Background
The Trails Act was enacted in 1968 to create a nationwide system of recreational trails. In 1983, Congress added a rail section, codified at
16 U.S.C. 1247(d)
, “to preserve for possible future railroad use rights-of-way not currently in service and to allow interim use of the land as recreational trails.”
Preseault
v.
ICC,
494 U.S. 1, 6 (1990). Through a process commonly known as “railbanking,” the Trails Act allows a rail carrier to transfer (or railbank) its interests in a right-of-way that is no longer needed for rail service, and that the rail carrier might otherwise remove from the Board's jurisdiction (
i.e.,
abandon), to a trail sponsor for use in the “interim” as a trail, with the rail carrier retaining the ability to reactivate rail service in the future. Specifically, the Trails Act provides that “in the case of interim use of any established railroad rights-of-way pursuant to donation, transfer, lease, sale, or otherwise in a manner consistent with this chapter [
i.e.,
as a trail], if such interim use is subject to restoration or reconstruction for railroad purposes, such interim use shall not be treated, for purposes of any law or rule of law, as an abandonment of the use of such rights-of-way for railroad purposes.”
16 U.S.C. 1247(d)
. The Trails Act also provides a limited role for the Board. It requires that “[if] a State, political subdivision, or qualified private organization is prepared to assume full responsibility for management of such rights-of-way and for any legal liability arising out of such transfer or use, and for the payment of any and all taxes that may be levied or assessed against such rights-of-way, then the Board shall impose such terms and conditions as a requirement of any transfer or conveyance for interim use in a manner consistent with this chapter [
i.e.,
as a trail], and shall not permit abandonment or discontinuance inconsistent or disruptive of such use.”
Id.
Regulatory Framework.
Two core principles pertaining to the Board's administration of the Trails Act have emerged through judicial and agency precedent. First, the Trails Act applies only to voluntary transfers of rights-of-way.
Nat'l Wildlife Fed.
v.
ICC,
850 F.2d 694, 696, 698 (D.C. Cir. 1988). It does not permit the Board to force interim trail use/railbanking upon an unwilling rail carrier.
Id.
Second, the Board's role under the Trails Act is “essentially ministerial.”
Goos
v.
ICC,
911 F.2d 1283, 1295 (8th Cir. 1990). “[B]y the plain terms of the statute,” the Board “has little, if any, discretion to forestall a voluntary agreement” effecting the transfer or conveyance of a right-of-way from a rail carrier to a potential trail sponsor for trail use.
Id.; see also
Citizens Against Rails-to-Trails
v.
Surface Transp. Bd.,
267 F.3d 1144, 1151, 1152 (D.C. Cir. 2001). Accordingly, the Board does not have discretion to decide whether interim trail use is desirable for a particular line.
Rail Abans.—Use of Rights-of-Way as Trails—Suppl. Procs.
(
Suppl. Procs.
), 4 I.C.C.2d 152, 156 (1987). And while the Trails Act contemplates that a line transferred under the Trails Act will in fact be used as a trail,
CSX Transp., Inc.—Aban. Exemption—in Pinellas Cnty., Fla.
AB 55 (Sub-No. 794X), slip op. at 10 (STB served Nov. 14, 2023), the Board is not involved in determining the type or level of trail use for a particular right of way,
CSX Transp., Inc.—Aban. Exemption—in Monroe & Owen Cntys., Ind.,
AB 55 (Sub-No. 514X), slip op. at 2 (STB served Sept. 30, 1997).
The ICC adopted regulations implementing the Trails Act in 1986.
See Rail Abans.—Use of Rights-of-Way as Trails (
49 CFR parts 1105
and
1152
)
(
1986 Rules),
2 I.C.C.2d 591 (1986). As discussed below, railbanking under the Board's regulations has involved a two-stage process: an initial period for negotiation between the carrier and the potential trail sponsor (which may be extended), followed by entry into an agreement between those parties that provides for interim trail use/railbanking subject to potential reconstruction and reactivation of the right-of-way for rail service. Only lines authorized for abandonment have been eligible for interim trail use/railbanking.
1986 Rules,
2 I.C.C.2d at 614;
see also Suppl. Procs.,
4 I.C.C.2d at 159 (“In order for lines to be eligible for trail use under [16 U.S.C.] 1247(d), the Commission will have already approved the line for abandonment under [49 U.S.C.] 10903 (or freed it from the need for approval under [49 U.S.C.] 1050[2]).”);
49 CFR 1152.29(c)
,
(d)
.
Specifically, during an abandonment proceeding, a prospective trail sponsor can invoke the Trails Act by filing a request with the Board within specified timeframes.
49 CFR 1152.29(a)
,
(b)
. Consistent with the Trails Act, the Board's regulations require that the prospective trail sponsor include with its request a statement of willingness to assume responsibility for management, legal liability, and payment of taxes related to the right-of-way, and an acknowledgement that interim trail use is subject to restoration of rail service at any time.
49 CFR 1152.29(a)
. If the rail carrier agrees to negotiate with a prospective trail sponsor, and if the line is otherwise authorized for abandonment, the Board issues either a Notice of Interim Trail Use (NITU) or a Certificate of Interim Trail Use (CITU), depending on the type of proceeding.
6
Id.
1152.29(c)(1), (d)(1). Per the Board's regulations, a NITU/CITU expressly authorizes the rail carrier to “discontinue service, cancel any applicable tariffs, and salvage track and materials.”
Id.
1152.29(c)(1)(i), (d)(1)(i). The NITU/CITU also authorizes a period of time (under the current regulations, a year, with possible extensions), during which the rail carrier and prospective trail sponsor may negotiate an interim trail use/railbanking agreement.
Id.
1152.29(c), (d). Parties must jointly notify the Board if they reach such an agreement during the NITU/CITU negotiating period.
49 CFR 1152.29(h)
. Once notification has been provided, the Board's Trails Act regulations require nothing more from rail carriers and trail sponsors, and no further action from the Board, as a predicate to transfer or convey a line for interim trail use/railbanking.
Under the current framework, the Board will only issue a NITU/CITU for
(
printed page 76176)
lines authorized for abandonment.
See
49 CFR 1152.29(c)
,
(d)
. A rail carrier, however, cannot exercise that abandonment authority during the NITU/CITU negotiating period or, if an interim trail use/railbanking agreement is reached, while the right-of-way is being used as a trail.
See Ala. & Fla. Ry.—Aban. Exemption—in Geneva, Coffee & Covington Cntys., Ala.,
AB 1073X, slip op. at 2 (STB served Mar. 3, 2015). In that sense, pursuant to the voluntary process, a NITU/CITU operates as a “regulatory barrier to consummation” of the rail carrier's abandonment authority.
See, e.g.,
id.; see also
49 CFR 1152.29(e)(2)
. If no railbanking/interim trail use agreement is reached by the expiration of the NITU/CITU negotiation period (and any extension thereof), or if the NITU/CITU is revoked, including because the trail sponsor has terminated trail use, the rail carrier may exercise its authority to abandon the line, without further action by the agency,
49 CFR 1152.29(c)(1)
,
(d)(1)
, provided that there are no unmet conditions imposed on abandonment, such as, for example, environmental conditions, that must be satisfied prior to consummation.
See Nat'l Ass'n of Reversionary Prop. Owners—Pet. for Rulemaking,
EP 749 et al., slip op. at 4 (STB served Oct. 2, 2018). Railroads must file a “notice of consummation” of abandonment if they wish to exercise abandonment authority.
Id.; see also
49 CFR 1152.29(e)
. Filing such a notice of consummation is the only legally recognized way to consummate abandonment authorization.
Honey Creek R.R., Inc.—Pet. for Declaratory Order,
FD 34869 et al., slip op. at 5 (STB served June 4, 2008). The notice must be filed within one year from the date on which the line was authorized for abandonment or 60 days from expiration of the last barrier to consummation (including a NITU/CITU negotiating period), whichever is later.
49 CFR 1152.29(e)
.
The Board retains jurisdiction over a rail line throughout the NITU/CITU negotiating period, any period of railbanking/interim trail use, and any period during which rail service is restored. Only after a NITU/CITU is no longer in effect and the railroad has lawfully consummated its abandonment authority is the Board's jurisdiction terminated.
See
16 U.S.C. 1247(d)
;
Hayfield N. R.R.
v.
Chi. & N. W. Transp. Co.,
467 U.S. 622, 633 (1984). At that point, whatever property interest the rail carrier has in the right-of-way, including any rail easement, becomes “ordinary real property” subject to the application of state law.
Id.
at 632. Thus, when a rail carrier operates a rail right-of-way pursuant to an easement that is limited to use for rail purposes, abandonment may result in the easement being extinguished under state law, thereby unencumbering the underlying land and allowing those who own the land in fee to take possession of the right-of-way.
Preseault,
494 U.S. at 8. Extinguishment of the easement is not possible, however, while the right-of-way remains within the Board's jurisdiction.
See, e.g.,
Grantwood Vill.
v.
Mo. Pac. R.R.,
95 F.3d 654, 659 (8th Cir. 1996) (“State law claims [for possession of the right-of-way] can only be brought
after
the [agency] has authorized an abandonment and after the railroad has consummated that abandonment authorization.”).
Takings Framework.
Courts have held that use of the Board's Trails Act regulations can result in a federal government taking of property. Such claims are litigated by and against the United States pursuant to the Tucker Act,
28 U.S.C. 1491(a)(1)
. Those claims have generally proceeded under one or both of the following theories.
First, a taking has been held to arise if the NITU/CITU delays or stops a rail carrier's abandonment of the right-of-way that otherwise would have occurred and, as a consequence, “state law reversionary property interests that would otherwise vest in the adjacent landowners are blocked from so vesting.”
Caldwell
v.
United States,
391 F.3d 1226, 1233 (Fed. Cir. 2004);
see, e.g.,
Sauer W. LLC
v.
United States,
151 F.4th 1339, 1344-45 (Fed. Cir. 2025);
Caquelin
v.
United States,
959 F.3d 1360, 1371 (Fed. Cir. 2020). This theory may support a claim for a temporary taking for the duration of the NITU/CITU, even if negotiations during the NITU/CITU negotiating period do not yield an interim trail use/railbanking agreement.
E.g., Memmer
v.
United States,
50 F.4th 136, 139 (Fed. Cir. 2022). This theory may also support a claim for a permanent taking on the ground that, once an interim trail use/railbanking agreement is reached, the NITU/CITU blocks abandonment of the rail carrier's easement “indefinitely.”
See e.g.,
id.
at 139.
Second, a taking has been held to arise if trail use resulting from invocation of the Board's processes exceeds the scope of the property rights transferred by the rail carrier to the trail sponsor (
e.g.,
if the rail carrier's easement is limited to use for railroad purposes and would not permit trail use as a matter of state law).
See, e.g.,
Preseault
v.
United States,
100 F.3d 1525, 1550 (Fed. Cir. 1996) (en banc) (plurality opinion) (finding a taking when, “pursuant to ICC Order,” the trail sponsor established trail use that “could not be justified under the terms and within the scope of the existing easements for railroad purposes”). The Court of Federal Claims has, at times, attributed this taking of new property rights to Board issuance of a NITU/CITU.
See, e.g.,
Haggart
v.
United States,
108 Fed. Cl. 70, 82 (2012) (“The power to exceed the scope of the easement was held by the federal government, acting through the STB. That power was exercised by the government on October 27, 2008 and November 28, 2008, when it issued the three NITUs.”);
see also Howard
v.
United States,
106 Fed. Cl. 343, 351 (2012) (framing one of the issues as “whether, when the STB issued the NITU and authorized recreational trail use on the railroad rights-of-way running through the plaintiffs' lands,” such “interim trail use [was] within the scope of the railroad easements that encumber plaintiff's property”). In
Kotis Assocs., LLC
v.
United States,
the Court of Federal Claims recently characterized the “STB's implementing regulations” as “assign[ing]” to the rail carrier a trail use “property right,” which it may then sell to the trail sponsor through the Board's “trail-use proceeding.” 176 Fed. Cl. 346, 356 (2025).

Under DOJ's proposal, the Board would modify its procedures to allow railroads to pursue interim trail use/railbanking by initiating an exemption proceeding for the purpose of obtaining authority to discontinue service over a line. (Pet. for Rulemaking 2.) DOJ argues that use of a discontinuance pathway would avoid disputes specific to abandonment proceedings and reduce the time typically required to conclude the Board's railbanking process, especially in circumstances in which a railroad and trail sponsor have already negotiated an agreement. Id.
at 18-22.) DOJ further proposes that abandonment no longer be authorized (at least in a discontinuance exemption proceedings) without further action from the Board if interim trail use/railbanking negotiations do not result in a trail use agreement; rather, the railroad would need to request abandonment authority should negotiations not yield an interim trail use agreement, and the Board would issue a subsequent decision indicating whether the rail carrier may abandon the line.

Id.

Id.

Discussion and Conclusions
Overview
In light of DOJ's petition, the Board has undertaken a comprehensive evaluation of its obligations under the Trails Act and the regulations implementing them. As explained below, the Board agrees with DOJ that the Board should propose a discontinuance pathway for interim trail use/railbanking. But, as the petition anticipates, the Board has also “identif[ied] additional opportunities to reduce regulatory burdens.” (Pet. for Rulemaking 19.) The Board additionally proposes to end its regulatory role in negotiations over interim trail use/railbanking and to replace NITU/CITUs with a Trails Act order authorizing the rail carrier to transfer its interest in the right-of-way to the trail sponsor, if necessary, after an agreement is reached. Consistent with Congress's statutory policy goals to “minimize the need for Federal regulatory control over the rail transportation system,” “ensure the development and continuation of a sound rail transportation system,” and “reduce regulatory barriers to entry into and exit from the industry,”
49 U.S.C. 10101(2)
, (4), (7), these further simplifications should substantially reduce the Board's regulatory footprint while better conforming the Board's processes to the Trails Act's text.
The Board proposes to abolish its existing process whereby it has issued NITU/CITUs at the negotiation stage for lines authorized for abandonment. Instead, any voluntary negotiations between a rail carrier and a potential trail sponsor would take place outside of the Board's processes and without any Board action. After an agreement is reached, the Board would, at the parties' joint request, authorize a rail carrier to transfer its interest in a right-of-way to a trail sponsor for interim trail use/railbanking, provided that the rail carrier owning the line has discontinued service on the line (pursuant to Board discontinuance authorization)
[
8
]
and no other rail carriers are licensed to operate there. Trails Act orders would be subject to the trail sponsor meeting the management, liability, and tax conditions required by the Trails Act, and subject to the line being available for rail service reactivation if needed.
See
16 U.S.C. 1247(d)
. The process would work as follows:
For a line authorized for discontinuance, the rail carrier and trail sponsor would jointly request in the discontinuance docket an order authorizing the rail carrier to transfer its interest in the right-of-way to a trail sponsor under the Trails Act, with the rail carrier certifying that it has discontinued service on the line and that no other carriers are licensed to operate there, and with the trail sponsor supplying information and representations of the kind currently required by
49 CFR 1152.29(a)(1)-(3)
.
For a line authorized for abandonment (without consummation
[
9
]
), the rail carrier and trail sponsor would file the above-described joint transfer request in the abandonment docket, and the rail carrier would additionally include in the request notice that it is relinquishing its authority to fully abandon the line.
For a line not authorized for abandonment or discontinuance, the rail carrier would seek discontinuance authority (via application, petition for exemption, or notice of exemption, as appropriate), and the parties would file their joint transfer request in that docket. Discontinuance would need to be authorized before or at the same time that the Board issues an order approving the transfer for interim trail use/railbanking.
If these conditions are met, the Board would issue an order authorizing the transfer, subject to the conditions that the trail sponsor “assume full responsibility” for managing the right-
(
printed page 76178)
of-way, for “legal liability arising out of [its] transfer or use,” and for taxes assessed on it.
16 U.S.C. 1247(d)
. In any Trails Act order, the Board would state that its order does not (1) exercise any power of eminent domain, (2) take or burden private property, (3) authorize the rail carrier or the trail sponsor to condemn or take private property, or (4) allow for use of property in excess of existing property rights.
The proposed amendments would accommodate the potential for reactivated rail service on a railbanked line, pursuant to existing policies.
[
10
]
The Board would also entertain petitions to transfer the line to a new trail sponsor, as well as requests to abandon the line in the event that interim trail use has ceased.
Under these proposed amendments, the Board would not conduct environmental or historic reviews of orders transferring rights-of-way to trail sponsors (beyond whatever review was required for the predicate grants of abandonment or discontinuance authority)
[
11
]
because the Board lacks discretion under the Trails Act to deny such a transfer that has been properly requested. Trails Act orders are not federal actions or undertakings, and neither the National Environmental Policy Act,
42 U.S.C. 4321
to 4347, nor the National Historic Preservation Act,
54 U.S.C. 300101
to 307108, apply.
[
12
]
As discussed in more detail below, these proposed amendments are intended to reduce regulatory burden by eliminating the need for parties to notify the Board of pending negotiations and for the carrier to secure abandonment authority as a prerequisite to interim trail use/railbanking. Nothing in the Trails Act imposes either requirement. Indeed, the only affirmative step that the Trails Act requires the Board to take is to impose certain conditions on “any transfer or conveyance” of the right-of-way for interim trail use, just as these proposed amendments do. The amendments are also consistent with the Trails Act's other, prohibitory commands that the Board not “treat[ ]” interim trail use “as an abandonment,” and, after transfer to a trail sponsor, “not permit abandonment or discontinuance inconsistent or disruptive of such use.”
16 U.S.C. 1247(d)
. These amendments should also reduce the United States's Trails Act-related takings liability, which has grown as the result of court decisions that do not reflect the Board's Trails Act role. (
See
Further Filing at 20 (arguing that “the most straightforward way to address the `temporary takings' is to reform the features of the Board's regulations that courts have sometimes found to operate as a temporary taking of property rights”).)
The Board does not propose to give this rule, if adopted, retroactive effect. These amendments would therefore not affect lines for which a NITU/CITU is already in place. In addition, because the rule does not regulate stakeholders' primary conduct and would not apply to cases in which negotiations are already ongoing, the Board does not anticipate that the proposed rule would endanger any serious reliance interests. Any parties that do have such interests, however, are encouraged to bring them to the Board's attention in comments.
The individual elements of the Board's proposal are discussed in more detail below. The proposed new regulatory text is set forth below, with the principal changes occurring in the new
49 CFR 1152.29
, and with minor conforming changes made to other provisions.
The Board will no longer issue CITUs/NITUs or otherwise concern itself with interim trail use/railbanking negotiations; instead, the Board will authorize transfer of the rail carrier's interest in the right-of-way to the trail sponsor once an agreement is reached.
Under existing regulations, the Board responds to expressions of trail-use interest by potential trail sponsors and carriers by issuing a NITU/CITU—a document that, among other things, authorizes the rail carrier to discontinue rail service and salvage track for an extendable one-year period while the rail carrier and trail sponsor negotiate.
49 CFR 1152.29(c)(1)
,
(d)(1)
. The Board has said that the NITU/CITU operates as a “legal barrier” to the carrier consummating abandonment authority on the line during the negotiation period (and after an agreement is reached), so that the NITU/CITU can have the effect of delaying the default one-year deadline to consummate abandonment authority.
E.g., Ala. & Fla. Ry.—Aban. Exemption—in Geneva, Coffee & Covington Cntys., Ala.,
AB 1073X, slip op at 2 (STB served Mar. 3, 2015);
see
49 CFR 1152.29(e)(2)
.
This complicated scheme governing voluntary negotiations between the rail carrier and the trail sponsor appears to represent unnecessary “Federal regulatory control over the rail transportation system.”
49 U.S.C. 10101(2)
. Accordingly, the Board proposes to eliminate it.
To start, there is no need for the Board to “authorize” any negotiations or negotiation period. Although the Board has sometimes described the NITU/CITU as “authorizing [the carrier] to negotiate” with would-be trail sponsors,
e.g., Norfolk S. Ry.—Aban. Exemption—City of Greensboro, N.C.,
AB 290 (Sub-No. 404X), slip op. at 1 (STB served Jan. 4, 2024), rail carriers do not actually need the Board's permission to engage in negotiations with potential trail sponsors. They may do so at any time. The existing regulations recognize as much,
see
49 CFR 1152.29(g)
(accommodating agreements reached after the prescribed negotiation period ends), and, as DOJ observes, “railroads often enter negotiations and reach tentative agreements with interested trail sponsors before initiating the exemption abandonment proceedings,” (DOJ Further Filing at 3-4 & n.6 (collecting numerous examples)). To the extent the NITU/CITU has been understood to authorize negotiations, therefore, it is unneeded.
Nor is a NITU/CITU needed to authorize the discontinuance of service or the salvage of track during negotiations. A rail carrier that wishes to discontinue service during trail-related negotiations can simply seek discontinuance authority; or, if the
(
printed page 76179)
carrier already has obtained but not consummated abandonment authority, it can simply file a notice that it is exercising discontinuance authority, which is a lesser-included power.
See, e.g.,
Norfolk S. Ry—Aban. Exemption—in Dayton, Montgomery Cnty., Ohio,
AB 290 (Sub-No. 390X) (STB served Feb. 12, 2021). And a rail carrier needs no authority to salvage track at all. “[T]he Board generally does not regulate a railroad's . . . decisions . . . regarding disposition of rail property,” including track salvage.
Permitting Reform—Envt'l Review Process,
EP 779, slip op. at 9 n.12. Even on an active rail line where there is a common carrier obligation, a carrier is not prohibited from salvaging track, so long as no shipper seeks service and the carrier “is prepared to restore the track should it receive a reasonable request for service.”
13
BNSF Ry.—Pet. for Declaratory Ord.,
FD 35164 et al., slip op. at 5-6 (STB served May 7, 2010).
Finally, there is no need for a NITU/CITU or any other Board action to “block” the carrier's consummation of abandonment during negotiations. To the extent that a NITU/CITU nominally has that effect today, it appears to do so only as an artifact of how the Board structured notices of consummation of abandonment when it created them in 1996. The Board determined that abandonment authority should generally expire unless the carrier files a notice of consummation within one year.
Aban. & Discon. of Rail Lines and Rail Transp. Under
49 U.S.C. 10903
,
61 FR 67876
,
67879
(Dec. 24, 1996) (promulgating
49 CFR 1152.29(e)(2)
). But to account for situations such as interim trail use/railbanking, the Board determined that the one-year deadline would not apply when there is a “legal or regulatory barrier[ ] to consummation,” and decided that a NITU/CITU would be one such barrier.
Id.
It is clear that the Board's aim was to effectuate an abandonment consummation deadline consistent with the Trails Act's prohibition on permitting abandonment during interim trail use/railbanking, but there is no language to suggest that the Board considered blocking abandonment consummations during negotiations to be an independent policy goal.
See id.
Nor would it have been. Interim trail use/railbanking has always been a voluntary process, and even today a rail carrier wishing to end negotiations and consummate abandonment can always ask the Board to vacate the NITU/CITU before the negotiation period expires.
City of Fishers—Pet. for Partial Revocation of Exemption,
FD 36137, slip op. at 7 (STB served July 31, 2019). As a result, any NITU/CITU function of blocking consummation of abandonment during negotiations is unnecessary.

14
]
Under the new proposed approach, the Board would not take action regarding trail use until the rail carrier and trail sponsor have reached an interim trail use/railbanking agreement and the parties have jointly filed with the Board a petition to authorize transfer of the rail carrier's interest in the right-of-way to the trail sponsor pursuant to
16 U.S.C. 1247(d)
and proposed
49 CFR 1152.29
.
The petition to transfer would represent that the rail carrier owning the line
[
15
]
and trail sponsor have reached an interim trail use/railbanking agreement for the right-of-way, that the rail carrier has discontinued rail service on the line or is in the process of seeking authority to do so (including contemporaneously with the petition), and that no other rail carriers are licensed to operate there. The petition would also contain substantially the same information and representations that are currently required by
49 CFR 1152.29(a)
, namely: (1) a map and description of the portion of the right-of-way proposed to be transferred, including mileposts; (2) a statement of the trail sponsor's willingness to assume full responsibility for managing the right-of-way, for paying any legal liability arising out of the transfer or any interim trail use, and for paying associated taxes; and (3) the trail sponsor's acknowledgments (a) that the transfer will be conditioned on the trail sponsor meeting its statutory responsibilities and not alienating or otherwise altering any portion of the transferred right-of-way in a manner that would be inconsistent with future reactivation for rail service and (b) that the Board has the authority and obligation to vacate the Trails Act order, requiring that the right-of-way be transferred away from the trail sponsor, if the right-of-way needs to be reactivated for rail service. In the petition, the carrier also would need to relinquish any unconsummated abandonment authority (if applicable), as explained below.
If these standards are met, and the line has been authorized for discontinuance, the Board would issue an order authorizing the transfer of the rail carrier's interest in the right-of-way to the trail sponsor and imposing the trail sponsor's statutory responsibilities as conditions of that transfer, as required by
16 U.S.C. 1247(d)
. The order would also condition the transfer on the trail sponsor not alienating or otherwise altering any portion of the transferred right-of-way in a manner that would be inconsistent with future reactivation for rail service.
This new approach better implements the mandate of the Trails Act, and in particular the operative sentence of section 1247(d) directing the Board to take action:
If a State, political subdivision, or qualified private organization is prepared to assume full responsibility for management of such rights-of-way and for any legal liability arising out of such transfer or use, and for the payment of any and all taxes that may be levied or assessed against such rights-of-way, then the Board shall impose such terms and conditions as a requirement of any transfer or conveyance for interim use in a manner consistent with this chapter . . . .
16 U.S.C. 1247(d)
. That language requires the Board to authorize and condition “any transfer or conveyance” of the railroad's interest in the right-of-way to the trail sponsor when the specified requirements are met—which is what the proposed rule does. Nothing in the Trails Act requires or even contemplates that the Board will regulate interim trail use/railbanking negotiations before an agreement is reached. Reducing the agency's regulatory role in this way better carries out the statutory policies to “minimize the need for Federal regulatory control over the rail transportation system . . . . ,” “reduce regulatory barriers to entry into and exit from the industry,” and “provide for the expeditious handling and resolution of [Board] proceedings . . . .”
49 U.S.C. 10101(2)
, (7), (15).
The new approach should also reduce takings liability for the United States to the extent it is based on a misunderstanding of the Board's role in the Trails Act process. The Federal Circuit has held that a NITU/CITU can effect a taking during the negotiations period because, in the court's view, the NITU/CITU “compels the railroad to
(
printed page 76180)
delay its abandonment.”
E.g., Memmer,
50 F.4th at 140. But interim trail use/railbanking is voluntary,
e.g., Nat'l Wildlife Fed'n,
850 F.2d at 702;
1986 Rules,
2 I.C.C.2d at 598—and so are interim trail use/railbanking negotiations. The Board has never denied a request to vacate a NITU/CITU from a rail carrier that desires to end negotiations in order to consummate abandonment before an interim trail use/railbanking agreement is reached.
See, e.g.,
City of Fishers,
FD 36137, slip op. at 7. Given the inherent voluntariness of negotiations, the NITU/CITU negotiating period thus appears to be creating takings liability for the United States while serving no apparent regulatory purpose. By ending Board involvement in the negotiation period altogether, the Board expects that courts would reassess the viability of takings claims against the United States that arise before an interim trail use/railbanking agreement is reached.
The Board will establish a discontinuance pathway to interim trail use/railbanking.
The Board additionally proposes to create a discontinuance pathway to interim trail use/railbanking. That is, the Board would no longer require abandonment authority as a predicate to interim trail use/railbanking, as the current regulations do, and would instead allow interim trail use/railbanking of any line that the Board has authorized for discontinuance if no other carriers are licensed to operate there. This proposal resembles the one in DOJ's petition and would be expected to achieve the same benefits, including reduced regulatory burdens, avoidance of unnecessary disputes, and a potential reduction in takings liability.
The Board's exit licensing procedures include authorizing the “abandonment” or “discontinuance” of rail lines.
49 U.S.C. 10903(a)(1)
. Once consummated, abandonment and discontinuance both end the rail carrier's common carrier obligation to provide service on the line on reasonable request.
E.g., Mfrs. Ry.—Discon. Exemption—in St. Louis Cnty., Mo.
(
Mfrs. Ry.
), AB 1075X, slip op. at 2 (STB served Feb. 6, 2013). The principal difference is that abandonment removes the line from the Board's exclusive jurisdiction.
Id.
At that point, the rail carrier's property rights in the right-of-way become “ordinary real property” subject to the application of state law,
Hayfield N. R.R.,
467 U.S. at 632, including laws that may provide for extinguishment of the rail carrier easement and possession of the underlying land by those who own it in fee. Discontinuance, by contrast, leaves the line in the Board's jurisdiction such that state laws that could result in loss of the right-of-way remain preempted and the option of resumed common carrier operations on the line is preserved without the need for new construction and/or operating authority from the Board.
Mfrs. Ry.,
AB 1075X, slip op. at 2;
see Preseault
v.
ICC,
494 U.S. 1, 5 n.3 (1990). The Board authorizes abandonment or discontinuance “only if . . . the present or future public convenience and necessity require or permit” it,
49 U.S.C. 10903(d)
, or if the proposed action is exempt from regulation under
49 U.S.C. 10502(a)
.
It is appropriate that the Board require
some
type of exit license as a predicate to interim trail use/railbanking, in that the Trails Act does not mandate that the Board allow interim trail use/railbanking on lines for which there remains an active rail transportation need. The Trails Act's purpose is to “preserve established railroad rights-of-way for future reactivation of rail service” and to keep rail lines within Board jurisdiction in the case of their “interim use” as a trail if the line is “subject to restoration or reconstruction for railroad purposes.”
16 U.S.C. 1247(d)
. That language would make little sense if a line were still needed for railroad purposes at the time that it was railbanked.
As discussed above, under the agency's existing regulations, only rail lines authorized for abandonment have been eligible for interim trail use/railbanking.
See
49 CFR 1152.29(c)
,
(d)
;
Suppl. Procs.,
4 I.C.C.2d at 159. But the Board does not appear previously to have considered whether discontinuance could also serve as an interim trail use/railbanking predicate.
The Board now concludes that interim trail use/railbanking should be permitted on lines over which the carrier is authorized to discontinue service and no other carriers are licensed to operate. The feature of lines authorized for abandonment that makes them suitable for interim trail use/railbanking is that the Board has found the public convenience and necessity to permit the cessation of common carrier rail service over them.
See
49 U.S.C. 10903(a)(1)
. The same is true of lines over which the carrier is authorized to discontinue service and no other carriers are licensed to operate.
See id.
In fact, discontinuance better fits the Trails Act.
See Preseault,
494 U.S. at 5 n.3, 8. Unlike abandonment, discontinuance leaves open “the option of resuming common carrier operations over the line in the future without obtaining new Board authority,”
Mfrs. Ry.,
AB 1075X, slip op. at 2—that is, leaves the line “subject to restoration or reconstruction for railroad purposes,”
16 U.S.C. 1247(d)
. As the Supreme Court put it, Congress in the Trails Act “deem[ed] interim trail use to be like discontinuance rather than abandonment.”
Preseault,
494 U.S. at 8. And under the existing regulations, the Board already authorizes discontinuance in every case of interim trail use/railbanking (and never allows the consummation of abandonment while a NITU/CITU is in place).
See
49 CFR 1152.29(c)
,
(d)
,
(e)(2)
;
16 U.S.C. 1247(d)
.
A discontinuance pathway could encourage interim trail use/railbanking by reducing the regulatory burden of initiating it. By their nature, abandonment determinations have higher stakes than discontinuance determinations because they authorize the permanent loss of the corridor to the rail network. For example, under the Board's “stranded segment” doctrine, the Board does not authorize abandonments that would isolate an adjoining segment from the rail system.
R.J. Corman R.R. Prop., LLC—Aban. Exemption—in Scott, Campbell, & Anderson Cntys., Tenn.
(
R.J. Corman
), AB 1296X, slip op. at 3 (STB served Nov. 17, 2022). Because abandonment is a prerequisite to interim trail use/railbanking under the Board's current regulations, the stranded segment doctrine has the effect of barring interim trail use/railbanking despite railbanked lines remaining within the Board's jurisdiction.
See Elk River R.R.—Aban. Exemption—in Kanawha & Clay Cntys., W. Va.,
AB 1314X, slip op. at 3-4 (STB served Mar. 25, 2022). Moreover, to avoid a rail line's permanent loss, a party may offer to purchase a line that the rail carrier seeks to abandon under the financial assistance provisions of
49 U.S.C. 10904
, but may only offer to subsidize operations on a line for which the carrier seeks discontinuance.
Offers of Financial Assistance,
EP 729, slip op. at 1 (STB served Dec. 7, 2015);
Mfrs. Ry.,
AB 1075X, slip op. at 6 n.6.
But the difference between abandonment and discontinuance is irrelevant in the very common situation in which rail carriers initiate abandonment proceedings only as a technical prerequisite for railbanking, with no intent to fully abandon. (
See
DOJ Further Filing at 3-4 & n.6 (collecting examples of rail carriers explicitly initiating abandonment proceedings only to facilitate interim trail use/railbanking).) A discontinuance pathway would enable those rail carriers to pursue interim trail use/railbanking without litigating—or requiring the Board to resolve—whether
(
printed page 76181)
the line's full abandonment would serve the public convenience and necessity.
[
16
]
It would avoid conflict with the Board's stranded segment doctrine.
See R.J. Corman,
AB 1296X, slip op. at 7 (STB served Nov. 17, 2022) (Member Fuchs joined by Member Schultz, concurring) (explaining that wasteful effort could have been avoided in ascertaining the regulatory status of a long-unused connected segment if the Board had allowed for a discontinuance pathway to railbanking instead);
Great Redwood Trail Agency—Adverse Aban.—Mendocino Ry. in Mendocino Cnty., Cal.,
AB 1305 (Sub-No. 1), slip op. 15 (STB served Feb. 19, 2026) (Member Hedlund, concurring) (similar);
see also Cent. Or. & Pac. R.R.—Aban. & Discon. of Serv.—in Coos, Douglas, & Lane Cntys., Or.,
AB 515 (Sub No. 2), slip op. at 12-13 (STB served Oct. 31, 2008) (stranded segments doctrine precluded unconditioned abandonment but not unconditioned discontinuance). A discontinuance pathway would also avoid potential forced sale proceedings under
49 U.S.C. 10904
where the rail carrier was not interested in abandoning in the first place (and was merely seeking abandonment authority as a means of railbanking the line). Such a sale makes little sense if the rail carrier intends all along to transfer its line for interim trail use/railbanking, where it will be subject to reactivation should the need arise (obviating the point of a sale).
A discontinuance pathway should also have the effect of further reducing the government's misplaced takings liability. As explained above, the Federal Circuit has held that a NITU/CITU effects a taking because it “block[s]” abandonment by the railroad and thus prevents “state law reversionary property interests that would otherwise vest in the adjacent landowners” from vesting.
Memmer
v.
United States,
50 F.4th 136, 145 (Fed. Cir. 2022) (quoting
Caldwell,
391 F.3d at 1233). But, as discussed above, interim trail use/railbanking is voluntary. The Board will only issue a NITU/CITU when the rail carrier consents, and thus is choosing to pursue interim trail use/railbanking and not pursue abandonment.
17
E.g., Nat'l Wildlife Fed'n
v.
ICC,
850 F.2d 694, 702 (D.C. Cir. 1988);
1986 Rules,
2 I.C.C.2d at 598. The existing regulations arguably obscure that fact by forcing rail carriers to formally request and obtain abandonment authority en route to interim trail use/railbanking, despite the rail carrier choosing to forgo use of that authority when it agrees to negotiate interim trail use/railbanking. The discontinuance pathway avoids any mistaken impression that Board regulation prevents an otherwise-willing rail carrier from consummating abandonment prior to transferring the line to a trail sponsor; under the discontinuance pathway, the rail carrier does not request abandonment authority and the Board does not grant it.
For similar reasons, the Board proposes modifying the abandonment pathway to interim trail use/railbanking. Specifically: if a rail carrier has already received unconsummated abandonment authority when it asks to transfer its interest in the right-of-way to the trail sponsor, the Board proposes that the petition to transfer must include, in addition to the statement that the rail carrier has consummated or is consummating its discontinuance authority,
[
18
]
a statement relinquishing the carrier's right to fully abandon the line and withdrawing any request for authority to do so.
This would be a change from the existing regulations, under which any abandonment authority granted prior to railbanking becomes usable again for a 60-day period following the end of interim trail use/railbanking.
See
49 CFR 1152.29(e)(2)
. But keeping abandonment authority pending in the background during interim trail use/railbanking comes at a cost to the United States, as it appears to have contributed to courts concluding that it is Board action (rather than voluntary carrier action) that prevents rail carriers from pursuing abandonment instead of interim trail use/railbanking.
See, e.g.,
Memmer,
50 F.4th at 145. Requiring rail carriers to formally relinquish that authority when they instead decide to railbank a line will foster clearer lines of accountability for not abandoning, and will better reflect the reality that interim trail use/railbanking is voluntary: when a rail carrier chooses to transfer a line to a trail sponsor for interim trail use/railbanking, the carrier is choosing, for the time being, not to abandon the line.
To be sure, this change does require an additional step in the situation in which a trail sponsor intends to terminate interim trail use over some or all of the right-of-way, and the rail carrier seeks to abandon that portion of the line. In that case, the current regulations allow either the carrier or the trail sponsor to request that the NITU/CITU be vacated and request that the line be “immediate[ly] authorized for abandonment.”
49 CFR 1152.29(c)
,
(d)
. Under the amended rules, however, it would be necessary to seek abandonment authority through a new request. But requests to vacate CITUs/NITUs under the current rules happen fairly infrequently (less than twice per year on average, and often pertaining to only a small portion of the railbanked right-of-way), and the paperwork required to obtain abandonment authority (including earlier-granted authority) should be largely duplicative of (and can incorporate by reference) what was required to obtain discontinuance or abandonment authority in the first instance. Ultimately the Board believes that the efficiency costs the new rule may impose would be outweighed by the gains of greater fidelity to the text of the Trails Act text, clarification of the Board's statutory role, and the potential for avoiding takings liability based on a mistaken understanding of the interim trail use/railbanking process.
The Board additionally confirms that, under the proposed discontinuance pathway, the line would not be available for purchase under the financial assistance provisions of
49 U.S.C. 10904
and
49 CFR 1152.27
. As noted, that option is available only for abandonments.
Mfrs. Ry.,
AB 1075X, slip op. at 6 n.8. But when a rail carrier seeks discontinuance authority (whether for the purpose of interim trail use/railbanking or not), interested persons will still have the usual opportunity to submit requests to subsidize operations for up to one year.
Id.
Should such a request be granted, discontinuance authority would not issue during the provision of financial assistance.
The Board would clarify in Trails Act orders that the Board is not exercising eminent domain or requiring use of the right-of-way in a manner inconsistent with whatever property rights are transferred from the rail carrier to the trail sponsor.
The proposal would also clarify the Board's ministerial role under the Trails Act.
Under the existing regulations, some courts have understood the NITU/CITU affirmatively to create a right to establish interim trail use on the right-of-way, even when the rail carrier's property rights over the right-of-way do not by their terms permit trail use.
(
printed page 76182)
These decisions have tended to view the Board as adjudicating property rights and, through the NITU/CITU, modifying those rights or even creating new property rights to allow trail-use to occur.
[
19
]
For example, the decision in
Kotis Associates LLC
v.
United States,
176 Fed. Cl. 346 (2025), described the Board as a “condemnation `court,' ” exercising eminent domain to take the underlying landholders' property without their participation.
Id.
at 357;
see also id.
at 370-71 (treating the NITU as a “judgment of immediate possession”). Based on the court's understanding of the Board's role,
Kotis Associates
gave “dispositive” weight to the NITU's description of the physical boundaries of the railbanked right-of-way—which simply reflected the trail sponsor's representations to the Board—notwithstanding documentary evidence indicating otherwise.
See id.
at 369-72. The court thus viewed the NITU as “taking” a substantial portion of the abutting landowners' property and transferring it to the trail sponsor because, in the court's view, “the NITU is the authoritative document through which Congress and the STB impose [a new] easement [for interim trail use/railbanking].”
Id.
at 371.
The proposed regulations would help ensure an improved understanding of the Board's very limited role in Trails Act administration. The Trails Act requires from the Board no more than that it impose certain conditions when a rail carrier wishes to transfer its right-of-way to a trail sponsor for use as a trail and that, after such a transfer, it not permit abandonment or discontinuance inconsistent with trail use.
16 U.S.C. 1247(d)
. The modest role for the Board in the Trails Act stands in contrast to other instances where Congress authorized the Board to “allow” one party to use or acquire the property “owned by” another. In those instances, Congress expressly granted the Board that authority and required the Board to establish compensation.
See
49 U.S.C. 11102(a)
(authorizing the Board to grant terminal trackage rights over facilities “owned by a rail carrier”);
49 U.S.C. 10907
(authorizing Board to force the sale of a rail line where certain findings of inadequate service have been made, and directing the Board to require such sale to be “at a price not less than the constitutional minimum value”);
49 U.S.C. 10904
(permitting the Board to require the sale of a line to be abandoned and requiring that it “determine the price and other terms of sale”);
cf.
49 U.S.C. 11102(c)
(requiring that Board establish “compensation” when requiring rail carriers to enter into reciprocal switching agreements). The Trails Act includes no similar provision nor, as the agency has long held, does it confer condemnation power.
1986 Rules,
2 I.C.C.2d at 597;
see also Preseault
v.
ICC,
494 U.S. at 15 & n.8, 16 (Trails Act is not “a program of direct federal trail acquisition”).
Moreover, whenever the Board authorizes the construction, acquisition, and operation of rail lines and combination of rail carriers under
49 U.S.C. 10901
and
11324
, it is up to the applicant to obtain the necessary property and contract rights that would enable it to exercise the regulatory authority issued by the STB and begin rail operations.
Allegheny Valley R.R.—Pet. for Declaratory Order,
FD 35388, slip op. at 3 (STB served Apr. 25, 2011) (explaining that the Board's acquisition authority “is permissive, not mandatory, and cannot be viewed as conveying property rights to an applicant, as property ownership rights are determined by state law.”);
Ohio River Partners LLC—Acquis. & Operation Exemption—Hannibal Dev., LLC,
FD 35984, slip op. at 3 (STB served Apr. 1, 2016) (same);
Tongue River R.R.—Constr. & Operations—W. Alignment,
FD 30186 (Sub-No. 3), slip op. at 16 n.50 (STB served Oct. 9, 2007) (“In rail construction cases . . . [t]he applicant is responsible for acquiring the land necessary to build the line.”). Just as the Board does not involve itself in an applicant's efforts to obtain whatever property and contractual rights it needs to establish rail service, it does not involve itself in the trail sponsor's efforts to secure whatever rights it may need to establish trail use. Indeed, such a role for the Board—one that requires or otherwise licenses the use of property beyond the scope of existing property rights—is inconsistent with the Board's “essentially ministerial” role under the Trails Act.
Goos,
911 F.2d at 1295. And it would be far more reaching than what the Board does when exercising its core rail regulatory responsibilities over which it has far greater discretion.
The Trails Act no doubt permits rail carriers to transfer any or all of whatever property interests the railroad has in the right-of-way to a state, municipality, or private organization for interim trail use/railbanking. From the Board's perspective, what is important is that the rail carrier's interests remain within the Board's jurisdiction and thus cannot be deemed abandoned as a matter of state law, and that the rail carrier's ability to reinstate service in the future otherwise cannot be undermined.
E.g., Idaho N. & Pac. R.R.—Aban. & Discon. Exemption—in Wash. & Adams Cntys., Idaho,
3 S.T.B. 50, 59 (1998) (explaining that the Board's principal concern after a railbanking agreement has been reached is that “nothing occur that would preclude a railroad's right to reassert control over the right-of-way”). Indeed, the Board's jurisdiction only preempts the remedies “provided under this part”—
i.e.,
the rail provisions of the Interstate Commerce Act,
49 U.S.C. 10101-11908
—not duties assigned to the Board under other provisions.
See Trevarton
v.
S. Dakota,
817 F.3d 1081, 1086 (8th Cir. 2016) (emphasizing that the Board's “exclusive jurisdiction under
49 U.S.C. 10501(b)
`is limited to remedies with respect to rail
regulation'
”);
Kan. & Okla. R.R.—Aban. Exemption in Hodgeman, Comanche, Kiowa, & Pratt Cntys., Kan.,
AB 853 (Sub-No. 1X), slip op. at 5 (STB served Apr. 30, 2020) (state and local laws are preempted if they interfere with railbanking). Whether the trail sponsor has the property rights needed to implement trail use is simply not relevant to the Board's regulation of the rail network.
[
20
]
In keeping with the Board's narrow statutory mandate under the Trails Act, the Board proposes to explicitly state in each order under
16 U.S.C. 1247(d)
that, by approving the transfer or conveyance of the right-of-way as required by the statute, the Board (1) is not exercising any power of eminent domain, (2) is not taking or burdening private property, (3) is not authorizing the rail carrier or the trail sponsor to condemn or take private property, and (4) is not allowing for use of property in excess of existing property rights. The Board would merely be authorizing the rail carrier to transfer its property rights in the right-of-way to the trail sponsor, with conditions.
The Board will have no role in the Trails Act process in cases in which the rail carrier itself wants to operate a trail.
From time to time, the Board has issued a NITU/CITU at the request of a
(
printed page 76183)
rail carrier seeking to establish interim trail use/railbanking on its own line, acting as its own trail sponsor.
See, e.g.,
Metro N. Commuter R.R.—Aban. Exemption—in Dutchess & Putnam Cntys., N.Y.,
AB 1311 (Sub-No. 1X), slip op. 2 & n.4 (STB served Feb. 7, 2024);
Great Redwood Trail Agency—Aban. Exemption—in Mendocino, Trinity, & Humboldt Cntys., Cal.,
AB 1305X, slip op. 5-6 & n.6 (STB served Oct. 25, 2022). In those cases, the Board has not required the rail carrier to file a notice that an agreement for interim trail use/railbanking has been reached, but instead to file a notice “confirming that it is implementing interim trail use/rail banking.”
Id.
It follows from the above discussion that, under the proposed new framework, the Board will no longer take affirmative action where a rail carrier (or non-carrier owner) intends to act as its own trail sponsor and establish interim trail use/railbanking itself on its own line. As explained, the Board's only affirmative role in interim trail use/railbanking is to approve and condition the “transfer or conveyance” of a rail carrier's rights over an unused right-of-way to a trail sponsor, where necessary. If no such transfer is needed, no affirmative action from the Board is required. The consequence should be a reduction in paperwork and simplified or eliminated regulatory proceedings in the situations where this rule applies.
As far as the Board's licensing procedures are concerned, a rail carrier wishing to use some or all of its right-of-way for trail use may do so on its own without seeking authority from the agency, so long as such trail use does not interfere with the provision of common carrier rail service.
See Great Redwood Trail Agency—Adverse Aban.—Mendocino Ry. in Mendocino Cnty., Cal.,
AB 1305 (Sub-No. 1), slip op. at 13 (STB served Feb. 19, 2026) (“There is generally no prohibition to a rail carrier permitting its right-of-way to be used for non-rail purposes so long as such uses do not interfere with common carrier rail service.”). And a rail carrier can seek discontinuance authority if it wishes to be relieved of its common carrier obligation during any such trail use. (Indeed, the rail carrier
must
seek discontinuance authority if the trail use would supplant, rather than coexist with, the rail line.) In such a case, as in any other, if a right-of-way is put to interim trail use and subject to reactivation for railroad purposes, that interim use “shall not be treated” by the Board “as abandonment of the use of such rights-of-way for railroad purposes.”
16 U.S.C. 1247(d)
.
The Board will similarly not take action in the case of interim trail use/railbanking by a non-carrier state or state subdivision that has acquired a rail line approved for abandonment under the Board's Common Carrier Status of States rules.
See
49 CFR 1150.22
;
Common Carrier Status of States, State Agencies & Instrumentalities, & Pol. Subdivisions,
363 I.C.C. 132 (1980),
aff'd sub nom. Simmons
v.
ICC,
697 F.2d 326 (D.C. Cir. 1982);
see also S. Dakota ex rel. Dep't of Transp.—Pet. for Declaratory Order,
FD 36697 (STB served Aug. 21, 2023) (issuing NITU where non-carrier state was “both the owner of the [line] and the trail sponsor”). Under those rules, a state's acquisition of a line that has been approved for abandonment, but for which the abandonment has not been consummated, is exempted from the Board's jurisdiction.
49 CFR 1150.22
. An operator that contracts with the state to provide service over the line incurs a common carrier obligation.
Id.
The operator is exempt from the statutory requirements governing the start-up and termination of operations found at
49 U.S.C. 10901
and
10903
, but must comply with the special rules in 49 CFR pt. 1150 subpart C.

Under the proposed new Trails Act framework, after an operator terminates service, the state will not need the Board's permission to establish interim trail use/railbanking, and there is no role for the Board to play because no transfer or conveyance of the right-of-way is necessary. If interim trail use does occur, that interim trail use “shall not be treated” as having consummated the abandonment if the right-of-way is subject to reactivation for railroad purposes.
16 U.S.C. 1247(d)
.
Environmental Review
The proposed action is categorically excluded from environmental review because it is a “rulemaking . . . that has no potential for significant environmental impacts.”
49 CFR 1105.6(c)(6)
. The proposed rule simplifies and clarifies Board procedures implementing the Trails Act and does not regulate industry actors' primary conduct. No extraordinary circumstances warrant the preparation of an environmental assessment or environmental impact statement.
Regulatory Flexibility Act
The Regulatory Flexibility Act of 1980 (RFA),
5 U.S.C. 601-612
, generally requires a description and analysis of new rules that would have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities. In drafting a rule, an agency is required to: (1) assess the effect that its regulation will have on small entities; (2) analyze effective alternatives that may minimize a regulation's impact; and (3) make the analysis available for public comment.
Id.
601-604. In its notice of proposed rulemaking, the agency must either include an initial regulatory flexibility analysis, 603(a), or certify that the proposed rule would not have a “significant impact on a substantial number of small entities,” 605(b). Because the goal of the RFA is to reduce the cost to small entities of complying with federal regulations, the RFA requires an agency to perform a regulatory flexibility analysis of small entity impacts only when a rule directly regulates those entities. In other words, the impact must be a direct impact on small entities “whose conduct is circumscribed or mandated” by the proposed rule.
White Eagle Coop.
v.
Conner,
553 F.3d 467, 480 (7th Cir. 2009).
The Board's proposed changes to its regulations here are intended to streamline, rationalize, and clarify its trail use procedures and they do not mandate the conduct of small entities. The changes proposed here are largely procedural and would not have a significant economic impact on Class III rail carriers or trail sponsors (whether as small businesses, not-for-profits, or small governmental jurisdictions) to which the RFA applies. The proposed rules, if promulgated, would no longer require prospective trail sponsors to request Board permission to negotiate for interim trail use/railbanking, or Board permission for rail carriers to consent to such requests. The proposed rules would also enable rail carriers to consummate abandonment authority if they are no longer interested in negotiating for interim trail use without waiting for the Board-ordered negotiation period to expire or asking that the order be vacated. As discussed below, the Board estimates that these changes would eliminate all paperwork requirements in approximately 45% of attempted railbanking negotiations.
See
infra 21 n.22. In the remaining cases, the Board does not expect that the new petition for Trails Act transfer would result in any greater burden than would the existing request for a NITU/CITU, and may even result in less. The proposed rules would, however, require that rail carriers (or trail sponsors acting on behalf of rail carriers) to seek abandonment authority should they wish to abandon lines over which the trail sponsor intends to terminate interim trail use. Because termination requests are infrequent, and because this
(
printed page 76184)
rulemaking does not modify the substantive standards for abandonment, including use of the class exemption at
49 CFR 1152.50
, the Board does not anticipate it will be any more difficult for such rail carriers to obtain that authority under the proposed rules. On balance, the Board expects the impact of the proposed rule would be a reduction in regulation and paperwork burden for small entities. Further, the Board asserts that the economic impact of the reduction in paperwork would be entirely beneficial to small entities as such entities would have reduced filing burdens associated with negotiating an interim trail use agreement. Therefore, the Board certifies under
5 U.S.C. 605(b)
that these proposed rules, if promulgated, would not have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities within the meaning of the RFA. This decision will be served upon the Chief Counsel for Advocacy, Office of Advocacy, U.S. Small Business Administration, Washington, DC 20416.
Paperwork Reduction Act
Pursuant to the Paperwork Reduction Act (PRA),
44 U.S.C. 3501-3521
, Office of Management and Budget (OMB) regulations at
5 CFR 1320.8(d)(3)
, and the Appendix, the Board seeks comments about the revisions in the proposed rules to the currently approved collection of Preservation of Rail Service (OMB Control No. 2140-0022) and Statutory Licensing Authority (OMB Control No. 2140-0023) regarding: (1) whether the collection of information, as modified in the proposed rule below, is necessary for the proper performance of the functions of the Board, including whether the collection has practical utility; (2) the accuracy of the Board's burden estimates; (3) ways to enhance the quality, utility, and clarity of the information collected; and (4) ways to minimize the burden of the collection of information on the respondents, including the use of automated collection techniques or other forms of information technology, when appropriate.
The proposed rule no longer requires the filing of a trail use request whenever a trail sponsor and rail carrier negotiate trail use for lines authorized for abandonment, or the filing of requests to extend the authorized negotiation period. The Board estimates the proposed rules would reduce the total annual hourly burden by 50 hours under Preservation of Rail Service (OMB Control No. 2140-0022) because not every negotiation for interim trail use/railbanking yields an agreement.
[
21
]
The proposed rules, however, will require a rail carrier (or a trail sponsor acting on behalf of a rail carrier) to seek abandonment authority should it wish to abandon a railbanked line for which a trail sponsor intends to terminate trail use. But because trail sponsors infrequently terminate trail use and because the filing should be substantially duplicative of the request for abandonment authority previously filed for the line, the Board expects that the proposed rules will increase the total hourly burden by only 20 hours under Statutory Licensing Authority (OMB Control No. 2140-0023). The Board welcomes comment on the estimates of actual time and costs of compliance with the proposed rules, as detailed in the Appendix. The proposed rules will be submitted to OMB for review as required under
44 U.S.C. 3507(d)
and
5 CFR 1320.11(b)
. Once the comment period ends, comments received by the Board regarding the information collection will also be forwarded to OMB for its review.
Executive Order 12866
(Regulatory Planning and Review) and
Executive Order 14192
(Unleashing Prosperity Through Deregulation)
Executive Order 12866
, as modified by
Executive Order 14215
, provides that the Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs (OIRA) will review all significant rules. OIRA has determined that this rule is significant under section 3(f) of
Executive Order 12866
. The STB anticipates requesting that the final rule be considered an
Executive Order 14192
deregulatory action.
The proposed rule is needed to simplify the Board's railbanking processes and reduce unnecessary takings liability for the United States. The Board has discretion to carry out the directives of
16 U.S.C. 1247(d)
through appropriate rules and regulations governing filing requirements and procedures for railbanking at the Board. The Board lacks discretion, however, to reject a railbanking request on the grounds that the particular rail line in question is not suitable for railbanking.
See Citizens Against Rails-to-Trails
v.
Surface Transp. Bd.,
267 F.3d 1144, 1152 (D.C. Cir. 2001);
Goos
v.
ICC,
911 F.2d 1283, 1295 (8th Cir. 1990).
The benefits of the proposed rule include eliminating any need for regulated entities to file paperwork with the Board in cases where interim trail use/railbanking negotiations occur but do not result in an agreement, which the Board estimates to be approximately 45% of cases.
See supra
21 n.22. In those cases, the existing regulations require the parties to seek and require the Board to issue a NITU/CITU (and require the rail carrier to seek vacatur of that NITU/CITU should it wish to end negotiations), but, under the proposed rule, a Board filing is required only after the parties have reached agreement. The Board estimates that each of the filings to be eliminated takes approximately five hours to complete. An additional substantial benefit of the rulemaking would be an expected reduction in the takings liability of the United States—and the costs of litigating those claims—particularly in cases where no interim trail use/railbanking agreement is reached. Whereas under the current regime a NITU/CITU has been held to effect a taking in those circumstances, under the proposed rule there would be no agency action and hence no takings claim or corresponding litigation. According to the Treasury Department website, Trails Act-related payments from the judgment fund over the last two years, including payment of interests and attorney fees, exceeded $50 million. These takings cases are against the United States and handled by DOJ, and the Board is not in a position to project what percentage of those awards and cost payments would not have occurred under the new rules or estimate the litigation costs incurred by DOJ. But the Board expects that the amount of expense saved by the proposed rule would be substantial.
In terms of costs of the rulemaking, the proposed reforms do require that rail carriers seek authority to abandon railbanked lines in cases where interim trail use has been terminated, whereas that authority is effectively automatic under the current regulations. However, trail sponsor requests to terminate trail use are infrequent, occurring on average no more than twice per year, and those requests will largely duplicate requests previously filed. Thus, the Board anticipates that this rule will be net deregulatory, as the benefits from less regulation of rail carrier and trail sponsor trail use negotiations will outweigh any increase in administrative or other costs borne by carriers, trail sponsors, or the Board.
(
printed page 76185)
The alternatives the Board considered included (1) the no-action alternative and (2) the proposal in the petition for rulemaking filed by DOJ. The Board rejected the no-action alternative because that alternative—
i.e.,
the situation in which the Board does nothing—would not solve the problem of the unnecessary filings and takings litigation expenses that are regular features of the status quo. The proposal the Board is putting forward resembles DOJ's proposal in many respects but is more comprehensive and makes other changes to align the Trails Act procedures with the Board's overall regulatory scheme.

Revise § 1152.29 to read as follows:
§ 1152.29
Prospective use of rights-of-way for interim trail use and railbanking.
(a)
Petition for Trails Act Transfer defined.
Under section 208 of the National Trails System Act,
16 U.S.C. 1247(d)
(“the Trails Act”), a carrier or other owner of a rail line can transfer its interest in the right-of-way to a state, political subdivision, or qualified private organization (“trail sponsor”) for interim trail use. The Board must approve and condition that transfer. An owner and trail sponsor seeking to obtain such approval must jointly file with the Board a Petition for Trails Act Transfer.
(b)
Content.
All Petitions for Trails Act Transfer must be filed jointly by the owner and the trail sponsor and must include:
(1) A map depicting, and an accurate description of, the right-of-way, or portion thereof (including mileposts), proposed to be transferred. This identification is for notice and administrative purposes only. It does not determine the location, width, extent, validity, or ownership of any property interest.
(2) A joint representation that the owner and the trail sponsor have reached an agreement to transfer the owner's property interest in the designated right-of-way to the trail sponsor for interim trail use.
(3) The owner's representations (i) that no rail carriers other than the owner are licensed to operate on the line and, if the owner is a rail carrier, (ii) that the owner has obtained Board authority to discontinue service on the line and has consummated that authority or that the owner is seeking Board authority to do so and will discontinue service immediately upon receiving such authority, and (iii) that the owner does not intend to fully abandon the line and is relinquishing any previously granted Board authority to do so, including a statement withdrawing any notice of exemption for abandonment that the owner has previously filed for the line, if applicable.
(4) The trail sponsor's representations that it is prepared to assume full responsibility for:
(i) Managing the right-of-way;
(ii) Any legal liability arising out of the transfer or use of the right-of-way (unless the trail sponsor is immune from liability, in which case the trail sponsor need only indemnify the owner against any potential liability); and
(iii) The payment of any and all taxes that may be levied or assessed against the right-of-way.
(5) The trail sponsor's acknowledgments:
(i) That the transfer will be conditioned on the trail sponsor meeting its responsibilities described in the preceding paragraph of this section, such that the trail sponsor's continued performance of those responsibilities will be a requirement of the transfer.
(ii) That the trail sponsor cannot alienate or otherwise alter any portion of the right-of-way in a manner that would be inconsistent with future reactivation for rail service, absent express Board permission.
(iii) That the Board has the authority and obligation to vacate the resulting Trails Act order if the right-of-way is needed for reactivation of rail service and that continued trail use inconsistent with reactivation will not be permitted.
(c)
Procedures for filing.
(1) Lines authorized for discontinuance. If the right-of-way is on a rail line on which the Board has authorized the owner to discontinue service, the parties shall jointly file the petition for transfer in the discontinuance docket.
(2) Lines authorized for abandonment. If the right-of-way is on a rail line that the Board has authorized the owner to abandon but for which the abandonment has not been consummated, the parties shall jointly file the petition for transfer in the abandonment docket.
(3) Other lines. If the right-of-way is on a rail line that the Board has not authorized for either abandonment or discontinuance by the owner, the owner shall request, in a new docket, discontinuance authority from the Board (via application, petition for exemption, or notice of exemption, as appropriate), and the parties shall file the petition for transfer in that new docket.
(d)
Effect of Trails Act Order.
A Board order granting a Petition for Trails Act Transfer under this section authorizes the owner to transfer its property rights in the right-of-way to the trail sponsor, with such conditions as the Board may impose. The order does not involve the exercise of any power of eminent domain. It does not take or burden private property. It does not authorize the owner or the trail sponsor to condemn or take private property. And it does not authorize the use of private property in excess of existing property rights.
(e)
Substitution of trail sponsor.
When a trail sponsor intends to terminate trail use and another person intends to become a trail sponsor by assuming financial responsibility for the right-of-way, then the current and future trail sponsors shall jointly file a petition to transfer the property interest in the right-of-way to the future trail sponsor. The filing must include the map and description of the right-of-way described in § 1152.29(b)(1) and the future trail sponsor's representations and acknowledgments described in § 1152.29(b)(4) and (b)(5).
(f)
Ending interim trail use/railbanking.
After a line has been transferred to a trail sponsor pursuant to these regulations, the Board will entertain petitions to vacate the Trails Act order and reactivate rail service on the line. The Board will also entertain requests to authorize the line for abandonment or take other appropriate action in the event that the trail sponsor intends to end the use of all or any portion of the right-of-way as a trail.

Because Board collections are submitted electronically to the Board, there is no cost for filing with the Board. Needs and Uses:
The Surface Transportation Board is, by statute, responsible for the economic regulation of common carrier freight railroads and certain other carriers operating in the United States. Under the laws the Board administers, persons seeking to preserve rail service may file pleadings before the Board to acquire or subsidize a rail line for continued service, to impose a public use condition, or to request a Trails Act transfer to a trail sponsor.
When a line is proposed for abandonment or discontinuance, affected shippers, communities, or other interested persons may seek to preserve rail service by filing with the Board: an offer of financial assistance (OFA) to subsidize or purchase a rail line for which a railroad is seeking abandonment or discontinuance (
49 U.S.C. 10904
), including a request for the Board to set terms and conditions of the financial assistance; a request for a public use condition (
49 U.S.C. 10905
); or a request for authority to transfer the line to a trail sponsor under the Trails Act (
16 U.S.C. 1247(d)
). Similarly, when a line is placed on a system diagram map identifying it as an anticipated or potential candidate for abandonment, affected shippers, communities, or other interested persons may seek to preserve rail service by filing with the Board a feeder line application to purchase the identified rail line (
49 U.S.C. 10907
). Additionally, the railroad owning the rail line subject to abandonment or discontinuance must, in some circumstances, provide information to the applicant or offeror, as included above.
As to trail use, under the proposed rule, the STB will issue a Trails Act order authorizing the transfer of the rail line to a trail sponsor under
16 U.S.C. 1247(d)
