AGENCY:
Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS), Department of Health and Human Services (HHS).
ACTION:
Notice.
SUMMARY:
This notice announces a $776.00 calendar year 2027 application fee for institutional providers that are initially enrolling in the Medicare or Medicaid program or the Children's Health Insurance Program (CHIP); revalidating their Medicare, Medicaid, or CHIP enrollment; or adding a new Medicare practice location. This fee is required with any enrollment application submitted on or after January 1, 2027, and on or before December 31, 2027.
DATES:
The application fee announced in this notice is effective on January 1, 2027.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Frank Whelan, (410) 786-1302.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
I. Background
In the February 2, 2011,
Federal Register
(
76 FR 5862
), we published a final rule with comment period titled “Medicare, Medicaid, and Children's Health Insurance Programs; Additional Screening Requirements, Application Fees, Temporary Enrollment Moratoria, Payment Suspensions and Compliance Plans for Providers and Suppliers”. This final rule finalized, among other things, provisions related to the submission of application fees as part of the Medicare, Medicaid, and the Children's Health Insurance Program (CHIP) provider enrollment processes.
As provided in section 1866(j)(2)(C)(i) of the Social Security Act (the Act) and in
42 CFR 424.514
, “institutional providers” that are initially enrolling in the Medicare or Medicaid programs or CHIP, revalidating their enrollment, or adding a new Medicare practice location are required to submit a fee with their enrollment application. An “institutional provider” for purposes of Medicare is defined at § 424.502 as “any provider or supplier that submits a paper Medicare enrollment application using the CMS-855A, CMS-855B (not including physician and non-physician practitioner organizations), CMS-855S, or associated internet-based PECOS enrollment application.” As we explained in the February 2, 2011, final rule (
76 FR 5914
), in addition to the providers and suppliers subject to the application fee under Medicare, Medicaid-only and CHIP-only institutional providers would include nursing facilities, intermediate care facilities for persons with intellectual disabilities (ICF/IID), and psychiatric residential treatment facilities; they may also include other institutional provider types designated by a State in accordance with their approved State plan.
As indicated in §§ 424.514 and 455.460, the application fee is not required for either of the following:
A Medicare physician or non-physician practitioner submitting a CMS-855I.
A prospective or revalidating Medicaid or CHIP provider—
++ Who is an individual physician or non-physician practitioner; or
++ That is enrolled as an institutional provider in Title XVIII of the Act or another State's Title XIX or XXI plan and has paid the application fee to a Medicare contractor or another State.
II. Provisions of the Notice
Section 1866(j)(2)(C)(i)(I) of the Act established a $500 application fee for institutional providers in calendar year (CY) 2010. Consistent with section 1866(j)(2)(C)(i)(II) of the Act, § 424.514(d)(2) states that for CY 2011 and subsequent years, the preceding year's fee will be adjusted by the percentage change in the consumer price index (CPI) for all urban consumers (all items; United States city average, CPI-U) for the 12-month period ending on June 30 of the previous year. Consequently, each year since 2011 we have published in the
Federal Register
an announcement of the application fee amount for the forthcoming CY based on this formula. Most recently, in the December 3, 2025,
Federal Register
(
90 FR 55738
), we published a notice announcing a fee amount for the period of January 1, 2026, through December 31, 2026, of $750.00. The $750.00 fee amount for CY 2026 was used to calculate the fee amount for CY 2027 as specified in § 424.514(d)(2).
According to Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) data, the CPI-U increase for the period of July 1, 2025, through June 30, 2026, was 3.5 percent. (See
https://www.bls.gov/​news.release/​archives/​cpi_​07142026.htm
). As required by § 424.514(d)(2), the preceding year's fee of $750 will be
(
printed page 76252)
adjusted by 3.5 percent. This results in a CY 2027 application fee amount of $776.25 ($750 × 1.035). As we must round this to the nearest whole dollar amount, the resultant application fee amount for CY 2027 is $776.
III. Collection of Information Requirements
This document does not impose information collection requirements that is, reporting, recordkeeping, or third-party disclosure requirements. Consequently, there is no need for review by the Office of Management and Budget under the authority of the Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995 (
44 U.S.C. 3501
et seq.
). However, it does reference previously approved information collections. The CMS-855A, CMS-855B, CMS-855I, and CMS-855S applications are approved under, respectively, OMB control numbers 0938-0685, 0938-1377, 0938-1355, and 0938-1056.
IV. Regulatory Impact Statement
A. Background and Review Requirements
We have examined the impacts of this rule as required by
Executive Order 12866
, “Regulatory Planning and Review”;
Executive Order 13132
, “Federalism“;
Executive Order 13563
, “Improving Regulation and Regulatory Review”;
Executive Order 14192
, “Unleashing Prosperity Through Deregulation”; the Regulatory Flexibility Act (RFA) (Pub. L. 96-354); section 1102(b) of the Social Security Act; section 202 of the Unfunded Mandates Reform Act of 1995 (
Pub. L. 104-4
); and the Congressional Review Act (
5 U.S.C. 804(2)
).
Executive Orders 12866 and 13563 direct agencies to assess all costs and benefits of available regulatory alternatives and, if regulation is necessary, to select those regulatory approaches that maximize net benefits (including potential economic, environmental, public health and safety, and other advantages; distributive impacts.). Section 3(f) of
Executive Order 12866
defines a “significant regulatory action” as any regulatory action that is likely to result in a rule that may: (1) have an annual effect on the economy of $100 million or more or adversely affect in a material way the economy, a sector of the economy, productivity, competition, jobs, the environment, public health or safety, or State, local, or tribal governments or communities; (2) create a serious inconsistency or otherwise interfere with an action taken or planned by another agency; (3) materially alter the budgetary impact of entitlements, grants, user fees, or loan programs or the rights and obligations of recipients thereof; or (4) raise novel legal or policy issues arising out of legal mandates, or the President's priorities.
A regulatory impact analysis (RIA) must be prepared for a regulatory action that is significant under section 3(f)(1) of
E.O. 12866
. As explained in this section of the notice, we estimate that the total cost of the increase in the application fee will not exceed $100 million. Therefore, this notice does not reach the $100 million economic threshold and is not considered a major notice.
B. Costs
The costs associated with this notice involve an increase in the application fee amount that certain providers and suppliers must pay in CY 2027. The CY 2027 cost estimates are as follows:
1. Medicare
Based on CMS data, we estimate that in CY2027 approximately:
8,392 newly enrolling institutional providers will be subject to and pay an application fee; and
35,148 revalidating institutional providers will be subject to and pay an application fee.
Using a figure of 43,540 (8,392 newly enrolling + 35,148 revalidating) institutional providers, we estimate an increase in the cost of the Medicare application fee requirement in CY 2027 of $1,132,040 (or 43,540 × $26 (or $776 minus $750)) from our CY 2026 projections.
2. Medicaid and CHIP
Based on CMS and State statistics, we estimate that approximately 30,000 (9,000 newly enrolling + 21,000 revalidating) Medicaid and CHIP institutional providers will be subject to an application fee in CY 2027. Using this figure, we project an increase in the cost of the Medicaid and CHIP application fee requirement in CY 2027 of $780,000 (or 30,000 × $26 (or $776 minus $750)) from our CY 2026 projections.
3. Total
Based on the foregoing, we estimate the total increase in the cost of the application fee requirement for Medicare, Medicaid, and CHIP providers and suppliers in CY 2027 to be $1,912,040 ($1,132,040 + $780,000) from our CY2026 projections.
The RFA requires agencies to analyze options for regulatory relief of small businesses. For purposes of the RFA, small entities include small businesses, nonprofit organizations, and small governmental jurisdictions. Most hospitals and most other providers and suppliers are small entities, either by nonprofit status or by having revenues of less than $9 million to $47. million in any 1 year. Individuals and States are not included in the definition of a small entity. As we stated in the RIA for the February 2, 2011, final rule (
76 FR 5952
), we do not believe that the application fee will have a significant impact on small entities.
In addition, section 1102(b) of the Act requires us to prepare a regulatory impact analysis if a rule may have a significant impact on the operations of a substantial number of small rural hospitals. This analysis must conform to the provisions of section 604 of the RFA. For purposes of section 1102(b) of the Act, we define a small rural hospital as a hospital that is located outside of a Metropolitan Statistical Area for Medicare payment regulations and has fewer than 100 beds. We are not preparing an analysis for section 1102(b) of the Act because we have determined, and the Secretary certifies, that this notice would not have a significant impact on the operations of a substantial number of small rural hospitals.
Section 202 of the Unfunded Mandates Reform Act of 1995 (UMRA) also requires that agencies assess anticipated costs and benefits before issuing any rule whose mandates require spending in any 1 year of $100 million in 1995 dollars, updated annually for inflation. In 2026, that threshold was approximately $193 million. The Agency has determined that there will be minimal impact from the costs of this notice, as the threshold is not met under the UMRA.
Executive Order 13132
establishes certain requirements that an agency must meet when it promulgates a proposed rule (and subsequent final rule) that imposes substantial direct requirement costs on State and local governments, preempts State law, or otherwise has Federalism implications. Since this notice does not impose substantial direct costs on State or local governments, the requirements of
Executive Order 13132
are not applicable.
In accordance with the provisions of
Executive Order 12866
, this notice was reviewed by the Office of Management and Budget.
The Administrator of the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS), Dr. Mehmet Oz, having reviewed and approved this document, authorizes Chyana Woodyard, who is the Federal Register Liaison, to electronically sign
(
printed page 76253)
this document for purposes of publication in the
Federal Register
.

Federal Register Liaison, Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services.

AGENCY:
National Park Service, Interior.
ACTION:
Notice of written determination.
SUMMARY:
The National Park Service determines that allowing bicycles on approximately 0.85 miles of new and existing multi-use trails within Kennesaw Mountain National Battlefield Park is consistent with the protection of the park's natural, scenic, and aesthetic values; safety considerations; and management objectives; and will not disturb wildlife or park resources.
DATES:
Comments on this written determination must be received by 11:59 EDT on December 28, 2026.
ADDRESSES:
You may submit comments on this written determination by either of the following methods:
(1)
Electronically:
Visit
https://parkplanning.nps.gov/​kemo
and click on the link entitled “Open for Comment”.
(2)
By hard copy:
Mail to Park Superintendent, Kennesaw Mountain National Battlefield Park, 900 Kennesaw Mountain Drive, Kennesaw, Georgia 30152.
Document Availability:
The Old 41 Highway Widening and Improvements Environmental Assessment and Finding of No Significant Impact provide information and context for this written determination and are available online at
https://parkplanning.nps.gov/​kemo
.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Patrick Gamman, Superintendent, Kennesaw Mountain National Battlefield Park, 770-427-4686,
patrick_gamman@nps.gov
.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
(
printed page 76262)
Background
The National Park Service (NPS), in cooperation with the Federal Highway Administration (FHWA), the Georgia Department of Transportation (GDOT), and Cobb County, completed an Environmental Assessment (EA) in June 2025 to evaluate proposed improvements of Old 41 Highway within Kennesaw Mountain National Battlefield Park. The project is needed to reduce traffic congestion, reduce the frequency and severity of crashes, improve traffic and pedestrian safety at intersections, and reduce the queuing of traffic along Old 41 Highway for approximately 0.71 miles in the area between Stilesboro Road and Kennesaw Avenue within the park. This area attracts a high volume of both pedestrian and bicycle traffic. Among the elements analyzed in the EA was the construction of a new multi-use trail path and tunnel beneath the south leg of the Old 41 Highway/Stilesboro Road intersection and impacts of bicycle use on the new trail and on connecting trails. Public review of the EA occurred between August and October 2025.
Based on documentation and analysis provided in the EA and associated decision file, on February 25, 2026, the Acting Regional Director for Interior Region 2 signed a Finding of No Significant Impact (FONSI). The Selected Alternative complies with the procedural requirements in existing NPS regulations for the designation of trails for bicycle use within park areas. Appendix A in the EA documents the NPS's evaluation of the pathway surface suitability and soil conditions for accommodating bicycle use, including any maintenance, minor rehabilitation, or armoring to achieve sustainable conditions. Appendix A also addresses lifecycle maintenance costs, safety considerations, strategies to prevent or minimize user conflict, and measures to protect natural and cultural resources and mitigate potential impacts.
Written Determination
NPS regulations in
36 CFR 4.30
require the NPS to determine that bicycle use on the existing Noonday Trail and the Mountain to River Trail, and in the new tunnel and on the connecting trail segments, is consistent with the protection of the park area's natural, scenic and aesthetic values, safety considerations and management objectives, and will not disturb wildlife or park resources. The EA and the FONSI provide information and context for this written determination, including additional analysis of the potential effects of bicycle use on park resources and visitors. The EA and FONSI are available online on the park's planning page at the link provided in the
ADDRESSES
section.
Park Significance, Purpose, and Values
Kennesaw Mountain National Battlefield Park encompasses approximately 2,923 acres of mostly hardwood forest that preserves a Civil War battleground of the Atlanta Campaign in Cobb County, Georgia. The park is located about 25 miles northwest of downtown Atlanta within the northern suburbs of the greater Atlanta metropolitan area, which has a population of about 5 million people. The name Kennesaw is derived from the Cherokee Indian “Gah-nee-sah” meaning cemetery or burial ground. This name became a self-fulfilling prophecy when the Battle of Kennesaw Mountain resulted in 5,350 casualties between June 19, 1864, and July 2, 1864.
Ultimately, more than 67,000 soldiers were killed, wounded, and captured during some of the heaviest fighting of Atlanta Campaign of the Civil War. The battle was a crucial engagement in General William T. Sherman's campaign to advance into Georgia and capture Atlanta, the Confederacy's key transportation and manufacturing center. Facing General Joseph E. Johnston's smaller Confederate force, Sherman's numerically superior army steadily pushed south through a series of engagements. At Kennesaw Mountain, Confederate troops held strong defensive positions, but Sherman eventually outflanked them and forced a retreat. The loss of Kennesaw Mountain opened the path to Atlanta, whose fall in September 1864 strengthened Union morale and contributed to President Abraham Lincoln's reelection.
The purpose of the park is to preserve, protect, and interpret, for the benefit and inspiration of the people, the historical and natural features of this major battle site in the American Civil War's 1864 Atlanta Campaign.
Significance statements express why a park's resources and values are important enough to merit designation as a unit of the National Park System. These statements are linked to the purpose of the park, and are supported by data, research, and consensus. Statements of significance describe the distinctive nature of the park and why an area is important within a global, national, regional, and systemwide context. They focus on the most important resources and values that will assist in park planning and management. The following significance statements have been identified for the park.
The park is the only nationally designated battle site that commemorates the 1864 Atlanta Campaign. Union victory in this campaign ensured the re-election of Abraham Lincoln and thereby the eventual preservation of the Union.
The park preserves 8.9 miles of original Civil War field fortifications, which were decisive elements in later stages of the American Civil War.
The park is the largely intact site of a major Civil War battle, contained within one of the largest contiguous federally managed public green spaces in a major metropolitan area of the United States.
The battlefield was set aside as an important cultural property dedicated to public inspiration and interpretation of the significant historic events that occurred here. The size of this forested historic battleground makes it the largest green space in the 13-county metropolitan Atlanta region that does not charge an entrance fee. As a result, approximately 1.18 million recreational visitors came to the battlefield in 2025 to enjoy its history and natural resources.
Fundamental resources and values of the park are those features, systems, processes, experiences, stories, scenes, sounds, smells, or other attributes that are essential to achieving the purpose of the park and maintaining its significance. The park's 2013 Foundation Document identifies the following fundamental resources and values of the park: (1) General Sherman's military strategy; (2) Cheatham Hill memorialization; (3) historic transportation corridors; (4) field fortifications; and (5) urban wildlands experience.
Natural, Scenic and Aesthetic Values
The new tunnel and connecting trail segments will be designed to uphold the natural, scenic, and aesthetic conditions of where they are located in the park, consistent with management zones established in the 1983 General Management Plan (GMP). The existing Noonday and Mountain to River Trails are each paved 10 feet wide trails. The new tunnel and connecting trail segments will have design specifications that are consistent with the Noonday Trail in terms of width and pavement material. Signage will primarily focus on wayfinding and will be limited and designed to be as visually unobtrusive as possible. Continuing to allow bicycle use on the existing trails will have no adverse impacts to natural, scenic, and aesthetic values because this use is
(
printed page 76263)
ongoing and has no effect to these resources along Old Highway 41. Furthermore, bicycle use enhances connectivity to county-wide trail networks while fostering a deeper enjoyment and appreciation of the surrounding landscape among users.
Safety Considerations
Given its location within the park, the project area experiences significant pedestrian and bicycle traffic. To accommodate these users, the construction of a tunnel beneath the south leg of the Old 41 Highway/Stilesboro Road intersection was included in the Selected Alternative. The existing Noonday Trail and the Mountain to River Trail, and the new tunnel will be connected with new trail segments. The tunnel will enable park visitors utilizing the park overflow lot to access park amenities without having to cross Stilesboro Road at grade, thereby eliminating potential conflicts between vehicles and bicyclists/pedestrians. Additionally, the existing side path along the south side of Old 41 Highway (comprising the Noonday Creek Trail west of Stilesboro Road and the Mountain to River Trail east of Stilesboro Road) will be preserved in its current location following the project's completion and the removal of the existing roadway pavement. This arrangement will help maintain a safe separation between the high traffic volumes on Old 41 Highway and pedestrian and bicycle users.
Monitoring of the Noonday Trail, Mountain to River Trail, the tunnel and connecting trail segments will be conducted to assess the effectiveness of the new facilities in meeting safety and accessibility goals. Monitoring will ensure that the established trail guidelines are met to reduce the likelihood of user conflicts and injuries. Conflicts and congestion will be minimized using wayfinding signs and the use of educational materials to educate users about trail rules and appropriate behavior.
Management Objectives
Overall management objectives for the park are guided by NPS Management Policies 2006, which direct superintendents to develop management plans that allow for recreation in National Park System units, but in a manner that avoids unacceptable impacts to park resources or values. See NPS Management Policies 2006, Section 8.2.2.1. They also emphasize the need for alternative transportation systems, especially those that promote nonmotorized means of accessing and moving within System units. See NPS Management Policies 2006, Section 9.2. Consistent with these NPS-wide policies, the NPS has established management objectives for the park in the GMP and Foundation Document and the Multi Use Trails Along Cheatham Hill road, Dallas Highway, and Burnt Hickory road EA with Cobb County and GDOT. These documents promote an appropriate balance between visitor access and enjoyment, and the protection of park resources. One way to further this management objective is to increase visitor appreciation and understanding of the resources and values of the park by providing experiences that foster deeper connections with them. This strategy enhances visitor satisfaction and promotes responsible recreation, as users are encouraged to experience and respect the natural and cultural resources found throughout the park.
Future maintenance and rehabilitation of the Noonday Trail, Mountain to River Trail, the tunnel and connecting trail segments will be the responsibility of Cobb County through a future maintenance agreement. A Cooperative Management Agreement between Cobb County and the National Park Service will outline the roles and responsibilities for maintaining these trails and connecting segments.
Wildlife and Park Resources
The EA and the FONSI concluded that resources in the park, including cultural and natural resources and sensitive species, will not be impaired or significantly impacted by continued bicycle use on the existing trails or expanded bicycle use on the new multi-use path and tunnel. Although trails that allow bicycle use are prone to short-term impacts along trail edges when bikers occasionally travel off trail into vegetated areas, the NPS can mitigate these impacts through trail design and visitor education. The plan would be implemented in an area that receives frequent human visitation. Local wildlife are habituated to human use of the landscape and typically avoid encounters with humans; as a result, continued public use of trails would not adversely affect wildlife. Bicycling and other non-motorized uses would not contribute to the loss of habitat that is detrimental to wildlife because visitors generally stay on or close to trails. Ongoing and planned trail maintenance by the park and Cobb County will reduce adverse impacts by addressing graffiti, trash, damaged trail surfaces or rutting along the pathways from bicycle and pedestrian use.
Electric Bicycles
The use of an electric bicycle (as defined in NPS regulations at
36 CFR 1.4
) may be allowed on park roads, parking areas, and administrative roads and trails that are otherwise open to bicycles. The Superintendent will designate the areas open to electric bicycles, or specific classes of electric bicycles, and notify the public pursuant to
36 CFR 1.7
, as set forth in
36 CFR 4.30(i)
.
Determination
Based upon the foregoing, the NPS determines allowing bicycle use on the 0.85 miles of the Noonday Creek Trail, Mountain to River Trail, tunnel and new connecting trail segments is consistent with the protection of the park's natural, scenic and aesthetic values; safety considerations; and management objectives; and will not disturb wildlife or park resources.
Patrick E. Gamman,
Superintendent.

AGENCY:

ACTION:
Final rule.
SUMMARY:
The NCUA Board (Board) is amending its regulations governing supervisory committee audits to eliminate unnecessary, redundant, and overly prescriptive provisions. The final rule is necessary to reduce regulatory burden, increase operational flexibility for federally insured credit unions (FICUs), and streamline the rules by removing requirements that are outdated or duplicative of other authorities. The intended effect of the final rule is to simplify compliance for FICUs without compromising the integrity of the audit process.
DATES:
This final rule is effective on December 28, 2026.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Ian Marenna, Associate General Counsel, Office of General Counsel at (703) 518-6450 or at 1775 Duke Street, Alexandria, VA 22314.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
I. Introduction
A. Background
On December 11, 2025, the Board published a notice of proposed rulemaking in the
Federal Register
proposing to amend its regulations at
12 CFR part 715
, which govern the supervisory committee audit and verification responsibilities for FICUs.
[
1
]
The proposal sought to partially or wholly eliminate several sections of this part to reduce regulatory burden, eliminate unnecessary and redundant provisions, and increase flexibility for FICUs. These changes are consistent with the Board's ongoing efforts to modernize its regulations and ensure they remain effective and efficient without imposing undue burdens. They are intended to provide FICUs with greater flexibility in meeting their audit compliance obligations while maintaining the integrity of the audit and verification process.
The primary purpose of this regulation is to ensure that FICUs meet required financial reporting objectives and establish practices and procedures sufficient to safeguard members' assets from error, conflicts of interest, self-dealing, and fraud.
The following is a description of the purpose and function of those sections as they currently exist. The changes the Board proposed, the comments received on the proposal, and the final rule are discussed in section II below.
Section 715.2 defines key terms used throughout the part. It establishes the meaning of technical terms such as
financial statements, financial statement audit,
GAAP, and GAAS. It also defines terms specific to the rule's framework, such as
compensated person,
which refers to an accounting or auditing professional compensated for performing more than one supervisory committee audit per year, and working papers, which are the records supporting the auditor's findings. This section distinguishes a formal
financial statement audit
from the broader su
pervisory committee audit
responsibility, which can be fulfilled through several alternative engagements.
Section 715.8 sets forth the requirements for the verification of member accounts. This requirement is derived from
12 U.S.C. 1761d
and obligates the supervisory committee to verify members' passbooks and accounts against the credit union's records at least once every two years. The regulation permits several methods for this verification, including a 100 percent controlled verification of all member share and loan accounts, a statistical sampling method, or a nonstatistical sampling method consistent with GAAS when performed by a state-licensed independent person.
Section 715.9 governs the engagement of an outside, compensated person to assist the supervisory committee. To ensure auditor independence, the section prohibits such a person from being related by blood or marriage to any management employee or official of the credit union. It also mandates that the engagement be formalized through a written engagement letter contracted directly with the supervisory committee. This letter must specify the terms, conditions, objectives, and compensation for the engagement; identify the basis of accounting to be used; and set a target date for the delivery of the written audit report. The engagement letter must also certify that regulators will be provided
(
printed page 76133)
unconditional access to the complete set of original working papers and acknowledge that these papers will be retained for at least three years.
Section 715.10 outlines the supervisory committee's responsibilities for the audit report and working papers. Upon receiving a written audit report, the committee must submit it to the board of directors and provide a summary of the audit to the members at the next annual meeting. If a member requests it, the committee must provide access to the full audit report. This section also holds the supervisory committee responsible for maintaining a complete set of original working papers for each audit and for providing the NCUA with unconditional access to these papers upon request.
Section 715.12 provides statutory remedies for the NCUA Board to address non-compliance by a federal credit union (FCU). The Board may compel a credit union to obtain a supervisory committee audit performed by an independent, state-licensed person if the credit union's supervisory committee fails to obtain a required annual audit or obtains one that does not meet the requirements of part 715. The Board may also compel a full financial statement audit if the credit union has experienced “serious and persistent recordkeeping deficiencies.” The rule defines a deficiency as “serious” if financial reporting objectives are not met and member assets are not safeguarded, and “persistent” if it continues beyond a reasonable period.
Section 741.202 applies supervisory committee audit and verification and other requirements of part 715 to all FICUs, which extends coverage to federally insured, state-chartered credit unions (FISCUs).
B. Legal Authority
The Board is issuing this final rule pursuant to its authority under the FCU Act. Under the FCU Act, NCUA is the chartering and supervisory authority for FCUs and the federal supervisory authority for FICUs.
[
2
]
The FCU Act grants NCUA a broad mandate to issue regulations governing both FCUs and all FICUs. Section 120 of the FCU Act is a general grant of regulatory authority and authorizes the Board to prescribe rules and regulations for the administration of the FCU Act.
[
3
]
Section 207 of the FCU Act is a specific grant of authority over share insurance coverage, conservatorships, and liquidations.
[
4
]
Section 209 of the FCU Act is a plenary grant of regulatory authority to issue rules and regulations necessary or appropriate to carry out its role as share insurer for all FICUs.
[
5
]
Accordingly, the FCU Act grants the Board broad rulemaking authority to ensure that the federally insured credit union industry and the Share Insurance Fund remain safe and sound.
Sections 115 and 202(a)(6) of the FCU Act set forth provisions addressing auditing and accounting requirements.
[
6
]
Section 115 of the FCU Act requires an FCU's supervisory committee to make an annual audit and submit a report of that audit to the FCU's board of directors and a summary of that report to the FCU's members at the next annual meeting.
[
7
]
Further, the supervisory committee is required to make supplemental reports as it deems necessary.
Section 202(a)(6)(A) of the FCU Act is a general grant of authority to the Board to prescribe audit standards that require an outside, independent audit by a certified public accountant for any fiscal year for which a FICU has not conducted an annual supervisory committee audit, has not received a complete and satisfactory supervisory committee audit, or during which the FICU has experienced persistent or serious recordkeeping deficiencies.
[
8
]
Section 202(a)(6)(C) of the FCU Act generally requires FICUs having assets of $10 million or more to use accounting principles consistent with GAAP in all reports or statements required to be filed with the Board. The Board, and state credit union supervisors under applicable state law, may require credit unions having less than $10 million in assets to follow GAAP. Section 202(a)(6)(D) of the FCU Act imposes audit requirements for larger FICUs. Specifically, a FICU having assets of $500 million or more is required to obtain an annual independent audit of its financial statements performed in accordance with GAAS, hereafter referred to as a “financial statement audit.” That audit must be performed by an independent certified public accountant or public accountant licensed to do so by an appropriate state or jurisdiction.
[
9
]
Additionally, if an FCU having total assets of less than $500 million but more than $10 million elects to obtain a financial statement audit, the audit must be performed consistent with the accountancy laws of the appropriate state or jurisdiction.
[
10
]
II. Final Rule
A. Overview
This final rule follows publication of the proposed rule and takes into consideration the comments received on the proposal. By the close of the public comment period on February 9, 2026, the Board had received 32 public comments. Comments were submitted by individuals, state credit union leagues and national trade organizations, FICUs, and an association of state credit union supervisors. All but one of the 32 comments received on the proposed rule supported the proposal. The remaining commenter did not offer support or opposition for the proposed rule, but instead spoke to cybersecurity standards as they relate to audits.
[
11
]
In generally supporting the rule, 15 commenters stressed that small FICUs struggle with compliance burden, often related to redundant and duplicative regulations and examination practices that necessitate resources on low impact areas that do not affect safety and soundness and take away from their ability to serve members. Other reasons commenters cited for generally supporting the rule included: reduced burden and improved flexibility while preserving strong oversight; promoting efficiency and clarity; and alignment with industry best practices. After careful consideration of the issues raised by the commenters, the Board has decided to adopt the proposal without change.
B. Final Rule and Discussion of Public Comments
This section of the preamble discusses the final rule, the significant issues raised by the commenters, and the Board's responses to the comments.
1. Section 715.2
The Board proposed amending §  715.2(h), which defines “[i]nternal control” for Part 715. The current regulation defines this term as the process designed by a FICU's board, officers, and employees to provide reasonable assurance of reliable financial reporting and safeguarding of
(
printed page 76134)
assets against unauthorized acquisition, use, or disposition. The definition also describes internal control components in detail, specifying five components and describing reliable financial reporting. As noted in the proposal, the second sentence of the paragraph, which enumerates the five components of an internal control structure, is overly prescriptive and risks becoming obsolete. This list is derived from a specific framework that may evolve over time. Removing this static definition, as was proposed, would make the regulation more durable and allow FICUs and auditors to apply current, industry-accepted frameworks for evaluating internal controls. The third sentence, which defines reliable financial reporting by referencing only the preparation of Call Reports, is unduly narrow and was also proposed for removal to provide a more comprehensive understanding of the term.
Ten commenters specifically supported modernizing the definition by removing the prescriptive list of internal control components and the reference to Call Report preparation to describe reliable financial reporting in favor of allowing FICUs and auditors to apply non-specified current and future auditing and risk management practices and allow for a more comprehensive understanding of what constitutes reliable financial reporting. Commenters felt this would eliminate unnecessary prescriptive requirements and provide regulatory relief by being flexible, technology and framework neutral, and capable of evolving while still ensuring reliable financial reporting and safeguarding of assets. One commenter specifically agreed that defining reliable financial reporting by referencing only the preparation of Call Reports is unnecessarily narrow.
One commenter requested that NCUA add a resource to help FICUs confirm current industry accepted processes for evaluating internal controls to eliminate inconsistencies when applying those processes. Two commenters asked NCUA to communicate supervisory expectations and apply them consistently, consistent with the FICU's size and complexity. They requested NCUA emphasize that no particular internal control framework is required or implied by the revised definition so that informal or unwritten expectations do not develop and negate the relief.
NCUA Response.
The final rule adopts the changes as proposed. The Board appreciates commenters' input and generally agrees with the cited benefits of the changes. Regarding the addition of a resource to help FICUs confirm current industry accepted processes for evaluating internal controls, the Board will consider whether additional guidance may be beneficial but is reluctant to prescribe specific resources FICUs should look to as this change is intended to provide greater flexibility. The Board agrees with the comments addressing the importance of communicating consistent supervisory expectations and applying them consistently. The Board believes the final rule will facilitate this. As requested, the Board also confirms that no particular internal control framework is required or implied by the revised definition.
2. Section 715.8
The Board proposed amending §  715.8(a), which details specific methods for the verification of member accounts. The FCU Act imposes a clear and self-executing duty on the supervisory committee to verify member accounts at least once every 2 years.
[
12
]
The regulation requires members' accounts to be verified against the records of the treasurer. The proposed change would amend this requirement to state more generally that members' accounts must be verified against the credit union's records. The proposal noted that, while the treasurer must maintain the records under the FCU Act, because the treasurer's records belong to the credit union the supervisory committee is responsible for checking these records against members' account records.
Twenty-three commenters specifically supported this change. Six expressed that the proposed change appropriately aligns the regulation with the statutory requirement while reflecting modern operational realities of system-based recordkeeping practices and preserving the supervisory committee's independent verification responsibility. Another said the change would streamline compliance without compromising the NCUA's oversight. Two commenters specifically agreed with the proposal's assessment that “the treasurer's records belong to the credit union” and the regulation can provide that members' accounts must be verified against the credit union's records. Fifteen commenters said easing the regulatory and exam burden related to the biennial account verification, which they felt a largely obsolete and low impact area, would help reduce the compliance burden on small FICUs.
NCUA Response.
The final rule adopts the change as proposed. The Board appreciates commenters' input and generally agrees with the cited benefits of the change.
3. Section 715.9
The Board proposed amending § 715.9(b), which provides details on engagement letters with outside, compensated auditors. The current provision requires the scope of work to be documented in an engagement letter contracted with the supervisory committee. The provision also details how the engagement letter must be signed by both parties. As noted in the proposal, the Board finds this additional detail and prescription unnecessary. Without this description, the provision is clear that the supervisory committee must enter into a contract with the outside, compensated auditor. Prescribing this process in greater detail adds to the body of regulations that FICUs must follow without any clear benefit. Therefore, the Board proposed to remove the final sentence of this provision.
Twenty-five commenters specifically supported eliminating the requirement for dual signatures on engagement letters as it would remove unnecessarily prescriptive language and streamline compliance without compromising the NCUA's oversight or audit quality. Fifteen commenters said the change would help reduce the compliance burden on small FICUs. One said reducing prescriptive regulatory requirements like this will cut down FICU paperwork burdens without reducing the stringency of Generally Accepted Auditing Standards (GAAS) or other standards applicable to these scopes of work. One commenter requested auditors review the changes.
NCUA Response.
The final rule adopts the change as proposed. The Board appreciates commenters' input and generally agrees with the cited benefits of the change.
4. Section 715.10
The Board proposed amending § 715.10(a) by removing the sentence that requires a supervisory committee to provide the NCUA with a copy of audit reports upon request. This provision is entirely redundant of the Board's existing authority. As noted in the proposal, the Board has broad statutory power under the FCU Act to access all books and records of any FICU during its examination and supervision activities.
[
13
]
This inherent authority includes the power to obtain audit reports, which are records of the credit union. Eliminating this duplicative regulatory language streamlines the rule
(
printed page 76135)
without in any way diminishing the agency's access to information or its oversight capabilities.
Eleven commenters specifically expressed support for this change, agreeing the FCU Act already provides the NCUA with broad authority to access all FICU books and records, including audit reports. Nine commenters said the change removes a duplicative regulatory requirement without reducing transparency or supervisory oversight.
Two of these commenters said they generally support the change but noted that the existing regulatory language has historically served as a clear and direct reference point for supervisory committees regarding their role in supporting exams. The commenters felt removing the explicit provision may raise questions for supervisory committee members, especially volunteer ones, about how audit materials are expected to be made available and under what circumstances. They suggested that to avoid uncertainty and promote consistent understanding the NCUA clarify through supervisory guidance or examiner communications that the amendment does not alter the NCUA's access rights or the expectation that audit reports will be provided promptly upon request during an examination or supervisory review. The commenters felt this would preserve transparency and cooperation while still achieving the proposal's deregulatory intent.
One commenter asked NCUA to clarify the requirements related to audit working papers to reflect modern audit practices, noting Part 715 assigns the supervisory committee responsibility for maintaining a complete set of original working papers and providing NCUA unconditional access, which can be read to require duplicative retention even when compensated auditors maintain the official working papers under professional standards. The commenter suggested clarifying that compliance is satisfied so long as the supervisory committee ensures prompt and complete access to all working papers upon request, regardless of whether they are maintained electronically by the auditor, and that electronic records are fully acceptable. The commenter said this would streamline compliance without limiting the agency's supervisory authority.
NCUA Response.
The final rule adopts the change as proposed. The Board appreciates commenters' input and generally agrees with the cited benefits of the change. The Board understands commenters' concern that removing the explicit provision may raise questions for supervisory committee members about how audit materials are expected to be made available and under what circumstances. The Board agrees, and reiterates here, that the amendment does not alter the NCUA's access rights or the expectation that audit reports will be provided promptly upon request during an examination or supervisory review and will endeavor to ensure examiners communicate these obligations consistently. The Board will consider additional guidance if it becomes necessary.
Finally, regarding the commenter's concern that the requirement to maintain a complete set of original working papers can be read to require duplicate retention by both the supervisory committee and the compensated auditor, the Board stresses that duplicate retention is not necessary. As the commenter notes, compliance is satisfied so long as the supervisory committee ensures retention of a complete set of original working papers and the ability to provide NCUA unconditional, complete, and prompt access to all working papers upon request. This has long been the NCUA's position and is evidenced in both a 1996 final rule preamble
[
14
]
adopting changes to part 715 and in the requirements in §§ 715.9(c)(7)-(8) that the engagement letter with the compensated auditor:
Certify that NCUA staff and/or the State credit union supervisor, or designated representatives of each, will be provided unconditional access to the complete set of original working papers, either at the offices of the credit union
or at a mutually agreed upon location,
for purposes of inspection; and acknowledge that working papers shall be retained for a minimum of three years from the date of the written audit report.
[
15
]
Regarding the acceptability of electronically maintained working papers, the Board stresses that electronically maintained working papers are acceptable and have been since the 1996 final rule.
[
16
]
5. Section 715.12
Finally, the Board proposed to remove two sentences from § 715.12(b). This provision currently describes the objective of a financial statement audit compelled by the NCUA and states that an “adverse opinion or disclaimer of opinion should be the exception rather than the norm.” As noted in the proposal, this language is unnecessary because GAAS already establishes the objectives of a financial statement audit. This commentary in the regulation is best read as guidance and could cause confusion if auditing standards evolve to provide different objectives or expectations for financial statement audits. Therefore, the Board proposed to remove the final two sentences of this provision to reduce potential confusion.
Nine commenters specifically expressed support for this change, noting that the change would eliminate unnecessary and potentially confusing regulatory language that duplicates existing professional auditing standards. They agreed that GAAS already establishes the objectives and expectations of a financial statement audit and retaining prescriptive regulatory language on those objectives is redundant and risks creating confusion if professional standards evolve. Commenters said that removing this language appropriately streamlines the regulation while preserving the NCUA's existing authority to require an audit when necessary and reducing the risk of confusion as auditing standards evolve. Several commenters also specifically agreed that the language that would be removed is guidance and not suitable for regulatory text.
NCUA Response.
The final rule adopts the change as proposed. The Board appreciates commenters' input and generally agrees with the cited benefits of the change.
6. Other Comments
FISCUs:
Five commenters raised concerns about application of Part 715, both in its current form and as proposed, to FISCUs through § 741.202 and urged NCUA to clarify which elements of Part 715 apply to FISCUs. The commenters noted that certain provisions, like those related to supervisory committees, are not universally required under all state laws and do not clearly apply to FISCUs in NCUA's regulations. They said additional guidance regarding how these provisions apply through incorporation by reference would
(
printed page 76136)
promote clarity and consistent implementation.
NCUA Response.
The Board appreciates the commenters' input. This is beyond the scope of this rulemaking, but the Board may consider the comments as part of any future amendments to part 715.
Supervisory Expectations:
Four commenters stressed that as prescriptive requirements are removed NCUA must provide clear supervisory messaging, accessible guidance, and consistent application across exams. Two of these commenters emphasized that regulatory burden stems not only from regulatory text, but also from how expectations are communicated, interpreted, and applied during exams. They said less prescriptive requirements place additional importance on remaining expectations being clearly articulated, readily accessible, and applied consistently to prevent increased compliance uncertainty and examiner variability that diminish the practical benefits of the proposed relief. One of these commenters noted the importance of supporting strong supervisory programs and clarity to both FICUs and state and federal regulators.
NCUA Response.
The Board appreciates the commenters' input and agrees that less prescriptive requirements increase the importance of NCUA clearly articulating standards and consistently applying the regulations. The NCUA will endeavor to do this.
Standards:
Three commenters noted support for a more flexible, principles-based framework, but encouraged NCUA to ensure this does not inadvertently diminish clarity around base supervisory recordkeeping expectations. Two of these commenters said that with reduced prescriptive requirements there is a risk of differing interpretations regarding the documentation sufficient to evidence compliance with the audit requirements. They requested NCUA clearly communicate, either in the final rule or accompanying guidance, that, while specific formats and processes are no longer prescribed, FICUs remain responsible for maintaining records that reasonably support audit conclusions and board oversight. The commenters felt that emphasizing outcomes and risk coverage rather than procedural detail would preserve Part 715's effectiveness while providing the intended flexibility. One commenter stressed that recordkeeping clarity is not merely procedural, but fundamental to enabling effective supervision by regulators and boards to ensure deficiencies can be identified, escalated, and corrected. They encouraged NCUA to remind FICU directors of their fiduciary obligation to ensure accurate and timely recordkeeping.
NCUA Response.
The Board appreciates the commenters' concerns and emphasizes that while the final rule is intended to provide greater flexibility and reduce regulatory burden, and thus does make part 715 more principles based, FICUs remain responsible for maintaining records that reasonably support their audit conclusions and demonstrate board oversight. As the commenter noted, the intent of the changes is not to lessen standards but to allow FICUs greater flexibility to demonstrate they are meeting those standards. The Board strongly agrees that it is essential that FICUs maintain accurate and timely recordkeeping and that FICUs understand their obligations to do so.
Appendix A:
One commenter asked the NCUA to eliminate Part 715 Appendix A, which contains minimum procedures for supervisory committee audits. They asked that the substance of any enforceable rules be moved to the body of Part 715 and any guidance be reissued as standalone guidance. They noted that NCUA's broader deregulatory project has proposed eliminating Part 748 Appendices A and B because they are guidance and reissuing them as non-binding guidance. They felt keeping Appendix A as is would confuse stakeholders.
NCUA Response.
The Board appreciates the commenters' input. This is beyond the scope of this rulemaking, but the Board will consider the comment as part of any future amendments to part 715.
Broader Deregulation Project:
One commenter asked NCUA to ensure changes are harmonized with other revisions and introduced with adequate implementation timelines.
NCUA Response.
The Board appreciates the commenters' input and emphasizes that it is implementing the deregulation project with the goal of making sure all changes are harmonized and implemented in a manner that allows FICUs sufficient time to adapt to the changes.
Passbooks:
Two commenters asked NCUA to modernize part 715 by replacing outdated language requiring verification of “passbooks” in
12 CFR 715.8
, which stems from
12 U.S.C. 1761d
, which refers to passbooks and accounts, to reflect today's electronic account records, online access, and digital confirmations, none of which rely on physical passbooks.
NCUA Response.
The Board appreciates the commenters' input. This is beyond the scope of this rulemaking, but the Board may consider the comments as part of any future amendments to part 715. The Board also notes that the FCU Act and the regulation refer to “accounts” more generally in addition to passbooks.

The changes in the final rule will reduce burden and confusion by streamlining certain provisions in the NCUA's audit regulations that apply to all FICUs. AGENCY:
National Credit Union Administration (NCUA).
ACTION:
Final rule.
SUMMARY:
The NCUA Board (Board) is amending its regulations for corporate credit unions by removing the requirement that a corporate credit union's asset and liability management committee (ALCO) must have at least one member who is also a member of the corporate credit union's board of directors. The final rule also removes filing requirements related to a corporate credit union's annual report and any management letter or other report issued by its independent public accountant. The intended effect is to reduce unnecessary regulatory burden and provide corporate credit unions with greater flexibility.
DATES:
This final rule is effective on December 28, 2026.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Office of General Counsel:
Rachel Ackmann, Senior Attorney, Office of General Counsel, at (703) 518-6540 or at 1775 Duke Street, Alexandria, VA 22314.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
I. Introduction
A. Background
In 2010, the Board comprehensively revised the regulations governing corporate credit unions to provide longer-term structural enhancements to the corporate system in response to the financial crisis of 2007-2009.
[
1
]
The provisions of the 2010 rule were intended to stabilize the corporate system and improve corporate credit unions' ability to function and provide services to natural person credit unions without undue risk. Since 2010, and as part of the Board's continuous reevaluation of its regulation of corporate credit unions, the Board has amended part 704 on several occasions.
[
2
]
In 2017, the Board amended corporate credit union capital standards to change the calculation of capital after a consolidation and to set a retained earnings ratio target.
[
3
]
In October 2020, the Board issued a final rule to amend several provisions relating to corporate credit union investments in credit union service organizations (CUSOs) and other provisions relating to corporate credit union governance.
[
4
]
Finally, in 2021, the Board amended part 704 to clarify that corporate credit unions may purchase subordinated debt instruments issued by consumer credit unions.
[
5
]
On December 11, 2025, the Board published a proposed rule to remove the requirement that a corporate credit union's ALCO have at least one board member and certain filing requirements related to a corporate credit union's annual report and other reports issued by its independent public accountant.
[
6
]
The proposed rule would have applied to both federally and state-chartered corporate credit unions.
B. Legal Authority
The Board is issuing this final rule pursuant to its authority under the Federal Credit Union Act (FCU Act). Under the FCU Act, NCUA is the chartering and supervisory authority for federal credit unions (FCUs) and the federal supervisory authority for federally insured credit unions (FICUs).
[
7
]
The FCU Act grants NCUA a broad mandate to issue regulations governing both FCUs and all FICUs. Section 120 of the FCU Act is a general grant of regulatory authority and authorizes the Board to prescribe rules and regulations for the administration of the FCU Act.
[
8
]
Section 207 of the FCU Act is a specific grant of authority over share insurance coverage, conservatorships, and liquidations.
[
9
]
Section 209 of the FCU Act is a plenary grant of regulatory authority to issue rules and regulations necessary or appropriate to carry out its role as share insurer for all FICUs.
[
10
]
Accordingly, the FCU Act grants the Board broad rulemaking authority to ensure that the federally insured credit union industry and the Share Insurance Fund remain safe and sound.
The FCU Act also includes an express grant of authority for the Board to subject federally chartered central, or corporate, credit unions to such rules, regulations, and orders as the Board deems appropriate.
[
11
]
Part 704 of the NCUA's regulations implements the requirements of the FCU Act regarding corporate credit unions.
[
12
]
II. Final Rule
A. Overview
This final rule follows publication of the proposed rule and takes into consideration the comments received on the proposal. By the close of the public comment period on February 9, 2026, the Board had received 12 public comments. Comments were submitted by an individual, FICUs, both natural person and corporate, state credit union leagues, a national association of state credit union supervisors, and national trade associations. After careful consideration of the issue raised by the commenters, the Board has decided to adopt the proposal without change.
B. Discussion of Public Comments
This section of the preamble discusses the significant issues raised by the commenters, and the Board's responses to the comments.
ALCO Committee Representation
The Board proposed to rescind the requirement for each corporate credit union's ALCO to have at least one member who is also a member of the board of directors. Two commenters objected to the proposed change. One natural-person FICU stated that the proposal removes a key layer of independent oversight and noted the increased premiums that natural-person FICUs paid following the corporate crisis. An individual stated that having
(
printed page 76126)
a board member on the corporate ALCO lessens moral hazard. The individual stated that when monitoring is weakened, managers face fewer constraints and may shift toward higher-risk strategies. The commenter stated that retaining board-level oversight will help sustain accountability, promote efficient risk-taking, and protect the long-run stability of the credit union system.
The Board agrees that strong oversight of the corporate's ALCO is critical for risk management. However, the Board does not believe it is necessary for a board member to be on the ALCO for the board of directors to fulfill its oversight function. Also, several other requirements more effectively ensure adequate oversight. First, part 704 requires that a corporate credit union operate according to a written asset and liability management policy that addresses certain defined components. Additionally, corporate credit union ALCOs must review asset and liability management reports monthly and should report regularly to the board of directors. Additionally, corporate credit union boards of directors must ensure that the corporate's financial performance is evaluated and that the objectives of the corporate credit union and the responsibilities of management are met.
[
13
]
Therefore, the Board does not believe that removing the requirement for a board member to be on the corporate credit union's ALCO presents safety and soundness risk.
All other commenters were supportive of the proposed change. These commenters discussed several benefits of the proposed rule, including additional flexibility, the ability to attract and include the right talent for effective risk management, and that the key risk reduction requirement is an established written asset liability management policy. The Board agrees and believes the change strikes the right balance between flexibility for the corporate credit union to determine its internal governance structure and ensuring corporate credit union boards retain responsibility for the strategic oversight of a corporate credit union's asset and liability management.
Filing Requirements for a Corporate Credit Union's Annual Report
The Board proposed to remove several of its filing requirements related to a corporate credit union's annual report. The proposed rule would have rescinded the requirement to file a copy of an annual report and any management letter or other report issued by its independent public accountant with the NCUA within 180 days after the end of the calendar year. The proposed rule also rescinded the requirement for the NCUA to make the annual report available for public inspection. Along with the proposed removal of these filing requirements, the proposal rescinded requirements related to untimely filings.
One individual commenter was opposed to the changes. The commenter stated that maintaining public access to annual audit reports preserves transparency. The Board does not believe removing this provision would affect transparency. The current provision has been in effect for over ten years and the Board is not aware of any public requests for access to corporate credit union annual reports. The Board believes the existing requirement is unnecessary and its removal will not affect transparency. The Board also notes that all member credit unions are given access to a preliminary annual report. A preliminary annual report is required because a corporate credit union may not have completed its annual report at the time of the annual meeting. The Board understands that most corporate credit unions voluntarily post final annual reports on their website. The Board will consider updating the rule in the future to require disclosure of the final annual report.
All other commenters were supportive of the proposed change. These commenters stated that the reports continue to remain subject to examiner review and the proposed rule removes duplicate and unnecessary filing requirements. Commenters also noted that this proposed change streamlines reporting obligations without limiting NCUA's access to information and that corporate credit unions must submit a preliminary annual report to the membership. One commenter stated that the requirements were of limited public benefit.
The Board agrees with commenters on eliminating these filing requirements as they impose an unnecessary and undue compliance burden on corporate credit unions that is disproportionate to their limited public benefit. The NCUA has access to corporate credit union records and audit reports through its examination authority.
[
14
]
The amendments only remove the requirements for the corporate credit union to file the documents with the NCUA and does not limit the NCUA's access to the information. NCUA examiners will continue to review these materials through the examination process.
The Board notes that other aspects of the NCUA's filing requirements will remain unchanged. Corporate credit unions will continue to be required to notify the NCUA within 15 days of losing an independent public accountant through dismissal or resignation.
The proposed rule also would have removed the requirement to report the engagement of an independent public accountant. The Board is more concerned with prompt notification for the dismissal or resignation of an accountant than about notification of the initial engagement. The NCUA has access to the engagement letter if necessary and does not need prompt notification. Additionally, a corporate credit union must submit a preliminary annual report to the corporate credit union's membership at its next calendar year's annual meeting.
Comments Outside the Scope of the Proposed Rule
The Board also received a few comments outside of the scope of the proposed rule. A few commenters sought additional regulatory relief. Some commenters requested that corporate credit unions receive 15 additional days to notify NCUA of losing an independent public accountant. Commenters asked for at least 30 days to ease compliance burden, instead of the current timeframe of 15 days. In addition, one association of credit union supervisors also stated the Board should provide greater flexibility for corporate credit unions to manage their balance sheets, particularly given the significantly higher capital levels corporate credit unions hold now compared to 2009 and 2010. The association believes that greater flexibility can be calibrated with supervisory risk mitigation to enhance the benefits to natural-person credit unions. Finally, two state leagues recommended additional changes that were not within the scope of the proposed rule. The changes including removing: (1) the prohibition on an individual serving as the representative of more than one organizational member; (2) the requirement for external auditors to file certain reports with NCUA; (3) the requirement that the enterprise risk management committee include at least one experienced risk management expert; and (4) the prohibition on the board chair simultaneously serving as an officer, director, or employee of a credit union trade association. The Board may
(
printed page 76127)
consider these recommendations for future rulemakings.
III. Regulatory Procedures
A. Executive Orders 12866, 13563, and 14192
Pursuant to
Executive Order 12866
(“Regulatory Planning and Review”), a determination must be made whether a regulatory action is significant and therefore subject to review by the Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs (OIRA), within the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) in accordance with the requirements of the Executive Order.
[
15
]
Executive Order 13563
(“Improving Regulation and Regulatory Review”) supplements and reaffirms the principles, structures, and definitions governing contemporary regulatory review established in
Executive Order 12866
.
[
16
]
This final rule was drafted and reviewed in accordance with
Executive Order 12866
and
Executive Order 13563
. OIRA has determined that this final rule is not a “significant regulatory action” as defined by section 3(f) of
Executive Order 12866
.
Executive Order 14192
(“Unleashing Prosperity Through Deregulation”) requires that any new incremental costs associated with new regulations shall, to the extent permitted by law, be offset by the elimination of existing costs associated with at least 10 prior regulations.
[
17
]
This final rule is not an
Executive Order 14192
regulatory action because this rule is not significant under
Executive Order 12866
. This final rule is considered an
Executive Order 14192
deregulatory action.
B. Regulatory Flexibility Act
The Regulatory Flexibility Act
[
18
]
generally requires an agency to conduct a regulatory flexibility analysis of any rule subject to notice and comment rulemaking requirements, unless the agency certifies that the rule will not have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities. If the agency makes such a certification, it shall publish the certification at the time of publication of either the proposed rule or the final rule, along with a statement providing the factual basis for such certification.
[
19
]
For purposes of this analysis, NCUA considers small credit unions to be those having under $100 million in assets.
[
20
]
The Board fully considered the potential economic impacts of the regulatory amendments on small credit unions.
There are no corporate credit unions under $100 million in assets. Accordingly, NCUA certifies the final rule will not have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small credit unions.
C. Paperwork Reduction Act
The Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995 (PRA) generally provides that an agency may not conduct or sponsor, and not withstanding any other provision of law, a person is not required to respond to, a collection of information, unless it displays a currently valid OMB control number. The PRA applies to rulemaking in which an agency creates a new or amends existing information collection requirements. For purposes of the PRA, an information collection requirement may take the form of a reporting, recordkeeping, or a third-party disclosure requirement. The NCUA has determined that the changes addressed in this notice do not create a new information collection or revise an existing information collection as defined by the PRA.
D.
Executive Order 13132
on Federalism
Executive Order 13132
encourages independent regulatory agencies to consider the impact of their actions on state and local interests.
[
21
]
NCUA, an agency as defined in
44 U.S.C. 3502(5)
, voluntarily complies with the executive order to adhere to fundamental federalism principles. This final rule applies to all corporate FICUs, including state-chartered credit unions. The NCUA expects that any effect on states or on the distribution of power and responsibilities among the various levels of government will be minor. The changes remove existing federal filing requirements for state-chartered corporate credit unions and do not negatively affect the division of responsibilities between the NCUA and state regulatory authorities with oversight of federally insured, state-chartered corporate credit unions.
E. Assessment of Federal Regulations and Policies on Families
NCUA has determined that this final rule will not affect family well-being within the meaning of Section 654 of the Treasury and General Government Appropriations Act, 1999.
[
22
]
The final rule is exclusively concerned with corporate credit union governance and filing requirements. The final rule is intended to reduce regulatory burden while maintaining a strong corporate system to support consumer credit unions in their provision of financial services to members. The potential positive effect on family well-being, including financial well-being is, at most, indirect.
F. Congressional Review Act
Subtitle E of the Small Business Regulatory Enforcement Fairness Act of 1996, also known as the Congressional Review Act (CRA), generally provides for congressional review of agency rules.
[
23
]
NCUA must submit a report to Congress and the Comptroller General when it issues a final rule, as defined by the CRA.
[
24
]
An agency rule, in addition to being subject to congressional oversight, may also be subject to a delayed effective date if the rule is a “major rule.” OIRA has determined that this rule is not a “major rule” within the meaning of the relevant sections of the CRA. NCUA will also file appropriate reports with Congress and the Comptroller General so this rule may be reviewed.
