For additional information or access to background documents, contact Jeremiah Singer, Human Factors/Engineering Integration (W46-430), (202) 366-7679, U.S. Department of Transportation, 1200 New Jersey Avenue SE, Washington, DC 20590.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Under the Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995 (
44 U.S.C. 3501
et seq.
), before an agency submits a proposed collection of information to OMB for approval, it must first publish a document in the
Federal Register
providing a 60-day comment period and otherwise consult with members of the public and affected agencies concerning each proposed collection of information. The OMB has promulgated regulations describing what must be included in such a document. Under OMB's regulation (at
5 CFR 1320.8(d)
), an agency must ask for public comment on the following: (a) whether the proposed collection of information is necessary for the proper performance of the functions of the agency, including whether the information will have practical utility; (b) the accuracy of the agency's estimate of the burden of the proposed collection of information, including the validity of the methodology and assumptions used; (c) how to enhance the quality, utility, and clarity of the information to be collected; and (d) how to minimize the burden of the collection of information on those who are to respond, including the use of appropriate automated, electronic, mechanical, or other technological collection techniques or other forms of information technology,
e.g.,
permitting electronic submission of responses. In compliance with these requirements, NHTSA asks for public comments on the following proposed collection of information for which the agency is seeking approval from OMB.
(
printed page 76304)
Title:
Driver Body Position and Readiness to Respond When Using L2 Systems.
OMB Control Number:
New.
Form Number(s):
Form 2202, Form 2203, Form 2204, Form 2205, Form 2206, Form 2207, Form 2208, Form 2209, Form 2210, Form 2211, Form 2212, Form 2213.
Type of Request:
New information collection.
Type of Review Requested:
Regular.
Requested Expiration Date of Approval:
Three years from date of approval.
Summary of the Collection of Information:
The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) of the U.S. Department of Transportation is seeking approval to conduct a one-time research study involving 12 voluntary information collections, up to 2,780 licensed drivers over 18 years old for a research study to examine driver body position and readiness to respond when using L2 features. The respondents will either participate in an online survey study or an in-person simulator study. Within this study, NHTSA's contractor, the Virginia Tech Transportation Institute (VTTI), and its subcontractors, University of Minnesota (UMN) and Keisler Social & Behavioral Research, will conduct the simulator and survey data collection sessions, respectively. The complete data collection effort is estimated at 1,606 burden hours to the study participants.
Survey Study:
2,750 participants will be recruited to participate in an online survey to assess driver's postures in L2 and non-L2 vehicles and the role of individual characteristics and driving environment on the adoption of various driving postures. The survey is expected to last 30 minutes. The survey questions will include standard socioeconomic metrics (
e.g.,
age, sex, location, household income, education), perceptions and attitudes towards L2 features, and typical driving postures that are assumed. The planned data collection activities discussed herein have been approved by Virginia Tech's Institutional Review Board.
Simulator Study:
30 participants will be recruited to participate in an in-person simulator study. Participants who meet the stated eligibility criterion and are interested in joining the study will complete a screening questionnaire which will screen for likelihood of simulation sickness, age, driver's license status, and height. Research staff will contact eligible participants and schedule their participation, based on their availability and available time slots in the study. After arriving at the study site, participants will complete the informed consent form. Participants will fill out a series of questionnaires, the One-time Questionnaire set, which asks questions about demographics and type of vehicle owned by the participant. Next, participants will complete a familiarization baseline drive to become accustomed to the driving simulator's behavior and L2 functions. Participants will then practice any secondary tasks that may have been developed to be included in the simulation. Following practice trials, participants will take the Pre-Drive Questionnaire, which is the pre-task Short Stress State Questionnaire (SSSQ). Participants will then be instructed to adopt a specific posture in the vehicle and monitor the drive along the straight roadway and the secondary task during each drive, while also taking over control of the vehicle when necessary. Participants will complete a total of four drives that vary in posture and take over scenario. Immediately following each drive, participants will complete a rating scale mental effort assessment and stress state post-questionnaire assessment, a wellness questionnaire to screen for simulation sickness, and an automation trust questionnaire called the Situation Trust Cale for Automated Driving before proceeding to the next drive. The planned data collection activities discussed herein have been approved by the University of Minnesota's Institutional Review Board.
Description of the Need for the Information and Proposed Use of the Information:
NHTSA's mission is to save lives, prevent injuries, and reduce economic costs due to road traffic crashes, through education, research, safety standards, and enforcement. To accomplish this mission, NHTSA has statutory authority to conduct crash injury research and collect relevant data in the interest of public health. Specifically, NHTSA is authorized to: (1) engage in research on all phases of highway safety and traffic conditions; (2) undertake collaborative research and development projects with non-federal entities for the purposes of crash data collection and analysis; and (3) conduct research and collect information to determine the relationship between motor vehicles and crashes, and personal injury or deaths resulting from such crashes. This information collection supports the department's strategic goal of safety.
The advancement in driver support systems (DSSs), particularly SAE Level 2 (L2) automation features, can result in situations where limited or no driver inputs are required to control the vehicle. While L2 features show promise for improved safety and vehicle operation, they have the potential to introduce new potential risks related to driver system misuse or misunderstanding of system limitations. These systems may, for example, struggle with complex roadway features and traffic situations, induce an unwarranted sense of security, and encourage driver disengagement.
[
1
]
Driver posture, especially as it relates to the position and orientation of the driver's limbs, is fundamental to the driving task. In the research literature, the term “posture” typically refers to naturally assumed body positions, while the term “pose” typically denotes prescribed or deliberate body positions, such as a specific way of standing, sitting, or lying that an individual assumes. Essential vehicle controls, like steering and braking, require manual actuation with the driver's hands and feet. Thus, one central goal of automobile design has always been to support and encourage a driver posture that allows safe and effective vehicle control during a wide array of driving scenarios. Fully manual driving facilitates that task to some extent, as it affords limited variance in postures that still allow effective vehicle control. However, this limitation is weaker for vehicle features that partially perform some vehicle control functions. Thus, DSSs that do not require continuous control inputs from the human driver could unintentionally result in drivers assuming postures that are ill-suited to the effective and efficient resumption of manual vehicle control (
e.g.,
responding to a takeover request, responding to an emerging hazard).
Three primary considerations are important. First, driver posture is not constant. Certain driving maneuvers (
e.g.,
backing) require substantial posture adjustments, and posture examinations should ideally account for that inherent variability. Second, in the context of normal vehicle operation, there is a general concept of a “standard driving position,” which in crashworthiness applications is operationalized to specific vehicle reference points. While this standard position is relevant in normal vehicle operation, it may not represent the frequency and duration of other driver postures, including slouched, reclining, leaning on some portion of the cabin, or sitting with crossed lower legs. Third, drivers differ in how they view DSS
(
printed page 76305)
features, how they believe they should/can safely engage with the features, and in their perceptions of the risk and safety of driving postures. Therefore, it is important to understand the range of behaviors and perceptions related to driving posture in the general driving population.
Ultimately, the objective of this work is to improve safety in L2 systems by (a) cataloguing the postures drivers assume during driving and under partial automation, (b) identifying their beliefs or perceptions surrounding those postures vis-à-vis the driving task, (c) understanding the reasons and factors that modulate why certain drivers tend to assume certain postures, and (d) deriving, based on those links, design guidance for potential countermeasures to encourage drivers to maintain positions that allow safely returning to the driving task.
The outcomes of this data collection will provide a wide variety of stakeholders with valuable information about the impact of driver posture, especially as it relates to the position and orientation of the driver's limbs when using L2 automation features, and readiness to respond to takeover requests.
NHTSA will use the information collected to produce a technical report containing summary statistics and tables. No identifying information or individual responses will be reported. The technical report will be made available to a variety of audiences interested in improving highway safety through the National Transportation Library.
Affected Public:
Survey Study:
The potential respondent universe is comprised of all U.S. licensed driving adults at least 18 years of age. The survey study will include two sample populations. One sample of 1,650 U.S. adult drivers will be matched to the U.S. general population as closely as possible on standard demographics (age, sex, race/ethnicity, education, U.S. region). An additional sample of 1,100 U.S. adult drivers will be recruited who drive vehicles with at least one L2 feature.
Simulator Study:
30 participants will be recruited for this study. The recruited study population will aim to represent the general driving public in Minnesota. The screening questionnaire will be used to screen for risk of simulation sickness, with participants who do not indicate experiences or behaviors associated with simulation sickness being invited to participate.
Estimated Number of Respondents:
Survey Study:
The target for the survey study is 2,750 participants, completing the entire survey; therefore, the research team will collect information for screening purposes from an estimated 3,929 potential participants.
Simulator Study:
The target for the simulator study is 30 participants who will be recruited to complete all four drives in the simulator; therefore, the research team will contact up to 70 potential participants for this study.
Frequency:
This is a one-time information collection.
Estimated Total Annual Burden Hours:
The total estimated burden for this one-time information collection is 1,608 hours total, or 536 annual burden hours (based on a 3-year period of performance). Further details are provided below.
This ICR includes 12 information collections, three for the survey study and nine for the simulator study, which are described below.
Survey Study:
1. Survey Screening Form (Form 2202)
Members of an online national survey panel will be invited to complete the survey. They will be invited via email and will click on a link in the email that will take them to a website that hosts the survey. An estimated 3,929 members will complete a series of screening questions. Participants are expected to take an estimated average of two minutes to complete the screening questions, resulting in a total of 131 burden hours.
2. Survey Study Informed Consent (Form 2213)
Individuals who meet the eligibility requirements will continue to the consent form. The consent form will take up to one minute to complete, resulting in a total of 46 burden hours.
3. Survey One-Time Questionnaire (Form 2203)
Individuals who meet the eligibility requirements and consent to participate will continue to the full survey on the website. The survey is expected to take up to 30 minutes to complete, resulting in a total of 1,375 burden hours.
Simulator Study:
4. Simulator Screening Questionnaire (Form 2204)
An estimated 70 participants (23 respondents annually), who have previously participated in UMN's Human Factors Safety Laboratory (HFSL) studies, will be contacted via email or phone call. The HFSL has an existing database of possible research participants who have indicated in the past that they would like to be contacted for future research studies. If necessary, advertisements will be posted to social media accounts after study approval, primarily on Facebook, X, Craigslist, and LinkedIn. These posts will be public so that anyone who routinely drives in Minnesota will be able to participate. The recruited study sample will aim to represent the general driving public. Respondents are expected to take an estimated average of three minutes to complete the questionnaire and will complete this questionnaire once, resulting in a total of four burden hours (one annual burden hour) for the screening of potential participants. Recruitment of study respondents will be from Minneapolis, Minnesota and its suburbs.
5. Participant Scheduling (Form 2205)
An estimated 30 participants (10 participants annually) will be contacted by email or phone and the research team member will coordinate with them about the best time to visit the laboratory at the University of Minnesota to participate in the study. Respondents are expected to take an estimated average of two minutes to complete the questionnaire and will complete this step once, resulting in a total of one burden hour (0.33 annual burden hour) for the scheduling of participants.
6. Simulator Study Informed Consent (Form 2206)
Thirty respondents (10 respondents annually) will complete informed consent, anticipating that either some respondents may choose not to proceed with the study or that the experimenter may determine that they should not participate (uncooperative, impaired, etc.). The visit to the UMN facility will begin with a consenting process that includes an overview of the study, an explanation of the consent form, and an opportunity for participants to ask questions and get clarification. Those individuals who consent to the study and enroll will complete the Informed Consent form and move on to the next process. This consent process and completion of the Informed Consent form, using the maximum of 30 respondents (10 annually), are expected to take five minutes and will be completed resulting in a total of three burden hours (one annual burden hour). This is a digital form, which participants are required to sign digitally.
7. One-Time Questionnaires (Form 2207)
Participants will complete the One-time Questionnaires. This set of
(
printed page 76306)
questionnaires also includes demographic questions asking about age, sex, education level, racial background, height and weight, state and zip code, household income, driving frequency and experience, region of habitation (urban, suburban, rural), and area the participant drives. Other questions include experience with Level 2 (L2) vehicle automation, and model of current vehicle owned, if any. This set of questions includes the Cognitive Failures Questionnaires, which asks about the propensity for attentional slips and forgetfulness, the Driver Behavior Questionnaire, which asks about typical driving behaviors performed by the participant, and a short survey of distracted driving behavior. Finally, the list of questions includes the Risk Propensity Scale and the Technology Readiness Index, the latter asking about the participant's favorability towards new technologies. The One-time Questionnaires, using a maximum of 30 respondents (10 annually), is expected to take 10 minutes and will be completed resulting in a total of five burden hours (two annual burden hours). This is a digital form, which participants are required to fill out digitally.
8. Baseline Drive Checklist (Form 2208)
A baseline drive will allow the participant to become familiar with the manual operation of the driving simulator, experience the vehicle under L2 conditions, and gain familiarity and experience with take-over requests/responses (TORs) (
i.e.,
familiarize participants with engaging and disengaging the L2 automation features). In addition, participants will be provided with practice trials of the selected secondary task (
i.e.,
both while stationary prior to the baseline drive and during the baseline drive). The Baseline Drive, using a maximum of 30 respondents (10 annually), is expected to take 12 minutes and will be completed, resulting in a total of 33 burden hours (11 annual burden hours. The Baseline Drive, using the maximum of 30 respondents (10 annually), is expected to take 12 minutes and will be completed resulting in a total of six burden hours (two annual burden hours).
9. Simulator Pre-Drive Questionnaire (Form 2209)
Participants will complete the Pre-Drive Questionnaire. This is the Short Stress State Questionnaire (SSSQ). The SSSQ assesses the change in task stress experienced by the participant during the simulator drive by measuring the participant's self-reported stress before (Pre-Drive Questionnaire) and immediately after (Post-Drive Questionnaires) the drive. The Pre-Drive Session Questionnaire is completed four times, using the maximum of 30 respondents (10 annually), is expected to take two minutes each time and will be completed resulting in a total of four burden hours (one annual burden hour).
10. Drive Session (Form 2210)
The simulation scenarios will expose participants to typical road environments where L2 automated features may be engaged to support hands-off, feet-off driving. The anticipated road environments will feature two- or four-lane highways with undivided and divided road designs that can support continuous driving at highway speeds for greater than 12 minutes. The driving scenarios will feature low-complexity roadway and traffic environments for the majority of the driving exposure time. Select scenarios will be introduced to each roadway environment at variable times to present realistic scenarios where the participant must assume manual control of the vehicle after the L2 automated features experience a system-limit failure where the vehicle experiences known circumstances that are outside of the operational design domain. In the cases of a system-limit failure, the vehicle will present a TOR to the participant with low to medium-low urgency. A secondary driving task, which will be beta tested and piloted, will be introduced to increase the driver's mental workload, encourage mental disengagement from the driving task and increase the difficulty of the manual takeover task. This is expected to be a mental processing task, which may include simple counting backwards by threes from a large number, such as 800. The Drive Session is completed four times, using a maximum of 30 respondents (10 annually). It is expected to take 12 minutes each time and will be completed resulting in a total of 24 burden hours (eight annual burden hours).
11. Post-Drive Questionnaires (Form 2211)
Participants will complete the Post-Drive Questionnaires. These include the Rating Scale Mental Effort (RSME) and the post-task Short Stress State Questionnaire (SSSQ). The RSME assesses how mentally demanding the drive was for the participant, and the SSSQ assesses the change in task stress experienced by the participant. This set of questionnaires also includes Situation Trust Scale for Automated Driving (STS-AD), and an abbreviated set of questions examining symptoms of simulation sickness (Wellness Questionnaire), to ensure the health and well-being of participants after the drive. The Post-Drive Questionnaires, using a maximum of 30 respondents (10 annually), is completed four times, and is expected to take four minutes each time. It will result in a total of eight burden hours (three annual burden hours).
12. Participant Payment Process (Form 2212)
Participants will go through the payment process paid with the Greenspire Clincard system, which provides participants with a debit card with the amount of compensation stipulated for the study. The participants will need to confirm some of their information with the key research team member completing this process, such as name, date of birth, and address information, which is required by the Greenspire system. This should take approximately one minute to complete. The Participant Payment Process, using the maximum of 30 respondents (10 annually), is expected to take about two minutes, resulting in a total of one burden hour (0.33 annual burden hours).
Estimated Total Annual Burden Cost:
The only cost burdens respondents will incur are costs related to travel to and from the research location for the simulator study. The costs are minimal and are expected to be offset by the honorarium that will be provided to the research participants. NHTSA estimates that, on average, each of the participants will travel less than five miles one-way to the research location (10 miles round trip), for a total of 300 miles for the entire study. Using the IRS standard mileage rate of $0.70 per mile,
[
2
]
each respondent is expected to incur no more than $7.00 in transportation costs. Therefore, NHTSA estimates that the total costs to respondents (N = 30) will be no more than $210.
Public Comments Invited:
You are asked to comment on any aspects of this information collection, including (a) whether the proposed collection of information is necessary for the proper performance of the functions of the Department, including whether the information will have practical utility; (b) the accuracy of the Department's estimate of the burden of the proposed information collection; (c) ways to enhance the quality, utility and clarity
(
printed page 76307)
of the information to be collected; and (d) ways to minimize the burden of the collection of information on respondents, including the use of automated collection techniques or other forms of information technology.

AGENCY:
Office of the Assistant Secretary for Community Planning and Development, HUD.
ACTION:
Notice.
SUMMARY:
This notice governs Community Development Block Grant disaster recovery (CDBG-DR) and Community Development Block Grant mitigation (CDBG-MIT) funds awarded under the appropriations acts identified below. In response to a grantee request, this notice provides a specific waiver and alternative requirement for the State of North Carolina for grants provided under the public laws cited herein.
DATES:
Applicability Date:
November 30, 2026.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
William J. Silva, Director, Office of Disaster Recovery, U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development, 451 7th Street SW, Room 7282, Washington, DC 20410, telephone number 202-708-3587 (this is not a toll-free number). HUD welcomes and is prepared to receive calls from individuals who are deaf or hard of hearing, as well as individuals with speech or communication disabilities. To learn more about how to make an accessible telephone call, please visit:
https://www.fcc.gov/​consumers/​guides/​telecommunications-relay-service-trs
.
Email inquiries may be sent to
Disaster_Recovery@hud.gov
.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
I. Authority To Grant Waivers
Public Laws 115-123 and 116-20 authorize the Secretary to waive or specify alternative requirements for any provision of any statute or regulation the Secretary administers in connection with the obligation by the Secretary, or use by the recipient, of grant funds, except for requirements related to fair housing, nondiscrimination, labor standards, and the environment. HUD may also exercise its regulatory waiver authority under
24 CFR 5.110
,
91.600
, and
570.5
.
The waiver and alternative requirement authorized in this notice is based upon a determination by the Secretary that good cause exists, and a determination by the Secretary that the waiver or alternative requirement is not inconsistent with the overall purposes of Title I of the Housing and Community Development Act of 1974 (
42 U.S.C. 5301
et seq.
) (HCDA). The basis for the waiver and alternative requirement is summarized in this notice.
II. Waiver and Alternative Requirement for Consultation With a Citizen Advisory Committee for the State of North Carolina's CDBG-MIT Grants for 2016 and 2018 Disasters
The Department received a request and justification of good cause from the State of North Carolina to waive the second paragraph of section V.A.3.c. of the notice published in
84 FR 45838
on August 30, 2019 (“the August 2019 Notice”), which requires CDBG-MIT grantees to form one or more citizen advisory committees. These committees are required to meet at least twice a year and solicit and respond to public comments and input, providing increased transparency to the public on the use of the CDBG-MIT allocation, and serving as an on-going public forum to continuously inform the grantee's CDBG-MIT projects and programs.
This waiver and alternative requirement, as further described below, applies to the following CDBG-MIT grants allocated to the State: (1) the allocation for disasters occurring in 2016 and 2018, funded by
Public Law 115-123
; and (2) the allocation for a disaster occurring in 2018, funded by
Public Law 116-20
. Both allocations are subject to the requirements published in
84 FR 45838
on August 30, 2019;
85 FR 60821
on September 28, 2020; and
86 FR 569
on January 6, 2021.
This waiver request aligns with HUD's requirements included in the notice titled,
Common Application, Waivers, and Alternative Requirements for Community Development Block Grant Disaster Recovery Grantees: The Universal Notice,
published on January 8, 2025, at
90 FR 1754
, as amended by Memorandums 25-02
[
1
]
and 25-03
[
2
]
(the “Universal Notice”). Section III.A.6.a. of the Universal Notice does not require the use of citizen advisory committees but instead encourages their use as a means to gather feedback and recommendations from the public at least annually.
The August 2019 Notice requires that, following HUD's approval of the Action Plan, each grantee form one or more citizen advisory committees to meet in an open forum at least twice a year. The primary function of these groups is to provide increased transparency to the public on use of the CDBG-MIT funds by soliciting and responding to public comments and to serve as an on-going public forum to continuously provide input on the CDBG-MIT funded projects and programs. Citizen advisory committees could also be a part of the process to prepare the initial CDBG-MIT Action Plan submitted to HUD, although not expressly required.
The State of North Carolina reports that despite efforts to engage and support the citizen advisory committees, member participation and community involvement have declined over the last few years. As a result, these groups no longer serve their intended purpose. To maintain the committees, the State made good faith attempts to increase attendance and participation, including widely advertising meetings through multiple channels. Despite these efforts, committee member attendance and participation continue to decline, often resulting in meetings
(
printed page 76260)
with minimal engagement. This trend reduces the committee's ability to provide meaningful input and limits its value as an advisory mechanism. Furthermore, these ongoing recruitment, retention, and engagement challenges require a disproportionate amount of staff time to manage, even as the committee's overall effectiveness wanes. Together, these factors demonstrate that the grantee's request is reasonable and that approving this waiver will reduce administrative burden, conserve resources, and streamline recovery efforts.
After reviewing the State of North Carolina's request and based on the good cause provided herein, the Department is waiving the alternative requirement found in the second paragraph of section V.A.3.c. of the August 2019 Notice. HUD notes the State's administrative and financial burden of forming a citizen advisory committee for its CDBG-MIT grants and, in alignment with section III.A.6.a. of the Universal Notice, waives this requirement. As an alternative requirement the grantee is subject to the requirement in section III.A.6.a. of the Universal Notice that states, “HUD encourages grantees to gather feedback and recommendations on key program decisions from a citizen advisory group at least annually.” If the State decides later that they do wish to work with a citizen advisory committee, the State can determine the cadence of the meetings and how the group would provide feedback to the grantee. This waiver and alternative requirement applies to the second paragraph of section V.A.3.c. of the August 2019 Notice as it relates to citizen advisory committees for CDBG-MIT funds under
Public Law 115-123
and
Public Law 116-20
for the State of North Carolina
only.
The State must continue to follow the first paragraph of section V.A.3.c. as it relates to the availability and accessibility of the Action Plan, substantial amendments, and performance reports, as well as other citizen participation requirements in section V.A.3.
III. Environmental Review
This notice does not direct, provide for assistance for, or otherwise govern real property acquisition, disposition, leasing, rehabilitation, alteration, demolition, or new construction and does not provide standards for construction, manufactured housing, or occupancy. Accordingly, under
24 CFR 50.19(c)(1)
, this notice is categorically excluded from environmental review under the National Environmental Policy Act of 1969 (
42 U.S.C. 4321
).

Department of Transportation
Federal Aviation Administration
14 CFR Part 39
[Docket No. FAA-2026-3474; Project Identifier MCAI-2025-01807-A; Amendment 39-23526; AD 2026-24-02]
RIN 2120-AA64
AGENCY:
Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), DOT.
ACTION:
Final rule.
SUMMARY:
The FAA is superseding Airworthiness Directive (AD) 2021-11-08, which applied to all Pilatus Aircraft Ltd. (Pilatus) Model PC-6, PC-6-H1, PC-6-H2, PC-6/350, PC-6/350-H1, PC-6/350-H2, PC-6/A, PC-6/A-H1, PC-6/A-H2, PC-6/B-H2, PC-6/B1-H2, PC-6/B2-H2, PC-6/B2-H4, PC-6/C-H2, and PC-6/C1-H2 airplanes. AD 2021-11-08 required revising the airworthiness limitations section (ALS) of the existing aircraft maintenance manual (AMM) or instructions for continued airworthiness (ICA) to incorporate new airworthiness limitations and adding an additional eddy current inspection of the fuselage wing fittings and wing-to-fuselage fittings if the last inspection was performed using an earlier version of the required material. Since the FAA issued AD 2021-11-08, the FAA has determined that new or more restrictive airworthiness limitations are necessary. This AD requires revising the ALS of the existing AMM or ICA for these airplanes. The FAA is issuing this AD to address the unsafe condition on these products.
DATES:
This AD is effective December 30, 2026.
The Director of the Federal Register approved the incorporation by reference of a certain publication listed in this AD as of December 30, 2026.
ADDRESSES:
AD Docket:
You may examine the AD docket at
regulations.gov
under Docket No. FAA-2026-3474; or in person at Docket Operations between 9 a.m. and 5 p.m., Monday through Friday, except Federal holidays. The AD docket contains this final rule, the mandatory continuing airworthiness information (MCAI), any comments received, and other information. The address for Docket Operations is U.S. Department of Transportation, Docket Operations, M-30, West Building Ground Floor, Room W12-140, 1200 New Jersey Avenue SE, Washington, DC 20590.
Material Incorporated by Reference:
For European Union Aviation Safety Agency (EASA) material identified in this AD, contact EASA, Konrad-Adenauer-Ufer 3, 50668 Cologne, Germany; phone: +49 221 8999 000; email:
ADs@easa.europa.eu
;
website:
easa.europa.eu.
FAA, Airworthiness Products Section, Operational Safety Branch, 1100 Main, Kansas City, MO 64105. For information on the availability of this material at the FAA, call (817) 222-5110. It is also available at
regulations.gov
under Docket No. FAA-2026-3474.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Doug Rudolph, Aviation Safety Engineer, FAA, 1600 Stewart Avenue, Suite 410, Westbury, NY 11590; phone: (816) 329-4059; email:
doug.rudolph@faa.gov
.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Background
The FAA issued a notice of proposed rulemaking (NPRM) to amend
14 CFR part 39
to supersede AD 2021-11-08, Amendment 39-21570 (
86 FR 30155
, June 7, 2021) (AD 2021-11-08). AD 2021-11-08 applied to all Pilatus Model PC-6, PC-6-H1, PC-6-H2, PC-6/350, PC-6/350-H1, PC-6/350-H2, PC-6/A, PC-6/A-H1, PC-6/A-H2, PC-6/B-H2, PC-6/B1-H2, PC-6/B2-H2, PC-6/B2-H4, PC-6/C-H2, and PC-6/C1-H2 airplanes. AD 2021-11-08 required revising the ALS of the existing AMM or ICA to incorporate new airworthiness limitations and adding an additional eddy current inspection of the fuselage wing fittings and wing-to-fuselage fittings if the last inspection was performed using an earlier version of the required material. The FAA issued AD 2021-11-08 to address reduced airplane controllability due to possible loss of structural integrity of certain parts.
The NPRM was published in the
Federal Register
on April 6, 2026 (
91 FR 17161
). The NPRM was prompted by EASA AD 2025-0281, dated December 11, 2025 (EASA AD 2025-0281) (also referred to as the MCAI), issued by EASA, which is the Technical Agent for the Member States of the European Union. The MCAI states that new or more restrictive tasks and limitations have been developed. These include adding life limits for the control column pitch trim relay. The MCAI also states that failure to accomplish these instructions could result in an unsafe condition.
In the NPRM, the FAA proposed to require revising the ALS of the existing AMM or ICA for the airplane and the existing approved maintenance or inspection program, as applicable, by incorporating new or more restrictive actions and associated thresholds and intervals, including any life limits, specified in EASA AD 2025-0281. The FAA is issuing this AD to address failure of certain parts, which could result in loss of control of the airplane.
You may examine the MCAI in the AD docket at
regulations.gov
under Docket No. FAA-2026-3474.
Discussion of Final Airworthiness Directive
Comments
The FAA received comments from two commenters. The commenters were Pilatus and an individual commenter. The commenters requested changes to the proposed compliance requirements, applicability, and cost estimates. The following presents the comments received on the NPRM and the FAA's response to each comment.
Request To Revise Cost Estimate
An individual commenter requested that the FAA revise the Costs of Compliance section of the NPRM to include the labor and parts costs associated with performing the eddy current inspections and replacing the control column pitch trim relay, rather than only including the cost of revising the maintenance or inspection program. The commenter stated that estimating a cost of $85 per airplane does not reflect the actual economic impact on operators. The commenter further stated that eddy current inspections require specialized personnel and equipment and that excluding those costs understates the regulatory burden on small-scale and independent operators.
The FAA disagrees with expanding the Costs of Compliance to account for the actions required by the ALS revision. The FAA does not include the costs associated with accomplishing future repetitive maintenance actions required by an ALS revision. The FAA estimates only the costs associated with
(
printed page 76139)
the actions directly required by the AD, the ALS revision in this AD. Although
14 CFR 91.403(c)
requires operators to perform the actions specified in the ALS after revising their maintenance or inspection program, those future actions are not requirements of this AD and are therefore not included in the Costs of Compliance. In contrast, AD 2021-11-08 included inspection and corrective action costs because those actions were directly required by that AD in addition to the ALS revision. The FAA did not change this AD as a result of this comment.
Request To Reduce Compliance Time
An individual commenter requested that the FAA revise paragraph (h)(3) of the proposed AD to require immediate physical tracking and inspecting the control column pitch trim relay within 10 flight hours if airplane records indicate that the relay is near or has exceeded its newly established life limit, rather than allowing a general 30-day administrative compliance period. The commenter stated that pitch trim relay failures can trigger an uncommanded trim runaway. The commenter further stated that, because Model PC-6 airplanes are heavily utilized in low-altitude utility, agricultural, and skydiving operations, an uncommanded pitch change offers the flight crew virtually zero altitude margin for recovery and threatens pilot and passenger survival.
The FAA disagrees with changing the proposed compliance time from 30 days to 10 flight hours. This AD requires revising the existing AMM or ICA and the existing approved maintenance or inspection program, as applicable. Once the ALS is revised, the AD has been fully complied with and the life limit or inspection change remains enforceable as a part of the ALS.
14 CFR 91.403(c)
specifies that no person may operate an aircraft for which airworthiness limitations have been issued unless those limitations have been complied with. Therefore, there is no need to further expand the requirements of the AD beyond that which was proposed because
14 CFR 91.403(c)
already imposes the appropriate required action after the airworthiness limitations are revised. The FAA has determined that the 30-day compliance period provides an acceptable level of safety. Operators are always permitted to accomplish the requirements of an AD at a time earlier than the specified compliance time. Operators wanting additional time to comply with the requirements of an AD may request adjustments to the compliance time under the provisions of paragraph (j) of this AD and
14 CFR 39.19
. The FAA will consider requests for an adjustment of the compliance time if data are submitted to substantiate that such an adjustment would provide an acceptable level of safety. The FAA did not change this AD as a result of this comment.
Request To Restrict Accomplishment of ALS Revision to Certified Mechanics
An individual commenter requested that the FAA revise paragraph (g)(2) of the proposed AD to require that the airworthiness limitations be performed and signed off only by an FAA-certified airframe and powerplant mechanic or an authorized repair station, rather than by a private pilot. The commenter stated that tracking life limits for electrical relays and scheduling eddy current inspections of wing-to-fuselage fittings require rigorous maintenance tracking. The commenter further stated that allowing administrative sign-offs by private operators increases the risk of accounting errors, which could result in affected components remaining in service beyond their established life limits or inspection intervals.
The FAA agrees with the commenter's request. The FAA acknowledges that incorporation of the airworthiness limitations into the maintenance records constitutes a maintenance record entry associated with an airworthiness limitation and a private pilot should not be allowed to perform and sign off that action. Accordingly, in this final rule, the FAA is not adopting paragraph (g)(2) of the proposed AD. The FAA has determined that not adopting paragraph (g)(2) is appropriate to ensure that incorporation and accomplishment of the airworthiness limitations are performed and documented in accordance with the applicable maintenance regulations by persons authorized to perform and approve such maintenance.
Request for Additional Requirements for High-Usage Airplanes
An individual commenter requested that the FAA revise paragraph (c) of the proposed AD to include a separate, accelerated inspection tier for Model PC-6 airplanes operated in high-cycle, unpaved short takeoff and landing (STOL) environments. The commenter stated that airplanes used in rugged backcountry or drop-zone operations experience increased structural stress and aerodynamic buffeting. The commenter further stated that this operational profile may accelerate wear, corrosion, and crack propagation in upper wing strut fittings when compared to standard cross-country operations.
The FAA disagrees with the commenter's request. The FAA has determined that the airworthiness limitations developed by Pilatus adequately address the risks associated with various operational profiles. The FAA did not change this AD as a result of this comment.
Request To Supersede AD 2009-18-03 R1 for the Upper Wing Strut Fittings
Pilatus stated that, in the “Actions Since AD 2021-11-08 Was Issued” section of the NPRM, EASA had superseded EASA AD 2007-0241R4, dated August 31, 2010 (equivalent action to FAA AD 2009-18-03 R1, Amendment 39-16570 (
76 FR 1990
; January 12, 2011) (AD 2009-18-03 R1)), and EASA AD 2020-0278, dated December 14, 2020, by issuing EASA AD 2025-0281. Pilatus stated that AD 2009-18-03 R1 requires before next flight inspections and initial and repetitive eddy current and visual inspections of the upper wing strut fittings. Pilatus further stated that the repetitive inspections were later incorporated into the AMM and ALS, with ALS revisions mandated by AD 2011-01-14, Amendment 39-16571 (
76 FR 5467
, February 1, 2011) (AD 2011-01-14).
Pilatus stated that AD 2009-18-03 R1 has not been superseded and therefore remains in effect with respect to the before next flight and initial inspection requirements. Pilatus further stated that, because the repetitive inspections are now contained in the AMM/ALS and performed in accordance with AD 2011-01-14, the before next flight inspection requirement is no longer necessary when continued compliance with the AMM/ALS is maintained. Pilatus requested that the FAA consider superseding or cancelling AD 2009-18-03 R1 given the later AMM/ALS revisions.
The FAA disagrees with the commenter. The current airworthiness limitations in this new AD cover inspections of the upper wing strut fittings and so do the previous airworthiness limitations covered by AD 2011-01-14. However, AD 2009-18-03 R1 cannot be superseded at this time because the current ALS does not address the initial inspection requirements that apply to airplanes that might have been inactive for extended periods and are subsequently returned to service. The initial inspection requirements for the upper wing strut fittings and spherical bearings of AD 2009-18-03 R1 remain applicable until the ALS is updated to address these requirements. The FAA
(
printed page 76140)
did not change this AD as a result of this comment.
Conclusion
These products have been approved by the civil aviation authority of another country and are approved for operation in the United States. Pursuant to the FAA's bilateral agreement with this State of Design Authority, that authority has notified the FAA of the unsafe condition described in the MCAI referenced above. The FAA reviewed the relevant data, considered any comments received, and determined that air safety requires adopting this AD as proposed. Accordingly, the FAA is issuing this AD to address the unsafe condition on these products. Except for minor editorial changes, this AD is adopted as proposed in the NPRM. None of the changes will increase the economic burden on any operator.
Material Incorporated by Reference Under
1 CFR Part 51
The FAA reviewed EASA AD 2025-0281, which specifies procedures for revising the aircraft maintenance program (AMP) by incorporating airworthiness limitations, tasks, and associated thresholds and intervals, including life limits and maintenance tasks. EASA AD 2025-0281 also specifies accomplishing applicable maintenance tasks and replacing components before exceeding the applicable life limits and performing corrective actions if any discrepancy is found during accomplishment of any task or replacement in paragraph (1) of EASA AD 2025-0281. This material is reasonably available because the interested parties have access to it through their normal course of business or by the means identified in the
ADDRESSES
section.
Differences Between This AD and the MCAI
Where EASA AD 2025-0281 specifies revising the approved aircraft maintenance program within 12 months after the effective date of EASA AD 2025-0281, this AD requires revising the ALS of the existing approved maintenance or inspection program, as applicable, within 30 days after the effective date of this AD.
Costs of Compliance
The FAA estimates that this AD affects 30 airplanes of U.S. registry.
The FAA estimates the following costs to comply with this AD:

Authority for This Rulemaking
Title 49 of the United States Code specifies the FAA's authority to issue rules on aviation safety. Subtitle I, section 106, describes the authority of the FAA Administrator. Subtitle VII: Aviation Programs, describes in more detail the scope of the Agency's authority.
The FAA is issuing this rulemaking under the authority described in Subtitle VII, Part A, Subpart III, Section 44701: General requirements. Under that section, Congress charges the FAA with promoting safe flight of civil aircraft in air commerce by prescribing regulations for practices, methods, and procedures the Administrator finds necessary for safety in air commerce. This regulation is within the scope of that authority because it addresses an unsafe condition that is likely to exist or develop on products identified in this rulemaking action.
Regulatory Findings
The FAA has determined that this AD will not have federalism implications under
Executive Order 13132
. This AD will not have a substantial direct effect on the States, on the relationship between the national government and the States, or on the distribution of power and responsibilities among the various levels of government.
For the reasons discussed above, I certify that this AD:
(1) Is not a “significant regulatory action” under
Executive Order 12866

AGENCY:
Drug Enforcement Administration, Department of Justice.
ACTION:
Final rule, technical amendment.
SUMMARY:
This final rule updates Drug Enforcement Administration regulations to change the name of Narcotic Treatment Programs to Opioid Treatment Programs. This action is a nomenclature change and makes no substantive changes to the definition of a narcotic drug in the Controlled Substances Act or the definition of a narcotic treatment program in the implementing regulations.
DATES:
This final rule is effective November 25, 2026.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Heather E. Achbach, Regulatory Drafting and Policy Support Section, Diversion Control Division, Drug Enforcement Administration; Telephone: (571) 776-3882.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Legal Authority
The Controlled Substances Act (CSA) grants the Attorney General authority to promulgate rules and regulations relating to the registration and control of the manufacture, distribution, and dispensing of controlled substances;
[
1
]
as well as the maintenance and submission of records and reports
[
2
]
that are necessary and appropriate for the efficient execution of his statutory functions.
[
3
]
The Attorney General is further authorized by the CSA to promulgate rules and regulations relating to the registration and control of importers and exporters of controlled substances.
[
4
]
The Attorney General has delegated these authorities to the Administrator of the Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA).
[
5
]
The CSA and its implementing regulations are designed to prevent, detect, and eliminate the diversion of controlled substances into the illicit market while ensuring an adequate supply is available for the legitimate medical, scientific, research, and industrial needs of the United States. Controlled substances have the potential for abuse and dependence and are controlled to protect the public health and safety. Through the enactment of the CSA, Congress has established a closed system of distribution by making it unlawful to handle any controlled substance except in a manner authorized by the CSA. To maintain this closed system of distribution, the CSA imposes registration requirements on handlers of controlled substances.
The CSA authorizes the Administrator of DEA (by delegation of authority from the Attorney General) to promulgate and enforce any rules, regulations, and procedures which he may deem necessary and appropriate for the efficient execution of his functions under the CSA.
[
6
]
DEA publishes the implementing regulations for these statutes in
21 CFR part 1300
to end.
Technical Amendment
The CSA requires practitioners who dispense schedule II narcotic drugs to individuals for maintenance treatment or detoxification treatment to obtain a separate registration with DEA.
[
7
]
DEA regulations currently refer to these programs as Narcotic Treatment Programs (NTPs), and DEA defines an NTP as “a program engaged in maintenance and/or detoxification treatment with narcotic drugs.”
[
8
]
These programs are certified through the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS), which regulates the services provided through the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration (SAMHSA). Unlike DEA, HHS and SAMHSA refer to these programs as “opioid treatment programs” or “OTPs,” defined as “a program engaged in OUD [Opioid Use Disorder] treatment of individuals with MOUD [Medication for Opioid Use Disorder] registered under
21 U.S.C. 823(h)(1)
.”
[
9
]
The HHS definition requires the program be registered with DEA to dispense maintenance or detoxification treatment medication as required by
21 U.S.C. 823(h)(1)
, which is within the CSA.
To operate a treatment program, registrants must comply with both DEA and HHS/SAMHSA requirements. This includes meeting SAMHSA accreditation requirements as an OTP, being licensed by the State in which the registrant operates, and obtaining a DEA registration number as an NTP. DEA believes that this nomenclature change will align the terminology used by DEA and HHS, as well as other Federal agencies and State counterparts, to simplify the certification and licensure process for entities engaging in OUD treatments. Neither the term OTP nor the term NTP is defined by the CSA; DEA is authorized to update its nomenclature to create the standard term of OTP within its regulations.
[
10
]
DEA regulations define an NTP as a program engaged in maintenance and/or detoxification treatment with narcotic drugs. This final rule makes no change to that definition or to the term “narcotic drug” as used throughout DEA regulations.
Regulatory Analysis
Administrative Procedure Act
An agency may find good cause to exempt a rule from certain provisions of the Administrative Procedure Act (APA), including those requiring the publication of a prior notice of proposed rulemaking and the opportunity for public comment, if such actions are determined to be unnecessary, impracticable, or contrary to the public interest.
[
11
]
The “unnecessary” prong of the APA good cause provision covers amendments that are “ `minor or merely technical' and of little public interest,”
[
12
]
or that involve “routine determination[s], insignificant in nature and impact, and inconsequential to the industry . . . and to the public.”
[
13
]
This rule contains only a technical amendment: it merely updates the nomenclature currently used by DEA for registrants engaged in OUD treatments to reduce confusion to registrants and align DEA's terminology with the terms “opioid treatment program” and “OTP,” as defined by HHS and SAMHSA. Therefore, DEA finds there is good cause within the meaning of the APA to issue this amendment as a final rule without prior notice and an opportunity for public comment.
Similarly, the APA provides that a delayed effective date is unnecessary when the agency finds good cause for dispensing with the delay. The APA's delayed-effective-date provision is
(
printed page 76152)
intended “to give affected parties time to adjust their behavior before the final rule takes effect.”
[
14
]
Here, regulated parties will not need any time to adjust their behavior to the changes made in this final rule because the rule does no more than update DEA terminology to reduce confusion for registrants by aligning DEA's language with HHS and SAMHSA language. As such, this final rule shall become effective on the date of publication of this action in the
Federal Register
.
In addition, the APA excepts from the requirements of notice and comment and a delayed effective date those rules that are non-substantive.
[
15
]
Substantive rules make “substantive changes in prior regulations” or “create new law, rights, or duties.”
[
16
]
Here, as already explained, this final rule makes no substantive changes in DEA's regulations because this rule simply updates DEA regulations to reduce confusion for registrants and align DEA's terminology with the terms “opioid treatment program” and “OTP,” as defined by HHS and SAMHSA.
Executive Orders 12866, 13563, and 14192
DEA has determined that this rulemaking is not a “significant regulatory action” under section 3(f) of Executive Order (E.O.) 12866, Regulatory Planning and Review. Accordingly, this final rule has not been submitted to the Office of Management and Budget (“OMB”) for review. This final rule has been drafted and reviewed in accordance with
E.O. 12866
, “Regulatory Planning and Review,” section 1(b), Principles of Regulation;
E.O. 13563
“Improving Regulation and Regulatory Review,” section 1(b), General Principles of Regulation; and
E.O. 14192
, “Unleashing Prosperity Through Deregulation.” This final rule is not subject to
E.O. 14192
because it is not a significant regulatory action under section 3(f) of
E.O. 12866
.
As stated above, this final rule is a nomenclature change to update language in DEA regulations to match the language currently used by other agencies. This final rule will not change any definitions, require any new applications, or make any substantive changes to the regulations. The purpose of this final rule is to reduce confusion regarding the term NTP, and it will have no economic impact.
Executive Order 12988
, Civil Justice Reform
This final rule meets the applicable standards set forth in sections 3(a) and 3(b)(2) of
E.O. 12988
, to eliminate ambiguity, minimize litigation, establish clear legal standards, and reduce burden.
Executive Order 13132
, Federalism
This final rule does not have federalism implications warranting the application of
E.O. 13132
. The final rule does not have substantial direct effects on the States, on the relationship between the Federal government and the States, or on the distribution of power and responsibilities among the various levels of government.
Executive Order 13175
, Consultation and Coordination With Indian Tribal Governments
This final rule does not have tribal implications warranting the application of
Executive Order 13175
. This final rule does not have substantial direct effects on one or more Indian tribes, on the relationship between the Federal Government and Indian tribes, or on the distribution of power and responsibilities between the Federal Government and Indian tribes.
Executive Order 14267
, Reducing Anti-Competitive Regulatory Barriers
This final rule does not reduce competition, entrepreneurship, and innovation.
Executive Order 14294
, Fighting Overcriminalization of Federal Regulations
Executive Order 14294
specifies that all notices of proposed rulemaking and final rules published in the
Federal Register
, the violation of which may constitute criminal regulatory offenses, should include a statement identifying that the rule or proposed rule is a criminal regulatory offense, the authorizing statute, and the mens rea requirement for each element of the offense. Because this final rule does not involve a criminal regulatory offense,
E.O. 14294
does not apply.
Regulatory Flexibility Act
The Regulatory Flexibility Act (RFA) (
5 U.S.C. 601-612
) applies to rules that are subject to notice and comment under section 553(b) of the APA. As explained above, DEA determined that there is good cause to exempt this final rule from notice and comment. This final rule is a nomenclature change that makes no change to any process. Consequently, the RFA does not apply to this final rule.
Unfunded Mandates Reform Act of 1995
In accordance with the Unfunded Mandates Reform Act (UMRA) of 1995,
2 U.S.C. 1532
, DEA has determined that this final rule would not result in any Federal mandate that may result “in the expenditure by State, local, and tribal governments, in the aggregate, or by the private sector, of $100,000,000 or more (adjusted annually for inflation) in any 1 year.” Therefore, neither a Small Government Agency Plan nor any other action is required under UMRA.
Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995
This final rule does not impose a new collection of information requirement or modify an existing collection of information requirement under the Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995,
44 U.S.C. 3501-3521
. This final rule does not impose new or modify existing recordkeeping or reporting requirements on State or local governments, individuals, businesses, or organizations. An agency may not conduct or sponsor, and a person is not required to respond to, a collection of information unless it displays a valid OMB control number.
Congressional Review Act
This final rule is not a major rule as defined by Subtitle E of the Small Business Regulatory Enforcement Act of 1996 (known as the Congressional Review Act or CRA). Because this is a rule of agency organization, procedure, or practice that does not substantially affect the rights or obligations of non-agency parties, the reporting requirement under
5 U.S.C. 801
does not apply.

ACTION:

SUMMARY:
This proposed rule would revise the Medicare Advantage (Part C), Medicare Prescription Drug Benefit (Part D), and Programs of All-Inclusive Care for the Elderly regulations to implement changes related to marketing and communications, drug coverage, enrollment processes, special needs plans, and other programmatic areas. Additionally, it would establish and implement a mandatory Medicare Advantage (MA) CMS Innovation Center model.
DATES:
To be assured consideration, comments must be received at one of the addresses provided below, no later than 5 p.m. Eastern Time on January 19, 2027.
ADDRESSES:
In commenting, please refer to file code CMS-4214-P2. Because of staff and resource limitations, we cannot accept comments by facsimile (FAX) transmission. Comments, including mass comment submissions, must be submitted in one of the following three ways (please choose only one of the ways listed):
1.
Electronically.

https://www.regulations.gov/​docket/​CMS-2026-3533
.
Follow the “Submit a comment” instructions.

By regular mail.
You may mail written comments to the following address ONLY: Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services, Department of Health and Human Services, Attention: CMS-4214-P2, P.O. Box 8013, Baltimore, MD 21244-8013. Please allow sufficient time for mailed comments to be received before the close of the comment period.
3.
By express or overnight mail.
You may send written comments to the following address ONLY: Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services, Department of Health and Human Services, Attention: CMS-4214-P2, Mail Stop C4-26-05, 7500 Security Boulevard, Baltimore, MD 21244-1850. Alissa Gross, (410) 786-1120—Parts C and D Payment Issues. Sara Klotz, (410) 786-1984—D-SNP Issues. Elisabeth Daniel, (667) 290-8793—Medicare Drug Price Negotiation Program Issues.

We post all comments received before the close of the comment period on the following website as soon as possible after they have been received:

Plain Language Summary:
In accordance with
5 U.S.C. 553(b)(4)
, a plain language summary of this proposed rule may be found at
https://www.regulations.gov/​
.
I. Executive Summary
A. Purpose
The primary purpose of this proposed rule is to amend the regulations for the Medicare Advantage (Part C) program, Medicare Prescription Drug Benefit (Part D) program, and Programs of All-Inclusive Care for the Elderly. This proposed rule includes a number of changes that would improve these programs for contract year 2028 as well as codify existing subregulatory guidance.
We note that, as with previous rules, the new marketing and communications policies in this rule are proposed to be applicable for all contract year 2028 marketing and communications, beginning October 1, 2027.
B. Summary of the Key Provisions
1. Establishing a “Healthy Food” Standard for MA Supplemental Benefits
CMS proposes to establish a “healthy food” standard applicable to all MA supplemental benefits that include food items. Specifically, the proposal would apply a CMS-defined healthy food standard, aligned with the HHS and USDA's 2025-2030 Dietary Guidelines for Americans, across both primarily health-related supplemental benefits and Special Supplemental Benefits for the Chronically Ill (SSBCI). Under this proposal, food items offered as supplemental benefits would be required to either meet the CMS-defined healthy food standard or be specifically recommended by a healthcare provider to meet an enrollee's medical needs.
2. Using a CMS Approval Mechanism for Use of the Disaster/Emergency Special Enrollment Period (SEP) and Other Technical Changes
We propose that use of the Disaster/Emergency SEP (
42 CFR 422.62(b)(18)
and
423.38(c)(23)
) requires prior CMS approval through the use of a CMS-operated mechanism. Initially, this SEP will be restricted to use through 1-800-MEDICARE only, similar to other SEPs, though CMS may consider expanding this to other mechanisms, including the Online Enrollment Center, in the future. This requirement would allow for CMS oversight of the SEP and the election mechanism to ensure appropriate use.
3. Seamless Continuation of Coverage for Newly Medicare-Eligible Individuals
CMS is considering creating an optional process for transitioning enrollees of commercial and Marketplace health plans into an MA plan under the same MA organization during an enrollee's initial coverage election period if they fail to elect other coverage. Congress established seamless conversion in section 1851(c)(3) of the Social Security Act (the Act) in 1997. CMS addressed seamless conversion in rulemaking (Medicare Program; Establishment of the Medicare Advantage Program,
70 FR 4588
) in 2005, and guidance was established that same year. CMS granted its first approval for an MA organization to implement seamless enrollment for June 2005. The second approval was granted for March 2010 and the third for January
(
printed page 76315)
2012. As of August 2016, CMS had approved 24 MA organizations to use the seamless enrollment mechanism, although not all approved organizations had begun to enroll individuals using this mechanism. We are considering to model a process and the participation requirements on the existing default enrollment mechanism for Medicaid beneficiaries. We are soliciting comments on a potential return to an opt-out process for seamless enrollment and the expected administrative and implementation issues and opportunities for plans intending to utilize seamless enrollment.
4. Cost Sharing Standards for Ground Ambulance and Emergency Services
CMS proposes changes to the MA cost sharing standards for ground ambulance and emergency services to better align beneficiary cost sharing across these services. Specifically, CMS proposes to apply a range of cost sharing limits for ground ambulance services based on maximum out-of-pocket (MOOP) type and to establish emergency services cost sharing limits that are actuarially equivalent to 15 to 20 percent of Original Medicare costs using the most recent Medicare fee-for-service projections.
CMS also proposes to update the applicable cost sharing limits for ground ambulance and emergency services annually through the sub-regulatory guidance process outlined in § 422.100(f)(7)(iii).
5. Enrollee Notification Requirements for Provider Terminations, Continuity of Care, and SEP Notice Consolidation
CMS proposes requirements for MA organizations to notify affected enrollees of provider terminations upon the effective date of the termination, revise the criteria for identifying affected enrollees using a 12-month lookback period, and establish a continuity of care requirement under which affected enrollees would continue to receive coverage at in-network cost sharing following a provider termination. The proposal would also define what qualifies as a “significant” change in an MA plan provider network and codify the notification requirements, evaluation criteria, and applicable timeframes used to determine when a provider termination triggers a SEP. The proposal would also align provider termination and SEP notification requirements so that affected enrollees receive a single notification regarding provider terminations and SEP eligibility, as applicable.
6. Enrollment Capacity Limits
CMS proposes to codify the process for MA organizations to request enrollment capacity limits during the annual bid submission process, and to rescind § 422.60(b)(3), which permits MA organizations to request enrollment capacity limits outside of the bid submission process, given concerns about the potential for contract gaming and alternative tools available to address any relevant risks to health and safety. CMS also proposes to establish a SEP for individuals who enroll in an MA plan that has reached its approved enrollment capacity limit, allowing those individuals to elect a different MA plan.
7. Use of Existing Interoperability API for Prior Authorization Transactions
CMS proposes to require MA organizations to include a provision in their contracts with in-network providers requiring providers to use the MA organization's HL7® Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources (FHIR®)-based Prior Authorization Application Programming Interface (API) to transmit information and documentation pertaining to prior authorization requests, and to require MA organizations to annually test and confirm the ability of their in-network providers to send and receive information through the FHIR-based Prior Authorization API.
8. Strengthening Maximum Fair Price Effectuation Policies for Medicare Advantage
a. Medicare Transaction Facilitator Requirements for Network Providers
CMS proposes to amend §  422.504 by adding paragraph (p) to require that any contract between the MA organization and a provider, or between a first tier, downstream, or related entity and a provider on the MA organization's behalf, for participation in one or more of the MA organizations' networks must include a provision requiring that if the provider furnishes or administers selected drugs payable under Part B during the period when such drugs are subject to a maximum fair price (MFP) (as defined in proposed § 422.2), the provider must be enrolled in the Medicare Drug Price Negotiation Program's (Negotiation Program) Medicare Transaction Facilitator (MTF) Data Module (DM) (or any successor to the MTF DM). Such provider must also maintain and certify up-to-date, complete, and accurate enrollment information with the MTF DM, in accordance with applicable terms and conditions of participation with the MTF DM, in a form and manner determined by CMS. The MTF DM helps support Primary Manufacturers of selected drugs effectuate the MFP by assisting necessary operations related to administration of the Negotiation Program and the Part C program, including creating and making available remittances or electronic remittance advices (ERAs), maintaining provider access to the complaints and disputes submission portal, and facilitating continued access to selected drugs payable under Part B. We believe this requirement, if finalized, would facilitate continued access to selected drugs that are payable under Part B for MA enrollees and providers by facilitating manufacturer effectuation of negotiated MFPs under the Negotiation Program.
b. Encounter Data Collection Requirements for Selected Drugs Payable Under Part B
To facilitate MFP effectuation by Primary Manufacturers and to help ensure prompt MFP refund payments by Primary Manufacturers to providers with respect to selected drugs payable under Part B administered or furnished to individuals enrolled in MA plans, encounter records for selected drugs payable under Part B and subject to an MFP warrant a submission deadline that is different from the risk adjustment encounter data submission deadline requirements of § 422.310(g). For the purposes of risk adjustment, MA organizations typically have 13 months following the service year of which payment is based (
i.e.,
the year before the payment year) to submit encounters to CMS for inclusion in final reconciliation. Therefore, if the final risk adjustment data submission deadline were used, providers could wait up to approximately 14 to 26 months to receive MFP refund payments, potentially causing financial hardship. To mitigate potential financial hardship on providers, which could impact Part C enrollee access to selected drugs payable under Part B and subject to an MFP, CMS proposes to amend §  422.504 by adding paragraph (q)(1)(i) to require encounter data submission for selected drugs payable under Part B and for which an MFP (as defined in proposed § 422.2) is in effect, within 30 days of the claim-from date to reduce the maximum amount of time a provider could wait to receive access to the MFP with respect to the administration or furnishment of selected drugs payable under Part B to MA enrollees. Additionally, to facilitate Primary Manufacturer effectuation of the MFP, with respect to the administration or
(
printed page 76316)
furnishment of selected drugs payable under Part B to MA enrollees, CMS proposes to amend §  422.504 by adding paragraph (q)(1)(ii) to require MA organizations to collect and submit the 11-digit National Drug Codes (NDC-11 codes) on each MA encounter data record for a selected drug payable under Part B for which an MFP is in effect on the claim-from date. Finally, CMS proposes to amend §  422.504 by adding paragraph (q)(2) to require the Chief Executive Officer (CEO), Chief Financial Officer (CFO), or an individual delegated with the authority to sign on behalf of one of these officers, and who reports directly to such officer, to certify (based on best knowledge, information, and belief) that the data the MA organization submits under § 422.504(q)(1) are accurate, complete, and truthful.
c. Medicare Advantage Out-of-Network Cost Sharing for Selected Drugs Payable Under Part B
CMS proposes to amend §  422.100(f)(6)(i) to require that any out-of-network cost sharing for selected drugs payable under Part B and subject to an MFP (as defined in proposed § 422.2) is calculated based on a price that does not exceed the MFP. CMS believes that this requirement is necessary to ensure that MA enrollees are not subject to benefit design that discriminates on the basis of health status-related factors or is likely to substantially discourage enrollment by certain MA-eligible individuals, as prohibited by section 1852(b)(1) of the Act.
9. Medicare Advantage/Part C and Part D Prescription Drug Plan Quality Rating System
We have continued to identify enhancements to the Star Ratings program over time to increase the health and well-being of enrollees. In this proposed rule, we are proposing changes to simplify and refocus the areas included in the Star Ratings, including changes to the measure set, building on the changes finalized in the “Medicare Program; Contract Year 2027 and Certain Contract Year 2026 Policy and Technical Changes to the Medicare Advantage Program, Medicare Prescription Drug Benefit Program, and Medicare Cost Plan Program” final rule, which appeared in the
Federal Register
on April 6, 2026 (
91 FR 17384
) (“Contract Year 2027 final rule”). The proposed measure set of 15 measures reflects our ongoing effort to sharpen the Star Ratings program's focus on clinical outcomes while continuing to encourage high performance on patient experience and would also include a small number of process measures in areas of high clinical importance where contracts' current performance is low. The measure removals would apply (that is, data will be collected and performance measured) for the 2028 measurement period and the 2030 Star Ratings.
In the Contract Year 2027 final rule, we also solicited comments on ways to simplify and modify the Star Ratings methodology to further improve quality of care. Consistent with that intent, we propose removing the reward factor and modifying the improvement measure hold harmless to apply only to contracts receiving 4.5 or higher stars for their highest rating. These changes to the measure set and methodology would streamline and simplify the Star Ratings while also raising the bar to achieve high Star Ratings and associated Quality Bonus Payments (QBPs) by incentivizing plans to improve performance and ensure the highest quality of care for their enrollees.
We are also proposing a change to the methodologies for setting cut points to account for the potential impact of the ADVaNCE MA model proposed in section VIII of this proposed rule, a substantive update to the Controlling Blood Pressure measure, a clarification related to displaying Star Ratings domains on the Medicare Plan Finder (MPF) website, language related to disclosing preliminary data shared with plans during the plan preview periods, and a clarification related to the extreme and uncontrollable circumstances policy.

CMS proposes changes to the MA application requirements for new MA contracts and service area expansions. Specifically, CMS proposes to revise the timing of network adequacy reviews by shifting those reviews from the MA application process to the first year of operation for newly approved contracts and service areas.
In addition, CMS proposes modifications to network adequacy requirements that are intended to promote competition, provide operational flexibility for MA organizations, and support beneficiary access to behavioral health services and telehealth.
Finally, CMS requests comment on potential changes to policies that can improve access to healthcare via adjustments to provider network adequacy standards, as well as other policy approaches to lower costs and improve competition in the MA program.
11. Updating Agent and Broker Compensation and Oversight
CMS is proposing to revise the MA and Part D agent and broker compensation framework to better align with statutory requirements, reflect current market practices, and respond to a recent court decision vacating portions of the April 2024 compensation regulations. The proposal would provide a new market-based approach definition for compensation, including distinctions between base compensation and supplemental compensation. The proposal would expand the safeguards designed to ensure that the use of compensation creates incentives for agents and brokers to enroll beneficiaries in the MA plan that is intended to best meet their health care needs. CMS proposes a methodology for identifying compensation outliers, which would enable CMS to disapprove outliers and require MA organizations and Part D sponsors to resubmit compensation amounts. The proposal would also require MA organizations and Part D sponsors to report actual base compensation amounts and details regarding supplemental compensation. CMS proposes to require MA organizations and Part D sponsors provide supporting documentation upon request and comply with new oversight and reporting requirements intended to strengthen transparency and program integrity.

Proposed changes include modifications to training and testing requirements, allowing greater flexibility for acceptance of third-party training programs, enhancing reporting of agent and broker terminations, prohibiting contracts with agents or brokers terminated from participation in the Federally Facilitated Exchange, and clarifying oversight responsibilities for MA organizations and Part D sponsors. In addition, CMS proposes to remove certain requirements that it believes are redundant or no longer necessary, while retaining key beneficiary protections through existing enrollment, marketing, and compliance safeguards. Collectively, these changes are intended to modernize compensation oversight, improve transparency, and ensure that compensation arrangements support beneficiary enrollment in plans that best meet their health care needs.
