II. Enhancements to the Medicare Advantage and Medicare Prescription Drug Benefit Programs
A. Establishing a “Healthy Food” Standard for MA Supplemental Benefits
1. Background
MA plans have the ability to offer items and services beyond what Original Medicare covers, known as supplemental benefits. Section 50322 of the Bipartisan Budget Act of 2018 (
Pub. L. 115-123
) expanded the scope of what MA plans may offer as supplemental benefits by amending section 1852(a)(3) of the Act to create Special Supplemental Benefits for the Chronically Ill (SSBCI).
[
1
]
SSBCI are supplemental benefits that MA plans may offer to qualifying eligible chronically ill enrollees and, unlike other supplemental benefits, are not required to be primarily health related. Rather, SSBCI may include items and services that have a reasonable expectation of improving or maintaining an enrollee's health or overall function, including food-related SSBCI.
MA plans may offer food-related supplemental benefits in different ways. For example, MA plans may offer meals on a limited basis following an acute
(
printed page 76319)
health event as a primarily health-related supplemental benefit available to all their enrollees. MA plans may also cover protein bars and nutritional drinks or shakes as primarily health-related over-the-counter (OTC) items available to all their enrollees. Additionally, plans may offer a Food and Produce benefit or meals provided on an unlimited or ongoing basis as SSBCI to their chronically ill enrollees.
[
2
]
MA plans have increasingly incorporated food-related benefits into their supplemental benefit design. For example, the percentage of MA plans offering Food and Produce as an SSBCI has grown from about 16 percent in 2024, to roughly a third (35 percent) in 2026. Moreover, around 60 percent of MA plans now offer a primarily health related meal benefit.
[
3
]
Additionally, based on 2025 CMS internal data received as part of Part C Reporting Requirements, beneficiaries utilized a Food and Produce SSBCI about 40 million times. These utilizations were recorded for 45 percent of eligible enrollees, making it one of the most popular benefits among eligible enrollees. Given that so many MA enrollees are using these benefits, they have real potential to meaningfully address nutrition-related chronic conditions, reduce avoidable hospitalizations, and support the overall well-being of Medicare beneficiaries.
As the availability and utilization of these benefits has expanded, CMS has also received recurring questions seeking examples of foods that qualify as healthy under these regulations versus those that do not—an issue that became especially prominent after CMS codified at § 422.102(f)(1)(iii)(I) in the Medicare and Medicaid Programs; Contract Year 2026 Policy and Technical Changes to the Medicare Advantage Program, Medicare Prescription Drug Benefit Program, Medicare Cost Plan Program, and Programs of All-Inclusive Care for the Elderly, hereafter referred to as the April 2025 final rule (
90 FR 15868
), that non-healthy food items are not permissible as SSBCI. Currently, there is no affirmative definition or standard in regulation for what constitutes healthy or non-healthy foods for purposes of SSBCI, although CMS specified in the April 2025 final rule that non-healthy foods are those that do “not assist in meeting the nutritional needs of a chronically ill enrollee” (
90 FR 15867
). As a result, MA plans currently exercise broad discretion in determining what foods qualify as healthy or non-healthy under the current regulations, which could result in inconsistent application of the prohibition on offering non-healthy food items as SSBCI. Additionally, a clear affirmative standard for what constitutes healthy food would promote CMS' ability to conduct meaningful compliance and enforcement work. For CMS to determine whether MA plans offer food benefits that are primarily health related or are appropriate as SSBCI, CMS is proposing to specifically require food-related supplemental benefits to be limited to “healthy food,” and to define what it means by “healthy food” for this purpose.
As food-related supplemental benefit spending continues to grow, so does the importance of ensuring that such spending is directed toward foods that genuinely support improved health outcomes. This aligns with the Make America Healthy Again (MAHA) initiative,
[
4
]
which emphasizes improving population health by addressing upstream drivers of chronic disease—particularly diet and nutrition, alongside broader efforts across HHS to translate the new 2025-2030 Dietary Guidelines for Americans (DGA)
[
5
]
into more practical standards for program design and administration. MAHA reflects a broader shift in federal health policy toward ensuring that public programs not only provide access to services, but also promote healthier choices, particularly in areas like food where poor nutrition can contribute to worsening health outcomes.
[
6
]
This edition of the DGA is organized around a simple principle: minimally processed, naturally nutrient-dense foods are the reference point for dietary guidance, and strong causal evidence is needed before recommending foods or ingredients that are highly processed. In practical terms, this means that minimally processed vegetables, fruits, meats, eggs, nuts, seeds, dairy, whole grains, beans, and seafood are the foundation for healthful diets. Clearly defining “healthy food” for purposes of MA supplemental benefit offerings supports MAHA's core objective of aligning federal health spending with interventions that improve long-term health and reduce diet-related disease.
Establishing a clear definition of “healthy food” to be required for supplemental benefit offerings directly supports these objectives by creating a consistent baseline for nutrition quality across the MA program—ensuring that all food-related supplemental benefits are contributing to better health outcomes rather than simply expanding access to food.
Based on a review of annual bid packages, CMS has noted that plan-issued debit cards are frequently used to administer a wide range of supplemental benefits, most notably Food and Produce offered as SSBCI. In the Contract Year 2027 final rule (
91 FR 17384
), CMS codified several safeguards for MA plans using debit cards to administer covered benefits. The purpose of that rule was, in part, to ensure enrollees were receiving the covered benefits to which they are entitled—as CMS had received numerous reports that MA plan debit card administration varied widely and that MA plans had varying success in ensuring enrollees received their approved, covered benefits through these cards. Adding a “healthy food” definition for purposes of MA supplemental benefits would build on these safeguards to help ensure enrollees receive only covered benefits.
2. HHS and USDA's 2025-2030 Dietary Guidelines for Americans
The new 2025-2030 DGA were released in January 2026. The 2025-2030 DGA rests on a documented evidence-review process: subject-matter experts were selected through a federal contracting process; standardized protocols—covering inclusion criteria, risk of bias, synthesis, and evidence grading—was set in advance by a methodology expert; the review relied on rapid systematic reviews, umbrella reviews, and literature syntheses; and the review was subject to external peer review coordinated by the NIH Office of Nutrition Research, with two independent reviewers assigned to each topic. Reviewer financial interests were disclosed as part of this process.
CMS recognizes that the information and guidelines contained in the DGA are based on the preponderance of the scientific and medical knowledge which is current at the time the DGA are prepared and is subject to ongoing refinement as new research emerges.
[
7
]
CMS believes this makes the DGA the most appropriate and reliable scientific anchor currently available for this definition, notwithstanding the inherent limitations of any evolving scientific field. Because the “healthy food” standard is anchored to the DGA rather
(
printed page 76320)
than to a fixed guideline or definition, the standard can evolve as the science changes and future DGA cycles are completed, rather than being bound to a static standard that cannot adapt over time. CMS seeks public comment on any additional evidence, data, or research that should be considered in finalizing this proposal.
The DGA emphasizes dietary patterns centered on whole, nutrient-dense foods, including proteins, fruits and vegetables, healthy fats, dairy, and whole grains. The DGA also encourages foods that are minimally processed and recommends limiting highly processed foods, refined carbohydrates, added sugars, excess sodium, sugar sweetened beverages, and other ingredients associated with poorer health outcomes such as artificial flavors, petroleum-based dyes, artificial preservatives, and low-calorie non-nutritive sweeteners. The DGA further emphasizes variety across both animal- and plant-based food sources and the importance of dietary patterns that support overall health, healthy aging, and chronic disease prevention. The DGA also includes recommendations specific to older adults, recognizing that while some older adults require fewer calories, they generally require equal or greater amounts of protein, vitamin B12, vitamin D, and calcium. Consistent with this recognition, the DGA recommends nutrient-dense foods and, where dietary intake or absorption is inadequate, medically supervised fortified foods or supplements under medical supervision. The DGA further addresses cardiovascular disease, obesity, and type 2 diabetes—conditions highly relevant to the Medicare population. For example, the DGA recommends for individuals at risk of calcium oxalate kidney stones, dietary oxalate should be monitored by avoiding foods such as spinach, chard, and rhubarb; limiting intake of potatoes, chocolate, nuts, beets, and bran; and ensuring adequate calcium consumption with meals.
Additionally, the DGA recommends vegetables, fruits, fiber-rich whole grains, and a variety of protein foods, while limiting saturated fat, added sugars, and sodium. The DGA states that adherence to the guidelines can help prevent or slow the progression of chronic disease, including cardiovascular disease, obesity, and type 2 diabetes, but advise individuals with chronic conditions to discuss their dietary needs with a health care professional. CMS seeks comment on whether other sources of information should be considered in addressing chronic conditions relevant to the Medicare population, such as the American Heart Association's recommendations. CMS notes that other federal programs also refer to the DGA. For instance, Section 339(2)(A)(i) of the Older Americans Act, codified at
42 U.S.C. 3030g-21(2)(A)(i)
, requires that meals funded under its nutrition programs “comply with the most recent Dietary Guidelines for Americans.” Individualized needs arising from conditions such as kidney disease, dysphagia, or diabetes are addressed separately under proposed § 422.102(h)(2) discussed later in this proposed rule. These recommendations are consistent with the goals of many food-related supplemental benefits offered by MA plans, including SSBCI which are intended to maintain or improve chronically ill enrollees' health and overall functioning through improved nutrition.
Consistent with these efforts, and based on our authority under section 1856(b)(1) of the Act to establish standards for MA plans consistent with, and to carry out, Part C, along with our authority in section 1857(e)(1) of the Act to adopt additional terms and conditions for MA contracts that are not inconsistent with the Part C statute and that are necessary and appropriate for the MA program, CMS proposes to establish a definition for what it considers “healthy foods” for purposes of MA supplemental benefits that aligns with the DGA and require that any food- or beverage-related supplemental benefit meet that definition. This standard is intended to ensure that such benefits are appropriately offered as supplemental benefits under Part C and are consistent with applicable statutory requirements.
3. “Healthy Food” Definition for MA Supplemental Benefits
The 2025-2030 DGA provide the nutritional foundation for this proposal. In developing this proposed definition, CMS worked closely with experts throughout HHS involved in the development of the DGA. The goal was to develop an MA-specific definition that is both consistent with the DGA nutritional principles and practical to administer within the MA supplemental benefit structure. CMS recognizes that the DGA provides broad nutrition guidance for the general population and is not written as regulatory standards for MA supplemental benefits. CMS therefore developed this proposed definition to translate the core nutritional principles reflected in the DGA into a clear, administrable standard for MA plans offering food-related supplemental benefits to Medicare beneficiaries.
In developing a “healthy food” standard for MA supplemental benefits, CMS considered adopting the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) criteria for use of the term “healthy” as a nutrient content claim. CMS determined that approach is not well suited to the MA program because it was developed as a voluntary labeling definition for a claim that appears primarily on packaged foods and relies on product-specific nutrient analyses, standardized serving sizes, and other requirements that do not readily apply to many foods provided through MA supplemental benefits, including prepared meals, medically tailored meals, and groceries or other items that may be administered through plan debit cards. Adopting the FDA criteria would also create additional operational and administrative burdens for plans and vendors and would tie MA policy to a set of criteria developed for a different statutory purpose. CMS believes that a DGA-based definition tailored to the MA program provides a more practical, administrable, and enforceable standard for food-related supplemental benefits while remaining aligned with current Federal nutrition policy.
CMS proposes to remove the existing provision at § 422.102(f)(1)(iii)(I) specifically prohibiting non-healthy food items as SSBCI and instead add a broad affirmative, standardized definition of “healthy food” applicable to all supplemental benefits that include food or beverage items. We propose to amend § 422.102 by adding paragraph (h) to provide that food and beverage items offered as supplemental benefits must meet the definition of “healthy food” in paragraph (h)(1). Under this proposal and consistent with the DGA, CMS would define “healthy food” at § 422.102(h)(1) as whole, nutrient-dense foods. For purposes of this definition, CMS intends the phrase “whole, nutrient-dense foods” to refer to minimally processed foods that are naturally rich sources of protein, fiber, essential fatty acids, vitamins, and minerals, and that contain no added sugars, refined starches, or chemical additives, and that provide meaningful nutritional value and support overall health, healthy aging, and physical functioning. Additionally, CMS seeks comment on this understanding of whole, nutrient-dense foods, and on whether CMS should establish a formal, codified definition of this term in future rulemaking.
To support clarity and consistent application by MA plans, CMS proposes to codify at § 422.102(h)(1)(i) through (viii) non-exhaustive examples of foods that align with this definition, including
(
printed page 76321)
proteins from a variety of animal and plant-based sources, such as eggs, poultry, seafood, red meat, and soy; fresh fruits and vegetables, as well as frozen, dried, or canned fruits and vegetables with no or limited added sugars; legumes including beans, lentils, chickpeas; nuts, seeds, and natural nut butters with limited added sugars; fats and oils such as olive oil, avocado oil, butter, and beef tallow; dairy products with limited added sugars; and fiber-rich whole grains such as sprouted bread, whole grain rye or pumpernickel bread, whole wheat pasta, buckwheat flour, and wheat or oat bran with limited added sugars. CMS selected these categories because they reflect a variety of foods commonly associated with healthy dietary patterns and align with nutritional principles emphasized throughout the DGA. CMS also seeks comment on whether the food-based examples at proposed § 422.102(h)(1)(i)-(viii) provide sufficient clarity and welcomes any suggestions for additional or alternative examples.
CMS notes that the proposed definition and examples at § 422.102(h)(1)(ii), (iv), (vi), and (vii) reference foods with “limited added sugars.” Consistent with the DGA, CMS intends these references to reflect the general principle that foods with lower amounts of added sugars more closely align with healthy dietary patterns and chronic disease mitigation. The DGA treats saturated fat and sodium as daily, whole-of-diet limits rather than item-level bans—specifically, saturated fat should not exceed 10 percent of total daily calories, and sodium should be less than 2,300 mg per day for individuals ages 14 and older. An item-level saturated fat ban would exclude whole foods the DGA otherwise promotes, such as full-fat dairy, eggs, and red meat; the DGA's Scientific Foundation (SF) finds that current evidence “does not provide causal support for reducing saturated fat below 10 percent of energy”. On the other hand, CMS's proposed definition already addresses sodium through food-based exclusions, consistent with the DGA's instruction that “highly processed foods that are high in sodium should be avoided”. As an alternative to this food-based approach, CMS is considering per-meal nutrient targets for food-related supplemental benefits—for example, sodium ≤600 mg and saturated fat ≤7 g per meal, consistent with the DGA's daily limits. CMS seeks comment on whether item-level numeric limits on sodium or saturated fat, as well as other nutrients, are warranted and, if so, what thresholds would be most appropriate given that food related supplemental benefits may include meals provided by a vendor or individual food items which may be purchased at a grocery store. CMS additionally seeks comment on the inclusion of examples of specific fats (such as butter and beef tallow) in its healthy food standard.
While this definition focuses on specific food items and not necessarily how those food items are prepared, CMS notes that foods which are baked, broiled, roasted, stir-fried, or grilled are preferable to those deep-fried, for example. CMS acknowledges that food preparation contributes to the overall healthfulness of a particular food item or meal. Since food related supplemental benefits may include either individual food items or full meals, CMS solicits comment on whether food preparation, and specific food additives, should be addressed in CMS' healthy food standard and what sources of information CMS should consider in adding such specifications.
In grounding this proposed standard in the DGA, CMS recognizes that nutrition science continues to evolve—which is why CMS has generally avoided highly prescriptive, item-level criteria in favor of the approach described above. If finalized as proposed, CMS intends to evaluate this definition on a regular basis consistent with the DGA's 5-year review cycle (
7 U.S.C. 5341(a)
) as well as monitor subsequent DGA revisions. Another reason CMS believes it is important to maintain flexibility in the healthy food standard rather than imposing fixed, item-level thresholds is to account for differences in enrollee populations and local market conditions. For example, rural enrollees may face unique challenges accessing foods meeting specific thresholds due to limited availability of grocery stores offering fresh fruits and vegetables. Maintaining flexibility in the standard allows plans to tailor their food related benefits better to suit their enrollee population, vendor arrangements and local markets.
CMS seeks comment on this approach, including whether establishing a quantitative threshold for added sugar, sodium, saturated fats or other nutrients would provide greater clarity and consistency for MA plans and, if so, what thresholds would be most appropriate.
4. Foods and Beverages That Generally Would Not Meet the Proposed Definition of Healthy Food for MA Supplemental Benefits
The 2025-2030 DGA generally emphasize dietary patterns centered on whole, nutrient-dense foods and recommend limiting foods that may be associated with negative health outcomes. Consistent with the principles reflected in the DGA and informed by input from subject matter experts involved in development of the DGA, CMS has created a list of certain categories of foods and beverages that generally would not align with the proposed definition of “healthy food” for purposes of MA supplemental benefits due to their nutritional composition and association with dietary patterns linked to poorer health outcomes.
[
8
]
This approach is also consistent with the standards governing MA supplemental benefits. Food-related supplemental benefits must either be primarily health related or, in the case of SSBCI, have a reasonable expectation of improving or maintaining the health or overall function of an eligible chronically ill enrollee. As such, CMS believes foods and beverages furnished through these benefits generally should align with dietary patterns that support those objectives.
CMS recognizes that stakeholders may have questions regarding how the proposed definition applies to processed foods and foods containing significant amounts of added sugars, refined carbohydrates, excess sodium, hydrogenated oils, and artificial additives. To help alleviate confusion, CMS generally would not consider the following categories of foods or beverages to meet the proposed definition of “healthy food” for MA supplemental benefits:
Fruit and vegetable juices that are not 100 percent fruit or vegetable juice.
Sugar-sweetened beverages, including sodas, energy drinks, sports drinks, flavored milks, sweetened iced teas, and other beverages with significant added sugars.
Refined grain products made primarily with refined white flour, including white bread, white pasta, pastries, muffins, cakes, cookies, crackers, tortillas, and similar products.
Processed meats containing added sugars, nitrates, nitrites, excess sodium, or chemical additives, including certain hot dogs, deli meats, sausages, bacon, and jerky products.
Frozen or ready-to-eat meals containing significant amounts of added sugars, excess sodium, or artificial preservatives.
Snack foods high in sodium, added sugars, refined white flour, refined oils,
(
printed page 76322)
or artificial additives, including chips, crackers, cookies, and similar snack products.
Foods where refined sugars are a primary ingredient, including candy, chocolate, syrups, jams, jellies, sweetened spreads, and similar confectionary products.
Margarine, shortening, and foods containing partially hydrogenated or hydrogenated oils.
CMS seeks comment on whether these categories provide sufficient clarity regarding foods that generally would not meet the proposed definition of “healthy food” for MA supplemental benefits.
5. Provider-Recommended Foods and Individualized Nutritional Needs
While this definition represents an important step in identifying what constitutes “healthy food” for MA plans, CMS recognizes that there are certain situations in which foods that meet this definition may not always be appropriate for a particular enrollee. For example, some elderly patients experience poor appetite, weight loss, and functional decline. In these situations, a physician may recommend an oral nutrient supplement that emphasizes caloric density and ease of intake over nutrient density. An example may include a patient who has difficulty swallowing solid foods, making certain whole food items inappropriate. Similarly, a lactose-intolerant enrollee whose provider recommends a nutritionally equivalent non-dairy milk alternative in place of dairy would qualify under this provision, even if the specific product may not otherwise meet the definition at § 422.102(h)(1). For example, a non-dairy milk alternative may contain significant amounts of added sugar or other additives, which as outlined in section II.A.4 of this proposed rule, would generally not meet the proposed standard. To preserve the treating provider's ability to make individualized recommendations for their patients, CMS proposes to add paragraph (h)(2) to § 422.102 to provide that any food or beverage recommended by an enrollee's health care provider to address the enrollee's medical condition or nutritional needs qualifies as “healthy food” for purposes of MA supplemental benefits provided that the item is not otherwise prohibited under § 422.102(f)(1)(iii) or other applicable law. CMS emphasizes that the definition of “healthy food” in proposed § 422.102(h)(1) establishes a general standard for MA supplemental benefit design and is not intended to supersede the individualized clinical judgment of a treating health care provider. CMS recognizes that nutritional needs may vary significantly based on an enrollee's medical condition, functional status, and overall clinical circumstances. Thus, proposed § 422.102(h)(2) is intended to preserve provider discretion by ensuring that foods or beverages recommended by a treating health care provider to address an enrollee's specific medical condition or nutritional needs remain permissible under § 422.102(h)(2). Under this proposal, any food or beverage item recommended by a provider for a specific enrollee's medical condition or nutritional needs would qualify as “healthy food” that may be offered as a supplemental benefit, even if it would not otherwise meet the proposed definition at § 422.102(h)(1). CMS notes that providers may incorporate individual care needs as well as other factors such as clinical standards of care for chronic health conditions. CMS is not proposing to require a prescription or other specific form of provider order for purposes of this provision. CMS emphasizes that this provision would not require MA plans to cover any particular food or beverage item solely because it is recommended by a provider, nor would it require MA plans to offer food-related supplemental benefits where they do not otherwise do so. Rather, this provision would apply only in circumstances where an MA plan already offers a food-related supplemental benefit and must determine whether a particular item is permissible under that benefit. In such cases, CMS would consider foods or beverages recommended by a provider to address an enrollee's medical condition to satisfy the proposed definition of “healthy food” for MA supplemental benefits and therefore be eligible for coverage under the terms of the applicable benefit.
CMS notes that while the DGA addresses specific chronic conditions such as cardiovascular disease, obesity, and type 2 diabetes—conditions highly relevant to the Medicare population—and provides general dietary guidelines, the DGA also states specifically that individuals with chronic conditions should consult their providers to establish individualized diets that are appropriate. This is consistent with CMS' proposal at 422.102(h)(2). CMS' proposal is not meant to guide individual enrollee dietary choices, but rather to establish a standard for what MA plans may cover as food related supplemental benefits. CMS seeks public comment on whether the provider-recommendation pathway adequately addresses situations where a nutrient-dense standard may conflict with an enrollee's individual clinical needs, including cases involving multiple chronic conditions with competing dietary requirements. CMS also seeks public comment on whether additional examples or clarifying language are needed to illustrate how this provision would apply across varying clinical circumstances and welcomes suggestions on how CMS can further balance a consistent nutrition standard with the clinical flexibility needed for a diverse, multimorbid population.
CMS notes that coordinated care plans are already required under existing MA regulations to maintain procedures that support effective and continuous patient care, including ensuring appropriate exchange of information among providers, ensuring that providers maintain enrollee health records consistent with MA plan standards, and informing enrollees of health care needs requiring follow-up and self-care measures (see § 422.112(b)(4) and (5)). CMS expects that where a provider recommends a specific food or beverage item to address an enrollee's medical condition or nutritional needs, this recommendation would be incorporated into the MA plan's existing care coordination and continuity of care functions under § 422.112. Consistent with § 422.112(b)(4)(ii) and (iii), MA plans would be expected to ensure providers maintain appropriate documentation within the enrollee record and that relevant information is appropriately shared among providers and care management personnel, as applicable. CMS also routinely conducts program audits and oversight activities of MA plans, and compliance with coordinated care requirements under § 422.112 may be reviewed as part of those activities. CMS may incorporate review of these activities, as appropriate, into existing oversight and auditing processes and may proceed with compliance actions should CMS discover plans are allowing foods inconsistent with the standard in proposed § 422.102(h)(1) and not recommended by their health care provider as proposed in § 422.102(h)(2).
CMS seeks comment on whether the proposed definition adequately accounts for individualized provider recommendations and the operational realities of MA plan administration, including whether existing MA care coordination and continuity of care processes under § 422.112 are sufficient to support and document provider-recommended food and beverage items.

While there may be some administrative burden on plans should CMS finalize this proposal, this administrative burden should not exceed the normal business operations that plans undertake to ensure their benefits adhere to CMS requirements. CMS notes that the proposed definition of “healthy food” for MA supplemental benefits at § 422.102(h) incorporates a non-exhaustive list of qualifying foods while preserving flexibility for MA plans to tailor food-related supplemental benefits to enrollee needs, local markets, and existing vendor arrangements. Any internal review or adjustment of food-related supplemental benefits that MA plans undertake to align with this definition would occur as part of the ordinary annual benefit design and bid preparation process. Since the beginning of the Part D program, we have interpreted section 1860D-2(b) of the Act to provide for two distinct types of standard prescription drug coverage—“Defined Standard coverage” and “actuarially equivalent standard coverage.” Section 1860D-2(b)(2)(A)(ii) of the Act provides that Part D sponsors offering actuarially equivalent standard coverage will be permitted to substitute cost-sharing requirements (including multi-tier benefit structures tied to Part D plan formularies and particular pharmacies in a Part D plan's network) for costs above the annual deductible and up to the catastrophic coverage limit, provided that those alternative cost-sharing requirements are actuarially equivalent to an average expected coinsurance of 25 percent for costs above the annual deductible and up to catastrophic coverage. Also, since the beginning of the Part D program, we have interpreted this provision to permit multi-tier benefit structures for actuarially equivalent standard coverage but not for Defined Standard coverage (
70 FR 4237
).
As is noted on page 55 of the Final Calendar Year 2015 Part D Call Letter, for a plan using a formulary (as defined at § 423.4), we expect that the formulary structure for Defined Standard coverage will be consistent with a plan benefit package (PBP) that does not include a multi-tier benefit structure. Similarly, we have stated in our Formulary Submission Module and Reports Technical Manual (available to appropriate reviewers in the HPMS via the following path: Plan Formularies/Formulary Review/CY 2027/Documentation/View Documentation/User Manual under FDR Documentation) that formularies that will only be associated with plans offering Defined Standard coverage must be submitted as having a single-tier benefit structure. We made an exception to this policy for a plan(s) offering Defined Standard coverage to use a formulary that is linked (via the formulary crosswalk) to at least one other plan with a multi-tier benefit structure (that is, a plan offering Actuarial Equivalent Standard, Basic Alternative, or Enhanced Alternative coverage). We made this exception because a given formulary (as defined in § 423.4) applies to all plans to which such formulary has been assigned, whereas any submitted multi-tier benefit structures are plan-specific and only apply to the individual plans that offer coverage other than Defined Standard. In other words, when a Part D sponsor assigns a formulary to both a plan offering Defined Standard coverage and one or more plans offering Actuarially Equivalent Standard, Basic Alternative, or Enhanced Alternative coverage, the plan offering Defined Standard coverage will cover the same list of drugs associated with that formulary. However, with respect to the plan offering Defined Standard coverage, the cost-sharing for all drugs on the formulary must be a single-tier benefit structure regardless of the tier structure that applies to the other plans assigned the same formulary.
The Final Calendar Year 2015 Part D Call Letter also instructed that all marketing materials for plans offering Defined Standard coverage reflect a single-tier benefit structure regardless of whether such plan offering Defined Standard coverage uses a formulary that is associated with other plans that offer multi-tier benefit structures.
Because we continue to receive questions from Part D sponsors about our policy that a plan offering Defined Standard coverage have a single-tier benefit structure, we are re-proposing our prior proposal from the CY 2024 Proposed Rule to codify this longstanding subregulatory policy. While we have made minor revisions to the proposed regulatory text to improve clarity, the underlying policy is unchanged from both our prior proposal and our longstanding subregulatory policy as established in the Final Calendar Year 2015 Part D Call Letter. Additionally, with regard to the formulary crosswalk policy, we have previously used the terms “associated,” “mapped,” “linked,” and “assigned” synonymously, but in order to minimize confusion, we have chosen to use the term “assign” in our proposed regulatory requirements.
First, we propose to define the term “formulary crosswalk” at § 423.100 as the process during bid submission through which a Part D sponsor assigns a formulary (as defined at § 423.4) to one or more Part D plans with single- or multi-tier benefit structures.
Second, we propose to add new paragraph (8) to § 423.120(b) to codify the single-tier benefit requirement for plans offering Defined Standard coverage. At new § 423.120(b)(8)(i), we propose to codify that a Part D sponsor must apply a single-tier benefit structure to a Part D plan offering Defined Standard coverage and such benefit must be administered consistent with Defined Standard coverage as defined at § 423.100. At new § 423.120(b)(8)(ii), we propose to codify that, except as provided in paragraph (iii), a Part D sponsor may not assign a formulary (as defined at § 423.4) with a multi-tier benefit structure to a plan offering Defined Standard coverage via the formulary crosswalk (as defined at § 423.100). Additionally, at new § 423.120(b)(8)(iii), we propose to codify an exception providing that when a Part D sponsor offers both Defined Standard coverage plan(s) and one or more other Part D plans with multi-tier benefit structures, the Part D sponsor may assign a formulary with a multi-tiered benefit structure to a plan offering Defined Standard coverage, provided that the benefit administered with respect to the Defined Standard plan is consistent with paragraph (i) of this section, and the formulary is marketed as a single-tier benefit structure (consistent with § 423.2267(e)(52)).
Finally, we propose to codify our subregulatory policy that a plan offering Defined Standard coverage reflect a single-tier benefit structure in all relevant communications, as defined at § 423.2260. Specifically, at new § 423.2267(e)(52), we propose to require that, when addressing the Part D plan's formulary, a plan offering Defined Standard coverage convey that all covered Part D drugs have a single-tier benefit structure. This model content would be included in all relevant communications (as defined at § 423.2260) that pertain to the formulary—including the complete and abridged formulary, Summary of

C. Ensuring Value for Enhanced Alternative Part D Plans (§ 423.104)
In this section, CMS proposes to clarify the specific changes that a Part D plan sponsor can make to increase the actuarial value of an Enhanced Alternative (EA) plan as compared to standard prescription drug coverage and to codify a requirement that Part D sponsors offering supplemental benefits under certain EA plans must demonstrate the added value by meeting a minimum 15 percent threshold differential, using the out-of-pocket costs (OOPC) model, when compared to Defined Standard (DS) coverage.
1. Background
CMS has the authority under section 1857(e)(1) of the Act, incorporated into Part D by section 1860D-12(b)(3)(D) of the Act, to establish additional contract terms that CMS finds “necessary and appropriate.” In addition, section 1860D-11(d)(2)(B) of the Act provides CMS with the authority to impose “reasonable minimum standards” for Part D plan sponsors.
Part D plan sponsors have the flexibility to offer non-DS plans, under which they can modify certain benefit parameters. This includes two types of basic plans—Actuarially Equivalent standard coverage and Basic Alternative coverage—in addition to EA coverage. EA coverage must meet the requirements of alternative prescription drug coverage and, in accordance with § 423.104(f), includes both required basic prescription drug coverage and supplemental benefits.
Section 11201 of the Inflation Reduction Act of 2022 (IRA) (
Pub. L. 117-169
) made significant changes to the Part D benefit design that affect the structure of the Part D benefit. Because the IRA did not modify the list of permissible supplemental benefits in section 1860D-2(a)(2)(A)(i) of the Act to include a reduction in the annual out-of-pocket (OOP) threshold, Part D plan sponsors may not lower the annual OOP threshold. Thus, under § 423.104(f)(1)(ii), the following supplemental benefits remain as possible enhancement features: coverage of drugs that are specifically excluded as Part D drugs under paragraph (2)(ii) of the definition of Part D drug under § 423.100 and/or any of the following changes or combination of changes that increase the actuarial value of benefits under the Part D plan above the actuarial value of defined standard prescription drug coverage:
Reduction (or elimination) of the DS deductible.
Reduction of cost sharing in the initial coverage phase.

CMS therefore believes it is critical to continue using a process for ensuring that beneficiaries receive value relative to the standard prescription drug benefit when they enroll in an enhanced plan in light of the supplemental premiums they may pay for these enhanced plans. This approach is consistent with CMS's broader efforts to promote healthy competition in the Part D marketplace and to advance transparency so that beneficiaries can identify the plan that best meets their individual needs. D. Ensuring Meaningful Differences Between Standalone PDPs (§ 423.265)
In this section, CMS proposes to codify a 15 percent value threshold to establish that an enhanced alternative (EA) PDP plan is meaningfully different from the basic plan offered by the same PDP sponsor within the same region. CMS also proposes a threshold such that the share of meaningful difference attributed to formulary robustness be greater than or equal to zero percent and that the share of meaningful difference attributed to benefit design be greater than 50 percent. CMS would use an out-of-pocket (OOPC) model to determine compliance with these thresholds, if codified.
1. Background
a. Legal Authority
CMS has the authority under section 1857(e)(1) of the Act, incorporated into Part D by section 1860D-12(b)(3)(D) of the Act, to establish additional contract terms that CMS finds “necessary and appropriate.” In addition, section 1860D-11(d)(2)(B) of the Act provides CMS with the authority to impose “reasonable minimum standards” for PDP sponsors. Under this authority, we can deny bids that are not substantially different from other bids submitted by the same PDP sponsor in the same service area with respect to the benefit package or plan costs (§ 423.272(b)(3)(i)). This is an important protection, as it helps to ensure beneficiaries can distinguish between the plans available to them and make the best choice for their needs. While the regulation uses the terms “substantial difference” and “substantially different,” we refer to this as our “meaningful difference” requirement to emphasize the importance of ensuring beneficiaries have meaningful plan choice.
b. History of the Part D OOPC Model
As discussed in the Final CY 2025 Part D Redesign Program Instructions,
[
22
]
CMS has used a Part D OOPC model since CY 2012 to conduct the annual standalone PDP meaningful difference evaluation and has refined it over the years based on experience and stakeholder feedback. The Part D OOPC model estimates the relative OOPC value (that is, the estimated beneficiary cost per month) for beneficiaries in PDPs. Annually, CMS has established meaningful difference value thresholds for the upcoming contract year by evaluating the estimated Part D OOPC values using the prior year's approved bid and formulary data. Between CY 2012 and CY 2022, CMS used an absolute dollar threshold to assess whether the estimated Part D OOPC value for the EA plan(s) is equal to or lower than the established dollar threshold compared to the estimated Part D OOPC value for the basic plan offered in the same region.
Beginning in CY 2023, CMS moved to an outlier approach to ensure that PDP offerings met the requirements under § 423.272(b)(3)(i) due to significant updates CMS made to the Part D OOPC model. To improve upon the accuracy and timeliness of estimated Part D OOPC values, CMS enhanced the model to estimate Part D OOPC values based on a cohort of a 0.1 percent sample of all Part D enrollees and their associated PDEs, as opposed to the previous approach of using the Medicare Current Beneficiary Survey (MCBS) data, which lagged in some cases by many years and required complex mapping of survey data.
Stakeholders supported these enhancements and agreed the change provided for a larger, more representative cohort, more timely data, and up-to-date drug estimates, compared to the fee-for-service cohort from the MCBS data. Based on commenters' additional feedback, CMS further enhanced estimated Part D OOPC values by accounting for therapeutic alternatives and formulary exception cost-sharing when a model drug is not on a PDP sponsor's formulary.
[
23
]
Since 2023, the current model simulates real-world beneficiary behavior and takes into account therapeutic alternative and exception tier cost sharing, whereas the model had historically estimated OOPC value for non-formulary drugs at their full cash price. The Medicare Payment Advisory Commission (MedPAC) stated that the actuaries MedPAC interviewed believe these combined enhancements were an improvement to the model and would make the meaningful difference requirement more rigorous.
[
24
]
Given the impact of these various model changes on Part D estimated OOPC values, CMS chose to temporarily evaluate bid submissions using a distribution analysis approach. We thus established an outlier threshold, rather than establishing an absolute dollar amount in advance, until we were able to gain more experience with the model updates. For CY 2023, CMS reviewed bid submissions for OOPC differences between basic and EA PDPs. We communicated concerns at the 75th percentile, which corresponded to a 7.5 percent difference between PDP basic and EA plan(s). In other words, any EA plan that did not have an estimated OOPC value that was 7.5 percent better than its respective basic plan's estimated OOPC value needed to further enhance its benefit. For CY 2024, CMS again used an outlier approach at the same 75th percentile, corresponding to a 10.65 percent difference threshold between basic and EA plan(s).
Section 11201 of the Inflation Reduction Act of 2022 (IRA) made amendments to section 1860D-2 of the Act that impact Part D plan benefit design by capping enrollees' annual OOP costs, eliminating the coverage gap phase, and eliminating cost-sharing in the catastrophic phase. As a result of these changes to the benefit, CMS adopted a new approach to assessing meaningful difference between an EA plan and a basic plan for standalone PDPs in CY 2025.
After consideration of the statutory changes under the IRA and the comments we received in response to the Draft CY 2025 Part D Redesign Program Instructions, we established an absolute percent threshold approach for evaluating PDP meaningful difference for CY 2025. This approach aligned with a longstanding CMS goal to move the meaningful difference evaluation from a variable absolute dollar differential to a
(
printed page 76328)
static percent differential. Once established, a percent differential does not require annual updates for inflation and establishes a stable, consistent requirement from year to year. This approach also considers the richness of the comparator basic plan in the evaluation; for instance, an EA plan will not need to meet the same dollar threshold when compared to basic plan with an estimated OOPC value of $100 as opposed to a basic plan with an estimated OOPC value of $150. This helps to alleviate the incentive to make the basic plan less rich to meet meaningful difference because a higher basic plan estimated OOPC value will result in a larger dollar threshold for the corresponding EA plan.
Specifically for CY 2025, CMS undertook an analysis of the historic threshold values used for the PDP meaningful difference requirements as shown in table II.D-1. This analysis looked at the annual meaningful difference dollar thresholds and calculated the average percent differences between the basic and the lower valued EA plan (that is, the EA plan with the higher estimated OOPC value when two EA plans are offered in the same region) for each PDP sponsor. We then prepared distributions and evaluated the percentile that was used to establish the meaningful difference dollar threshold for each year. Averaging the years together, we determined that a meaningful difference threshold of eighteen percent between the basic and EA plans would align with the observed dollar differentials from previous years.
Given the limited enhancements available to plans under Part D benefit redesign, we acknowledged that this may no longer be a reasonable expectation. For CY 2024, for example, all plans achieved close to a 12 percent difference without having an established threshold to target when preparing their bids. Therefore, for CY 2025, as a middle ground between these two values of 12 percent and 18 percent, we required a 15 percent difference between a PDP sponsor's basic plan and EA plan(s) offered in the same region.
All PDP sponsors met or exceeded the 15 percent threshold for CY 2025. However, after careful consideration of concerns raised by PDP sponsors, and considering that the inclusion in the OOPC model of maximum fair prices (MFPs) for initial price applicability year 2026 would have a greater impact on basic plan estimated OOPC values, thus potentially making it slightly more difficult to meet meaningful difference, CMS lowered the meaningful difference threshold to 10 percent for CY 2026. At that time, CMS believed that lowering the OOPC differential between PDP basic and EA plans to 10 percent balanced the challenges PDP sponsors faced in differentiating between basic and EA plans, while continuing to ensure that the enhancements offered to beneficiaries in EA plans are meaningful. However, in evaluating the CY 2026 bids, CMS found that nearly all PDP sponsors achieved a 15 percent difference or better between their basic and EA plan(s). While the threshold remained at 10 percent for the subsequent CY 2027 bid submissions, all PDP sponsors met or exceeded a 15 percent difference.
2. Establishing Meaningful Differences Between Bids (§ 423.265(b)(2)(i)).
CMS proposes to modify the regulatory text at § 423.265(b)(2)(i) to codify that a bid would satisfy the requirement to be meaningfully different if it meets thresholds established by CMS through the OOPC model that CMS releases in advance of each contract year (and that CMS proposes to describe at § 423.104(f)(1)(ii)(D)(2)). The Part D OOPC model takes the drug utilization of a sample cohort of Part D beneficiaries and conducts a simulated processing of claims using each plan's bid submission, including formulary data, to estimate a monthly Part D OOPC value. The OOPC model release would additionally include a simulated Defined Standard (DS) benefit scenario. The Part D OOPC model would generate four values that CMS would use to evaluate meaningful difference, as shown in table II.D-2. These outputs would include the estimated OOPC value of the basic plan (basic OOPC); the estimated OOPC value of the basic plan's formulary using a simulated DS benefit scenario (referred to as DS basic OOPC); the estimated OOPC value of the EA plan (EA OOPC); and the estimated OOPC value of the EA plan's formulary using a simulated DS benefit scenario (referred to as DS EA OOPC). We are also proposing minor revisions to the regulatory text at § 423.265(b)(2)(i) to replace the term “significantly different” with “meaningfully different” which is the term CMS has adopted in historical guidance.
a. Overall Meaningful Difference Threshold (§ 423.265(b)(2)(i)(A))
CMS further proposes a meaningful difference calculation and threshold requirement for standalone PDPs that would establish that an EA PDP is meaningfully different from the basic plan offered by the same PDP sponsor within the same region. First, CMS would codify a calculation to establish the absolute value for meaningful difference by subtracting the EA OOPC from the basic OOPC. We would then calculate a percent difference by taking this difference, dividing it by the basic
(
printed page 76329)
OOPC, and multiplying by 100. These calculations are shown in table II.D—2. Second, given our experience with the OOPC model, described in section II.D.1.b. of this proposed rule (History of the Part D Out-of-Pocket (OOPC) Model), CMS would codify a requirement that a PDP sponsor must meet a 15 percent difference threshold to establish that an EA PDP is meaningfully different from the basic plan that it offers within a region. These proposals would be codified by revising § 423.265(b)(2)(i) and adding new paragraph (A).
b. Meaningful Difference Derived From Formulary Robustness Versus Benefit Design Thresholds (§ 423.265(b)(2)(i)(B))
In addition to proposing to codify the current meaningful difference threshold policy, CMS proposes to codify an ancillary threshold policy. The proposal would require that in order for an EA plan to meet the meaningful difference requirement, the share of meaningful difference attributed to formulary robustness must be greater than or equal to zero percent and the share of meaningful difference attributed to benefit design must be greater than 50 percent. Currently, CMS determines the proportion of meaningful difference derived from formulary robustness, which is distinct from benefit design (inclusive of tier placement parameters), for the EA plan. We use the outputs from the DS benefit scenario to review these proportions. To determine the proportion of the estimated OOPC value provided by formulary robustness in a given EA plan, we subtract the DS EA OOPC from the DS basic OOPC, divide this difference by the meaningful difference, and multiply by 100. To determine the proportion of estimated OOPC value provided by benefit design, we subtract the formulary robustness proportion from 100. These calculations are also shown in table II.D-2. We would codify our proposals by adding a new paragraph (B) to § 423.265(b)(2)(i).
CMS is proposing to codify the metrics for formulary robustness and benefit design, as compared to the DS benefit, so that we can compare plans that may use a wide range of different formulary designs and benefit structures. Based on past CMS experience in bid review, there were instances in which a PDP sponsor's EA plan within a region applied higher cost sharing to individual formulary tiers when compared to its basic plan in that region. Such PDP sponsors achieved an adequate OOPC differential by adding drugs to the formulary without offering a richer benefit (for example, lower deductible or lower copays) compared to the basic plan. CMS does not consider this type of enhancement to be entirely transparent to the beneficiary. We also note that such an enhancement is of limited scope, given that only beneficiaries who utilize the added drugs benefit from the enhancement. Further, in responding to CMS's meaningful difference review concerns, PDP sponsors often responded by simply adding drugs to their formularies, particularly those that are high cost but with low utilization, rather than improving the benefit.

In the Final CY 2026 Part D Redesign Program Instructions,

III. Strengthening Current Medicare Advantage and Medicare Prescription Drug Benefit Program Policies
A. Using a CMS Approval Mechanism for Use of the Disaster/Emergency Special Enrollment Period and Other Technical Changes (§§ 422.62, 422.66, 423.32, 423.36 and 423.38)
1. Background and Proposed Provisions
Section 1851(c) of the Act provides the Secretary with the authority to establish a process by which MA enrollment elections (hereinafter referred to as “elections”) are made and changed, including the form and manner in which they are changed. Section 1851(c)(2)(A) and (B) of the Act specifies that the election process shall permit individuals to make MA elections by filing an appropriate election form with an MA organization. Section 1851(e)(4)(D) of the Act authorizes the Secretary to create special enrollment periods (SEPs) for an individual to disenroll from an MA plan or elect another MA plan if the individual meets an exceptional condition provided by the Secretary.
Section 1860D-1(b)(1)(B) of the Act provides that in adopting the Part D enrollment process, the Secretary “shall use rules similar to (and coordinated with) the rules for” MA plans under specified provisions of section 1851 of the Act, including section 1851(c) and (e) of the Act. Section 1860D-1(b)(3)(C) of the Act authorizes the Secretary to establish Part D SEPs for Medicare-eligible individuals to enroll in a Part D plan if they meet certain exceptional circumstances.
Consistent with these sections of the Act, in 1998, we published a final rule (
63 FR 34968
) to codify the Part C election process required under section 1851(c) of the Act at § 422.66. In 2005, we published a final rule (
70 FR 4194
) to codify the Part D election process required under section 1860D-1(b)(1)(B) of the Act at §§ 423.32 and 423.36. The Parts C and D subpart B regulations set forth our requirements with respect to the election process under §§ 422.60 (election process), 422.66 (coordination of enrollment and disenrollment
(
printed page 76331)
through MA organizations), 423.32 (enrollment process), and 423.36 (disenrollment process).
In 2020, we published a final rule (
85 FR 33796
) that codified the SEP for individuals affected by a government-entity-declared disaster or other emergency (hereinafter referred to as the “Disaster SEP”) (§§ 422.62(b)(18) and 423.38(c)(23)), which was previously limited to Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA)-declared emergencies or disasters. In 2026, we published a final rule (
91 FR 17384
) to codify long-standing policy that certain SEPs required CMS approval for use through the use of CMS-operated mechanisms as determined by CMS, such as 1-800-MEDICARE or the Online Enrollment Center, or other means, such as the receipt of a notice of eligibility. In that rule, we established §§ 422.66(g), 423.32(k), and 423.36(g), which specified the SEPs with this limitation. Language was also added to the SEPs under §§ 422.62 and 423.38 to indicate that CMS approval was required for use and how approval would be provided. We codified these limitations in order to better oversee the use of SEPs which may not be appropriate for plans to use without prior CMS eligibility determination and approval. In that rule, we provided as examples the SEPs for individuals who are impacted by a contract violation or by conduct that was sanctioned by CMS. In these examples the organizations making the SEP eligibility determinations are not neutral arbiters of eligibility, as they have a financial interest in deeming the conduct of other organizations as a contract violation or they lack the complete information about the circumstances of the sanctioned conduct.
As explained in the contract year 2026 final rule, CMS developed this limitation because of concerns about the capacity of organizations to properly assess eligibility for SEPs where organizations do not or could not have complete context, or where they may have financial interests that cause them to not be neutral arbiters of eligibility. As discussed elsewhere in this rule, CMS is now proposing to extend this limitation to apply to another situation where additional CMS oversight over the utilization of a particular SEP may be appropriate, specifically, where there is evidence to suggest that the SEP is being misused. In such cases, we believe that it may be necessary to require CMS approval for use of a particular SEP, in order to prevent misuse of the established election periods and the resulting enrollment abuses, including the potential for enrollment fraud.
To that end, we believe the Disaster SEP has been misused since it was codified and should require CMS approval prior to use. Shortly after the Disaster SEP was codified, we began to receive questions from external interested parties about the applicability of the SEP to various state and local disaster and emergency declarations. This was understandable since plans were adjusting to the new relevance of state and local declarations, given that the SEP previously was limited only to FEMA declarations. However, these inquiries soon became reports of suspected misuse of the SEP, which we started receiving in 2021 and continue to receive from plans, state departments of insurance, agents/brokers, and industry groups. In short, external interested parties report that some plans ignore the eligibility criteria of the SEP and treat disaster/emergency declarations as an open enrollment period, no matter the real or potential impact of the disaster/emergency on the individual utilizing the SEP. We have also received allegations that some plans are using this SEP for enrollment in areas where there has not been a disaster/emergency declaration.
This misuse of the Disaster SEP stems from an incorrect application of the eligibility criteria at §§ 422.62(b)(18)(iv) and 423.38(c)(23)(iv), which requires that eligible individuals did not make an election during another election period for which they were eligible “due to the emergency or major disaster.” By its ordinary meaning, “due to the emergency or major disaster” requires that the individual was prevented from making another election as a result of that emergency or disaster, or that the effects of the emergency or disaster prevented the individual from taking advantage of another election period. The easiest example of such a disaster would be a major hurricane that resulted in evacuations, power outages, disruption to mail delivery, or property damage, such that the displacement of the individual along with other effects made them unable to submit an enrollment application during another valid election period, like the Annual Enrollment Period.
The principal policy justification for the Disaster SEP is that eligible individuals would have used the other election period but were prevented from doing so by something beyond their control that they could not have been expected to foresee. An SEP provides a remedy for eligible individuals impacted by an emergency or disaster by replacing the other election period that would have been used. Based on the reports of external interested parties, some plans were not assessing for eligibility based on the actual effects of the disaster, that is, that the disaster prevented the individual from making an election during another election period. These reports indicated that plans were either using any emergency or disaster declaration akin to an open enrollment period and/or were not checking that the individual was eligible for an election period at an earlier point in time and had been unable to make an election during the timeframe of that earlier election period because of the emergency or disaster. The Disaster SEP is not so broadly written and application in such a manner entirely defeats the purpose of an SEP meant to provide protection to a specific group of individuals and provide a remedy.
After receiving numerous reports of suspected misuse, we undertook an internal analysis of enrollments that were submitted using the Disaster SEP. As a starting point, we reviewed disaster declarations between 2022 and 2024 that were previously reported to us by external parties as questionable sources of SEP eligibility. Among these reports were the actual lists of disasters that certain plans had provided to their agents/brokers as eligible to the Disaster SEP. CMS reviewed these lists and it is our understanding, based on external reports, that these were to be used as a reference by agents and brokers when accepting enrollments and included every active declaration, regardless of the actual likelihood of that disaster causing someone to miss an enrollment period, thereby making them eligible for the Disaster SEP. CMS has received reports that these types of materials were frequently made available through online broker portals and typically included details about declared disasters, affected counties, and SEP start and end dates.
Using this information, we identified disaster declarations (during the above time period) that were the only active declaration at the time in a particular geographic area and, based on the underlying circumstances, were unlikely to lead to an individual missing an election period as a result of the that disaster. We confirmed they were the only declared disaster by reviewing county, state, and federal disaster declarations in the same area to determine whether other declarations were active that could account for enrollments over the applicable period. We also found examples where enrollments were submitted in states and counties that had no active disaster declarations during part or all of the applicable period. The specific
(
printed page 76332)
emergencies examined in our analysis included: a heat emergency (30 days of high temperatures); hurricanes that resulted in minimal damage; the death of former First Lady Rosalynn Carter; inflation; mpox and polio; and the 2024 solar eclipse. This analysis was intentionally limited to disaster declarations that were unlikely to have prevented an individual from using another election period and that CMS had received complaints or reports of possible misuse of the SEP.
Our analysis identified 55,642 enrollments occurring between January 2022 and August 2024 in our sample of eight states which were likely cases of misuse, either because there was no active disaster declaration in that area at that time or the disaster was unlikely to have impacted an individual's ability to make an election. Nationwide, there were 1,180,848 total enrollments using the Disaster SEP over the same time period. While the 55,642 inappropriate uses of the Disaster SEP represent only 4.7% of the total uses over the same timeframe, given the frequency with which the SEP is utilized and the volume of complaints we receive regarding misuse, we believe that our limited analysis confirmed that misuse is occurring, which is unlikely to be limited to the eight states in our analysis. Therefore, even though our analysis cannot be used to establish a nationwide error rate, we believe that there is widespread misuse of the Disaster SEP. Since our analysis, utilization of the Disaster SEP has only grown, with 777,898 elections in 2025 alone, highlighting the need for stronger oversight of this frequently used SEP given the observed evidence of misuse. CMS continues to receive reports of suspected misuse of the SEP from external interested parties, supporting our belief that the eligibility criteria for the SEP are being misapplied or misunderstood.
To address suspected and reported misuse of the Disaster SEP, we propose that use of the Disaster SEP would require prior CMS approval through the use of a CMS-operated mechanism. CMS is proposing that initially, this SEP would be restricted to use through 1-800-MEDICARE only, similar to other SEPs, though we may consider expanding this to other mechanisms, including the Online Enrollment Center, in the future. This requirement would allow for CMS to exercise oversight over the Disaster SEP and the election mechanism to ensure appropriate use prior to the election request being filed with the plan. This change would not limit an individual's ability to access the SEP if they are eligible but would ensure that the SEP is not being used inappropriately. Agents and brokers will still be able to assist individuals making elections using this SEP and have their involvement in the enrollment request captured by providing their National Producer Number, which is transmitted to the plan along with the enrollment request.
Consistent with our previous rulemaking (
91 FR 17384
), we propose to codify the requirement for CMS approval in the description of the SEP at §§ 422.62(b)(18)(ii) and 423.38(c)(23)(ii) and propose to include the Disaster SEP on the list of SEPs that require CMS approval at §§ 422.66(g)(2)(iv), 423.32(k)(2)(iv), and 423.36(g)(2)(iv). In response to our request for comments on the 2026 rule, a commenter even suggested that CMS limit the Disaster SEP to only CMS-operated mechanisms in the same way that we described the limitation for the other SEPs. We believe that implementing this limitation in a similar fashion to the other SEPs identified in the 2026 final rule provides a consistent framework for the process of making an election and the filing with the plan, without the need to create a new or unique verification processes for the Disaster SEP or future SEPs that might be misused.
We are proposing a limitation on the way in which this SEP is accessed by beneficiaries to create a more consistent enrollment process and application of eligibility criteria for the Disaster SEP. We are concerned that inconsistent application and misuse of the Disaster SEP creates an uneven playing field, undermining fair enrollment standards and contributing to market instability. Specifically, this misuse can foster misleading or aggressive marketing, financial conflicts of interest, disruption in the continuity of care, and erosion of program integrity—all leading to increased administrative burden and Medicare program costs. Limiting the use of this SEP to a CMS-operated mechanism would level the playing field for organizations and should mitigate the negative consequences that can occur from the misuse of the Disaster SEP. Because of the higher level of oversight that we have over CMS-operated mechanisms, we can more easily ensure that the Disaster SEP is offered in cases where it is warranted, that is, in cases where the individual's unique circumstances clearly show that they were affected by a disaster and missed another opportunity to make an election, rather than the current state of the SEP where it is offered broadly and without regard to its eligibility criteria.
We conclude that the proposed changes to the regulatory text will not adversely impact agents and brokers, plan sponsors, or beneficiaries. During disasters, beneficiaries can be particularly vulnerable to high-pressure sales and marketing tactics. For those who have missed an enrollment period due to an emergency or disaster, it can be challenging to know which plans are available and best meet their coverage needs. For beneficiaries who want to utilize an agent or broker for assistance, this proposal supports that process. Beneficiaries can opt to contact their trusted agent or broker to perform the normal counseling functions, that is, reviewing the beneficiary's providers, prescriptions, pharmacies, costs, benefits, and available MA or Part D plans to help them to determine their best coverage options. When the beneficiary or the beneficiary and the agent call 1-800-MEDICARE to effectuate the enrollment, the beneficiary or the agent, as stated previously, can provide the agent/broker's National Producer Number for any due compensation. For those beneficiaries without existing agent/broker relationships, by contacting 1-800-MEDICARE, beneficiaries can ensure they will receive neutral comparisons across all eligible plans. This may help them make more informed decisions and protect their interests at a critical time.
Further, we conclude that the proposed regulatory change would not have a negative impact on the Medicare Trust Funds or result in a paperwork burden. All information impacts related to the procedural steps plans must take to receive and process election requests are currently approved by OMB under control numbers 0938-0753 (CMS-R-267) for Part C and 0938-0964 (CMS-10141) for Part D.
2. Alternative Considered
We considered an alternative proposal to address the suspected and reported misuse of the Disaster SEP. That alternative consideration is described in the following discussion:
Historically, CMS conveyed and effectuated disaster/emergency SEPs on an ad hoc basis specific to certain larger-scale disasters and emergencies via subregulatory guidance—the first appearing in our guidance manual, Chapter 2 of the Medicare Managed Care Manual, and Chapter 3 of the Medicare Prescription Drug manual in 2006 for Hurricanes Katrina, Rita, and Wilma. See also December 1, 2014, HPMS memo entitled “Enrollment Opportunities for Individuals Affected by the Winter Storms in Western New
(
printed page 76333)
York,” which described the availability of an SEP for individuals affected by winter storms that prevented them from using the Annual Enrollment Period (AEP). In 2018, CMS established the SEP for a FEMA-Declared Weather-Related Emergency or Major Disaster in Chapter 2 of the Medicare Managed Care Manual and Chapter 3 of the Medicare Prescription Drug Manual, which limited eligibility for this SEP to individuals affected by disasters and emergencies identified in FEMA declarations and did not include state and local government-entity declarations. In our 2020 rule (
85 FR 9002
), we proposed to codify the SEP for a FEMA-Declared Weather-Related Emergency or Major Disaster as it had existed in our subregulatory guidance. However, in response to public comments on that proposed rule, this was revised to include state and local government entities. In the final rule (
85 FR 33796
), we stated that based on comments requesting that the SEP be available for all government-entity disaster/emergency declarations, we would revise the SEP so it was not “solely contingent upon a FEMA declaration” and was consistent with our “goal of providing an enrollment or disenrollment opportunity to an individual who missed an election period due to circumstances beyond his or her control” (
85 FR 33868
).
Based on reports of misuse of the Disaster SEP, which we started receiving in 2021 from plans, state departments of insurance, agents/brokers, and industry groups, as well as our own analysis of how often and under what circumstances this SEP is being used, we considered an alternative approach of limiting the use of the Disaster SEP to FEMA-declared events, which are formal, documented federal actions with clear start/end dates and geographic boundaries (by county/area). Using a FEMA-declared event as the basis for granting a disaster SEP would give CMS, plans, and agents an unambiguous basis for determining SEP eligibility, as using one federal standard ensures beneficiaries in similar emergency situations are treated the same way regardless of which state they live in, avoiding a patchwork of differing state/local definitions of “emergency.” Broadening the SEP trigger to any state or local emergency declaration (which can be issued more frequently, with lower thresholds, or for a broader range of events such as minor weather events or localized incidents), creates more opportunities for agents/brokers to misuse the SEP to enroll or switch beneficiaries improperly (tying back to the “steering” concerns we discussed earlier) outside of normal enrollment periods.
We note that, in the event an individual is impacted by a state or local disaster/emergency event that is not a FEMA-declared event, CMS can allow an SEP, on a case-by-case basis, for exceptional circumstances related to enrollment into or disenrollment from an MA or Part D plan. Consistent with current practice, CMS will consider granting an enrollment or disenrollment opportunity in situations such as a circumstance beyond the individual's control that prevented them from submitting a timely request to enroll in or disenroll from a plan during a valid election period, or to ensure access to services, and when, without the approval of an enrollment exception, there could be adverse health consequences for the individual.
We welcome comments on the proposal to limit the use of the Disaster SEP to require CMS approval through the use of CMS-operated mechanisms such as 1-800-MEDICARE, as well as the considered alternative approach to limit the Disaster SEP to FEMA-declared weather-related events or emergencies only.
3. Technical Correction
Separately, in the contract year 2027 proposed rule we inadvertently omitted two SEPs for which it is our longstanding guidance and practice to require that the beneficiary at issue have CMS approval for the use of that SEP through the use of a CMS-operated election mechanism, such as 1-800-MEDICARE or the Online Enrollment Center (OEC), or other means, such as receipt of a notice. To correct this oversight and ensure that regulations align with current subregulatory guidance, we propose to codify the same limitations for the following SEPs:
SEP for individuals who are enrolled or not enrolled in Part D due to an error by a federal employee (§§ 422.62(b)(21) and 423.38(c)(3)).
CMS regulations at §§ 422.62(b)(21) and 423.38(c)(3) currently provide for an SEP for individuals whose enrollment or non-enrollment in an MA-PD or stand alone Part D plan was erroneous due to an action, inaction, or error by a Federal employee. Requiring CMS approval for the use of this SEP is consistent with CMS's longstanding application of this SEP. As articulated in CMS's current regulations, this SEP is only available upon a CMS determination that the SEP applies, meaning that a plan, broker, or beneficiary cannot independently declare that a federal employee made an error and thereby create an election period. In practice, CMS reaches such determinations based upon a review of CMS/federal records, as applicable incidents may involve what a 1-800-MEDICARE representative or another federal employee said or did, when it occurred, and whether that conduct actually caused the erroneous enrollment/non-enrollment. Additionally, requiring CMS approval protects enrollment integrity, as without centralized approval, plans could reach different conclusions about what constitutes a “federal employee error,” potentially creating inconsistent or unauthorized corrective enrollment actions. Lastly, the approval itself starts the SEP clock. This is particularly important: unlike many SEPs triggered automatically by an external event, this SEP begins with CMS approval, so there must be an authoritative CMS determination.
SEP for individuals affected by a significant change in provider network (§ 422.62(b)(23)).
CMS regulations at § 422.62(b)(23) provide an SEP for individuals affected by a significant change in their plan's provider network. Requiring CMS approval for the use of this SEP is consistent with CMS's longstanding application of this SEP, which, as described in Chapter 4 of the Medicare Managed Care Manual,
Benefits and Beneficiary Protections,
section 110.1.2, entitled
Significant Changes to Networks,
involves a rigorous review by CMS of the totality of the circumstances to decide whether a termination is significant. The MA organization whose network changed should not be the final arbiter of whether its own network disruption is sufficiently significant to give members a right to leave. By requiring a CMS determination of “significance,” this policy prevents different MA organizations from applying different definitions of “significant” and ensures that the SEP is applied consistently across plans and beneficiaries. Even after CMS finds a significant network change, the SEP is only available to those enrollees within the plan who are actually affected by the termination. Therefore, we are proposing to codify longstanding practice that this SEP should be granted under a CMS approval mechanism.
