B. Start, End, and Effective Dates for Special Election Periods (§§ 422.62 and 423.38)
Special election periods (SEPs) provide opportunities for Medicare beneficiaries to make enrollment and disenrollment elections outside of the annual election period when specific life events or circumstances occur. SEPs ensure that beneficiaries maintain access to appropriate coverage when circumstances arise that could affect their enrollment options. These SEPs address a wide range of situations, including changes in eligibility status, loss of other coverage, plan terminations, disasters or emergencies, and other exceptional circumstances. Sections 1851(e), 1860D-1(b)(1)(B)(iii), and 1860D-1(b)(3) of the Act authorize CMS to establish SEPs.
Current regulations at §§ 422.62 and 423.38 establish the circumstances under which an individual is eligible to use an SEP. While §§ 422.68(d) and 423.40(c) provide a default effective date for SEP elections, the regulations do not consistently describe the start and end dates of SEP eligibility windows or the exceptions to the default effective date. Additional details about when specific SEPs begin and end, and when coverage becomes effective are currently described primarily in sub-regulatory guidance, specifically, the Medicare Advantage and Part D Enrollment and Disenrollment Guidance (the “Enrollment Guidance”), section 30.6. In addition, the availability of retroactive enrollment, where applicable, is not consistently reflected in regulatory text. To provide transparency, promote consistent administration of SEPs across MA and Part D programs, and provide beneficiaries and plan sponsors with a single regulatory source describing SEP availability and operation, we are proposing to codify timeframes and the availability of retroactive enrollment for certain SEPs. Because the proposed revisions reflect longstanding CMS policies and current operational practice, these changes would not alter beneficiary rights or plan responsibilities.
First, we are proposing to amend §§ 422.62 and 423.38 to specify the start and end dates of the following SEPs:
The SEP for individuals whose plan or contract is non-renewed effective January 1, including service area reductions (nonrenewal) would be revised at §§ 422.62(b)(1) and 423.38(c)(6) to add subparagraph (i) to reflect that the SEP begins December 8 of the contract year and ends the last day of the following February.
The SEP for individuals whose plan or contract is terminated (Termination or Modification by MA organization, Part D Sponsor, or Mutual Consent) would be revised at §§ 422.62(b)(1) and 423.38(c)(6)) to add paragraph (ii) to reflect that the SEP begins 2 months before the termination effective date and ends the month after the month of termination.
The SEP for individuals whose plan or contract is terminated (CMS termination of contract) would be revised at §§ 422.62(b)(1) and 423.38(c)(6) to add paragraph (iii) to reflect that the SEP begins one month before the termination effective date and ends 2 months after the termination effective date.
The SEP for individuals who change permanent residence would be revised at §§ 422.62(b)(2) and 423.38(c)(7) to reflect that the SEP begins the date of the change in permanent residence or the month before the change in permanent residence for an individual who notifies the MA organization or Part D sponsor in advance of the change. An individual who leaves an MA plan service area on a temporary basis for an extended period of time but continues to maintain a permanent residence in the service area must be disenrolled if the extended absence exceeds six consecutive months, or up to 12 months if the MA plan offers a visitor/traveler benefit. For Part D plans, this period of allowable temporary absence from the service area is 12 consecutive months. For tracking purposes, MA organizations and Part D plan sponsors typically consider a possible temporary absence from the service area to begin upon notification from the enrollee, receipt of non-urgent or non-emergent out-of-area claims, receipt of returned mail or similar indications that an enrollee is out of the service area. The SEP for an individual disenrolled for exceeding the aforementioned periods of allowable temporary absence from the service area begins the first day of the sixth month (or up to the 12th month if a visitor/traveler benefit applies) for MA and, for Part D, the SEP begins the first day of the 12th month, when the MA organization or Part D sponsor has not been able to confirm the individual's residency status. The SEP would end 2 months following the month it begins or 2 months following the month of the move, whichever is later.
The SEP for Contract Violations would be revised at §§ 422.62(b)(3) and 423.38(c)(8) to add paragraphs (b)(3)(iii) and (c)(8)(iv), respectively, to specify that the SEP begins once CMS determines that a violation occurred and ends 90 calendar days after CMS' determination.
The SEP for individuals who involuntarily lose creditable prescription drug coverage would be revised at § 423.38(c)(1) to specify that the SEP begins the date the individual is notified of loss or reduction of creditable coverage and ends 2 calendar months after loss/reduction or receipt of notice, whichever is later.
The SEP for individuals not adequately informed of loss of creditable coverage would be revised at § 423.38(c)(2) to specify that the SEP begins the month CMS determines individual is eligible and ends two calendar months following CMS determination.
The SEP for individuals who disenroll from Part D to enroll in/maintain other creditable coverage would be amended at § 422.62(b)(14) to add paragraph (iii) and at § 423.38(c)(18) to specify that the SEP begins upon disenrollment from a Part D plan and ends on the 1st day of the following month in which disenrollment request is received by the plan.
The SEP for other exceptional circumstances would be amended at redesignated §§ 422.62(b)(28) and 423.38(c)(37) to state the SEP begins upon CMS determination and notification to enrollee and ends on a case-by-case basis, as determined by CMS.

While current guidance provides that the effective date for an enrollment or disenrollment made under the SEP for other exceptional circumstances may be either prospective or retroactive based on the individual's circumstances, as determined by CMS, this is not currently reflected in regulatory text. We are proposing to revise §§ 422.62(b)(27) and 423.38(c)(36) to codify that the effective date of coverage under this SEP may be prospective or retroactive, consistent with current guidance and practice. We note that this codification does not limit CMS's discretion to evaluate individual circumstances; rather, it provides a clear regulatory basis for a determination that CMS already makes on a case-by-case basis. In determining whether a prospective or retroactive effective date is appropriate, CMS considers the individual's specific circumstances, including but not limited to, circumstances beyond the individual's control that prevented timely enrollment, situations involving misleading or incorrect information provided by a plan representative, or situations where access to care could be adversely affected without an enrollment exception. For example, CMS may consider a retroactive enrollment for a case in which an individual enrolled in a Medicare drug plan based on incorrect formulary information, such that there is no coverage for necessary medications under the current plan, and waiting for a prospective enrollment in a plan that meets the individual's needs would be problematic.
We note that the SEP for individuals who elect into or out of employer-sponsored coverage (§§ 422.62(b)(4) and 423.38(c)(11)) and the SEP for individuals who involuntarily lose creditable prescription drug coverage (§§ 422.62(b)(19) and 423.38(c)(1)) already include language in regulation reflecting the availability of a choice of prospective effective dates, and therefore no amendment is proposed for those SEPs with respect to this issue.

C. Request for Comment: Seamless Continuation of Coverage for Newly Medicare-Eligible Individuals (§ 422.66)
Section 1851(c)(3)(A)(i) of the Act provides that, in general, an individual who fails to make an election between Original Medicare and MA during their initial election period is deemed to have
(
printed page 76337)

However, section 1851(c)(3)(A)(ii) of the Act provides the Secretary the authority to establish procedures under which an individual who is enrolled in a health plan (other than a MA plan) during their initial election period, and who fails to elect to receive other coverage may be deemed to have elected an MA plan offered by the organization that offers the individual's current non-MA plan. This second option is referred to as seamless continuation of coverage.
Consistent with this section of the Act, in 1998, we

27

63 FR 34968

42 CFR 422.66(c)
and the seamless continuation of coverage process at § 422.66(d). This initial codification implemented the seamless continuation of coverage process outlined in section 1851(c)(3)(A)(ii) of the Act, whereby individuals enrolled in a health plan offered by the organization may be deemed to have elected an MA plan offered by that same organization. In the 2005 final rule (
70 FR 4588
), CMS addressed the seamless continuation of coverage enrollment process and modified it to include MA-PD plans for the 2006 start of the Part D program. In 2018, we published the final rule (
83 FR 16440

The 2018 final rule also created a default enrollment process for MA dual eligible special needs plans, found at § 422.66(c)(2). Default enrollment allows for certain dual eligible individuals to be deemed to have elected an MA special needs plan. The requirements for default enrollment are codified at
42 CFR 422.66(c)(2)
. Not all D-SNP plans are eligible; the MA organization must have an affiliated Medicaid managed care plan and an approved D-SNP. Participating MA organizations are approved by both the state Medicaid agency and CMS, and MA organizations must be at least 3-star rated, a low enrollment contract, or a new MA plan. The 3-star rating requirement set a quality standard for plan participation in an auto-enrollment mechanism for Medicare Advantage for the first time. Participating plans must also not have any prohibition on new enrollment imposed by CMS. Dual eligibles receive advance notice of the intent to be default enrolled into a D-SNP and have the opportunity to opt out of the enrollment. As discussed further in this section, we are considering reestablishing the seamless continuation of coverage process with some modifications that are similar to the requirements in the existing default enrollment process.
Congress established seamless conversion in section 1851(c)(3) of the Social Security Act in the Balanced Budget Act of 1997. CMS addressed seamless conversion in rulemaking (CMS-4069-F) in 2005, and guidance was established that same year. CMS granted its first approval of an MA organization to offer seamless conversion in June 2005. The second approval was granted for March 2010 and the third for January 2012. In the 2018 final rule (
83 FR 16440
), we discussed the reasoning for changing seamless continuation of coverage from a default process, in which an individual would need to affirmatively opt out of automatic MA enrollment, to an opt in process. Specifically, we noted in the final rule that beneficiary advocates had requested additional consumer protections and that MA organizations found it difficult to comply with the opt out enrollment process and approval parameters. Advocates believed that automatic enrollment deprived beneficiaries of an active choice and cited cases in which beneficiaries alleged having been enrolled without their knowledge or consent. Advocates argued that a decision as important as choosing the way in which a newly Medicare-eligible individual receives Medicare should require an intentional “opt in” choice. Accordingly, we finalized an “opt in” policy in the 2018 final rule.
While we believe an “opt in” policy was previously appropriate, to improve outreach to newly eligible beneficiaries and ease the transition from commercial or Marketplace coverage to MA, we are considering a seamless continuation of coverage mechanism, similar to the opt-out process that existed prior to the 2018 final rule, but with several enhancements. Congress established seamless conversion in section 1851(c)(3) of the Act in 1997. We would modify § 422.66(d) to allow for the seamless continuation of coverage for enrollees of commercial or Marketplace plans into MA plans operated by the same organization, as provided in section 1851(c)(3)(A)(ii) of the Act. We believe this would address the administrative issues that led to the 2018 changes. Additionally, returning to an opt-out seamless continuation of coverage process would address prior beneficiary protection concerns by using the quality and notification requirements that, as discussed elsewhere in this rule, have proved successful in the default enrollment process. Further, we believe this change would result in the positive effects of maintaining coverage under the same organization, including continuity of care and simplicity for beneficiaries by preserving existing electronic health records, case management programs and approved prior authorizations, reducing the risk of temporary coverage losses during the transition to Medicare. Additionally, seamless continuation of coverage provides the newly Medicare-eligible individual with the option to transition to a Medicare health plan that is offered by the same organization the individual chose for their coverage prior to becoming eligible for Medicare. Since May 2020 CMS has made available to MA organizations a Medicare Beneficiary Identifier (MBI) lookup tool that can be used to process seamless continuation of coverage. This addresses some operational concerns that led to the 2018 changes, namely the transition at the time from health insurance claim numbers (HICNs), which no longer allowed plans to use an enrollee's SSN to determine their HICN. After the transition to HICNs but prior to release of the tool, plans had to wait for monthly CMS eligibility files to confirm when an enrollee was approaching Medicare eligibility, which made it difficult to meet the 60-day advance notice requirement for seamless continuation of coverage. The lookup tool gives MA organizations direct, real time access to Medicare systems, allowing them to proactively search for an individual's Medicare status.
We have also benefited from our experience in implementing the default enrollment mechanism for D-SNPs currently described in
42 CFR 422.66(c)(2)
, which has shown that the additional protections included in the codification of default enrollment in 2018 were successful in responding to the concerns raised several years earlier. Prior to implementing default enrollment, CMS created a robust process for review of MA organizations' proposals for implementing default enrollment and also developed a centralized electronic repository for all proposal-related materials. Under this enhanced review process, MA organizations upload for CMS review a detailed description of their default enrollment process and all related enrollee notices and member materials. As part of this process, CMS reviews all member materials, including the
(
printed page 76338)
advance notice, to ensure they are accurate and include all required elements, such as information on the individual's right to opt out of the enrollment, up to and including the day prior to the enrollment effective date, how to opt out and how to obtain information on other Medicare options. CMS maintains a record of communications between CMS and the MA organizations regarding any defects in the materials that need to be addressed, revised materials submitted to CMS and the final disposition of CMS' review. These technological advancements significantly enhanced CMS' oversight of the MA organization's plan for meeting the default enrollment requirements, just as CMS review of member materials has helped to ensure consistent and accurate messaging to beneficiaries regarding default enrollment across all MA organizations that choose to offer this enrollment mechanism.
Under the opt-out seamless enrollment process that CMS is considering, beneficiaries who do not opt out of seamless enrollment would also have access to enrollment periods, during which they could change their MA plan or return to Original Medicare. During the first 3 months of Medicare entitlement, all newly Medicare-eligible beneficiaries can use the MA Open Enrollment Period, as described in
42 CFR 422.62(a)(3)(ii)
, to switch to a different MA plan or disenroll from MA to return to Original Medicare, with Medigap guaranteed issue rights from the Medigap Open Enrollment Period as outlined in section 1882(s)(2)(A) of the Act, which lasts for the first 6-months the individual is at least both aged 65 and enrolled in Medicare Part B. Additionally, under § 422.62(c), an MA eligible individual who elects an MA plan during their initial enrollment period that surrounds their 65th birthday may disenroll from MA and elect coverage under Original Medicare at any time during the first 12 months of their MA enrollment. This individual would have Medigap guaranteed issue rights as outlined in section 1882(s)(3)(B)(vi) of the Act. Depending on their individual circumstances, they may also be eligible for an SEP that could be used to change MA plans or return to Original Medicare. If an MA SEP is used to return to Original Medicare, the individual would also have Medigap guaranteed issue rights as outlined in section 1882(s)(3)(B)(ii) of the Act.
CMS is considering whether to model the seamless continuation of coverage enrollment process on the existing default enrollment process by: (1) requiring MA organizations to obtain CMS approval prior to engaging in use of the seamless enrollment mechanism; (2) requiring that approved MA organizations must meet quality standards by having at least a 3-star rating (or by meeting the definition of “low enrollment contract” or “new MA plan” if the MA organization does not have a star rating); and (3) requiring advance notice to the individual of the organization's intent to seamlessly enroll them into an MA plan, along with details about plan benefits and cost. To ensure that individuals are aware of the seamless continuation of coverage and their Medicare coverage options, the advance notice would be required to be issued no fewer than 60 calendar days before the proposed MA enrollment effective date, that is, the first of the month in which the individual is entitled to Part A and enrolled in Part B. The notice would include clear information on the MA plan, as well as instructions to the individual on how to opt out of (decline) the seamless continuation of coverage and how to enroll in Original Medicare or a different MA plan. (As with all communications, notices must comply with applicable anti-discrimination law, including laws requiring effective communication for individuals with disabilities.
See for example,
45 CFR 92.101
et seq.
and
45 CFR 84.77
.) We would require that MA organizations must submit enrollment transactions to CMS no fewer than 60 calendar days prior to the effective date of MA enrollment.
The process we are considering would specify that an MA organization may implement a seamless continuation of coverage enrollment process in which a newly Medicare-eligible individual enrolled in a commercial or Marketplace plan it offers may be deemed to have elected an MA plan offered by the same organization. It would require that MA organizations obtain CMS approval prior to participating in the seamless continuation of coverage process. CMS would require that the organization identify in its proposal each commercial or Marketplace plan (by contract/plan ID) for which it is requesting approval to implement a seamless continuation of coverage enrollment process. We would specify that for each such plan the organization must include in its identification and notification processes all of the eligible enrollees within that specific plan, that is, commercial or Marketplace plan enrollees who are approaching Medicare eligibility and reside in the service area of the MA plan into which they would be enrolled. Approval for MA organizations granted under this process would be for a period not to exceed 5 years and may be suspended or rescinded prior to the expiration of this period if the organization is not in compliance with the seamless continuation of coverage requirements. Additionally, we would require that MA organizations must send proposals to participate in seamless continuation of coverage to CMS and that the proposal to use a seamless continuation of coverage process must include details on the proper identification of eligible current enrollees, describe outreach activities, and acknowledge enrollment transaction processing requirements. MA organizations would need to have the means to identify eligible individuals 90 calendar days in advance of the date of their initial Medicare eligibility and must include all individuals, regardless of the reason for eligibility (age, disability, end-stage renal disease). MA organizations would be required to provide a description of outreach activities associated with seamless continuation of coverage and include a copy of the written notice. MA organizations would also be required, when submitting a proposal to utilize seamless continuation of coverage, to acknowledge the requirement to send the appropriate enrollment transaction to CMS no fewer than 60 calendar days prior to the effective date of enrollment.
Additionally, MA organizations would have to have at least a 3-star rating (or meet the definition of “low enrollment contract” or “new MA plan,” as those terms are defined in CMS's regulations at
42 CFR 422.252
, if the MA organization does not have a star rating) and must not have any prohibition on new enrollment imposed by CMS to participate in seamless continuation of coverage.
Enrollment transaction submission requirements and notification requirements would specify that MA organizations would need to inform individuals who qualify for seamless continuation of coverage of the intent to enroll them in an MA plan. This notice would need to be sent at least 60 calendar days prior to the effective date of the enrollment and must include information on the differences in premium, benefits and other costs, including cost sharing, between the individual's current plan, Original Medicare, and the intended MA plan, and the process for accessing care under the MA plan. If the seamless conversion would result in the individual being enrolled in an MA plan type with more restrictive provider access and network rules, such as PPO to HMO, the notice
(
printed page 76339)
would have to include an explanation of these differences. We would require that the notice must also include information on how to obtain information on the provider networks and prescription drug formularies of the commercial plan and the MA plan so that they may identify any differences. The notice would have to include information on how to opt out of the seamless continuation of coverage, the alternative options for Medicare health and drug coverage (for example, Original Medicare, other Medicare health and drug plan options), the availability of Medigap (Medicare Supplemental Plans) and consequences of enrolling in an MA plan if the individual later chose to change to Original Medicare and Medigap, whether or not guaranteed issue (GI) rights exist, and the MA trial right period. MA organizations would be required to transmit the necessary enrollment information to CMS no fewer than 60 days prior to the effective date of the enrollment.
We remain invested in improving longitudinal care coordination and welcome input on other channels through which we could provide incentives for care continuity for both newly Medicare-eligible beneficiaries and existing MA plan enrollees. In other CMS programs, there are ongoing efforts to improve care coordination including the consideration of multi-year plan terms, for example, in the ACA market (
91 FR 29526
). We are interested in ideas that could improve longitudinal care coordination and provide a longer-term incentive for plans to manage members' health with preventive and follow-up care across multiple years rather than one enrollment cycle.
We are seeking public comment on a policy to return to an opt-out process for seamless continuation of coverage and on the expected administrative issues that plans would face in implementing the seamless continuation of coverage enrollment process. We also seek comment on the 90-day requirement to identify eligible individuals and the 60-calendar day notice and submission requirement for such an opt-out process, as described earlier in this section. We ask for comments on the feasibility of these timelines and whether a shorter requirement, or longer timeline, such as a 60-calendar day requirement for identification and a 30-calendar day requirement for notice and submission, would be more appropriate, or 120-calendar day and 90-calendar day respectively. We also seek public comment on ideas related to improving incentives for longitudinal care coordination in the MA program.
CMS is also seeking comment on whether additional eligibility criteria for MA organization participation in seamless enrollment would be appropriate. Specifically, adding a minimum length of time that an individual must have been enrolled in an MA organization's commercial plan offering as an additional eligibility criterion for seamless enrollment into their MA plan. A length of prior enrollment requirement could provide assurance that the individual both intended to enroll in the commercial plan and was satisfied enough with that organization that they intended to remain enrolled. In such a case, we believe that continuation of coverage would be appropriate, due to the individual's existing relationship with that organization. This requirement would limit seamless continuation of coverage to only individuals who have been continuously enrolled in a plan offered by the same parent organization for a specified minimum period of time prior to the individual's Medicare entitlement date. We also seek comment on whether 12 or 24 months would be an appropriate minimum length of time for this requirement and whether this would be an effective means of protecting beneficiaries. If a requirement is finalized, it would be included in addition to the other eligibility criteria described previously. We also seek comment on what types of information might best ensure a beneficiary is able to compare their current commercial plan offering to the MA plan that they would be enrolled in through seamless enrollment, so that they are fully informed during the enrollment period. These would be potentially included in the notice to beneficiaries. While cost difference is a significant factor when considering new coverage, we are requesting comment on what other information should be required in the notice to beneficiaries that we could adopt in the forthcoming final rule.
CMS is also seeking comment on the inclusion of additional regulatory language to prohibit organizations from utilizing commercial health data to selectively include healthier individuals into their MA plans. We are considering adding an explicit prohibition on the use of historical utilization data, claims data, or risk scores in determining eligibility for seamless enrollment. Our intent in adding this would be to emphasize that the only permissible criteria for identifying enrollees for seamless conversion would be initial age/disability-based Medicare eligibility, current active enrollment in the organization's commercial plan and permanent residence in the MA plan service area.
Lastly, we also seek comment on limiting seamless continuation of coverage to only MA organizations with star ratings of 4 or higher and whether a 4-star rating requirement is an appropriate protection for beneficiaries enrolled through an opt-out process or whether this would overly limit the pool of potential MA organizations that would utilize seamless continuation of coverage.
CMS is soliciting public comment on whether the additional and/or revised criteria noted previously may be appropriate. We also welcome comments on the following topics, to inform future rulemaking and policy efforts. We are interested in ways to increase early engagement for individuals newly eligible for Medicare. We seek public comments on ways to improve pre-enrollment outreach efforts for newly eligible beneficiaries. We seek comments on opportunities to simplify enrollment into MA for individuals approaching Medicare eligibility, including enrollment encouragement efforts to select the Medicare coverage option that is best suited for these individuals. We also seek comments on expanding opportunities for a streamlined transition from the individual's prior coverage to MA, similar to seamless and default enrollment, but for groups not captured by seamless or default enrollment. We also seek comments on ways to increase plan participation in programs such as seamless and default enrollment, particularly for dual eligible populations.

1. Background
Based on CMS's analyses (including analyses of contract year 2026 MA plan cost sharing data and contract year 2027 Medicare FFS data projections), CMS is concerned that the existing ground ambulance and emergency room cost sharing standards may be resulting in: (1) inadequate cost sharing for MA plans in connection with emergency services compared to the cost to provide the benefit and (2) high cost sharing for ground ambulance services for MA enrollees and uncollectable bad debt concerns for ground ambulance providers.
First, the current dollar limits for emergency services were based on contract year 2021 Medicare FFS data projections and do not reflect recent trends in increasing Original Medicare costs to provide these services (as shown in Table X.8, based on contract year 2027 Medicare FFS data projections). For example, the $150 emergency services dollar limit was actuarially equivalent to 20 percent of the contract year 2021 Medicare FFS median projection ($755); in comparison an updated actuarially equivalent value based on the most recent Medicare FFS median data projection (CY 2027, $973) would equate to $195. If MA organizations are also experiencing an increase in their total financial liabilities for emergency
(
printed page 76344)
services over this time period, without a corresponding increase to the cost sharing limit, the cost sharing could be inadequate for this benefit.

38
]
CMS analyzed contract year 2026 MA plan data to determine if MA plans were establishing emergency services cost sharing at the maximum allowable amount. Based on the information in Tables III.D-1, III.D-3, III.D-6, and III.D-8, most contract year 2026 MA plans established cost sharing for emergency services at the highest allowable amount for the plan's MOOP type. In brief, the weighted average MA plan emergency services cost sharing amount is $130 (Table III.D-3) and this correlates to how 45 percent of MA plans have an intermediate MOOP type (Table III.D-8) and are currently subject to a $130 emergency services dollar limit.
CMS compared the MA emergency services cost sharing information (based on contract year 2026 MA plan data) with other available data in Original Medicare and certain types of private health insurance plans. For example, based on the information in Table III.D-3, contract year 2026 MA plans have on average cost sharing for emergency services that is $110 to $87 less than comparable industry figures (the difference between the weighted average MA plan copayment for emergency services and the cost sharing for the same service in Original Medicare and employer plans—the “overall” row). This data point highlights how MA organizations are not, on average, receiving cost sharing for emergency services at amounts that are on par with the most recent cost sharing for this service in Original Medicare or employer plans under the current regulations.
CMS also considered the effect of the statutory requirement (Section 1852(a)(1)(B)(i) of the Act) for MA organizations to submit bids that are at least actuarially equivalent to coverage in Original Medicare. Specifically, if MA organizations are experiencing a financial impact in one area of their benefit design then they may increase cost sharing for other benefits to achieve actuarial equivalence with Original Medicare on a per member per month basis (as required by § 422.100(j)(2)). As a result, it is possible that the current emergency services cost sharing limits may in combination with § 422.100(j)(2)'s requirement be resulting in cost sharing increases or benefit reductions elsewhere—solely to make up for the potential financial loss received in emergency services cost sharing.
Second, MA organizations may be increasing cost sharing costs for non-emergency benefits, such as ground ambulance services, to: (1) make up for any potential financial loss due to the current cost sharing limit for emergency services and (2) maintain actuarial equivalence with Original Medicare overall per § 422.100(j)(2). While CMS analyzed average MA plan cost sharing for other service categories, MA plans may be particularly incentivized to raise cost sharing for ground ambulance services because: (1) there is significant flexibility in the current 50 percent coinsurance limit (for which CMS has not set an actuarially equivalent copayment limit) and (2) contract year 2026 MA plans established cost sharing amounts for ground ambulance services that are significantly in excess of cost sharing for that service in Original Medicare. In comparison, as shown in Tables III.D-9 and III.D-10, for other service categories (including air ambulance services), CMS is not finding potentially excessive cost sharing. As shown in Table III.D-10, for most of the other service categories subject to a 50 percent coinsurance limit (without an actuarially equivalent copayment limit set by CMS) on average MA plans have coinsurances around 20 percent, the cost sharing standard under Original Medicare. For example, CMS found MA plans are establishing cost sharing for air ambulance services on average at 20 percent while their cost sharing amounts for ground ambulance services (on average, $275) significantly exceeds cost sharing in original Medicare for those services (20% or $120 based on contract year 2027 projections). For example, the OACT determined that the mean (weighted average) rather than the median of the distribution of the cost of ground ambulance trips was more appropriate to use for purposes of setting an actuarially equivalent copayment limit because the cost per trip is close to a bell-shaped curve (normal distribution). As a result, CMS used the most recent (contract year 2027 projections at the time of issuing this proposed rule) weighted average Medicare FFS allowed amount for each category to calculate illustrative cost sharing limits. 3. Statutory and Regulatory Limitations on Benefit Design Changes
Plan benefit design changes may be made in response to multiple factors, including new cost sharing requirements. If this proposal is finalized, MA organizations will have the flexibility to offset any potential cost changes related to providing ground ambulance services (if they were not already establishing cost sharing amounts equivalent to or below the illustrative amounts from Table III.D-2). For example, MA organizations may choose to increase their emergency services cost sharing amount up to the illustrative amounts from Table III.D-1. In addition to or in lieu of making changes to cost sharing for emergency services, MA organizations that have to reduce their ground ambulance cost sharing amounts may make other changes to their benefit designs to meet the overall actuarial equivalence requirement from § 422.100(j)(2). For example, MA organizations may change MOOP amounts or cost sharing for other services.
MA organizations may make changes to their plan benefit design that comply with existing statutory and regulatory requirements. This includes sections 1852(a)(1)(B)(i), 1852(b)(1), and 1854(a)(5) and (6) of the Act. Section 1852(a)(1)(B)(i) of the Act provides that the MA organization must cover, subject to limited exclusions, the benefits under Parts A and B (that is, basic benefits as defined in § 422.100(c)(1)) with cost sharing that does not exceed or is at least actuarially equivalent to cost sharing in Original Medicare in the aggregate; this is repeated in a bid requirement under section 1854(e)(4) of the Act. CMS has addressed and implemented this requirement in several regulations, including §§ 422.100(j)(2), 422.101(e), 422.102(a)(4), and 422.254(b)(4).
Section 1852(b)(1) of the Act prohibits discrimination by MA organizations on the basis of health status-related factors and directs that CMS may not approve an MA plan if CMS determines that the design of the plan and its benefits are likely to substantially discourage enrollment by certain MA eligible individuals. Section 1854(a)(5) and (6) of the Act provide that CMS is not obligated to accept every bid submitted and may negotiate with MA organizations regarding the bid, including benefits. Under section 1854(a)(5)(C)(ii) of the Act, CMS is also authorized to deny a plan bid if the bid proposes too significant an increase in enrollee costs or decrease in benefits from one plan year to the next. This proposal would not limit CMS' negotiation authority under section 1854 of the Act and § 422.256 but would provide cost sharing standards for an acceptable benefit design for CMS to apply in reviewing and evaluating bids.
MA organizations must also comply with applicable Federal civil rights laws that prohibit discrimination. None of the proposals in this proposed rule limit application of applicable anti-discrimination requirements. These existing statutory antidiscrimination requirements, regulatory actuarial equivalence requirements, the competitive nature of the MA program, and the additional proposed flexibility for emergency services cost sharing are sufficient guardrails to prevent MA organizations from making discriminatory changes to their benefit designs in response, if this proposal is finalized. However, as discussed in the following section, CMS solicits comment on whether implementing this

E. Enrollee Notification Requirements for Provider Terminations, Continuity of Care, and SEP Notice Consolidation §§ 422.62, 422.111, 422.112, and 422.2267
1. Summary of Proposals
CMS is proposing several changes to regulations regarding provider network terminations. First, CMS is proposing to revise the enrollee notification and continuity of care requirements applicable to MA organizations under §§ 422.111(e), 422.112(b), and 422.2267(e)(12). These changes would revise the timing and content of required enrollee notices for provider terminations and establish new minimum continuity of care standards to protect enrollees during provider network transitions. CMS is also proposing to modify §§ 422.2267(e)(12)(ii)(D) and 422.62(b)(23)(iii) to require MA organizations to include special election period (SEP) eligibility information in
(
printed page 76350)
the provider termination notice when CMS has determined that the affected enrollee is eligible for the SEP described at § 422.62(b)(23).
Finally, CMS is proposing to codify longstanding criteria used to identify whether a provider termination constitutes a significant change in a plan provider network at § 422.112(d), thereby triggering eligibility for the SEP at § 422.62(b)(23), and to align the SEP lookback period at § 422.62(b)(23)(ii) with the lookback period used for the provider termination notice.
2. Introduction
MA organizations have considerable discretion to select the providers with whom they contract in order to build high-performing, cost-effective provider networks. They may make changes to those networks at any time during the contract year, provided they continue to furnish all Medicare-covered services in a nondiscriminatory manner, meet established access and availability standards and timely notice requirements, and ensure continuity of care for enrollees. This flexibility is supported by section 1854(a)(6)(B)(iii) of the Social Security Act (the Act), which prohibits CMS from requiring MA organizations to contract with a particular provider.
MA organizations must provide enrollees notice when a network provider's contract terminates. CMS established these enrollee notification requirements at § 422.111(e) in the “Medicare Program; Medicare+Choice Program” final rule, which appeared in the
Federal Register
on June 29, 2000 (
65 FR 40170
). More recently, in the Medicare Program; Contract Year 2024 Policy and Technical Changes to the Medicare Advantage Program, Medicare Prescription Drug Benefit Program, Medicare Cost Plan Program, and Programs of All-Inclusive Care for the Elderly final rule (
88 FR 22120
), hereinafter referred to as the “April 2023 final rule”, CMS established specific enrollee notification requirements for without-cause and for-cause provider contract terminations and added specific and more stringent enrollee notification requirements when primary care and behavioral health provider contract terminations occur. CMS also revised § 422.2267(e)(12) to specify the required content of the provider termination notice.
Under current regulations at § 422.111(e), CMS codified distinct time periods, by provider type, as part of the enrollee notification requirements regarding changes to provider networks. MA organizations are required to provide enrollees with advance notice (30 to 45 days depending on the provider type) when a provider is terminated from the MA plan's network. This advance notice is intended to allow enrollees sufficient time to identify a new in-network provider or, where applicable, exercise a SEP to change MA plans.
However, CMS has observed that provider contract negotiations frequently continue after advance notices are issued, and that in many cases terminations do not ultimately occur. As a result, enrollees may make unnecessary changes to their care arrangements (including switching providers or disenrolling from their current plan). Additionally, current regulations do not include standardized continuity of care requirements following an actual provider termination, leaving a potential gap in enrollee protections during the transition period.
The requirement for written notification to enrollees regarding their eligibility for the SEP for Significant Change in Provider Network (§ 422.62(b)(23)(iii)) is currently separate and distinct from the requirement that MA plans provide enrollees advance notice of routine provider terminations (§§ 422.111(e) and 422.2267(e)(12)). MA organizations must comply with different notice standards, timing requirements, and recipient populations. As a result, MA plans may be required to send multiple notices regarding related provider network changes and, in some cases, more than one notice to the same enrollee.
To address the gaps identified above, CMS is proposing changes to §§ 422.111(e), 422.112(b), 422.2267(e)(12), and 422.62(b)(23)(iii) that will reduce operational complexity and compliance risk for MA organizations and streamline communications for enrollees.
Under § 422.62(b)(23), individuals affected by a significant change in a plan provider network are eligible for a SEP that permits disenrollment from the MA plan that has changed its network. CMS has not codified the criteria it uses to identify a significant change in a plan provider network for purposes of triggering this SEP. This has resulted in inconsistent plan reporting, potentially uneven application of enrollee protections, and a lack of transparency regarding when affected enrollees are eligible for a SEP. Therefore, CMS is proposing to codify the process, including establishing notification requirements, evaluation criteria, and applicable timeframes.
Finally, CMS is proposing to revise the application of “affected enrollee” at § 422.62(b)(23)(ii) to align it with the enrollee population already identified in the provider termination notice requirements at § 422.111(e). This would more effectively target the enrollee population with an active and meaningful relationship with their provider and support the consolidation of the provider termination notice and the SEP eligibility notice into a single communication to affected enrollees.
3. Proposed Regulatory Changes
a. Identification of Affected Enrollee: Provider Termination Notification (§ 422.111(e))
Prior to the April 2023 final rule, CMS addressed the meaning of “affected enrollee” through subregulatory guidance in Section 110.1.2.3 of Chapter 4 of the Medicare Managed Care Manual, which identified affected enrollees as those “assigned to, currently receiving care from, or have received care within the past three months from a provider or facility being terminated.” That three-month lookback standard applied uniformly across all provider types.
In the April 2023 final rule, CMS codified the enrollee notification requirements at § 422.111(e) and established distinct lookback periods to identify affected enrollees based on the provider type. For primary care and behavioral health provider terminations, CMS codified a 3-year lookback period at § 422.111(e)(1)(iii). For all other specialty types, CMS retained the 3-month lookback standard at § 422.111(e)(2)(iii). Additionally, the April 2023 final rule included in § 422.111(e)(1)(iii) a separate category of enrollees “currently assigned” to the terminating primary care provider, which was designed primarily for HMO-model MA plans in which enrollees are required to designate a primary care provider as a condition of enrollment.
To identify affected enrollees, CMS is proposing to replace the existing provider-type-specific lookback framework with a uniform 12-month lookback for all provider types. The three-month lookback for specialty provider terminations does not reliably capture enrollees with a meaningful care relationship with the terminating provider. Enrollees may see specialists on a routine annual or semiannual basis, and under the current standard, those enrollees are not recognized as affected enrollees for purposes of receiving a provider termination notice. A uniform 12-month lookback captures enrollees with a meaningful, active care
(
printed page 76351)
relationship with a terminating provider of any type (including specialists seen on a semiannual or annual basis who are missed by a 3-month window), while avoiding the overly broad 3-year lookback period, which could extend to enrollees who do not have an ongoing care relationship with a terminated provider. Moreover, the current framework requires MA organizations to run separate lookback queries and maintain two separate enrollee populations for a single provider contract termination. A uniform 12-month lookback period would allow the MA organization to identify all affected enrollees using a single standard applied to the same contract termination.
Therefore, CMS proposes to modify § 422.111 by removing the existing provider-type-specific lookback framework and adding a paragraph at § 422.111(e)(3) that establishes a notification requirement for all enrollees who are currently receiving care, or have received care within the past 12 months, from a contracted provider being terminated. Under the proposed rule, MA organizations would identify affected enrollees through a single query, maintain one list, and issue one notice. A uniform standard also supports the consolidation of the provider termination notice and, where applicable, the significant provider termination SEP eligibility notice into a single communication directed to a single, consistently defined enrollee population.
CMS is also proposing to remove the “currently assigned” category described at § 422.111(e)(1)(iii). Primary care physician (PCP) assignment is a structural feature of plan design in HMO-model MA plans, in which enrollees are required to designate a PCP as a condition of enrollment. In PPO and other plan structures, formal PCP assignment is not a standard feature. As a result, whether an enrollee falls within the “currently assigned” category depends not on the nature of their care relationship with the provider but on the type of MA plan in which they are enrolled. CMS does not consider MA plan structure to be an appropriate basis for determining which enrollees are entitled to a provider termination notice. Furthermore, § 422.111(e)(1)(iii) does not define what it means to be “currently assigned” to a provider, or how MA organizations should identify which enrollees fall within this category. The absence of a regulatory definition has produced inconsistent application by MA organizations regarding who is actually eligible as an affected enrollee. The proposed 12-month lookback would replace this ambiguous category with a clear standard that applies consistently across all MA plan structures.
CMS believes that a uniform 12-month lookback would capture enrollees who have a meaningful, active care relationship with a terminating provider of any type, while excluding those whose relationship with the provider is too far back in time to warrant notification. It eliminates the need for separate lookback queries per provider type and supports the consolidation of the provider termination notice and, where applicable, the significant provider termination SEP eligibility notice into a single communication.
CMS solicits public comment on whether a uniform 12-month lookback period is the appropriate standard for identifying affected enrollees to receive the provider termination notice under § 422.111(e)(3). CMS is interested in whether this period appropriately captures enrollees with a meaningful, active care relationship with a terminating provider of any type, whether the lookback period should vary depending on the type of provider being terminated, or whether CMS should consider an alternate timeframe, such as a 6-month lookback. CMS also invites comment on whether removing the “currently assigned” category would exclude enrollees with an active care relationship with a terminating primary care provider, and whether any additional protection is warranted for enrollees who are formally assigned to a provider but have not had a clinical encounter within the past twelve months.
b. Timing for Enrollee Notification Requirements for Provider Terminations and Continuity of Care (§§ 422.111(e) and 422.112(b))
CMS proposes to require MA organizations to send a notification to affected enrollees of a provider termination within 5 business days of the effective date of the termination, rather than in advance of the termination. This change is intended to ensure that enrollees receive accurate and final information before taking action (such as changing MA plans or switching providers), thereby reducing unnecessary disruptions to care arrangements caused by premature or speculative notices. Based on CMS's experience, provider negotiations frequently result in a contract agreement; however, a final agreement may not be reached until shortly before the effective termination date. Therefore, at § 422.111(e), CMS is proposing to revise paragraph (2) to indicate MA organizations must provide enrollees notice of a termination of a contracted provider within 5 business days of the termination effective date regardless of whether the termination was for cause or without cause. CMS is proposing to remove the good faith effort standard for for-cause terminations because MA organizations would be required to notify enrollees within five business days of the termination, rather than 30 or 45 days in advance of the termination. CMS expects this later timeline to be feasible for both types of terminations. This proposed rule would shift the timing of required enrollee notifications of provider terminations and establish new minimum continuity of care standards to protect MA enrollees during provider network transitions that result from provider terminations.
Because CMS is proposing to revise the provider notification timing, CMS is also proposing a new continuity of care period designed to give affected enrollees sufficient time to transition to a new in-network provider without interruption to their coverage or an increase in their cost-sharing obligations. CMS expects that if an organization mails the notice within 5 business days of the termination date, it will arrive in a reasonable amount of time for enrollees to make any applicable changes or take action based on the contents of the notice.
These continuity of care requirements would be additional standards to implement the statutory requirement under section 1852(a) of the Act that MA organizations provide to their enrollees (by furnishing directly or through contracted providers, arranging for, or paying for) basic benefits (that is, all Part A and Part B benefits with limited exceptions) and such supplemental benefits the MA organization elects to offer. CMS has authority to adopt standards to carry out the applicable MA provisions in Title XVIII of the Act and to add new contract terms as necessary, appropriate, and not inconsistent with the statute in sections 1856(b) and 1857(e)(1) of the Act. Consistent with that authority, CMS is proposing to add to the current continuity of care regulations at § 422.112(b) by creating a new paragraph (9) to require that upon the termination of a contract between an MA organization and a provider or facility, the MA organization must continue to provide coverage for basic benefits, including items and services furnished by the terminated provider to affected enrollees at the applicable in-network cost-sharing rate for a
(
printed page 76352)
minimum coverage period of 90 days beginning on the termination effective date. The MA organization would be required to pay the provider pursuant to the requirements at § 422.214 for out-of-network providers. CMS would consider enrollees to have been affected by the provider termination if, per § 422.111(e)(3), the enrollees are currently receiving care from, or have received care within the past 12 months from, the terminated provider. This will ensure operational consistency between the notice and continuity of care requirements and will allow time for enrollees to transition to a new, in-network provider without disruption to coverage or an increase in cost-sharing. This continuity of care requirement does not extend to payments to providers that have been terminated for cause, including where the provider is excluded by the OIG or included on the preclusion list as described at §§ 422.222 and 422.224.
CMS requests comment on whether the proposed shift to notification within 5 business days of the termination, regardless of whether the termination was for cause or without cause, is appropriate, and whether MA organizations have operational constraints that would affect their ability to issue the provider termination notice within 5 business days of the effective date of the termination. CMS invites comments on whether the proposed 90-day continuity of care period is appropriate, or alternative timelines should be adopted, and whether MA organizations have operational constraints that would affect their ability to implement the proposed continuity of care requirements at § 422.112(b)(9) for the enrollee population defined at § 422.111(e)(3).
c. Technical Cross-Reference Corrections (§§ 422.111(e) and 422.2267(e)(12))
CMS is also making several additional technical changes to the provider termination notice requirements. CMS is proposing to add an exception to § 422.2267(e)(12)(ii)(C) for situations when an individual provider has died. Current CMS regulations require MA organizations to explain how an enrollee can request continuation of care with their current provider, but that instruction does not make sense when the provider is deceased. In those cases, CMS is proposing that the provider termination notice content communicate to the enrollee how to identify a new in-network provider, how to transfer their records, and how any applicable continuity of care protections would work if the termination were due to the death of the provider.
CMS is also proposing to remove the telephonic notice requirement at § 422.111(e)(1)(i) in its entirety, retaining only the requirement to provide written notice. Currently, § 422.111(e)(1)(i) requires MA organizations to provide written notice and make one attempt at telephonic notice to affected enrollees who have not opted out of calls regarding plan business as described in § 422.2264(b). CMS is proposing to remove both the telephonic notice requirement and the cross-reference to § 422.2264(b). With respect to the telephonic notice requirement, CMS received feedback indicating that the requirement added operational burden and enrollee confusion without a meaningful benefit.
Finally, CMS is proposing to update the content requirements at § 422.2267(e)(12)(ii) so that the provider termination notice reflects the effective date of the termination as proposed above. The provider termination notice would continue to include the same information currently required. CMS believes that the current advance notice framework imposes unnecessary operational burden on MA organizations by requiring the issuance of enrollee notifications while contract negotiations remain active, often resulting in notices that must be later retracted when a termination is averted. Aligning notification with the termination effective date eliminates this duplicative work and reduces administrative burden without compromising enrollee protections. Where continuity of care protections under § 422.112(b)(9) apply, MA organizations must include in the notice the minimum coverage period beginning on the termination effective date, that coverage is provided at the applicable in-network cost-sharing rate, and that coverage applies to basic benefits furnished by the terminated provider. As a conforming change, CMS is also proposing to remove § 422.2267(e)(12)(iii). That paragraph specifies that the telephonic notice required under § 422.111(e)(1)(i) must relay the same information as the written provider termination notice. Because CMS is proposing to remove the telephonic notice requirement from § 422.111(e)(1)(i), § 422.2267(e)(12)(iii) would no longer serve its original purpose and would be removed. CMS is also correcting an incorrect cross-reference in § 422.2267(e)(12)(ii)(D). That subparagraph currently directs enrollees to request consideration for a SEP “as specified in § 422.62(b)(26),” but that provision is being renumbered to § 422.62(b)(28) in this proposed rule. CMS is proposing to revise § 422.2267(e)(12)(ii)(D) to cite the correct regulation.
CMS solicits comment on all proposed technical changes to the provider termination notice requirements in this section.
d. SEP Eligibility Information in the Provider Termination Notice (§§ 422.2267(e)(12)(ii)(D) and 422.62(b)(23)(iii))
Currently, the written notice required to inform enrollees of their eligibility for the SEP based on a Significant Change in Provider Network (§ 422.62(b)(23)(iii)) operates separately from the advance notice MA organizations must provide for routine provider terminations (§§ 422.111(e) and 422.2267(e)(12)). Each notice obligation carries its own standards, timing, and intended recipients. Accordingly, MA organizations may need to issue more than one notice concerning related provider network changes, including multiple notices to the same enrollee where applicable.
To streamline these communications, CMS proposes to modify §§ 422.2267(e)(12)(ii)(D) and 422.62(b)(23)(iii) to require an MA organization to include information about SEP eligibility in the provider termination notice in cases where CMS has determined that the affected enrollee is eligible for the SEP described at § 422.62(b)(23), that is, if the termination has been determined by CMS to be a significant change in the MA plan's provider network under the new § 422.112(d) as proposed in section III.E.3.e of this proposed rule. Specifically, CMS is proposing to require under § 422.62(b)(23)(iii) that when CMS has determined that a provider termination is significant, MA organizations include information regarding an enrollee's eligibility for a SEP in the provider termination notice required under § 422.111(e), and how to use the SEP as described in § 422.2267(e)(12)(ii)(D).
Effectively, this means that for any provider termination, affected enrollees will only receive a single notification from the MA organization. If CMS determines that a provider termination is significant, that notification will inform the enrollees that they are eligible for a SEP. This change is intended to reduce operational burden and compliance risk for MA organizations while simplifying and clarifying communications for enrollees.
Not every enrollee who receives a provider termination notice is eligible for the significant provider termination SEP under § 422.62(b)(23). For cases in
(
printed page 76353)
which the termination has been determined not significant in accordance with § 422.112(d), the MA organization would not include significant provider termination SEP content in the notice. Nonetheless, all enrollees may also request access to the exceptional circumstances SEP under § 422.62(b)(28), which provides a separate pathway for enrollees facing coverage disruptions. That SEP is not automatic; it depends on an individual's unique circumstances and is determined on a case-by-case basis and is available regardless of whether the provider termination qualifies as significant. The criteria and process for the significance determination are being proposed in this rule under § 422.112(d), as addressed in section III.E.3.e.(2) of this proposed rule.
