e. Significant Change in Plan Provider Network (§ 422.112(d) and § 422.62(b)(23)(ii))
(1) Background
When a mid-year provider termination constitutes a “significant” change in a plan's provider network, affected enrollees are eligible for a SEP that allows them to enroll in another MA plan or to disenroll to Original Medicare. CMS is authorized to establish SEPs under section 1851(e) of the Act, including section 1851(e)(4) of the Act, which authorizes the Secretary to establish SEPs for individuals who meet other exceptional conditions specified by the Secretary, and § 1852(b)(1) of the Act, which governs MA organization obligations regarding enrollment and disenrollment.
The SEP for Significant Change in Provider Network was established in CY 2015 in response to significant mid-year network disruptions affecting MA enrollees and was subsequently codified at § 422.62(b)(23) in the Medicare Program; Contract Year 2021 Policy and Technical Changes to the Medicare Advantage Program, Medicare Prescription Drug Benefit Program, and Medicare Cost Plan Program Final Rule (
85 FR 33796
). In that final rule, CMS specified that significant changes in provider networks are those that go beyond individual or limited provider terminations that occur during the routine course of plan operations, and that have the potential to substantially impact a large number of the MA plan's enrollees, such as terminated relationships with multispecialty group practices or hospital systems.
Under the current framework, when CMS determines that a change in an MA plan's provider network is significant, affected enrollees are eligible for the SEP and may use it to request enrollment in another MA plan or to disenroll to Original Medicare from the MA plan that has changed its network. As described at § 422.62(b)(23)(ii), enrollees are “affected” by a significant network change and eligible for this SEP when they are assigned to, are currently receiving care from, or have received care within the past three months from a provider or facility being terminated from the MA plan's provider network. The SEP begins the month the individual is notified of eligibility and extends an additional two calendar months thereafter under § 422.62(b)(23)(i).
CMS has provided subregulatory guidance on significant network changes in Chapter 4 of the Medicare Managed Care Manual. Under that guidance, MA organizations have been directed to notify CMS of any provider termination that the MA organization deems to be a significant provider termination at least 90 days prior to the effective date. After receiving such notification, CMS reviews to determine whether the change in provider network is significant. The timeframe for CMS determinations has varied depending on the circumstances of each case. If CMS determines that a provider termination represents a significant change in the MA plan's provider network, the CMS Account Manager for the MA organization notifies the MA organization of the determination and of the requirement to issue written notification to affected enrollees of their eligibility for the SEP for significant change in provider network, the start and end dates of the SEP, how to make use of the SEP, and Medigap guaranteed issue rights in accordance with section 1882(s)(3)(D) of the Act. CMS provides model language regarding the SEP and Medigap guaranteed issue rights for the MA organization to use in its notice to affected enrollees.
As a separate requirement, MA organizations must notify affected enrollees of any changes in a provider network resulting from a termination (with or without cause) of a contract with a provider organization pursuant to §§ 422.111(e) and 422.2267(e)(12). Currently, the requirement for written notification to enrollees regarding their eligibility for the SEP for Significant Change in Provider Network (§ 422.62(b)(23)(iii)) is separate and distinct from the requirement that MA organizations provide enrollees advance notice of routine provider terminations (§§ 422.111(e) and 422.2267(e)(12)). As discussed in section III.E.3.d of this preamble section, CMS is proposing to consolidate these two notice requirements into a single communication to affected enrollees; the proposals in this section are designed to support and streamline that consolidation.
Despite the existence of this SEP framework, CMS has not previously codified in regulation the specific criteria it uses to evaluate whether a provider termination is significant. This approach has created a significant operational gap with material consequences for beneficiaries and program administration. MA organizations exercise discretion when deciding whether a change is significant and, accordingly, whether to notify CMS. Because CMS has not codified the criteria it uses to evaluate significance, MA organizations apply varying internal standards—some may not report a termination to CMS because they do not believe it meets the significance threshold, while others may apply different or inconsistent criteria. This inconsistency means that CMS may not be evaluating all terminations that meet its significance threshold, and that some enrollees who are eligible for a SEP are not appropriately notified of their eligibility and thus unable to use this protection.
Therefore, CMS proposes to codify the criteria used to identify a significant change in a MA plan provider network. This approach preserves the distinction between routine provider terminations and those that are sufficiently disruptive to warrant SEP eligibility, while providing transparency, consistency, and accountability.
(2) Notification Thresholds and Timeline (§ 422.112(d))
CMS is proposing to establish notification thresholds for significant provider terminations at new § 422.112(d). The proposal would require an MA organization to notify CMS of a contracted provider termination that meets either of the following thresholds at least 60 days prior to the effective date of the termination for without-cause terminations and when practicable for for-cause terminations: (i) at least 10 percent of the MA plan's enrollees would be affected by the provider termination under § 422.62(b)(23)(ii); or (ii) the provider termination would constitute at least 10 percent of the MA plan's network for a given specialty type
(
printed page 76354)
under §§ 422.116(b)(1) or (2). When a termination meets either threshold, it would be deemed “significant.” Upon notification, CMS would inform the MA organization of the requirement to issue written notification to affected enrollees of their eligibility for a SEP, the start and end dates of the SEP, how to make use of the SEP, and Medigap guaranteed issue rights in accordance with § 1882(s)(3)(D) of the Act. CMS would provide model language for the MA organization to use when notifying affected enrollees of their SEP eligibility in accordance with § 422.62(b)(23)(iii) and § 422.2267(e)(12)(ii), as addressed in section III.E.3.d of this proposed rule.
The first threshold, enrollee impact, focuses on the direct effect of the termination on the MA plan's enrollee population. A termination that affects at least 10 percent of an MA plan's enrollees, in accordance with the definition of “affected enrollee” at § 422.62(b)(23)(ii), represents a disruption that merits CMS's awareness and the award of a SEP. This threshold is directly tied to the beneficiary protection rationale underlying the SEP: when a substantial portion of a plan's enrollees lose access to a provider with whom they have an established care relationship, those enrollees should have the opportunity to seek coverage from a plan that includes their provider.
The second threshold, specialty network, focuses on enrollee access limitations due to changes to the plan's provider network. A termination that eliminates 10 percent or more of a plan's contracted network for a given specialty type under § 422.116(b)(1) or (2) represents a material reduction in enrollee access to covered services in that specialty. This threshold fits within CMS's existing framework under § 422.116, under which CMS already evaluates networks by specialty category and provider counts. The specialty network threshold recognizes that substantial contraction in a specialty network may impair access to medically necessary services, especially for beneficiaries in smaller MA plans, for which the loss of a single provider or practice group can represent a disproportionate share of available contracted capacity. Applying the enrollee impact threshold alone may miss these types of terminations, for which the enrollee impact is significant due to diminished access to a given specialty.
CMS believes a 10 percent threshold represents a balanced approach that appropriately distinguishes material network changes from routine contracting activity, while providing greater transparency, consistency, and predictability for beneficiaries, MA organizations, and CMS oversight operations. CMS chose percentage-based thresholds, as opposed to fixed provider counts, because percentage-based thresholds account for variation in plan enrollment size, network size, geography, and specialty concentration. A fixed provider count that is appropriate for a large urban network may be wholly inadequate to capture a significant disruption in a rural specialty market. For example, the loss of nine providers may be insignificant in a large urban network with hundreds of contracted specialists but devastating in a rural specialty market where those nine providers represent the majority of available contracted capacity. A percentage-based threshold scales appropriately across these varying contexts.
The 10 percent threshold represents the point at which a network change transitions from routine contracting activity to a disruption of sufficient scale to merit CMS awareness and enrollee notification. A lower threshold would be overinclusive, capturing routine contracting fluctuations that do not rise to the level of a significant network change and imposing unnecessary administrative burden on MA organizations and CMS. A higher threshold would be under-protective, permitting substantial network disruptions to proceed without CMS review or enrollee notification. A 10-percent threshold reasonably balances these competing concerns and is consistent with CMS's longstanding internal practice for evaluating significance.
CMS solicits comment on whether 10 percent is the appropriate threshold for the enrollee impact under proposed § 422.112(d)(1)(i). CMS is interested in whether a lower threshold would better protect beneficiaries in markets where even a smaller percentage of affected enrollees represents a significant disruption, or whether a higher threshold would more appropriately limit the significance determination to truly material network changes. CMS also invites comment on whether the threshold should vary based on plan size, market type, or other factors. Additionally, CMS solicits comment on whether 10 percent is the appropriate threshold for the specialty network under proposed § 422.112(d)(1)(ii). CMS is interested in whether this threshold appropriately captures network disruptions that impair access to covered services in a given specialty, and whether it should be calibrated differently for different specialty types, geographic markets, or plan types.
The proposed 60-day advance notification requirement for without-cause terminations aligns with the existing § 422.202(d)(4) provider notification timeframe, making it feasible for MA organizations and consistent with existing operational practice. Because the proposed rule codifies objective, quantitative thresholds, MA organizations will already have confirmed that they have met the threshold before notifying CMS, which will streamline CMS's internal review process. The 60-day window would be sufficient for CMS to review a significance determination and provide model language to the MA organization before the termination takes effect. This approach is expected to reduce burden on MA organizations relative to the current subregulatory guidance, which directs MA organizations to notify CMS 90 days in advance. CMS understands that for-cause terminations may occur without 60-days advanced notice, and therefore, MA plans may not be able to notify CMS 60 days before the termination date. Accordingly, CMS proposes to codify that MA plans notify CMS when practicable for for-cause terminations.
CMS maintains the right to inquire about provider terminations that were not reported by an MA organization when external information (including congressional inquiries, beneficiary complaints, or other sources) suggests that a significant termination may have occurred. The proposed codification of significance determination criteria does not limit CMS's existing oversight authority; it supplements that authority by establishing clear, enforceable reporting obligations. Because the significance determination criteria would now be codified in regulation, MA organizations would be on notice of the circumstances under which they are required to report a provider termination to CMS. Failure to report a qualifying termination in accordance with proposed § 422.112(d) would be subject to compliance action. MA organizations have previously requested clarity regarding reporting thresholds; codification would provide both the clarity they have sought and the accountability that the program requires.
CMS solicits comment on whether the proposed 60-day advance notification requirement for MA organizations to notify CMS of without-cause significant provider terminations and when practicable for for-cause terminations under § 422.112(d) is appropriate, and whether MA organizations have operational constraints that would affect
(
printed page 76355)
their ability to notify CMS within these timeframes.
(3) Identification of “Affected Enrollee” for the SEP (§ 422.62(b)(23)(ii))
Current § 422.62(b)(23)(ii) provides that an enrollee is affected by a significant network change when the enrollee is assigned to, currently receiving care from, or has received care within the past 3 months from a provider or facility being terminated from the provider network. CMS is proposing to replace this framework with a uniform 12-month lookback for all provider types and to remove the “assigned to” category, for the same reasons CMS is making those changes to the provider termination notice requirement at proposed § 422.111(e)(3): the 3-month lookback does not reliably capture enrollees with a meaningful care relationship with the terminating provider for SEP purposes. A uniform 12-month lookback would capture enrollees with a meaningful, active care relationship with a terminating provider of any type, including specialists seen on a semiannual or annual basis who would be missed by a three-month window.
CMS believes this proposed change would provide particular benefit to beneficiaries in rural areas, beneficiaries with complex care needs, and beneficiaries who depend on continuity with a specific provider. In rural markets, provider networks are often smaller, and the loss of a single provider or practice group can represent a disproportionate share of available contracted capacity. A significant termination in a rural market may leave beneficiaries with few or no in-network alternatives, making timely SEP notification critical to protecting their access to medically necessary services. Similarly, beneficiaries with complex care needs who have established ongoing treatment relationships with a specialist are particularly vulnerable to disruptions caused by mid-year provider terminations, and the proposed framework is designed to ensure that those affected beneficiaries are identified and notified appropriately.
CMS is also proposing to remove the “assigned to” category from § 422.62(b)(23)(ii). As discussed in section III.E.3.a of this proposed rule, PCP assignment is a structural feature of HMO-model MA plans and does not apply consistently across PPO and other plan structures.
Under the current framework, the enrollee population identified as “affected” for SEP purposes under § 422.62(b)(23)(ii) differs from the enrollee population identified for provider termination notice purposes under § 422.111(e), even though both determinations are made by the MA organization using the same underlying data. This inconsistency requires MA organizations to identify and manage two separate enrollee populations for what is, in effect, a single network disruption event. A uniform standard would eliminate the need for MA organizations to run separate queries and maintain separate enrollee populations by provider type and would directly support the consolidation of the provider termination notice and the SEP eligibility notice into a single communication—a consolidation that is only operationally feasible when both notices are directed to the same enrollee population.
CMS solicits comment on the proposed uniform 12-month lookback period to determine whether an enrollee is affected by a significant network change at § 422.62(b)(23)(ii). CMS invites comment on whether this period appropriately captures enrollees with an established care relationship with the terminated provider, and whether alternative lookback periods would better serve the purposes of the SEP. Finally, CMS invites comment on any other aspects of the proposals described in this section, including the alignment of the affected enrollee definition with the enrollee populations identified in § 422.111(e)(3).
F. Network Adequacy Exception Request Rationales (§ 422.116)

on December 10, 2024 (

CMS proposed to eliminate the rationale that the “provider does not contract with any organization or contracts exclusively with another organization” (meaning MA organization) as a basis for an exception. In the proposed rule, CMS indicated that in removing this rationale, CMS's intent was to limit the reasons that an organization would be able to bypass the established network adequacy criteria for a given specialty/county and provide greater incentives for MA organizations to establish contracts with providers that are located within the established time and distance standards. Based on comments received through the comment process for the December 2024 proposed rule, CMS has decided to reconsider this proposal and is proposing to codify all existing exception request rationales, including the rationale: “provider does not contract with any organization or contracts exclusively with another organization.”
Under CMS's authority to set standards to implement and carry out the MA statute (in section 1856(b)(1) of the Act), CMS codified network adequacy standards at § 422.116 under the final rule, Medicare Program; Contract Year 2021 Policy and Technical Changes to the Medicare Advantage Program, Medicare Prescription Drug Benefit Program, and Medicare Cost Plan Program, which appeared in the

In the June 2020 final rule, CMS codified regulations allowing MA organizations to submit exceptions to the network adequacy standards in § 422.116, including the circumstances under which an MA organization may request an exception (§ 422.116(f)(1)) and the factors that CMS considers when evaluating an MA organization's request for an exception (§ 422.116(f)(2)) as well as examples of how those factors are applied. An MA plan may request the exception permitted under § 422.116(f)(1)(i) if (A) certain providers or facilities are not available for the MA plan to meet the network adequacy criteria as shown in the Provider Supply file for the year for a given county and specialty type and (B) the MA plan has contracted with other providers and facilities that may be located beyond the limits in the time and distance criteria, but are currently available and accessible to most enrollees, consistent with the local pattern of care.

CMS explained in the Medicare Advantage and Section 1876 Cost Plan Network Adequacy Guidance that while the time and distance standards vary by county and specialty type, and are generally attainable across the country, there are unique instances where a given county's supply of providers/facilities is such that an MA organization would not be able to meet the network adequacy criteria. The exceptions process allows MA organizations to provide evidence to CMS when the health care market landscape has changed or is not reflected in the current CMS network adequacy criteria. The organization must include conclusive evidence in its exception request that the CMS network adequacy criteria cannot be met because of changes to the availability of providers/facilities, resulting in insufficient supply.
Per § 422.116(f)(1)(i), an MA plan may request an exception to network adequacy criteria when both of the following occur: (A) certain providers or facilities are not available for the MA plan to meet the network adequacy criteria as shown in the Provider Supply file for the year for a given county and specialty type; and (B) the MA plan has contracted with other providers and facilities that may be located beyond the limits in the time and distance criteria, but are currently available and accessible to most enrollees, consistent with the local pattern of care.
As part of CMS's evaluation of MA networks using § 422.116, MA organizations must first submit their Health Service Delivery (HSD) tables, containing all their network providers, to CMS. CMS processes and reviews the network submissions against its established regulatory standards through use of an automated system located in the Health Plan Management Systems (HPMS) network management module. This automated module within HPMS evaluates the networks based on CMS's current network time and distance standards. Once the evaluation is complete, CMS, through HPMS, provides MA organizations with an Automated Criteria Check (ACC) report. The ACC report contains CMS's determination of whether the standards in § 422.116 have been met or not met, and the report displays where the MA organization's specific county/specialty combinations, within the given service area, are passing and failing those standards. MA organizations may decide to submit an exception request for those parts of their network submission that were found to be failing CMS's network time and distance standards by using the exception request template found in HPMS, in accordance with CMS procedural instructions.
After submission, CMS evaluates exception requests based on the criteria noted in § 422.116(f)(2), including whether the current access to providers and facilities is different from the HSD reference and Provider Supply files for the year (see § 422.116(a)(5)), whether the MA organization demonstrates that network access is consistent with or better than the original Medicare pattern of care, and whether approval of the exception is in the best interest of beneficiaries. The exception request is then either approved or denied. Once the CMS exception request review is complete, the results of CMS's determination are uploaded into HPMS with an approval or denial status for MA organizations to view. If an exception request is denied, CMS will provide feedback with the exception disposition, including, as applicable, a sampling of the providers that CMS lists in the Provider Supply File that are available for the MA organization to contract with that would allow the MA organization to meet the time and distance standards for the specific county/specialty type. MA organizations must resubmit all previously approved exception requests whenever CMS requests an organization to upload its HSD tables to review an MA organization's network(s).
CMS received mixed feedback regarding the proposal to codify exception request rationales with one change to remove the rationale, “provider does not contract with any organization or contracts exclusively with another organization” in the December 2024 proposed rule. With regard to the portion of the proposal related to removing the “provider does not contract” rationale, supporters noted that the change would improve both network adequacy reviews and oversight of MA organizations' networks, while other commenters indicated that eliminating the exception rationale would decrease flexibility for MA organizations and make it harder to assemble provider networks in rural areas or areas with limited providers. Commenters on this portion of the proposal also noted that MA organizations cannot force contractual relationships with providers so having this rationale provides latitude in building networks and maintains enrollee choice. Finally, commenters argued that with the proposal to remove the rationale, CMS would be inappropriately inserting itself into contracting negotiations between MA plans and providers. Otherwise, commenters were largely supportive of the overall proposal for CMS to codify the long-standing network adequacy exception request rationales.
CMS agrees that codifying the exception request rationales will improve network adequacy reviews, making them more consistent and based on codified standards. Additionally, CMS agrees that MA organizations should retain flexibility in contracting, which the rationale “provider does not contract with any organization or contracts exclusively with another organization” gives in the network review process. Therefore, based on comments received on the initial proposal and to continue to strengthen CMS's network adequacy review process and rules related to exception requests, CMS is proposing to codify the following (including the rationale, “provider does not contract with any MA organization or contracts exclusively with another MA organization”) as valid rationales when an MA plan submits substantial and credible evidence, in the form and manner requested by CMS, to demonstrate that an exception request meets the requirements under § 422.116(f)(1)(i):
Provider is no longer practicing (for example, deceased, retired).
Provider does not provide services at the office or facility address listed in the Provider Supply file in paragraph (a)(5)(ii) of this section.
Provider does not provide services for the specialty type listed in the Provider Supply file in paragraph (a)(5)(ii) of this section.
Provider has opted out of Medicare (in compliance with § 422.204(b)(4)).
Provider does not contract with any MA organizations or contracts exclusively with another MA organization.
Provider is a sanctioned provider on the List of Excluded Individuals and Entities (in compliance with § 422.204);
(
printed page 76357)
or provider is on the CMS preclusion list (in compliance with § 422.222).
Provider has the potential to cause beneficiary harm.
Provider is at capacity and is not accepting new patients.
One, or more, of the listed rationales may be used to explain the reason that an MA plan has failed to demonstrate that its network meets the minimum requirements of § 422.116(a) through (e) but MA organizations should provide CMS with as comprehensive of an explanation as possible, including supporting documentation, regarding why an exception should be granted under the standards in § 422.116(f).
As discussed in the December 2024 proposed rule, current subregulatory guidance
[
44
]
states that CMS considers certain exception rationales under an “other” category. This guidance indicates that MA organizations may use the “other” category to request other exceptions, for example, “provider does not contract with any organization,” “the provider has the potential to cause beneficiary harm,” or “the provider is inappropriately credentialed.” CMS is proposing to eliminate the “other” category, but to codify certain examples listed as permissible rationales. As described previously, CMS is proposing to codify the exception rationale “provider does not contract with any organization.” CMS is also proposing to codify the exception rationale, “provider has the potential to cause beneficiary harm”, as this exception rationale serves to safeguard the best interests of beneficiaries against any potential risks posed by providers. Finally, CMS is not proposing to codify the exception rationale “the provider is not properly credentialed” currently permitted in the “other” category. CMS regulations under § 422.204 place the responsibility for credentialing and recredentialing of providers on MA organizations and not CMS. While a provider's lack of proper credentials may support a rationale based on potential to cause beneficiary harm, CMS is not proposing to codify a separate, formal exception rationale specific to credentialing.
CMS's current subregulatory guidance also includes an exception rationale for “use of Original Medicare telehealth providers and mobile providers”. CMS is not proposing to codify the “use of Original Medicare telehealth providers and mobile providers” as an available exception rationale because the use of Original Medicare telehealth providers and mobile providers is an available avenue for fulfilling network adequacy requirements, rather than a means of satisfying the exception requirements under § 422.116(f)(1)(i)(A) and § 422.116(f)(1)(i)(B). MA organizations may contract with Original Medicare telehealth providers and mobile providers to meet network adequacy requirements, so they may be submitted in their HSD tables. CMS's guidance states that for organizations using Original Medicare telehealth providers, services must meet the requirements for “telehealth services” under section 1834(m) of the Act (for example, provider types, eligible originating sites, geography, and currently approved list of Medicare telehealth services), as well as the requirements for “communication technology-based services” not subject to the section 1834(m) of the Act limitations (brief communication technology-based service/virtual check-in, remote evaluation of pre-recorded patient information, and inter-professional internet consultation). The MA organization must demonstrate that it meets all applicable requirements. CMS's guidance also states that if an MA organization uses mobile providers (for example, mobile x-ray suppliers, orthotics and prosthetics mobile units), they must be qualified and furnish services through scheduled appointments.
As CMS has indicated in subregulatory guidance, for purposes of the exception described in § 422.116(f)(1)(i), CMS will not accept an MA organization's assertion that it cannot meet current CMS network adequacy criteria because of a general “inability to contract” that is not reflected in one of the exception request rationales. CMS does not require an MA organization to contract with any particular provider or facility, and MA organizations have significant discretion in how they meet network adequacy standards. But MA organizations must establish a sufficient network to ensure enrollee access to appropriate providers as required by section 1852(d)(1) of the Act. CMS does not consider a general representation that an MA organization is unable to contract with otherwise available providers to be a sufficient basis for allowing an exception to network adequacy criteria.
With this proposal, CMS is codifying long-standing rules related to network adequacy exception request rationales; therefore, CMS does not believe there is any additional paperwork burden to be considered. However, CMS will submit these proposed changes through PRA CMS-10636 under control number 0938-1346 for OMB review. CMS welcomes comment on these proposals, including the exhaustive list of exception request rationales proposed here, and whether there are additional rationales to consider that are in the best interest of beneficiaries. In addition, CMS is soliciting comment on potential unintended consequences from this proposal, including potential changes in the provider landscape, that could limit MA plan choice and/or availability in certain areas of the country.

for MA Medical Savings Account (MSA) plans (
63 FR 35094
).
Historically, Medicare+Choice plans commonly requested enrollment capacity limits during their bid submission. Once the program shifted from Medicare+Choice to Medicare Advantage, the number of requests declined as MA plans gained a larger market share. Moreover, prior to the CY 2027 bid submission, CMS had not received any requests for an enrollment capacity limit as part of the bid over the last decade.
Until recently, CMS had not issued specific instructions related to submission of an enrollment capacity limit as part of a plan's bid submission in the Health Plan Management System (HPMS) platform. In the Preliminary Contract Year 2027 Standards for Part C Benefits, Bid Review, and Evaluation memo, CMS reminded MA organizations of the option to submit a proposed enrollment capacity limit and included instructions for how to submit this request in HPMS with their bid. Following the preliminary bid guidance, multiple parties inquired about factors that CMS would use to evaluate and accept the proposed limit. However, section 1854(a)(1)(A)(iii) of the Act and
42 CFR 422.254(c)(4)
and
(e)(1)
do not provide specific requirements or criteria by which CMS should review limits submitted as part of a bid. Given this, CMS provided additional information on how CMS would review these requests and addressed questions in the Final Contract Year 2027 Standards for Part C Benefits, Bid Review, and
(
printed page 76358)
Evaluation memo. For 2027, CMS received 66 bid submissions with proposed enrollment capacity limits and accepted all limits as meeting the minimum threshold for acceptance based on the bid guidance. Here, CMS proposes to codify a process for how it will review enrollment capacity limits submitted as part of the bid.
CMS is proposing to codify procedures for submitting an enrollment capacity limit in HPMS consistent with the way MA plans submitted these requests in CY 2027. That is, for CY 2028 and beyond, interested plans must submit their proposed limit, along with a short narrative explaining the basis for the identified limit for CMS review, with their annual bid. Requesting an enrollment capacity limit is entirely voluntary. Enrollment capacity limits accepted as part of the bid submission process would be in effect for the duration of the calendar year and MA organizations would be prohibited from disenrolling existing members to reach an approved limit (
42 CFR 422.74(a)
). Under this proposal, CMS would only accept enrollment capacity limits at or above current enrollment as of June 1st of the year preceding the contract year for the planned service area (for example, the plan's current enrollment as of June 1, 2027, would be the minimum enrollment capacity limit allowable in CY 2028 bids for the planned service area). This approach allows plans to determine what increase in enrollment they could reasonably accommodate and address concerns about unexpected large enrollment increases due to competitors exiting the service area. CMS expects that MA organizations should have the ability to maintain their current enrollment if they are operating in good standing and provide quality care to enrollees. Under this proposal, requesting an enrollment capacity limit is optional and may be requested at or above current enrollment as of June 1st of the year preceding the contract year for the planned service area. CMS encourages, but is not proposing to require, plans to factor in projected enrollment growth between June 1 and the start of the plan year when determining what enrollment capacity number to request, if any.
Of note, the majority of enrollment capacity limits submitted in the CY 2027 bids were significantly higher than the minimum threshold (only 15 of the 66 plans requested an enrollment limit representing 0-10% growth over current enrollment, with many plans setting a limit that would represent significant growth in enrollment if it were met). This indicates that some plans are utilizing enrollment capacity limits to protect against an unexpected increase in enrollment rather than limiting any additional enrollment beyond their current enrollees. For CY 2027, CMS provided guidance that new plans, which do not have current enrollment, interested in including an enrollment capacity limit in their bid should utilize the assumptions on their plan's projected enrollment used in the Bid Pricing Tool to inform their proposed limit.
For CY 2028 and subsequent years, CMS is proposing a similar approach, with some modifications. If an MA organization is submitting a bid for a new plan benefit package (PBP) for a new contract, the plan should use its projected enrollment and bid assumptions to propose an enrollment capacity limit. Similarly, if an MA organization adds a new PBP to an existing contract, while all other PBPs of the same type within the contract continue to operate for the upcoming year, the plan can use their projected enrollment and bid assumptions to propose a limit. CMS will consider two or more PBPs to be the same type when they are both the same type of special needs plan (SNP) or the same type of non-SNP. For example, two PBPs are the same type if they are both C-SNPs that focus on diabetes or if they are both facility-based I-SNPs. Of note, all PBPs within a single contract are either health maintenance organizations, preferred provider organizations, cost plans, or medical savings account plans by default.
For an MA organization that is closing a PBP and also opening a new PBP (or PBPs) of the same type under the same contract, CMS will only approve an enrollment capacity limit that is at least as high as the current June enrollment for the proposed service area for the existing PBP(s) that are non-renewing. Take for example a 2027 contract with four health maintenance organization PBPs: a D-SNP, C-SNP and two non-SNPs. For 2028, the MA organization plans to non-renew the C-SNP PBP and one of the non-SNP PBPs, and create a new non-SNP PBP. The minimum threshold for the new non-SNP PBP in this example would be the June 1, 2027, enrollment for the proposed service area from the non-renewing non-SNP PBP only. This approach will also apply to new PBPs where MA organizations are seeking to cross-walk enrollees from a non-renewing PBP into the new PBP. However, acceptance of an enrollment capacity limit is not contingent on CMS allowing the proposed cross-walk exemption.
In instances where an MA organization is non-renewing multiple PBPs and opening a new PBP of the same type under the same contract, the minimum threshold for the new PBP should be the current June 1st enrollment for the proposed service area in aggregate. Conversely, if there are two new PBPs with one non-renewing plan, CMS would compare the June enrollment for the non-renewing plan to the aggregate of limit(s) requested in the two new PBPs as the minimum threshold that would be accepted. In each of these scenarios, it is important to note that the minimum threshold is based on the current June 1st enrollment for the proposed service area for the upcoming bid year. This means that if an MA organization is opening a new PBP for an existing contract in one service area and closing a PBP of the same type in an entirely different service area, there would be no minimum threshold for that new PBP. This proposed update would avoid incentivizing MA organizations to close existing plans and open new plans in the same service area under the same contract in order to avoid the minimum threshold proposed by CMS and would promote similar access to new plans for individuals enrolled in non-renewing MA plans.
For the 2027 contract year, CMS encouraged plans to consider projected enrollment growth between the timing of the bid submission and the start of the plan year on January 1, 2027, when proposing an enrollment capacity limit in their bid. CMS is soliciting comments on the proposed minimum threshold of June 1st enrollment preceding the contract year or whether a higher minimum should be established (for example, a specified percentage higher than current enrollment) for what CMS may approve. Setting a higher minimum threshold could prevent plans exceeding their approved enrollment capacity limit for the upcoming year prior to the Annual Enrollment Period (AEP), thus essentially being closed to beneficiaries who would like to switch plans (for example, to a higher-rated plan or one with a specific in-network provider). CMS encouraged plans to take this potential scenario into account for the CY 2027 bid submission by suggesting plans incorporate some buffer in their enrollment capacity limit requests. CMS could formalize this recommendation by setting a higher numerical limit necessary for approval (for example, 5 percent, 10 percent, or another growth percentage above the current enrollment as of June 1st for the preceding plan year). CMS also seeks comment on the approach to new PBPs and how the minimum threshold is
(
printed page 76359)
applied in the different scenarios articulated above.
Beyond the numerical minimum threshold, CMS received several inquiries regarding whether additional factors would be used to evaluate and accept the proposed limit after issuing the CY 2027 guidance. Section 1854(a)(1)(A)(iii) and
42 CFR 422.254(c)(4)
and
(e)(1)
do not provide specific requirements or criteria by which CMS should review enrollment capacity limits. For CY 2027, there were no other factors used to evaluate acceptance of proposed limits beyond confirmation that the requested limit was at or higher than the minimum threshold and submission of a supporting narrative. Because CMS has an obligation to ensure that there is access to care for enrollees and beneficiary choice, CMS is proposing to codify that plans would be required to provide a written narrative explaining how they arrived at the requested limit (for example, their current enrollment, provider networks, available access to care or other metrics). Under this proposal, if an MA organization submits an enrollment capacity limit with their bid that is lower than the minimum threshold or fails to provide the required written narrative, CMS would offer the MA organization a chance to cure their submission prior to making a final determination.
CMS is seeking comment on what additional criteria, if any, CMS should use to evaluate limits proposed by MA organizations in bid submissions and may consider incorporating additional criteria from public comments in the final rule. In developing this proposal, CMS considered defining additional requirements for qualifying justifications that the plan would need to demonstrate in their submitted narrative. For example, CMS could require that MA plans provide a summary of current enrollment, capacity of the anticipated provider networks, timeliness in care for current enrollees, quality performance, and any current and anticipated operational challenges (for example, challenges hiring sufficient care managers, IT infrastructure) as part of their rationale to demonstrate how additional enrollment beyond their proposed limit could potentially jeopardize quality of care. Under this scenario, CMS could then base approval decisions on the strength of the submitted rationale. Further, CMS could put forward criteria that would allow CMS to reject a proposed enrollment capacity limit, such as if there are limited MA offerings in a particular area and multiple plans request enrollment capacity limits at or near the minimum threshold.
CMS recognizes that MA plans already make business decisions as part of their bid and employ marketing strategies that might impact enrollment. CMS also believes that enrollment capacity limits submitted with the bid should be considered another tool for plans to ensure that they are able to provide high-quality care and ensure provider access for their current enrollees and these proposed procedures to align with this understanding.
In summary, CMS is proposing to codify procedures regarding enrollment capacity limits submitted in the bid in recognition that these submissions are permitted by statute and appropriate as a formal component of the bid submission process. To effectuate these changes, CMS is proposing to revise § 422.254(c)(4) and § 422.254(e)(1) to establish criteria for CMS review of requests submitted as part of the bid by inserting the following language under each section: “(i) Proposed enrollment capacity limits must not be below the current enrollment as of June 1 of the year preceding the contract year for the planned service area. (ii) Plans submitting a proposed enrollment capacity limit must include a supporting narrative that describes how the limit was derived. (iii) For a plan in a new contract or a new plan to be offered under an existing contract without any non-renewing plans in the proposed service area for the contract year, there is no minimum limit for acceptance. (iv) For a new plan to be offered under an existing contract, the proposed enrollment capacity limit must not be below the aggregate current enrollment as of June 1 of the year preceding the contract year for the planned service area for any non-renewing plans of the same plan type within the contract.”
1. Enrollment Capacity Limits Submitted Outside the Bid via
42 CFR 422.60(b)(3)
Currently, MA plans may also request an enrollment capacity limit outside of the bid submission process. In 2000, CMS finalized a regulation at
42 CFR 422.60(b)(3)
that it would consider “enrollment limit requests for an M+C plan service area, other than those submitted with the adjusted community rate proposal, or for a portion of the plan service area, only if the health and safety of beneficiaries is at risk, such as if the provider network is not available to serve the enrollees in all or a portion of the service area” (
65 FR 40170
). CMS noted that this change was spurred by the bid submission deadline moving several months earlier due to the Balanced Budget Refinement Act of 1999 and in recognition that there may be other reasons Medicare+Choice plans may want to submit these requests outside of the bid submission. The preamble language did not further describe how CMS would define the health and safety standard but did state that “the circumstances under which a capacity limit will be approved after the ACRP date would likely occur when a portion of a provider network that furnishes an M+C plan becomes unavailable during the course of a contract year.” In 2005, CMS updated the language to the current text: “CMS considers enrollment limit requests for an MA plan service area, or a portion of the plan service area, only if the health and safety of beneficiaries is at risk, such as if the provider network is not available to serve enrollees in all or a portion of the service area” (
70 FR 4588
). When proposing the update, CMS noted that there could be several scenarios when an MA organization may need to restrict enrollment for capacity reasons because their ability to serve the potential number of enrollees it previously estimated it could would be significantly impacted, such as when a plan loses a sizable contract with a health system or physician group (
69 FR 46866
). In the final rule (
70 FR 4588
), CMS stated that the “ability to request a capacity limit is an important element of the MA program that helps ensure that plan enrollees will have sufficient access to needed providers and services. CMS's approval of a capacity limit request indicates that CMS agrees with the requesting MA organization that its defined network of providers is sufficient to deliver health care only to a limited number of plan members.” However, CMS did not define or provide additional examples of scenarios when the health and safety of beneficiaries is at risk, or how to objectively evaluate plans' capacity to absorb additional enrollees with their current provider networks. For example, if one large competitor leaves a market, and there are many available plans, enrollees may be dispersed across multiple plans, thus avoiding any potential shocks and any resulting harm that may be experienced by the receiving plans and their enrollees.
Since these rules were promulgated, CMS has received very few enrollment capacity limit requests outside of the bid submission. In fact, the few that were received in 2025 were the first in many years. When reviewing the 2025 requests, CMS reviewed the materials
(
printed page 76360)
shared by MA organizations for their specific plans to determine whether the health and safety standard at § 422.60(b)(3) was met. CMS interprets the health and safety standard at § 422.60(b)(3) to be based on present and documented risk to enrollees. Where an MA organization seeks a post-bid enrollment capacity limit based solely on anticipated challenges and the projected downstream impact to enrollees, these rationales are inherently speculative. Such requests cited concerns related to large organizations exiting markets or reducing plan offerings, anticipated operational challenges, expected increases in enrollment, provider network capacity, and potential effects on quality measures and Star Ratings. To date, CMS has denied all of these requests because the supporting evidence was speculative in nature, relying on projected market fluctuations and hypothetical enrollment shifts. In reviewing the market exits, CMS noted the impacted service areas had a variety of plans that could receive displaced enrollees. Moreover, none of the requesting plans demonstrated a concrete risk to beneficiary health and safety.
Since § 422.60(b)(3) was first promulgated, additional tools and policies have been developed within the MA program to address the concerns around provider access and protecting enrollees that were the impetus for this policy. CMS has broad authority to impose intermediate sanctions under
42 CFR part 422 Subpart O
for a variety of reasons. CMS also has flexibility to determine which sanctions are imposed, with discretion on whether to prohibit marketing by a plan, impose an enrollment sanction, and/or impose civil money penalties. When an MA organization fails to comply with program requirements, including requirements related to access to providers and services, CMS may, where appropriate, impose intermediate sanctions, restrict new enrollment into the plan, and allow current enrollees to switch plans via a special election period (SEP) (
42 CFR 422.62(b)(5)
,
42 CFR 423.38(c)(12)
). The availability of intermediate sanctions provides protection for enrollees, without placing undue constraints on enrollee plan choices and access.
Moreover, CMS is concerned that allowing requests for enrollment capacity limits outside of the formal bid process and based on projected risk to enrollees has the potential for introducing contract gaming and limiting fair competition between plans. CMS is cognizant of ensuring that any enrollment capacity limit, if granted, is structured in a way that avoids creating or exacerbating opportunities for contract gaming: plans with approved capacity limit requests may potentially have an easier time managing a smaller enrollment base which may allow them to stem any financial losses from increased utilization compared to bid projections or other unanticipated negative impacts to plan margins in a given contract year compared to plans that endeavor to maintain broad MA network access and serve larger enrollee populations despite smaller or negative margins. CMS believes that risk is increased for requests made outside of the bid process. While § 422.60(b)(3) provides that such requests may only be granted where the health and safety of beneficiaries is at risk, CMS is concerned that plans may view these requests as a potential financial tool—allowing plans to use these mid-year capacity limits as a mechanism to make business decisions outside of the bid period, and with information about the landscape they would not have had during the plan year. Several of the requests CMS received in prior years either directly or indirectly indicated the request was driven by financial concerns, rather than any risk to beneficiary health and safety. In light of these potential gaming concerns, CMS is proposing to limit the availability of enrollment capacity limits to the bid process.
Because CMS currently only considers an enrollment limit request outside of the bid submission process if there are present and documented risks to enrollee health and safety as set forth in § 422.60(b)(3), and CMS has other more robust tools available to intervene in these instances, CMS is proposing to remove the paragraph at § 422.60(b)(3) and revise § 422.60(b)(1) to make the request process applicable to enrollment capacity requests submitted as part of bid submission. These changes would remove the ability of plans to submit a capacity limit request outside of the bid submission. If a plan is concerned about the capacity of their provider network in delivering quality and timely care or other concerns about beneficiary outcomes, it can reach out to its CMS Regional Office account manager about these challenges. Where appropriate, CMS may issue intermediate sanctions, which can include suspending the plan's enrollment of Medicare beneficiaries and other actions.
Enrollees in plans subject to enrollment sanctions are eligible for a SEP that would allow them to choose another MA plan or Original Medicare. In addition, one of the primary rationales for allowing MA organizations to request enrollment limits outside of the bid process was to provide relief in the event of significant changes in provider networks, as reflected in the language of § 422.60(b)(3) identifying a lack of provider network availability as a potential basis for granting a request. It is important to note that CMS currently provides a SEP when there is a significant provider termination, as allowed under § 422.62(b)(23). Therefore, CMS has other protections in place to address the motivating concerns that prompted CMS to allow post-bid enrollment requests based on beneficiary health and safety risks. CMS also notes that extremely few requests of this nature were received prior to 2025, when some national MA organizations reduced their service areas. Even if such requests were a common occurrence, multiple plans identifying concerns that would be significant enough to meet the threshold of risk to health and safety would raise broader compliance concerns for the overall MA program. For example, if numerous MA organizations report that large provider groups have terminated their network contracts, and such terminations pose a sufficient risk to beneficiary health and safety, CMS could use existing compliance mechanisms to investigate the underlying circumstances. Such an investigation may examine compliance with network adequacy standards or the plan's obligation for arranging for and covering any medically necessary covered benefit outside of the plan provider network, but at in-network cost sharing, when an in-network provider or benefit is unavailable or inadequate to meet an enrollee's medical needs.
For these reasons, CMS is proposing to remove § 422.60(b)(3), thus removing the ability for plans to request an enrollment capacity limit outside of the bid process based on a risk to beneficiary health and safety. For further clarification of this point, CMS also proposes to revise § 422.60(b)(1) to indicate that all requests for enrollment capacity limits must be submitted with the bid with the following language: “(1) MA organizations may submit information on enrollment capacity of plans as part of the annual bid submission described at § 422.254(c)(4) or § 422.254(e)(1), as applicable.”
2. Enrollment Processes for Plans With a CMS-Approved Capacity Limit
As part of the CY 2027 bid process, CMS received several questions about the enrollment processes for plans with a capacity limit. The final CY 2027 bid guidance noted that all plans must
(
printed page 76361)
accept valid requests to enroll during all election periods until an established enrollment capacity limit is met.
[
45
]
This guidance is consistent with the requirements in
42 CFR 422.60(a)(1)
and
422.62(a)
, which CMS is not proposing to modify and would continue to be required. That is, a plan with an established enrollment capacity limit must accept all valid enrollments in the order they are received until the capacity limit is reached. For example, if the plan's enrollment exceeds the enrollment capacity limit submitted in the bid and accepted by CMS for CY 2028 at the start of the AEP in October 2027, it may not accept AEP enrollments for the January 1, 2028, enrollment start date. However, the plan must accept election requests using other election periods with 2027 effective dates (with the last possible effective date December 1, 2027). If the plan's enrollment is below the enrollment capacity limit before or at any point during the AEP, it must accept valid enrollment requests in the order they are received until the limit is met. When a plan is closed to new enrollment due to an enrollment capacity limit, the plan must remain closed to all prospective enrollees until space becomes available through natural attrition. If a plan receives valid enrollment requests after an enrollment capacity limit has been reached, the plan would deny those requests. If denied, an individual who wishes to enroll in the plan would need to wait until the plan is once again open and submit a new enrollment request. The individual would need to be eligible for an election period at the time of this subsequent request. Up until the enrollment capacity limit is reached, the plan must accept individuals based upon enrollments received in chronological order and in a manner that does not discriminate on the basis of any factor related to health as described in § 422.110.
CMS now discusses in greater detail its proposal for how plans would be required to operationalize an accepted enrollment capacity limit. Given that bid capacity limits would only be available when requested in connection with the bid submission under the proposed revisions to § 422.60(b), the proposed enrollment process requirements applicable to enrollment capacity limits obtained through the bid submission process would be codified at § 422.60(b)(2). Currently, § 422.60(b)(2) sets forth a rule for how a plan must prioritize accepting enrollment requests if the plan's enrollment falls below their enrollment capacity limit after previously having reached the capacity limit and being closed to new enrollment. Under this proposed rule, a plan would know well in advance of a contract year if they have an approved capacity limit and would have the ability to proactively manage their new enrollment closely. Plans with an established enrollment capacity limit would be responsible for maintaining a constant awareness of whether enrollment has met that limit, as they would need to determine the point in time at which they would cease accepting new enrollment requests. As a matter of course, plans are responsible for following CMS regulations on enrollment and submitting enrollments to CMS via MARx. Plans receive real-time responses from CMS for enrollment transactions submitted through MARx's user interface (UI) and Medicare Daily Transaction Reply Reports (DTRRs). Plans must monitor their enrollment data and should proceed cautiously when they are nearing their enrollment capacity limit to ensure they reach but do not exceed it. Once a plan is nearing its enrollment capacity limit, it may need to break batches of enrollments into smaller units so as not to exceed the enrollment capacity limit. If a plan receives several enrollment requests on one day, such that accepting all of them would exceed its enrollment capacity limit, the plan would accept and process to completion, as it would any other enrollment request, only those enrollment requests that were received while the plan's enrollment capacity limit had not yet been reached. The plan would deny any enrollment requests that, based on the time and date they were initially received by the plan, were received after the capacity limit had been reached. If a plan, during the processing of enrollments on a given day, determines that its enrollment capacity limit has been reached, the plan must continue processing those enrollment requests it received before the capacity limit was reached and may not disenroll those additional individuals. Only those enrollment requests that are received by the plan after the enrollment capacity limit has already been reached would be directly impacted by the capacity limit by having the enrollment request denied.
There may be circumstances in which an individual submits a valid enrollment request when there are still spaces available in the plan, but the plan reaches the enrollment capacity limit prior to submitting the enrollment transaction to CMS. Similarly, a plan may receive an incomplete application when the plan has not reached the enrollment capacity limit but then subsequently reach the capacity limit before the missing (but required) information is obtained. CMS would expect plans to accept these applications and process them to completion, including submitting the enrollment transaction to CMS as appropriate. Again, beneficiaries enrolled in excess of an approved enrollment capacity limit may not be disenrolled.
To conform with this approach, CMS is proposing to revise § 422.60(b)(2) to be “MA organizations must deny enrollment applications at the point of initial receipt once their CMS-approved enrollment capacity limit has been reached” and to remove 2(i) and 2(ii).
Under proposed § 422.60(b)(2), when individuals apply to an MA plan with an approved enrollment capacity limit, they would receive a denial notice if the enrollment capacity limit has been reached at the time the enrollment request is initially received by the plan. Currently, as described in the MA and Part D Enrollment and Disenrollment Guidance, section 50.4, plans must send denial notices within 10 calendar days of receipt of an enrollment request, or the expiration of the time for a request for additional information from the applicant, if applicable. It is therefore possible that an individual who applies late in an election period may not receive the denial notice before the end of their election period or may receive the notice without sufficient time to find and apply to a new plan. Although all individuals have the option of calling 1-800-MEDICARE to request a SEP for other exceptional circumstances, CMS is including in this proposal a new SEP to address this potential scenario and ensure that these individuals are not prevented from making an election through no fault of their own.
Section 1851(e)(4)(D) of the Act provides the Secretary with the authority to establish SEPs for exceptional conditions, during which an individual may request enrollment in, or disenrollment from, an MA plan. Therefore, CMS proposes to create a new SEP at
42 CFR 422.62(b)(27)
to ensure that individuals denied enrollment because of an enrollment capacity limit have the opportunity to make an election into an available health plan. This SEP would require
(
printed page 76362)
that the individual was eligible for an election period, attempted to enroll in an MA plan during that election period, was denied enrollment because of a CMS-approved capacity limit, received the enrollment denial notice, and was then unable to make another election during that original election period, because that election period had expired. CMS also proposes to renumber the existing SEP for other exceptional conditions at § 422.62(b)(27) as (b)(28). Because individuals who would be denied enrollment in a particular MA plan because of an enrollment capacity limit may prefer a standalone Part D plan instead of a different MA plan, CMS also proposes an analogous Part D SEP for other exceptional conditions at § 423.38(c)(36). The eligibility criteria for this SEP would be identical to that of the proposed new SEP at § 422.62(b)(27). CMS proposes to renumber the existing Part D SEP for other exceptional circumstances at § 423.38(c)(36) to (37). To conform with the proposed renumbering of existing § 422.62(b)(27) to (28) CMS is proposing to update the cross reference at § 422.66(g)(2)(iv). Similarly, to conform with the proposed renumbering of existing § 423.38(c)(36) to (37), CMS is proposing to update cross references at newly redesignated § 423.32(k)(2)(v) (as discussed in section III.A) and § 423.36(g)(2)(v).
At redesignated §§ 422.62(b)(27) and 423.38(c)(36) CMS proposes that the new SEP would begin the date the individual is notified of the enrollment denial and ends two calendar months after notification.
CMS proposes to limit use of this SEP to a CMS-operated mechanism, like 1-800-MEDICARE, consistent with the reasoning described in previous rulemaking (
91 FR 17384
,
17433
) and in the proposal for section III. A. Using a CMS Approval Mechanism for Use of the Disaster/Emergency Special Enrollment Period at §§ 422.62 and 423.38 that is also included in this proposed rule. In the case of the proposed capacity limit SEP, this is a situation where it would be inappropriate for the receiving MA organization to evaluate the applicant's eligibility because the receiving plan would not have the information it would need to determine eligibility for the SEP, such as details of the approved capacity limit, at what point the limit was reached, whether enrollment has subsequently dropped below the limit, whether the applicant was eligible for an election period when they requested enrollment in the capacity-limited plan, whether the applicant was denied enrollment due to the plan having reached the capacity limit, and whether there was insufficient time for the applicant to request enrollment in a different plan after having been denied enrollment. In this case, only CMS has all the necessary information to consider an individual's eligibility for this proposed new SEP. CMS proposes to include this limitation to CMS-operated mechanisms in both the requirements of the proposed SEP at § 422.62(b)(27) and in the list of SEPs that require prior CMS approval at § 422.66(g)(2). CMS is also proposing to specify that the SEP specified in the new proposed § 423.38(c)(36) would require CMS approval before an individual can use the SEP to make an election for Part D.
CMS is seeking public comment on alternatives to the standard for SEP eligibility described in our proposal, given that some individuals who are denied enrollment in an MA plan due to a capacity limit may be notified of the denial late in the election period they used to request enrollment in that plan and, as such, may not have sufficient time to identify and request enrollment in another plan prior to the expiration of that election period. CMS seeks comment on whether our consideration of this scenario is warranted and, for someone who receives a denial notice late in an election period, what would be the appropriate amount of time prior to the end of the election period to establish the SEP start date.
For CY 2027, CMS has encouraged plans with an accepted enrollment capacity limit to publicly post on their website when their plan has reached their limit to avoid potential beneficiary frustration if they try to enroll in a plan that does not have additional capacity. Therefore, CMS is considering whether to add additional regulatory language to require plans to post their accepted enrollment capacity limits and/or a notice when the limit has been reached on their public websites as part of marketing regulations at
42 CFR part 422 Subpart V
and
42
CFR 422.2265. For example, the MA plan would be required to display a message on its website that informs potential enrollees that enrollment in the plan has reached capacity and that it is no longer open for new enrollments. CMS seeks comment on this topic.
This proposal maintains the statutory framework allowing MA organizations to determine their capacity to accept new enrollees when submitting bids, while protecting against contract gaming concerns and challenges in CMS's ability to fairly and accurately determine whether to approve enrollment capacity requests outside of the bid process. The proposed approach also ensures the MA organization's ability to request an enrollment capacity limit on a level playing field across organizations through the bid submission process, while reducing the complexity of CMS review.
As CMS is proposing to maintain the ability for plans to request an enrollment capacity limit in the bid, plans would be expected to carefully assess their ability to absorb additional growth considering current market volatility when determining whether to include a proposed enrollment capacity limit in the plan's bid submission. This would ensure that, in the event a large MA organization exits a market unexpectedly, remaining plans in the market have proactively established an upper bound for the number of new enrollees they could realistically accommodate.
The estimated financial impact of this proposal is expected to be minimal. While there may be an increased number of plans submitting, and ultimately being approved for, an enrollment capacity limit as part of their bid submission, any added administrative burden on CMS (to review and approve/deny the request) or MA organizations (to make the request and then track enrollment) would be negligible and can likely be achieved using existing resources. Further, CMS is also removing the ability for plans to request a capacity limit outside of the bid process. However, because this was not a common occurrence as noted earlier, there is no burden reduction from this change. CMS requests comments on this proposal, including the proposed approach for CMS to review requests for enrollment capacity limits submitted during the bid and the removal of the ability to request a limit outside of the bid submission process. CMS is interested in comments about this proposal's impact on MA organizations' decision-making regarding offering plan benefit packages in specific service areas and other market implications, particularly on whether it supports competition and avoids contract gaming. Commenters should also note any anticipated impact to beneficiary access, choice, and outcomes.

2. Background on the Medicare Transaction Facilitator and Manufacturer Effectuation of MFPs With Respect to MA
Section 1193(a) of the Act instructs CMS to enter into agreements (a “Medicare Drug Price Negotiation Program Agreement,” hereinafter referred to as a “Negotiation Program Agreement”) with willing manufacturers of selected drugs (as described in section 1192(c) of the Act) with respect to a price applicability period (as defined in section 1191(b)(2) of the Act). After entering into a Negotiation Program Agreement with CMS and in accordance with section 1193(a) of the Act, any “Primary Manufacturer” (as defined in section 40 of the final guidance for initial price applicability year 2028) of a selected drug that continues to participate in the Negotiation Program and reaches agreement upon an MFP must provide access to the MFP to MFP-eligible individuals (as defined in section 1191(c)(2) of the Act) and to pharmacies, mail order services, and other dispensing entities dispensing selected drugs covered under Part D (hereinafter “dispensing entities”) with respect to such MFP-eligible individuals. As discussed in the final guidance for initial price applicability year 2028 and the draft guidance, starting with drugs selected for initial price applicability year 2028 or with a renegotiated MFP for initial price applicability year 2028, Primary Manufacturers are also required to provide access to the MFP of a selected drug to hospitals, physicians and other providers of services or suppliers that furnish or administer selected drugs payable under Medicare Part B (hereinafter “Part B provider(s)”) with respect to such MFP-eligible individuals.
[

In sections 40.4 of the final guidance for initial price applicability year 2028 and the draft guidance, we stated that a Primary Manufacturer must provide access to the MFP to dispensing entities and Part B providers, as applicable, in one of two ways: (1) prospectively ensuring that the price paid by the dispensing entity or Part B provider when acquiring the drug is no greater than the MFP, or (2) retrospectively providing reimbursement for the difference between the dispensing entity or Part B provider's acquisition cost and the MFP. The MTF, as currently operationalized for selected drugs covered under Part D in 2026 and 2027, has two distinct modules, the MTF DM and the MTF Payment Module (hereinafter “MTF PM”), where the latter is a voluntary option to pass payment for MFP refunds (that is, the amount the Primary Manufacturer has determined is equal to the difference between the dispensing entity and/or Part B provider's acquisition cost and the MFP) from Primary Manufacturers to dispensing entities. As discussed in the draft guidance, CMS intends to expand MTF DM and MTF PM functionality to allow pass through of MFP refunds from Primary Manufacturers to Part B providers, in addition to dispensing entities, in 2028. The combined data and payment facilitation functionalities present in the MTF DM and the MTF PM, respectively, attempt to address the interest expressed by dispensing entities, Part B providers and manufacturers to have a single platform for transmitting the data necessary for program administration and supporting MFP refund payments to create greater efficiency, standardization, and predictability in the execution of a high volume of continuous payments.

b. MTF DM Verification of MFP Eligibility
Consistent with the processes for selected drugs covered under Part D, CMS has discussed in the draft guidance that for selected drugs payable under Part B, the MTF DM would support verification that a selected drug was furnished or administered to an MFP-eligible individual, as described in section 40.4.2.1.2 of the draft guidance. With respect to selected drugs payable under Part B that are furnished or administered to Part C enrollees, CMS does not receive actual Part C claims from MA organizations; rather, we receive MA encounter data records that MA organizations submit for risk adjustment. MA encounter data records are not claims; they are records of healthcare services provided to Part C enrollees, including furnished or administered drugs payable under Part B, containing information about patient-provider encounters. Under the Negotiation Program, as discussed in section 40.4.2.1.2 of the draft guidance, CMS intends to use MA encounter data records as the source of information to provide claim-level data elements to Primary Manufacturers for selected drugs payable under Part B that are furnished or administered to an individual enrolled in an MA plan for 2028. For MA encounter data records for Part B items and services, the MTF DM would provide Primary Manufacturers with data that were submitted by the MA organization to the Medicare Advantage Encounter Data System (EDS).
[
62
]
That is, under this approach, once an MA organization submits an MA encounter data record to the EDS, no further action is required by the MA organization to review or verify the claim-level data elements extracted from the MA encounter record before the data elements are transmitted from the MTF DM to the Primary Manufacturer.
CMS, using EDS, will also perform verification steps to validate that the individual was enrolled in an MA plan under Part C on the date of service reported on the encounter data record. Encounter data records that have been verified as related to services rendered to individuals enrolled in an MA plan under Part C on the date of service reported are then transmitted to the Integrated Data Repository (IDR). Data in the IDR from the encounter data record that is associated only with a selected drug payable under Part B would be transmitted to the MTF DM, which would prepare the file of claim-level data elements for MFP-eligible claims for transmittal to the applicable Primary Manufacturer. Prior to transmission to the Primary Manufacturer, the MTF DM would confirm that the data reflect furnishing or administration of a selected drug payable under Part B and subject to an MFP by confirming the Healthcare Common Procedure Code Set (HCPCS) code on the MA encounter record received from the IDR contains a selected drug that is subject to an MFP on the claim-from date based on presence of the Selected Drug List and MFP File and, that a modifier indicating furnishing or administration of a selected drug or 11-digit National Drug Code (NDC-11) for a selected drug, as applicable, appears on such record. Therefore, considering that the Part C enrollment status of the individual will have been twice verified, by the MA organization and EDS, and that furnishing or administration of the selected drug will have been verified by the MTF DM before the data elements are sent from the MTF DM to the Primary Manufacturer, the data elements will have been verified as involving a selected drug payable under Part B that was furnished or administered to an MFP-eligible individual.
c. MFP Payment Window
For operational consistency with manufacturer prompt payment requirements for selected drugs covered under Part D and to ensure Part B providers receive MFP refunds promptly, as discussed in section 40.4.2.1.3 of the draft guidance, we intend to require the same 14-day prompt MFP payment window for selected drugs payable under Part B as for selected drugs covered under Part D. In the draft guidance, we stated that unless the Part B provider's acquisition cost for the selected drug is equal to or less than the MFP, or, as detailed in section 40.4.5 of the draft guidance, the Primary Manufacturer establishes that section 1193(d)(1) of the Act (related to 340B discounts) applies, CMS would require that the Primary Manufacturer transmit payment of an amount that provides access to the MFP within 14 calendar days of when the MTF sends the claim-level data elements that verify the selected drug was furnished or administered to an MFP-eligible individual to the Primary Manufacturer (“14-day prompt MFP payment window”). For Part D claims, Original Medicare (“OM”) claims, and MA encounters, the MTF DM's transmission of the claim-level data elements to the Primary Manufacturer starts the 14-day prompt MFP payment window, within which the Primary Manufacturer must transmit the claim-level payment elements (described further in sections 40.4.3 and 40.4.4 of the draft guidance) for each claim or encounter, as applicable, identified in the claim-level data elements that the MTF DM transmits to the Primary Manufacturer and, if applicable, would be required to transmit payment of an amount that provides access to the MFP when an MFP refund is appropriate. A Primary Manufacturer electing to provide access to the MFP via a retrospective refund would meet its obligation to make the MFP available by transmitting payment of an amount that provides access to the MFP within 14 calendar days of when the claim-level data elements are sent to the Primary Manufacturer by the MTF DM.
