3. Requirement for MA Organizations' Contracts With Network Providers To Require Enrollment in the MTF DM
CMS has broad contracting authority with respect to MA organizations under section 1857(e) of the Act. Section 1857(e)(1) of the Act authorizes the Secretary to adopt contract terms and conditions as necessary and appropriate and not inconsistent with the Part C statute. Under this authority, we propose to modify the regulation at § 422.504 (regarding Contract provisions) to establish that any contract between the MA organization and a provider (as defined in § 422.2), or between a first tier, downstream, or related entity and a provider on the MA organization's behalf, for participation in one or more of the MA organization's networks, must include a provision requiring that if the provider furnishes or administers selected drugs payable under Part B during the period when such drugs are subject to an MFP (as defined in proposed § 422.2), the provider must be enrolled in the MTF DM (or any successor to the MTF DM) in a form and manner to be determined by CMS. We emphasize that under the proposed regulation, such provision must require the provider “to be enrolled” in the MTF DM, as opposed to merely requiring the provider “to enroll” in the MTF DM, to establish an ongoing obligation that the provider maintain its enrollment in the MTF DM. We also propose that such provision must require such provider to maintain and certify to CMS that the enrollment information provided in the MTF DM is accurate, complete, and up to date, in accordance with applicable terms and conditions of participation with the MTF DM, in a form and manner to be determined by CMS. We propose amending §  422.504 by adding paragraph (p) to codify this requirement.
Consistent with section 1857(e)(1) of the Act, such a requirement would be necessary and appropriate and not inconsistent with the Part C statute. As previously mentioned, the MTF DM would contain several key functionalities that are necessary and appropriate for operations related to administration of the Negotiation Program and the Part C program. Through each of the functionalities outlined below, enrollment in the MTF DM of providers that furnish or administer selected drugs payable under Part B would help ensure continued beneficiary access to selected drugs that are payable under Part B by MA organizations.
First, the MTF DM would provide providers enrolled in the MTF DM with ERAs
[
63
]
to reconcile MFP refund payments when a Primary Manufacturer chooses to pass payment to the provider through the MTF PM. To meet industry standards in the creation of an accurate ERA, up-to-date banking information for a provider is needed. As part of a provider's enrollment in the MTF DM, the provider would affirm the payment account information, and the corresponding payment information would be used to deposit the MFP refund payment issued by the Primary Manufacturer for MFP-eligible claims in the form of an electronic funds transfer deposit. For Primary Manufacturers that make payments outside of the MTF PM, we intend to make information available to the Primary Manufacturer through the MTF DM, such as the provider's banking information and designated destination for ERAs.
These ERAs would assist providers that furnish or administer selected drugs payable under Part B in closing out their open accounts receivable, thereby minimizing cashflow interruptions. Specifically, the information contained in the ERA will connect the MFP refund amount paid by the Primary Manufacturer with how the payment was made, including the associated electronic funds transfer information, if applicable. We expect this would enable providers to review their accounts receivables (consistent with each provider's own standard business practices) for each claim and determine whether a Primary Manufacturer has paid all the claims the provider believes are MFP-eligible claims, in the amounts the provider believes are sufficient to effectuate the MFP. Moreover, we have consistently heard from interested parties that without an ERA, providers would not have means to determine which claim they were paid an MFP refund on, and which claim they were not.
Second, there would be streamlined access for providers enrolled in the MTF DM to submit complaints and disputes within the MTF DM to help identify issues with timely MFP refund payment, supporting providers in continuing efficient operations and preventing undue financial hardship, while maintaining accuracy of MA encounter data records and payment. Allowing providers streamlined access to this system will support the administration of the Negotiation Program and the Part C program. Through the MTF Helpdesk Portal web page,
[

]
a provider can submit a complaint related to MFP availability, which CMS will review. While providers are encouraged to remediate with the manufacturer directly if they believe that they have not received a retrospective refund payment necessary to effectuate the MFP, providers may use the complaint and dispute system referenced above to alert CMS if the provider believes Negotiation Program requirements are not being met.
Third, the MTF DM would serve as a central repository for information about providers enrolled in the MTF DM that self-report that they anticipate material cashflow concerns due to the reliance on retrospective MFP refunds within the 14-day prompt MFP payment window. Consider a scenario in which a provider purchases a selected drug at the average sales price (ASP). Providers may experience a temporary cashflow gap while waiting for payment from the MA organization and a retrospective MFP refund payment from the Primary Manufacturer. However, upon receiving the MFP refund payment, the provider's temporary cashflow gap is reduced, the extent of which is determined by the MA organization's payment terms for selected drugs payable under Part B. Assuming a consistent utilization rate for the drug, any temporary negative cashflow should be offset by the subsequent MFP refund payment. The timing and consistency of this pattern should lead to a more stable cashflow and lower likelihood of a long-term cash deficit over time. During MTF DM enrollment, we will ask providers to self-identify whether they are a provider that anticipates having material cashflow concerns at the start of the initial price applicability year in connection with Primary Manufacturers' effectuation of MFP. The types of entities we anticipate may self-report

through this process include independent physician clinics, providers that furnish or administer a high volume of drugs payable under Part B, providers who predominantly rely on drug administration revenue to maintain business operations, rural providers, and sole community hospitals. The information self-reported by providers will be provided to Primary Manufacturers to assist in the development of their MFP effectuation plans, which must include a process for mitigating material cashflow concerns for providers. The MTF DM will also be available to providers enrolled in the MTF that need to update their self-identification with respect to material cashflow concerns, as we anticipate that indication could change over time.
Fourth, we intend that providers enrolled in the MTF DM would be able to view the status of available credits and MFP refunds from Primary Manufacturers through the MTF DM. The ability to track credits and MFP refunds could also help providers better manage their cashflow or aid their financial planning by providing insight into credits incurred based on adjustments to prior claims that may be applied to future MFP refund payments.
Fifth, the MTF DM would collect and share financial information, including banking information, belonging to providers enrolled in the MTF DM with Primary Manufacturers that pay MFP refunds to providers outside the MTF PM. As such, during MTF DM enrollment, providers will have the ability to approve MTF DM use of the provider's financial information as reported in the Medicare Provider Enrollment, Chain, and Ownership System (PECOS), including the banking information that will inform where MFP refunds (as applicable) will be routed; providers opting not to use the PECOS data will have the ability to manually complete the MTF DM enrollment process, including provision of banking information. We believe that collecting and sharing of providers' bank account information with Primary Manufacturers will address interested parties' concerns related to the lack of an established channel to support MFP refund payments made outside the MTF PM and help providers to continue efficient operations.
In sum, we believe that enrollment in the MTF DM by providers that furnish or administer selected drugs payable under Part B would facilitate continued beneficiary and provider access under the MA program to selected drugs that are payable under Part B. Manufacturers and providers have asked the agency to undertake a role in assuring that MFP refund payments to providers can be made efficiently, and the MTF DM has an important role in that process. With less financial uncertainty, providers are better positioned to continue furnishing or administering selected drugs payable under Part B to MA enrollees. Of the approximately 16,000 providers that furnished or administered drugs selected for initial price applicability year 2028 that are payable under Part B to OM or MA enrollees in CY 2025, approximately 88 percent of National Provider Identifiers associated with those approximately 16,000 providers were included on an MA encounter record for such a drug in CY 2025. Therefore, given the large number of providers that furnish or administer drugs payable under Part B to MA enrollees, we believe this proposed requirement would help reach a substantial number of providers that serve MA enrollees. Requiring MA organizations' network contracts to require enrollment in the MTF DM by providers that furnish or administer selected drugs payable under Part B will help promote successful MFP effectuation by Primary Manufacturers under the Negotiation Program and facilitate continued access to selected drugs payable under Part B for MA enrollees and providers.
For the reasons stated previously, we propose to require at § 422.504(p) that any contract between an MA organization and a provider (as defined in proposed § 422.2), or between a first tier, downstream, or related entity and a provider on the MA organization's behalf, for participation in one or more of the MA organization's networks include a provision that if the provider furnishes or administers selected drugs payable under Part B during the period when such drugs are subject to an MFP (as defined in proposed § 422.2), the provider must be enrolled in the MTF DM (or any successor to the MTF DM), which would entail an ongoing obligation that the provider maintain its enrollment in the MTF DM, in a form and manner to be determined by CMS. We also propose at § 422.504(p) that such provision must require such provider to maintain and certify up-to-date, complete, and accurate enrollment information with the MTF DM, in accordance with applicable terms and conditions of participation with the MTF DM, in a form and manner determined by CMS.
4. Requirement—Submission of Encounter Data Records for Selected Drugs Payable Under Part B
To facilitate MFP effectuation by Primary Manufacturers and to help ensure prompt payments by Primary Manufacturers to Part B providers to provide access to the MFP with respect to selected drugs payable under Part B furnished or administered to individuals enrolled in MA plans, encounter data records for selected drugs payable under Part B warrant a submission deadline that is different from the risk adjustment encounter data submission deadline requirements at § 422.310(g). For the purposes of risk adjustment, MA organizations typically have 13 months following the service year of which payment is based (that is, the year before the payment year) to submit encounters to CMS for inclusion in final reconciliation. If CMS relied on such encounter data records to identify claims for selected drugs payable under Part B furnished or administered to enrollees of Part C plans for transmission to Primary Manufacturers for the manufacturer's MFP effectuation purposes, Part B providers could wait up to approximately 14 to 26 months to receive access to the MFP (for example, 13 to 25 months for the MA organization to submit encounter data records to the EDS, plus approximately 1 to 3 days for the encounter data records to move from EDS to the MTF DM, 2 days for the MTF DM to transmit claim-level data elements to the Primary Manufacturer, plus up to an additional 14 days for the Primary Manufacturer to transmit an MFP refund payment, and up to 5 banking days for payment transactions to process). If the Primary Manufacturer does not prospectively make the MFP available to the Part B provider, then the lag between when the Part B provider receives payment from the MA organization and when the Part B provider receives the MFP refund payment from the Primary Manufacturer could impose a financial strain on Part B providers given that anticipated MFP refunds could be a material percent of the Part B provider's purchase price. To mitigate potential financial hardship on Part B providers, which could impact Part C enrollee access to selected drugs payable under Part B, and to more closely align the timeline for MFP refund payments to providers that furnish or administer selected drugs payable under Part B to MA enrollees with the timeline for MFP refund payments to dispensing entities that dispense selected drugs covered under Part D, CMS believes it is appropriate to create a separate new requirement for submission of MA encounter data records, as described at § 422.310(d)(5), for selected drugs payable under Part B for which an MFP (as defined in proposed § 422.2) is in effect on the

This proposed new requirement would not affect or supersede existing risk adjustment submission deadlines specified at § 422.310(g) for Part B drugs or for any other items or services provided to MA enrollees. As stated at proposed § 422.504(q)(1), CMS will use this data for risk adjustment purposes unless the MA organization submits risk adjustment data required under § 422.310 by the final risk adjustment submission deadline under § 422.310(g).
In section 40.4.2.1.2 of the draft guidance, we stated that we are evaluating whether to propose a new requirement that MA organizations submit encounter data records for encounters for selected drugs payable under Part B on a timeline that is shorter than the MA risk adjustment submission timeline under § 422.310 to ensure Part B providers receive timely payment of MFP refunds by Primary Manufacturers who elect a retrospective reimbursement model. CMS received and reviewed comments from interested parties on the draft guidance related to the consideration of an earlier submission deadline requirement for encounters for selected drugs payable under Part B and used these comments to inform policy development for this rulemaking. After considering such comments and for the reasons discussed below, CMS proposes to require encounter data submission for selected drugs payable under Part B for which an MFP (as defined in proposed § 422.2) is in effect on the claim-from date, within 30 days of the claim-from date to reduce the maximum amount of time a provider that furnishes or administers a selected drug payable under Part B to an MA enrollee could wait to receive access to the MFP.
We do not receive Part C claims for drugs payable under Part B directly from MA organizations; we receive MA encounter data records that MA organizations submit for the purpose of risk adjustment. This encounter data record contains claims information for items and services provided to individuals enrolled in an MA plan. While CMS uses MA encounter data records primarily in the development and application of a risk adjustment payment model, we may also use and release these data for other purposes not inconsistent with § 422.310(f). As discussed in the draft guidance, we intend to use MA encounter data records to facilitate manufacturer effectuation of the MFP for selected drugs payable under Part B and furnished or administered to individuals enrolled in an MA plan under Part C as the data includes many fields from the underlying claim that are necessary to facilitate the Primary Manufacturer's obligation to make the MFP available. Therefore, at this time, we believe that use of certain data elements from MA encounter data records in lieu of the actual claim provides the minimum necessary information needed to facilitate Primary Manufacturer effectuation of the MFP for selected drugs payable under Part B and furnished or administered to individuals enrolled in an MA plan under Part C. To minimize the reporting burden imposed on MA organizations, rather than requiring MA organizations to send data elements directly to Primary Manufacturers or directly to the MTF DM, we intend to leverage MA encounter data records submitted by MA organizations to CMS to obtain data elements associated with Part C claims for selected drugs. These data elements will subsequently be transmitted to Primary Manufacturers via the established MTF DM data exchange. Data in the IDR would be transmitted to the MTF DM, which would prepare the file of claim-level data elements for MFP-eligible claims for transmittal to the applicable Primary Manufacturer.
As codified in § 422.310(g), the final risk adjustment data submission deadline is no earlier than January 31 of the year following the payment year. Therefore, the risk adjustment data submission timeline typically allows MA organizations 13 months following the service year of which payment is based (that is, the year prior to the payment year) to submit encounters to CMS for inclusion in final reconciliation. We are concerned that the typical 13- to 25-month timeline for encounter data submission could result in material cashflow concerns for Part B providers furnishing or administering selected drugs payable under Part B to MA enrollees during a price applicability period, were we to rely on risk adjustment encounter data records submitted pursuant to § 422.310(g) for facilitating Primary Manufacturer MFP effectuation. Part B providers experiencing such cashflow concerns may opt not to purchase selected drugs payable under Part B. This decision could affect the care provided to MA enrollees' by limiting access to these drugs. Therefore, unless CMS establishes a separate deadline for submission of encounter data records for encounters associated with selected drugs payable under Part B, compared to the anticipated MFP refund payment timelines for OM and Part D, the MFP refund payment timeline for MA encounters would be significantly longer. For reference, for selected drugs payable under Part B, OM claims would be typically processed by Medicare Administrative Contractors within 7 to 14 days, up to 2 days for the MTF DM to transmit claims-level data elements to the Primary Manufacturer, up to 14 days for the Primary Manufacturer to transmit an MFP refund payment, and up to 5 banking days for payment transactions to process, resulting in an approximate 21- to 28-day timeline for the Part B provider to receive the MFP refund with respect to an OM claim. For selected drugs covered under Part D, the Part D plan sponsor has 7 days to submit Prescription Drug Event records to CMS through the Drug Data Processing System (DDPS), from which the MTF DM receives data on selected drug claims. Then the MTF DM transmits the claims-level data elements to the Primary Manufacturer within two days, the Primary Manufacturer transmits an MFP refund payment within 14 days, and the MTF PM processes payment transactions within 5 banking days, resulting in an approximate 21- to 28-day timeline for the dispensing entity to receive the MFP refund.
Section 1857(e)(1) of the Act authorizes the Secretary to adopt contract terms and conditions, including requirements to provide information, as the Secretary may find necessary and appropriate and that are not inconsistent with the Part C statute. We specify that these requirements will equally apply to MA organizations participating in capitated payment arrangements with their contracted providers. Specifically, at § 422.504 (q)(1)(i), we are proposing to require MA organizations to submit encounter data

Although this proposal to submit MA encounter data records for selected drugs payable under Part B and subject to an MFP would result in a longer MFP refund timeline for MA encounters as compared to Part D or OM claims, we believe this proposal appropriately balances giving MA organizations sufficient time to process claims and submit associated encounters while minimizing the time lag as much as possible for the MFP refund (as applicable) to be paid to Part B providers.

CMS has used this authority to implement contract provisions that require MA organizations to report specific information to CMS for a variety of purposes, with the overall goal of improving the Part C program. 80 FR 7912
) to implement provisions at § 422.504(o) that require that every MA organization develop, maintain, and implement a business continuity plan that meets certain minimum standards. One of the purposes of this requirement is to ensure consistency across plan sponsors that allow beneficiaries to access health care services.
With the implementation of the Negotiation Program, we believe additional requirements for MA organizations are necessary and appropriate for consistency across MA organization operation that ultimately protect beneficiaries from coverage disruptions and facilitate access to the MFP (as defined in proposed § 422.2) for providers in accordance with section 1193(a)(3)(B) of the Act. As discussed in section I.2 of this proposed rule and consistent with the claims-level data elements discussed in section 40.4.2.1 of the draft guidance and listed in Table 6 of the draft guidance, the MTF DM would transmit to the Primary Manufacturer additional information about each claim that may be necessary in calculating the retrospective MFP refund, if applicable, including, but not limited to, the claim line NDC. Primary Manufacturers are required to provide access to the MFP to providers that furnish or administer selected drugs payable under Part B to MFP-eligible individuals. Ensuring timely access to retrospective MFP refund payments for providers is an important policy goal for CMS in administering the Negotiation Program, and helps to ensure providers furnishing or administering selected drugs payable under Part B subject to an MFP are not disincentivized from furnishing or administering such drugs to beneficiaries enrolled in MA plans under Part C, which in turn protects continued access to such selected drugs for MA enrollees. Accordingly, we have concluded that it is necessary and appropriate to use our authority under section 1857(e)(1) of the Act to propose specific data collection requirements for MA organizations to collect and submit certain data on encounter data record submissions for selected drugs payable under Part B for which an MFP (as defined in proposed § 422.2) is in effect to ensure that Primary Manufacturers have the minimum necessary information needed to effectuate the MFP for selected drugs payable under Part B furnished or administered to individuals enrolled in Part C.
As discussed in detail below and as discussed in the draft guidance, we believe it is necessary and appropriate to require MA organizations to collect NDC-11 data on each MA encounter data record for selected drugs payable under Part B for which an MFP (as defined in proposed § 422.2) is in effect and submit such data to CMS. The
(
printed page 76373)
proposed requirement to collect and submit NDC-11 codes at § 422.504(q)(1)(ii) is intended to facilitate MFP effectuation and protect access to selected drugs for MA enrollees by collecting information to allow identification of claims for selected drugs payable under Part B. Collecting this information supports accurate and timely MFP refund payments to Part B providers that bill MA organizations, which helps ensure providers are not disincentivized from furnishing or administering selected drugs to individuals enrolled in MA plans. In section 40.4.1.2 of the draft guidance, we detailed a challenge regarding the use of HCPCS codes for selected drugs payable under Part B, whereby a Primary Manufacturer may not be able to identify whether a claim billed with a HCPCS code is MFP-eligible. Because a single HCPCS code could include or correspond with multiple NDCs, including NDCs for both selected and non-selected drugs, it may not always be possible to determine from the HCPCS code alone whether the specific drug furnished or administered to a beneficiary is a selected drug with an applicable MFP. For example, a generic drug that relies on a selected drug that is approved under a New Drug Application (NDA) as its listed drug in the Orange Book and is approved after the selected drug is selected (and before such selected drug is deselected from the Negotiation Program) may be assigned to the same HCPCS code as the selected drug.
As described in section 40.4.1.2 of the draft guidance, this challenge is illustrated by the following scenario: drug X is a selected drug for initial price applicability year 2028, has one NDC-11 assigned to HCPCS code J1234, and is marketed under one approved NDA. Drug Y, a generic drug that has drug X as its listed drug, is determined to be approved and marketed on a date between November 2, 2026, and March 31, 2028. In this scenario, selected drug X would remain a selected drug for calendar year 2028, meaning the MFP would apply for 2028, and drug X would not cease to be a selected drug until January 1, 2029, as described in section 70 of the final guidance for initial price applicability year 2028. If drug X and drug Y share the same HCPCS code, for the period of time for which drug X and drug Y are both approved and marketed and before drug X is deselected from the Negotiation Program, the Primary Manufacturer of drug X cannot readily determine, based on the HCPCS code alone, whether a given claim for J1234 represents the furnishing or administration of drug X's NDC-11, and therefore whether the MFP for drug X should apply.
To address this scenario, we are considering different approaches, outlined in section 40.4.1.2 of the draft guidance, to identify MFP-eligible claims where an MFP-eligible NDC-11 for a selected drug has been administered or furnished to an MFP-eligible individual. One option to address the scenario described above is to require reporting of the NDC-11 for each claim for a selected drug payable under Part B. For that purpose, we are proposing to require MA organizations to collect and submit NDC-11s on each encounter data record for selected drugs payable under Part B for which an MFP (as defined in proposed § 422.2) is in effect on the claim-from date. This requirement only applies to HCPCS codes that include a selected drug payable under Part B for which an MFP is in effect on the claim-from date, including HCPCS codes that only include the selected drug. We believe it is necessary to require NDC-11 reporting even in instances where the HCPCS code alone would demonstrate that a selected drug payable under Part B was furnished or administered, to facilitate operational simplicity and support automation, as well as to allow for greater precision in the calculation of whether refunds are necessary to make the MFP available, and in what amount.
An alternative option considered and discussed in section 40.4.1.2 of the draft guidance, is requiring the use of a claims modifier to indicate whether an MFP-eligible NDC for a selected drug was furnished or administered. As an alternative to the collection of NDC-11s, we are considering requiring the collection and submission of modifiers by MA organizations on all claims for drugs payable under Part B submitted for a HCPCS code that includes a selected drug subject to an MFP. Specifically, we could establish two modifiers that would be reported on MA encounters submitted for a HCPCS code that includes a selected drug: one modifier to indicate an MFP-eligible NDC for a selected drug was furnished or administered and a second modifier to indicate an NDC for a non-selected drug was furnished or administered. For example, when a HCPCS code that includes a selected drug is used, the illustrative “JM” modifier would be used to report that an MFP-eligible NDC for a selected drug was furnished or administered and the illustrative “JN” modifier would be used to report that an NDC for a non-selected drug was furnished or administered. CMS solicits comment on whether the collection and submission of HCPCS modifiers is preferable over the proposed collection and submission of NDC-11s and for what reasons. We anticipate that collection and submission of NDC-11s or these modifiers would support the verification that a selected drug payable under Part B for which an MFP is in effect on the claim-from date was furnished or administered to an MFP-eligible individual as discussed in section 40.4.2.1.2 of the draft guidance and would support timely MFP refund payments.

7. Medicare Advantage Out-of-Network Cost Sharing for Selected Drugs Payable Under Part B
As discussed in section 80 of the draft guidance, pursuant to the requirement in section 11001(c) of the IRA that CMS use program instruction or other forms of program guidance to implement section 11001 of the IRA, including amendments made by such section, for 2028, CMS intends to establish through guidance for 2028 that when an MA plan uses coinsurance, the dollar amount of in-network coinsurance for selected drugs payable under Part B for individuals enrolled in MA plans must be calculated based on a price that is no more than the MFP. In the draft guidance, CMS solicited comments on whether, consistent with this intended policy for in-network coinsurance, a potential requirement to establish that MA plans must calculate the 50 percent out-of-network coinsurance cap for selected drugs payable under Part B based on the MFP would implement necessary and sufficient safeguards to ensure MA enrollees are not subject to benefit design that discriminates on the basis of health status-related factors or is likely to substantially discourage enrollment by certain MA-eligible individuals, as prohibited by section 1852(b)(1) of the Act. CMS used the comments submitted in response to the comment solicitation to inform policy development for this rulemaking.
CMS has broad contracting authority with respect to MA organizations under section 1857(e) of the Act. Section 1857(e)(1) of the Act authorizes the Secretary to adopt contract terms and conditions as necessary and appropriate and not inconsistent with the Part C statute. Furthermore, under section 1852(b)(1) of the Act, CMS shall not approve an MA plan if its design and its benefits are likely to substantially discourage enrollment by certain MA eligible individuals with the organization. Under these authorities, we propose to modify the regulation at § 422.100(f)(6)(i) to establish that for selected drugs payable under Part B that are subject to an MFP (as defined in proposed § 422.2) and furnished or administered by an out-of-network provider, 50 percent coinsurance or an actuarially equivalent copayment value under
42 CFR 422.100(f)(6)(i)
must be calculated based on a price that is equal to or less than the MFP for out-of-network cost sharing. CMS believes the proposed modification to the regulation, if finalized, would be necessary and appropriate and would implement safeguards to ensure MA enrollees are not subject to discriminatory benefits or discriminatory costs for basic benefits.
Consistent with section 1852(b)(1) of the Act, such a requirement would be necessary to ensure that MA plans (including Employer Group Waiver Plans) are not designed to substantially discourage enrollment by MA-eligible individuals who are furnished or administered selected drugs payable under Part B. Under section 80 of the draft guidance, the maximum dollar amount of in-network coinsurance an MA enrollee may be charged for a selected drug payable under Part B is based on the MFP of such selected drug in the same manner as it would have been if the individual had been enrolled under OM. This proposal would similarly ensure that MA enrollees who obtain a selected drug out of network receive the benefit of the MFP for coinsurance purposes and would ensure MA plans are not designed to substantially discourage MA-eligible individuals who are furnished or administered selected drugs payable under Part B from enrolling in MA.
To illustrate the impact on beneficiary out-of-pocket costs, take an example selected drug with an ASP of $125 and an MFP of $100. In a situation under which the MA organization's total financial liability for an out-of-network provider furnishing or administering a selected drug payable under Part B is ASP + 6 percent, the total cost for the drug would be $132.50. Beneficiary coinsurance calculated at the maximum for out-of-network services of 50 percent would be $66.25. At MFP + 6 percent, the total cost for the drug would be $106. Under our proposed change to the regulation, beneficiary coinsurance calculated at the maximum for out-of-network services would be no greater than $53, savings of $13.25.
We believe that the proposed changes to the regulatory text would not have an impact on the Medicare Trust Fund. There is no collection of information related to this change and, therefore, no change to paperwork burden to MA plans or individuals.

J. Low Performer Icon (LPI) Notice (§§ 422.2267 and 423.2267)
Sections 1851(d)(1) and 1860D-1(c) of the Act require CMS to take the necessary actions to provide Medicare beneficiaries with information regarding coverage options to promote active and informed enrollment decisions. As part of this responsibility, CMS has established the Medicare Star Ratings system to provide beneficiaries with information regarding the quality and performance of MA and Part D plans.
As described in
42 CFR 422.162
and
423.186
, CMS calculates an overall Star Rating, Part C summary rating, and Part D summary rating for each MA-PD contract, and a Part C summary rating for each MA-only contract using a 5-star rating system, with 1 being the lowest rating and 5 being the highest. Contracts that receive one or two stars are designated as “low performing” and receive an icon designating such status. Since 2012, CMS has mailed a low performing icon (LPI) notice to beneficiaries enrolled in MA, MA-PD, or standalone Part D plans that have received an overall Star Rating of less than 3 stars (that is, ratings of 1, 1.5, 2, or 2.5 stars) for 3 or more consecutive contract years in order to inform beneficiaries that their plan has demonstrated consistently low performance and encourage them to review other plan options available in
(
printed page 76375)
their area. The notice also informs beneficiaries of their ability to use a special enrollment period (SEP) to enroll in a plan that is not identified as a low-performing plan. CMS currently produces and mails this notice as CMS Product No. 11627.
We are proposing to codify a requirement at §§ 422.2267(e)(31) and 423.2267(e)(33) that plans meeting the LPI notice threshold furnish the CMS-approved LPI notice directly to their enrollees rather than CMS mailing the notice on the plans' behalf. Under this proposal, plans that have received an overall Star Rating of less than three stars for three or more consecutive contract years would be responsible for providing a standardized notice to affected beneficiaries. We are proposing that plans must furnish the notice no later than November 15 of each contract year to beneficiaries enrolled during the current plan year. We believe this deadline is appropriate because it falls after CMS releases updated Star Ratings on Medicare Plan Finder, ensuring the notice reflects the most current Star Ratings information available, and ensures beneficiaries receive the notice during the annual election period (AEP), which runs from October 15 through December 7, providing them with sufficient time to review their plan options and exercise their SEP rights. If finalized, this requirement would apply beginning with Star Ratings issued for contract year 2028, which means that plans that are designated with the LPI for 2028 would have to mail notices no later than November 15, 2027.
CMS would continue to develop and approve the notice content and would require plans to use the CMS-approved LPI notice with only minimal alterations, consistent with the standardized materials requirements under §§ 422.2267(b) and 423.2267(b). We believe this approach would improve transparency and accountability by clearly establishing plan responsibility for furnishing the notice while ensuring that beneficiaries continue to receive consistent and accurate information regarding plan performance and available enrollment options, and applicable SEP rights that are currently provided through the notice.
Current regulations do not expressly require low-performing plans to furnish the notice directly to their enrollees. We believe codifying this requirement would establish a clear and durable regulatory framework to promote consistent administration of the notice requirement and align communication responsibilities. We recognize that affected plans would incur costs associated with furnishing the notice to enrollees. However, because plans routinely communicate with their members and maintain enrollee mailing information, we believe plans are operationally positioned to implement this requirement.

(

L. PACE Retroactive Effective Dates (§ 460.158)
Sections 1894(f)(2) and 1934(f)(2) of the Act direct CMS to incorporate into regulation the requirements applied to Programs of All-inclusive Care for the Elderly (PACE) demonstration programs under the PACE protocol as published by On Lok, Inc., the parent company of On Lok Senior Health Services, to the extent consistent with the provisions of sections 1894 and 1934 of the Act. The Act also authorizes CMS to modify or waive certain provisions of the PACE protocol in the development of the regulation, if the modification or waiver were not inconsistent with and would not impair the essential elements, objectives, and requirements of sections 1894 and 1934 of the Act.
The CMS-1201-F rule (
71 FR 71244
) published in the
Federal Register
on December 8, 2006, finalized HCFA-1903-IFC, the interim final rule with comment period published in the
Federal Register
on November 24, 1999 (
64 FR 66234
). CMS-1201-F established requirements for PACE under the Medicare and Medicaid programs, including regulations at § 460.158 related to the effective dates of enrollment into a PACE program. Section 460.158 specifies that the participant's enrollment in the program is effective on the first day of the calendar month following the date the PACE organization receives the signed enrollment agreement. We defined a participant as an individual enrolled in a PACE program and also identified a Medicare beneficiary who is enrolled in a PACE program as a Medicare participant and a Medicaid recipient who is enrolled in a PACE program as a Medicaid participant. As eligibility to enroll in a PACE program is not restricted to an individual who is either a Medicare beneficiary or Medicaid recipient, we acknowledge that the start or end date of an individual's enrollment in PACE is not directly linked to Medicare or Medicaid entitlement. While Medicare or Medicaid entitlement may impact a PACE participant's premium or cost sharing obligations, the lack of such entitlement cannot be used as a basis for denying PACE enrollment or involuntarily disenrolling a PACE participant, as neither Medicare nor Medicaid entitlement is required. An individual's enrollment in the PACE program is effective the first day of the calendar month following the date the PACE organization receives the signed enrollment agreement, regardless of the individual's Medicare or Medicaid status at that time.
CMS issued an HPMS memo titled “Medicare Enrollment for PACE Participants with Prospective or Retroactive Medicare Entitlement” on October 19, 2012 stating that PACE enrollment effective dates when an individual obtains retroactive Medicare entitlement could be up to one year prior to the month the request is received by the CMS Account Manager. However, this policy is not codified in regulation. The HPMS memo further explained that requests for retroactivity are limited to cases where the individual receives a retroactive Medicare entitlement award from SSA or becomes entitled to Medicare for a reason other than age (for example, disability, ESRD) that was not immediately identified and addressed by the PACE organization in a timely manner. PACE organizations with participants who later become entitled to Medicare, for example, as in cases in which an individual receives a retroactive Medicare entitlement determination from SSA or becomes entitled to Medicare for a reason other than aging into Medicare (for example, disability, ESRD), should use the retroactive process to effectuate the change in the participant's status to reflect Medicare entitlement.
Subregulatory guidance in Chapter 4 of the PACE manual specifies that CMS expects PACE programs to follow the procedures described in the Medicare Advantage & Prescription Drug Plan Communications User Guide (PCUG) to successfully submit accurate transactions to CMS within the current operating month cycle. As we reiterated in the HPMS memo entitled “Clarification of Enrollment of PACE Participants for Medicare Payment” on August 28, 2025, plans are expected to submit MARx transactions within a five-month period that begins one month before the participant becomes eligible
(
printed page 76377)
for Medicare. However, following the guidance in the earlier 2012 HPMS memo, PACE organizations had been able to submit enrollments for PACE participants who obtain retroactive Medicare entitlement to the CMS Account Manager and request an effective date of up to a year retroactive from the month the retroactive request was submitted to CMS. This guidance potentially allows PACE organizations to delay the submission of timely Medicare status transactions after they are informed of the PACE participants' new entitlement to Medicare. When there is a delay in submitting the appropriate transaction that reflects the PACE participant's Medicare status, it may result in PACE coverage conflicting with other program enrollments, such as MA, Part D, and LI NET, and incorrect capitation payments made to the PACE organization based on conflicting Medicare entitlement statuses reflected in MARx. For example, an individual who should be enrolled in PACE with dually-eligible status is enrolled in PACE with Medicaid-only status, or an individual who should be enrolled in PACE with Medicare-only status is still considered private pay for PACE.
When a current PACE participant gains Medicare entitlement and the retroactive request overlaps with prior MA, Part D, or LI NET coverage, the CMS Account Manager must contact the MA organization, Part D sponsor, or LI NET sponsor to determine if the prior coverage period can be cancelled and the PACE Medicare status effectuated for a retroactive date, in order to ensure that the other plan has not been used and that services have not been provided to the individual before moving forward with the retroactive request. If appropriate, then CMS's Retroactive Processing Contractor (RPC) makes the update, and the Medicare capitation payment is given to the correct plan of record for the retroactive period to avoid double payment. The majority of retroactive enrollments submitted by PACE organizations have effective dates that are fewer than 90-calendar days from the month the CMS Account Manager receives the request from the PACE organization. A small percentage of PACE enrollments have retroactive effective dates that are more than one year from the month the CMS Account Manager receives the request from the PACE organization, and even fewer go back more than two years. In 2023, 12 percent of retroactive enrollment requests had effective dates dating back more than one year from the month the CMS Account Manager received the request from the PACE organization. In 2024, this increased to 16 percent and, in 2025, it slightly decreased to 14 percent. Despite the relatively low percentage of enrollments with effective dates that go back more than one year from the month the CMS Account Manager receives the request from the PACE organization, each retroactive enrollment request places additional burden on PACE organizations to submit documentation to CMS and on CMS Account Managers to review and make a determination. When retroactive requests date back for an extended period of time, the complexity of the review increases significantly. CMS Account Managers must assess potential overlaps with prior plan coverage, coordinate with the RPC and, in some cases, contact other plan sponsors to confirm whether coverage was provided during the retroactive period. Timely and accurate Medicare entitlement status is critical to ensuring PACE participants receive the correct level of benefits and that capitation payments accurately reflect the Medicare and/or Medicaid entitlement status of PACE participants. Delays in updating Medicare entitlement status can result in beneficiaries being incorrectly classified—for example, as Medicaid-only or private pay—potentially affecting the scope of services they receive, and the financial obligations placed upon them.
We propose to codify at § 460.158(b)(1) a retroactive timeframe of up to 3 months prior to the month the retroactive request is received when a PACE participant becomes entitled to Medicare retroactively. Codifying this timeframe provides PACE organizations with clarity and stability regarding this policy that was previously outlined in sub-regulatory guidance. By codifying a 3-month retroactive window, CMS aims to protect PACE participants from the adverse consequences that may result from conflicting information regarding enrollment status, plan premium, cost sharing and coverage for past periods, while continuing to provide PACE organizations with a reasonable timeframe to identify and submit retroactive Medicare status requests. Limiting the retroactive window to 3 months would reduce the frequency of these complex, resource-intensive reviews and allow CMS Account Managers to monitor timely and accurate enrollment processing.
CMS acknowledges that there may be cases that necessitate retroactive effective dates that extend beyond the 3-month retroactive timeframe, although we expect these to be rare. CMS recognizes that there may be instances in which strict application of this timeframe may not be appropriate for PACE participants and organizations alike. Accordingly, we propose that CMS may approve a retroactive effective date beyond the 3-month time period from the month the CMS Account Manager receives the retroactive effective date request when CMS makes a determination that neither the PACE organization nor the participant bears responsibility for the circumstances that gave rise to the need for a retroactive effective date request. This proposal seeks to improve the timeliness of retroactive PACE submissions, reduce the potential for retroactive Medicare status change requests that overlap with other coverage, and reduce the overall number of retroactive submissions that exceed the codified timeframe of 3 months.
In addition, we propose to codify at § 460.158(b)(2) the limited reasons for when a retroactive request may be approved, which include when an individual receives retroactive Medicare entitlement from SSA or becomes entitled to Medicare for a reason other than aging into Medicare (for example, disability, ESRD). We also propose redesignating the current regulation text at § 460.158 as § 460.158(a) and adding a new heading.
CMS believes that codifying a 3-month retroactive limit will incentivize PACE organizations to act promptly to submit PACE participant status updates to CMS upon learning of a participant's retroactive Medicare entitlement and therefore minimize adverse impacts on PACE participants. Under the current subregulatory guidance, the availability of up to a 12-month retroactive window may have inadvertently reduced the urgency for PACE organizations to submit timely Medicare status transactions. By establishing a timeframe in regulation, CMS expects PACE organizations to develop internal processes to identify and act on retroactive entitlement determinations in a timely manner to reduce the overall volume of delayed submissions and associated payment reconciliation issues.
We request comments on whether the proposed 3-month retroactive timeframe is appropriate, or whether a shorter or longer timeframe would better serve the needs of PACE participants and PACE organizations.

Because the ingredient cost for a 30-day equivalent supply of a Part D drug is the negotiated price net of dispensing fees, administration fees, and sales tax, and because section 1860D-2(d)(1)(D) of the Act caps the negotiated price for a selected drug at the MFP plus dispensing fees, the ingredient cost for a 30-day equivalent supply of a selected drug cannot exceed the MFP. This stands in contrast to other covered Part D drugs for which the ingredient cost is not prospectively known. This approach reflects that, for most Part D drugs, the most recent complete data available at the time of annual bid and formulary submissions is the claims history from the plan year ending 12 months prior, and that drug prices historically have not decreased year over year. Similarly, for newly FDA-approved drugs that have little or no claims history, paragraph (A)(6) relies on the Part D sponsor's estimate of the ingredient cost portion of its negotiated prices because the ingredient cost for such drugs is not known in advance. ), the ingredient cost reflected on the PDE is used to determine the ingredient cost for a 30-day equivalent supply of a Part D drug for purposes of the specialty-tier cost threshold determination. As stated in the Contract Year 2022 Final Rule, negotiated prices in the PDE record are composed of ingredient cost, administration fee (when applicable), dispensing fee, and sales tax (when applicable). Because the ingredient cost generally accounts for most of the negotiated price, and has fewer variables than the negotiated price overall, the ingredient cost represents the most transparent, least complex, and most predictable of all the components of negotiated price upon which to base the determination of the specialty-tier cost threshold. The ingredient cost reflected on the PDE is therefore the negotiated price for the drug net of any dispensing fees, administration fees, and sales tax.
Section 1860D-2(d)(1)(D) of the Act, as added by section 11001 of the IRA, requires that, for a selected drug with an MFP in effect for a price applicability period, the negotiated price used for payment shall be no greater than the MFP for such drug plus any dispensing fees. Because the ingredient cost reflected on the PDE represents the negotiated price net of dispensing fees, administration fees, and sales tax, and because the statute caps the negotiated price for a selected drug at the MFP plus dispensing fees, the ingredient cost for a 30-day equivalent supply of a selected drug cannot exceed the MFP.
Section 423.104(d)(2)(iv) requires that a drug's ingredient cost for a 30-day equivalent supply exceed the specialty-tier cost threshold for the drug to be eligible for specialty-tier placement. For most Part D drugs, CMS has had to establish methodologies, based on claims history under paragraph (A)(5) or sponsor estimates for newly FDA-approved drugs under paragraph (A)(6), to determine whether that ingredient cost exceeds the specialty-tier cost threshold because the ingredient cost is not known in advance. Those methodologies are not applicable to selected drugs with an MFP in effect because, under section 1860D-2(d)(1)(D) of the Act, the negotiated price for a selected drug shall be no greater than the MFP plus any dispensing fees, meaning that the ingredient cost, which is a component of that negotiated price, cannot exceed the MFP during the price applicability period. Because the MFP is published in advance, CMS and Part D sponsors will prospectively know whether a selected drug's maximum ingredient cost exceeds the specialty-tier cost threshold for the applicable contract year and whether the drug is eligible for specialty-tier placement, without CMS needing to apply the methodologies set forth at paragraphs (A)(5) and (A)(6). In other words, the methodologies set forth at paragraphs (A)(5) and (A)(6) for determining specialty-tier eligibility are not applicable to selected drugs during their price applicability period because the MFP for a selected drug is published and CMS can prospectively determine specialty-tier eligibility for the selected drug based on the published MFP for the applicable contract year.
Historical PDE claims data from prior contract years likely will no longer be reflective of the drug's ingredient costs when a drug becomes a selected drug and its MFP goes into effect. As a result, using historical PDE claims data to determine specialty-tier eligibility for selected drugs would produce misleading results for selected drugs during their price applicability period as that data reflects ingredient costs from prior contract years, before the MFP for a selected drug took effect. Because the specialty tier is reserved for drugs whose ingredient costs exceed the specialty-tier cost threshold, it would be inconsistent with both the statute and the regulatory definition of the specialty tier at § 423.104(d)(2)(iv) to base approval of specialty-tier placement for a selected drug on the drug's historical cost when the MFP in effect for the applicable contract year no longer exceeds the threshold and is prospectively known.
We are therefore proposing, consistent with the April 23, 2026 HPMS memorandum, to make explicit in our regulations that for selected drugs as defined at § 423.100, CMS will only approve placement on the specialty tier for those selected drugs that have an MFP in effect, as adjusted for inflation, if applicable, for the upcoming contract year that exceeds the specialty-tier cost threshold. If the MFP for a selected drug does not exceed the specialty-tier cost threshold, then, consistent with section 1860D-2(d)(1)(D) of the Act, the ingredient cost for a 30-day equivalent supply of that drug cannot exceed the threshold, and the selected drug would not be eligible for specialty-tier placement. In other words, we are proposing that we would not use claims data reported on previous years' PDEs to determine if a selected drug is eligible for placement on the specialty tier. Instead, we are proposing to use the MFP, which is a published, known
(
printed page 76380)
maximum price, to prospectively determine specialty-tier eligibility for the applicable contract year.
We note that, while the MFP represents the statutory maximum amount for the negotiated price (net of dispensing fees) for a selected drug, a Part D sponsor's actual negotiated price for that drug may be lower than the MFP. However, for purposes of determining eligibility for specialty-tier placement, CMS is proposing to use the MFP, as adjusted for inflation, if applicable, not the sponsor's negotiated price, as the basis for the specialty-tier eligibility determination. This approach ensures a consistent, prospective standard across all Part D plan sponsors, and reflects that the MFP is the published, known maximum price against which eligibility can be objectively assessed.
When a Part D sponsor's negotiated price is lower than the MFP, but the MFP exceeds the specialty-tier cost threshold, we are proposing that the drug would be eligible for specialty-tier placement. This approach is consistent with how CMS currently applies the existing PDE-based methodology, under which claims data are used as a standardized benchmark to determine whether a Part D drug's costs exceed the specialty-tier cost threshold. The MFP-based placement standard that we are proposing in this proposed rule would operate similarly by using the MFP as a standardized benchmark for determining whether a selected drug is eligible for specialty-tier placement.
This proposal is consistent with the intent of the specialty tier, which is intended to encompass high-cost drugs whose ingredient costs exceed the specialty-tier cost threshold. Because the MFP represents the statutory maximum amount for the ingredient cost for a selected drug during the price applicability period, the MFP is the appropriate measure for prospectively determining specialty-tier eligibility for such drugs.
We are therefore proposing to add new § 423.104(d)(2)(iv)(E)(
3
) to specify that, for a selected drug, as defined at § 423.100, with an MFP, as defined at section 1191(c)(3) of the Act, in effect for the applicable contract year, CMS would approve placement of that drug on the specialty tier only if the MFP in effect for the contract year exceeds the specialty-tier cost threshold set in accordance with § 423.104(d)(2)(iv)(A) for that contract year. We also propose to revise newly redesignated § 423.104(d)(2)(iv)(E)(
1
) to add an exception for selected drugs.
N. Request for Information (RFI) on an Interim Medicare Part D Payment Reconciliation
1. Background
CMS makes prospective payments to Part D plan sponsors for various subsidies, including the low-income cost-sharing (LICS) subsidy, selected drug subsidy, and reinsurance. Pursuant to our authority under sections 1860D-14(c)(1)(C) and (c)(2), 1860D-14D, and 1860D-15(d)(1) of the Act, and in accordance with §§ 423.315, 423.329, and 423.343, these subsidies are paid prospectively based on information in the approved basic bid and other data provided by CMS, such as enrollment data, which updates payments throughout the year. Following the end of the coverage year, CMS performs a final Part D payment reconciliation to compare the finalized prospective payments and the corresponding actual costs reported on prescription drug event (PDE) records and, in the case of reinsurance, direct and indirect remuneration (DIR) data. CMS then makes payment adjustments according to the rules for each payment methodology. Payment adjustments can be positive or negative.
During the Part D payment reconciliation, CMS also performs the risk corridor calculation pursuant to section 1860D-15(e) of the Act and in accordance with § 423.336. This calculation utilizes the total DIR amount. The purpose of the risk corridor calculation is to limit a plan's exposure to unexpected expenses not already included in the reinsurance subsidy or considered through health status risk adjustment. The federal government and the plan share the profits or losses resulting from expenses for the basic benefit within defined symmetrical risk corridors around a target amount. The payment can be positive, negative, or zero.
Under current regulations at §§ 423.336(c) and 423.343(c), (d), and (e), sponsors are required to submit the necessary data for reconciliation, including PDE and DIR data, within 6 months following the end of the coverage year. This final data is certified by Part D sponsors in accordance with § 423.505(k)(3) and (5) and is used to calculate the final subsidy amounts as well as the final risk corridor payment. This process ensures payment accuracy for both CMS and Part D sponsors.
CMS is seeking feedback on implementation of an additional, earlier reconciliation process, known as “Interim Reconciliation” (IR), as a mechanism to address uncertainty in bidding that could result from various market factors and lead to actual costs significantly exceeding bid estimates. The plan's bid reflects the revenue needed to provide beneficiaries with the Medicare prescription drug benefit, which CMS pays through prospective subsidy payments.
When the bid closely aligns with actual costs, the Part D payment reconciliation results in smaller payment adjustments. However, these reconciliation payments can be volatile, influenced by shifts in drug utilization, drug pricing, plan bidding behavior, and statutory changes to the Part D benefit year to year. If a plan underestimates utilization, drug mix, or liability in its bid, CMS pays more during the Part D payment reconciliation. Conversely, if a plan overestimates these costs, CMS recoups payments as determined by the reconciliation calculations. For instance, the introduction of new hepatitis C prescription drug treatments significantly increased drug spending and consequently increased reconciliation amounts for coverage years 2013 through 2015. By 2016 and 2017, reconciliation amounts had stabilized as historical experience began to reflect these new drug treatments, resulting in improving bid accuracy and formulary management. Similarly, there was also a sharp increase in reconciliation amounts for coverage year 2024, likely driven by uncertainty with the Inflation Reduction Act Part D redesign. As plan sponsors gain more experience with the redesigned Part D benefit there will be less uncertainty with bidding assumptions, which is anticipated to stabilize the reconciliation payment amounts.
2. The Interim Reconciliation (IR) Concept
The IR would serve as a reconciliation process that would begin in January immediately following the coverage year, prior to the final data (PDE and DIR) submission deadline. Payment adjustments to remit or recover the estimated IR amounts would most likely occur with the March payment following the coverage year.
CMS would include the LICS, selected drug subsidy, and reinsurance calculations in the IR. The risk corridor payment would not be included in the IR because the information necessary to calculate such payment—specifically, the final Direct Subsidy Amount determined during the Final Risk Adjustment reconciliation—would not yet be available.
The estimated IR amount would be calculated based on PDE data with dates of service through December 31st as of mid-January following the coverage year
(
printed page 76381)
(referred to here as the PDE data cut-off). CMS will need an estimate of the total DIR amount for the IR. We could require that each plan provide an estimated total DIR amount based on their actual claims experience through December 31st. The plan would submit this estimate to CMS in January following the coverage year. Alternatively, we could estimate the total DIR amount based on the sponsor's approved bid for the coverage year. To estimate the total DIR amount for IR, we would apply a ratio as follows: the projected total DIR amount in the bid divided by the projected drug costs in the bid, then multiplied by the actual drug costs as reflected in the PDE data as of the PDE data cut-off. We have concerns regarding the alternative approach, particularly if the projected total DIR amount included in the bid significantly differs from the actual experience (which as we state above is the issue we would be attempting to address with an IR process), and we request comments on this approach below.
Using this preliminary data, CMS would determine interim amounts for the LICS, reinsurance, and selected drug subsidy. This process would lead to an IR payment adjustment, with some sponsors receiving payments from CMS while others would be required to remit payments to CMS at the time of the IR payment adjustment. Our IR simulation using coverage year 2024 data show that a number of plans would have been required to remit payment to CMS at the time of the IR payment adjustment had the IR process been in place for coverage year 2024.
Based on our analysis, we could consider an IR process that would allow plans to voluntarily opt in. Under this voluntary process, we anticipate that plans would estimate their potential IR reconciliation amount and make an informed decision regarding participation. However, if a plan's estimate is inaccurate and results in an amount owed to CMS through IR, CMS will recoup the calculated IR amount. Due to the timing between the IR and the final Part D payment reconciliation, we anticipate that an IR would not be eligible for reopening under § 423.346 or for appeal under § 423.350.
IR payment adjustments would be fully reconciled during the final Part D payment reconciliation, which takes place after the June data submission deadline and uses final, certified PDE and DIR data. The risk corridor calculation will also be completed at this time as part of the standard final Part D payment reconciliation process.
3. Request for Public Comment
CMS is soliciting comments on this IR concept to assess its necessity and feasibility, evaluate potential impacts on Part D sponsors, and determine whether such a policy would be beneficial for the Part D program. We are interested in feedback from all Part D sponsors, with a particular interest in understanding the potential effects on smaller, regional health plans.
Specifically, we are requesting comments, data, and examples regarding the following:
Potential Benefits and Risks:
++ Considering the pattern that CMS has observed, where using more representative historical data leads to improved bids and greater reconciliation stability, is it necessary to introduce a new and complex IR process?
++ What do you see as the primary benefits of an IR, if any? Conversely, what are the most significant risks or potential unintended consequences for sponsors and beneficiaries?
Operational and Administrative Impact:
++ What would be the administrative burden and operational challenges for your organization to participate in an IR? Please comment on any required system modifications, resource allocation, and the processes involved in tracking and validating IR calculations.
++ During which month of the coverage year would your organization have sufficient information to determine whether to opt in to a voluntary IR? Given the information provided in this RFI, what is the likelihood that your organization would choose to opt in to an IR?
Financial Impact:
What effect would an interim payment or recoupment in March following the coverage year have on your organization's cash flow and overall financial stability? If possible, please provide quantitative examples to illustrate the potential impact.
Accuracy and Data Reliability:
++ Provide feedback regarding the two possible methods for estimating the total DIR amount. Discuss the feasibility of providing an estimated total DIR amount in January following the coverage year, utilizing actual claims experience through the coverage year. Comment on the alternative approach and the accuracy of an IR that depends on an estimated total DIR amount from your bid. What is the usual difference between your bid-projected DIR and your final, actual DIR?
++ Comment on the completeness of PDE data available mid-January following the coverage year for dates of service through December 31st. What percentage of your total PDE data for a coverage year is typically submitted after mid-January following the coverage year? What percentage of your accepted PDE data for a coverage year is typically adjusted or deleted after mid-January following the coverage year? Provide examples of how PDE data evolves between January and the final June submission. How might this affect the accuracy of the IR calculations?
++ Provide comments on potential incentives that may lead to the submission of inaccurate DIR estimates. Additionally, offer insights regarding PDE data submissions, specifically addressing whether an IR could incentivize non-compliance with PDE timeliness requirements by delaying the submission of adjustment or deletion PDE records beyond the 90 calendar days allowed after discovering or receiving notification of an issue necessitating changes to previously submitted and accepted PDE records, as outlined in § 423.325(a)(2).
Bidding and Market Effects:
In what ways could an IR influence your organization's approach to bid development for upcoming plan years?
Please be advised that this is a request for information only. This RFI is issued exclusively for informational and planning purposes; it does not constitute a solicitation, a promise to issue a solicitation in the future, or a commitment to implement the policy described.

IV. Medicare Advantage/Part C and Part D Prescription Drug Plan Quality Rating System (§§ 422.166 and 423.186)
A. Introduction
CMS develops and publicly posts a 5-star rating system for Part C,
[
80

more commonly referred to as Medicare Advantage (MA), and Part D plans as part of its responsibility to disseminate comparative information, including information about quality, to beneficiaries under sections 1851(d) and 1860D-1(c) of the Act. The Part C and D Star Ratings system is used to determine quality bonus payment (QBP) ratings for MA plans under section 1853(o) of the Act and the amount of MA beneficiary rebates under section 1854(b) of the Act. We use multiple data sources based on the collection of different types of quality data under section 1852(e) of the Act to measure the quality and performance of contracts, such as CMS administrative data, surveys of enrollees, and information provided directly from health and drug plans. CMS regulations, including §§ 417.472(j) and (k), 422.152(b), 423.153(c), and 423.156, require plans to report on quality improvement and quality assurance and to provide data that help beneficiaries compare plans. The methodology for the Star Ratings system for the MA/Part C and Part D programs is codified at §§ 422.160 through 422.166 and 423.180 through 423.186, respectively, and we have specified the measures used in setting Star Ratings through rulemaking. In addition, the cost plan regulation at § 417.472(k) requires cost contracts to be subject to the Parts 422 and 423 Medicare Advantage and Part D Prescription Drug Program Quality Rating System (
83 FR 16526
and
16527
). As a result, the regulatory changes proposed here would apply to the quality ratings for MA plans and cost plans.
We have continued to identify enhancements to the Star Ratings program to ensure it is aligned with the CMS Quality Strategy
[
81
]
as it evolves over time to increase the health and wellbeing of enrollees. In this proposed rule, we propose removing additional measures to continue to simplify and refocus the areas included in the Star Ratings, building on the changes to the measure set finalized in the Contract Year 2027 final rule. The proposed measure set of 15 measures reflects our ongoing effort to sharpen the Star Ratings program's focus on clinical outcomes while continuing to encourage high performance on patient experience and would also include a small number of process measures in areas of high clinical importance where better performance would improve quality of care for beneficiaries. The proposed revised measure set would continue to motivate high performance on patient experience while reducing the emphasis on process-oriented measures that assess whether a specific action was completed, rather than whether that action meaningfully improved an enrollee's health or experience. We believe this greater emphasis on outcome measures better reflects the actual effects of care on enrollees' health and wellbeing, and more directly captures whether contracts are delivering the care enrollees need.
In the Contract Year 2027 final rule we also solicited comments on ways to simplify and modify the Star Ratings methodology to further improve quality of care. Consistent with that policy goal and some of the comments we received on the Star Ratings proposals in the rule, we propose removing the reward factor. We are also proposing modifying the improvement measure hold harmless to apply only to contracts receiving 4.5 or higher stars for their highest rating. These changes to the measure set and methodology would streamline and simplify the Star Ratings. They would also raise the bar for achieving high Star Ratings and associated Quality Bonus Payments (QBPs), incentivizing plans to improve performance and deliver the highest quality of care for their enrollees. We believe these proposed changes will create a Star Ratings program directly aligned with the outcomes and patient experiences that matter most to Medicare enrollees. We also propose a change to the methodologies for setting cut points to account for the potential impact of the ADVaNCE MA model proposed in section VIII. of this proposed rule. We also propose a substantive update to the Controlling Blood Pressure measure, a clarification related to displaying Star Ratings domains on the Medicare Plan Finder (MPF) website, language related to disclosing preliminary data shared with plans during the plan preview periods, and a clarification related to the extreme and uncontrollable circumstances policy.

1. Updating Measure—Controlling Blood Pressure (Part C)
Consistent with § 422.164(c)(1), we continue to review measures that are nationally endorsed and in alignment with private sector organizations, such as the National Committee for Quality Assurance (NCQA) and the Pharmacy Quality Alliance (PQA). As discussed in the Advance Notice of Methodological Changes for Calendar Year (CY) 2025 for Medicare Advantage (MA) Capitation Rates and Part C and Part D Payment, NCQA, the measure steward, was exploring updates to the Controlling High Blood Pressure (CBP) measure. NCQA has decided to move forward with updates to this measure. CMS is proposing to replace the current version of the CBP measure with the updated version, referred to as the Blood Pressure Control for Patients with Hypertension (BPC-E) measure, starting with the 2029 measurement year and 2031 Star Ratings. Both the current (CBP) and the updated (BPC-E) measures assess the percentage of
(
printed page 76385)
members 18-85 years of age who had a diagnosis of hypertension and whose blood pressure was adequately controlled (<140/90 mm Hg) during the measurement year. Both measures use the same blood pressure threshold, numerator, age range, and exclusions. For CBP, beneficiaries are captured in the denominator when they have two or more outpatient, telephone, or virtual visits on different dates of service with a diagnosis of hypertension. Since the updated measure expands the denominator, it is a substantive change as defined at § 422.164(d)(2). The only two changes from CBP to BPC-E are the change in denominator to allow beneficiaries to be included if they have at least one outpatient, telephone, or virtual visit with a diagnosis of hypertension and at least one dispensed antihypertensive medication, and the transition to ECDS reporting. Both the legacy measure (CBP) and the new measure (BPC-E) will be collected for the 2027 and 2028 measurement years. The existing CBP measure will continue to be in Star Ratings through the 2028 measurement year and 2030 Star Ratings. We are proposing to replace the existing CBP measure with the updated BPC-E measure for the 2029 measurement year and the 2031 Star Ratings. The updated BPC-E would continue to be referred to as the “CBP” measure in the Star Ratings, although the current version would be replaced with BPC-E as of the 2031 Star Ratings. The updated measure would be on the display page for the 2029 and 2030 Star Ratings and would be included in the 2031 Star Ratings if finalized through rulemaking. C. Cut Point Methodology Changes to Account for Potential Impact of ADVaNCE MA Model (§§ 422.166(a)(2) and (3) and 423.186(a)(2) and (3))
In section VIII. of this proposed rule, CMS proposes to implement the Aligning Data and Value to Nurture Competition and Efficiency in Medicare Advantage (ADVaNCE MA) model. Because this model would test different quality and payment incentives for MA contracts in selected states, the ADVaNCE MA model may impact how model contracts perform on the quality measures included in the Part C and D Star Ratings. While Star Ratings would not be calculated for model contracts, removing the model contracts from the calculation of the Star Ratings measure cut points for non-model contracts could result in shifting of the cut points that is unrelated to the performance of non-model contracts. Therefore, CMS proposes to calculate the Star Ratings measure cut points for MA contracts using adjusted measure scores for model contracts to avoid biasing the cut points for non-model contracts and to avoid impacting non-model contracts' Star Ratings. The adjusted measure scores for model contracts would account for the estimated average impact of the ADVaNCE MA model on measure scores and would only be calculated for measures that are the same across model and non-model contracts. These adjusted model contract scores would only be used for the purpose of calculating Star Ratings cut points for star assignments of non-model contracts. The adjusted scores for model contracts would not be publicly available and would be available to all Part C and D plan sponsors only for measures included in the de-identified sample measure data provided in the Health Plan Management System (HPMS) during the second plan preview period.
