We propose to treat the improvement measures differently from the other Star Ratings measures because the improvement measures assess year-over-year change in performance rather than the level of performance in a given year. We assume that model contracts, in the absence of the ADVaNCE MA model, would have experienced year-over-year performance changes similar to those of non-model contracts. Therefore, excluding model contracts from the improvement measures would not substantially shift cut points. However, we anticipate that year-over-year changes in performance for model contracts may differ from non-model contracts because of their participation in the model. Model contracts may also differ in the year-to-year correlations of the measure scores that are included in the improvement measures, relative to the non-model contracts. Both factors would affect improvement measure stars. Excluding model contracts from the improvement measure score and cut point calculations would avoid model contracts impacting the improvement measure stars for non-model contracts.
The reward factor ranges from 0.0 to 0.4 and is added to the overall and summary ratings to incentivize consistently high performance. We propose adding language at §§ 422.166(f)(1)(i) and 423.186(f)(1)(i) to exclude model contracts from the calculation of the weighted variance and weighted mean thresholds used to determine the reward factor for the duration of the ADVaNCE MA model, and removing language that references the reward factor calculations for the 2022 Star Ratings only. During the model, ADVaNCE MA model contracts will not receive Star Ratings and could cause some shifting of the thresholds; thus, we propose to exclude ADVaNCE MA model contracts from these calculations. We note, however, that if CMS finalizes the removal of the reward factor starting with the 2030 Star Ratings as proposed in section V.G. of this proposed rule, there would be no need to adjust the reward factor during the ADVaNCE MA model or to finalize the proposed additional language at §§ 422.166(f)(1)(i) and 423.186(f)(1)(i).
The categorical adjustment index (CAI) is a factor that is added to or subtracted from an overall or summary Star Rating (or both) to adjust for the average within-contract (or within-plan as applicable) disparity in performance associated with the percentages of beneficiaries who are dually eligible for Medicare and enrolled in Medicaid, beneficiaries who receive a Low Income Subsidy or have disability status in that contract (or plan as applicable). We propose adding language at §§ 422.166(f)(2) and 423.186(f)(2) to exclude model contracts from the calculation of the CAI for the duration of the ADVaNCE MA model. During the model, ADVaNCE MA model contracts will not receive Star Ratings; thus, we propose to exclude ADVaNCE MA model contracts from these calculations.
We solicit comment on these proposed changes to the Star Ratings methodology to account for the potential impact of the ADVaNCE MA model. We propose implementing these changes beginning with the 2031 Star Ratings for the duration of the proposed ADVaNCE MA model.

E. Plan Preview of Star Ratings (§§ 422.166(h)(2) and 423.186(h)(2))
During the first plan preview, CMS expects MA organizations and Part D sponsors to closely review the methodology and their posted numerical data for each measure in HPMS prior to display on MPF. The second plan preview includes data revisions made as a result of the first plan preview and provides preliminary Star Ratings for each measure, domain rating, summary rating, and overall rating. During the second plan preview, MA organizations and Part D sponsors should again review their data closely. Following the second plan preview, CMS makes any necessary corrections identified by contracts or CMS during the preview periods and then finalizes the Star Ratings.
Our goal is for Medicare beneficiaries to make informed plan decisions that take into consideration the cost, benefits, and quality of the plans in their geographic area. To that end, based on our authority under sections 1856(b)(1), 1857(e)(1), and 1860D-12(b)(3)(D) of the Act, which grant the Secretary authority to establish by regulation standards that are consistent with and to carry out the statute and to include additional contract terms and conditions that are not inconsistent with the statute and that the Secretary finds necessary and appropriate, we are proposing language at §§ 422.166(h)(2) and 423.186(h)(2) to codify that MA organizations, PDPs, and first tier, downstream, and related entities may not publicly disclose any preliminary data displayed in HPMS until the Star Ratings have been finalized and released on MPF. Data displayed in HPMS during the plan preview periods are preliminary and subject to change. Public release of these preliminary data creates a risk that Medicare beneficiaries will rely on inaccurate quality information to make a plan selection since Medicare beneficiaries may hear about the preliminary ratings through the media or other communication channels. CMS develops and publicly posts the Star Ratings as part of its responsibility to disseminate comparative information to beneficiaries in order to promote an active, informed selection among available coverage options, as required by sections 1851(d) and 1860D-1(c) of the Act. Medicare beneficiaries exposed to preliminary Star Ratings data may not have sufficient information to understand that these ratings are preliminary and subject to change, and they may rely on these data to make plan selections without confirming the final ratings once they are released on MPF. Thus, to minimize the risk that Medicare beneficiaries will rely on preliminary and potentially inaccurate information and to promote the active, informed selection of coverage options, we are proposing that no preliminary Part C and D Star Ratings data can be disclosed to the public until CMS releases the final Star Ratings data on MPF in mid-October.

G. Reward Factor (§§ 422.166(f)(1) and 423.186(f)(1))
The reward factor described at §§ 422.166(f)(1) and 423.186(f)(1) was included in the Part C and D Star Ratings program beginning with the 2009 Star Ratings with the purpose of creating additional incentives for high and stable relative performance across measures by discouraging contracts from having a lot of variation in performance across measures (that is, a mix of low and high performance across measures). In the Contract Year 2024 final rule, we finalized the removal of the reward factor along with the addition of the health equity index (HEI) reward. Subsequently, in the Contract Year 2027 final rule, we finalized a policy that retained the reward factor in lieu of implementing the HEI reward for two reasons: (1) to incentivize improvement efforts on clinical care, outcomes, and patient experience, rather than on improvement among certain populations, and (2) to keep the Star Ratings methodology consistent while we explored ways to simplify and modify the methodology to further drive quality improvement.
While we believe it was important to retain the reward factor methodology for consistency while we explored ways to simplify and streamline the Star Ratings methodology, we also stated in the Contract Year 2027 final rule that CMS would consider whether the historical reward factor should continue to be part of the Star Ratings in the future. As we explained in the Contract Year 2024 final rule, the reward factor is less effective in serving its intended purpose in the Star Ratings as overall contract performance has continued to increase. At the beginning of the Star Ratings program, the distribution of ratings across contracts looked very different, with overall performance much lower than it is today. Over time, we have established additional methodological enhancements to foster performance improvement across measures, such as the addition of the Health Plan Quality Improvement and the Drug Plan Quality Improvement measures as described at §§ 422.164(f) and 423.184(f). The improvement measures are weighted 5 and reward contracts for improving performance from the prior year across measures. The linkage between Star Ratings and QBP ratings has further motivated MA organizations to perform well across measures. As a result, contract performance has improved and become more consistent across Star Ratings measures over time.
These considerations suggest that the reward factor may no longer be necessary; thus, we are proposing in this rule the removal of the reward factor. If CMS finalizes the removal of the reward factor from the Star Ratings methodology, contracts would still have incentives to perform well and improve because high performance on individual Star Ratings measures, including the Health Plan Quality Improvement and the Drug Plan Quality Improvement measures, translates into better overall and summary ratings.
Removing the reward factor would place downward pressure on Star Ratings and would create additional incentives for contracts to improve performance. This is consistent with our objectives to simplify the Star Ratings methodology and further drive quality improvement on the refocused set of Star Ratings measures finalized in the Contract Year 2027 final rule and proposed in this rule.
We solicit comment on our proposal to remove the reward factor from the Star Ratings beginning with the 2030 Star Ratings.
H. Improvement Hold Harmless (§§ 422.166(g)(1) and 423.186(g)(1))
In the “Medicare Program; Contract Year 2019 Policy and Technical Changes to the Medicare Advantage, Medicare Cost Plan, Medicare Fee-for-Service, the Medicare Prescription Drug Benefit Programs, and the PACE Program” final rule, we discussed that one of the goals of the Part C and D Star Ratings program is to drive quality improvement for plans and providers (
83 FR 16521
). In that final rule, CMS adopted, at §§ 422.166(g)(1) and 423.186(g)(1), a hold harmless provision for the inclusion of the Part C or Part D or both improvement measures for contracts with 4 or more stars for their highest rating (that is, the overall rating for MA-PDs, the Part C summary rating for MA-only contracts, and the Part D summary rating for PDPs). Under this provision, the highest rating is calculated both with and without the improvement measures; contracts with 4 or more stars without including the improvement measures are held harmless from having the highest rating reduced by the addition of the improvement measures. The original intent of this hold harmless provision was to recognize that higher performing contracts have less room to improve (
83 FR 16578
).
Upon further reflection, the hold harmless provision for the highest rating may suppress improvement incentives for 4 star contracts, because these contracts still have the potential to increase scores across measures and thus their Star Ratings. This is particularly important as we propose to further refocus the measure set and to remove the reward factor. We want to ensure that all contracts are motivated to reach the highest levels of performance across the refocused set of Star Ratings measures. In order to encourage continued improvement across measures for contracts with 4 stars for their highest rating, we propose to modify § 422.166 at paragraphs (g)(1)(i) and (ii) and § 423.186 at paragraphs (g)(1)(i) and (ii) to apply the improvement measure hold harmless provision to only contracts with 4.5 and 5 stars for their highest rating beginning with the 2030 Star Ratings.

V. Strengthening Current Medicare Advantage Special Needs Plans Program Policies
A. Reducing Model of Care (MOC) Burden, Improving Special Needs Plans (SNP) Care Coordination Requirements, and Updating HRA Outreach Requirements (§ 422.101)
Congress permanently authorized special needs plans (SNPs) through section 50311(a) of the Bipartisan Budget Act (BBA) of 2018. Under section 1859(f)(2) through (4) of the Act, SNPs are required to restrict enrollment to Medicare beneficiaries who are: institutionalized individuals, who are currently defined in § 422.2 as those residing or expecting to reside for 90 days or longer in a long-term care facility, and institutionalized equivalent individuals who reside in the community but need an institutional level of care when certain conditions are met (Institutionalized Special Needs Plan or I-SNP); individuals entitled to medical assistance under a State plan under Title XIX (Dual eligible SNP or D-SNP); or other individuals with certain severe or disabling chronic conditions who would benefit from enrollment in a SNP (Chronic condition SNP or C-SNP).
Section 1859(f)(5)(A) of the Act imposes specific care management requirements for all SNPs effective January 1, 2010. As a result, all SNPs are required to implement care management requirements that have two core components: an evidence-based model of care (MOC) and care management services for each enrollee.
CMS is proposing to amend and add new regulations at § 422.101(f) in order to, first, adequately address gaps in care management by SNPs based on findings from the CMS SNP audit process, second, reduce unnecessary plan and provider burden associated with SNP MOC training requirements, and third, amend current health risk assessment (HRA) requirements to take into account technological advancements employed by MA organizations when communicating with enrollees. Specifically, CMS proposes to: amend § 422.101(f)(1)(vii) to require that person-centered goals and objectives in individualized care plans (ICPs) be specific to all active needs and diagnoses based on available data and input from the enrollee, address supplemental benefits available to the enrollee under the plan, and ensure that the ICP is shared among a designated group; amend interdisciplinary care team (ICT) regulations at § 422.101(f)(1)(ix) to better suit the unique populations served by SNPs; remove MOC training requirements at § 422.101(f)(2)(ii) to alleviate SNP and provider burden; and amend § 422.101(f)(1)(iv) to remove the prohibition on automated phone calls when conducting outreach to enrollees for the purpose of completing an HRA. Collectively, these proposals are intended to reduce care coordination gaps identified through CMS program audits, improve the person-centeredness of SNP care planning, and reduce regulatory burden associated with current SNP care coordination requirements.
1. Improving SNP Care Coordination and Communication
Section 164 of the Medicare Improvements for Patients and Providers Act added care management provisions for all SNPs as set forth in section 1859(f)(5) of the Act (
42 U.S.C. 1395w-28(f)(5)
). The mandate requires SNPs to implement a care management model with two core components. The first core component is an evidence-based MOC with an appropriate network of providers and specialists to meet the specialized needs of the SNP target population. The second core component is a set of care management services that includes: a comprehensive initial HRA and annual reassessments; an ICP with goals and measurable outcomes; and an ICT to manage care. Section 1859(f)(5) is the foundation for much of CMS's MOC regulatory standards. Section 422.101(f)(1) requires MA organizations offering SNPs to implement a MOC with care management as the centerpiece, designed to meet the specialized needs of the plan's targeted enrollees.
During the review of SNP care coordination findings in the CMS Medicare Parts C and D program audits, CMS routinely sees plans struggle to complete HRAs and/or annual assessments in a timely manner, create and develop ICPs that comply with all requirements, and facilitate ICT meetings between their enrollees' key providers and care managers. Audits have also demonstrated that some SNPs are more adept at employing HRAs, ICPs, and ICTs as care management tools. The use of these care management tools is meant to improve the care of special needs individuals enrolled in SNPs, and the proposed care management amendments to § 422.101(f) are intended to improve SNP performance in carrying out statutorily required care coordination practices.
CMS is proposing to amend the SNP ICP requirements at § 422.101(f)(1)(vii), which require MA organizations offering SNPs to develop a comprehensive ICP within 90 days of conducting a comprehensive initial HRA, or within 90 days after the effective date of enrollment, whichever is later, that meets additional requirements at paragraphs (f)(1)(vii)(A)-(D). CMS has identified opportunities to improve the content of ICPs. For example, CMS reviewed ICPs that did not reflect needs and conditions that often have significant impacts on beneficiary health outcomes and experiences, were only loosely related to the needs and preferences of enrollees, or that did not contain measurable outcomes. To address some of these findings, CMS is proposing several amendments to § 422.101(f)(1)(vii).
First, CMS proposes to insert new language at § 422.101(f)(1)(vii)(C) that ICPs should document all active needs and diagnoses for the enrollee based on available data. In addition to the requirement at paragraph (vi) of this section, the SNP must utilize available enrollee-specific data, including but not limited to current diagnoses, health status information, and other clinical data where available. Over the years, CMS has found that some plans will produce ICPs that do not address aspects of the enrollee's current healthcare needs. Although CMS recognizes that information collected during an HRA—along with involvement of the enrollee and/or enrollee's personal representative, as applicable—is valuable in developing an ICP, SNPs are expected to formulate an ICP based on all information gathered and should draw from enrollee-specific data, including but not limited to, current diagnoses and health status information and other clinical data where available, claims and prescription history, prior authorization records, discharge summaries, or other information from the enrollee's providers when HRA material is not available. Therefore, the proposed new language at § 422.101(f)(1)(vii)(C) requires SNPs to use enrollee-specific data, including but not limited to current diagnoses, health status information, and other clinical data where available. Note that section 1859(f)(5)(B)(iii) of the Act and § 422.101(f)(1)(vi) require that SNPs ensure the results from the comprehensive initial and annual HRA conducted for each enrollee are addressed in the enrollee's ICP. This amendment would assist SNPs in
(
printed page 76393)
meeting and completing ICP requirements when enrollees are unable to participate or when limited information is gathered from the HRA process.
CMS also proposes to amend the existing requirement at § 422.101(f)(1)(vii)(C), which requires that SNPs identify, as part of the ICP process, person-centered goals and objectives (as prioritized by the enrollee), including measurable outcomes as well as specific services and benefits to be provided. CMS proposes to redesignate § 422.101(f)(1)(vii)(C) as § 422.101(f)(1)(vii)(D) with revisions and reorder the current language at § 422.101(f)(1)(vii)(D) as § 422.101(f)(1)(vii)(F). CMS proposes revising this section to require that, when enrollee input is obtainable from the HRA or other consultations with the enrollee, the ICP documents discussions between the enrollee and the ICT regarding all active needs, diagnoses, and available resources for those needs. Documentation must include when the enrollee has chosen not to focus on an active need or diagnosis. The ICP must reflect the enrollee's chosen person-centered goals and objectives (as prioritized by the enrollee), including measurable outcomes, as well as specific services and benefits to be provided. This would help ensure SNPs create ICPs that appropriately reflect a discussion of all active needs and available resources for the enrollee as well as the enrollee's chosen goals, resulting in more comprehensive care planning, improved care coordination, and better health outcomes.
Consistent with a person-centered approach, the ICP should reflect the enrollee's identified goals, preferences, and priorities, even when additional health conditions or needs are identified through the HRA or available data. For example, if an enrollee uses tobacco but does not wish to pursue smoking cessation, the ICP should document that tobacco use was identified and discussed, and that cessation resources were offered, as well as the enrollee's decision not to prioritize smoking cessation at that time. The ICP should then reflect the enrollee's chosen goals and priorities rather than include interventions the enrollee has declined. Another example is where an enrollee needs support for one or more Activities of Daily Living (ADLs), but through discussion as part of the ICP development, the SNP has identified that the enrollee has sufficient caregiver support within the home and does not want to receive other supports. In this scenario, the plan would document the discussion and relevant facts of the circumstance, with the conclusion that the enrollee does not wish to prioritize this need and then specify the enrollee's chosen goals and priorities as identified through the discussion.
In addition, CMS proposes adding a new paragraph at § 422.101(f)(1)(vii)(E) regarding situations in which an enrollee does not participate in the ICP process or does not participate in the HRA process. Specifically, if the enrollee declines to participate or cannot be reached, the SNP must identify person-centered goals and objectives for the enrollee based on available data so that they are addressed in the ICP, including measurable outcomes as well as specific services and benefits to be provided. If an enrollee does not participate meaningfully in these processes, the SNP must identify person-centered goals and objectives for the enrollee based on all available data to ensure a comprehensive ICP. CMS has noted in the past that the ICP is an essential tool for managing care for all SNP beneficiaries, regardless of whether they complete or participate in an HRA. Additionally, MA regulations at § 422.152(g)(2)(v) require that, as part of a SNP's quality improvement program, it must implement an ICP for each beneficiary. However, observations from audits and other activities have identified that when enrollee input was not obtained through the HRA for some SNPs, the ICPs lack detail or enrollee-specific information. This proposed change, taken with the proposed new language at § 422.101(f)(1)(vii)(C), will ensure that ICPs are specific to each enrollee by utilizing other information available to the plan.
CMS still maintains that obtaining enrollee input through the HRA is the best way to develop a comprehensive, person-centered ICP. CMS will continue to monitor SNP compliance with HRA and ICP requirements through the SNP audit process and notes that many organizations continue to have high unable to reach rates. CMS requests comments on methods that organizations can use to lower these unable to be reached rates.
Next, CMS proposes adding a new requirement at § 422.101(f)(1)(vii)(G) to ensure that SNPs take available supplemental benefit offerings included in the enrollee's specific plan benefit package (PBP) into account when creating an ICP to address the enrollee's needs or to make enrollees aware of supplemental benefits under their plan. Specifically, as proposed, SNPs would identify in the enrollee's care plan the available and relevant supplemental benefits as described in § 422.102 and notify enrollees who have been identified as eligible for such benefits that those benefits are accessible to address their identified care needs. In providing the ICP to the enrollee and/or enrollee's personal representative, SNPs would be required to proactively inform enrollees of both eligibility and availability of supplemental benefits under their plan that address the enrollee's identified care needs as part of the ICP process. As noted above, SNPs are already required to take HRA information into consideration when drafting an ICP and CMS proposes codifying a requirement that SNPs use available enrollee-specific information to complete an ICP when the enrollee is unavailable to complete an HRA and/or ICP. It is likely that some SNPs are already informing enrollees of available supplemental benefits relevant to the enrollee's identified care needs as part of the ICP creation process. CMS acknowledges that supplemental benefit offerings vary significantly across MA plans and contract years and clarifies that SNPs would be expected to consider benefits available under the enrollee's specific PBP, including Special Supplemental Benefits for the Chronically Ill (SSBCI) for which the enrollee is eligible, but not benefits available under other plans or programs. When reviewing and updating the ICP, the ICT should consider any supplemental benefits available to the enrollee under the enrollee's specific PBP, as applicable, and identify those benefits in the ICP when they support the enrollee's care goals and needs. Extending the requirement for the ICP to account for supplemental benefits would further increase the effectiveness of the ICP, enhance existing care coordination requirements under§ 422.101(f), and improve quality outcomes, particularly given the critical role supplemental benefits can play in providing medical and non-medical items and services not covered by Medicare Parts A and B.
Next, CMS proposes to add a new requirement at § 422.101(f)(1)(vii)(H) that would require SNPs to share and make accessible the ICP with the following parties: the enrollee; the enrollee's personal representative, if applicable and consistent with
45 CFR 164.502(g)
; the ICT required under § 422.101(f)(1)(ix); and, for facility-based institutional special needs plans (FI-SNPs), the enrollee's long-term care facility. Of note, the sharing of the ICP must be consistent with current statutory and regulatory requirements regarding the sharing of protected health
(
printed page 76394)
information. SNP audit findings indicate that SNPs are inconsistent in providing a copy of the ICP to the enrollee or making it available through an easily accessible platform, such as a plan portal. This proposal would expand access beyond the enrollee to include their personal representative, in alignment with the HIPAA Privacy Rule at
45 CFR 164.502(g)
, as well as members of the enrollee's ICT. CMS is not proposing to designate a specific method for communicating the ICP to the parties identified in the proposed rule. MA organizations are best positioned to identify an appropriate method of communication. However, any form of dissemination should permit individuals to readily retrieve, store, and secure the ICP as they see fit, consistent with HIPAA and other applicable privacy and security requirements. This requirement would also apply to enrollees who did not participate in an HRA, as SNPs are required to develop ICPs for all enrollees.
Lastly, CMS proposes to revise § 422.101(f)(1)(ix) to strengthen the current statutory and regulatory framework requiring SNPs to employ an ICT in providing coordination of enrollee care. Section 1859(f)(5)(A)(ii)(III) of the Act requires SNPs to use an ICT in the management of care. In addition, for C-SNPs, section 1859(f)(5)(B)(i) of the Act requires the ICT to include providers with demonstrated expertise, including training in an applicable specialty, in treating individuals similar to the targeted population of the plan. CMS implemented these statutory requirements in regulation at § 422.101(f)(1)(ix) to apply to all SNP types. In addition to relabeling paragraph (ix) as “Interdisciplinary Care Team (ICT),” CMS proposes to add several new requirements specifying the types of providers that, at a minimum, should be part of an enrollee's ICT.
First, CMS proposes adding at § 422.101(f)(1)(ix)(A) a general ICT requirement applicable to all SNP types—D-SNPs, C-SNPs, and I-SNPs—that would require SNPs to include, at a minimum, the following: a primary care provider or a member of their clinical staff such as nurse practitioners, physician assistants, or registered nurses, acting as the provider's representative, a care manager, any behavioral health care provider actively treating or coordinating care for the enrollee, and at least one other individual with clinical training or expertise who is delivering or coordinating care for the enrollee. If the enrollee is not receiving treatment or care coordination from a behavioral health provider, the SNP is not required to have a behavioral health provider serve on that enrollee's ICT. Second, CMS proposes adding at § 422.101(f)(1)(ix)(B) an additional ICT requirement specific to C-SNPs to ensure that the ICT includes a specialist provider who focuses on the specific chronic disease(s) of focus. For C-SNPs that serve enrollees with multiple chronic conditions, the ICT only needs to include one specialist. Next, CMS proposes adding at § 422.101(f)(1)(ix)(C) an additional ICT requirement specific to I-SNPs serving institutionalized individuals and/or institutionalized-equivalent individuals as defined at § 422.2. For I-SNP enrollees who are institutionalized, the ICT would also be required to include a member of the clinical team providing care from the enrollee's long-term care facility. For I-SNP enrollees who are institutionalized-equivalent but reside in the community, the ICT would also be required to include a home health provider, nurse, or other individual providing care in the home, as applicable based on the enrollee's care needs. Last, CMS proposes adding at § 422.101(f)(1)(ix)(D) an additional ICT requirement specific to D-SNPs. For D-SNP enrollees who are full-benefit dually eligible and residing in the community, the ICT would be required to include a home health provider, nurse, personal care aide, or other individual providing care in the home.
CMS is proposing these requirements to strengthen the value of ICTs by including the providers most critical to the enrollee's care and well-being. CMS believes the participation of these providers will close any gaps that may exist in the enrollee's care by providing a forum for sharing and exchanging information key to maintaining the enrollee's health. However, CMS acknowledges that requiring the inclusion of specific providers on the ICT may not directly increase provider participation in the ICT process, which audits have shown to be a recurring issue for many SNPs. CMS reiterates that the general requirement at paragraph (ix)(A) applies in addition to the type-specific requirements at (ix)(B), (ix)(C), and (ix)(D), not in lieu of them. CMS is seeking public comment on whether there are additional requirements CMS should consider in future rulemaking that would increase provider participation in the ICT process. In addition, CMS did consider whether to further specify ICT requirements based on the needs of enrollees, such as those that have a higher risk of poor health outcomes or greater needs for care coordination, drawing from observations in the Financial Alignment Initiative and other similar efforts. However, given the populations served by SNPs, it is anticipated that all SNP enrollees would benefit from strengthened ICT requirements. CMS requests comment on this approach and whether further specifying ICT requirements based on enrollee risk would be beneficial.
2. MOC Training and Reducing Plan and Provider Burden
CMS is proposing to remove the current requirement at § 422.101(f)(2)(ii) requiring SNPs to have appropriate staff (employed, contracted, or non-contracted) trained on the SNP MOC to coordinate and/or deliver all services and benefits. The original regulation at § 422.101(f)(2) was established to ensure that MA organizations offering SNPs maintained a robust and effective care management infrastructure capable of meeting the complex needs of their targeted enrollee populations. At its core, the requirement that SNPs have appropriate staff—whether employed, contracted, or non-contracted—trained on the SNP's MOC was intended to operationalize the broader statutory mandate that SNPs provide specialized, coordinated care to vulnerable beneficiaries.
Over the years, SNPs and their provider partners have consistently communicated to CMS that the MOC training requirement, as written, imposes a significant and disproportionate administrative burden. Plans report that while they can reasonably ensure that their employed staff receive MOC training, extending that obligation to both in-network and non-contracted providers presents substantial logistical and operational challenges. SNPs note that attempting to track, document, and verify MOC training completion for a broad and ever-changing universe of both in-network and non-contracted providers consumes significant administrative resources without producing a commensurate improvement in care coordination outcomes. Additionally, in-network providers are often torn between clinical obligations and meeting the many administrative requirements associated with contemporary healthcare, for example prior authorization forms and clinical documentation requirements. Moreover, non-contracted providers, by definition, do not have a formal relationship with the plan and therefore have no contractual obligation to participate in plan-sponsored training activities.
(
printed page 76395)
Provider organizations and professional associations have similarly raised concerns that the training requirement places an undue burden on individual clinicians and care teams who may serve patients enrolled in multiple SNPs—each with its own distinct MOC and training curriculum. Providers note that complying with MOC training requirements across numerous plans is not only time-consuming but also creates confusion when training content varies significantly from plan to plan.
In light of this sustained stakeholder feedback, CMS's own observations through program oversight, and to align with
Executive Order 14192
's call to alleviate unnecessary regulatory burden,
[

the proposal to remove § 422.101(f)(2)(ii) reflects a recognition that the regulation, as currently structured, imposes administrative costs that are not proportionate to its demonstrated impact on care quality or enrollee outcomes. CMS continues to expect that SNPs will maintain a well-trained and capable care management workforce. However, this expectation can be more effectively advanced through other existing regulatory requirements—including the broader MOC framework, care coordination standards, and quality improvement program requirements—without the specific prescriptive training mandate that has proven difficult to implement and enforce consistently across the diverse range of providers involved in SNP care delivery. If finalized, CMS and NCQA will revise the current matrix for MOC evaluation and approval to remove tracking of MOC training. CMS is seeking public comment on the removal of this requirement.
3. Modernizing HRA Outreach Requirements for SNPs
Under the current regulatory framework at § 422.101(f)(1)(iv), SNPs are required to make at least three attempts to reach an enrollee, excluding any automated phone calls, on different days and at different times of day in order to schedule a comprehensive initial or annual HRA. If the enrollee remains unresponsive after three attempts, the SNP must send a follow-up letter. Additionally, SNPs are required to document all outreach attempts and, where applicable, the enrollee's decision not to participate. These requirements were designed to ensure that SNPs make meaningful, good-faith efforts to engage enrollees in the HRA process. However, the lack of clarity around emerging technologies, like Super Intelligence (SI)-enabled platforms that can be used for outreach, and the explicit prohibition on automated phone calls, has increasingly limited the ability of SNPs to leverage modern communication technologies that some enrollees may prefer and that have become standard practice in healthcare outreach.
[
87
]
CMS is proposing to amend § 422.101(f)(1)(iv) to remove the prohibition on automated phone calls subject to applicable Federal and State communications, accessibility, and privacy requirements, and to afford SNPs the flexibility to use a broader range of communication technologies when conducting outreach to enrollees for the purpose of completing an HRA. This proposed change reflects CMS's recognition that the communication landscape has evolved significantly since the original regulation was promulgated. Enrollees today increasingly interact with healthcare organizations through digital channels, including text messages, secure patient portal communications, and automated interactive voice response systems. Requiring SNPs to rely exclusively on non-automated, live-agent phone calls as the primary mode of HRA outreach is no longer consistent with how many beneficiaries prefer to communicate with their health plans.
Under the proposed amendment, SNPs would be permitted to use automated phone calls, SI-assisted outreach, text message communications, and secure portal messaging methods that comply with applicable privacy and security requirements as part of their HRA outreach efforts to meet the three-attempts requirement under § 422.101(f)(1)(iv)(A). This flexibility is intended to allow SNPs to tailor their outreach strategies to the communication preferences of their enrollee populations, consistent with the person-centered care principles that underpin the MOC framework. For example, a SNP serving a predominantly younger dual-eligible population may find that text message outreach yields significantly higher response rates than live phone calls, while a SNP serving an older institutionalized population may choose to rely on direct staff contact as the most effective approach. The proposed amendment would allow each SNP to determine the most appropriate and effective outreach modality for its specific population, rather than mandating a one-size-fits-all approach. CMS understands that many SNPs already employ some of these outreach tools, but an additional intent of this proposed rule is to eliminate any ambiguity that may exist with the current regulation and potential outreach methods that plans could use to communicate with enrollees.
Importantly, the proposed amendment does not eliminate the requirement that SNPs make meaningful outreach efforts to reach enrollees for HRA completion. SNPs would still be expected to document their outreach attempts and, where applicable, the enrollee's decision not to participate. The core accountability framework—including the requirement to send a follow-up letter when an enrollee has not responded—would be retained to ensure that SNPs continue to make good-faith efforts to engage all enrollees in the HRA process. The proposed change is narrowly focused on removing the prohibition on automated outreach and expanding the permissible methods of contact, not on reducing the overall standard of care coordination expected of SNPs.
This proposed amendment is consistent with CMS's broader policy goals of reducing administrative burden on plan sponsors while simultaneously improving the quality and effectiveness of care coordination for SNP enrollees. Recent reporting data indicates that across all SNPs, the mean percent of new enrollees that were unreachable for an initial assessment was roughly 20 percent, with 37.52 percent unreachable for the annual assessment in 2024. Notably, there were very small percentages of enrollees refusing to participate in either the initial or annual assessments, which indicates that there are significant opportunities to improve assessment completion rates through enhanced outreach strategies. By permitting the use of modern communication technologies—including SI-assisted outreach tools that can personalize messaging, optimize contact timing, and adapt to enrollee response patterns—CMS aims to increase HRA completion rates, improve the timeliness of care plan development, and ultimately enhance health outcomes for the vulnerable populations served by SNPs. In particular, communications through patient portals that are compliant with the HIPAA Privacy and Security Rules offer a secure and enrollee-friendly channel that protects beneficiary privacy and security while enabling more efficient and responsive outreach than traditional mail or live phone contact alone.
(
printed page 76396)
CMS also recognizes that the adoption of SI and automated communication technologies in healthcare is accelerating, and that regulatory frameworks must evolve to keep pace with these developments. Allowing SNPs the flexibility to incorporate these tools into their HRA outreach processes positions the program to benefit from ongoing technological innovation while maintaining the robust enrollee protections and care coordination standards that are central to the SNP program. As with any regulatory change, CMS may reevaluate this position if there are unintended consequences, impacts on compliance with other regulations, or potential beneficiary harms following implementation.
Lastly, CMS also proposes amending paragraph (f)(1)(iv) to permit CMS to review SNP HRA communication policies and/or procedures upon request. If finalized, CMS intends to review HRA communication and outreach policies through the annual MOC submission process. For instance, NCQA and CMS could potentially ask SNPs to provide an overview of their HRA outreach and communication process, including whether they use SI and automated communication technologies, how plans are operationalizing HRA refusals, and documentation of outreach attempts for enrollees across different communication modalities. CMS anticipates that corresponding changes would be made to the MOC matrix through an update of OMB Control Number 0938-1296 (CMS-10565) titled, “Medicare Advantage Model of Care Submission Requirements.” CMS will continue to assess individual enrollee outreach attempts through the regular program audit processes.
CMS estimates that this proposal will reduce SNP burden, which is discussed in section IX.B.5. of the proposed rule. CMS is seeking comments on all foregoing proposals. Specifically, CMS is looking for feedback on whether SNPs should be required to document each enrollee's preferred method of HRA communication at the time of enrollment and use the enrollee's stated preference as the primary outreach modality for HRA scheduling. Lastly, CMS also welcomes comments from the public on the required composition for the SNP ICTs, including additional requirements by SNP type, and whether additional or different providers, staff, or other professionals should be added for the interdisciplinary care team.
B. Improvements for Specials Needs Plans (§§ 422.2, 422.66, and 422.101)
1. Require Certain Chronic Condition Special Needs Plans and Institutional Special Needs Plans To Coordinate With Medicaid for Dually Eligible Individuals (§ 422.101)
In 2025, there were approximately 12.5 million people dually eligible for Medicare and Medicaid. Dually eligible individuals totaled 20 percent of the Medicare population in 2022 but accounted for 36 percent of Medicare spending. Similarly, dually eligible individuals comprised 13 percent of all Medicaid beneficiaries but accounted for 27 percent of Medicaid spending in 2022. Dually eligible individuals frequently encounter fragmentation in the health care system as they navigate the Medicare and Medicaid programs. CMS has been working to improve care and reduce avoidable expenditures through policies that integrate care for dually eligible individuals. Integrated care refers to delivery system and financing approaches that (1) maximize person-centered coordination of Medicare and Medicaid services; (2) create a seamless experience for dually eligible individuals; and (3) mitigate cost-shifting incentives between the two programs.
C-SNPs restrict enrollment to special needs individuals with one or more specific severe or disabling chronic conditions as defined at § 422.2. The Bipartisan Budget Act of 2018 (BBA of 2018) (
Pub. L. 115-123

Some examples of these conditions include chronic alcohol use disorder and other substance use disorders, autoimmune disorders, cancer, cardiovascular disorders, chronic heart failure, dementia, diabetes mellitus, HIV/AIDS, chronic lung disorders, chronic and disabling mental health conditions, and neurological disorders. Dually eligible individuals represented the vast majority of I-SNP enrollees at approximately 90 percent of total enrollment each year given their needs for long-term care. The higher proportion of dually eligible individuals in other SNP types is not unexpected—dually eligible individuals frequently have higher rates of chronic disease and those enrolled in I-SNPs have significant long-term care needs, which can be costly and impact spenddown to Medicaid eligibility.

Additionally, C-SNPs with high proportions of dually eligible individuals frequently have benefit designs that specifically attract dually eligible individuals. In an analysis of the 108 C-SNPs with dually eligible individuals representing 60 percent or more of total enrollment in CY 2026, 90 percent of the C-SNPs have the highest possible Part D deductible ($615). Of these C-SNPs with a high proportion of dually eligible enrollees, 89 percent had the maximum Part A and B out-of-pocket limit ($9,250) and another 7 percent of these plans had Part A and B out-of-pocket limits between $6,500 and $8,850. Most dually eligible individuals do not benefit from lower levels of Part A and B out-of-pocket limits since Medicaid covers their Part A and B cost-sharing. Similarly, C-SNPs that target dually eligible individuals do not have the same incentives as other MA plans to charge lower Part D deductibles and premiums because the Part D low-income subsidy covers the Part D deductible and premiums. While CMS recognizes that dually eligible individuals can enroll in any type of MA plan based on their unique preferences, the data suggests such benefit designs result in higher proportions of dually eligible individuals enrolled in certain C-SNPs because non-dually eligible individuals would have high out-of-pocket costs, which makes the plans unattractive for these individuals. Another factor that could contribute to dually eligible individuals enrolling in C-SNPs is their high prevalence for chronic conditions, which we discuss later in this section. We also recognize that a dually eligible individual may choose a C-SNP over a D-SNP due to their own unique preferences.
We support options that continue to emphasize beneficiary choice of health plans but maintain concern for the quality of care received by dually eligible individuals. Much of the feedback we received from our C-SNP request for information (RFI) in the November 2025 proposed rule supported a system where dually eligible individuals who are enrolled in a C-SNP or I-SNP can access high-quality integration, including accessing their Medicaid and Medicare benefits without delay and have access to quality person-centered care coordination. The central argument was that dually eligible individuals deserve the same level of coordinated care regardless of which SNP type they are enrolled in. A dominant theme from the commenters was support for extending the D-SNP care coordination requirements to C-SNPs and I-SNPs serving dually eligible individuals, particularly regarding coordination with Medicaid for long-term services and supports (LTSS) and behavioral health. Some plans recommended that CMS standardize care coordination requirements across D-SNPs, C-SNPs, and I-SNPs for full-benefit dually eligible individuals, including integrated health risk assessments and care plans.
A commenter noted that dually eligible individuals experience significantly higher prevalence of severe and disabling chronic conditions than Medicare-only beneficiaries. Thus, overlap between dual eligibility and C-SNP enrollment is clinically expected and reflects appropriate targeting of chronic conditions, not circumvention of program requirements. A commenter also stated that C-SNPs offer supplemental benefits that are targeted for treating the designated chronic condition as well as specialized

Another commenter noted that C-SNPs can provide more tailored care coordination for complex populations such as persons with end-stage renal disease (ESRD). In C-SNPs, this population may experience more timely access to specialists such as nephrologists compared to other plan types where wait times may be increased or out-of-network arrangements may be more frequent. Relatedly, a commenter noted that C-SNPs can better help manage disease progression and potentially delay the need for higher levels of care.

Some commenters opposed any new care coordination requirements for C-SNPs and I-SNP. These commenters highlighted that SNPs, including C-SNPs and I-SNPs, currently have requirements to coordinate delivery of care across healthcare settings, providers, and services to ensure continuity of care. They believed that any new care coordination requirements would likely be redundant and refocus C-SNPs on enrollees' dually eligible status rather than their chronic conditions.
To ensure full-benefit dually eligible individuals enrolled in C-SNPs and full-benefit dually eligible individuals enrolled in I-SNPs who reside in the community receive the benefits of care coordination with Medicaid similar to those enrolled in D-SNPs, we propose to add a requirement at § 422.101(f)(2)(iii)(B) that C-SNPs and IE-SNPs, where 60 percent or more of the plan's total enrollment is enrollees who are entitled to Medicaid, as determined by CMS using the January enrollment of the current year, coordinate with Medicaid across healthcare settings, providers, and services for full-benefit dually eligible enrollees. We propose to add a similar requirement at new § 422.101(f)(2)(iii)(C) for full-benefit dually eligible HI-SNP enrollees who reside in the community. We explained in the RFI included in the November 2025 proposed rule that the challenges with C-SNPs and I-SNPs enrolling high percentages of dually eligible individuals are similar to the challenges of D-SNP look-alikes, which are non-SNP MA plans that enroll 60 percent or more dually eligible individuals as a percent of their total enrollment. (
90 FR 54981
) For purposes of our proposal, we recommend setting the threshold at 60 percent or more dually eligible individuals as a percentage of total enrollment consistent with how CMS defines D-SNP look-alikes at § 422.514(d). As we explained in the April 2024 final rule addressing D-SNP look-alikes, the 60-percent threshold indicates a level of dually eligible enrollment that would not be the result for any plan that simply reflected the concentration of dually eligible enrollees in its service area. (
89 FR 30708
) This analysis also includes service areas where C-SNPs and I-SNPs are offered so the 60-percent threshold is appropriately applicable to C-SNPs, IE-SNPs, and HI-SNPs as well. Under this proposal, C-SNPs, IE-SNPs, and HI-SNPs would be required to identify full-benefit dually eligible individuals enrolled in their plan, strategies for coordinating Medicaid covered services in response to enrollee needs, and methods for coordination. For HI-SNPs, the proposed requirement would only apply to full-benefit dually eligible individuals who reside in the community. Section 1856(b)(1) of the Act authorizes the Secretary to establish by regulation standards consistent with, and to carry out, Part C. Additionally, section 1857(e)(1) of the Act authorizes the Secretary to establish MA organization contract terms and conditions that are necessary and appropriate and not inconsistent with other Part C statutory requirements. We believe that our proposed contract terms requiring certain C-SNPs, IE-SNPs, and HI-SNPs to assist full-benefit dually eligible individuals in accessing Medicaid benefits is not inconsistent with the Part C statute and is necessary and appropriate to ensure full-benefit dually eligible individuals have access to services that could prevent future acute care events and avoid any duplication of benefits across the two programs.
While we note that § 422.101(f)(2)(iii) already requires MA organizations offering SNPs to coordinate the delivery of care across healthcare settings, providers and services to assure continuity of care, it does not specifically include coordination with Medicaid. Medicaid covers key services including long-term services and supports (LTSS), behavioral health, durable medical equipment (DME), dental, vision, transportation, and caregiver supports. We believe that it is beneficial for MA plans to coordinate with Medicaid to ensure full-benefit dually eligible individuals have access to the Medicaid services they need to manage chronic conditions and other care needs. Dually eligible individuals have a high prevalence for chronic conditions. Sixty-three percent of dually eligible individuals have three or more chronic conditions. Sixty-four percent of full-benefit dually eligible individuals have a behavioral health diagnosis, such as depression or serious mental illness, and 37 percent of full-benefit dually eligible individuals use LTSS.

The definition of C-SNPs in section 1859(b)(6)(B)(i)(II) of the Act states that enrollees in these plans require intensive care coordination. Dually eligible enrollees often have greater needs for the types of services that are covered under Medicaid. Without coordination for the services that are provided under Medicaid, there can potentially be a larger gap in fulfilling the needs of these enrollees. At a minimum, it can delay care or services which could result in the potential for acute or chronic conditions to worsen or the need for institutional equivalent individuals to receive a higher level of care.

We are not proposing to require C-SNPs, IE-SNPs, and HI-SNPs with high proportions of dually eligible individuals to coordinate with Medicaid for partial-benefit dually eligible individuals because the only Medicaid benefits these individuals receive is coverage of Medicare cost-sharing. However, due to eight-to-nine percent of partial-benefit dually eligible individuals becoming full-benefit dually eligible individuals each year, we believe it is important that these plans are ready to coordinate with Medicaid when a partial-benefit dually eligible individual reaches full-benefit eligibility and thus are proposing to include them in the 60-percent threshold.

If this proposal is finalized, the C-SNPs, IE-SNPs, and HI-SNPs that meet this threshold would be required to coordinate with Medicaid across healthcare settings, providers, and services for full-benefit dually eligible enrollees for the upcoming year. We are limiting the proposal to exclude I-SNP enrollees who meet the definition of institutionalized in § 422.2. We believe that IE-SNP and HI-SNP enrollees who reside in the community could benefit most from the enhanced care coordination, as their care is likely to be more fragmented which results in the need to coordinate with more resources, similar to persons in D-SNPs and C-SNPs. In contrast, I-SNP enrollees who are institutionalized receive more centralized care coordination with facility-based staff that is likely to be familiar with how to coordinate with Medicaid due to the proportion of people in the facility being eligible for Medicaid. However, we solicit comments regarding whether enhanced care coordination requirements should apply to all I-SNPs and all I-SNP enrollees given the importance of coordinating care and benefits for dually eligible individuals residing in long-term care nursing facilities.

They have access to data on dual eligibility status through Monthly Membership Report data that CMS shares with MA plans for each beneficiary enrolled in the plan. Through the Monthly Membership Report file, all MA plans, including C-SNPs, IE-SNPs, and HI-SNPs, can ascertain whether enrollees are partial- or full-benefit dually eligible individuals. Also, MA plans receive the MA Medicaid Status Data File, which includes monthly dually eligible statuses and corresponding dually eligible status code report.

We note that there will likely be differences in the amount and types of coordination needed for enrollees based on their risk stratification level and their current needs.
Some types of coordination could include outreach to the enrollee's Medicaid MCO to inform the Medicaid MCO that the enrollee had a recent inpatient hospital admission and was discharged back to the community with services the C-SNP, IE-SNP, or HI-SNP has put in place, like home health. The C-SNP, IE-SNP, and HI-SNP may need to coordinate with the Medicaid plan and/or directly with Medicaid providers to ensure appropriate long-term services and supports, such as a personal care aide or personal emergency response system device, are in place to ensure the enrollee is safe in the community, managing any chronic conditions, and ideally avoids a readmission. A C-SNP, IE-SNP, and HI-SNP could take the same approach with enrollees receiving Medicaid via fee-for-service, such as coordinating with a section 1915(c) home-and-community based waiver services coordinator or Medicaid case worker. A May 2026 Health Affairs article notes that Colorado's Medicaid agency, the Department of Health Care Payment and Financing, leverages D-SNP admission, discharge, and care transition data to develop reports for options counseling teams and train D-SNP teams to make direct referrals to options counseling.
