2. Amend Definition of Fully Integrated Dual Eligible Special Needs Plan (§ 422.2)
D-SNPs are a type of MA plan that are intended to integrate or coordinate care for beneficiaries who are dually eligible for both Medicare and Medicaid more effectively than standard MA plans or Original Medicare by focusing enrollment and care management on dually eligible individuals. Since the Medicare Prescription Drug, Improvement, and Modernization Act of 2003 (MMA) (
Pub. L. 108-173
) first authorized D-SNPs' creation, subsequent legislation has been enacted that has extended their authority to operate and set forth additional programmatic requirements. In 2008, sections 164 and 165 of the Medicare Improvements for Patients and Providers Act (MIPPA) (
Pub. L. 110-275
) amended sections 1859 and 1852(a) of the Act to require D-SNPs to: limit cost sharing for certain dually eligible beneficiaries, provide each prospective enrollee, prior to enrollment, with a comprehensive written statement that describes the benefits and cost-sharing protections to which the beneficiary is entitled under Medicaid and which are covered by the plan, and contract with the State Medicaid agency to provide benefits, or arrange for the provision of Medicaid benefits, which may include long-term care services consistent with State policy, to which such individual is entitled. Notwithstanding this requirement, section 164(c)(4) of MIPPA stipulated that a State is in no way obligated to contract with a D-SNP and limit the imposition of cost-sharing on full-benefit dually eligible individuals and qualified Medicare beneficiaries. In 2010, section 3205 of the Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act (
Pub. L. 111-148
) revised section 1853(a)(1)(B) of the Act to permit the Secretary to apply a frailty payment under Program of All-Inclusive Care for the Elderly (PACE) payment rules to certain D-SNPs that are fully integrated with capitated contracts with States for Medicaid benefits, including long-term care, and that have similar average levels of frailty (as determined by the Secretary) as the PACE program. Most recently, section 50311(b) of the Bipartisan Budget Act of 2018 (BBA of 2018) (
Pub. L. 115-123
) amended section 1859 of the Act to require integration of the Medicare and Medicaid benefits provided to enrollees in D-SNPs. In particular, the BBA of 2018 requires: (1) development of unified grievance and appeals processes for D-SNPs; and (2) establishment of new standards for integration of Medicare and Medicaid benefits for D-SNPs.
CMS has promulgated regulations in accordance with legislation. In the Contract Year 2012 Medicare Advantage and Part D final rule, which appeared in the April 15, 2011
Federal Register
on (
76 FR 21432
, hereafter referred to as the April 2011 final rule), we finalized a definition of fully integrated special needs plan (FIDE SNP) at § 422.2 in accordance with section 3205 of the Affordable Care Act, stating that a FIDE SNP is a CMS approved MA-PD D-SNP that, among other things, enrolls special needs individuals entitled to Medicare and Medicaid, has a capitated contract with a State Medicaid agency that includes coverage of specified primary, acute, and long-term care benefits and services, consistent with State policy, coordinates the delivery of covered Medicare and Medicaid health and long-term care services using aligned care management and specialty care network methods for high-risk beneficiaries, and employs policies and procedures approved by CMS and the State to coordinate or integrate member materials, enrollment, communications, grievance and appeals, and quality improvement. Further, we finalized in the April 2011 final rule that a FIDE SNP must provide dually eligible individuals access to Medicare and Medicaid benefits under a single managed care organization.
In the Contract Year 2020 Medicare Advantage and Part D final rule, which appeared in the April 16, 2019
Federal Register
(
84 FR 15680
), we established requirements in accordance with section 50311(b) of the BBA of 2018. In that rulemaking, we amended the definition of FIDE SNP at § 422.2 to align with the definition of D-SNP, finalized in that same rule. These amendments to the FIDE SNP definition included replacing terminology to create cohesion between regulation and statute, codifying subregulatory guidance, and amending language regarding coordination of care. In this final rule, we added language to the definition of FIDE SNP to require a FIDE SNP to provide access to Medicare and Medicaid benefits under a single entity that holds both an MA contract with CMS and a Medicaid managed care organization contract.
FIDE SNPs fully integrate care for dually eligible beneficiaries under a single managed care organization and have the highest level of integration among D-SNPs. Just like HIDE SNPs and coordination-only D-SNPs, FIDE SNPs must have a contract with the State Medicaid agency that complies with the contracting requirements in § 422.107(c). However, to be designated a FIDE SNP, a plan must also include coverage of primary, acute, and long-term services and supports including coverage of nursing facility services for a period of at least 180 days during the plan year, behavioral health benefits, and provide coverage of home health services, medical supplies, equipment, and appliances. As of January 2026, there are 101 FIDE SNPs across 17 states.
The current requirement in § 422.2 that the same legal entity must hold the contract for the D-SNP as well as the contract for the Medicaid managed care organization (MCO) has created a high bar for eligibility for a FIDE SNP designation. While all plans that are currently designated FIDE SNPs meet the requirements set forth in the definition of FIDE at § 422.2 and the contracting requirements at § 422.107(c), there are other plans that meet all the same elements for contracting requirements at § 422.107(c) and for FIDE SNPs as outlined in the definition at § 422.2, aside from the requirement that the contracts be held under a single entity. Because these plans do not have the same legal entity, the plan is designated as a HIDE SNP.
In the interest of promoting integration, we adopted a definition of FIDE SNP in the 2020 rule that, among
(
printed page 76402)
other things, codified longstanding subregulatory guidance that required the same legal entity to hold both contracts. Since then, CMS has received feedback indicating that this requirement places unnecessary constraints on plan flexibility and isn't necessary to promote integration as it was intended to do. To maximize plan flexibility, we are proposing to remove this requirement.
Section 1859(f)(8)(D)(i)(II) of the Act describes D-SNPs that “meet the requirements of a fully integrated plan described in section 1853(a)(1)(B)(iv)(II),” other than the requirement to have similar average levels of frailty as the PACE program. Section 1853(a)(1)(B)(iv)(II) allows for the application of a frailty adjustment for “a specialized MA plan for special needs individuals described in section 1859(b)(6)(B)(ii) that is fully integrated with capitated contracts with States for Medicaid benefits, including long-term care, and that have similar average levels of frailty (as determined by the Secretary) as the PACE program.” These provisions do not require a single legal entity to hold both the MA contract with CMS and the State Medicaid agency contract, provided the SNP is fully integrated with capitated contracts with the State for Medicaid benefits.
Further, based on feedback received since the “same legal entity” requirement was codified in the regulatory definition of a FIDE SNP, we do not believe this requirement creates a plan that provides more integrated care than a HIDE SNP that meets the bar of FIDE SNP designation outside of the same legal entity requirement. As a result, we are proposing to amend the definition of FIDE SNP at § 422.2 to remove the requirement that the D-SNP provide access to Medicare and Medicaid under a single entity that holds both an MA contract with CMS and a Medicaid MCO and replace it with the same requirement applicable to contracts held by HIDE SNPs under § 422.2: the requirement that the plan provides coverage of Medicaid benefits under a capitated contract that is between the State Medicaid agency and the MA organization, the MA organization's parent organization or another entity that is owned and controlled by its parent organization, or a local nonprofit public benefit corporation of which the MA organization, MA organization's parent organization, or another entity that is owned and controlled by its parent organization is a founding member where the local nonprofit public benefit corporation is responsible for the delivery of physical, behavioral, and dental health services. This proposed amendment to the FIDE SNP definition at § 422.2 would continue to meet the statutory requirement at section 1853(a)(1)(B) of the Act that a FIDE SNP is fully integrated with capitated contracts with States for Medicaid benefits, as the enrollees of such a plan would have access to their Medicare benefits, provided under an MA contract with CMS, and their Medicaid benefits, provided under a Medicaid managed care organization contract, under the control of a single parent organization, but would provide more contracting flexibility for plans interested in providing a FIDE SNP.
The current definition of FIDE SNPs in § 422.2 identifies, in paragraphs (2)-(6), additional requirements that a MA plan must meet to be considered a FIDE SNP. Requirements include that a FIDE SNP have a capitated contract with a State Medicaid agency that requires coverage of primary and acute care services including Medicare cost sharing, long-term services and supports including coverage of nursing facility services for a period of at least 180 days during the plan year, behavioral health services, home health services, medical supplies, equipment, and appliances, in addition to coordinating the delivery of covered Medicare and Medicaid services using aligned care management and specialty care network methods for high-risk beneficiaries, and using integrated materials and processes for enrollment, communications, grievance and appeals, and quality improvement. FIDE SNPs must also maintain exclusively aligned enrollment, which is the requirement that, per State policy, the FIDE SNP may only enroll individuals who are enrolled in, or in the process of enrolling in, the affiliated Medicaid managed care plan. We are not proposing to amend any of the elements in paragraphs (2)-(6) of the FIDE SNP definition at § 422.2. As such, the proposed definition allowing the Medicare and Medicaid contracts to be held by separate legal entities under common organizational control would continue to require FIDE SNPs to be fully integrated with capitated contracts with States for Medicaid benefits, including long-term care, as set forth in section 1853(a)(1)(B)(iv)(II).
We note that our only proposed change would be to amend the requirement that the FIDE SNP is required to provide dually eligible individuals access to Medicare and Medicaid benefits under a single entity that holds both an MA contract with CMS and a Medicaid managed care organization contract. We are not proposing any other amendment to the FIDE SNP or HIDE SNP definitions at § 422.2. We are not proposing any substantive change to the types or amounts of benefits that are required to be offered to HIDE SNPs or FIDE SNPS and all other requirements would remain identical to what they are today.
If finalized, this amended definition would have the impact of creating more FIDE SNPs. Currently, based on internal analysis of contract year 2026 plans, we believe that there are six HIDE SNPs that, aside from the requirement that a FIDE SNP must provide dually eligible individuals access to Medicare and Medicaid benefits under a single entity holding both the MA contract with CMS and the Medicaid managed care organization contract, would meet the definition of FIDE SNP. Therefore, we believe that additional plans could be considered for frailty payments if this proposal is finalized. We believe that amending this definition will open up the market for more plans to become FIDE SNPs and remove an unnecessary barrier for plans. But given the high bar that plans would continue to have to meet to be considered a FIDE SNP, we do not believe that there will be a substantial increase in plans that would newly meet the FIDE SNP definition under the proposed revision.
We solicit comment on all aspects of our proposal and assumptions, including whether to include in the definition of FIDE SNP the allowance for a capitated contract to be held by a local nonprofit public benefit corporation of which the MA organization, MA organization's parent organization, or another entity that is owned and controlled by its parent organization is a founding member where the local nonprofit public benefit corporation is responsible for the delivery of physical, behavioral, and dental health services. This allowance, currently applicable to HIDE-SNPs, was finalized in the April 2025 Final Rule to address a unique scenario presented by coordinated care organization structures in Oregon, in which there is a capitated contract between the State Medicaid agency and a local nonprofit public benefit corporation of which the MA organization is a founding member.
We invite comment on the effect of this proposal and request suggestions for potential refinement.
3. Update to Default Enrollment for States Transitioning From Medicaid Fee-for-Service to Medicaid Managed Care (§ 422.66)
Section 1851(c)(3)(A)(ii) of the Act provides the Secretary with authority to establish, by regulation, a process under which an individual who is enrolled in
(
printed page 76403)
a non-MA health plan offered by an MA organization may be deemed to have made an election to enroll in an MA plan offered by that organization upon becoming entitled to Medicare benefits. This provision grants the Secretary broad discretionary authority to define the parameters of such enrollment processes, including the populations eligible for such enrollment and the conditions under which such enrollment may be effectuated.
We initially addressed default enrollment upon conversion to Medicare in rulemaking (
70 FR 4606
through
4607
) in 2005, indicating that we would retain the flexibility to implement this provision through future instructions and guidance to MA organizations. Such subregulatory guidance was established later that year and was applicable to contract year 2006. As outlined previously in Chapter 2 of the Medicare Managed Care Manual, now the MA and Part D Enrollment and Disenrollment Guidance, we established an optional enrollment mechanism, whereby MA organizations may develop processes and, with CMS approval, provide seamless continuation of coverage by way of enrollment in an MA plan for newly MA eligible individuals who are currently enrolled in other health plans offered by the MA organization (such as commercial or Medicaid plans) at the time of the individuals' initial eligibility for Medicare. The guidance emphasized that seamless continuation of coverage should not be limited to situations in which an enrollee becomes eligible for Medicare by virtue of age, but extended to all newly eligible Medicare beneficiaries, including those whose Medicare eligibility was based on disability. We did not mandate that MA organizations implement a process for seamless continuation of coverage but, instead, gave MA organizations the option of implementing such a process for their enrollees who were approaching Medicare eligibility. From its inception, the guidance required that individuals receive advance notice of the proposed MA enrollment and have the ability to “opt out” of such an enrollment prior to the effective date of coverage.
The Contract Year 2019 final rule titled, “Medicare Program; Contract Year 2019 Policy and Technical Changes to the Medicare Advantage, Medicare Cost Plan, Medicare Fee-for-Service, the Medicare Prescription Drug Benefit Programs, and the PACE Program” (
83 FR 16440
, April 16, 2018), established the regulatory framework for an enrollment process under section 1851(c)(3)(A)(ii) of the Act as it relates to enrollment of Medicaid enrollees into dual eligible special needs plans (D-SNPs) at the time of their initial coverage election period (ICEP), which was given the term “default enrollment”. The framework for default enrollment was established at § 422.66(c) and requires that the default enrollment process into D-SNPs be subject to all of the following conditions:
Upon enrollment into the D-SNP, the individual remains enrolled in an affiliated Medicaid managed care plan and is dually eligible for Medicare and Medicaid.
The State has approved use of this default enrollment process and provided Medicare eligibility information to the MA organization.
The MA organization provides the individual with a notice that meets CMS requirements.
The individual does not decline the default enrollment prior to the effective date and does not elect to receive coverage other than through the MA organization.
CMS has approved the MA organization to use the default enrollment process before any enrollments are processed.
The MA organization has a minimum overall quality rating from the most recently issued Star Ratings of three stars or is a low enrollment contract or new MA plan.
The MA organization does not have any prohibition on new enrollment imposed by CMS.
In the Contract Year 2019 final rule (
83 FR 16440
and
16496
), we included our reasoning for proposing and finalizing this provision, stating that the option of default enrollment can be particularly beneficial for Medicaid managed care enrollees who are newly eligible for Medicare. When the parent organization of the Medicaid managed care plan also offers a D-SNP, default enrollment promotes enrollment in a plan that offers some level of integration of care, which could include acute care, behavioral health, long-term care services and supports (LTSS), including institutional care, and home and community-based services (HCBS). Since the implementation of default enrollment, our analysis of default enrollment transactions shows a high level of retention among individuals who are default enrolled. In 2025, 80 D-SNPs were approved for default enrollment. In our review of the 40,980 individuals who were default enrolled in CY 2025, 76 percent remained enrolled in the integrated D-SNP after their enrollments were effective and 70 percent remained enrolled three months after their default enrollments were effective. Since the finalization of the Contract Year 2019 rule, a number of States have transitioned their Medicaid program from a fee-for-service (FFS) delivery system to a Medicaid managed care delivery system. We anticipate two additional states may make such a transition within the next 3 years.
During these State-initiated transitions, individuals who are in their Medicare ICEP and meet the other criteria for default enrollment cannot be default enrolled into a D-SNP newly affiliated with a Medicaid managed care plan because they are not enrolled in the Medicaid managed care plan prior to their Medicare ICEP. This is not due to any choice or action by the individual but rather is a function of the timing of the State's transition. Under current regulations, individuals who become Medicare-eligible after a State has transitioned their Medicaid beneficiaries to a managed care delivery system are eligible for default enrollment into a D-SNP, whereas individuals who become Medicare-eligible during the transition period are excluded solely because they were not previously enrolled in Medicaid managed care plan.
This system-timing issue creates a gap for individuals who are Medicare-eligible but are in the process of being transitioned from Medicaid FFS to Medicaid managed care. Those individuals cannot be enrolled via the default enrollment mechanism simply because the State has not yet completed the individual's transition to Medicaid managed care. We believe this creates an unfair system for Medicaid enrollees who become Medicare eligible during a State's transition to Medicaid managed care that excludes individuals based on the timing of how their Medicare eligibility date aligns with their State's transition into Medicaid managed care. Default enrollment promotes integration between Medicare and Medicaid coverage. To alleviate this barrier and ensure that as many individuals as possible are eligible for default enrollment during a State's transition to Medicaid managed care, we are proposing new regulation text to allow default enrollment into a D-SNP for individuals who are eligible for Medicare and who are in the process of transitioning from Medicaid FFS into a Medicaid managed care plan affiliated with the D-SNP, as part of a State-initiated transition to Medicaid managed care. We are proposing that default enrollment under this proposed expansion must be coordinated with, and is contingent upon, the individual's concurrent enrollment into the affiliated
(
printed page 76404)
Medicaid managed care plan, such that integrated Medicare and Medicaid coverage is effectuated simultaneously, and that an MA organization may not effectuate default enrollment under this proposal prior to the individual's enrollment in the affiliated Medicaid managed care plan. This proposal presents a narrow update to the existing default enrollment regulations. These proposed additions would only apply to default enrollment transactions that are effective the first day of the month in which a State transitions an individual from Medicaid FFS to Medicaid managed care. Beyond that point in time, the existing default enrollment regulations would apply because individuals eligible for default enrollment are already enrolled in a Medicaid managed care plan affiliated with an eligible D-SNP.
We are proposing this change pursuant to the statutory authority described in section 1851(c)(3)(A)(ii) of the Act, which states that the Secretary may establish procedures whereby an individual currently enrolled in a non-MA health plan offered by an MA organization at the time of his or her ICEP is deemed to have elected an MA plan offered by the organization if he or she does not elect to receive Medicare coverage in another way. As we highlighted previously in this preamble, default enrollment into a D-SNP that is contingent upon and concurrent with the individual's enrollment in the affiliated Medicaid managed care plan would meet the requirement that the individual be enrolled in a non-MA health plan offered by an MA organization.
We propose to add a new § 422.66(c)(2)(i)(A) to permit default enrollment when the individual is eligible for full Medicaid benefits and is concurrently transitioning from Medicaid FFS to a Medicaid managed care plan affiliated with the MA organization offering the D-SNP. The individual's concurrent enrollment into the affiliated Medicaid managed care plan and default enrollment into the D-SNP must effectuate simultaneously. We also propose to add new § 422.66(c)(2)(i)(B)(1) to require that for any State transitioning from Medicaid fee-for-service to Medicaid managed care and seeking to initiate concurrent default enrollment, the State will identify the individuals eligible for enrollment in the affiliated Medicaid managed care plan consistent with beneficiary choice in § 438.52, including the ability to make an affirmative Medicaid plan selection, and disenrollment protections at § 438.56, including beneficiaries' rights to disenroll for cause at any time and without cause during the 90 days following the date of the beneficiary's initial enrollment into the MCO. In particular, the proposed expansion of default enrollment would retain beneficiary choice of at least two MCOs, prepaid inpatient health plans (PHIPs), or prepaid ambulatory health plans (PAHPs) consistent with § 438.52. While States would identify individuals to be default enrolled into a D-SNP affiliated with a Medicaid managed care plan, those individuals would have the opportunity to opt out of the default enrollment and make a different enrollment choice for their Medicare and Medicaid coverage. The proposal ensures that individuals subject to default enrollment retain the ability to disenroll consistent with § 438.56. States utilizing the default enrollment mechanism would only transmit eligibility information to D-SNPs for individuals who would be concurrently enrolled in the Medicaid managed care plan affiliated with the D-SNP. States could include language in their State Medicaid agency contract to approve the use of the default enrollment process. Finally, we propose to move language currently at § 422.66(c)(2)(i)(A) that defines an affiliated Medicaid managed care plan for purposes of this section to new paragraph § 422.66(c)(2)(i)(H) for clarity.
The Medicaid managed care enrollment, default, and passive processes framework at § 438.54 provides a parallel regulatory structure under which States may assign individuals to Medicaid managed care plans as part of a transition from Medicaid FFS to Medicaid managed care. Under this framework, when a State transitions its Medicaid population from FFS delivery to a managed care delivery system and elects to use a default enrollment process, individuals who do not make an affirmative plan selection within a designated choice period are assigned using a default enrollment process to a participating Medicaid managed care plan by the State. The default assignment framework is accompanied by a set of mandatory beneficiary protections that are built directly into the regulatory structure at § 438.56. For States that elect to use a passive enrollment process, before a Medicaid passive assignment takes effect consistent with §§ 438.52, 438.54(c), and 438.10(e), individuals must receive advance written notice informing them of the proposed Medicaid managed care plan assignment, their right to make an affirmative selection of a different plan, and the process for doing so. For States that choose to limit disenrollment, consistent with § 438.56(c), Medicaid managed care plan contracts must provide that an individual may request disenrollment for cause at any time and without cause during the 90 days following the individual's initial enrollment into the Medicaid managed care plan or during the 90 days following the date the State sends the enrollment notice, whichever is later. These protections reflect the statutory requirements of sections 1932(a)(3) and (4) of the Act, which conditions a State's authority to require managed care enrollment on the provision of meaningful choice, adequate notice, and accessible disenrollment rights. The proposed amendment to § 422.66(c)(2) expressly preserves these disenrollment rights for individuals default enrolled under our proposal, ensuring that individuals subject to default enrollment retain the ability to disenroll  consistent with § 438.56, which governs Medicaid managed care disenrollment rights, and with existing default enrollment protections under § 422.66(c)(2)(i)(D) and § 422.66(c)(2)(iv)(B).
The proposed amendment to § 422.66(c)(2) is designed to align the Medicare default enrollment framework with this parallel Medicaid structure, ensuring that individuals transitioning to Medicaid managed care can be simultaneously enrolled in both the affiliated Medicaid managed care plan and the D-SNP so that integrated Medicare-Medicaid coverage is not disrupted. The concurrent enrollment requirement proposed at § 422.66(c)(2)(i)(A)(
2
)(
i
), if finalized, would ensure that individuals are not default enrolled into a D-SNP before enrollment in the affiliated Medicaid managed care plan is effectuated, thereby preserving the coordinated coverage arrangement contemplated by the default enrollment process. Without this alignment, a dually eligible individual could be enrolled in a D-SNP for Medicare coverage while remaining in Medicaid FFS, an outcome inconsistent with the default enrollment process.
The concurrent enrollment requirement implements the proposal's requirement that default enrollment into a D-SNP be coordinated with enrollment in an affiliated Medicaid managed care plan such that both the D-SNP and affiliated managed care plan enrollment effectuate simultaneously. By coordinating the Medicare default enrollment process with the applicable Medicaid managed care enrollment process, the proposed rule, if finalized,
(
printed page 76405)
would require the two enrollment actions occur concurrently, consistent with beneficiary choice under § 438.52 and the disenrollment protections under § 438.56, thereby supporting integrated Medicare and Medicaid coverage during the transition to Medicaid managed care.
We emphasize that this proposed expansion does not diminish any existing beneficiary protections under § 422.66(c), including advance notice requirements and opt-out rights. As outlined in the current default enrollment framework, individuals identified for default enrollment under this proposed provision would receive advance written notice in plain language per § 422.66(c)(iv), and, as required by § 422.2267, in their preferred language, explaining the nature of the default enrollment, the implications for their access to care, and their right to opt out or make an alternative enrollment election.
As required under existing § 422.66(c)(2)(iv), the default enrollment notice provides information on the differences in premium, benefits and cost sharing between the individual's current Medicaid managed care plan and the D-SNP and the process for accessing care under the D-SNP; the individual's ability to decline the enrollment—up to and including the day prior to the enrollment effective date—and either enroll in Original Medicare or choose another MA plan; and a general description of alternative Medicare health and drug coverage options available to an individual in his or her ICEP. The default enrollment notice requirements provide the beneficiary with at least a 60-day period in which to review his or her Medicare options to decline enrollment or disenroll after the enrollment is effective. CMS reaffirms that clear, accessible communication with individuals identified for default enrollment is a critical protection, particularly given the potential impact of MA plan enrollment on provider access and care continuity. We believe that this 60-day advance notice requirement under § 422.66(c)(2)(iv) provides the same type of beneficiary protections and choice as the 90-day Medicaid managed care disenrollment window under § 438.56(c). As such, the 60-day advance notice requirement under § 422.66(c)(2)(iv) complements the 90-day Medicaid managed care disenrollment window under § 438.56(c).
For individuals eligible for default enrollment into a D-SNP on the effective date the State transitions them from Medicaid FFS to Medicaid managed care, the 60-day advance notice for default enrollment under § 422.66(c) is designed to work in concert with—not in lieu of—the 90-day Medicaid managed care disenrollment window afforded to individuals under § 438.56(c). The 60-day notice that the D-SNP sends to individuals serves a dual purpose: it serves as the official communication of the D-SNP enrollment and simultaneously informs the beneficiary of their right to decline enrollment (opt-out) or to disenroll. For situations in which a State enrolls an individual into a Medicaid managed care plan, the required 60-day advance notice of default enrollment into the D-SNP provides potential enrollees with the opportunity to opt out of the default enrollment and disenroll from the affiliated Medicaid managed care plan with or without cause as the 60-day advance notice of default enrollment window is within the 90-day Medicaid disenrollment window. We believe this approach ensures that the 60-day default enrollment notice under § 422.66(c)(2)(iv) and the 90-day Medicaid managed care disenrollment window under § 438.56(c) would operate in alignment, by providing individuals with a clear and consistent understanding of their enrollment rights across both Medicare and Medicaid. We solicit comment on how best to coordinate the 90-day Medicaid managed care disenrollment window and 60-day D-SNP default enrollment notice requirements.
If finalized, these proposed revisions would strengthen the alignment between Medicare and Medicaid enrollment processes by ensuring that individuals transitioning to Medicaid managed care are not disadvantaged by the timing of State program changes. By enabling concurrent enrollment into affiliated Medicaid managed care plans and D-SNPs as part of a State-initiated transition to Medicaid managed care, the proposal promotes greater integration, continuity, and equity in coverage for dually eligible individuals. This approach preserves existing beneficiary protections while better supporting States and MA organizations in advancing person-centered, integrated care.
We solicit comment on all aspects of our proposal and assumptions. In particular, we solicit comments on how to coordinate the 90-day Medicaid managed care disenrollment period under § 438.56(c) with the 60-day default enrollment notice requirements under § 422.66(c)(2)(iv). We also solicit comment on whether there are other Medicaid managed care regulations and operational processes that we need to consider as we finalize this proposal. Finally, we solicit comment on whether States will have the capacity to approve default enrollment if the State is transitioning its payment systems and how the timing of those transitions will need to be effectuated.

D. Introduce Additional Choice and Competition With Integrated D-SNPs (§§ 422.2; 422.514). 1. Expanding the Definition of HIDE SNP (§§ 422.2 and 422.514)
Background and Policy Framework
CMS policy regarding dually eligible beneficiaries is to (1) promote integrated care; and (2) promote the principles of choice and competition in D-SNP markets as a means of encouraging innovation and ensuring beneficiaries have the opportunity to choose from a range of high-quality plans offered by competing MA organizations. First, as we stated in the C-SNP and I-SNP Request for Information (RFI) published in the November 2025 proposed rule, meaningful integration means ensuring that dually eligible beneficiaries receive seamless, coordinated care that addresses their full range of Medicare and Medicaid needs and mitigates cost-shifting incentives between the two programs. As further described below, integration, in this context, requires that a single plan or coordinated arrangement assumes clinical and financial responsibility for benefits provided under both Title XVIII and Title XIX of the Act, so that beneficiaries experience their Medicare and Medicaid coverage as a unified whole rather than as separate, fragmented programs.
Second, we recognize that the landscape of managed care contracting has evolved, and that network dynamics and organizational structures may vary across States and markets in ways that affect how plans can feasibly deliver integrated financing and benefits. CMS has received feedback from interested parties that certain regulatory policies aimed at promoting more integrated care models have had the unintended consequence of discouraging choice and competition in certain markets. We therefore believe it is appropriate to consider a range of arrangements through which MA organizations can demonstrate the clinical and financial accountability that is the hallmark of meaningful integration, rather than prescribing a single structural model that may not reflect the realities of today's managed care marketplace.
Regulatory History
To promote integration, our rulemaking has tended to rely on common ownership requirements to foster structural integration and alignment between a D-SNP and an affiliated Medicaid managed care organization (MCO), at least for purposes of defining FIDE SNPs and HIDE SNPs in § 422.2, and more recently for purposes of § 422.514(h).
The statutory foundation for these integration requirements is found in section 1859(f)(8)(D)(i) of the Act, which establishes that, beginning in 2021, D-SNPs must meet one or more integration requirements to the extent permitted under State law, including: (1) coordinating long-term services and supports or behavioral health services, or both, in accordance with a minimum set of Secretary-determined
(
printed page 76407)
requirements; (2) meeting the requirements of a fully integrated plan in section 1853(a)(1)(B)(iv)(II) of the Act (other than level-of-frailty requirements) or entering into a capitated contract with the State Medicaid agency to provide long-term services and supports or behavioral health services, or both; or, (3) where the D-SNP and a Medicaid MCO share a common parent organization, having that parent organization assume clinical and financial responsibility for benefits provided under both Medicare and Medicaid with respect to any individual enrolled in both plans. While the statute requires a common parent organization to assume clinical and financial responsibility for Medicare and Medicaid benefits with respect to any individual enrolled in both a D-SNP and a Medicaid MCO under the common parent, it does not mandate common ownership as a prerequisite for integration—rather, common ownership has been a component of CMS's regulatory framework for FIDE SNPs and HIDE SNPs at § 422.2, and applicable integrated plans (AIPs) at § 422.561 as a mechanism through which integration is achieved. In turn, corporate structures that facilitate the common assumption of clinical and financial responsibility for both Medicare and Medicaid benefits have effectively been the standard that CMS has used to operationalize integration requirements through successive rulemakings establishing and refining the definitions of FIDE SNP and HIDE SNP at § 422.2, and AIP at § 422.561. This reliance on the assumption of clinical and financial responsibility lies at the core of integration.
This can first be seen beginning with the Contract Year 2012 Medicare Advantage and Part D final rule, which appeared in the
Federal Register
on April 15, 2011 (hereafter referred to as the April 2011 final rule;
76 FR 21432
), where we finalized that a FIDE SNP must provide dually eligible individuals access to Medicare and Medicaid benefits under a single managed care organization. In the April 2019 final rule (
84 FR 15700
), we amended the FIDE SNP requirement to specify that access to Medicare and Medicaid benefits must be provided under a single legal entity that holds both the MA contract with CMS and a Medicaid MCO contract. In that same rulemaking, we established the definition of HIDE SNP as a type of D-SNP offered by an MA organization that has—or whose parent organization or another entity that is owned and controlled by its parent organization has—a capitated contract with the Medicaid agency in the State in which the D-SNP operates that includes coverage of long-term services and supports (LTSS), behavioral health services, or both, consistent with State policy.
As part of the April 2019 final rule, we finalized the definition of AIP as FIDE SNPs and HIDE SNPs in which Medicare and Medicaid enrollment is aligned (per the definition at § 422.2) with the companion Medicaid MCOs for those D-SNPs, thereby making it feasible for these plans to implement unified grievance and appeals processes. At that time, we limited the universe of potential AIPs to FIDE SNPs and HIDE SNPs with exclusively aligned enrollment to ensure, first, that all enrollees are covered with the same scope of benefits, and second, that the plans implementing unified grievance and appeals offered a sufficiently substantial range of Medicaid benefits to make the unification of Medicare and Medicaid processes meaningful for beneficiaries and worthwhile for States and plans (

).
The April 2019 final rule finalized the definition of aligned enrollment at § 422.2, which refers to D-SNP enrollment where the enrollee's Medicaid benefits are covered under a Medicaid MCO contract between the State and: (1) the MA organization offering the D-SNP; (2) the D-SNP's parent organization; or (3) an entity that is owned and controlled by the D-SNP's parent organization. In the April 2019 final rule, we explained that this definition clarifies that financial and clinical responsibility for the enrollee is held by the MA organization or its parent organization (
84 FR 15708
).
We have since received feedback reflecting that additional arrangements beyond common ownership may also facilitate the assumption of common clinical and financial responsibility for both Medicare and Medicaid benefits. Accordingly, while the integration option described in section 1859(f)(8)(D)(i)(III) of the Act is limited to a situation in which the MA organization and the affiliated MCO share a common parent organization, a D-SNP operating under an alternative corporate arrangement where the organization offering the D-SNP assumes clinical and financial responsibility for both Medicare and Medicaid benefits, such that the State Medicaid agency contract can be attributed to the D-SNP for integration purposes, may be sufficiently integrated to meet other integration options identified in section 1859(f)(8)(D)(i) of the Act. We are therefore proposing an amendment that would allow such D-SNPs to qualify as HIDE SNPs where other integration requirements are met.
We previously recognized that the assumption of clinical and financial responsibility for both Medicare and Medicaid benefits can be achieved through contractual arrangements, not only through common ownership, in the Contract Year 2023 MA and Part D final rule, which appeared in the
Federal Register
on May 9, 2022 (hereafter referred to as the May 2022 final rule;
87 FR 27704
). In that rule, we amended the definition of AIP at § 422.561 to expand the range of qualifying arrangements between Medicaid managed care plans and D-SNPs. Specifically, we recognized that certain contractual arrangements between the D-SNP and the Medicaid MCO that do not meet the definition of a FIDE SNP or HIDE SNP may nonetheless satisfy the policy objectives underlying the AIP framework without requiring that the D-SNP and the Medicaid MCO share a common parent. As finalized § 422.561, we established that the following arrangement may additionally meet the definition of AIP:
The D-SNP, by State policy, has enrollment limited to those beneficiaries enrolled in a Medicaid MCO, where—
There is a capitated contract between the MA organization, the MA organization's parent organization, or another entity that is owned and controlled by its parent organization—
++ A Medicaid agency; or
++ A Medicaid managed care organization as defined in section 1903(m) of the Act that contracts with the Medicaid agency; and
++ Through the capitated contract, Medicaid benefits including primary care and acute care, including Medicare cost-sharing as defined in section 1905(p)(3)(B), (C), and (D) of the Act, without regard to the limitation of that definition to qualified Medicare beneficiaries, and at a minimum, one of the following: Home health services as defined in § 440.70, medical supplies, equipment, and appliances as described in § 440.70(b)(3), or nursing facility services are covered for the enrollees.
Current Landscape and Rationale for Proposed Change
Since codifying the changes at § 422.561 in the May 2022 final rule, we have become aware of other similar contracting arrangements that we believe would allow for the level of integration of clinical and financial responsibility necessary for HIDE SNPs—and possibly FIDE SNPs—but do not meet the common ownership requirements currently codified in the HIDE SNP definition. We continue to
(
printed page 76408)
hear from interested parties that requiring common ownership under a single parent organization is not necessary to achieve meaningful integration between D-SNPs and Medicaid MCOs, and that such a requirement may discourage competition and limit beneficiary choice in certain markets.
In response to the C-SNP and I-SNP RFI published in the November 2025 proposed rule, commenters noted that CMS's current focus on structural alignment—requiring the same parent organization for both the MA organization offering the D-SNP and affiliated Medicaid MCO—reflects an outdated approach to Medicare-Medicaid care coordination. Commenters noted that technology has transformed the integration and coordination landscape through ease of data sharing and opportunities to establish delegated integration models where MA plans would lead overall care coordination while partnering with Medicaid plans without requiring Medicare-Medicaid plan integration through common ownership.
One example of an arrangement that we believe could allow sufficient integration of clinical and financial responsibility to offer a HIDE SNP, but does not meet the current common ownership requirement, is when a State Medicaid agency has a capitated Medicaid MCO contract with an entity, and that entity has a contractual relationship with one or more MA organizations that offer one or more D-SNPs. In this arrangement, the Medicaid managed care plan has an executed Medicaid MCO contract with the State and contracts with the MA organization(s) offering the D-SNPs, with the MA organization(s) offering the D-SNPs taking on clinical and financial responsibility for both Medicare and Medicaid benefits. In this example, the MA organization(s) offering the D-SNPs would be contractually responsible for conducting the health risk assessments, establishing individualized care plans, conducting ongoing care coordination of Medicare and Medicaid benefits, reviewing and authorizing Medicare and Medicaid benefits, unifying appeals and grievance processes, and paying Medicare and Medicaid claims for enrollees, which reflects the assumption of clinical and financial responsibility for Medicare and Medicaid benefits. A second example involves two separate MA organizations that offer D-SNPs and do not have a common parent, forming a joint venture as a Medicaid MCO that has an executed Medicaid contract with the State. Each MA organization offering a D-SNP may contract with the joint venture and meet all the requirements to be a HIDE SNP or FIDE SNP, except for common parent ownership. In the second example, each MA organization offering the D-SNP would have clinical and financial responsibility for the Medicare and Medicaid benefits, meaning that the MA organization offering the D-SNP would be contractually responsible for conducting the health risk assessments (HRAs), establishing individualized care plans (ICPs), conducting ongoing care coordination of Medicare and Medicaid benefits, reviewing and authorizing Medicare and Medicaid benefits, unifying appeals and grievances processes, and paying Medicare and Medicaid claims for the enrollees. In both examples, if the MA organization offering the D-SNP contractually assumes clinical and financial responsibility for Medicare and Medicaid benefits with respect to any individual enrolled in the D-SNP and receiving Medicaid benefits through the capitated Medicaid contract, we find it appropriate under those circumstances to attribute the State Medicaid agency contract to the D-SNP, such that the D-SNP can appropriately be considered to have entered into, and to be providing coverage of Medicaid benefits under, the capitated Medicaid contract as contemplated by section 1859(f)(8)(D)(i)(II) of the Act. We are therefore proposing to amend the HIDE SNP definition to allow for such contractual arrangements.
1. Proposed Amendment to the HIDE SNP Definition
We are proposing to broaden the HIDE SNP definition to allow for more flexible and innovative arrangements between D-SNPs and Medicaid MCOs, which could create more opportunities for organizations to serve dually eligible individuals and expand integration approaches used by States. Specifically, we are proposing to add a new paragraph (1)(iv) to the HIDE SNP definition at § 422.2 to include D-SNPs offered by an MA organization that provides coverage of Medicaid benefits under a capitated contract that meets the following requirements: the capitated contract is between the State Medicaid agency and an entity that has a contractual relationship with the MA organization that requires the MA organization to assume clinical and financial responsibility for Medicare and Medicaid benefits with respect to individuals enrolled in the D-SNP who receive their Medicaid benefits through the capitated contract. We believe this change will open the integrated D-SNP market to other organizations, which in turn will provide more beneficiary choice and promote competition.
To meet the proposed amendment to the HIDE SNP definition, D-SNPs would still need to meet all other requirements of the current HIDE SNP definition at § 422.2, including having a capitated contract covering Medicaid LTSS or Medicaid behavioral health services, as required per the integration standards at Section 1859(f)(8)(D)(i)(II) of the Act. We believe that permitting this type of joint venture contracting arrangement would retain the existing level of integration required of a HIDE SNP while also allowing more flexibility with respect to corporate structure. This proposed definition would thereby promote competition and choice in D-SNP markets. While we recognize that similar arguments regarding contractual accountability could be applied to the FIDE SNP definition, we are not proposing to extend this change to the FIDE SNP definition at this time. Modifying the FIDE SNP definition in this manner raises distinct considerations, particularly with respect to the frailty adjustment methodology, and we believe it would be premature to make additional structural changes to the FIDE SNP definition given that we are already proposing modifications to the FIDE SNP definition in this rulemaking.
We are also proposing to broaden the aligned enrollment definition at § 422.2 to include D-SNPs meeting the proposed expanded HIDE SNP definition. Under the current definition, aligned enrollment refers to enrollment in a D-SNP of full-benefit dually eligible individuals whose Medicaid benefits are covered under a Medicaid MCO contract between the applicable State and the D-SNP's MA organization, the D-SNP's parent organization, or another entity that is owned and controlled by the D-SNPs parent organization. We propose to expand this existing definition of aligned enrollment to include enrollment in a D-SNP of full-benefit dually eligible individuals whose Medicaid benefits are covered under a capitated contract between the applicable State and an entity that has a contractual relationship with the MA organization that requires the MA organization to assume clinical and financial responsibility for Medicare and Medicaid benefits for any individuals so enrolled.
Finally, we are proposing updates to § 422.514(h) to clarify that D-SNPs meeting the proposed expanded HIDE SNP definition would be subject to the requirements at § 422.514(h). Under current policy at § 422.514(h)(1) beginning in Contract Year 2027, where
(
printed page 76409)
an MA organization offers a D-SNP and the MA organization, its parent organization, or any entity that shares a parent organization with the MA organization also contracts with a State as a Medicaid MCO that enrolls full-benefit dually eligible individuals in the same service areas (even if there is only partial overlap of the service areas), the MA organization: (a) may only offer, or have a parent organization or share a parent organization with another MA organization that offers, one D-SNP for full-benefit dually eligible individuals except as otherwise provided in § 422.514(h)(3); and (b) must limit new enrollment in the D-SNP to individuals enrolled in, or in the process of enrolling in, the Medicaid MCO. Per § 422.514(h)(2), beginning in Contract Year 2030, such D-SNPs must only enroll (or continue to enroll) individuals enrolled in (or in the process of enrolling in) the affiliated Medicaid MCO, except that such D-SNPs may continue to implement deemed continued eligibility requirements as described in § 422.52(d). We propose updates at § 422.514(h)(1) to apply these requirements to entities meeting the proposed expanded HIDE SNP definition and avoid creating a potential loophole to circumvent the § 422.514(h) requirements.
We solicit comments on all aspects of this proposal, including the following:
FIDE SNP and AIP Definitions:
Whether we should apply the proposed change to FIDE SNPs, and whether we should consider other updates to the HIDE SNP, FIDE SNP, and AIP definitions to capture other types of contractual arrangements that might adequately allow for D-SNP integration.
Enrollment Restriction:
Whether, similar to the definition of AIP, a contractual relationship should only be recognized in the context of an arrangement where enrollment is limited to the contracted Medicaid MCO, as a means of ensuring that the goals of integrated care are fully realized for all enrollees.

Whether a contractual relationship where the parent organization or MA organization offering the D-SNP assumes clinical and financial responsibility for Medicare and Medicaid benefits with respect to individuals enrolled in the D-SNP who receive their Medicaid benefits through the capitated contract is an appropriate integration standard to apply for the flexible arrangements proposed in this rulemaking. Is this the appropriate allocation of roles between the MA organization offering the D-SNP and the Medicaid MCO where the MA organization offering the D-SNP is ultimately accountable for performance? If so, what should be the role of the Medicaid MCO with respect to operations and functions to ensure the integration of care? Also, are there risks with our proposed amendment and other guardrails CMS should consider to ensure accountability and protect beneficiaries?

Whether there are any unintended consequences of applying the § 422.514(h) requirements to arrangements under the proposed expansion of the HIDE SNP definition rather than continuing to limit § 422.514(h) requirements to D-SNPs based on common ownership.

Whether there are examples of other types of contractual relationships that might meet our proposed amendment to the HIDE SNP definition and whether there are examples of other types of contractual relationships that meet some but not all our proposed requirements.
2. Request for Information on Need for Additional Flexibility in the Current Integrated Dual Eligible Special Needs Plan Policy To Expand Choice for Dually Eligible Individuals
Background and Policy Framework
The Contract Year 2025 Medicare Advantage and Part D final rule, which appeared in the
Federal Register
on April 23, 2024 (hereafter referred to as the April 2024 final rule;
89 FR 30448
), included several provisions to simplify options for dually eligible individuals and promote greater alignment of dual eligible special needs plans (D-SNPs) and Medicaid managed care organizations (MCOs). In the April 2024 final rule (

through

Per § 422.514(h)(2), beginning in Contract Year 2030, such D-SNPs must only enroll (or continue to enroll) individuals enrolled in (or in the process of enrolling in) the affiliated Medicaid MCO, except that such D-SNPs may continue to implement deemed continued eligibility requirements as described in § 422.52(d). To minimize enrollment disruption associated with achieving compliance, in the April 2024 final rule, we finalized a provision at § 422.530(c)(4)(iii) that would provide a new crosswalk exception to allow one or more MA organizations that share a parent organization and offer D-SNPs subject to the new limits to crosswalk enrollees (within the same parent organization and among consistent plan types) when the MA organization chooses to non-renew or consolidate its current D-SNPs to comply with the new rules at §§ 422.504(a)(20) and 422.514(h).

We expect the current § 422.514(h) policy to reduce the number of D-SNPs each parent organization offers for full-benefit dually eligible individuals in a service area, reducing the competitive advantage that large parent organizations hold over small ones so they can offer a more comparable number of D-SNP offerings in a service area and stopping a parent organization with multiple MA organizations in a service area from diluting the market with multiple D-SNP offerings that do not meaningfully differentiate their offerings. These are policy goals for CMS. For example, in Miami-Dade County in Florida in 2026, there are 33 D-SNPs for full-benefit dually eligible individuals offered by 12 MA parent organizations. One parent organization offered 10 of these D-SNPs, a second parent organization offered eight of these D-SNPs, and the remaining parent organizations offered three or fewer D-SNPs for full-benefit dually eligible individuals. The main differentiating features of the D-SNPs offered by the same parent organization in CY 2026 are the value of flex cards and dental benefits. For CY 2027, under the current § 422.514(h) policy, these offerings for full-benefit dually eligible individuals reduced to 18 D-SNPs offered by 11 MA parent organizations, evening the competition among parent organizations.
Interested parties have raised concerns, however, that the current § 422.514(h) policy reduces beneficiary choice of D-SNPs. For example, limiting parent organizations to offer one D-SNP for full-benefit dually eligible individuals in a service area could discourage some full-benefit dually eligible individuals from enrolling in a D-SNP when they are not ready to receive both Medicare and Medicaid benefits from one parent organization.
Additionally, in a market such as Pennsylvania where coordination-only D-SNPs compete against integrated D-SNPs subject to the restrictions of § 422.514(h) as described above, interested parties have raised concern that these integrated D-SNPs are at a competitive disadvantage. These disadvantages include limitations on the potential pool of enrollees available to plans subject to § 422.514(h) that may only enroll beneficiaries enrolled in an affiliated Medicaid MCO as compared to coordination only D-SNPs that face no such restrictions. For example, in Pennsylvania, there are three MA parent organizations that have Medicaid MCO contracts with the State and offer HIDE SNPs. Under the current § 422.514(h) policy, these three parent organizations are not allowed to offer a coordination-only D-SNPs enrolling full-benefit dually eligible individuals in the same service area as their HIDE SNP. Starting in CY 2027, any individuals newly enrolling in their HIDE SNP must be enrolled in or in the process of enrolling in the affiliated Medicaid MCO, consistent with § 422.514(h). These parent organizations cannot compete for full-benefit dually eligible individuals who are not enrolled in their affiliated Medicaid MCO whereas the coordination-only D-SNPs can compete for those individuals. Based on current experience of some of these parent organizations, individuals who enrolled in the HIDE SNP with unaffiliated Medicaid MCO enrollment become acquainted with the parent organization and change their Medicaid MCO enrollment to align with the HIDE SNP. In this example, allowing these parent organizations to offer a coordination-only D-SNP for full-benefit dually eligible individuals would improve competitiveness in the D-SNP market as well as offer an opportunity for individuals to enroll first in the coordination-only D-SNP for their Medicare coverage. As these individuals become acquainted with the parent organization, they may enroll in the HIDE SNP and affiliated Medicaid MCO to have fully integrated Medicare and Medicaid coverage.
CMS policy regarding dually eligible beneficiaries is two-fold. First, it is to promote integrated care—a goal we have long pursued through our regulatory framework for D-SNPs. Second, CMS policy is to promote the principles of choice and competition in D-SNP markets as a means of encouraging innovation and ensuring beneficiaries have the opportunity to choose from a range of high-quality plans offered by competing MA organizations.
3. Potential Policy Change for Comment Solicitation
We solicit comments on a potential policy change to address the aforementioned concerns, allow more beneficiary choice and competition in D-SNP markets, and continue to promote integrated care. In particular, we solicit comment on whether an effective solution would be an amendment to § 422.514(h) to allow D-SNPs with affiliated Medicaid MCOs to also offer a coordination-only D-SNP for full-benefit dually eligible individuals in the same service area as their D-SNP subject to the requirements of § 422.514(h). Would allowing each D-SNP with an affiliated Medicaid MCO to offer one coordination-only D-SNP sufficiently address the need to provide an additional option for full-benefit dually eligible individuals without adding D-SNPs to the market that do not offer meaningful differences? Under this idea, the coordination-only D-SNP could enroll both full- and partial-benefit duals even if the full-benefit dually eligible individuals are enrolled in an unaffiliated Medicaid MCO. This would mean that full-benefit dually eligible individuals who do not want to enroll with the same parent organization for both Medicare and Medicaid benefits could enroll in the coordination-only D-SNP for Medicare and enroll in a
(
printed page 76411)
different parent organization for Medicaid. If we were to propose such a change, States that want to continue to limit D-SNP offerings to only D-SNPs with an affiliated Medicaid MCO could continue to do so through their SMAC.
The extent to which MA organizations could take advantage of this idea would depend on State policy. For Contract Year 2026, there are 13 States and U.S. Territories that have integrated D-SNPs and do not allow coordination only D-SNPs in any service area in the State or only allow coordination only D-SNPs for partial-benefit dual eligible beneficiaries such that the proposed exception would not apply based on State policy. Additionally, many States have made changes to their D-SNP markets for Contract Year 2027 via the executed Contract Year 2027 SMACs to comply with existing requirements at § 422.514(h). States may be reluctant to undo these changes in future years and allow coordination-only D-SNPs for full-benefit dually eligible individuals in the same service area as HIDE SNPs or AIP D-SNPs offered by the same parent organization. However, in Contract Year 2026, there are at least 11 States that have integrated D-SNPs and allow enrollment of full benefit dually eligible individuals in coordination-only D-SNPs in the same service area as integrated D-SNPs, including Pennsylvania and South Carolina.

VI. Reducing Regulatory Burden and Costs in Accordance With
Executive Order 14192
A. Burden Reduction in the MA Application Process and MA Network Adequacy (§ 422.116)
Section 1852(d)(1) of the Act permits an MA organization to select the providers from which an enrollee may receive covered benefits, provided that the MA organization, in addition to meeting other requirements, makes such benefits available and accessible in the service area with promptness and in a manner that assures continuity in the provision of benefits. Further, §  422.112(a) generally requires that a coordinated care plan maintain a network of appropriate providers that is sufficient to provide adequate access to covered services to meet the needs of the population served.
1. Shifting Network Adequacy Reviews From the MA Application
In the “Medicare Program; Contract Year 2021 Policy and Technical Changes to the Medicare Advantage Program, Medicare Prescription Drug Benefit Program, and Medicare Cost Plan Program” final rule, which appeared in the
Federal Register
on June 2, 2020 (
85 FR 33796
) (hereinafter referred to as the June 2020 final rule), CMS codified, with some modifications, network adequacy criteria and access standards (previously outlined in subregulatory guidance) at §  422.116. The provisions at §  422.116 establish standards for measuring network adequacy and access under a contracted provider network in accordance with section 1852(d)(1) of the Act and §§  422.112(a) and 422.114(a)(1). In addition, CMS codified the then-existing policy that CMS would not deny an application based on the evaluation of the applicant's network for a new or expanding service area. Under that policy, an applicant was required to attest that it had an adequate network for access and availability of applicable provider and facility types at the time of the application for a new or expanding service area, and CMS reviewed networks for pending service areas after an application was approved but before the MA organization was operational in the new or expanded service area.
Subsequently, in the “Medicare Program; Contract Year 2023 Policy and Technical Changes to the Medicare Advantage and Medicare Prescription Drug Benefit Programs; Policy and Regulatory Revisions in Response to the COVID-19 Public Health Emergency; Additional Policy and Regulatory Revisions in Response to the COVID-19 Public Health Emergency” final rule, which appeared in the
Federal Register
on May 9, 2022 (
87 FR 27704
) (hereinafter referred to as the May 2022 final rule), CMS finalized an amendment at § 422.116(a)(2)(ii) to require MA organizations to submit a compliant network for review at the time of an MA application and provide that CMS may deny an application on the basis of an evaluation of the applicant's network for the new or expanding service area.
In the May 2022 final rule, CMS explained that the timing of network adequacy submissions for pending service areas affected the timely, complete, and accurate submission of bids. CMS stated that providing network adequacy determinations before the bid deadline, within the MA application timeline, would allow organizations to make decisions regarding their intended service areas before submitting bids and would mitigate operational issues associated with service area changes after the bid deadline. In that rule, CMS also finalized a temporary 10-percentage-point credit toward the percentage of beneficiaries residing within published time and distance standards for all combinations of county designations and provider/facility specialty types specified in §  422.116(d) in the proposed contracted network for a new or expanded service area. In response to public comments, CMS also allowed Letters of Intent (LOIs) to be used in lieu of signed provider contracts—at the time of application and for the duration of the application review. These flexibilities were intended to account for the fact that the network adequacy review for an MA application for a new or expanding service area occurs almost a year before the applicable contract year begins.
When a network adequacy review is performed in conjunction with an MA application, there is a very short window of time for MA organizations to complete the application process and
(
printed page 76412)
demonstrate compliance with network adequacy requirements. MA organizations submit provider networks for review using the Health Service Delivery (HSD) tables and submit the data through the Network Management Module (NMM) in the Health Plan Management System (HPMS), where CMS's automated review of network adequacy, also known as the Automated Criteria Check (ACC), is triggered. MA organizations may cure deficiencies identified through the ACC by resubmitting HSD tables with additional contracted providers or facilities, or by submitting valid exception requests during CMS specified timelines. If network deficiencies remain unresolved after the cure period, CMS may issue a notice of intent to deny the application under § 422.502(c)(2). MA organizations may also withdraw counties they wanted to operate in as submitted with their application during the application review process if they are unable to satisfy the network adequacy standards for those counties. If at least one deficiency (for a county/specialty type combination) remains unresolved after CMS issues a notice of intent to deny the application, CMS may deny the application and the MA organization may request a hearing under § 422.660. If the MA organization is not successful at the hearing, they may also appeal to the CMS Administrator under § 422.692. Unless the MA organization is successful in an administrative appeal, the application is denied.
Under the current process MA organizations must submit comprehensive application materials in mid-February of the year prior to the year in which they wish to operate, CMS reviews those materials, including the network information, and issues notices of intent to deny in mid-April and denials in mid-May in order to provide MA organizations time to exercise their appeal rights. In contrast, CMS's ongoing oversight of active provider networks operates on a three-year cycle known as the Triennial Review. This annual operational review evaluates one-third of all contracts and their entire active service areas. However, unlike the stricter application-stage process that may lead to application denial, organizations found to be out of compliance with network adequacy standards during the Triennial Review may be referred for compliance and/or enforcement actions.
An adequate network requires that MA organizations meet Medicare access and availability requirements through direct contracting with network providers consistent with the prevailing community pattern of health care delivery in the areas where the network is being offered. Since CMS began including the network adequacy review in the MA application cycle, MA organizations have had difficulty establishing networks so far in advance of the contract start date, even with the flexibilities afforded during the application process. CMS has heard from applicants that the timing of the MA application submission period is insufficient for MA organizations to build high-quality provider networks. In addition, MA applicants have suggested that the network adequacy requirements disproportionately affect smaller MA organizations seeking to expand to certain regional, rural, and medically underserved areas, thereby inhibiting competition among plans and limiting beneficiary choice.
Since implementing application-stage network adequacy reviews, CMS has denied applications for network adequacy reasons, including in circumstances when an MA organization may only be failing network adequacy for the lack of a singular provider and where approving the application could have increased competition and enrollee choice in various service areas. Although MA organizations receive the new applicant credit and may use LOIs to establish an adequate network, CMS has found that those flexibilities have not always resolved the difficulties of establishing a contracted network so far in advance and within a short window to demonstrate compliance. Additionally, CMS has observed instances where an MA organization submitted HSD tables based largely on LOIs, rather than signed contracts. That was not the intended use of LOIs, which were meant to provide flexibility rather than serve as a placeholder for a fully compliant network.
CMS has also experienced continued bid timeline challenges. For example, when an MA organization exercises its hearing rights under § 422.660, the timeline for resolving the hearing can interfere with finalizing bids and may delay plan corrections and contract execution. Delays in those pre-operational steps create downstream issues for MA and MA-PD systems, such as contracts not being included in enrollment processes, contract information not being displayed timely on Medicare Plan Finder, challenges with automatic continuation or transition of a beneficiary's enrollment from one plan to another, and beneficiary reassignments. To reduce burden on MA organizations and CMS, and consistent with
Executive Order 14192
, “Unleashing Prosperity Through Deregulation” (
90 FR 9065

2. Consolidating Outpatient Behavioral Health Network Adequacy Requirements
In the “Medicare Program; Contract Year 2024 Policy and Technical Changes to the Medicare Advantage Program, Medicare Prescription Drug Benefit Program, Medicare Cost Plan Program, and Programs of All-Inclusive Care for the Elderly” final rule, which appeared in the
Federal Register
on April 12, 2023 (
88 FR 22120
) (hereinafter referred to the April 2023 final rule), CMS finalized amendments to § 422.116 adding time and distance standards and minimum ratios for two new provider-specialty types, Clinical Psychology and Clinical Social Work. In the “Medicare Program; Changes to the Medicare Advantage and the Medicare Prescription Drug Benefit Program for Contract Year 2024—Remaining Provisions and Contract Year 2025 Policy and Technical Changes to the Medicare Advantage Program, Medicare Prescription Drug Benefit Program, Medicare Cost Plan Program, and Programs of All-Inclusive Care for the Elderly (PACE)” final rule, which appeared in the
Federal Register
on April 23, 2024 (
89 FR 30448
) (herein after referred to as the April 2024 final rule), CMS finalized a new facility-specialty type, Outpatient Behavioral Health (OBH), including time and distance standards and minimum provider number requirements. As a result of these changes, MA organizations must independently satisfy each of the network adequacy standards for Clinical Psychology, Clinical Social Work, and OBH. CMS also added Clinical Psychology, Clinical Social Work, and OBH to the list at § 422.116(d)(5) of specialties for which an MA organization may receive a 10-percentage-point telehealth credit if its contracted provider network includes one or more telehealth providers of that specialty type furnishing additional telehealth benefits, as defined in § 422.135, for covered services.
At the time of the April 2023 final rule, CMS received several comments that opposed the proposal to add new behavioral health specialty types to the network adequacy evaluation, citing concerns that shortages of behavioral health providers could hinder MA plans' ability to meet network adequacy standards. However, CMS determined that finalization of the proposal was appropriate at that time, indicating that the network adequacy standards are updated annually based on the supply of providers and that MA organizations unable to meet network standards have the option to submit an exception.
Since implementing separate behavioral health specialty types into the network adequacy standards, CMS has received industry feedback that the behavioral health standards may have introduced unintended consequences, such as skewed negotiating leverage and reduced provider competition and supply in MA networks, which may increase the cost of care.
While performing network adequacy reviews, CMS has also found that MA organizations have submitted some of the same Clinical Social Work and Clinical Psychology providers on their HSD tables to satisfy both the OBH time and distance and minimum number standards and the separate Clinical Psychology and Clinical Social Work standards. For example, CMS examined network submissions by MA organizations during the formal 2025 triennial review period and found that 94.5 percent of OBH submissions were also submitted with another behavioral health specialty, meaning that the majority of MA organizations submitted the same providers under multiple behavioral health specialty types. In the April 2024 final rule, CMS stated that “MA organizations may not submit a single provider for purposes of meeting the Outpatient Behavioral Health requirement if they have already submitted that provider under another specialty. For example, MA organizations would not be permitted to submit a single provider as a psychiatry, clinical social work, or clinical psychologist provider specialty and as an Outpatient Behavioral Health facility.” However, CMS has come to understand, based on analysis of fee for service Medicare claims data from August 1, 2021, through July 31, 2022, that beneficiaries use similar psychotherapy services across the behavioral health provider types CMS monitors. For example, psychotherapy services provided to individuals with mental health or substance use disorders may be similar among clinical psychology, clinical social work, and certain specialties allowable under OBH. They may also provide other services as well, such as medication monitoring or care management.
Accordingly, to reduce administrative burden and increase flexibility with network adequacy submissions, and to mitigate potential market impacts associated with redundant network adequacy specialty type designations, CMS proposes to consolidate Clinical Psychology and Clinical Social Work provider-specialty types into the OBH facility-specialty type. Under this proposal, MA organizations would be able to satisfy the OBH network adequacy standards using any combination of qualifying providers or facilities included in § 422.116(b)(2)(xiv), including clinical psychologists and clinical social workers. This would expand the pool of providers and facilities eligible to meet the OBH network adequacy requirements and directly address concerns about duplicative submissions, provider supply, and contracting leverage.
In the amended OBH facility-specialty type definition at § 422.116(b)(2)(xiv), CMS is also proposing to include certified peer support specialists and community health workers that meet the requirements for auxiliary personnel acting under the supervision of a physician (or other eligible practitioner) described at § 410.26(a)(1). Peer support specialists are qualified mental health or substance use professionals who leverage their own lived recovery experience to guide others. They provide non-judgmental mentoring, help clients navigate treatment systems, and assist in building independent living and recovery plans. Community health workers (CHWs) are frontline public health professionals who serve as a trusted liaison between healthcare

These changes make Community Health Integration and Principal Illness Navigation services separately payable under original Medicare to account for resources when clinicians involve certain types of health care support staff such as community health workers, care navigators, and peer support specialists in furnishing medically necessary care.
