3. Proposed Revision to the Network Adequacy Telehealth Credit (§ 422.116(d)(5))
Section 1852(d)(1) of the Act requires an MA organization using a network of providers to make covered benefits available and accessible to each enrollee within the plan's service area with reasonable promptness and in a manner that assures continuity in the provision of benefits. Consistent with this statutory requirement, § 422.116 establishes minimum provider and facility number requirements and maximum time and distance standards that network-based MA plans must satisfy.
Under § 422.116(d)(4), an MA plan must demonstrate that at least 90 percent of beneficiaries residing in large metro and metro counties, and at least 85 percent of beneficiaries residing in micro, rural, and Counties with Extreme Access Considerations (CEAC), have access to at least one provider or facility of each applicable specialty type within the published time and distance standards. Section 422.116(d)(5) currently provides a 10-percentage-point credit toward the applicable percentage for certain provider specialty types when an MA plan includes in its contracted network one or more telehealth providers that furnish additional telehealth benefits, as defined in § 422.135.
CMS established the telehealth credit in the June 2020 final rule to recognize the additional access and choice that contracted telehealth providers can furnish while maintaining the role of telehealth as a supplement to, rather than a replacement for, an adequate in-
(
printed page 76415)
person provider network. See
85 FR 33796
,
33855
. The existing regulatory framework preserves in-person access. Under § 422.116(e)(1), a telehealth-only provider may not count toward the minimum provider number requirement. In addition, § 422.135(c) requires an MA plan furnishing additional telehealth benefits to furnish in-person access to the specified Part B service at the election of the enrollee and to advise enrollees that they may receive the service either in person or through electronic exchange.
In the April 2024 final rule, some commenters recommended that CMS increase the telehealth credit from 10 percentage points to 30 percentage points. Other commenters expressed concern that a larger credit could result in overreliance on telehealth and could reduce access to providers who furnish timely in-person services. CMS stated that the Agency would remain open to considering future adjustments to the telehealth credit based on evidence, stakeholder feedback, and the evolving role of telehealth in the delivery of health care. See
89 FR 30448
,
30494
.
CMS is now proposing to revise § 422.116(d)(5) to increase the current 10-percentage-point telehealth credit to a value greater than 10 percentage points such as 30 percentage points or to another appropriate level within that range of increase. Although CMS is not setting specific amendatory language for § 422.116(d)(5) in this proposed rule, CMS is describing the substance and range of the policy under consideration and soliciting comment on the appropriate amount and structure of the credit. After considering public comments, CMS may finalize an increased uniform credit of up to 30-percentage points or finalize no change to the existing 10-percentage-point credit under § 422.116(d)(5).
CMS's quantitative network adequacy standards are an important beneficiary protection to ensure that MA plans maintain sufficient contracted networks and that covered services are geographically accessible. At the same time, in markets with limited provider supply or concentrated provider systems, an MA plan may have relatively few practical contracting alternatives for satisfying the applicable network adequacy standards. The interaction between limited provider supply and quantitative network requirements may make network development more difficult, may affect the ability of MA organizations to enter or remain in certain service areas, and may provide substantial negotiating leverage to a small number of providers or provider systems whose participation is necessary for a plan to satisfy the standards.
Contracted telehealth providers may broaden the range of providers available to MA enrollees, facilitate more timely access to clinically appropriate services, and reduce geographic barriers to care. Recognizing meaningful telehealth capacity in the network adequacy methodology may support the availability of MA plan choices in areas where development of an in-person network is particularly challenging.
However, telehealth must not be treated as a complete substitute for an adequate in-person network. Certain services require a physical examination, diagnostic testing, procedures, or other in-person components. Some beneficiaries may also prefer in-person care or may be unable to use telehealth effectively because of limitations involving broadband access, technology, digital literacy, privacy, or other circumstances. The appropriate telehealth credit therefore should recognize the access value of telehealth without materially undermining required access to timely and clinically appropriate in-person care.
A 30-percentage-point credit, for example, would constitute a substantial change from the existing policy. Before application of other available network adequacy credits, a plan receiving a 30-percentage-point telehealth credit could satisfy the 90-percent standard applicable in large metro and metro counties at 60 percent. It could satisfy the 85-percent standard applicable in micro, rural, and CEAC counties at 55 percent. CMS therefore seeks feedback, including specific evidence, on whether a credit at this level—or at another level above the current 10 percent, whether 30 percent or another appropriate level within that range—appropriately reflects the access furnished through telehealth, and conversely in-person, and what safeguards, if any, should accompany an increase.
Any increase in the telehealth credit would continue to operate within the broader network adequacy framework. CMS is not proposing any change that would permit a telehealth-only provider to satisfy the minimum provider number requirement under § 422.116(e), eliminate the requirement under § 422.135 that enrollees retain access to the covered service through an in-person visit, or relieve an MA organization of its obligation to make covered benefits available and accessible consistent with section 1852(d)(1) of the Act and §§ 422.112 and 422.116.
CMS is considering several possible structures. First, CMS could apply a uniform credit greater than 10 percent to every provider specialty type currently identified in § 422.116(d)(5) and applicable to every county type.
Second, CMS is considering an alternative approach of varying the credit by county classification. For example, a lower credit could apply in large metro and metro counties where provider supply and broadband access may differ from those in less densely populated areas, while a larger credit, such as the proposed 30 percent credit, could apply in micro, rural, or CEAC counties. Telehealth may be particularly valuable in rural and CEAC counties, where beneficiaries may otherwise face limited provider supply, substantial travel distances, and difficulty obtaining timely specialty care. An increased telehealth credit could support MA plan availability in these areas and could provide beneficiaries with access to providers who would otherwise not be reasonably available. At the same time, rural beneficiaries may be more likely to experience limitations involving broadband availability, reliable internet service, access to devices, private locations from which to receive care, transportation for necessary in-person follow-up, and digital literacy. CMS would not finalize an increased credit unless, after considering the public comments and available evidence, CMS concludes that the policy is consistent with the access requirements in section 1852(d)(1) of the Act and appropriately protects access to in-person care. CMS is particularly interested in data concerning the effect of the current credit, and the likely effect of an increased credit, on provider contracting, appointment availability, travel burdens, beneficiary choice, health outcomes, and MA plan availability in micro, rural, and CEAC counties.
Third, CMS could vary the credit by provider specialty type, based on factors such as the clinical appropriateness of telehealth for that specialty, the extent to which services ordinarily require an in-person component, observed patterns of telehealth utilization, and provider supply. CMS has previously analyzed Medicare claims data for telehealth services to identify which provider specialty types warrant a telehealth credit. CMS considered utilization and supply of providers across specialty types over multiple years tracked through the network adequacy reviews. A uniform credit amount for all specialty types risks overlooking meaningful differences in how beneficiaries access care from different types of providers. Therefore, CMS proposes, as another alternative, to
(
printed page 76416)
increase the credit to up to 30 percent for specialty types that had a high telehealth utilization, including but not limited to dermatology, psychiatry, neurology, otolaryngology and cardiology. Under this alternative, the remaining telehealth eligible specialty types under 422.116(d)(5) would continue to receive the 10 percent telehealth credit.
Lastly, CMS could maintain the existing 10 percent credit with no changes to the specialty types under 422.116(d)(5) based on feedback to the proposals in this proposed rule.
Section 422.116(d)(6) separately provides a 10-percentage-point credit for affected provider and facility types in a State with Certificate of Need (CON) laws or other State-imposed anticompetitive restrictions that limit the number of providers or facilities in the State or in a county. The CON credit and the telehealth credit address different circumstances: the CON credit addresses State-imposed restrictions affecting provider or facility supply, while the telehealth credit recognizes additional access furnished through contracted telehealth providers. MA organizations may receive both the 10-percentage-point CON credit and telehealth credit, if applicable.
CMS solicits comments on all aspects of the potential changes described in this section, including the alternative approaches CMS is considering, and specifically request comment on the following:
What percentage-point credit greater than 10 would appropriately recognize the access furnished by contracted telehealth providers without undermining access to in-person care? Is a 30-percent threshold the appropriate level, or would another credit within the 10 to 30-percent range more accurately reflect the value that telehealth providers contribute to a contracted network and better achieve the goals of network adequacy and beneficiary access? CMS asks commenters to provide data or other evidence supporting the recommended amount.
Should CMS adopt a uniform credit, or should the credit vary by county type, provider specialty type, or another factor? If the credit should vary, what methodology and values should CMS use?
Would an increased credit reduce, maintain, or improve beneficiary access to timely in-person care? What safeguards would prevent an MA plan from using the credit as a substitute for contracting with an adequate number and distribution of in-person providers?
What effects would an increased credit have in large metro, metro, micro, rural, and CEAC counties? In particular, would a larger credit improve access and MA plan availability in rural communities, or could it reduce the availability of local in-person providers in these areas?
To what extent do limited provider supply, provider-market concentration, or difficulties in contracting with particular providers or provider systems prevent MA organizations from satisfying network adequacy standards? Would an increased telehealth credit meaningfully improve plan competition or help MA organizations build a network of providers, and what evidence supports that conclusion?
Would a 30-percent telehealth credit, or another appropriate level within the 10 to 30 percent range, adequately incentivize MA plans to maintain or expand telehealth provider networks in rural and underserved communities?
Would a 30-percent telehealth credit, or another appropriate level within the 10 to 30 percent range, have any unintended consequences that could reduce the availability or quality of telehealth services for rural beneficiaries?
Would rural beneficiaries experience differential impacts compared to urban or suburban beneficiaries as a result of the proposed changes, and how should those differences be addressed?
Should additional protections, incentives, or complementary policies be considered to safeguard access to telehealth services in rural areas?
How does the proposed change align with existing federal initiatives and programs aimed at improving rural health access, including those administered by CMS and other federal agencies?
CMS solicits comments on all aspects of these proposals.
4. RFI on Network Adequacy Topics
In addition to the foregoing proposals, CMS requests comment more broadly on strategies to address negotiating leverage that may result from network adequacy requirements, particularly in behavioral health and primary care, due to shortages of providers, that may increase the cost of care for the MA program.
First, CMS seeks input on potential adjustments to time and distance standards that could increase access to behavioral health and primary care services for enrollees. Specifically, the following questions:
Should CMS modify the time and distance standards for providers that regularly furnish telehealth services? If so, should the modification differ by county classification (for example, reducing the time and distance standards by 40 percent for urban counties and 50 percent for rural counties)?
What are the tradeoffs between relaxing time and distance standards to expand the qualifying provider pool and the potential impact on beneficiary access to in-person care? How should CMS weigh these tradeoffs?
Second, CMS also seeks comment on potential structural changes to network adequacy requirements that may broaden the qualifying provider pool and reduce disproportionate negotiating leverage. Specifically the following questions:
Should CMS permit nurse practitioners and physician assistants to satisfy primary care network adequacy requirements when they furnish primary care services and are licensed or certified to do so under applicable State law?
Are there other provider types or care settings that should be eligible to satisfy behavioral health or primary care network adequacy requirements? For example, should Rural Health Clinics be eligible to meet the primary care network adequacy requirements? Should Federally Qualified Health Centers be eligible to meet the behavioral health or primary care network adequacy requirements?
CMS seeks comment on whether regulatory changes would improve access and reduce burden on MA organizations in primary care and behavioral health.
Finally, are there other policy approaches, including the utilization of super intelligence to improve access to care, not described previously that CMS should consider, to advance competition, lower costs, and preserve or strengthen beneficiary access to behavioral health and primary care services in the MA program? How should CMS approach these viewpoints given the potential tradeoffs between competition, cost reduction, and beneficiary access?

1. Removing the Requirement for CMS Approval of Plan Use of the Medicare Card Image Found In §§  422.2262(a)(1)(xvii) and 423.2262(a)(1)(xvi)
As a part of the Medicare Program; Contract Year 2024 Policy and Technical Changes to the Medicare Advantage Program, Medicare Prescription Drug Benefit Program, Medicare Cost Plan Program, and Programs of All-Inclusive Care for the Elderly Final Rule which appeared in the
Federal Register
on April 12, 2023 (hereafter referred to as the April 2023 Final Rule) (
88 FR 22120
), CMS finalized regulations at §§  422.2262(a)(1)(xix) and 423.2262(a)(1)(xviii) (later redesignated as §§ 422.2262(a)(1)(xvii) and 423.2262(a)(1)(xvi) in Medicare Program; Contract Year 2027 and Certain Contract Year 2026 Policy and Technical Changes to the Medicare Advantage Program, Medicare Prescription Drug Benefit Program, and Medicare Cost Plan Program,
91 FR 17583
, hereafter referred to as the April 2026 final rule) with an aim to strengthen beneficiary protections and improve MA and Part D marketing. CMS placed discrete limits around the use of the Medicare name, logo, and Medicare card, including requiring that the use of the Medicare card image (MCI) be permitted only after review and approval from CMS.
CMS implemented these regulations in response to concerns from external stakeholders about marketing activities and documents that appeared to be from Medicare, CMS, or the Federal Government, when in fact, the documents originated from non-governmental entities. For example, CMS noted instances in which third-party internet sites included the word Medicare in the URL, television advertisements where beneficiaries might assume that the advertising was from CMS or the Medicare program, and complaints received through 1-800-MEDICARE detailing instances in which beneficiaries thought they were contacting Medicare and were in fact contacting a MA or Part D plan, its agent or broker, or other associated third-party marketing organization (TPMO). These instances heightened CMS' concern that these advertisements were inconsistent with regulations at §§  422.2262(a)(1)(i) and 423.2262(a)(1)(i), which prohibit MA organizations and Part D Sponsors from misleading, confusing, or providing materially inaccurate information to current or potential enrollees as well as the regulations at §§ 422.2274(c) and 423.2274(c) which require MA organizations and Part D sponsors to hold first tier, downstream, and related entities that represent the MA organization or Part D sponsor to those same standards.
Upon issuance of the April 2023 Final Rule, CMS implemented operations to manage the MCI submission and disposition process. This included developing review rubrics, approval/denial language, a policy for non-English materials, workload tracking, and communications to MA organizations, Part D sponsors, and TPMOs. Currently CMS generally approves submissions for educational use, for example, side-by-side comparisons of the MCI and the MA organizations' card. Additionally, materials that contain clear disclaimer language, for example, `Not affiliated with or endorsed by the Federal Government or the Medicare program,' typically receive approval. Submissions which could be mistaken as endorsed by Medicare or the Federal Government are disapproved. The MA organization or TPMO then has the option to modify the material and resubmit for rereview.
After implementing this review process, it has become apparent that CMS approves the substantial majority of MCI requests received. Among the denied submissions, the primary deficiency was a failure to make sufficiently clear that the image originated from a non-governmental entity or that it was not endorsed by the Federal Government. It has also become apparent to CMS that the requirement to pre-review MCI is overly burdensome on entities using the MCI in their material as well as on the government resources reviewing those materials. CMS already maintains robust oversight authority over marketing materials, authority that includes the ability to take action when an image is improperly attributed to a governmental entity or falsely implies Federal endorsement. The current additional layer of MCI review, that is, the individual review of the use of the MCI, has not shown to provide any meaningful protection in either detection or enforcement beyond what CMS can already provide under other existing mechanisms. Based on CMS's experience reviewing MCI submissions, CMS has determined that there is nothing inherent in the use of the MCI that warrants a separate or heightened review process compared to other communications or marketing content subject to the requirements of
42 CFR part 422, subpart V
, and
42
CFR part 423, subpart V.
The MCI pre-review requirement stands in notable contrast to how CMS regulates other potentially sensitive elements of MA and Part D marketing materials. Numerous other components of communications and marketing materials, including plan benefit summaries, cost-sharing disclosures, provider network representations, and formulary information, carry significant potential to mislead or confuse beneficiaries, yet none of these elements are subject to the same individualized, pre-authorization review process that has been applied to the MCI. Instead, communications and marketing materials are subject to the broader oversight framework established under
42 CFR part 422, subpart V
, and
42
CFR part 423, subpart V, including CMS's authority to review materials submitted under §§ 422.2261 and 423.2261, prohibit misleading or inaccurate communications under §§ 422.2262(a)(1)(i) and 423.2262(a)(1)(i), and take appropriate compliance or enforcement action where warranted. Between CMS's existing review mechanisms and processes currently in place, CMS expects that if the MCI pre-approval requirement was eliminated as proposed here, communications marketing materials that use the MCI would still receive sufficient oversight.
While CMS recognizes that the MCI pre-review requirement was adopted based on genuine underlying concerns about potentially abusive use of the MCI in marketing materials, the operational experience gained since implementation of the MCI pre-review requirement has provided CMS with additional information regarding the practical
(
printed page 76418)
operation and effectiveness of the requirement. The fact that CMS has approved the substantial majority of MCI submissions received since the review process was established suggests that the problem the requirement was designed to address (that is, widespread or systematic misuse of the MCI in a manner likely to mislead beneficiaries into believing they were dealing with a governmental entity) has not materialized at the scale or frequency that originally prompted regulatory action. As previously noted, CMS relies on robust, generally applicable oversight mechanisms to protect beneficiaries from misleading representations across all other categories of communications marketing content, including content that directly affects beneficiary enrollment decisions and financial obligations. Based on the operational experience gained since implementation of the MCI pre-review requirement, it appears that these oversight mechanisms and general prohibitions on misleading marketing conduct will also be sufficient to address concerns related to MCI use. Imposing a unique, resource-intensive pre-review requirement exclusively on the MCI, while relying on post-submission review and enforcement for all other marketing content, creates an inconsistency that is difficult to justify on beneficiary protection grounds and is precisely the type of unnecessary regulatory burden that
Executive Order 14192
directs agencies to eliminate.
CMS reviews and evaluates marketing materials in the Marketing Module of the Health Plan Management System (HPMS), as required under §§ 422.2261(a)(2) and 423.2261(a)(2). As a part of this process, CMS uses different criteria, including material content, to focus on particular types of marketing materials. Marketing materials reviewed by CMS that include the MCI will continue to be subject to the review standards under §§ 422.2261(d) and 423.2261(d), including if the use of the MCI is misleading or confusing, as CMS did before the MCI was singled out for specialized, targeted, and individualized pre-review. In addition, if this rule is finalized and CMS later identifies concerns with the use of the MCI or would like to monitor how the MCI is being used, CMS could add MCI as a specific material content to the marketing module submission process. This would enable MA organizations, Part D sponsors, and third parties that submit marketing materials to specifically indicate if the material includes the MCI.
CMS acknowledges that there may be legitimate reasons for industry stakeholders to use the MCI in communication materials. For example, differentiating between an MA organization or Part D sponsor's card and the Medicare card, displaying the MCI when reminding beneficiaries about an upcoming MA Open Enrollment Period, or using the MCI to help beneficiaries understand how to identify their Medicare Beneficiary Identifier are examples of legitimate use of the MCI. CMS is not proposing to remove the requirement that the MCI, as well as the Medicare name, CMS logo, and products or information issued by the Federal Government, not be used in a misleading way. Rather, CMS is proposing to remove only the requirement that use of the MCI is permitted only with prior authorization from CMS.
CMS notes that existing regulations at
42 CFR 422.2262(a)(1)(i)
and
423.2262(a)(1)(i)
prohibit MA organizations and Part D sponsors from engaging in activities that could mislead or confuse Medicare beneficiaries and prohibit these entities from providing information that is inaccurate or misleading. Additionally, the existing regulations at
42 CFR 422.2274(c)
and
423.2274(c)
direct MA organizations and Part D sponsors to oversee their first tier, downstream, and related entities, as well as TPMOs, that represent the plans to ensure those entities abide by the requirements at
42 CFR Subpart V
, including §§ 422.2262(a)(1)(i) and 423.2262(a)(1)(i). Therefore, CMS has concluded that sufficient beneficiary protections already exist in regulation and CMS' systems such that requiring CMS approval to use the MCI is unnecessary, as it does not offer enough benefit to justify continuation of the approval process. As indicated previously, CMS will leverage particular aspects of the already-established Marketing Module in HPMS if CMS becomes aware of the need for a targeted review of use of the MCI.
To ensure the use of the MCI is not misleading, CMS strongly recommends that, when MA organizations, Part D sponsors, and TPMOs representing MA organizations and Part D sponsors create materials that use the MCI, they include language, such as a disclaimer, so that a reasonable person would not incorrectly conclude that the image or message originated from, or is endorsed by Medicare, CMS, HHS, or the Federal Government. Doing so will help to keep the material in compliance with the requirement at §§ 422.2262(a)(1)(i) and 423.2262(a)(1)(i) that prohibit MA organizations and Part D sponsors from misleading Medicare beneficiaries or misrepresenting the MA organization or Part D sponsor.

Executive Order 14192
, Unleashing Prosperity Through Deregulation, CMS is proposing to amend the regulatory language found at
42 CFR 422.2262(a)(1)(xvii)
and

2. Removing a Redundant Requirement for the Use of Plan Star Ratings
CMS instituted the Star Ratings program in 2007. The program was designed as a tool for consumers to quickly and reliably evaluate the quality of MA and Part D plans with ratings from one to five stars. In addition to quality, CMS hoped to drive improvements in care on the part of these plans. The program rates Cost, MA, and Part D plans on various measures including clinical care, patient experience, and drug safety. CMS has continually updated the methodology with significant refinements and changes regarding the calculation of the elements of measure that determine Star Ratings. CMS has included incentives for the Star Ratings program regarding enrollment as well, creating special enrollment periods allowing beneficiaries to enroll in plans with 5 stars or leave plans with fewer than 3 stars outside of the normal MA enrollment periods. The utility and reliability of the Star Ratings program have made it an integral element of the MA and Part D programs. CMS has codified the regulatory requirements for the development and use of the Star Ratings program in §§ 422.160, 422.162, 422.164, 422.166, 423.182, 423.184, and 423.186. CMS has codified the regulatory requirements for use of Star Ratings in marketing materials in §§ 422.2263(c) and 423.2263(c).
As such, CMS maintains a strong interest in the integrity of the program and how Star Ratings are marketed to Medicare beneficiaries. CMS has maintained many requirements for the use of Star Ratings in advertising and member education since the institution of the program. These requirements have served as guardrails to provide plans with a picture of the purpose CMS intended the Star Ratings program to serve. The requirements, in several iterations, existed as guidance in the Medicare Managed Care Manual until January of 2021 when they were codified. On January 19, 2021, CMS issued the Medicare and Medicaid
(
printed page 76419)
Programs; Contract Year 2022 Policy and Technical Changes to the Medicare Advantage Program, Medicare Prescription Drug Benefit Program, Medicaid Program, Medicare Cost Plan Program, and Programs of All-Inclusive Care for the Elderly Final Rule (
86 FR 5864
), referred to hereafter as the January 2021 Final Rule. In this rule, CMS codified requirements for disclaimer language at §§ 422.2267(e)(31) and 423.2267(e)(33) as part of the list of MA and Part D required materials and content. These requirements indicated that the disclaimer must convey that MA organizations and Part D sponsors are evaluated yearly by CMS to determine accurate Star Ratings and that the Star Ratings are based on a 5-star rating system. The regulatory requirements also indicated that MA organizations and Part D sponsors must convey the disclaimer or the information in the disclaimer whenever Star Ratings are mentioned in marketing materials, except on small objects such as pens, rulers, or other give-away items. On May 9, 2022, in the Medicare Program; Contract Year 2023 Policy and Technical Changes to the Medicare Advantage and Medicare Prescription Drug Benefit Programs; Policy and Regulatory Revisions in Response to the COVID-19 Public Health Emergency; Additional Policy and Regulatory Revisions in Response to the COVID-19 Public Health Emergency Final Rule (
87 FR 27899
), hereafter referred to as the May 2022 Final Rule, CMS amended these paragraphs by moving them without change to §§ 422.2267(e)(33) and 423.2267(e)(35). As a whole, the requirements provided regulatory instructions for the use of disclaimer language related to Star Ratings used in marketing.
Accuracy in communication of Star Ratings is essential for the reliability and operation of the program, particularly to protect beneficiaries' awareness of the quality of the plans they are choosing. Yet, there is a level of duplication between the Star Ratings requirements found under §§ 422.2263(c) and 423.2263(c) and the Star Ratings disclaimer requirements under §§ 422.2267(e)(33) and 423.2267(e)(35). The language in §§ 422.2263(c) and 423.2263(c) is more robust than the language at §§ 422.2267(e)(33) and 423.2267(e)(35). Those sections indicate that a plan is required to mention the contract year that the Star Rating represents. This indicates that the Star Rating is produced yearly. The language at §§ 422.2263(c) and 423.2263(c) also indicates that any mention of the Star Rating must be clear that the rating is out of five stars. The introductory language in §§ 422.2263(c) and 423.2263(c) also indicate that the requirements described in those sections apply whenever MA organizations and Part D sponsors use CMS-issued Star Ratings in communications and marketing materials. CMS has determined that the intended beneficiary protections inherent in the requirements regarding Star Ratings in §§ 422.2267(e)(33) and 423.2267(e)(35) are unnecessary because they are also captured under the regulatory requirements at §§ 422.2263(c) and 423.2263(c).
Taken together, the requirements at §§ 422.2263(c) and 423.2263(c) fully encompass the consumer protections that the disclaimer requirements at §§ 422.2267(e)(33) and 423.2267(e)(35) were designed to provide. The disclaimer requirements were intended to ensure that beneficiaries understand that Star Ratings are evaluated annually and are based on a five-star scale—information that is already mandated, and conveyed with greater specificity, under the more comprehensive Star Ratings marketing requirements, which require identification of the specific contract year rather than a general reference to annual evaluation. Maintaining a separate, duplicative disclaimer requirement creates unnecessary regulatory burden for MA organizations, Part D sponsors, and CMS, and risks introducing compliance ambiguity where plans may interpret two overlapping but textually distinct standards as imposing different obligations. Furthermore, redundant disclosure requirements can undermine the clarity and readability of beneficiary-facing materials, reducing rather than enhancing the effectiveness of consumer communication. Removing the disclaimer requirement would therefore streamline compliance obligations and improve the quality of beneficiary communications while preserving the full scope of beneficiary protections already established in regulation.
Aside from the Star Ratings-specific regulatory requirements under §§ 422.2263(c) and 423.2263(c), CMS notes that the general communications requirements in §§ 422.2262(a)(1)(i) and 423.2262(a)(1)(i), which prohibit MA organizations and Part D sponsors from misleading, confusing, or providing materially inaccurate information to current or potential enrollees offer a level of protection to the use of Star Ratings in advertisements. Additionally, one of the criteria by which CMS defines marketing and identifies marketing material is the use of measuring or ranking standards. The regulatory definition at §§ 422.2260 and 423.2260 for “Marketing” includes the use of measuring or ranking standards and specifically identifies Star Ratings as an example of such standards in paragraph (2)(ii). This means that virtually all advertisements that include Star Ratings fall under the definition of marketing and therefore must abide by the more stringent requirements for marketing materials present in §§ 422.2263 and 423.2263.
To prevent confusion on the part of plans regarding the use of Star Ratings in marketing to beneficiaries, and in keeping with
Executive Order 14192
, Unleashing Prosperity Through Deregulation, which appeared in the
Federal Register
on February 6, 2025 (
90 FR 9065
), CMS is proposing to amend the regulation found at
42 CFR 422.2267(e)(33)
and
423.2267(e)(35)
to remove the requirement for MA organizations and Part D sponsors to use the Star Ratings Disclaimer.
We invite comments on this proposal.
3. Removing the Requirement for Mailing Statements

4. Removing the Requirement To Notify Users When Leaving the Plan's Website
Various versions of the Medicare Managed Care Manual's instructions for MA organizations and Part D sponsors' marketing and communications chapter have included instructions for the required use of exit disclaimers, notifying users when clicking a link on the website would open or take a user to a third-party website. This long-standing requirement was established in the interest of beneficiary protection as well as the integrity of the MA and Part D programs when the internet was still in its early stages. In the January 2021 Final Rule, CMS codified these longstanding requirements for MA organization and Part D sponsor websites in §§ 422.2265(a)(1)(ii) and 423.2265(a)(1)(ii). In these regulatory provisions, CMS indicated that a plan's website must notify users that they are leaving the plan's Medicare website when the users click on a link that leads outside of the plan, such as to a first-tier or downstream entity or a third-party vendor.
As the MA and Part D programs have developed and matured, so have the use of exit disclaimers on websites. Exit disclaimers are now a longstanding and widely accepted practice to clearly notify users when they are leaving an organization's website and accessing third-party content. Organizations routinely use them to reduce potential liability, avoid the appearance of endorsing third-party content, and clearly communicate when users are leaving the organization's controlled environment. Privacy and compliance resources (for example, business websites
[
100
]
indicating common and best practices in the execution of financial business), recognize exit disclaimers as a best practice for promoting transparency, managing user expectations, and clarifying that organizations are not responsible for third-party content. Likewise, CMS understands that financial institutions frequently include third-party website disclaimers that expressly state they are not responsible for the security, accuracy, availability, malware, viruses, or copyright compliance of external websites.
Since the use of exit disclaimers has become a common practice, and in keeping with
Executive Order 14192
Unleashing Prosperity Through Deregulation, which appeared in the
Federal Register
on February 6, 2025 (
90 FR 9065
), CMS is proposing to remove the regulatory language found at §§ 422.2265(a)(1)(ii) and 423.2265(a)(1)(ii). Given the widespread use of exit disclaimers across both the public and private sectors, CMS anticipates that MA organizations and Part D sponsors will continue to use exit disclaimers on their websites when directing users to external websites beyond the organization's or sponsor's control.
We invite comments on this proposal.
C. Updating Agent and Broker Compensation and Oversight and Modifications To Streamline and Reduce Marketing Requirements (§§ 422.2260, 422.2271, 422.2272, 422.2274, 423.2260, 423.2271, 423.2272, and 423.2274)
CMS is proposing to make changes to its regulations governing agent and broker compensation and oversight, and training and testing requirements. CMS is also proposing to make modifications to streamline and reduce certain marketing requirements. Section 1851(h) of the Act governs the approval of marketing material and application forms for Medicare Advantage organizations. Section 1860D-1(b)(1)(B)(vi) of the Act directs that the Secretary use rules similar to and coordinated with the MA rules at section 1851(h). Sections 1851(j)(2)(D) and 1860D-4(l) of the Act require that CMS create limitations and guidelines to ensure that the use of compensation creates incentives for agents and brokers to enroll individuals in the MA plan or Part D plan that is intended to best meet their health care needs. Sections 1851(j)(2)(E) and 1860D-4(l) of the Act also require that CMS establish limitations on MA organizations and Part D sponsors using agents, brokers, and other third parties that have not completed an initial training and testing program and an annual retraining and testing program. In addition, Section 1856(b)(1) provides for the Secretary to establish by regulations and other standards to carry out other parts of the Statute regarding the Medicare + Choice (Medicare Advantage) program. Furthermore, Section 1860(D)-12(f)(1) provides that the Secretary may periodically review the standards under the section and revise the standards if the Secretary determines revisions are appropriate.
CMS is proposing changes to its regulations governing agent and broker compensation and oversight to take into consideration the ruling from the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Texas in

v.
HHS

In this proposed rule, CMS is proposing to establish a transparent framework for agent and broker compensation requirements better suited to the current, more established MA and Part D markets. These proposed changes would move away from regulatory limits on MA and Part D compensation and instead move towards emphasizing data transparency and enforceable guardrails.
Agents and brokers are an integral part of the MA and Part D industries, helping millions of Medicare beneficiaries learn about and enroll in Medicare Advantage and Medicare Prescription Drug Plans (PDPs) by providing expert guidance on plan options in their local area, while assisting with everything from comparing costs and coverage to applying for financial assistance. In September 2008, CMS published the Revisions to the Medicare Advantage and Prescription Drug Benefit Programs interim final rule (
73 FR 54237
), hereafter referred to as the “September 2008 interim final rule”. This was CMS's first regulation to establish requirements for agent and broker compensation, which included compensation limitations, training and testing, and other safeguards. In that rulemaking, CMS noted that these reforms addressed concerns that the previously unregulated compensation structure resulted in financial incentives for agents and brokers to only market and enroll beneficiaries in specific plans
(
printed page 76421)
and not others due to larger commissions. The larger commissions potentially resulted in beneficiaries being directed toward plans that were not the best suited to meet their health care needs.
In the September 2008 interim final rule, CMS noted that “[d]epending on the circumstances, agent and broker relationships can be problematic under the Federal anti-kickback statute if they involve, by way of example only, compensation in excess of fair market value (FMV), compensation structures tied to the health status of the beneficiary (for example, cherry-picking), or compensation that varies based on the attainment of certain enrollment targets.” (
73 FR 54239
). These and other fraud and abuse risks existed and continue to exist among the relationships between MA organizations, Part D sponsors, and third-party marketing organizations (TPMOs), including agents, and brokers. CMS noted in the September 2008 interim final rule that the HHS Office of the Inspector General (OIG) advisory opinion process was available to parties seeking OIG's opinion as to the legality of a particular arrangement. That advisory opinion process remains available and can be found on the OIG's website at
http://oig.hhs.gov/​fraud/​advisoryopinions.html
.
In the final rule “Medicare Program; Changes to the Medicare Advantage and the Medicare Prescription Drug Benefit Program for Contract Year 2024-Remaining Provisions and Contract Year 2025 Policy and Technical Changes to the Medicare Advantage Program, Medicare Prescription Drug Benefit Program, Medicare Cost Plan Program, and Programs of All-Inclusive Care for the Elderly (PACE)” which appeared in the
Federal Register
on April 23, 2024, (
89 FR 30448
), hereafter referred to as the “April 2024 final rule,” CMS significantly modified the regulations governing agent and broker compensation paid by MA organizations and Part D sponsors. In the April 2024 final rule, CMS made changes to compensation requirements to address new issues in the marketplace. In that rule, we explained that the regulatory changes were prompted in part because CMS observed that there was an increase in additional payments to agents and brokers characterized as administrative payments. We noted in the April 2024 final rule that CMS had observed web-based advertisements for agents and brokers to work with, or sell, particular plans where the agents and brokers were offered bonuses and perks, such as trips and extra cash framed as allowable administrative add-ons in exchange for enrollments. CMS also noted the increase in complaints from a host of different organizations, including state partners, beneficiary advocacy organizations, and MA organizations, among others. A common theme of these complaints was that agents and brokers were being paid in excess of the maximum enrollment-based compensation allowed under the current regulation under the guise that the additional payments were for administrative services. We also noted beneficiary complaints accusing agents and brokers of enrolling them without their consent, as well as complaints that after enrollment, beneficiaries found the plan's benefits, such as provider networks, did not align with what the beneficiary was told by the agent or broker.
The April 2024 final rule limited MA organizations and Part D sponsors, as well as TPMOs with which they contract (such as Field Marketing Organizations (FMOs)), from structuring payments to agents and brokers that allowed for separate payments that circumvented compensation caps. CMS also noted that the amounts in these separate payments appeared to be increasing. In that final rule, at a high level, CMS finalized four major changes related to agent and broker compensation: (1) establishing a flat compensation rate versus a maximum FMV amount; (2) including administrative payments, as defined under §§ 422.2274(e) and 423.2274(e), as a part of compensation; (3) increasing compensation FMV to account for the removal of administrative payments; and (4) prohibiting MA organizations and Part D sponsors from entering into contract terms with an agent, broker, or other TPMO, that have a direct or indirect effect of creating an incentive that would reasonably be expected to inhibit an agent or broker's ability to objectively assess and recommend which plan best fits the health care needs of a beneficiary. At the time, CMS believed that the impact of these changes would better align with the statutory requirements to ensure that the use of compensation creates incentives for agents and brokers to enroll individuals in the plan that best fits a beneficiary's health care needs.

Following the court's granting of summary judgment, CMS reverted to the compensation

requirements within §§ 422.2274 and 423.2274 which had applied prior to the April 2024 final rule; those requirements limit compensation payments to no more than the CMS-defined FMV and provide that administrative payments may not exceed the value of those services in the marketplace. However, CMS notes that the regulations finalized in the April 2024 final rule are still reflected in the CFR, even though those vacated provisions are not operative.
Since publication of the April 2024 final rule, CMS has observed additional market changes in how compensation is being used. In discussions with various state insurance commissioners, reviews of notices issued by states, agent and broker trade groups, and information provided by MA organizations, CMS has been made aware that some MA organizations and Part D sponsors have elected to stop paying initial and/or renewal compensation for some products. This has created a new market force for CMS to consider. Whereas historically the concern and regulatory focus have been on excessive compensation influencing an agent or broker's decision as to what MA or Part D plan to enroll a beneficiary, this newly emerging trend may have the opposite effect. That is, an MA organization or Part D sponsor could use a lack of compensation as a potential tactic to reduce enrollments into a given plan option, by making that option less desirable to be sold by an agent or broker as compared to the organization's other plan offerings. Under the currently applicable regulatory requirements, it is the MA organization's or Part D sponsor's decision on whether to use agents and brokers to sell their products, whether or not to pay compensation to such agents and brokers, and how much they will pay, provided that such compensation conforms with CMS's regulatory requirements, does not violate the Federal anti-kickback statute, and complies with all other applicable requirements, including all fraud and abuse laws. CMS wants to be clear that under the new requirements in this proposed rule, these decisions would remain with MA organizations and Part D sponsors, provided that any compensation offered to agents and brokers is not determined to be a base compensation outlier for enrolling beneficiaries into their plans and, moreover, that such compensation does not violate the Federal anti-kickback statute and otherwise complies with all applicable statutes, regulations, and guidance. CMS notes that the relationships between MA organizations, Part D sponsors, and TPMOs, including agents and brokers, regarding compensation could still violate the Federal anti-kickback statute or other applicable laws and regulations, depending on the facts and circumstances.
To better align with the statute, ensure current regulations are in the best interest of the program, reflect industry practices, reduce regulatory duplication, and most importantly to ensure appropriate beneficiary safeguards, CMS is proposing changes, modifications, and re-designations of requirements currently at §§ 422.2260, 422.2272, 422.2274, 423.2260, 423.2272, and 423.2274. To better segment the various requirements, CMS is also proposing the creation of new §§ 422.2271 and 423.2271 where many of the current requirements in §§ 422.2272, 422.2274, 423.2272, and 423.2274 will be redesignated. CMS is also proposing to relocate and update existing definitions and to establish new definitions under §§ 422.2260 and 423.2260.
1. Updating Definitions Under §§ 422.2260 and 423.2260
First, CMS is proposing to move the definitions at §§ 422.2274(a) and 423.2274(a) to §§ 422.2260 and 423.2260. Currently, definitions for Subpart V are split between §§ 422.2260 and 423.2260 and 422.2274(a) and 423.2274(a). CMS believes consolidating definitions for Subpart V within §§ 422.2260 and 423.2260 will streamline CMS's regulations. In this move, CMS proposes to redesignate, with minor conforming changes, the definitions for “initial enrollment year,” “like plan type,” “plan year and enrollment year,” “renewal year,” and “unlike plan type.” CMS is proposing to modify the definitions of “compensation” and “fair market value” and add a definition for “base compensation outlier.” Following are CMS's specific proposals for the definition of “compensation,” “fair market value,” and “base compensation outlier.”
a. Updating the “Compensation” Definition
CMS currently defines “compensation,” at §§ 422.2274(a) and 423.2274(a), to include “monetary or non-monetary remuneration of any kind relating to the sale, renewal, or services related to a plan or product offered by an MA organization . . .” The existing definition in §§ 422.2274(a) and 423.2274(a) further provides examples of compensation (for example, bonuses, gifts, etc.), as well as the regulatory updates to compensation from CY 2024 to CY 2025. As previously noted, following the court's summary judgment, CMS reverted to the compensation requirements within §§ 422.2274 and 423.2274 that were in effect prior to the April 2024 final rule. Taking into consideration the court's ruling and to align with industry trends, CMS is now proposing to redefine “compensation.” CMS is proposing to retain the current language regarding monetary or non-monetary remuneration for the new compensation definition but is proposing to eliminate regulatory language concerning CY 2024 and CY 2025 compensation, as well as the phrase “or services related to” which was added in the April 2024 final rule. CMS is proposing to further distinguish compensation into two types, base compensation and supplemental compensation, creating the two sub-definitions of compensation types under new paragraphs (1) and (2) at §§ 422.2260 and 423.2260, both of which must be Fair Market Value. Under new paragraph (1), CMS proposes to define “base compensation” and under paragraph (2), CMS proposes to define “supplemental compensation.”
[
112
]
CMS proposes to define “base compensation” as “any monetary remuneration for the actual initial or renewal enrollment, as referenced in §§ 422.2274(a) and 423.2274(a).” In other words, base compensation is an amount paid for each enrollment into a MA or Part D plan by an agent or broker. CMS proposes to define “supplemental compensation” as “any monetary or non-monetary remuneration, above and beyond base compensation, related to the sale and renewal of a plan or product offered by an MA organization [Part D sponsor], such as bonuses, gifts, prizes or awards. Supplemental compensation is an additional incentive offered by an MA organization or Part D sponsor to agents and brokers, often tied to a performance metric. For example, an MA organization may provide supplemental compensation in the form of a bonus to agents who have a renewal retention rate of 90 percent, or a bonus based on enrollee satisfaction survey results.
b. Updating the “Fair Market Value” Definition
Next, CMS is proposing to modify the “fair market value” definition, currently defined at §§ 422.2274(a) and
(
printed page 76423)
423.2274(a). The term “fair market value” has been used since the origination of compensation requirements in 2008. “Fair market value” is currently defined as what CMS has determined could reasonably be expected to be paid for an enrollment or continued enrollment into an MA or Part D plan. Since 2008, CMS has determined a FMV maximum each year. Taking into consideration the court's ruling and industry trends, CMS is proposing to modify this definition to no longer establish a maximum FMV for compensation. In developing the modified proposed definition, CMS looked at concepts in existing definitions of fair market value and general market value under
42 CFR 411.351
. CMS adapted the concepts found in these two definitions to re-define FMV in such a way that ensures the compensation being paid to an agent or broker reflects normal market forces, rather than favoritism, coercion, or hidden incentives, and that any such payments be based on prevailing market rates for comparable services.
CMS believes an updated definition is necessary given the changes in compensation, as outlined in this preamble, and to more closely align the MA and Part D programs with how agents and brokers are compensated in the commercial market, as well as compensation associated with assisting consumers with enrollment in Qualified Health Plans (QHPs) through the Federally Facilitated Exchanges (FFEs). Under this new FMV definition, CMS is proposing to eliminate the maximum allowable compensation structure under the current FMV definition and is proposing the updated FMV definition to state that FMV means the compensation amount (which includes base and supplemental compensation) that would be paid to a licensed insurance agent or broker at the time the parties enter into an arrangement, as the result of bona fide bargaining between well-informed parties acting at arm's length and under comparable market conditions. Furthermore, the proposed fair market value definition applies to compensation, both base compensation and supplemental compensation, including monetary and non-monetary remuneration. Although CMS is proposing an outlier review only for base compensation, supplemental compensation must also meet the proposed fair market value standard, including consistency with prevailing market rates for comparable services. The absence of a supplemental compensation outlier methodology does not exempt supplemental compensation from that standard. As previously noted, all compensation arrangements must not violate the Federal anti-kickback statute and must comply with other applicable laws and regulations.
This proposed definition would also require that compensation be consistent with prevailing market rates for comparable services and must not reflect consideration of any business generated between the parties, except as expressly permitted by applicable law and regulation. As previously mentioned, in developing this new proposed definition, CMS utilized the concept of “bona fide bargaining between well-informed parties acting at arm's length,” found in the definition of “general market value” under § 411.351. Although this definition of general market value pertains to financial relationships between physicians and entities furnishing designated health services, CMS believes that the way it frames a market value standard is equally appropriate for CMS's updated FMV definition. In proposing this updated definition, CMS sought to ensure that the resulting compensation rates reflect typical market forces and are not influenced by parties working in tandem to artificially inflate values for their mutual benefit.
Under this proposal, MA organizations and Part D sponsors would be permitted to set their own compensation amounts for initial and renewal enrollments, provided they fall within the applicable newly proposed definitions and guardrails outlined as a part of this proposed rule. CMS also notes that, based on research including discussions with MA organizations and Part D sponsors, state regulators, and agent and broker trade groups, these proposed changes better align with industry standards in other insurance markets where compensation caps are not typically utilized. In fact, as previously noted, in drafting this proposal, CMS looked at how agents and brokers who assist consumers with enrollment in QHPs offered through the FFEs are compensated. Under this program, CMS regulations do not cap the compensation these agents and brokers receive, though under
45 CFR 156.200(f)
, a QHP issuer must pay the same agent and broker compensation for QHPs offered through an FFE that the QHP issuer pays for similar health plans offered outside of the exchange.
CMS originally implemented FMV caps in 2008, at a time when there were concerns that compensation rates would dramatically increase without a limit in place, which could result in problematic behaviors by some agents and brokers, ultimately leading to enrollments that did not best meet a beneficiary's health care needs. As previously noted, CMS has heard more recently from some state Departments of Insurance that MA organizations and Part D sponsors have stopped paying compensation for enrollment in some products. MA organizations and Part D sponsors stop paying compensation for various reasons which may include limiting financial losses in certain plans, or attempting to minimize the number of new enrollees in particular plans to ensure adequate access is available to current members or because an MA organization or Part D sponsor may not have the administrative capabilities to provide services to a significant number of additional enrollees. Considering the rise of some MA organizations and Part D sponsors not offering any enrollment compensation to agents and brokers for enrollments into certain plans, CMS is now concerned that agents and brokers will avoid enrolling beneficiaries into these plans.
In the release of the Contract Year 2027 Plan Benefit Package and Bid Pricing Tool Software and Related Technical Bidding Guidance for Employer/Union-Only Group Waiver Plan, CMS reminded MA organizations of the option to request an enrollment capacity limit for a given plan benefit package as part of the bid submission process. Additionally, in this proposed rule at section III.G, CMS is proposing to codify a process for how CMS will review enrollment capacity limits. In addition, CMS is proposing a minimum threshold for what would be accepted as part of the bid. CMS believes this proposed rule, if finalized, may reduce the need of MA organizations and Part D sponsors to try to limit enrollment in particular plans by not paying compensation.
Taking into consideration the court's ruling, as well as how the broader industry uses and pays compensation, CMS also considered different alternatives for compensation. CMS considered continuing with the existing methodology which sets an FMV ceiling for compensation, adjusted each year based on MA and Part D growth factors. CMS also considered providing plans with complete flexibility to set their compensation rates, with no provision for CMS to analyze or address compensation outliers, resulting in the market determining compensation amounts without oversight to ensure compensation amounts do not result in the steerage of beneficiaries into specific plans. CMS also considered requiring MA organizations and Part D sponsors to pay the same base compensation amount across all product lines,
(
printed page 76424)
resulting in one base compensation rate for each contract, regardless of the type of product being sold. CMS believes this latter option would provide the least amount of flexibility for MA organizations and Part D sponsors.
We solicit comments on the proposed changes to compensation, the alternatives described earlier that CMS has also considered, as well as other ideas that interested stakeholders may have for the best way to ensure the use of compensation creates incentives for agents and brokers to enroll Medicare beneficiaries into the health plan that best meets their needs.
c. Defining “Base Compensation Outliers”
CMS is proposing to add a definition for a base compensation outlier at §§ 422.2260 and 423.2260. Similar to concerns expressed in the past when FMV was originally calculated, CMS is concerned that certain MA organizations or Part D sponsors paying significantly more than other MA organizations or Part D sponsors could have an undue influence on agent and broker behavior. As noted previously, CMS is proposing to allow the market to dictate an acceptable level of base compensation. However, CMS wants to guard against an MA organization or Part D sponsor offering a level of compensation so high that it could negatively influence an agent or broker's objectivity.
CMS is proposing that the base compensation outlier be defined as any base compensation amounts, submitted to CMS by any MA organizations and Part D sponsors to CMS, pursuant §§ 422.2271(b)(3)(ii) and 423.2271(b)(3)(ii) that are above the 3rd quartile, as calculated in a distribution, using a box plot method and determined by CMS pursuant §§ 422.2274(b) and 423.2274(b). Base compensation outliers will be determined using all base compensation amounts submitted by all MA organizations and Part D Sponsors.
[
113
]
Box plots are a graphical distribution of data split into quartiles, with the median at the center and lower and upper quartiles at the 25th and 75th percentiles. A box plot has “fences” developed using the interquartile range, which is calculated as Q3-Q1. Any point beyond an inner fence is considered a mild outlier. Any points beyond an outer fence are considered extreme outliers.
If finalized, MA and Part D outlier analyses would be calculated separately.
2. Proposed Updates to §§ 422.2272 and 422.2274 Under New 422.2271

b. Requirements Under New §§ 422.2271(b) and 423.2271(b)
As noted previously, CMS is proposing a new §§ 422.2271(b) and 423.2271(b) titled “MA [Part D] reporting requirements.” This proposed section will include provisions that require MA organizations and Part D sponsors to report specific information to CMS.
Current regulations at §§ 422.2272(d) and 423.2272(d) require MA organizations and Part D sponsors to report terminations of agents or brokers to the State in which the agent or broker is appointed, and the reason for termination as required by State law. CMS believes that all agent or broker terminations based on Federal law, CMS regulations, or relevant State laws should be reported to CMS. In addition, since agent and broker licensure is a state function, states also need to know of all agent and broker violations of Federal law, CMS regulations, or relevant State laws. To ensure both CMS and states receive information regarding these agent and broker terminations, CMS is proposing to consolidate the existing termination reporting requirements under new requirements at §§ 422.2271(b)(1) and 423.2271(b)(1) and include the requirement to report to both CMS and the applicable state. CMS believes that MA organizations and Part D sponsors reporting for cause terminations to CMS itself will strengthen CMS's ability to provide greater oversight over inappropriate marketing activities and help protect beneficiaries from harm. Specifically, MA organizations and Part D sponsors reporting these terminations within 15 days will allow CMS to track these terminations in real time and will strengthen CMS's ability to identify bad actors. Current regulations require that agents and brokers be trained on the plan products and any details specific to each plan product they intend to sell. CMS believes that training and testing on the nuances of cost sharing, benefits, and service areas for each individual plan is unnecessary since the agents and brokers have that information readily available when selling a plan. Additionally, it is in the best interest of the MA organization or Part D sponsor to ensure that an agent or broker is appropriately trained on unique plan information, regardless of regulatory requirements. This proposal will significantly reduce the burden on all agents, brokers, MA organizations, and Part D sponsors.
CMS is also proposing, under new §§ 422.2271(c)(2)(iii) and 423.2271(c)(2)(iii), to add a provision permitting MA organizations and Part D sponsors to accept third-party training and testing, or training and testing from another MA organization or Part D sponsor, provided they meet the requirements in (c)(2)(i) and (ii) of this section. Provided MA organizations and Part D sponsors use this option, these proposed updates to the training and testing requirements should result in a significant burden reduction for agents, brokers, TPMOs, MA organizations, and Part D sponsors, while still maintaining appropriate beneficiary protections and safeguards.
CMS is also proposing to move with slight modifications the current requirements at §§ 422.2274(c)(8) and 423.2274(c)(8), to new §§ 422.2271(c)(3) and 423.2271(c)(3). The current requirements state that marketing consulting fees cannot be charged to Medicare beneficiaries when considering enrollment into an MA or Part D plan. CMS views agents and brokers selling MA or Part D plans as an extension of the MA organization or Part D sponsor. As such, it is CMS's policy to ensure beneficiaries receive information and enrollment services provided by an MA organization or Part D sponsor without having to pay. At the same time, CMS has been made aware that some states have separate licenses, for example for health care consulting, that fall outside of the license required to be an agent or broker (or “producer” in state terms). Under new §§ 422.2271(c)(3) and 423.2271(c)(3), CMS is proposing to maintain the position that beneficiaries should not be charged fees for information regarding Medicare products being sold by an agent, broker or TPMO. However, CMS does not intend to interfere with state laws that permit fees to be paid under a separate license, such as a health care consultant license, which are outside of CMS's purview as it applies to agent and broker oversight.
CMS is proposing to modify the new §§ 422.2271(c)(3) and 423.2271(c)(3) to say that fees may not be charged to the beneficiary, by an agent, broker or TPMO, when the agent, broker or TPMO is operating under a health insurance license under State law. By limiting CMS's requirement to health insurance licenses, CMS continues to protect beneficiaries, while not interfering with State laws governing health consultant licenses. Moreover, the proposed requirement eliminates the ambiguity associated with what constitutes “marketing consulting” fees, under the current definition.

d. Requirements Proposed To Be Removed
CMS is also proposing to remove redundancy from existing requirements. Currently, requirements at §§ 422.2274(b)(3) and 423.2274(b)(3) state that agents and brokers who represent plans must “secure and document a Scope of Appointment prior to meeting with potential enrollees.” Additionally, §§ 422.2274(c)(9)(ii) and 423.2274(c)(9)(ii) require the establishment and maintenance of a system for confirming that agents and brokers complete the scope of appointment (SOA) for all marketing appointments (including telephonic and walk-in). These requirements are largely duplicative of the requirements in §§ 422.2264(c)(3)(i) and 423.2264(c)(3)(i), which currently require an agreed upon and recorded SOA. Therefore, CMS proposes to remove the duplicative and unnecessary SOA requirements currently at §§ 422.2274(b)(3), 422.2274(c)(9)(ii), 423.2274(b)(3), and 423.2274(c)(9)(ii) since the requirement to establish and maintain a system for confirming agents and brokers complete the SOA for all marketing appointments is already in regulation at §§ 422.2264(c)(3)(i) and 423.2264(c)(3)(i). In addition, the removal of these regulations will streamline requirements in line with
E.O. 14192
, Unleashing Prosperity Through Deregulation.
CMS is also proposing to remove §§ 422.2274(c)(6) and 423.2274(c)(6), which require MA organizations and Part D sponsors to have in place, on an annual basis, a full compensation structure by October 1st for the following plan year. CMS is proposing to remove these provisions to align with the overall proposed changes in the regulation, including the proposed requirement at §§ 422.2271(b)(3)(ii) and (iii) and 423.2271(b)(3)(ii) and (iii) to require MA organizations and Part D sponsors to provide actual base and supplemental compensation amounts defined by the proposed definitions under §§ 422.2260 and 423.2260. CMS believes the proposed changes to agent and broker compensation requirements, which include the submission of actual compensation data by the last Friday in July, supersedes the need for a full compensation structure in place by October 1st. Removing these requirements is also in line with
E.O. 14192
, Unleashing Prosperity Through Deregulation.
Next, CMS is also proposing to remove the requirement at §§ 422.2274(c)(7) and 423.2274(c)(7), which requires MA organizations and Part D sponsors to oversee their FDRs and their submission of agent and broker marketing materials to HPMS. Currently, at §§ 422.2261(a) and 423.2261(a), CMS requires MA organizations and Part D sponsors to submit marketing materials into HPMS. In addition, §§ 422.2261(a)(2) and 423.2261(a)(2) further specify that marketing materials developed by TPMOs must also be submitted into HPMS. Given the duplicative nature of these requirements, CMS is proposing to remove §§ 422.2274(c)(7) and 423.2274(c)(7), in line with
E.O. 14192
, Unleashing Prosperity Through Deregulation.
CMS is also proposing to remove requirements at §§ 422.2272(b), 422.2274(c)(9)(i), 423.2272(b), and 423.2274(c)(9)(i). At §§ 422.2272(b), and 423.2272(b), current requirements state that, in marketing, MA organizations and Part D sponsors must “establish and maintain a system for confirming that enrolled beneficiaries have, in fact, enrolled in the MA plan, and understand the rules applicable under the plan.” Similarly, at §§ 422.2274(c)(9)(i) and 423.2274(c)(9)(i), CMS requires that MA organizations and Part D sponsors, through their oversight of FDRs, ensure
(
printed page 76429)
that agents and brokers, “establish and maintain a system for confirming” that “beneficiaries enrolled by agents or brokers understand the product, including the rules applicable under the plan.” CMS believes these requirements are largely duplicative with other requirements that already exist in regulations, both for ensuring the beneficiary understands the rules applicable under the plan, and for establishing and maintaining a system to confirm a beneficiary's enrollment in a plan. For example, CMS requires the pre-enrollment checklist (PECL) at §§ 422.2267(e)(4) and 423.2267(e)(4) which requires plans to provide a standardized communications material to prospective enrollees so that enrollees understand important plan benefits and rules. For telephonic enrollments, the contents of the PECL must be reviewed with the prospective enrollee prior to the completion of the enrollment. The PECL requires references to information on the evidence of coverage (EOC), provider directory, pharmacy directory, formulary, premiums, copayments, coinsurance, emergency and urgent coverage, plan-type rules and the effect on current coverage. CMS believes that this checklist, which must be reviewed with prospective enrollees prior to the completion of enrollment, sufficiently covers what a beneficiary needs to understand prior to enrolling with a plan.
Furthermore, other required materials at §§ 422.2267 and 423.2267 ensure that documents, such as the enrollment notice, EOC, and the provider directory, are sent to new enrollees within required timeframes. These documents clearly provide beneficiaries with sufficient information about their enrollment in a plan. CMS notes that there are also various beneficiary protections in place, including the possibility of providing special enrollment periods when appropriate, or, if warranted, processing a retrospective enrollment to place the beneficiary back into their prior coverage, if a beneficiary makes an adverse enrollment decision based on misrepresentation or otherwise non-compliant sales tactics.
Similarly, CMS is proposing to remove the requirement at §§ 422.2274(c)(12) and 423.2274(c)(12), which requires that plans, in their oversight of their FDRs, ensure that, prior to an enrollment, CMS's required questions and topics regarding beneficiary needs in a health plan choice are fully discussed. CMS believes this requirement duplicates the PECL requirement at §§ 422.2267(e)(4) and 423.2267(e)(4), which requires the PECL to be presented to enrollees before enrollment so prospective enrollees understand plan rules, including provider directories, premiums, copayments, effect on current coverage as well as other topics. Furthermore, CMS believes the proposed MA organization and Part D sponsor oversight requirements in §§ 422.2271 and 423.2271 will provide additional protections to beneficiaries in that MA organizations and Part D sponsors will ensure enrollees are fully informed of the details regarding their enrollment into an MA or Part D plan. Therefore, having both requirements, that is to cover what is required under §§ 422.2274(c)(12) and 423.2274(c)(12), as well as being required to provide the PECL or read its content may be unnecessary and confusing for agents, brokers, and beneficiaries alike. Removing these duplicative requirements is also in line with
E.O. 14192
, Unleashing Prosperity Through Deregulation.
CMS is proposing to remove §§ 422.2274(c)(13) and 423.2274(c)(13). These provisions currently require MA organizations and Part D sponsors to ensure that, beginning with contract year 2025, no provision of a contract with an agent, broker, or other TPMO has a direct or indirect effect of creating an incentive that would reasonably be expected to inhibit an agent or broker's ability to objectively assess and recommend which plan best fits the health care needs of a beneficiary. CMS is proposing to remove this requirement in light of the court's ruling as detailed previously.
CMS is proposing to remove §§ 422.2274(g)(1), 422.2274(g)(2)(i), 423.2274(g)(1), and 423.2274(g)(2)(i). Sections 422.2274(g)(1) and 423.2274(g)(1) require that MA organizations and Part D sponsors, when doing business with a TPMO, either directly or indirectly through an FDR, when a TPMO is not an FDR, ensure that the TPMO adheres to applicable MA organizations' and Part D sponsors' requirements. CMS is proposing to remove this requirement because it is duplicative and unnecessary. CMS's definition of TPMO at §§ 422.2260 and 423.2260 “means organizations and individuals, including independent agents and brokers, who are compensated to perform lead generation, marketing, sales, and enrollment related functions as a part of the chain of enrollment (the steps taken by a beneficiary from becoming aware of an MA [Part D] plan or plans to making an enrollment decision). TPMOs may be a first tier, downstream or related entity (FDRs), as defined under § 422.2, but may also be entities that are not FDRs but provide services to an MA [Part D] plan or an MA [Part D] plan's FDR.” This definition is inclusive of both entities that are and are not FDRs and is referenced throughout these requirements. Therefore, MA organizations and Part D sponsors are already required to ensure that TPMOs they directly or indirectly contract with adhere to all MA and Part D requirements. Additionally, this language is also reiterated in newly proposed requirements in the introductory paragraphs §§ 422.2271 and 423.2271, which state that “MA organizations [Part D sponsors] are responsible for the actions of their first tier, downstream, related entities (FDRs) and TPMOs, that represent the MA organization [Part D sponsor] and must ensure the following requirements in paragraphs (a) through (c) of the section are met.” Removing these requirements is also in line with
E.O. 14192
, Unleashing Prosperity Through Deregulation.
Regulations at §§ 422.2274(g)(2)(i) and 423.2274(g)(2)(i) require FDRs and TMPOs to disclose subcontracted relationships used for marketing, lead generation, and enrollment to the MA organizations and Part D sponsors. CMS finalized this requirement in “Medicare Program; Contract Year 2023 Policy and Technical Changes to the Medicare Advantage and Medicare Prescription Drug Benefit Programs; Policy and Regulatory Revisions in Response to the COVID-19 Public Health Emergency; Additional Policy and Regulatory Revisions in Response to the COVID-19 Public Health Emergency” which appeared in the

In addition, the subcontracting arrangements, including disclosure requirements, entered into between MA organizations and Part D
