e. Modified Compensation Requirements for Existing §§ 422.2274 and 423.2274
As previously noted, compensation requirements were initially implemented in the September 2008 interim final rule. Since 2008, there have been significant changes in how MA organizations and Part D sponsors market and enroll Medicare beneficiaries into their Part C and Part D plans. Prior to the initial compensation requirements, including FMV, in the September 2008 interim final rule, MA organizations were paying excessively high compensation, potentially resulting in beneficiaries being enrolled in a plan based on compensation and not based on the plan best met the beneficiary's health care needs. Except for the changes in compensation for CY 2025, which were subsequently vacated by court order, CMS's policies governing compensation for agents and brokers in the MA and Part D programs have largely been unchanged, even though industry practices have changed substantially and the MA and Part D programs have matured.
In proposing new compensation regulations, CMS reviewed how compensation is treated for agent-assisted QHP enrollments. CMS also reached out to State Insurance Commissions and MA organizations for information regarding commercial plans and specific payment amounts for Medicare health plans. For agent-assisted QHP enrollments, CMS does not set compensation rates; rather, it generally allows the market to determine the value of the services provided by agents and brokers.
[
121
]
QHP issuers determine how much compensation will be paid to agents and brokers for each consumer enrollment through the FFEs. For QHP issuers, CMS generally allows the market to determine compensation rates.
[
122
]
CMS does not regulate other payments, such as administrative payments or override payments, instead letting the market also drive the value of those services. CMS, in discussions with State Departments of Insurance, was also informed that states generally do not set compensation rates for commercial products. As with the compensation QHP issuers offer to agents and brokers who assist consumers with enrollment in coverage through the FFEs, states let the marketplace determine the value of an enrollment in a commercial health plan.
CMS also sought specific compensation data from a small sampling of MA organizations based on various sizes and service areas for contract year 2026. This effort was undertaken to obtain more specific data on how much MA organizations pay and to whom they pay compensation. CMS's request was completely voluntary, with more than half of the MA organizations asked choosing to participate. CMS requested MA organizations provide contract year 2026 actual compensation payment amounts at the plan level, if different rates were paid. Furthermore, CMS requested specific amounts if MA organizations paid different amounts based on other factors including specific agents/agencies or types of products sold (for example, PPO vs. HMO). CMS reviewed data collected from MA organizations and observed a range of compensation structures, including uniform compensation rates throughout the year, midyear changes to $0 compensation, and differing compensation rates by plan type. In some contracts, full compensation was paid for D-SNP enrollments while $0 compensation applied to standard HMO or PPO enrollments under the same contract. CMS believes the variability observed across organizations and contracts could result in differing financial incentives depending on the product being recommended and, in some circumstances, could raise concerns about the potential for compensation differences to influence agent and broker recommendations. CMS believes these observations provide additional support for the proposal, discussed later in this section, to require consistent compensation for like product lines (for example, HMO) across contracts, which could help reduce the potential influence of compensation differences on recommendations.
CMS is proposing to modify the introductory paragraph of current §§ 422.2274 and 423.2274 to align with the proposed changes noted later. The current introductory paragraph refers to the requirements in paragraphs (a) through (f), identifying which paragraphs are applicable to MA organizations and Part D sponsors who use agents and brokers to sell their plans and to MA organizations and Part D sponsors who make payments to third parties. CMS is proposing to revise the introductory paragraph to accurately reflect the proposed revisions to §§ 422.2274 and 423.2274.
Currently, the regulations at §§ 422.2274(d) and 423.2274(d) state that MA organizations and Part D sponsors must ensure they meet the requirements in paragraphs (d)(1) through (5), which address general rules and types of compensation, in order to pay compensation and that the compensation requirements only apply to independent agents and brokers. CMS proposes to redesignate §§ 422.2274(d) and 423.2274(d), titled “compensation
(
printed page 76431)
requirements” as §§ 422.2274(a) and 423.2274(a) to align with our other proposals. CMS is also proposing to make modifications to the introductory paragraph at §§ 422.2274(a) and 423.2274(a), which currently states that if MA organizations and Part D sponsors use agents and brokers paragraphs (a) through (e) must be met. CMS is proposing to modify the language to state that MA organizations and Part D sponsors must comply with the requirements in paragraphs (1)-(8) of §§ 422.2274(a) and 423.2274(a) in paying and recovering compensation, as that more accurately reflects the specific requirements in new proposed paragraphs (1)-(8), further described later.
CMS is proposing to remove in their entirety the requirements, in §§ 422.2274(d)(1)(i) and 423.2274(d)(1)(i), that MA organizations and Part D sponsors may only pay agents or brokers who meet certain requirements. CMS is proposing at §§ 422.2271(c) and 423.2271(c) that MA organizations and Part D sponsors must ensure agents and brokers meet specified requirements. CMS believes these new proposed requirements cover the current language at §§ 422.2274(d)(1)(i) and 423.2274(d)(1)(i).
Although vacated by the court, current regulations at §§ 422.2274(d)(1)(ii) and 423.2274(d)(1)(ii) state that, beginning in contract year 2025 MA organizations and Part D sponsors would be limited to amounts outlined in this section. Based on the court's ruling, CMS is proposing to remove §§ 422.2274(d)(1)(ii) and 423.2274(d)(1)(ii). Additionally, CMS is proposing to redesignate §§ 422.2274(d)(1)(iv) and 423.2274(d)(1)(iv) to §§ 422.2274(a)(6) and 423.2274(a)(6).
Current regulations at §§ 422.2274(d)(1)(iii)-(iv) and 423.2274(d)(1)(iii)-(iv) state that MA organizations and Part D sponsors may determine their payment schedule and may only pay compensation for the number of months a beneficiary is enrolled in the plan. CMS is proposing to redesignate §§ 422.2274(d)(1)(iii) and 423.2274(d)(1)(iii) to §§ 422.2274(a)(2) and 423.2274(a)(2) with clarifying edits. CMS is proposing to maintain the requirement that MA organizations and Part D sponsors may determine their compensation payment schedule but proposes to remove the language currently in §§ 422.2274(d)(1)(iii) and 423.2274(d)(1)(iii) which provide examples of payment schedules, such as monthly or quarterly. Additionally, CMS is proposing to remove the language in §§ 422.2274(d)(1)(iii) and 423.2274(d)(1)(iii) that payments must be during the year of the beneficiary's enrollment, which were originally implemented to ensure agents and brokers were paid timely. MA organizations and Part D sponsors contract with their downstream entities. In general, CMS does not interfere with these contracts and should not regulate payment schedules between MA organizations and Part D sponsors with agents and brokers. CMS believes the agent and broker and the MA organization or Part D sponsor should determine and negotiate an appropriate payment schedule.
Next, CMS is proposing to redesignate and modify the introductory language at §§ 422.2274(d)(2) and (3) and 423.2274(d)(2) and (3). The newly redesignated language will be at §§ 422.2274(a)(3) and (4) and 423.2274(a)(3) and (4). Since CMS is proposing to modify the definition of FMV, CMS is proposing to eliminate the reference in these requirements to pay compensation at or below FMV, as CMS is proposing to no longer establish a maximum FMV for compensation.
CMS is not proposing any additional changes to the existing requirements at §§ 422.2274(d)(2)(i) and (ii) and (3)(i) and (ii) and 423.2274(d)(2)(i) and (ii) and (3)(i) and (ii) and proposes to maintain the other requirements regarding initial and renewal enrollments provided within these subparagraphs. CMS is proposing to redesignate §§ 422.2274(d)(2)(i) and (ii) and 423.2274(d)(2)(i) and (ii) to §§ 422.2274(a)(3)(i) and (ii) and 423.2274(a)(3)(i) and (ii) and redesignate §§ 422.2274(d)(3)(i) and (ii) and 423.2274(d)(3)(i) and (ii) to §§ 422.2274(a)(4)(i) and (ii) and 423.2274(a)(4)(i) and (ii).
CMS is proposing to add a new requirement at §§ 422.2274(a)(1), requiring MA organizations to pay the same base compensation to all agents and brokers for the same product line under a contract. This requirement would only be applicable to MA organizations based on their product lines. Since Part D sponsors only offer one product line, CMS is proposing to add a new requirement at § 423.2274(a)(1), that the Part D sponsor would be required to pay the same compensation for all plans under that contract. To further explain, an MA organization would be required to pay the same base compensation to all agents and brokers for all HMO plans offered under each contract. If the MA organization also has a PPO plan under the same contract as the HMO plan, the MA organization would be able to pay a different base compensation rate for that PPO than it does for the HMO, provided the MA organization pays all agents and brokers the same base compensation amount for that PPO. To reiterate, the same base compensation must apply to all enrollments for a particular product line offered under a contract. For purposes of this regulatory requirement, CMS is proposing to define a “product line” as one of the following: HMO, PPO, PFFS, RPPO, MSA, and Cost plans. CMS separated the various product lines that an MA organization may offer along these lines because each of these product lines have different rules, such as having to go in-network (HMO), or having the option of going in or out of network with different cost sharing (PPO). CMS is proposing this requirement to ensure an agent or broker does not steer a beneficiary into a particular plan, within a product line, based on compensation.
Since CMS does not require plans to compensate agents and brokers, CMS is considering including in this proposed requirement at §§ 422.2274(a)(1) and 423.2274(a)(1), that, MA organizations and Part D sponsors, may either pay the same base compensation for all PBPs of a similar product line as described previously, or they may pay $0 base compensation for any of those PBPs. CMS notes that the same base compensation or $0 would be the only permitted variations in base compensation across the same product lines. In other words, CMS would permit plans to offer either a specified base compensation amount or $0 for all their PBPs of a similar product line. As an example, if a plan has 3 HMO PBPs, a plan could pay agents and brokers $200 for two of their HMO PBPs and $0 for the final HMO PBP in base compensation.
In drafting this proposal, CMS also considered different types of compensation guardrails. The Agency considered requiring the same base compensation amount for all plans across all product lines under the same contract. In this scenario MA organizations would only be permitted to pay one base compensation amount for every product line, which includes all plans, for those plans in which the MA organization chooses to pay base compensation. For instance, if one MA organization has two HMOs, one PPO, and one Private Fee-for-Service plan, the MA organization would have to pay the same base compensation for all four plans, if base compensation is paid at all.
CMS also considered requiring MA organizations and Part D sponsors to pay the same base compensation across
(
printed page 76432)
plans operating within the same geographic service area or counties. For example, an MA organization or Part D sponsor may offer three plans, regardless of product line, that operate in the same four counties (Counties A, B, C, and D). Under this approach, the MA organization or Part D sponsor could establish different base compensation amounts by geographic area. It could pay one base compensation amount in County A, a different amount in County B, and another amount in Counties C and D. Within each designated geographic area, the MA organization or Part D sponsor would be required to pay the same base compensation amount for all three plans—regardless of product line—operating in the same county. Accordingly, all three plans would be required to have the same base compensation amount in County A; all three plans would be required to have the same, base compensation amount in County B; and all three plans would be required to have the same, base compensation amount in Counties C and D. The base compensation rates in each of those counties could differ.
Finally, CMS considered whether these six plan types (HMO, PPO, PFFS, RPPO, MSA, and Cost plans) are the appropriate plan types, or if other delineations are more appropriate, such as designating SNPs as a different type of plan and even further designating each SNP (D-SNP, I-SNP, and C-SNP) as different plan types. CMS is soliciting comments and suggestions as to whether these proposed guardrails are necessary, if the proposed guardrails are the most appropriate, or whether one of the alternatives to the proposed guardrails will best ensure that the use of compensation creates incentives for enrolling a beneficiary into a plan that best meets their health care needs or whether different guardrails would better serve the beneficiary.
To conform with the proposed changes, CMS is proposing to redesignate, without modifications, §§ 422.2274(d)(4) and (5) and 423.2274(d)(4) and (5) to §§ 422.2274(a)(7) and (8) and 423.2274(a)(7) and (8).
The current regulations at §§ 422.2274(c)(5) and 423.2274(c)(5) contain compensation reporting requirements, which CMS has proposed earlier to be moved and modified to new §§ 422.2271(b)(3) and 423.2271(b)(3). This existing requirement also prohibits MA organizations and Part D sponsors from changing their compensation rates and ranges following the last Friday in July. Although the current requirement at §§ 422.2274(c)(5) and 423.2274(c)(5), does not permit changes to be made after the July deadline, this prohibition has not resulted in a strict prohibition of changes. As described previously, many MA organizations and Part D sponsors have traditionally submitted an intended compensation range of $0 for the minimum and FMV for the maximum, meaning that they could change their compensation throughout the year, provided they pay a compensation rate between the minimum and maximum range provided. With CMS proposing to collect the actual base compensation amounts, that plans will pay to independent agents and brokers, and supplemental compensation, CMS wants to ensure MA organizations and Part D sponsors retain the flexibility to make midyear changes to compensation amounts allowed within the current regulatory requirements. Therefore, CMS is proposing to redesignate and modify this section of existing requirements at §§ 422.2274(c)(5) and 423.2274(c)(5) to §§ 422.2274(a)(5) and 423.2274(a)(5), to permit MA organizations and Part D sponsors to change their compensation rates.
CMS proposed, in §§ 422.2274(a)(1) and 423.2274(a)(1), that MA organizations and Part D sponsors pay the same base compensation based on product line. If finalized as proposed, an MA organization or Part D sponsor who modifies their base compensation amount during the year, must apply that change to all PBPs under the same product line under a contract. As an example, if an MA organization has three different HMO plans under a contract, the MA organization must adopt the updated compensation level for all three HMOs. Since Part D sponsors only have one product type, the same changes must be made to all plans under that contract. As previously discussed, CMS is considering whether MA organizations and Part D sponsors should be permitted to make an individual change in compensation for a plan within a product line, if that change is to $0 compensation. For example, if an MA organization has three HMO plans under the same contract, for which the compensation rate for all three HMO plans is $350 for an initial enrollment, CMS is considering permitting the MA organization to change the compensation rate to $0 only for one of the HMO plans, without being required to change the compensation rate for either of the other two HMO plans under that same contract. CMS is soliciting comments on the proposal and this alternative.
CMS is also proposing, at §§ 422.2274(a)(5) and 423.2274(a)(5), to require that MA organizations or Part D sponsors who plan to change their base and/or supplemental compensation during the year, must provide advanced notice of these changes to CMS, and that those changes must be made in the form and manner prescribed by CMS. The Health Plan Management System (HPMS) is the current system used to collect plan submitted compensation data. Any changes in compensation would be effective 30 days after the change is made. CMS solicits comments on the proposed 30-day timeframe and whether CMS should consider a shorter timeframe, such as 15 days, or a longer timeframe, such as 45 days, or should not allow base and/or supplemental compensation to be changed once submitted. e. Base Compensation Outlier Review Requirements
CMS is proposing new §§ 422.2274(b) and 423.2274(b), which states that CMS reviews all base compensation submissions to identify outliers as defined at §§ 422.2260 and 423.2260. CMS is proposing to conduct an outlier analysis to ensure the base compensation amounts are within FMV, as described earlier in this proposal. CMS proposes to deny base compensation amounts that are determined to be base compensation outliers, as defined in §§ 422.2260 and 423.2260. Similar to concerns expressed in the past when the compensation requirements were first developed,

CMS is concerned that certain MA organizations or Part D sponsors paying significantly more than other MA organizations or Part D sponsors could have an undue influence on an agent or broker. This guardrail will ensure agents and brokers are not enrolling a beneficiary in a plan based on an unusually high base compensation.
As previously discussed, CMS is proposing to determine base compensation outlier amounts annually, following the proposed compensation data submission by the last Friday of July. Following submission CMS proposes to identify any base compensation outliers for MA organizations and Part D sponsors separately. That is, the MA organization outlier review would include MA only plans and MA plans that include Medicare prescription drug coverage, and stand-alone Part D plans will be a part of the separate Part D sponsor outlier review. CMS is proposing to notify MA organization and Part D sponsors of their base compensation outlier status prior to the start of marketing, October 1 of each year, with the aim of providing sufficient time for them to modify base compensation as needed to bring the base compensation outlier amounts within the acceptable range. MA organizations and Part D sponsors who fail to modify base compensation below the CMS determined outlier amount would be prohibited from paying base compensation until the submitted amount is below the CMS threshold. This prohibition would only apply to the product line's submitted base compensation rates that are above the FMV, and would not apply to other product lines that were not considered base compensation outliers.
Base compensation outlier amounts would not be recalculated if, at other times of the year, MA organizations or Part D sponsors change their base compensation. Any revised base compensation would be reviewed against CMS' initial base compensation outlier analysis for that plan year to ensure that it is not an outlier. If the updated base compensation amount is identified as an outlier, CMS would deny the base compensation, requiring a resubmission by the MA organization or Part D sponsor.
CMS does not propose to permit MA organizations or Part D sponsors to request a re-review or provide a reconsideration process. Since the proposal is based on a review of all base compensation amounts submitted by all MA organizations and Part D sponsors, as part of the annual submission process described in CMS's proposed regulation text at §§ 422.2271(b)(3) and 423.2271(b)(3), base compensation outliers will be determined using the box plot method described earlier and will result in in the final outlier determinations. Since the data is reported to CMS, the Agency cannot influence what constitutes an outlier. Therefore, no re-review or reconsideration process is necessary given outlier numbers will be determined by the box plot method and not changed or influenced by CMS. CMS notes that if there were an error on CMS's calculation of the outlier, CMS would recalculate the outlier and notify MA organizations and Part D sponsors.

f. Supplemental Compensation
Section 1851(j)(2)(D) of the Act requires the Secretary to establish guidelines to ensure that the use of compensation creates incentives for agents and brokers to enroll individuals in the Medicare Advantage plan that is intended to best meet their health care needs. As a component of agent and broker compensation, supplemental compensation may affect these incentives and, therefore, may affect the plans that agents and brokers market or recommend to beneficiaries. CMS notes that compensation being proposed under supplemental compensation, such as bonuses, gifts, etc., are considered part of the current compensation definition and are historically subject to CMS' FMV. This proposal separates base compensation and supplemental compensation into two categories to account for the different types of compensation paid to agents and brokers. CMS' proposal eliminates the previous FMV cap on the rate paid for an enrollment and instead identifies outliers based on determining the FMV for base compensation, as submitted by MA organizations and Part D sponsors. Since base compensation is defined as a monetary amount, a base compensation outlier review is substantially easier than an outlier review for supplemental compensation, which can be monetary or non-monetary. CMS recognizes that significant differences in supplemental compensation among plans could create financial incentives that affect an agent's or broker's recommendations. However, at this time, CMS does not believe the Agency has sufficient information to propose an oversight mechanism for supplemental compensation akin to the outlier review process proposed for base compensation.
CMS has not historically received information indicating how MA organizations and Part D sponsors design and provide for bonuses, gifts, etc. Given CMS' current lack of data regarding these arrangements, regulating supplemental compensation at this time is challenging. CMS's understanding is that MA organizations and Part D sponsors structure supplemental compensation programs in substantially different ways often tied to performance metrics, including financial bonuses based on factors such as enrollee retention, enrollee satisfaction, quality measures, or other performance metrics. In addition, some MA organizations and Part D sponsors have offered, or may be interested in offering, non-monetary supplemental compensation, such as gifts, trips, awards, or other benefits. CMS's understanding is that these arrangements differ in their structure, frequency, eligibility requirements, valuation, and the metrics used to determine whether an agent or broker receives supplemental compensation that is fair market value. Moreover, an MA organization's or Part D sponsor's compensation arrangements must not violate the Federal anti-kickback statute and must comply with all other applicable laws and regulations.
For these reasons, CMS is not proposing to establish an outlier threshold or validation process for supplemental compensation at this time. Instead, CMS believes it is appropriate to first pursue the proposed supplemental compensation reporting requirements discussed earlier and as proposed in §§ 422.2271(b)(3)(iii) and 423.2271(b)(3)(iii). If finalized, CMS would implement those reporting requirements and evaluate the information collected under those requirements. The initial year of reported supplemental compensation would be contract year 2028, allowing CMS to better understand the types of supplemental compensation agents and brokers receive, the frequency and monetary value of such compensation, the metrics or conditions used to determine supplemental compensation, and variation in compensation arrangements across MA organizations and Part D sponsors.
(
printed page 76437)
After gaining experience with the reporting requirements and reviewing the data collected, CMS could evaluate whether supplemental compensation arrangements raise concerns, warranting additional oversight and, if so, whether an outlier analysis or another approach would be appropriate. Any such analysis would need to account for the substantial variation in supplemental compensation arrangements and ensure that comparisons are sufficiently meaningful. CMS would also need to consider whether MA organizations and Part D sponsors should be evaluated separately, whether comparisons should occur at the organization, plan, agent or broker, geographic, or national level, and how non-monetary compensation and compensation tied to different performance metrics should be valued and compared.
While CMS is not proposing a supplemental compensation outlier methodology in this rule, the Agency recognizes the supplemental compensation may influence the plan or plans an agent or broker recommends to a beneficiary. To protect beneficiaries, CMS believes additional guardrails need to be put in place for supplemental compensation. The Agency considered different alternatives as described later in this proposal. CMS is soliciting comments on the potential supplemental compensation guardrail approaches identified earlier. CMS is providing these examples to illustrate potential future approaches and solicit comment; they do not represent an exhaustive list, nor do they represent proposed outlier thresholds or methodologies. The Agency is also interested in other approaches to ensure supplemental compensation results in an agent or broker recommending the plan that best meets the health care needs of a beneficiary.
One possible approach could be to examine the highest amount of supplemental compensation that an agent or broker could receive under an organization's or sponsor's compensation arrangement. Another possible approach could be to collect supplemental compensation using monetary or value ranges, or “buckets.” Such an approach could provide more information regarding the distribution of supplemental compensation while potentially reducing reporting burden compared with reporting each individual payment. However, the usefulness of this approach would depend on how the ranges are established and whether compensation arrangements can be meaningfully compared within and across those ranges.
CMS could also examine differences in supplemental compensation among plans offered by the same MA organization or Part D sponsor. Such an analysis could help identify circumstances in which substantially greater supplemental compensation is associated with enrollment in a particular plan. Alternatively, CMS could consider comparisons across organizations or sponsors on a broader geographic or national basis. Each approach presents challenges because differences in compensation may reflect differences in plan characteristics, markets, performance metrics, or compensation structures rather than incentives to steer beneficiaries toward particular plans.
Another approach could focus on supplemental compensation received by individual agents or brokers relative to their peers. Such an approach could potentially identify unusually high payments, but determining an appropriate peer group would be particularly important. Differences in enrollment volume, geographic market, experience, performance, retention, or other factors could result in legitimate differences in supplemental compensation. CMS could also consider whether information regarding actual supplemental compensation payments should be evaluated together with information regarding enrollments facilitated by agents and brokers. This information could help CMS better understand the relationship, if any, between supplemental compensation and enrollment activity. However, such an approach would require additional data collection and could raise questions regarding the appropriate level of reporting and analysis. A related approach could examine aggregate supplemental compensation and enrollment. CMS could, for example, collect the total supplemental compensation paid by an MA organization or Part D sponsor and the total number of enrollments facilitated by agents and brokers during the applicable period. CMS could then calculate supplemental compensation on a per-enrollment basis and evaluate variation across organizations or sponsors. Although this approach could reduce the need for agent-level reporting, aggregate measures may obscure substantial variation among individual compensation arrangements and may not account for supplemental compensation tied to outcomes other than enrollment.
Similarly, CMS is interested in whether organizations, sponsors, or plans that do not offer supplemental compensation should be included in any future analysis. Including zero supplemental compensation amounts could substantially affect averages, distributions, or statistical thresholds, particularly where supplemental compensation is not widely used. Reporting supplemental compensation, as a newly proposed concept, if finalized, will provide CMS information on how many MA organizations or Part D sponsors elect to use supplemental compensation as a part of the total agent and broker compensation package.
As this discussion illustrates, designing a meaningful outlier methodology requires carefully balancing the need to identify potentially concerning supplemental compensation arrangements against the reality that differences in supplemental compensation often reflect legitimate variation in plan characteristics, market conditions, and agent or broker circumstances. CMS believes that collecting data under the reporting requirements proposed in this rule, if finalized, would be an important first step, and we look forward to stakeholder input that will help inform whether and how a future outlier methodology could be developed in a way that is both effective and appropriately tailored to the diversity of supplemental compensation arrangements in the marketplace.
CMS solicits comments on all parts of supplemental compensation outliers. In particular, CMS seeks comments on whether supplemental compensation arrangements could create incentives that warrant additional CMS oversight; what information CMS would need to determine whether such concerns exist; whether the reporting requirements described in this rule would provide sufficient information for that purpose; and what additional data, if any, would be necessary. CMS also seeks comments on whether any of the illustrative approaches described previously could provide a meaningful method for identifying potentially concerning supplemental compensation arrangements, what limitations or unintended consequences those approaches might present, and whether commenters recommend alternative approaches.
CMS further solicit comments on the appropriate unit of comparison for any future analysis, including whether comparisons should be made at the MA organization or Part D sponsor, plan, agent or broker, geographic, or national level; how CMS could account for differences in the structure and purpose of supplemental compensation arrangements; how non-monetary compensation should be valued;
(
printed page 76438)
whether organizations or plans that do not offer supplemental compensation should be included in an analysis; and whether actual compensation and enrollment data would provide useful information sufficient to justify the additional reporting burden. CMS will consider stakeholder feedback in determining whether additional rulemaking or other action concerning supplemental compensation is warranted.
g. Referral Fee Requirements
CMS is proposing to remove limitations on referral fees, currently at §§ 422.2274(f) and 423.2274(f). Referral fee limitations were originally established in October 2011. At that time, CMS was made aware of excessive referral fees, upwards of what the maximum FMV ($402) for compensation was at that time. Moreover, with a cap placed on compensation, there was a concern that referral fees were being used as a means of circumventing the existing compensation requirements. CMS implemented a cap on referral fees to address these concerns and to limit the incentives of agents to enroll beneficiaries into particular plans, without regard to whether the plan met the beneficiary's health care needs.
[
125
]
Similar to the changes being proposed in this proposed rule regarding limitations on compensation, CMS believes that the marketplace should determine the value of a referral. MA organizations and Part D sponsors are in the best position to determine to whom referrals should be paid and the amount of referral that should be paid. Unlike the compensation reporting requirements being proposed at this time, CMS is not proposing to collect referral fee data, nor will CMS be establishing regulations to identify referral fee outliers. However, CMS will still review complaints and take appropriate action if violations occur such as agents or brokers steering or cherry-picking beneficiaries based on referral fees. CMS reiterates that if this proposed change is adopted, MA organizations and Part D sponsors would still be required to remain in compliance with all fraud and abuse laws, including the Federal anti-kickback statute.
Finally, as an alternative to finalizing the changes proposed in this section, CMS is considering amending §§ 422.2274 and 423.2274 to remove the vacated provisions and restore the corresponding regulatory text in effect prior to the April 2024 final rule. This alternative would align the CFR with the agent and broker compensation and oversight requirements that CMS is currently applying. CMS solicits comments on this alternative as well as all the proposals discussed in this section.
D. Removing the Requirement for a TPMO Disclaimer (§§ 422.2267 and 423.2267)
As a part of the Medicare Program; Contract Year 2023 Policy and Technical Changes to the Medicare Advantage and Medicare Prescription Drug Benefit Programs; Policy and Regulatory Revisions in Response to the COVID-19 Public Health Emergency; Additional Policy and Regulatory Revisions in Response to the COVID-19 Public Health Emergency final rule, which appeared in the
Federal Register
on May 9, 2022 (hereafter referred to as the May 2022 final rule) (
87 FR 27704
), and as a part of a broader effort to address concerns with TPMOs, CMS finalized regulations at §§ 422.2267(e)(41) and 423.2267(e)(41) to improve regulatory oversight of Third-Party Marketing Organizations (TPMOs). One provision required Medicare Advantage (MA) organizations and Part D sponsors to ensure that TPMOs with which MA organizations and Part D sponsors directly or indirectly do business verbally convey a standardized disclaimer during sales calls with beneficiaries. The disclaimer, as finalized, consisted of the following statement: “We do not offer every plan available in your area. Any information we provide is limited to those plans we do offer in your area. Please contact
Medicare.gov
or 1-800-MEDICARE to get information on all of your options.”
The following year, CMS issued the Medicare Program; Contract Year 2024 Policy and Technical Changes to the Medicare Advantage Program, Medicare Prescription Drug Benefit Program, Medicare Cost Plan Program; and Programs of All-Inclusive Care for the Elderly final rule, hereinafter referred to as the April 2023 final rule (
88 FR 22120
). In this final rule, CMS amended §§ 422.2267(e)(41) and 423.2267(e)(41), revising the existing disclaimer to require TPMOs to notify the beneficiary of the number of organizations and the number of plans the TPMO offers in the beneficiary's service area. This disclaimer is only applicable for TPMOs that sell on behalf of more than one MA organization or Part D sponsor.
In the April 2023 final rule, CMS also added State Health Insurance Assistance Programs (SHIPs) as a source of information for beneficiaries in the disclaimer and required TPMOs to convey the applicable disclaimer within the first minute of a sales call, among other requirements, for the TPMO to communicate the disclaimer through other electronic means or materials. Specifically, any TPMO, as defined under §§ 422.2260 and 423.2260, that sells plans on behalf of more than one MA organization or Part D sponsor, must electronically convey the TPMO disclaimer when communicating with a beneficiary through email, online chat, or other electronic means of communication, prominently display the disclaimer on TPMO websites, and include the disclaimer in any marketing materials, including print materials and television advertisements, developed, used, or distributed by the TPMO.
Most recently, as part of the Medicare Program; Contract Year 2027 and Certain Contract Year 2026 Policy and Technical Changes to the Medicare Advantage Program, Medicare Prescription Drug Benefit Program, and Medicare Cost Plan Program final rule which appeared in the
Federal Register
on April 6, 2026, (hereafter referred to as the April 2026 final rule) (
91 FR 17384
), CMS finalized regulations at §§ ;422.2267(e)(41) and 423.2267(e)(41), updating the TPMO disclaimer requirements by changing the timing of verbal disclosure from the first minute of the call to “prior to the discussion of any benefits,” and removing the reference to SHIPs from the disclaimer. The requirements in §§ 422.2267(e)(41)(i), (iii), (iv), and (v) and 423.2267(e)(41)(i), (iii), (iv), and (v) did not change. In the April 2026 final rule, CMS received numerous comments from stakeholders urging CMS to completely rescind the TPMO disclaimer requirement. In response, CMS noted that eliminating the TPMO disclaimer was not proposed and thus, out of scope for removal in the April 2026 final rule. However, CMS committed to taking the commenters' input under advisement.
In the April 2026 final rule, CMS also discussed the findings noted in the April 2023 final rule about the review of sales and enrollment calls. As noted in that April 2023 final rule, the review found that only one plan option from one MA organization was discussed in over 80 percent of the calls. CMS used the call monitoring findings to justify the changes in the April 2023 final rule, specifically creating a new disclaimer for TPMOs that contracted with every MA organization or Part D sponsor in a service area. CMS continued to believe that these findings should be considered when refining regulations, including the April 2026 final rule.
(
printed page 76439)
CMS created the TPMO disclaimer to address a concern that TPMOs were not providing beneficiaries with information about all their health care plan options, which is a practice viewed as potentially misleading. However, industry stakeholders have indicated in subsequent meetings with CMS that it is common industry practice for agents and brokers to evaluate plan offerings based on a beneficiary's unique needs and present the plan or plans they believe will best meet the beneficiary's health care needs. CMS previously viewed the absence of information about all plan options available in the beneficiary's service area as evidence that beneficiaries were being denied information necessary to make an informed choice, thus necessitating the disclosure information in the TPMO disclaimer. However, CMS now recognizes that the complaints observed in the aforementioned sales calls may not reflect the majority of agent and broker interactions with beneficiaries. CMS also recognizes that limiting the number of plans presented to a beneficiary may reduce beneficiary confusion by appropriately excluding plans that are not for a beneficiary suited (for example, a chronic care special needs plan for a beneficiary with no health issues). The current TPMO disclaimer fails to recognize that the agent or broker may be able to provide more efficient and understandable advice to beneficiaries by researching multiple options and presenting the plan or plans that appear best suited to meet the beneficiary's health care needs.
Further, as it applies to the TPMO disclaimer, CMS recognizes that the call monitoring findings discussed in the April 2023 and April 2026 final rules should be interpreted in the context of the data source from which they were derived. The calls reviewed by CMS were drawn from marketing misrepresentation complaints in the Complaints Tracking Module (CTM) and, accordingly, reflected calls often involving non-compliance with CMS's marketing requirements under subpart V of parts 422 and 423. Those complaint-based calls were appropriately considered in identifying problematic marketing practices. However, because the calls were selected based on complaints, they were not intended to represent a random or comprehensive sample of all beneficiary interactions with agents and brokers or to establish that the TPMO disclaimer would have addressed the underlying causes of the non-compliance.
CMS now believes that, in many instances, the conduct reflected in those calls was more attributable to ill-intentioned or ill-informed agents and brokers failing to accurately disclose the full scope of the products to the beneficiary or steering them toward an option despite reasonable indications that it was not in the beneficiary's best interest—conduct already addressed through existing marketing requirements—rather than the absence of a TPMO disclaimer. As a result, the finding that more than 80 percent of calls discussed only one plan may reflect the characteristics of complaint-based calls rather than the broader population of sales calls conducted by well-intentioned and informed agents and brokers. As previously mentioned, CMS recognizes that it may be common industry practice for agents and brokers to evaluate a beneficiary's unique health care needs and recommend the plan or plans they reasonably believe are the best fit, rather than discussing every available plan. Accordingly, CMS recognizes that the trend identified in the earlier call monitoring findings of agents and brokers discussing only one recommended plan, standing alone, may not have been indicative of inappropriate marketing or beneficiary harm, and that is therefore unclear whether requiring the TPMO disclaimer would have remedied the concerns reflected in the complaint-based calls.
CMS's conclusion is further supported by a more recent review of approximately 25 calls associated with marketing misrepresentation complaints submitted to 1-800-MEDICARE between January 2026 and March 2026. Although CMS acknowledges the limited sample size, the review identified recurring concerns involving beneficiaries' inability to access preferred providers because those providers were outside the plan's network, failures to clearly explain that a beneficiary's existing coverage would end, and agents and brokers not providing complete information regarding plan benefits and cost sharing. During these calls, however, beneficiaries did not inquire about other available plans, even when agents provided the TPMO disclaimer informing beneficiaries that additional options were available, as required. These findings suggest that the beneficiary complaints were driven by incomplete or misleading information regarding the recommended plan, rather than by a lack of awareness that other plans existed. Accordingly, where an ill-intentioned or ill-informed agent or broker limits the information provided to a beneficiary or otherwise fails to comply with CMS's marketing requirements, CMS now questions whether requiring the TPMO disclaimer meaningfully changes the outcome of the interaction. Instead, the more effective means of addressing these concerns may be through enforcement of existing marketing requirements that prohibit misleading or incomplete communication and require appropriate oversight of agents and brokers.
CMS also considered the practical burdens associated with the TPMO disclaimer in reassessing whether it remains an appropriate regulatory requirement. The disclaimer imposes compliance obligations on TPMOs, MA organizations, and Part D sponsors, including requirements to incorporate prescribed language into verbal and electronic communications, train agents and brokers on its use, monitor compliance, and update marketing materials and systems when the disclaimer is revised. Although each of these obligations may be modest in isolation, together they create ongoing administrative and operational burdens that are warranted only if the disclaimer provides meaningful benefits to beneficiaries.
CMS also believes the disclaimer may unnecessarily interrupt what is intended to be a trust-based discussion between a beneficiary and an agent or broker. Requiring agents and brokers to deliver a standardized disclosure before engaging in a substantive discussion of a beneficiary's health care needs may delay the conversation and divert attention from information that is more relevant to the beneficiary's enrollment decision. As discussed previously, CMS now understands that it is common industry practice for well-intentioned and informed agents and brokers to evaluate a beneficiary's individual circumstances and recommend the plan or plans they reasonably believe best meet the beneficiary's needs. In that context, a disclaimer emphasizing that the agent or broker does not offer every available plan may create unnecessary confusion without providing information that meaningfully improves the beneficiary's ability to make an informed enrollment decision. Because CMS no longer believes the TPMO disclaimer effectively addresses the conduct underlying beneficiary complaints, CMS believes these burdens outweigh any incremental benefit provided by the disclaimer.
CMS continues to believe that protecting beneficiaries from misleading or confusing marketing practices remains a fundamental objective of the Medicare marketing regulations. However, based on the information discussed previously, CMS no longer believes that the TPMO disclaimer is the
(
printed page 76440)
appropriate regulatory mechanism to further that objective. Instead, CMS believes that other existing requirements under §§ 422.2262(a)(1)(i), 423.2262(a)(1)(i), 422.2274(c), and 423.2274(c), and proposed requirements under
42 CFR parts 422
and 423 subpart V more effectively target the causes of beneficiary complaints and will allow the agency to continue to pursue entities that continue to mislead beneficiaries by providing inaccurate or incomplete information while avoiding a disclosure requirement that has not demonstrated meaningful benefits for beneficiaries.
For example, §§ 422.2274(c) and 423.2274(c) require MA organizations and Part D sponsors to oversee first tier, downstream, and related entities (FDRs) that represent the MA organization or Part D sponsor to ensure agents and brokers abide by all applicable State and Federal laws, regulations, and requirements. Protections are provided through MA organizations and Part D sponsors monitoring TPMOs to ensure they are abiding by all requirements. CMS notes that in section I.B.11 of this proposed rule CMS is proposing significant changes to §§ 422.2274(c) and 423.2274(c). However, under this proposal the requirement to oversee FDRs would remain, but would be redesignated to new proposed §§ 422.2271(a)(2) and 423.2271(a)(2).
Likewise, the broad provisions at §§ 422.2262 and 423.2262, already prohibit TPMOs from engaging in marketing practices that are misleading, confusing, or provide materially inaccurate information to beneficiaries. Thus, CMS believes the TPMO disclaimer requirement is a redundant application of the general marketing regulations already in place.
Beyond the broad anti-misleading provisions at §§ 422.2262 and 423.2262, CMS notes that existing regulations establish a comprehensive framework requiring transparency in beneficiary communications. Under §§ 422.2262(a) and 423.2262(a), CMS prohibits plans from engaging in a defined set of actions, which establish clear boundaries for plan conduct. Taken together, these provisions create overlapping layers of protection. A TPMO operating in compliance with these existing requirements would, by definition, already be communicating its limitations to beneficiaries in a truthful and non-deceptive manner. As noted, the disclaimer requirement, as originally conceived, was a reactive measure designed to address a specific gap in beneficiary awareness at a particular point in the program's development. The regulatory landscape has since matured considerably. Moreover, in this rule under “Enhancing Agent and Broker Compensation and Oversight,” CMS is proposing extensive changes to the existing agent/broker compensation and oversight structure, as addressed in section VI.C of this proposed rule. An example of these proposed changes includes requiring MA organizations to pay the same compensation to agents and brokers for similar product types offered under a contract, intended to reduce the use of compensation to influence enrollment decisions. In addition, beneficiaries can take advantage of certain important beneficiary protections such as potential SEPs, including retrospective enrollments, when appropriate, if a beneficiary makes an adverse enrollment decision based on misrepresentation or otherwise non-compliant sales tactics. CMS believes that the guardrails included in the Enhancing Agent and Broker Compensation and Oversight provision, coupled with existing beneficiary protections, render the TPMO disclaimer unnecessary.
Based on information identified in calls, beneficiary protections already in place, and additional proposed guardrails, CMS believes the disclaimer is no longer necessary. Therefore, for the reasons cited previously, and in keeping with
Executive Order 14192
, Unleashing Prosperity Through Deregulation, which appeared in the
Federal Register
on January 31, 2025 (
90 FR 9065
), We are proposing to rescind the regulatory language found at §§  422.2267(e)(41) and 423.2267(e)(41).
We invite comments on this proposal.
E. Expanding Electronic Delivery of Required Enrollee Communications (§§ 422.2267 and 423.2267)
On January 19, 2021, CMS issued the Medicare and Medicaid Programs; Contract Year 2022 Policy and Technical Changes to the Medicare Advantage Program, Medicare Prescription Drug Benefit Program, Medicaid Program, Medicare Cost Plan Program, and Programs of All-Inclusive Care for the Elderly final rule (
86 FR 5864
), referred to hereafter as the January 2021 final rule. In this rule, CMS codified requirements in
42 CFR 422.2267(d)(2)(i)
and
423.2267(d)(2)(i)
permitting MA organizations and Part D sponsors, without prior authorization from the enrollee, to mail a hard copy notice informing enrollees how to electronically access the Evidence of Coverage (EOC), Provider and Pharmacy Directories, and Formulary. The notice must also explain how enrollees may request hard copies of those materials. Since the January 2021 final rule, electronic delivery of materials has become more common across the health care and insurance sectors. CMS believes many enrollees increasingly expect access to plan materials through websites, portals, and other electronic channels. Based on CMS's experience administering §§ 422.2267(d)(2)(i) and 423.2267(d)(2)(i), CMS has not identified complaints suggesting that enrollees' access to the Evidence of Coverage (EOC), Provider and Pharmacy Directories, or Formulary has been materially impaired by providing these materials electronically, provided that a hard-copy notice is furnished and enrollees retain the right to request paper copies.
CMS is proposing to expand the scope of required materials and content eligible for electronic delivery without prior authorization from the enrollee. Currently, §§ 422.2267(d)(2) and 423.2267(d)(2) permit electronic delivery in two circumstances. First, under §§ 422.2267(d)(2)(i) and 423.2267(d)(2)(i), MA organizations and Part D sponsors may mail new and current enrollees a notice describing how to electronically access the EOC, Provider and Pharmacy Directories, and Formulary without obtaining prior authorization from the enrollee, subject to the notice and hard-copy request requirements in those paragraphs. F. Treatment of Compound Drug Products (§ 423.120)
Multi-ingredient compounds are products extemporaneously prepared by pharmacies to provide drug therapies that are not commercially available as finished products approved by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) in the same dose, formulation, and/or combination of ingredients. In the April 15, 2011 final rule titled, “Medicare Program; Changes to the Medicare Advantage and the Medicare Prescription Drug Benefit Programs for Contract Year 2012 and Other Changes” (
76 FR 21432
) (hereinafter referred to as the Contract Year 2012 final rule), CMS codified requirements at § 423.120(d) related to how Part D plan sponsors must treat multi-ingredient compounds in the Part D program. Those requirements specify at § 423.120(d)(1)(i) and (ii) that only compounds that contain at least one ingredient that independently meets the definition of a Part D drug, and that do not contain any ingredient that is covered under Part B as prescribed and dispensed or administered, may be covered under Part D. Compounds meeting both criteria are referred to as Part D compounds. The Contract Year 2012 final rule also established requirements related to when Part D compounds must be considered formulary drugs for purposes of determining enrollee cost sharing, and when transition rules apply (see § 423.120(d)(1)(iii) and (iv)).
The Contract Year 2012 final rule also codified a requirement at § 423.120(d)(2) that Part D plan sponsors establish consistent rules for beneficiary payment liability for ingredients of a Part D compound that independently meet the definition of a Part D drug, and for non-Part D ingredients. Specifically, for low income subsidy-eligible individuals (LIS), Part D plan sponsors are required to apply the copayment amount described in § 423.782 for a Part D compound based on whether the most expensive ingredient that independently meets the definition of a Part D drug is a generic or brand name drug (see § 423.120(d)(2)(i)). Finally, at § 423.120(d)(2)(ii), CMS specified that Part D plan sponsors must—through their contract with the pharmacy—prohibit pharmacies from balance billing the enrollee for the cost of any non-Part D ingredient of a Part D compound, including drugs described under § 423.104(f)(1)(ii)(A).
CMS's intent in codifying the balance billing prohibition for non-Part D ingredients was to provide transparency to Part D enrollees with respect to out-of-pocket costs associated with covered Part D compounds, and to establish a more straightforward approach for enrollees, Part D sponsors, and pharmacies, without interfering with the ability of pharmacies to negotiate prices that provide adequate reimbursement for compounds. We noted in the Contract Year 2012 final rule our belief that Part D sponsors and pharmacies have negotiated how Part D compounds
(
printed page 76442)
are priced in general and that such prices adequately account for any non-Part D ingredients, which usually account for a small portion of the overall cost, regardless of how an individual paid claim represents payment for individual ingredients (
76 FR 21523
).
While we continue to believe this is true with respect to most Part D compounds, we have observed in recent years situations involving covered Part D compounds with substantial non-Part D ingredient costs, including costs that far exceed those of the Part D ingredient(s). In these limited situations, standard practices whereby the plan absorbs the costs for the non-Part D ingredients (without charging the enrollee or reporting the non-Part D costs to CMS) or reimburses the pharmacy for the non-Part D ingredients as part of the dispensing fee, are both inadequate and improper.
Existing Part D compound policies are intended to ensure enrollee access to Part D drugs when there is no commercially available formulation to meet an individual's specific treatment needs, such as an allergy to an inactive ingredient or a need for a different dosage form or custom dosage requirements. The prohibition on balance billing for non-Part D ingredients is not meant to be a vehicle by which Part D enrollees can obtain drugs that are otherwise not payable under Part D, nor is it intended to leave Part D plan sponsors or pharmacies that agree to provide Part D compounds with significant non-Part D expenses for these claims.
While the existing policy prohibiting balance billing for the cost of non-Part D ingredients was intended as an enrollee financial protection, when the financial impact on the pharmacy is significant, it understandably deters pharmacies from providing compounding services for multi-ingredient compounds that include Part D drugs.
Only costs associated with covered Part D drugs, as defined at § 423.100, can be paid for under the Part D benefit. As such, longstanding CMS policy limits Part D coverage of Part D compounds to only: (1) the ingredient costs associated with the ingredients that independently meet the definition of a Part D drug; and (2) any dispensing fees, as defined at § 423.100, which can include the costs associated with preparing the compound such as labor costs and costs of inactive, non-Part D ingredients necessary to prepare the compound (for example, flavored compounding syrup). Because of the scenarios described earlier and our concerns with how our current policy on balance billing operates in those scenarios, we propose to revise our policy to remove the requirement that Part D plan sponsors' contracts with network pharmacies must prohibit balance billing for the cost of non-Part D ingredients, effective for plan years beginning January 1, 2028. Specifically, we propose to add the phrase, “For plan years beginning before January 1, 2028,” at § 423.120(d)(2)(ii) to eliminate the prohibition on balance billing beginning with the 2028 plan year.
Under our proposal, only the requirement to prohibit balance billing would be removed. This proposal would not prevent Part D plan sponsors and pharmacies from continuing to negotiate reimbursement for Part D compounds under their contracts, and Part D sponsors may choose to continue to prohibit balance billing. We are proposing this change to address a specific scenario involving non-Part D ingredients that represent a substantial portion of the costs for a Part D compound. Outside of that scenario, and because the costs associated with preparing the compound are included in our definition of dispensing fees, CMS expects that Part D compounds would generally continue to be available to enrollees without additional out-of-pocket costs if this proposal is finalized.
We propose to make additional technical corrections to improve accuracy and readability of § 423.120(d) by striking the word “both” and adding the word “for” in the introductory text at paragraph (d)(2) and revising paragraph (d)(2)(i) to refer to “subsidy eligible individuals (as defined at § 423.4)” instead of “low income subsidy-beneficiaries”.
We estimate that this proposal, if finalized, would have a negligible overall impact on the government, Part D sponsors, and pharmacies. Since 2011, compounds have accounted for significantly less than one percent of total PDEs and total Part D drug spend.
We seek comment on whether and how the prohibition on balance billing for non-Part D ingredients of Part D compounds has impacted Part D sponsors, pharmacies, and Part D enrollees, our proposed changes, and our estimate on anticipated effects if this proposal is finalized.

B. Updating I-SNP Crosswalk Terms—Technical Change (§ 422.530)
This proposal would amend
42 CFR 422.530(b)(2)(ii)
by replacing the current Institutional Special Needs Pan (I-SNP) subtype terminology with updated terminology that reflects the definitions finalized in the April 2024 final rule (
89 FR 30448
). The proposed amendments would replace references to “Institutional SNP,” “Institutional Equivalent SNP,” and “Institutional/Institutional Equivalent SNP” with the terms defined at § 422.2: Facility-based Institutional Special Needs Plan (FI-SNP), Hybrid Institutional Special Needs Plan (HI-SNP), and Institutional-Equivalent Special Needs Plan (IE-SNP).
SNPs are MA coordinated care plans authorized under section 1859(f) of the Act and designed to provide targeted care to, and limit enrollment to, specific groups of special needs individuals as defined at § 422.2. I-SNPs are a category of SNPs that restrict enrollment to individuals who reside in an institution or who require an equivalent level of care.
As part of the April 2024 final rule, CMS finalized four definitions at § 422.2 to clarify the specific standards applicable to I-SNPs.
These definitions clarify the standards applicable to I-SNPs and distinguish the three I-SNP subtypes from each other and from other MA plans and other MA SNPs. The I-SNP subtype definitions rely on the definitions of “institutionalized” and “institutionalized-equivalent” in § 422.2, including the list of eligible facilities in the definition of “institutionalized.”
Under § 422.530(a)(1), a crosswalk is the movement of enrollees from one plan (or plan benefit package (PBP)) to another plan (or PBP) under a contract between the MA organization and CMS. MA plans may crosswalk enrollees only in the circumstances specified in § 422.530(b), or through an approved exception under § 422.530(c).
Currently, § 422.530(b)(2)(ii) sets forth the following permissible I-SNP crosswalk scenarios using the prior subtype terminology:
Renewing Institutional SNP that transitions enrollees to an Institutional/Institutional Equivalent SNP.
Renewing Institutional Equivalent SNP that transitions enrollees to an Institutional/Institutional Equivalent SNP.
Renewing Institutional/Institutional Equivalent SNP that transitions eligible enrollees to an Institutional SNP.
Renewing Institutional/Institutional Equivalent SNP that transitions eligible enrollees to an Institutional Equivalent SNP.
Non-renewing Institutional/Institutional Equivalent SNP that transitions eligible enrollees to another Institutional/Institutional Equivalent SNP.
These provisions use terminology that predates the April 2024 final rule and must be updated to reflect the new Institutional Special Needs Plan (I-SNP) subtype definitions now codified at § 422.2.
CMS is proposing to amend § 422.530(b)(2)(ii) by replacing the current I-SNP subtype terminology with updated terminology consistent with the definitions finalized in the April 2024 final rule. The amended text of § 422.530(b)(2)(ii) would be revised to read as follows:
The following crosswalk scenarios are permissible for I-SNPs:
++ Renewing Facility-based Institutional special needs plan (FI-SNP) that transitions enrollees to a Hybrid Institutional special needs plan (HI-SNP).
++ Renewing Institutional-equivalent special needs plan (IE-SNP) that transitions enrollees to a HI-SNP.
++ Renewing HI-SNP that transitions eligible enrollees to a FI-SNP.
++ Renewing HI-SNP that transitions eligible enrollees to an IE-SNP.
++ Non-renewing HI-SNP that transitions eligible enrollees to another HI-SNP.
The proposed amendments are necessary to ensure regulatory consistency between the crosswalk provisions at § 422.530(b)(2)(ii) and the updated I-SNP subtype definitions finalized in the April 2024 final rule. Without these conforming amendments, the crosswalk provisions would continue to reference outdated terminology that does not correspond to the defined I-SNP subtypes, creating potential confusion for MA organizations and beneficiaries.
The proposed amendments do not alter the substantive crosswalk policies currently in effect. Rather, they would update the terminology used to describe the permissible crosswalk scenarios to align with the new I-SNP subtype definitions. The permissible crosswalk scenarios under this proposal correspond to the same types of transitions currently permitted under § 422.530(b)(2)(ii). CMS does not anticipate burden impacts for this technical update and is not scoring this update in the COI section. Section 423.315 sets forth the general payment provisions for the Medicare Part D program. Paragraph (d) describes the low-income subsidies, specifically, the premium and cost-sharing subsidies, paid on behalf of certain subsidy-eligible individuals. See
section 1860D-2(b)(3)(A) of the Act. Additionally, as it applies to plan years prior to 2025, we do not believe that the reference to the initial coverage limit is necessary. VIII. Aligning Data and Value To Nurture Competition and Efficiency in Medicare Advantage (ADVaNCE MA) Model
A. Introduction and Background
1. Introduction and Goals of the ADVaNCE MA Model
Under the authority of section 1115A of the Act, the CMS Innovation Center proposes to implement and test a mandatory, 10-year model: the Aligning Data and Value to Nurture Competition and Efficiency in Medicare Advantage (ADVaNCE MA) model. We are proposing the ADVaNCE MA model would begin January 1, 2029, and end December 31, 2038, with bid submissions for the first year of the model, calendar year (CY) 2029, due in June 2028. In addition, there would be a pre-implementation period beginning
(
printed page 76445)
on June 8, 2027, the CY 2028 bid deadline, and ending December 31, 2028, during which pre-performance contracting and operational activities required for appropriate implementation would occur.
MA covers more than half of all Medicare beneficiaries. The ADVaNCE MA model is designed to test potential avenues to further incentivize quality improvement among MA organizations, promote local competition, reduce program expenditures, and address concerns for potential fraud, waste, and abuse or avoidable costs to the Medicare program.
[
127 128 129 130 131
]
The ADVaNCE MA model would test approaches to addressing some of the structural mechanisms in question through three core components:
CMMI Inferred Risk Adjustment Model: Explore, through shadow testing, an innovative risk adjustment methodology that builds upon the current CMS Hierarchical Condition Category (HCC) risk adjustment model by integrating multiple, existing data sources already available to CMS, including Original Medicare (OM) claims data, MA encounter data, enrollment data, and new technologies. The learnings from the shadow test are expected to inform future risk adjustment policy.
The Diamond Ratings System: A redesigned quality program implemented in Mandatory States (defined below) would replace the current MA and Part D Star Ratings and Quality Bonus Payment (QBP) system with a localized, cohort-based, quality framework that incentivizes continuous improvement; enables beneficiaries to make meaningful, geographically relevant plan comparisons in their local areas; and promotes competition in the Medicare Advantage program;
Targeted Supplemental Benefits for Low-Income Subsidy (LIS)-Eligible Individuals: New regulatory flexibilities would allow MA organizations to offer certain supplemental benefits, currently mostly available to qualifying chronically ill beneficiaries, to Part D LIS-eligible individuals. These benefits have a focus on high-value preventive care and serious illness support through nutrition, caregiver supports, and transportation for non-medical needs that aim to improve quality outcomes; and
Dialysis Carveout for Beneficiaries with End-Stage Renal Disease: CMS is considering, but not currently proposing, to exclude payment for dialysis services from MA for beneficiaries with end stage renal disease (ESRD) as a component of the ADVaNCE MA Model. Under this concept, for beneficiaries with ESRD, dialysis providers would bill OM directly and be reimbursed through the ESRD Prospective Payment System (PPS). If finalized as a part of the ADVaNCE MA model, in future rulemaking, additional details with respect to interactions under the ESRD PPS would be provided.
Sections 1102(a) and 1871(a)(1) of the Act provide the Secretary with the authority to implement regulations necessary to administer the Medicare program. In addition, section 1115A of the Act authorizes the Secretary to test innovative payment and service delivery models that reduce program expenditures while preserving or enhancing the quality of care furnished to beneficiaries. Section 1115A(b) of the Act authorizes the Secretary to select and test payment and service delivery models subject to the requirements and considerations specified in that subsection. The proposed ADVaNCE MA model would be tested pursuant to the model selection criteria of section 1115A(b)(2)(A) of the Act.
The CMS Innovation Center, under its statutory authority, is proposing the ADVaNCE MA model to test alternative approaches to payment and service delivery in MA for purposes of evaluating whether these approaches would improve or maintain quality, while reducing program expenditures. Goals of the ADVaNCE MA model include spurring local plan competition, enhancing beneficiary choice and value, and protecting taxpayers by safeguarding against improper payments and fraud, waste, and abuse. On the whole, savings are also anticipated, for instance, through the removal of “double bonus counties” and through supplemental benefit offerings that existing medical literature supports will decrease hospitalizations and improve enrollee health, the ADVaNCE MA model would be primarily evaluated on two factors: (1) the quality of care furnished through the model, and (2) changes in expenditures.
The ADVaNCE MA model is grounded in the CMS Innovation Center's 2025 Strategic Direction, which established three inter-related pillars to build healthier lives and Make America Healthy Again: (1) promote evidence-based prevention; (2) empower people to achieve health goals; and (3) drive choice and competition. These pillars are anchored in the Center's statutory obligation to protect taxpayers.

The alignment of each ADVaNCE MA model core component with these strategic pillars is detailed throughout this introductory section.

The methodology is intended to help beneficiaries understand differences in quality performance between contracts. The ADVaNCE MA model seeks to enable dual eligible special needs plans (D-SNP)-specific comparisons based on quality, and more specific geographically based quality rankings to inform beneficiary choice. The ADVaNCE MA model presents an opportunity to explore whether a different approach to quality measurement could complement the existing framework, support greater transparency, broaden benefit availability, and bolster a more dynamic competitive environment across MA organizations of all sizes.
