3. Mandatory Nature of the ADVaNCE MA Model
We propose the ADVaNCE MA model as a mandatory test, in Mandatory States, as we believe doing so is essential to evaluate the ability of the ADVaNCE MA model to improve
(
printed page 76448)
quality of care and reduce program expenditures. We also believe a mandatory test is appropriate because the ADVaNCE MA model would test changes to MA payment, quality incentives, and risk adjustment that are intended to operate across local markets and, therefore, require broad participation within select geographic areas. As such, we believe that requiring MA organizations with eligible plans in Mandatory States to participate would reduce the potential for self-selection bias, improve the representativeness of participating MA organizations across geographic areas, and support sufficient participation to generate meaningful results. We discuss specific proposals relating to mandatory participation and Mandatory States in more detail in section VIII.D. of this proposed rule.
We also believe that a mandatory test of this model is appropriate because there are several limitations when conducting a voluntary test. In a voluntary model test, participants may be able to choose to join the model after the performance period has already begun depending on model parameters. This can present significant evaluation challenges. As noted in the Fourth Evaluation Report of the Medicare Advantage Value-Based Insurance Design (VBID) model-the only prior CMS Innovation Center model test focused on the MA program, which concluded in 2025-VBID participation increased substantially over time (from 144 plans in 2020 to 1,400 in 2024), resulting in the majority of VBID plans being first-year implementers throughout the model timeline, limiting the ability of evaluation results to “fully capture VBID's long-term effects on outcomes.”
[
153
]
The evaluation report also found that the significant rise in VBID model population contributed to other evaluation limitations. That is, “self-selection into the model presented particular challenges for D-SNPs. By 2023, the majority of eligible D-SNPs had joined the model test, leaving a smaller and possibly a skewed selected sample of nonparticipating D-SNPs to serve as comparators.”
[
154
]
In short, a continued influx of model participants each year (and decline in available comparators) could limit our ability to evaluate the impact of the ADVaNCE MA model, and is why, in part, we are proposing a mandatory framework.
Depending on the terms of the model, a voluntary model test may also permit participants to cease their model participation before the end of the model performance period. CMS has noted that, “in some cases, voluntary participation can limit potential savings and impede evaluation due to selection bias as participants may opt in if they project that the financial incentives in the model are in their favor and drop out when potential losses are projected.”
[
155
]
As noted previously, in VBID, the participants could shift year to year with contracts participating in the model one year but not the next, which caused problems for the evaluation. Under the ADVaNCE MA model, all applicable MA plan types in a Mandatory State would be required to participate, as discussed in section VIII.D.2.a of this proposed rule. This ensures maximum consistency and fuels the ability of the model to meet its goals and the mission of the CMS Innovation Center to identify, test, and scale new ways to pay for and deliver better healthcare.
Moreover, the CBO previously noted that the CMS Innovation Center has greater potential to meet its statutory obligations related to program cost and quality were it to shift to mandatory models, stating “[The CMS Innovation Center] might also achieve larger savings in its second decade if it reduced the potential for selective participation by shifting from voluntary to mandatory models.”
[
156
]
That is, voluntary models may be more susceptible to attrition and volatility, particularly since high-volume participants may choose to cease model participation prior to the end of the model test period (due to market, financial, or regulatory factors, for example), exacerbating sample size and selection bias issues over time. The ADVaNCE MA model would be prone to many of the drawbacks of voluntary models, which is in part, why we are proposing it as a mandatory model.
We believe a robust and consistent evaluation of the ADVaNCE MA model necessitates sustained participation in the ADVaNCE MA model, which would be fostered by a mandatory model design. Such participation over time also can aid the statistical calculations underlying the evaluation of the Diamond Ratings system that require sufficient participation over multiple years to generate reliable, population-level results, as proposed at § 516.200(a) and described in section VIII.F.
4. Summary
The proposed aspects of the model described in this section build on information gathered from the RFIs described above.
a. Risk Adjustment
The ADVaNCE MA model proposes to shadow test a CMMI Inferred Risk Adjustment Model that builds upon the current HCC framework by integrating multiple, additional data sources already available to CMS, including OM claims data, MA encounter data, enrollment data, and new technologies. The shadow test will begin during the pre-implementation period and run in parallel with the existing risk adjustment methodology; at this time, we are not proposing risk adjustment related payment changes under the ADVaNCE MA model to be tied to shadow test results. The purpose of the shadow test is to generate learnings about how new approaches may improve the accuracy of risk adjustment, determine if its use reduces susceptibility to upcoding, and test if its use better reflects beneficiaries' actual health status and care needs. These learnings are expected to inform future risk adjustment policies in the ADVaNCE MA model. The specific design of the CMMI Inferred Risk Adjustment Model is described in detail in section VIII.E of this proposed rule.
b. Diamond Ratings System
The Diamond Ratings system for the ADVaNCE MA model would test an innovative design for quality assessment and quality based payment. A key mechanism for achieving this is measuring quality at a more granular geographic level in cases in which contracts previously spanned multiple states. This approach would spur local quality improvement, help beneficiaries make meaningful, geographically relevant plan comparisons, and encourage plans to more meaningfully compete on the basis of quality of care. The Diamond Ratings system would also test if replacing the payment thresholds in the current, statutorily based QBP adjusted benchmark methodology can create more incentives for plans to improve quality by more directly linking incremental
(
printed page 76449)
performance differences with incremental payment impacts and utilizing ranking rather than threshold based rewards through a more competitive funding environment among all plans. The specific design of the Diamond Ratings system is described in detail in section VIII.F of this proposed rule.
c. Supplemental Benefits
To test potential alternatives to the supplemental benefit structure described earlier in section VIII.G.3.(d) of this proposed rule, we propose to allow targeting of certain supplemental benefits to LIS-eligible individuals under the ADVaNCE MA model. That is, ADVaNCE MA model participants would be allowed to target certain supplemental benefits specifically to Part D LIS-eligible individuals, as defined at
42 CFR 423.34(b)(2)
. This is intended to assess whether such flexibilities would enable ADVaNCE MA model participants to support access to preventive care and address drivers of unnecessary healthcare expenditures and adverse health outcomes for high-need beneficiaries, and whether doing so would reduce program expenditures and improve overall quality of care. The ADVaNCE MA model expands the offering of benefits available through Special Supplemental Benefits for the Chronically Ill (SSBCI), by making certain supplemental benefits available to LIS-eligible individuals. This would level the playing field for disparately resourced MA organizations since some may currently face challenges implementing existing supplemental benefit authorities due to limited funding, staffing, and/or data systems. As proposed in § 516.300(a)(1)(i) through (iii), the ADVaNCE MA model would allow MA organizations to offer the following supplemental benefits to LIS-eligible individuals:
Healthy food and produce.
Transportation for non-medical needs (TNMN).
Supports for caregivers of enrollees.
Of these three benefits, healthy food and produce and TNMN are currently allowable only as SSBCI. We believe that testing these flexibilities could empower enrollees and caregivers, encourage innovative and value-driven benefit designs, improve quality, reduce avoidable healthcare utilization, and encourage more meaningful competition. These benefits may have cascading impact, not only among MA organizations but among healthy food and transportation vendors, also resulting in improved quality of care for enrollees. For example, based on responses to our 2024 RFI on MA Data as well as external research, CMS believes enabling smaller, more local MA organizations to offer certain prevention-oriented benefits could reduce barriers to relationships between MA organizations and smaller, local vendors (such as family-operated grocers, local farmers, and community transportation providers).

]
The inclusion of such vendors in MA organizations' supplemental benefit networks may impact their continued operation and/or competition on price and quality with larger, national vendors (which more national MA organizations may contract with) to better ensure supplemental benefit access across multiple States/non-contiguous service areas.
d. Dialysis Payments
We are considering, but are not currently proposing, a policy to carve-out outpatient dialysis payments from the MA benefit for beneficiaries with ESRD that live in Mandatory States. Since the 21st Century Cures Act allowed beneficiaries with ESRD to enroll in MA, as of December 2024, 55 percent of the Medicare beneficiaries with ESRD were enrolled in MA. Currently, MA organizations negotiate dialysis payment rates directly with facilities rather than using the OM ESRD PPS rates. However, there are two dominant providers who control 75 percent of market share, meaning they have significant leverage over the payment rates in MA. A 2026 MedPAC study indicated MA organizations pay, on average, 22 percent more for dialysis treatment than OM, a trend that has occurred for many years.
[

The goal of this policy would be to lower MA dialysis costs without reducing access to dialysis for beneficiaries. We request comments on this potential policy, including its costs, benefits, and other impacts, as well as any alternative approaches that would achieve the desired policy aims of reducing spending in this area, promoting choice and competition, and best serving the needs of beneficiaries with ESRD.
5. Alignment With the CMS Innovation Center's Strategic Vision To Make America Healthy Again
The CMS Innovation Center's 2025 Strategic Direction established a vision to build healthier lives grounded in three pillars: (1) promote evidence-based prevention; (2) empower people to achieve health goals; and (3) drive choice and competition. These pillars are anchored in the CMS Innovation Center's statutory obligation to protect taxpayers.
[
160
]
As detailed throughout this proposed rule, the ADVaNCE MA model is designed to operationalize each of these pillars. Table I-1 summarizes the proposed innovations of the ADVaNCE MA model for each of the three pillars and supporting principle of protecting taxpayers.
a. Promote Evidence-Based Prevention
The CMS Innovation Center's prevention pillar incentivizes model participants to promote access to timely preventive services and encourages investments in chronic disease management. It expands the use of beneficiary engagement incentives tied to health promotion and sustained lifestyle changes and encourages the use of metrics to track preventive outcomes, including metrics focused on reducing the progression of chronic illness.
The ADVaNCE MA model progresses this pillar by allowing plans to target certain supplemental benefits aimed at promoting prevention: healthy food and produce, TNMN, and supports for caregivers of enrollees. Healthy food and produce and TNMN—currently available only to chronically ill MA beneficiaries who qualify for SSBCI—have the potential to prevent the onset of chronic illness and delay progression of existing chronic conditions. Additionally, supports for caregivers of enrollees may prevent beneficiaries (especially those who are experiencing advanced illness or functional and cognitive decline) from disease progression that might otherwise require more intensive institutional care. These flexibilities are intended to test if CMS can realize improved health outcomes and reduced Medicare expenditures for high-needs beneficiaries by directly tying these alternative benefit designs to
(
printed page 76450)
health prevention and long-term, sustained lifestyle changes.
b. Empower People To Achieve Health Goals
The CMS Innovation Center's empowerment pillar focuses on equipping people with tools, information, and processes that better connect them to their health data and support informed health decisions. This includes increasing data access, aligning financial incentives with health outcomes, and publishing data on provider, plan cost, and quality performance to support beneficiary decision-making.
The ADVaNCE MA model advances this pillar in two ways. First, the Diamond Ratings system would test whether reporting an MA parent organization's performance at the State level by cohort and delivering localized comparative quality data to beneficiaries enables more informed plan selection. Second, the supplemental benefit flexibilities for LIS-eligible individuals, including targeting of healthy food and produce, TNMN, and supports for caregivers of enrollees, are intended to assess whether such benefits may empower beneficiaries and caregivers to engage in prevention-based activities and enable beneficiaries to remain in the community longer.
c. Drive Choice and Competition
The CMS Innovation Center's competition pillar promotes stronger market-based incentives that encourage providers and MA organizations to deliver higher-value care and expands information on high-value coverage options to stimulate beneficiary choice and competition.
The ADVaNCE MA model advances this pillar through the Diamond Ratings system, which is designed to encourage stronger local-level competition among MA organizations by measuring and reporting quality at the State level by cohort, and by utilizing forced ranking. This alternative, more localized framework, is intended to provide beneficiaries with meaningful and clear quality comparisons between MA organizations and create direct incentives for MA organizations to compete on quality within the Mandatory States. Additionally, the supplemental benefit flexibilities proposed under the ADVaNCE MA model are intended to promote competition among healthy food and transportation vendors through contracts with MA organizations that are offering targeted benefits to LIS-eligible individuals, driving value. Finally, in considering moving MA dialysis payments to OM, we hope to drive competition in the dialysis market.
d. Protecting Taxpayers
All three pillars of the CMS Innovation Center's Strategic Direction are anchored in the obligation to protect taxpayers. The ADVaNCE MA model moves this forward by: (1) shadow testing a CMMI Inferred Risk Adjustment Model; (2) refining quality reporting and payment; (3) testing whether permitting MA organizations to target to LIS-eligible individuals reduces the future costs of chronic disease through preventive supplemental benefits; and (4) considering changes to dialysis payment structure.

C. Statutory Authority and ADVaNCE MA Model Length
1. Statutory Authority
Section 1115A(a)(1) of the Act (
42 U.S.C. 1315a
) authorizes the CMS Innovation Center to test innovative payment and service delivery models expected to reduce Medicare, Medicaid, and Children's Health Insurance Program (CHIP) expenditures while preserving or enhancing the quality of care furnished to the beneficiaries of such programs. Section 1115A(b) authorizes the Secretary to select and test payment and service delivery models subject to the requirements and considerations specified in that subsection. In addition, section 1115A(c) of the Act authorizes the Secretary to expand (including implementation on a nationwide basis), through rulemaking, the duration and scope of successful models if certain requirements are met—namely, reducing spending without reducing the quality of care or improving quality without increasing spending.
2. ADVaNCE MA Model Test
At § 516.2, we propose that the ADVaNCE MA model would operate across three periods that would comprise the model test: a pre-implementation period; a 10-year model performance period; and a post-implementation period, as detailed further in this section.
a. Pre-Implementation Period
We propose at § 516.2(a) to establish a pre-implementation period that encompasses the period beginning on June 8, 2027, the CY 2028 bid deadline, and ending December 31, 2028, during which pre-performance contracting and operational activities required for appropriate implementation of the ADVaNCE MA model would occur. We believe that the pre-implementation period is necessary to engage in preparation activities so that both CMS and ADVaNCE MA model participants are ready to begin the ADVaNCE MA model on the start date of the model performance period described in subparagraph VIII.C.2.b. below. Under the proposal, we would consider the shadow testing of the CMMI Inferred Risk Adjustment Model described in section VIII.E of this proposed rule to be an operational activity that would begin during the pre-implementation period, though we note that, as described in section VIII.C.2.a, this activity would continue beyond the pre-implementation period.
We seek comment on our proposal at § 516.2(a) to establish a pre-implementation period, on the proposed length of the pre-implementation period, and the proposed contracting and operational activities to be conducted during the pre-implementation period.
b. Model Performance Period
At § 516.2(b), we propose that the ADVaNCE MA model performance period would consist of 10 consecutive performance years, each aligned with the calendar year, beginning January 1, 2029, and ending December 31, 2038, unless the ADVaNCE MA model is terminated earlier either in accordance with
42 CFR 512.165
or to effectuate an expansion of the model in accordance with section 1115A(c) of the Act.
We considered employing a shorter ADVaNCE MA model performance period of five years. However, as discussed in sections VIII.F. and G. of this proposed rule, the ADVaNCE MA model would introduce new approaches to quality measurement and the associated payments, as well as supplemental benefits flexibilities, which, collectively, would constitute new efforts in MA and require substantial time to test, implement, and evaluate. For example, as described in section VIII.F of this proposed rule, the model's proposed-Diamond Ratings-
system would
replace the MA and Part D Star Ratings program's statutorily required approach
for
adjusting payments with a continuous payment scale. As proposed, there would be a three-year gap between when quality measurement data are collected and the point at which the outcomes would influence ADVaNCE MA model participant payments. For example, under the terms of the model, quality ratings based on the applicable measurement period data impacting the 2031 Diamond Ratings would not influence ADVaNCE MA payments until CY 2032. Consequently, a five-year ADVaNCE MA model performance period, CY 2029 through CY 2033, would result in CMS having only two years of payment data from the point at which an ADVaNCE MA model participant's payments were influenced by the Diamond Ratings system before the model would conclude. Further, we expect ADVaNCE MA model participants' quality of care in response to the model to improve over time as they gain more experience, which could impact their bids and quality improvement practices in later years, potentially making results from the earlier years of the model less representative of future years. As such, we believe that a five-year model would have too short an implementation period to observe these changes, thereby limiting insights into the Diamond Ratings system's impacts on quality and payments. Furthermore, one of the goals of the proposed Diamond Ratings system is to promote local competition, which can take several years as it incentivizes organizations to enter new markets. A five-year model would allow there would only be two years of data to evaluate the effects of the ADVaNCE MA model's impact on MA market competition and the resultant effects on quality and costs, which we believe is not likely to be enough time for the competition to increase. Finally, MA data, such as encounter data, is typically not sufficient for analytics until up to two years after the completion of the service CY, meaning, we are unlikely to have sufficient data to accurately determine next steps for the model after only a five-year period. We believe this limited timeline would restrict our ability to make informed decisions about potential next steps for the model, such as nationwide expansion.

Consequently, we believe that a five-year performance period ending in 2033 would provide insufficient evidence to evaluate the ADVaNCE MA model's proposed quality program's impact on quality of care, payment changes, and market competition.
We also considered interim performance-period lengths of six through nine years. Similar to the logic for a five-year performance period, given the lag between the measurement period and the associated payment, ADVaNCE MA model lengths of six or seven years also would not allow for enough payment data to accumulate to-properly evaluate the payment results before the conclusion of the ADVaNCE MA model. From there, recognizing that past mandatory models, such as the Comprehensive Care for Joint Replacement (CJR) model,
38
were eight years in length, we further considered performance periods of eight and nine years. However, experience has shown that the greater the complexity of a model, the more likely it is that midstream changes are required, which then extend a model's performance period. For example, over the course of the CJR model, joint replacement surgeries went from being primarily inpatient procedures to being primarily outpatient procedures. This fundamental shift in the clinical landscape required numerous midstream model changes and model extensions. Model extensions tend to be destabilizing for stakeholders, because the policy landscape is constantly shifting. Because the ADVaNCE MA model would create the Diamond Ratings system while simultaneously implementing changes to supplemental benefits, we believe that a longer performance period would ensure market stability in order to allow the expected outcomes of quality improvement and increased competition, goals that we believe will take time to materialize.
After consideration of these alternatives, we believe a 10-year ADVaNCE MA model performance period would provide ADVaNCE MA model participants with the time necessary to make operational and strategic investments to accommodate the model's requirements and would allow CMS to conduct a robust evaluation of the model's impacts on MA costs and quality, while giving sufficient time for ADVaNCE MA model participants to effectuate changes to competition and care delivery. We believe a 10-year performance period would increase the likelihood-that these investments would have sufficient time to produce measurable effects and that CMS would have sufficient evidence to evaluate the model within the time constraints of CMS Innovation Center model test periods. If we believe we have gained sufficient evidence to make decisions about the model in fewer than 10 years, we could seek to end the model earlier pursuant to § 512.165, or, alternately, to expand the model in accordance with section 1115A(c) of the Act. We believe that preemptively choosing a shorter model performance period would increase the risk that there will not be sufficient time to see the full impact of the model.
We considered a model start date of January 1, 2030, or later, but we believe that our proposed start date affords sufficient preparation time for CMS and ADVaNCE MA model participants to implement and operationalize the necessary changes. We also believe that the potential positive impact of the proposed ADVaNCE MA model is significant enough to warrant beginning the test as soon as practicable. Furthermore, initiating the ADVaNCE MA model performance period in CY 2029 would be sufficient to accommodate the Federal rulemaking process, allowing us to conduct thorough outreach to interested parties and gather critical feedback from commenters.
We seek comment on our proposal in § 516.2(b) to establish a 10-year model performance period, on the alternatives of five years through nine years, and potential alternate model lengths. We also seek comment on the proposed ADVaNCE MA model start date of January 1, 2029 for PY one, on the alternately considered start date of January 1, 2030, and the corresponding adjustment to dates of the ADVaNCE MA model performance period.
c. Post-Implementation Period
We propose at § 516.2(c) to establish for the ADVaNCE MA model a post-implementation period consisting of the three consecutive payment years that would immediately follow the model performance period (
e.g.,
if the model performance period ends December 31, 2038, the post-implementation period would begin January 1, 2039, and end December 31, 2041). Further, we propose that the main purpose of the post-implementation period is for CMS to provide final payments associated with the model's Diamond Ratings system as described in section VIII.F of this proposed rule. As previously discussed in this section and further elaborated in section VIII.F.4. of this proposed rule, ADVaNCE MA model payments would begin in CY 2032 and continue for 10 years. We believe this proposal is appropriate to ensure that ADVaNCE MA model participants align their care delivery with the Diamond Ratings system's incentive structure throughout the entirety of the model's applicable performance period.
As described in greater detail in section VIII.F.1.a., CMS alternatively considered proposing a final measurement period for the ADVaNCE MA model applicable to the 2037 Diamond Ratings, which would have resulted in a shorter, seven-year period in which an ADVaNCE MA model participant's first and final ADVaNCE MA payments would occur (CY 2032 and CY 2038, respectively). This alternative would have no post-implementation period. We considered this alternative as a means to accommodate the transition of ADVaNCE MA model participants back to the Star Ratings system and QBP system in CY 2039, following the conclusion of the model's performance period. However, we concluded that this consideration did not outweigh the importance of ADVaNCE MA model participants aligning their quality strategies and approaches with the Diamond Ratings system's incentive structure throughout the ADVaNCE MA model's entire applicable performance period, which we believe would strengthen the model's ability to generate reliable evaluation data by eliminating confounding factors that may arise from transitioning back to the Star Ratings system and QBP system during the model's performance period.
We seek comment on our proposal in § 516.2(c) for a post-implementation period of the three consecutive payment years that would immediately follow the model performance period to provide final payments associated with the model's Diamond Ratings System, as well as the alternative described that would lead to a seven-year overall payment period, as well as any additional approaches to the model's payment period that CMS should consider.
D. Mandatory Participation, ADVaNCE MA Model Participants, Geographic Areas and Contract Structure Requirements for Operations
1. Mandatory Participation
As discussed in section VIII.A.3 of this proposed rule, we believe that a mandatory model design is necessary to support a sound evaluation of the ADVaNCE MA model. We are proposing to establish at § 516.100(a) that participation in the ADVaNCE MA model would be mandatory for all MA organizations that operate one or more
(

Under the proposal, all MA organizations that operate eligible plans during the ADVaNCE MA model's performance period would be required to participate in the model and offer eligible plans under contracts that meet requirements proposed in section VIII.D.4.b of this proposed rule. Note that proposals to establish and describe eligible plans and Mandatory States are discussed in sections VIII.D.2 and 3, respectively, of this proposed rule, and that the contract structure requirements for the ADVaNCE MA model are discussed in detail in section VIII.D.4. In the sections that follow, we describe our rationale for proposing mandatory participation and the scope of MA organizations subject to that requirement.

a. Rationale for Mandatory Participation
We considered making the ADVaNCE MA model voluntary. We believe that a mandatory model is necessary to ensure that a sufficient number of MA organizations participate in the ADVaNCE MA model, such that the model test is representative of the Nation and that CMS will be able to conduct a sound evaluation of the model's effects on cost and quality of care, in accordance with section 1115A(b)(4) of the Act.
CMS' past experience with models shows that potential model participants can be reluctant to participate voluntarily in any model in which their Medicare payments could be subject to change, and we do expect that this dynamic would be present with respect to the ADVaNCE MA model, specifically. Because payments under the Diamond Ratings system would be based on an MA organization's relative performance within its local market (see the discussion of Diamond Ratings system scoring methodology in section VIII.F.3 of this proposed rule), we believe that MA organizations that anticipate a competitive advantage under this new payment structure would be more likely to participate voluntarily than organizations that do not anticipate such an advantage. Under a voluntary design, this dynamic would be likely to produce a participant pool skewed toward organizations expecting favorable outcomes, rather than one representative of the national distribution of MA organizations. Additionally, we believe that voluntary participation in the model would make evaluations more challenging because, under a voluntary participation scenario, different MA organizations within the same service area could operate under different quality payment structures: some organizations' payments would be predicated on the Diamond Ratings system of the ADVaNCE MA model, as described in section VIII.F.4, while others would continue to be in the standard MA and Part D Star Ratings and QBP system, which operates under a fundamentally different structure. Having MA organizations in the same market operate under different quality payment structures would complicate evaluation results. Because the ADVaNCE MA model would establish a new quality payment structure, CMS acknowledges that individual contracts may experience changes in payment based on the application of policies under the ADVaNCE MA model's Diamond Ratings system. The first payment under the Diamond Ratings system would not occur until 2032, which is the first time that we expect ADVaNCE MA model participants may experience increases or decreases in associated payments relative to their previous QBP. Because the Diamond Ratings system payments are based on relative performance within a market, and we cannot definitively predict how each ADVaNCE MA model participant within a market would perform in the model, we do not have specific estimates for any potential participant for their payment rates during the ADVaNCE MA model's performance period as this method of measurement is unique to the Diamond Ratings system and ADVaNCE MA model requirements. CMS will continue efforts to ensure MA organizations are able to provide uninterrupted, high-quality care to beneficiaries by considering and incorporating feedback received through comments to this proposed rule and by releasing additional guidance via Health Plan Management System (HPMS) memos prior to the ADVaNCE MA model start date to ensure ADVaNCE MA model participant readiness.
To facilitate the generalizability of model evaluation results, and as described in more detail in this section, we believe that mandating participation would minimize the risk of potential distortions in the model's effects on outcomes resulting from self-selection as described earlier in section VIII.A.3.
We seek comment on our proposal to make participation in the ADVaNCE MA model mandatory.
b. Scope of Mandatory Participation
There are two major elements to the proposed mandatory construct for the ADVaNCE MA model: eligible plan types and geographic areas. We discuss the eligible plan types for which mandatory participation would apply in section VIII.D.2 and the proposal for geographic areas in VIII.D.3. Under these proposals, all MA organizations offering eligible plans within the Mandatory States would be subject to ADVaNCE MA model requirements. Plans offered by MA organizations in States other than the Mandatory States would not be subject to ADVaNCE MA model requirements. To accommodate this scope, our proposals discussed in section VIII.D.2 would require MA organizations operating eligible plan types for which mandatory participation would apply to organize into contracts that meet the requirements described in section VIII.D.4 of this proposed rule. As noted in section VIII.D.1 above, at § 516.100(a), we propose to establish the participation unit at the contract level in accordance with § 516.150 and as discussed in section VIII.D.4 of this proposed rule. We considered establishing participation units at the level of MA plans rather than MA contracts. While we believe this alternative participation unit would have been simpler for MA organizations to implement and for CMS to include or exclude specific plan types from the model, operational considerations led us to ultimately propose MA contracts as the participation unit. Specifically, the current infrastructure of the MA program relies on several information systems to collect and calculate integral metrics for MA organizations at the contract level. For example, HPMS, which handles the data collection and reporting activities that MA and Part D plans must complete, organizes nearly all plan-level data by MA contract number. The MA and Part D Star Ratings and QBP system evaluates quality at the contract level, which shapes the benchmarks that plans within an MA contract bid against to set base capitated payment rates; CMS then adjusts these rates further through risk adjustment at the contract level. CMS also determines compliance, oversight, and sanctions—including termination circumstances under
42 CFR 422.510
and MLR requirements under
42 CFR part 422 Subpart X—at
the contract level. Accordingly, an MA-based model

Therefore, we are not proposing an alternative participation unit, to ensure the operational feasibility of the ADVaNCE MA model.
We seek comment on our proposal to use MA contracts as our unit of participation.
2. Plan Eligibility

We believe this broad approach to inclusion would create a representative testing environment that reflects the MA landscape and enables CMS to better assess the ADVaNCE MA model's reforms across different plan structures.
We considered defining eligible and ineligible plans for the ADVaNCE MA model by service area. However, we believe this approach is unnecessary. We considered two alternatives to our proposal to make D-SNPs of all integration levels eligible plan types for the ADVaNCE MA model. First, we considered proposing the exclusion of all D-SNPs because of the complex coordination requirements between Medicare and Medicaid services and varying levels of integration across different D-SNP configurations, which we recognized could complicate the implementation of the ADVaNCE MA model. Second, we considered proposing that all non-AIP CO D-SNPs participate in the ADVaNCE MA model because they historically hold the highest share of D-SNP enrollees and offer the minimum required level of integration. Though we recognize that more highly integrated D-SNP types, such as FIDE SNPs and HIDE SNPs, must meet extensive Medicare-Medicaid coordination, enrollment, and benefit coverage requirements, we considered that non-AIP CO D-SNPs could adapt to the ADVaNCE MA model's temporary changes while still providing meaningful data on their impact. We rejected these first two alternatives as we believe that broader participation of D-SNPs in the ADVaNCE MA model would strengthen the model's evaluation by increasing sample sizes, improving demographic heterogeneity, and producing more statistically robust and generalizable findings. Further, including D-SNPs of all integration levels ensures that all D-SNPs in a Mandatory State that do not opt out—as discussed in section VIII.D.2.c—operate under a cohesive set of rules. While dually eligible beneficiaries enrolled in C-SNPs and general MA plans would continue to have access to the model's benefits, CMS believes it is important that the model's potential benefits extend to dually eligible beneficiaries across all D-SNP integration levels. Broad inclusion of D-SNPs also avoids uneven incentives across the market that may distort D-SNP behavior and undermine the integrity of the ADVaNCE MA model's test conditions.

Broadly, we believe that by including plan types in the ADVaNCE MA model where it is feasible to do so, we strengthen the model's evaluation by increasing sample sizes and capturing results from the model's application to a variety of plan types, ultimately improving the generalizability of findings across eligible plan types. 42 CFR 422.138(a)

However, we determined that these differences do not represent a barrier to participation and that inclusion of PFFS plans strengthens the model's evaluation as described above. b. Ineligible Plan Types
We propose at § 516.100(b)(2) that an ineligible plan is one of the following plan types (listed at clauses (i) through (iv), respectively): (1) Institutional SNPs (I-SNPs); (2) Medical Savings Accounts (MSAs); (3) Regional Preferred Provider Organization (RPPOs); and (4) EGWPs. (1) I-SNPs
We propose in § 516.100(b)(2)(i) that I-SNPs are ineligible for the ADVaNCE MA model. I-SNPs are MA plans that restrict enrollment to MA-eligible individuals who meet the definition of institutionalized or institutionalized-equivalent (
42 CFR 422.2
), a population with particularly complex care needs that is highly sensitive to changes in plan benefit structures. We believe that including I-SNPs in the ADVaNCE MA model would introduce implementation and evaluation complexity that differs materially from the plan types otherwise proposed for inclusion for two primary reasons. First, I-SNP enrollees are among the highest-need beneficiaries in the MA program, and we believe that subjecting this population to the operational and benefit structure
(
printed page 76458)
changes associated with ADVaNCE MA model participation could risk unnecessary disruptions to the specialized care and benefits they currently receive. While we recognize that a proportion of enrollees in other SNP types may also have high acuity needs or reside in skilled nursing facilities, I-SNPs are uniquely defined by and designed around the institutionalized population, making the potential risks of disruption more acute and uniform across their enrolled populations. Second, I-SNPs represent a relatively small share of total MA enrollment, and as a result, their inclusion would contribute minimally to the model's overall sample size and would not meaningfully impact the model's ability to generate generalizable findings. Accordingly, we propose to exclude all I-SNP subtypes from the ADVaNCE MA model.
We solicit comments on our proposal to make I-SNPs ineligible for the ADVaNCE MA model.
(2) MSA Plans
We propose at § 516.100(b)(2)(ii) that MSA plans are ineligible for the ADVaNCE MA model. MSA plans have a fundamentally different payment and benefit structure compared to other MA plan types, such as HMOs and Local PPO plans, which we believe imposes the risk of skewing model evaluations. Specifically, unlike eligible plan types proposed for inclusion in the model, MSA plans do not directly submit bids against county-level benchmarks and are not paid based on a comparison of plan bids against county level benchmarks. Because the ADVaNCE MA model's payment approach is designed around the bid-to-benchmark payment structure common to other MA plan types, incorporating MSA plans would require substantial modifications to the ADVaNCE MA model's payment methodology and risk skewing model evaluations by introducing a structurally distinct comparator. Further, MSA plans generally lack provider networks that could be leveraged to improve quality through care coordination, which is the underlying foundation of the Diamond Ratings system, discussed in section VIII.F of this proposed rule. Overall, we believe excluding MSA plans would ensure that the ADVaNCE MA model could be implemented consistently across participating plan types without requiring substantial modifications to the ADVaNCE MA model's proposed payment approach to accommodate fundamentally different payment structures.
We solicit comments on our proposal to make MSA plans ineligible for the ADVaNCE MA model.
(3) RPPOs
We propose in § 516.100(b)(2)(iii) that RPPO plans are ineligible for the ADVaNCE MA model. We recognize that RPPOs use a different payment methodology than the majority of MA plans. Unlike most MA plans, whose benchmarks are based on county rates, the benchmark for an RPPO plan is determined using a blend of the statutory regional benchmark and the weighted average of RPPO plan bids within the region which would create an uneven payment structure across plan types in the context of the ADVaNCE MA model. Excluding RPPO plans, as proposed, would allow for more consistent implementation across participating plan types while avoiding unnecessary complications associated with regional plan structures.
We solicit comments on our proposal to make RPPO plans ineligible for the ADVaNCE MA model.
(4) EGWPs
We propose in § 516.100(b)(2)(iv) that EGWPs are ineligible for the ADVaNCE MA model. EGWPs have a distinct regulatory and contractual framework (notably with respect to bidding requirements and enrollment mechanisms) and non-representative enrollee population relative to the MA plan types that we are proposing to be eligible for the ADVaNCE MA model. The bidding requirements for EGWPs differ from the standard MA bid submission process used by the other MA plan types we propose as eligible and would require consideration of additional payment policies unique to this plan type. Including EGWPs may also add complexity in navigating contracts between CMS, MA organizations, and employers or unions when implementing mandatory requirements for the ADVaNCE MA model. Beyond these complexities, EGWP enrollment processes and timelines observe unique flexibilities that are not available to individual MA plans, which we believe would limit the generalizability of the model's findings. Accordingly, we propose to exclude EGWPs from the ADVaNCE MA model.
We solicit comments on our proposal to make EGWPs ineligible for the ADVaNCE MA model.

3. Geographic Areas
We propose to describe at § 516.100(e) the geographic areas that would be included in the ADVaNCE MA model. Specifically, as discussed further in section VIII.D.3.b below, we propose to use States, including the District of Columbia (herein collectively referred to as “States”), as the selected geographic areas that determine mandatory participation in the ADVaNCE MA model. Under this proposal, all MA organizations that meet the participation requirements discussed in section VIII.D.2.a. of this proposed rule and operate within a Mandatory State would be subject to the ADVaNCE MA model, consistent with the contract-level participation framework discussed in section VIII.D.4. We further propose to exclude all U.S. Territories from eligibility as discussed in section VIII.D.3.c below, as well as any State that, based on the Monthly Enrollment by Contract/Plan/State/County data, MA State/County Penetration, and Special Needs Plan (SNP) Data made publicly available for the timeframe described, had fewer than 1,000 beneficiaries enrolled in eligible plans. For Alaska and Connecticut, the applicable timeframe is July 2024. For all other States, the applicable timeframe is March 2026. The reason for these timeframes is discussed in section VIII.D.3.c relating to the exclusions and is explained more broadly in section VIII.D.3.d.
We would use a three-step process to determine the specific Mandatory States that would participate in the model, as described in more detail in this section. First, as described in section VIII.D.3.c of proposed rule, we propose to exclude States that do not meet our geographic inclusion criteria. Second, as described in section VIII.D.3.d. of this proposed rule, we propose to classify States into groups on the basis of their similarity across composite variables. Third, as described in section VIII.D.3.e. of this proposed rule, we propose to randomly select States from within each group.
a. Alternatives Considered
In developing the proposed ADVaNCE MA model, we considered several alternative approaches to using entire States for defining the geographic and organizational units that would be used for reportability of Diamond Ratings scores (see section VIII.F of this proposed rule). These alternatives included: (1) retaining the use of Original Contract Service Areas without modification; (2) using Office of Management and Budget (OMB)-defined Combined Statistical Areas (CSAs), or
(
printed page 76461)
combinations of multiple CSAs, as the geographic unit; and (3) other organizational grouping configurations. After careful analysis, we determined, as discussed below, that none of these alternatives adequately achieved the policy objectives of the ADVaNCE MA model and, accordingly, we are not pursuing them.
(1) Original Contract Service Areas
We considered proposing existing MA contract service areas, that is, the geographic boundaries already established under each MA contract with CMS, as the sole basis for defining the geographic unit of participation and reportability. Under this approach, MA organizations would have been evaluated for reportability solely within the boundaries of their existing contract service areas, as those areas are defined at the time of bid submission.
We believe that using existing contract service areas would inhibit the goals of the model around competition based on quality. Relying solely on existing contract service areas without modification would be inconsistent with our goal of testing the ADVaNCE MA model's impact on program expenditures and quality within a regional market that was applicable to a beneficiary's care experience. Additionally, utilizing the original contract service areas can lead to comparison of possibly incontiguous areas of the county, making the presentation of quality information to potential or current MA enrollees confusing. Though Star Ratings utilizes this approach, the use of a set geographic area was paramount to the Diamond Ratings program to promote local competition and geographic region easily understood by beneficiaries.
We also considered whether contract service areas could be combined on an ad hoc or manual basis, for example, by grouping geographically proximate or administratively related service areas without the application of a systematic, replicable algorithm. We determined that this approach would introduce inconsistency, lack transparency, and be difficult to administer uniformly for similarly situated MA organizations at scale across the full population of MA organizations participating in the ADVaNCE MA model. We believe that such potential inconsistency and lack of transparency could undermine the models' goal of enhancing competition.
(2) Combined Statistical Areas
We also considered the use of OMB-defined CSAs, which are broad geographic units that aggregate adjacent Core-Based Statistical Areas (CBSAs) based on economic and commuting ties, as the geographic unit for reportability determinations under the ADVaNCE MA model. We further considered whether combinations of multiple CSAs could be constructed to serve as adequate reportability units for the purposes of the Diamond Ratings system, with sufficient enrollment size. While the level of granularity, especially for the Diamond Ratings system, is desirable to CMS for its additional level of geographic detail, after careful analysis, we determined that neither the OMB CSA approach nor the multiple-CSA approach was appropriate for the ADVaNCE MA model for the reasons set forth below.
OMB-defined CSAs are delineated based on economic and social integration among adjacent metropolitan and micropolitan statistical areas, as reflected in commuting patterns and other indicators of functional interdependence.
[
169
]
While this framework serves important purposes in Federal statistical and administrative programs, it was not designed to reflect the geographic structure of MA contracting. MA contracts are organized at the county level and are established through county-level elections that reflect market strategy, network adequacy, and operational capacity, not the economic integration criteria that underlies OMB's CSA delineations.
[
170
]
Additionally, CBSAs and therefore CSAs can cross state lines. Because the ADVaNCE MA model, as proposed, would include D-SNPs, such potential spanning of State lines would introduce the complication that within the mandatory geographic unit there could be inconsistent State-level policies for dually eligible beneficiaries. Therefore, we believe that CSAs would complicate and impede aspects of the ADVaNCE MA model.
OMB-defined CSAs also do not provide comprehensive coverage of the United States. As of the most recent OMB delineations, a substantial portion of the U.S. population and a corresponding share of MA beneficiaries reside in counties that are not included within any CSA, including counties that are part of standalone Metropolitan Statistical Areas, Micropolitan Statistical Areas, or that fall outside all OMB-defined metropolitan and micropolitan delineations entirely.
[
171
]
Because MA enrollment can occur nationally, in non-CSA counties, a reportability framework anchored to CSA boundaries would systematically exclude or disadvantage MA organizations with significant enrollment in non-CSA counties. This would create unfair differences in treatment among similarly situated organizations and undermine the ADVaNCE MA model's goal of broad, representative participation across the national MA market. Additional detail regarding the process to create a nationally representative set of Mandatory States can be found in section VIII.D.3.d. of this proposed rule (Stratification Methodology).
We further considered whether the limitations of individual CSAs could be addressed by constructing reportability from combinations of multiple CSAs (for example, by aggregating adjacent or regionally proximate CSAs to achieve enrollment denominators sufficient for quality reporting under the Diamond Ratings system). We rejected this approach for several reasons, as described in this section.
First, there is no established Federal framework for systematically combining OMB-defined CSAs into larger geographic units for administrative or programmatic purposes. OMB's statistical area delineations are intended to reflect functional economic relationships among adjacent communities; combining multiple CSAs into larger composite units would depart from the underlying conceptual basis of the OMB framework and produce geographic units that lack a coherent administrative or analytical rationale.
Second, the construction of multiple CSA combinations would require significant discretion in determining which CSAs to aggregate and on what basis. Whether combinations were defined by geographic contiguity, enrollment size, market concentration, or other criteria, the resulting units would be difficult to define transparently and apply consistently. This discretionary complexity was part of the reason this option was considered and not proposed. Even if we were able to determine a reasonable method for
(
printed page 76462)
constructing multi-CSA units, such an approach would not capture the non-CSA areas and therefore would not solve the above-described problems stemming from that exclusion.
(3) Other Organizational Configurations
We considered alternative organizational configurations, including approaches that would have applied uniform national or regional thresholds without regard to contract service area boundaries, or that would have grouped MA organizations across cohort designations. These alternatives were considered but not proposed for the following reasons.
First, our analysis indicates that the impact of any grouping methodology would not be uniform across parent organizations. Smaller parent organizations or those in the lower enrollment quartiles experienced negligible changes in reportability regardless of the grouping approach applied. This reflects the structural reality that smaller parent organizations may either have widely dispersed enrollment that is insufficient to meet reportability thresholds within any given service area or have enrollment that is so geographically concentrated that reportability is determined primarily by whether their service area falls within a specific geographic area. Alternative configurations applying uniform thresholds would not have resolved these underlying structural challenges and would have introduced additional administrative complexity without commensurate benefit.
Second, approaches that ignored contract service area boundaries would have obscured meaningful geographic variation in MA market structure and enrollment patterns, undermining the goal of geographic integrity of quality measurement and further complicating the ADVaNCE MA model's evaluation design. Additionally, ignoring contract service area boundaries would have complicated payments between CMS and MA organizations, which are completed at the contract level, including payments under the Diamond Ratings system. While we acknowledge there would be mandated alterations to contracts to abide by the service area requirements within Mandatory States, we believe this approach allows us to keep operations as similar as possible to payments absent the model.
Third, configurations that grouped parent organizations in a way that did not allow for cohort designations were rejected because these cohorts reflect meaningful clinical and organizational distinctions among MA contracts. We believe that collapsing these distinctions solely to achieve reportability thresholds would compromise the comparability of quality measures across similarly situated plans and reduce the analytical validity of ADVaNCE MA performance assessments.
We seek comment on whether CSAs, CBSAs, or some other geographic unit would be better suited for the ADVaNCE MA model than using entire States.
b. Rationale for States as the Geographic Unit
As described above, we are proposing to designate entire States as the mandatory geographic unit of participation for the ADVaNCE MA model. We believe States are the most appropriate geographic unit for the ADVaNCE MA model for the following reasons:
Representative breadth:
CMS officially recognizes five types of counties for purposes of MA network adequacy: Large Metropolitan, Metropolitan, Micropolitan, Rural, and Counties with Extreme Access Considerations.
[
172
]
Each county type has unique characteristics and other MA attributes. States naturally incorporate all five county types, making them ideal for capturing the full range of MA market dynamics and ensuring the ADVaNCE MA model's findings are generalizable to the different county types for potential nationwide adoption in the future. In particular, if this model is expanded, including potentially being implemented on a nationwide basis, pursuant to section 1115A(c) of the Act, we believe that a geographic unit that encompasses the full variety of county types would best serve such an expansion in the context of MA because MA employs county specific policies, like contract service areas.
[
173
]
Operational alignment with contract-level participation:
In section VIII.D.4. of this proposed rule, we discuss our proposals for ADVaNCE MA model contract restructuring. When the geographic unit is defined at the State level as we are proposing, that contract restructuring can be implemented cleanly along State lines, ensuring that the contracts that result from the proposed restructuring as described in that section are either wholly within or wholly outside a Mandatory State. We believe that this approach is more straightforward to implement and administer than geographic units that would require intra-State contract splitting or county-level carve-outs.
Mitigation of adverse selection and market avoidance
: We believe that statewide implementation would make it harder for potentially eligible MA organizations to avoid ADVaNCE MA model participation because they would not be able to do so without materially exiting an entire State market. Under a CSA-based approach, MA organizations could potentially adjust service areas or product offerings at a more localized level to avoid selected geographies while continuing to operate elsewhere in the same State. We believe that statewide participation would reduce opportunities for that type of geographic avoidance and would apply the ADVaNCE MA model more uniformly across similarly situated organizations within the selected State.
Rural access and guardrails:
We believe that statewide participation would allow high-performing MA organizations operating in rural areas to benefit from the Diamond Ratings system (described in section VIII.F of this proposed rule) rather than excluding rural counties or creating uneven treatment within a State, as would be a consequence of CSA delineation. We believe that this approach would be consistent with CMS's commitment to rural MA beneficiaries by ensuring that they are not systematically excluded from the benefits of ADVaNCE MA model participation.
Simplicity and stability of State definitions:
States are the simplest geographic unit to define for purposes of the ADVaNCE MA model scope. Unlike CBSAs and CSAs, which are subject to periodic OMB delineation updates, including annual adjustments and a mid-decade boundary adjustment, State boundaries are stable and do not require ongoing administrative adjustment.
[
174
]
We expect that stability in State boundaries would reduce operational burden for CMS and ADVaNCE MA model participants over the course of the ADVaNCE MA model, particularly in light of our proposal in section VIII.C.2 to implement the model over a 10-year performance period. States also are a concept that beneficiaries are familiar with, which will be important for the model, for example, because the Diamond Ratings system would appear differently from the Stars Ratings system in Medicare Plan Finder (as discussed further in section VIII.F.3 of the proposed rule). Having the ADVaNCE
(
printed page 76463)
MA model's geographic area be defined as Mandatory States also simplifies the dual eligibility criteria necessary to operationalize the D-SNP cohort as described in section VIII.D.4.
CMS seeks comment on our proposal at § 516.100(e)(1) to use States as the geographic unit for the ADVaNCE MA model.

d. Stratification Methodology
We propose at § 516.100(e)(1)(i) to identify Mandatory States, including the District of Columbia, for the ADVaNCE MA model through a stratified random sampling methodology. Our goal with stratification is to select, in a fair way, a small set of States that reflect the heterogeneity of the Nation on characteristics that CMS considers relevant to the ADVaNCE MA model. Individual States may have unique or similar profiles with respect to the combinations of these characteristics. We believe that such characteristics consist of market competitiveness, size
(
printed page 76464)
of the MA market, MA market structure, and market geographic homogeneity. We believe that stratifying States based on the profiles generated by the below-described process support the production of a nationally representative sample and longer-term use of the model.
[
178
]
Further, pursuant to section 1115A(b)(4) of the Act, the proposed stratification of States would support CMS's ability to evaluate the quality of care furnished under the model and changes in program spending due to the model.
CMS determined from power calculations for the proposed evaluation, discussed in section VIII.D.3.e, that 12 States would be a sufficient sample size to test the model. Below and in the following section VIII.D.3.e, we propose a method to determine, in a fair and impartial manner, the 12 States to be selected as Mandatory States, using random selection while obtaining a nationally representative sample.
Our analysis allows for selecting multiple measures from the State characteristics for stratification described below, rather than stratifying on only one or a narrow subset of measures within a characteristic or a subset of characteristic—because profiles of States are multidimensional. We considered an alternative approach of stratifying States upon a subset of the proposed measures. However, we believe that a profile accounting for the multiple, relevant measures of characteristics described below would better reflect similarities and differences among State MA markets leading to a representative sample. We used a similar stratification approach as the Home Health Value Based Purchasing Model which incorporated several characteristics into the stratification process to group States before randomly selecting Mandatory States.
[
179
]
State MA markets may have more or different characteristics relevant to the model than State home health markets and thus we determined it was appropriate to include all the measures described later in the section to construct State profiles for the ADVaNCE MA model stratified random sample.
We propose applying a principal components analysis (PCA) to reduce the set of potentially interrelated measures to a smaller set of composite variables, which we would use to define the groups from which States would be selected. PCA is a widely used method in data science and machine learning that uses weighted combinations of related measures to construct a smaller number of composite variables that retain the most important multidimensional patterns present in the underlying data.
[
180
]
In other words, the PCA process includes information from all the proposed State characteristics and the underlying measures related to the ADVaNCE MA model by creating a smaller number of composite variables in place of many individual characteristics and measures. One composite variable can capture the biggest patterns in the data, and a second variable can capture other important, independent ways in which States differ.
We propose using two composite variables, drawn from measures representing State market characteristics, to construct groups of States. The extent to which any individual characteristic or measure representing a characteristic contributes to a composite variable is determined by how strongly it correlates with that component's underlying pattern of variation. Two PCA-derived composite variables captured more variation across States than any two individual measures from the original set, which we believe supports the use of PCA over simpler two-measure stratification.
We used the statistical software Stata and the function “pca” to carry out the PCA process to create the two composite variables. Through this process we examined 13 potential composite variables, but ultimately determined that for purposes of the ADVaNCE MA model, two was an appropriate number. In determining the number of composite variables to retain, we considered the Kaiser-Guttman Rule, under which a composite variable is retained only if its eigenvalue exceeds one.
[
181
]
Our first two composite variables had eigenvalues of 6.26 and 1.72; the third had an eigenvalue of 1.05. Because the Kaiser-Guttman Rule alone can lead to over-extraction,
[
182
]
we did not rely on it exclusively. We confirmed a two-variable solution using Cattell's Scree Test, Horn's Parallel Analysis, and accepted cumulative variance thresholds for the social sciences (our cumulative variance with two composite variables was 0.61).
[
183
]
Because the third composite variable's eigenvalue was only marginally above one and each supplemental method supported a two-variable solution, we retained two composite variables.
We included the proposed characteristics, as represented by their underlying measures, based on both their theoretical relevance to how markets might behave under the ADVaNCE MA model and the extent to which the combinations best explained variation across States.
Under this methodology, the characteristics described below would be used to construct the two composite variables that would determine the final groups.
Market Competition:
One of the goals of the ADVaNCE MA model is to enhance competition between plans in health care markets as a mechanism to improve quality. Competition can occur between MA and OM and between plans within the MA market. Because the proposed Diamond Ratings system discussed in section XIII.F would use parent organization level cohorts, we focus on competition between parent
(
printed page 76465)
organizations. The level of competition within MA varies across States. The impact of the ADVaNCE MA model may differ depending upon the level of competition that exists prior to implementation of the ADVaNCE MA model. We believe that including States with varying levels of competition prior to the ADVaNCE MA model is important to enable the production of results that will generalize nationally.
The Size of the MA Market:
The market capture opportunity in a State, in terms of potential enrollee volume, might impact the response to the ADVaNCE MA model. We measure the size of the MA market in terms of the number of enrollees in D-SNPs and in other eligible plan types as well as market penetration of MA among all Medicare enrollees. A larger Medicare population reflects a larger market and a greater market capture opportunity. A State with higher MA penetration also reflects a larger market. Including States of varying MA market sizes would support the production of results that are generalizable nationally.
Market Structure:
The extent to which the ADVaNCE MA model would alter the State's MA market structure may impact the response to the ADVaNCE MA model. We would assess market structure based on the number of MA contracts by contract characteristics relevant to the model, as well as the existence of Medicaid managed care programs for full benefit dual eligible enrollees, as these programs can intersect with D-SNP contracts. The extent to which a State's MA contracts between CMS and MA organizations would need to be split, as described in section VIII.D.4 of this proposed rule, to comply with the ADVaNCE MA model is an example of an alteration to a State's MA market structure that can differ across States. While stratification based on competition can encompass the number of parent organizations within a State, stratification based on market structure enables additional inclusion of the traits of the contracts these entities oversee. Including States with varying levels of exposure to multi-State contracts and intersection with Medicaid managed care would support the production of results that are generalizable nationally.
Market Urban/Rural Homogeneity:
Rural and urban markets within a State can differ and may have differential impacts across numerous domains including network adequacy requirements (
42 CFR 422.116
), market competition, and plan designs. The effects of the ADVaNCE MA model on States are likely to vary systematically by patterns of homogeneity related to rurality or urbanicity. We would measure geographic heterogeneity based on the percentage of MA enrollees within a State residing in rural counties. Including States across the range of patterns of rurality is important to enable the production of results that will generalize nationally.
We used 13 measures to represent the characteristics described above. We chose these measures based on their relevance to the ADVaNCE MA model and availability to CMS as of April 2026, the time at which CMS needed to begin making decisions about the stratification process. Specifically, we used publicly available Monthly Enrollment by Contract/Plan/State/County data, MA Contract Service Area by State/County data, MA State/County Penetration data, and Special Needs Plan (SNP) data to construct the below described measures for enrollment, Herfindahl-Hirschman Index (HHI), market share, number of parent organizations, numbers of contracts, and MA penetration. For Alaska and Connecticut, the applicable timeframe was July 2024, the midpoint of the most recent year for which the MA penetration data were available for these States, for the enrollment, HHI, market share, number of parent organizations, and MA penetration measures. For the number of contract measures and all other States, the applicable timeframe was March 2026. We used internal analyses to construct the below described measure for Medicaid managed care programs for full benefit dual enrollees. We used the 2024 Master Beneficiary Summary File and 2020 Rural-Urban Commuting Area Codes (RUCA) codes to construct the below described measure regarding rurality. Because the characteristics and individual measures are highly related, individual measures may fit into more than one of the four characteristics.
We chose to use two HHI measures, as measured by the number of MA enrollees per parent organization. We incorporate an HHI measure for all MA enrollees in eligible plans (measure one) as well as a measure for D-SNP enrollees (measure two), because the proposed Diamond Ratings system discussed in section VIII.F would look at a separate D-SNP cohort, and we recognize that a market's D-SNP concentration may differ from its market concentration for its General Enrollment population. HHI is a common measure for market concentration used in MA literature.

The number of groups and number of States within each group would be dependent upon the similarities and differences in the profiles of States produced under this analysis of composite variables, based on the above-described measures and characteristics, when trying to capture meaningful patterns of differences between States. Where more States are clustered together due to having similar profiles based upon the composite variable values, a group would be larger in size (consisting of more total States). The purpose of grouping similar States together is to facilitate creating a small set of Mandatory States that represent the Nation as a whole. If, for example, 40 States were similar with respect to the characteristics that we determined are relevant to the model, but the other 10 States were unique with respect to those same characteristics, creating two more groups of five states each would adequately differentiate those states from each other, the result would be one group of 40 States and two additional groups of five States each. If six States were an adequate sample to test the model, we would select two States from the group of 40 and two from each group of five, resulting in six total States selected as Mandatory States. The first group would have a two-in-40, or 5 percent, chance of selection into the model as Mandatory States, while the States in the other two groups would have a two-in-five, or 40 percent chance, due to the relative sizes of the groups. The chances of being selected into the ADVaNCE MA model as a Mandatory State depends upon the number of States in each group based upon the PCA stratification.
As we discuss in more detail below, we determined that using seven groups enabled sufficient differentiation between groups of similar States. The two PCA-derived composite variables resulted in clusters of States in which the composite variables each comprised an axis, and we examined how the States clustered to determine the groupings. Specifically, PCA enabled groupings based on the clusters.
In deciding the appropriate number of groups of States, we incorporated both statistical and policy-based considerations. As a policy matter, we sought to advance our goals of fairness of selection among eligible States and national representativeness of the Mandatory States. As a statistical matter, we sought to create groups that would facilitate precise estimates and a sufficient sample size to support evaluation of the ADVaNCE MA model. First, we wanted to avoid creating a group with only one State, in which that State would have a 100 percent chance of selection, and to make the likelihood of selection as similar as possible across States while still pursuing national representativeness. We, therefore, preferred groups of a similar size in terms of the number of States, while still accommodating the possibility that some States had less common market characteristics and should be grouped together on that basis. Second, we wanted to avoid too few groups that would combine a greater number of States into the same group and increase the risk of dissimilarities within grouped States that could reduce representativeness, as measured by their composite variable values. Dissimilar observations within a group could reduce the precision of statistical estimates, relative to an internally homogeneous group.
[

]
Such dissimilarity could require a larger sample size to reach adequate statistical power to detect model effects. Third, we wanted to avoid having too many groups, which would separate similar States into different groups unnecessarily. Standard statistical practice dictates using the minimum number of groups necessary to achieve meaningful internal homogeneity.

Within the statistical software Stata, we used the function `cluster kmeans [two composite variable names], k([number of groups]) start(segments)' to assign States to groups. K-means clustering is a method commonly used in quantitative analysis and applied statistics that allows us to group States by minimizing the Euclidean distances between each State and its assigned cluster centroid, based on the two continuous composite variables that we derived through the process described earlier in this section.

Once the number of groups was set, this function impartially assigned each State to a group based on its composite variable values, without further discretion on our part, minimizing the risk that groupings reflect arbitrary or biased manual selection. One resulting group contains four States. We reviewed this group specifically and determined that its members are substantively similar based on the characteristics we deemed important in generating a nationally representative sample and differed substantively from the other States, supporting our use of this group despite its smaller size relative to the other groups.

Higher group numbers also tend to be associated with lower HHI values and percentages of MA enrollees residing in rural counties.
