e. Random Selection of States From Groups
We carefully considered many selection methodologies, including selecting States on a non-random basis to be Mandatory States. Ultimately, our proposal in § 516.100(e)(1) would employ stratified random sampling to select Mandatory States. Under the proposal, we would use a selection methodology based on a randomized sampling of States within each of the groups constructed using the methodology described earlier in section VIII.D.3.e of this proposed rule. As we discussed above in section VIII.D.3.d, we determined that using seven groups enabled sufficient differentiation between groups of similar States.
We conducted simulations of the proposed randomization-within-groups strategy to ensure that our approach can produce unbiased samples of States, ensure that no State was excluded unintentionally, confirm no State appeared more than once across groups, and verify no single State's characteristics disproportionately influenced any group. If the proposed methodology is finalized, the random selection process would be run once to determine the list of Mandatory States. We will include the finalized methodology and the list of Mandatory States in the final rule. We determined that a randomized selection of States could be accomplished using the function “sample” within the statistical software Stata, an industry standard and scientifically valid computer algorithm and software widely used among researchers. The simulations of the randomized selection of States were run on each of the previously described groupings using exactly the same process, and, therefore, reflect a commonly accepted method of randomized sampling. The proposed computer algorithm omits any human interaction once it runs.
We conducted power analyses to identify detectable changes in quality measures tracked under the Diamond Ratings system, comparing a potential group of parent organization cohorts in 12 potential Mandatory States and a potential group of parent organization cohorts in 38 potential eligible but not selected States, using a Type I error of 0.05, Type II error of 0.2 (implying a power of 0.8), and a one-sided test in which we anticipate quality measures will improve under the ADVaNCE MA model. The analysis shows that, if 12 eligible States are selected for the ADVaNCE MA model, as proposed, we would be able to detect between a 2.84 and a 3.48 annual percent increase in mean Diamond score, all else being equal. This increase in mean Diamond score is within the range that CMS expects to achieve. The range in potential detectable scores is due to varying the assumption of the number of years of data available for the years immediately preceding the model performance period. We tested the possibility of using between one and three years of such data. Across all iterations, we consistently assumed that the covariance between any pair of annual scores remains constant across years.
In consideration of sampling efficiency and maintaining generalizability while being cognizant of the ADVaNCE MA model's footprint, we would select the minimum number of States that we believe is necessary to achieve adequate statistical power to detect ADVaNCE MA model effects representative of the national MA landscape. From the seven groups we constructed under the methodology described above in section D.3.d of this proposed rule, we propose to select one to two States per group, with two States chosen from Groups one through five and one State chosen from Groups six and seven, the smallest groups. Through this selection process, we would select a total of 12 (24.0 percent) eligible States across which the ADVaNCE MA model would be implemented. A State's probability of being selected as a Mandatory State to participate in the ADVaNCE MA model would depend on the group it falls in and would range from 16.7 percent to 28.6 percent:

f. Stability and Publication of the Mandatory State List
We propose at § 516.100(e)(2) that the list of Mandatory States would remain fixed and would not be revised or updated across performance years of the ADVaNCE MA model except as may be required under applicable State or Federal law, including the authority of the Secretary to expand models under section 1115A(c) of the Act. We believe that a stable, fixed geographic scope is essential to the integrity of the ADVaNCE MA model's evaluation design and to providing MA organizations, State Medicaid Agencies, and other affected parties with the regulatory certainty needed to make long-term operational and investment decisions.
Maintaining a fixed Mandatory State list is important to the integrity of the ADVaNCE MA model evaluation. Because the ADVaNCE MA model spans 10 performance years, a stable set of participating States ensures that changes in MA organization participation reflect ADVaNCE MA model dynamics rather than geographic variation introduced by mid-ADVaNCE MA model revisions. Altering the Mandatory State list after implementation would compromise the comparability of outcomes across performance years, making it difficult to accurately detect and attribute changes to the ADVaNCE MA model itself.
Accordingly, we propose that no mechanism will exist for adding or removing States from the mandatory participation list after the final rule is published, except as may be required under applicable State or Federal law. We note that section 1115A(b)(3)(B) of the Act does provide that the Secretary has the statutory authority to modify the design and implementation of the model, which may include the list of Mandatory States, if certain statutory requirements are not met.
We propose that the final list of Mandatory States would be published in the
Federal Register
as part of the final rule establishing the ADVaNCE MA model. We propose that, once the Mandatory States are finalized, all MA organizations meeting the ADVaNCE MA model participant criteria, discussed earlier in section VIII.D.2.a, and operating in a Mandatory State as of January 1, 2029, would be required to participate in the ADVaNCE MA model.
We seek comment on this approach, including whether any circumstances should permit modification of the Mandatory State list after finalization.
4. Contract Structure Requirements for Operations
a. General Requirements and Need for Contract-Level Restructuring
Consistent with the proposal at § 516.100(a) and described in section VIII.D.1 that mandatory participation applies at the unit of an MA contract, we propose MA contract requirements at § 516.150 that would apply to all ADVaNCE MA model participants. As such, we propose at § 516.150(a) that ADVaNCE MA model's contract requirements would apply to any MA organization that plans to have a contract under
42 CFR 422.504
in a given contract year during the ADVaNCE MA model's performance period described in § 516.2(b) (discussed in section VIII.C.2.b of this proposed rule) that includes one or more eligible plans, described in § 516.100(b) (discussed in section VIII.D.2 of this proposed rule) that operate in a Mandatory State as defined under § 516.5 and discussed in section VIII.D.3 of this proposed rule. Under the proposal, MA organizations with eligible plans in the model would need to consider the ADVaNCE MA model's policies when preparing their MA contract applications, Change of Ownership requests, and CY 2029 bid submissions. The work that would be required during the ADVaNCE MA model's pre-implementation period (discussed in section VIII.C.2.a of this proposed rule) would support implementation for all MA organizations that operate eligible plans, as defined under § 516.100(b), for both the General Enrollment Cohort and the D-SNP cohort, within the Mandatory States identified using the criteria specified in § 516.150.
The relationship between an MA organization and CMS is established and governed by a contract executed pursuant to section 1857 of the Act and
42 CFR 422.504
. Each MA contract is assigned to a single legal entity and is identified by a unique contract identifier, or number. Under the current framework, a single MA contract may encompass multiple plan offerings of varying attributes, such as SNP and employer group plans, under the same MA plan type, as defined at
42 CFR 422.4
. Further, both the contract itself and the plans offered thereunder may operate across service areas that span more than one State. Consequently, an existing MA contract may include plans whose service areas extend both within and outside of a Mandatory State.
We believe that this multi-State contract structure would be incompatible with the administration of the ADVaNCE MA model, as the model's payment, quality, and Medicaid coordination requirements would necessitate a State-specific contract framework, for the reasons discussed below. First, the ADVaNCE MA model would require State-specific data reporting and payment methodologies. Because these methodologies would be applied at the contract level, a contract with plans that span both Mandatory States and non-Mandatory States could not be cleanly subject to ADVaNCE MA model requirements without creating ambiguity in how those requirements would apply to the non-mandatory portions of the contract. Second, we must be able to distinguish ADVaNCE MA model contracts from non-ADVaNCE MA contracts for purposes of monitoring, evaluation, and payment. A mixed-State contract would require CMS to administer different payment and quality methodologies within a single contract, creating unnecessary complexity and making accurate payment reconciliation and program oversight substantially more difficult.
We propose at § 516.150(b)(1) that, beginning in CY 2029, ADVaNCE MA model participants would be required to operate State-specific contracts for eligible plans, as described in proposed § 516.100(b)(1)(i) through (iv), whose service areas would fall entirely within a single Mandatory State. We further propose that such contracts must be designated in the General Enrollment Cohort, as defined in proposed § 516.5. Additionally, we propose at § 516.150(b)(2) that, beginning in CY 2029, ADVaNCE MA model participants that offer D-SNPs would be required to operate State-specific contracts containing only D-SNPs, as defined in proposed § 516.100(b)(1)(v), whose service areas fall entirely within a single Mandatory State, subject to the requirements in proposed § 516.100(c) (pertaining to State opt-out described in section VIII.D.2.c of this proposed rule). We further propose that such contracts must be designated as D-SNP cohort contracts, as defined in § 516.5. We believe that this additional separation is necessary to ensure that the Diamond Ratings system Cohort comparisons described in section VIII.F of this proposed rule, which would compare MA organizations within Cohorts defined in part by plan type, and any

b.  ADVaNCE MA Contract Structure and Splits
We propose to establish at § 516.150(c) an administrative process by which CMS, on behalf of MA organizations, would identify and apply contract number splits to an existing MA contract that contains both eligible and ineligible plans as described in proposed § 516.100(b). We propose, at § 516.150(c)(1), to establish eligibility criteria for existing MA contracts subject to contract splits. Specifically, we propose at (i)-(iii) that an existing MA contract would be subject to a contract split if it operates one or more eligible plans within a Mandatory State's service areas and either operates across multiple States or is confined within a Mandatory State while offering either a mix of eligible plans and ineligible plans or a mix of both eligible D-SNPs and eligible plans that are not D-SNPs.
We propose at § 516.150(c)(2)(i) that for CY 2029, CMS will split existing MA contracts meeting the proposed criteria at § 516.150(c)(1) into non-ADVaNCE MA contracts, General Enrollment cohort contracts, and D-SNP cohort contracts as applicable on behalf of applicable MA organizations without requiring the submission of application materials. Specifically, we would restructure the service areas of contracts involved in the split process to reflect the previously established service areas of plans that qualify for either (1) ADVaNCE MA model contracts meeting the requirements proposed at § 516.150(b)(1) and (2); or (2) non-ADVaNCE MA model contracts. E. Risk Adjustment
1. Background
Risk adjustment allows CMS to pay MA organizations based on the health risk of the beneficiaries they enroll, rather than paying the same average amount for every beneficiary. Risk adjustment is accomplished through calculation of a risk score, a relative measure of a beneficiary's predicted health care expenditures based on demographic characteristics and documented health conditions. Risk scores are used to calculate risk adjusted payments to MA organizations. By adjusting plan payments to reflect a beneficiary's expected health care costs, CMS is able to make more accurate plan payments for enrollees with differences in expected costs, which are determined based on data that MA organizations submit to CMS.
By increasing payment for beneficiaries who are expected to require more costly care and decreasing payment for beneficiaries expected to require less costly care, risk adjustment is intended to reduce incentives for MA organizations to preferentially cover healthier beneficiaries and avoid sicker ones.
[
190
]
Accurate risk adjustment also helps support more meaningful comparisons between MA organizations' populations.
CMS, as required by section 1853(b) of the Act, annually provides MA organizations notification of proposed changes in the MA capitation rate methodology and risk adjustment methodology, and provides an opportunity for comment on the proposed changes prior to announcing the capitation rate for each MA payment area and the risk and other factors to be used in adjusting such rates for a given CY. CMS recently fully implemented the 2024 CMS-HCC (v28) risk adjustment model first introduced for the 2024 payment year. In addition to updating the data years of the model and a reclassification of the HCCs to base them on the International Classification of Diseases, Tenth Revision, Clinical Modification (ICD-10-CM) codes, rather than ICD-9-CM codes, the 2024 CMS-HCC model included additional constraints and the removal of several HCCs in order to improve payment accuracy.
CMS believes it is important to assess and update the CMS-HCC risk adjustment model regularly and continues to investigate new ways to accurately predict spending. As referenced in the RFI on Future Directions in Medicare Advantage (Risk Adjustment and Quality Bonus Payments)
[
191
]
released in 2025, this includes exploring the use of Super Intelligence (SI)/Machine Learning (ML) and inferred risk adjustment models within MA. We will continue to leverage the feedback that was collected in response to the RFI in the development of any SI/ML-inferred risk adjustment models.
2. CMMI Inferred Risk Adjustment Model
As part of the ADVaNCE MA model, CMS proposes to shadow test the use of risk scores generated from a CMMI Inferred Risk Adjustment Model starting in CY 2028, meaning this would begin during the ADVaNCE MA model's pre-implementation period. Shadow testing means that, in CY 2028, CMS will calculate risk scores for all MA organizations using a CMS developed CMMI Inferred Risk Adjustment Model and will release the scores privately to each MA organization for their applicable enrollees only via HPMS and the Medicare Advantage and Prescription Drug (MARx) system for informational purposes. These new risk scores would not be used for payment in the ADVaNCE MA model in CY 2028; CMS would continue to use a CMS-HCC risk adjustment model used for all MA organizations. The purpose of this shadow test is so MA organizations can evaluate the differences between the two risk adjustment models, the CMS-HCC model and the CMMI Inferred Risk Adjustment Model. The shadow test for our new risk adjustment model would be solely implemented by CMS, there are no additional obligations placed on
(
printed page 76471)
MA organizations to implement this shadow test.
As the new CMMI Inferred Risk Adjustment Model is developed, we are considering an approach that would integrate multiple factors designed to improve the accuracy of predicting beneficiaries' health risk. These factors might include the use of the comprehensive sets of data that CMS has available (that is, OM claims data, MA encounter data, enrollment data), new Super Intelligence and machine learning methodologies, clinical and inferential risk logic, such as leveraging select prescription drug classes that more directly imply the conditions for which an individual is being treated, and other advanced statistical methods not used in the current risk adjustment model.
In advance of releasing the initial round of CMMI inferred risk scores in CY 2028, CMS will release the finalized technical specifications of the CMMI Inferred Risk Adjustment Model, research papers, and other public facing materials in 2027.
We anticipate that we could, in future rulemaking, propose using risk scores generated from the CMMI Inferred Risk Adjustment Model for payment for ADVaNCE MA model participants in future years. Should we decide that such a policy is appropriate, the use of the CMMI Inferred Risk Adjustment Model for payment in the ADVaNCE MA model would be subject to completion of testing and validation, and additional rulemaking.
We seek comment on this proposal, the potential, future use of a CMMI Inferred Risk Adjustment Model for payment for ADVaNCE MA model participants, and the factors listed above or others for consideration in the development of a CMMI Inferred risk Adjustment Model.
3. Coding Pattern Adjustments
As set forth in section 1853(a)(1)(C)(ii) of the Act, within MA there is a required minimum 5.9 percent coding pattern adjustment, which in effect lowers the average MA risk score by 5.9 percent. This adjustment is made to reflect differences in coding patterns between MA plans and providers under Parts A and B.
[
192
]
Despite possible nuances in the intensity of these coding pattern differences between a given MA contract and OM, the same coding pattern adjustment is applied to all MA plans.
While some of the difference in coding intensity between contracts may be attributable to differences in patient populations, CMS has noted that incentives created by risk adjustment may drive coding for payment maximization purposes, particularly around diagnoses that involve a substantial amount of discretion.
[
193
]
To better understand the effect of coding intensity at a more granular level we are considering leveraging the Demographic Estimate of Coding Intensity (DECI) method that has been used by MedPAC
[
194
]
to analyze the effect of coding intensity at the parent organization level. This method attempts to estimate coding intensity by comparing the difference in MA to OM diagnosis-based risk scores with the difference in MA to OM demographic-only predicted risk. Although the DECI method begins to estimate coding intensity at a more granular level, separating variation in risk scores driven by coding practices versus true condition prevalence within the underlying population becomes more difficult as you evaluate at a parent organization or contract level.
[
195
]
To address differences in the effect of coding intensity between MA contracts and/or parent organizations, we are interested in gathering feedback on methodologies that could scale the coding pattern adjustment such that it is higher for contracts that are proven to disproportionately utilize coding as a means to generate higher risk scores and lower for contracts that are not engaging in such behavior. We note that if we were to propose a coding pattern adjustment for some contracts below the 5.9% statutory minimum, we would also have to waive § 1853(a)(1)(C)(ii)(III)-(IV) in future rulemaking. This tiered coding intensity adjustment would rely on CMS' ability to accurately evaluate the effect of coding intensity at a contract level via analyses such as the DECI method, the difficulties of which are previously discussed.
We seek comments to inform possible proposals that would be included in future rulemaking on reliable methods, such as the DECI method mentioned above, to evaluate the effect of coding intensity at the parent organization and contract level and on approaches to a tiered coding intensity adjustment that would increase the adjustment for high outlier contracts while potentially lowering it for others. With regards to a tiered coding intensity adjustment, we seek input on the definition of a high outlier contract including what thresholds of coding intensity could warrant a higher or lower adjustment and what could the maximum and minimum adjustment be.

F. ADVaNCE MA Diamond Ratings System
The MA and Part D Star Ratings system evaluates MA contract quality, which directly influences QBPs, as authorized under section 1853(o) of the Act, and the amount of MA rebates, as authorized under section 1854(b) of the Act. In this proposed rule, as part of the ADVaNCE MA model, we are proposing to test the ADVaNCE MA Diamond Ratings system, a new quality framework that would replace participation in the MA and Part D Star Ratings and QBP system for eligible contracts in Mandatory States. The Diamond Ratings system would adopt all provisions of the Star Ratings program unless otherwise stated within this rule and at §§ 516.600(h) through (j) and 516.605. The Diamond Ratings system would provide payments based on quality performance (Diamond Ratings) within a Mandatory State. The Diamond Ratings system would compare performance of ADVaNCE MA model participants within cohorts of either General Enrollment contracts (contracts without any D-SNPs or ineligible plan types) (“General Enrollment cohorts”) or D-SNP contracts (contracts that exclusively contain D-SNPs) (“D-SNP cohorts”). This proposed Diamond Ratings system bases its innovations in the three pillars of the CMS Innovation Center Strategy mentioned earlier: (1) promoting evidence-based prevention; (2) empowering people to achieve their health goals; and (3) driving choice and competition.
At § 516.5, we propose to define “ADVaNCE MA model Diamond Ratings system” as the quality assessment and payment framework described in Subpart C of proposed part 516, which covers our proposals addressing quality measurement, performance and payment years, scoring methodology, ADVaNCE MA Overall Diamond
(
printed page 76472)
Ratings, ADVaNCE MA Individual Measure Diamonds, and the ADVaNCE MA Payment methodology.
Our proposed Diamond Ratings system would test pivotal reforms to MA quality by:
Assessing quality of MA contracts in each Mandatory State at the parent organization level and within cohorts to hold parent organizations accountable for the quality of care for all enrollees while accounting for differences in populations between cohorts. There are two cohorts, (1) the collection of eligible contract types that are not D-SNPs are all grouped into the “General Enrollment cohort” and (2) all D-SNP contracts are grouped into the “D-SNP cohort.” The cohort delineation is done for all contracts held by a parent organization within a Mandatory State. Of note, as described in § 516.100(c), if a State opts out their D-SNPs from ADVaNCE MA, then that State would only have General Enrollment cohorts participating in the model. Differing from the current Categorical Adjustment Index
[
196
]
used in the MA and Part D Star Ratings to account for certain differences in a contract's enrolled population, the Diamond Ratings system proposes a cohort approach that would help ensure D-SNPs serving higher needs enrollees would not be penalized due to differences in health status relative to enrollees in General Enrollment contracts and so that beneficiaries considering D-SNPs will have quality scores most applicable to their performance within the State.
Ensuring performance is incrementally acknowledged:
Departing from the current approach of linking bonus payments to a single, discrete quality threshold, as required by sections 1853(o) and 1854(b)(1)(C)(v) of the Act, the Diamond Ratings system would use an incremental scale to ensure even small differences in quality performance can be rewarded.
Providing more granularly displayed quality ratings:
The Diamond Ratings system would display ADVaNCE MA Overall Diamond Ratings and ADVaNCE MA Individual Measure Diamonds, where possible, in smaller increments (for example, one-tenth) on Medicare Plan Finder. The current MA and Part D Star Ratings measure Stars are displayed in whole-Star increments and the MA and Part D Star Ratings system overall and summary ratings are displayed in half-Star increments.
Restructuring payment:
The Diamond Ratings system would include benchmark adjustments and rebates with the intention of offering rewards based on the ADVaNCE MA model participants' relative performance.
In crafting proposals for the Diamond Ratings system, we sought to: (1) ensure predictability and fairness of quality scoring by assessing performance along an incremental scale; (2) avoid large swings in payment for minor changes in performance; and (3) stimulate competition between ADVaNCE MA model participants in Mandatory States by evolving the rewards structure to recognize quality differences on an incremental scale.

3. Performance Scoring Methodology for the Diamond Ratings System
At § 516.215, we are proposing a scoring methodology for the Diamond Ratings system. In this section, we describe how ADVaNCE MA model participants' performance on the ADVaNCE MA Diamond Ratings system measure set would be assessed for the public display of ADVaNCE MA Individual Measure Diamonds and ADVaNCE MA Overall Diamond Ratings. We propose that the scoring and ratings in the Diamond Ratings system would assess quality at the parent organization level within each cohort and Mandatory State, would allow incremental improvements in performance to be reflected in payment, reducing the link between bonus payments and a single, discrete quality threshold within the statutory QBP system, and would account for differences in enrollee populations through cohort-based assessments within each parent organization and Mandatory State.
a. Cohort Grouping in the Diamond Ratings System
Currently, the MA and Part D Star Ratings system accounts for certain differences in a contract's enrolled population, such as social risk factors, by adjusting overall and summary MA and Part D Star Ratings using a Categorical Adjustment Index (CAI). Additionally, some other measures in the MA and Part D Star Ratings program have additional adjustment applied.

The CAI adjusts for average within-contract disparity in performance associated with the percentages of DE, LIS, and disabled enrollees within that contract, as described at

and
42 CFR 423.186(f)(2)

At § 516.600(j)(4), we are proposing to waive
42 CFR 422.166(f)(2)
and
42 CFR 423.186(f)(2)
. Instead, we contemplate that the Diamond Ratings system would group participants within the Mandatory States into either a General Enrollment cohort or a D-SNP cohort based on the contract type. Measure level case-mix adjustments would be maintained for purposes of the Diamond Ratings.
At § 516.215(a), for scoring purposes, we are proposing to assign all of a parent organizations' participating contracts to one of two cohorts based on contract type offerings within the Mandatory State. The proposed cohort structure of the performance scoring methodology in the ADVaNCE MA Diamond Ratings system would account for differences in enrollee populations and allow for separate assessment of quality outcomes and comparisons for General Enrollment and D-SNP populations.
Our goal in proposing this cohort structure for the Diamond Ratings system is to further incentivize participating parent organizations to exert the full range of their influence and capabilities to deliver the highest quality care possible to their D-SNPs, and to be equally, but separately, accountable for the quality of their General Enrollment plans. We acknowledge this cohort structure does not account specifically for dual-eligible beneficiaries who have chosen General Enrollment contracts for their care but believe that this is the best way to focus on duals who select dual-specific plans.
We believe this proposal has the potential to incentivize higher quality of care in large part due to the changes in scoring methodology and competitive structure, and that the parent organizations of ADVaNCE MA model participants would be held accountable in both absolute and relative terms for their performance across both General Enrollment and D-SNP contracts. First, we believe that the scoring methodology, discussed further in sections VIII.F.3.b. through VIII.F.3.e., of this proposed rule rewards incremental progress, encouraging ADVaNCE MA model participants to work to achieve the absolute highest rating possible for their ADVaNCE MA Overall Diamond Ratings display as beneficiaries would use this information in selecting plans during each enrollment period. Second, we believe that the relative ADVaNCE MA payment structure, discussed further in section VIII.F.4. of this proposed rule, would incentivize ADVaNCE MA model participants to constantly strive to be the highest performer amongst their peers in the same Mandatory State and cohort in order to receive the largest adjustments to their benchmarks and rebates.
The use of cohorts would also incentivize better quality by providing greater transparency in performance differences. While the ADVaNCE MA model participants within the General Enrollment cohort may include dual eligible, LIS, and disabled enrollees, the D-SNP cohort would consist only of
(
printed page 76477)
dual eligible enrollees actively enrolled in D-SNPs and provide a distinct ADVaNCE MA Overall Diamond Rating for the D-SNP contracts under a parent organization within a Mandatory State, providing a clearer view into their specific quality performance. Thus, we believe the cohort structure would generate more relevant quality measurement information for dual eligible enrollees by reporting quality data in a way that empowers them to make the best choice when selecting between both General Enrollment and D-SNP-specific plan offerings and make it possible to make a selection based on the highest quality D-SNP on Medicare Plan Finder.
Additionally, the cohort structure narrows potential disparities in payments for ADVaNCE MA model participants that have more D-SNPs. An ADVaNCE MA model participant's quality performance for the General Enrollment cohort would be compared with all other ADVaNCE MA model participants' quality performance within the General Enrollment cohort for the same Mandatory State. Similarly, a D-SNP's quality performance would be compared with all other ADVaNCE MA model participants' D-SNP quality performance within the D-SNP cohort for the same Mandatory State.
We seek comment on our proposal to use two cohorts, one for General Enrollment contracts and another for D-SNP contracts, for scoring purposes in the Diamond Ratings system.

For the Diamond Ratings system, we are proposing at § 516.215(b) that the data reported for the measures by each ADVaNCE MA model participant under § 516.205 would be pooled with measure data reported by all other ADVaNCE MA model participants within the same parent organization, same cohort, and same Mandatory State using enrollment-weighted averages based on enrollment data from July of the measurement period, except for survey-based measures, consistent with the process used for consolidated contracts in the MA and Part D Star Ratings system under

The survey-based measures would use the enrollment at the time the sample is pulled for the rating year for all ADVaNCE MA model participants within the same parent organization and same cohort in the same Mandatory State. Accordingly, all ADVaNCE MA model participants under a single parent organization and within the same cohort and same Mandatory State would receive one set of measure scores for each Diamond Ratings system quality measure. We believe that reporting measure data pooled across ADVaNCE MA model participants under each parent organization within each cohort would both provide more meaningful data for beneficiaries and help reduce complexity when selecting between plans on Medicare Plan Finder. Currently when beneficiaries search for plans in Medicare Plan Finder, they may see many different Star Ratings for each of the numerous contracts offered by a single parent organization.These ratings may represent the combined quality of care from a service area and network outside of the beneficiary's State of residence. Because ADVaNCE MA Overall Diamond Ratings would be specific to the quality of care received by beneficiaries within the Mandatory State, beneficiaries would be guaranteed that the quality ratings they see would reflect quality experienced by other beneficiaries in their Mandatory State. Furthermore, for a beneficiary choosing between multiple contracts under the current MA and Part D Star Ratings system, the beneficiary may encounter multiple plan choices across different carriers with identical Star Ratings. Under our proposal, we believe that the newly calculated ADVaNCE MA Overall Diamond Ratings could offer beneficiaries an option to quickly stratify their search by quality before looking to other factors, such as premiums, for the plan selection.
Under this proposed framework, ADVaNCE MA model participants under the same parent organization in a Mandatory State may have up to two distinct sets of measure scores, one for the General Enrollment cohort and one for the D-SNP cohort. For example, consider a parent organization that has three participating contracts in a Mandatory State, where one contract represents an HMO network that exclusively has General Enrollment contract offerings, the second contract represents a PPO network that exclusively has General Enrollment contract offerings, and a third contract that exclusively has D-SNP contract offerings. The HMO contract and PPO contract would independently collect measure data, according to the data collection requirements for contracts as specified by the MA and Part D Star Ratings system. The measure data for these two contracts under the General Enrollment cohort would be pooled together to create one set of measure scores to represent the performance of those ADVaNCE MA model participants under the same parent organization in the same Mandatory State within the General Enrollment cohort across all ADVaNCE MA measures. The third D-SNP contract would also independently collect measure data to create one set of measure scores that represents the ADVaNCE MA model participant's performance within the D-SNP cohort within the Mandatory State. We believe that pooling the measure data across like ADVaNCE MA model participants within the same parent organization, same cohort, and same Mandatory State ensures that the measure scores reflect the quality of care specific to the services provided within the same State for similar enrollees, and parent organization, based on similar provider networks. It would also ensure that all contracts receive equitable resources from parent organizations, because the lowest performing contracts' scores are combined with the highest performing contracts.

(1) Minimum Reporting Requirements
The MA and Part D Star Ratings system requires that a contract have measure scores for at least 50 percent of measures required to be reported for the contract to have the summary rating calculated in accordance with

Similar to the MA and Part D Star Ratings system, we are proposing at § 516.215(d)(1)(i) that improvement measures will be excluded from the count of measures needed to be reported to receive an overall score. Unlike the MA and Part D Star Ratings system, reportability would be assessed at the parent organization, cohort, Mandatory State-level. As described earlier in section VIII.F.3.b. of this proposed rule (Measure Scoring), measure data reported by all ADVaNCE MA model participants under the same parent organization in the same cohort and within each Mandatory State would be pooled together to calculate one set of measure scores; therefore, minimum reporting would, in effect, be calculated at the parent organization-level. For example, consider a parent organization in a Mandatory State that has three participating contracts in the General Enrollment cohort. Each participating contract would collect and report data on each measure as it would under the MA and Part D Star Ratings system. However, under the Diamond Ratings system, for each measure, the measure calculations would be performed such that the measure denominator would include all enrollees under the parent organization's three participating contracts within the General Enrollment cohort for the Mandatory State. If future measure changes are made to the ADVaNCE MA Diamond Ratings system measure set, ADVaNCE MA model participants would still be required to meet the minimum reporting requirements described here, such that ADVaNCE MA model participants would need to have measure scores for at least 50 percent of the total measures (as pooled with other ADVaNCE MA model participants with the same parent organization in the same cohort and same Mandatory State). Additionally, we note that as proposed in § 516.200(a)(3), if an ADVaNCE MA model participant fails to adhere to reporting or data integrity requirements for a measure required under § 516.205(a), such non-missing zero measure would contribute to the measures required to meet the minimum reporting requirements. The proposed process for calculating the overall score for all eligible ADVaNCE MA model participants is described in the sections that follow in this proposed rule.
We considered an alternative minimum reporting requirement that would require an ADVaNCE MA model participant to have measure scores for at least 50 percent of the total available measure weights to receive an overall score and ADVaNCE MA Overall Diamond Rating. Such an approach would sum the category weight assigned to each measure in the measure set (that is, Intermediate Outcome measures receive a weight of three, Process Measures receive a weight of one) and require that the sum of the weights of all measures that an ADVaNCE MA model participant reports equal at least 50 percent of that total. This option to use measure weights to establish the minimum reporting requirements for the Diamond Ratings system would result in contracts that are able to report more highly weighted measures to be more likely to receive a score. We believe these highly weighted measures, including outcome and improvement measures, would be most important in defining quality, and would ensure that at least some outcome measures are reported by ADVaNCE MA model participants in order to have sufficient reporting. However, we are not proposing to use measure weights in determining whether minimum reporting requirements have been met at this time in order to minimize the number of changes and to remain aligned with reportability in the MA and Part D Star Ratings system.
We seek public comment on our minimum reporting requirement proposal.

4. ADVaNCE MA Payment
We are proposing an ADVaNCE MA payment approach for each cohort in a Mandatory State that provides benchmark adjustments and plan rebate percentages relative to performance on ADVaNCE MA Overall Diamond Ratings

We believe our approach both leverages the existing infrastructure of the QBP ratings that is familiar to MA organizations and reduces the importance of discrete quality thresholds in the current statutorily required payment structure. Further, we believe this approach could incentivize incremental quality improvement and establish a framework that would support an overall reduction of program expenditures.
As discussed further in this section, our proposed payment approach would reward all ADVaNCE MA model participants for improvements in quality by using incremental scales to determine changes to benchmarks and rebates. The QBP ratings existing approach, required by section 1853(o) of the Act, provides contracts with a four-Star Rating or above with a five-percentage point increase in the development of their benchmarks. Also, low enrollment contracts and new contracts under new parent organizations do not have calculated ratings and are provided a 3.5 percentage point increase in the development of their benchmarks. The quality bonus increase (either zero, 3.5, or five percentage points) is added to the applicable percentage defined at section 1853(n)(2)(B) of the Act and MA contracts with a four-Star Rating or above in qualifying “double bonus” counties receive a 10-percentage point increase for quality as required by section 1853(o)(2) of the Act. While there is an increased rebate retention for plans with 3.5 stars compared to three stars, the statutorily required approach provides no quality bonus increase for contracts with a QBP rating of less than four stars, resulting in an “all or nothing” approach that does not incentivize incremental improvements for poorly performing plans. The ADVaNCE MA model, as discussed in more detail in the next section, would instead incentivize all parent organizations of ADVaNCE MA model participants to make improvements in quality by establishing an incremental scale that would reward each ADVaNCE MA model participant relative to their performance and remove the double bonus structure, as proposed in § 516.600(j)(2) and described further in section VIII.H.3.b.(1) of this rule. This is a departure from the current system and it is important to note that Diamond Ratings are not directly comparable in their calculation to Star Ratings and are calculated using a different algorithm that limits direct comparisons between the two. We further believe that by establishing the incremental scale relative to each Mandatory State and cohort with three or more parent organizations that we are ensuring ADVaNCE MA model participants are receiving payment adjustments relative to other ADVaNCE MA model participants that are serving similar types of enrollees (General Enrollment or D-SNP cohort) and in similar market conditions (their Mandatory State). This linear function would effectively rank parent organizations in a Mandatory State and by cohort so that the value of a given ADVaNCE MA Overall Diamond Rating (in terms of a quality bonus increase to their applicable percentage) is relative to the performance of other ADVaNCE MA model participants in the same Mandatory State and cohort, as we discuss in further detail below.
Specifically, we are proposing that we would establish a ceiling where the ADVaNCE MA model participant with the highest ADVaNCE MA Overall Diamond Rating for a cohort within a Mandatory State would receive the highest percentage increase, a five-percentage point bonus to their applicable percentage. This means that the top performing ADVaNCE MA model participant in each Mandatory State and for each cohort would receive a five-percentage point increase to their applicable percentage, regardless of their relative performance on a national scale. This could mean that in one Mandatory State the highest scoring ADVaNCE MA model for the General Enrollment cohort could have 4.6 Diamonds while the highest scoring ADVaNCE MA model participant for the D-SNP cohort could have 3.8 Diamonds and both ADVaNCE MA model participants could receive a five-percentage point bonus increase to their applicable percentage. Using this logic, if the lowest ranked plan unexpectedly leaves the market, by default, the next lowest ranking plan would experience a decrease in their benchmark, regardless of quality performance.
For ADVaNCE MA model Mandatory States and cohorts with three or more parent organizations that are able to report an ADVaNCE MA model Overall Diamond Rating, we are similarly proposing at § 516.230(b)(1), that the ADVaNCE MA model participant with the lowest ADVaNCE MA model Overall Diamond Rating for a cohort within a Mandatory State would not receive an increase to their applicable percentage, or in other words, a zero percentage point increase. As proposed at § 516.230(b)(1), all other ADVaNCE MA model participants would receive an increase to their applicable percentage correlated with their ADVaNCE MA model Overall Diamond Rating based on a linear scale between the highest and lowest performing participants for their Mandatory State and cohort. This could mean that in one Mandatory State the lowest scoring participant for the General Enrollment cohort could have 2.1 Diamonds while the lowest scoring participant for the D-SNP cohort could have 2.3 Diamonds and both participants would not receive any bonus, that is, a zero-percentage point increase, to their applicable percentage.

(2) ADVaNCE MA Mandatory States and Cohorts With Two Parent Organizations That Have ADVaNCE MA Model Participant(s) That Receive an ADVaNCE MA Overall Diamond Rating
Under § 516.230(b)(2), we propose the applicable benchmark percentage increases for Mandatory States and cohorts with two parent organizations with ADVaNCE MA model participant(s) that receive an ADVaNCE MA Overall Diamond Rating. Specifically, at § 516.230(b)(2)(i), we propose that the ADVaNCE MA model participant(s) with the higher ADVaNCE MA Overall Diamond Rating for the Mandatory State and cohort would have their applicable benchmark percentage increased by five percentage points. For the ADVaNCE MA model participant(s) with the lower of the two ADVaNCE MA Overall Diamond Ratings, we propose under § 516.230(b)(2)(ii) that if such rating is greater than or equal to the enrollment-weighted average ADVaNCE MA Overall Diamond Rating across all ADVaNCE MA model participants of the same cohort across all Mandatory States, their applicable benchmark percentage would be increased by 2.5 percentage points. If their ADVaNCE MA Overall Diamond Rating is less than the enrollment-weighted average ADVaNCE MA Overall Diamond Rating across all ADVaNCE MA model participants of the same cohort across all Mandatory States, we propose that the applicable benchmark percentage for such a participant would be increased by zero percentage points. We believe that in the context of a Mandatory State and cohort that only has two parent organizations with ADVaNCE MA model participant(s) that can report ADVaNCE MA Overall Diamond Ratings, it is appropriate to vary the increase to the applicable benchmarking percentage relative to the broader performance across all Mandatory States for the cohort, so that the ADVaNCE MA model participant(s) with the lower ADVaNCE MA Overall Diamond Rating is evaluated in the context of the national performance of the ADVaNCE MA model.
Finally, in a Mandatory State and cohort that has only two parent organizations with ADVaNCE MA model participants that receive ADVaNCE MA Overall Diamond Ratings, we are proposing under § 516.230(b)(2)(iii) that if the ADVaNCE MA model participants receive ADVaNCE MA Overall Diamond Ratings that are within 0.2 Diamonds of each other then the benchmark adjustment would depend on whether the ADVaNCE MA Overall Diamond Ratings are greater than or equal to the enrollment-weighted average ADVaNCE MA Overall Diamond Rating across all Mandatory States for the same cohort. If the ADVaNCE MA model participant's ADVaNCE MA Overall Diamond Rating is above the average, the benchmark must be increased by five percentage points. If such ADVaNCE MA Overall Diamond Rating is less than the enrollment-weighted average ADVaNCE MA Overall Diamond Rating across all Mandatory States for the same cohort, the applicable benchmarking percentage for the ADVaNCE MA model participants must be increased by 2.5 percentage points. If the scores straddle the average, both will receive a five-percentage point increase.
For example, if the two ADVaNCE MA model participants in the General Enrollment cohort receive ADVaNCE MA Overall Diamond Ratings of 2.6 Diamonds and 2.8 Diamonds and the enrollment-weighted average ADVaNCE MA Overall Diamond Rating across all Mandatory States for the General Enrollment cohort is 3.4 Diamonds, then both ADVaNCE MA model participants would receive a 2.5 percentage point increase to their applicable benchmark percentages. However, if the two ADVaNCE MA model participants were to score 4.3 Diamonds and 4.8 Diamonds for the same cohort and Mandatory State (a difference of 0.5 Diamonds) and the enrollment-weighted average ADVaNCE MA Overall Diamond Rating is 3.4 Diamonds, the ADVaNCE MA model participant with the higher ADVaNCE MA Overall Diamond Rating would receive a five percentage point increase to their applicable benchmark percentage and the ADVaNCE MA model participant with the lower ADVaNCE MA Overall Diamond Rating that is still above the enrollment-weighted average would receive a 2.5 percentage point increase to their applicable benchmark percentage, as proposed previously, because it is above the enrollment-weighted average ADVaNCE MA Overall Diamond Rating for the cohort. Similarly, if the two ADVaNCE MA model participants receive ADVaNCE MA Overall Diamond Ratings of 3.6 Diamonds and 3.1 Diamonds for the same cohort and Mandatory State, and the enrollment-weighted average ADVaNCE MA Overall Diamond Rating is 3.4 Diamonds, then the ADVaNCE MA model participant with the higher ADVaNCE MA Overall Diamond Rating would receive a five percentage point increase to their applicable benchmark percentage and the ADVaNCE MA model participant with the lower ADVaNCE MA Overall Diamond Rating that is below the enrollment-weighted average would receive a zero percentage point increase to their applicable benchmark percentage, as proposed previously, because it is below the enrollment-weighted average ADVaNCE MA Overall Diamond Rating.
As an alternative, we considered proposing that in a Mandatory State and cohort with only two parent organizations that have ADVaNCE MA model participant(s) that receive an ADVaNCE MA Overall Diamond Rating, that the ADVaNCE MA model participant(s) with the higher ADVaNCE MA Overall Diamond Rating would receive a five percentage point increase to their applicable benchmark percentage and the ADVaNCE MA model participant(s) with the lower ADVaNCE MA Overall Diamond Rating would receive a zero percentage point increase to their applicable benchmarking percentage, regardless of how their performance compares with other ADVaNCE MA Mandatory States. We believe this could also be appropriate as it effectively applies the linear scale we have proposed for Mandatory States and cohorts with three or more participants to those with two participants.
An additional alternative considered would be to weigh the coinciding benchmarks to account for distance from the average score, especially in the instance of scores within 0.2 Diamonds. The goal of the current proposal (above) is to ensure that parent organizations are not unfairly penalized against each other, but to also encourage parent organizations to consistently seek to improve quality against the national average. The associated benchmark bonuses assigned to those below the national average are designed not to overly penalize plans, but to provide an opportunity to improve. However, one potential limitation with this approach is that it may create a steep threshold that the ADVaNCE MA model is being designed to avoid. (4) Insufficient Data, Low Enrollment, and New Entrants
We also propose changes to benchmark percentage increases for ADVaNCE MA model participants that do not meet the minimum reporting requirements, meet the definition of low enrollment, are new entrants to the ADVaNCE MA model, and/or are new entrants to a Mandatory State.
At § 516.230(b)(4), we propose that parent organizations in Mandatory States with insufficient data, as defined in § 516.5, would receive an increase to their applicable benchmark of 3.5 percentage points. We note that under both our proposed definition of low enrollment and under our minimum reporting requirements, measure data is pooled with all other ADVaNCE MA model participants under the same parent organization in the same cohort and in the same Mandatory State. We also propose that new entrants, as defined at § 516.5, would also receive an increase to their applicable benchmark of 3.5 percentage points.
At § 516.230(b)(5), we propose that for new ADVaNCE MA model participants that enter a Mandatory State in CY 2030 or subsequent years of the model, the applicable benchmarking increase would be 3.5 percentage points for the new ADVaNCE MA model participant for their first three years in the model. We believe this would incentivize existing parent organizations to enter into a Mandatory State or expand into additional Mandatory States. We also considered providing a 2.5 percentage point increase but are proposing a 3.5 percentage point increase because it provides benchmarking percentages that are similar to the MA and Part D Star Ratings system under
42 CFR 422.258(d)(7)(v)
, and we believe this would provide predictability for ADVaNCE MA model participants that are familiar with the MA and Part D Quality Bonus Payment system.
We considered two alternatives each for new ADVaNCE MA model participants that fall into group (1) parent organizations with existing MA contracts outside of the ADVaNCE MA Mandatory State, or (2) parent organizations that have contracts in another Mandatory State, and that enter a Mandatory State in year two or subsequent years of the Model.
For the first group, we considered determining the applicable benchmarking percentage increase by calculating an enrollment-weighted average of the highest rating for the parent organization's contracts in all other States. We first considered applying QBPs based on their enrollment weighted Star Ratings, maintaining the payment thresholds as experienced in the MA and Part D Quality Bonus Payment system. While we believe this option would reflect the familiarity of the current MA and Part D Quality Bonus Payment system for a new participant in the ADVaNCE MA model, we believe this is less aligned with the intention of the model to reduce the effects of the current payment thresholds.
We also considered using their enrollment-weighted average Star Ratings within the linear increase formula as described earlier in this section to determine the applicable benchmark percentage increase. While we believe this option would enable a new ADVaNCE MA model participant to more quickly integrate within the ADVaNCE MA Payment structure, we believe there may be timing challenges in the calculations of the enrollment-weighted average Star Ratings within a bidding cycle and inequivalence in comparing their enrollment-weighted average Star Ratings against ADVaNCE MA Overall Diamond Ratings.
For the second group, we considered determining the applicable benchmarking percentage increase by calculating an enrollment-weighted average of the ADVaNCE Overall Diamond Ratings for the parent organization's contracts in other Mandatory States within the ADVaNCE MA model. Similarly, we first considered applying QBP ratings based on their enrollment-weighted ADVaNCE MA Overall Diamond Ratings, maintaining the payment thresholds applicable to QBPs. Under the MA and Part D Star Ratings program, pursuant to
42 CFR 422.266(a)(2)(ii)
, contracts that receive a rating of at least 4.5 stars receive a 70 percent rebate, contracts that receive between 3.5 and 4.5 stars receive a 65 percent rebate, and contracts that receive less than 3.5 stars receive a 50 percent rebate as required by section 1854(b)(1)(C)(v) of the Act.
At § 516.230(c), we are proposing that the ADVaNCE MA model would similarly leverage the existing regulatory structure for rebates under
42 CFR 422.266
; however,
42 CFR 422.266(a)(2)(ii)
would not apply and proposed § 516.230(c)(1) through (5) would apply instead. Thus, rather than a fixed distribution of rebates as currently exists, we are proposing at § 516.230(c)(1) that we would use an incremental scale, similar to the scale used for determining the applicable percentage change in benchmarks under § 516.230(b)(1), to assign rebate percentages to ADVaNCE MA model participants specific to their Mandatory State and cohort based on their ADVaNCE MA Overall Diamond Ratings. We believe this incremental scale would ensure that ADVaNCE MA model participants receive rebates that incrementally increase with their ADVaNCE MA Overall Diamond Ratings so that participants are incentivized to make even small improvements in quality. We further believe that by establishing the incremental scale relative to each Mandatory State and cohort that we are ensuring participants are receiving rebate percentages relative to other ADVaNCE MA model participants that are serving similar types of enrollees (General Enrollment or D-SNP cohort) and in similar market conditions (their Mandatory State). This linear function would effectively rank ADVaNCE MA model participants in a Mandatory State and by cohort so that the value of a given ADVaNCE MA Overall Diamond Rating (in terms of a rebate percentage) is relative to the performance of other model participants in the same Mandatory State and cohort, as we discuss in further detail below.

Similarly, if the two ADVaNCE MA model participants receive ADVaNCE MA Overall Diamond Ratings of 3.6 Diamonds and 3.1 Diamonds for the same cohort and Mandatory State, and the enrollment-weighted average ADVaNCE MA Overall Diamond Rating is 3.4 Diamonds, then the ADVaNCE MA model participant with the higher ADVaNCE MA Overall Diamond Rating would receive a rebate percentage of 70 percent and the ADVaNCE MA model participant with the lower ADVaNCE MA Overall Diamond Rating that is below the enrollment-weighted average would receive a rebate percentage of 50 percent, as proposed previously, because it is below the enrollment-weighted average ADVaNCE MA Overall Diamond Rating.
As an alternative, we considered proposing that in a Mandatory State and cohort with only two parent organizations with ADVaNCE MA model participant(s) that receive an ADVaNCE MA Overall Diamond Rating, that the participant(s) with the higher ADVaNCE MA Overall Diamond Ranking would receive a flat 70 percent rebate, regardless of their performance. The participant(s) with the lower ADVaNCE MA Overall Diamond Rating would receive 50 percent rebate, regardless of their performance. We believe this could also be appropriate as it effectively applies the linear scale we have proposed for Mandatory States and cohorts with three or more participants to those with two participants.
An additional alternative considered would be to weigh the coinciding rebates to account for distance from the average score, especially in the instance of scores within 0.2 Diamonds. The goal of the current proposal (above) is to ensure that parent organizations are not unfairly penalized against each other, but to also encourage parent organizations to consistently seek to improve quality against the national average. The associated benchmark bonuses assigned to those below the national average are designed not to overly penalize plans, but to provide an opportunity to improve. However, one potential limitation with this approach is that it may create a steep threshold that the ADVaNCE MA model is being designed to avoid. An alternative strategy that we considered is, instead of having a specific reward percentage based on if the dyad is above or below the national average, to set the benchmark and rebate proportional to the national average so that dyads that are far below the national average have lower bonuses and rebates and those that are far above the national average have higher comparatively. This could potentially be done by assigning scores according to the national distribution of Diamond (for example, if the dyad's scores are below the 25th percentile nationally they receive a 25 percent lower benchmark and rebate, or if they perform above the 75th percentile, they receive a higher score).
We seek comment on the reward structure with two parent organizations in a Mandatory State and cohort, as well as the listed alternatives including alternative ways to reward against the national average.

G. Supplemental Benefits To Enhance Access to Prevention and Caregiver Support
1. Background
In the Part C program, MA organizations may offer supplemental benefits to enrollees—items or services that are not covered by OM and for which the MA organization incurs a non-zero direct medical cost or, for Special Supplemental Benefits for the Chronically Ill (SSBCI), a non-zero direct non-administrative cost.

]
With the exception of SSBCI, supplemental benefits must be primarily health related. Under
42 CFR 422.100(c)(2)(ii)
, supplemental benefits are “primarily health related” if they are used to diagnose, prevent, or treat an illness or injury; compensate for physical impairments; act to ameliorate the functional/psychological impact of injuries or health conditions; or reduce avoid emergency and health care utilization.”

207
]
CMS has provided examples of allowable primarily health related supplemental benefits, such as support for caregivers of enrollees, in sub-regulatory guidance.
[

With some exceptions, MA organizations must offer supplemental benefits uniformly to all enrollees in a plan benefit package.

Through SSBCI, MA organizations can offer primarily health related supplemental benefits, non-primarily health related supplemental benefits, or both non-uniformly to certain qualifying enrollees, so long as the supplemental benefits have a reasonable expectation of improving or maintaining the health or overall function of the enrollee. Specifically, MA organizations can offer SSBCI to enrollees who have at least one complex and life-threatening chronic condition, high risk of hospitalization, and require intensive care coordination. In April 2019, we released guidance

As discussed previously in section VIII.A of this proposed rule, in 2025, the CMS Innovation Center released a renewed strategy

comprised of three pillars: (1) promoting evidence-based prevention, (2) empowering people to achieve their health goals, and (3) driving choice and competition for people. We stated that future models would seek to increase the access and uptake of primary, secondary, and tertiary prevention. That is, activities to avoid disease occurrence, detect early signs of disease before symptoms, and slow the progression of existing chronic disease, respectively. Given these strategic pillars—and their relevance to supplemental benefits—we are proposing under the ADVaNCE MA model to enhance access to certain supplemental benefits relating to nutrition, transportation, and caregiver support. As discussed later in this section of the proposed rule, we believe each of these three areas (nutrition, transportation, and caregiver support) have the potential to address the strategic pillars, improve quality, and reduce future health care expenditures.
Importantly, when designing the proposed ADVaNCE MA model, we leveraged lessons learned from the VBID model and its associated costs. We believe our proposed supplemental benefit policies would better enable CMS to reduce Medicare expenditures, relative to the VBID model. Prior evaluations found the VBID model was associated with increases in targeted beneficiaries' risk scores (and, therefore, increased costs to CMS), likely driven by the model's design elements which encouraged beneficiaries to engage with providers, “creating opportunities to identify additional diagnoses that increased beneficiaries' risk scores.”

As discussed in section III.A of this proposed rule, a clear affirmative standard for what constitutes healthy food would promote CMS' ability to conduct meaningful compliance and enforcement work. For CMS to determine whether MA plans offer food benefits that are primarily health related or are appropriate as SSBCI, CMS is proposing to specifically require food-related supplemental benefits to be limited to “healthy food,” and to define what it means by “healthy food” for this purpose. As food-related supplemental benefit spending continues to grow, so does the importance of ensuring that such spending is directed toward foods that genuinely support improved health outcomes. Establishing a clear definition of “healthy food” to be required for supplemental benefit offerings directly supports these objectives by creating a consistent baseline for nutrition quality across the MA program—ensuring that all food-related supplemental benefits are contributing to better health outcomes rather than simply expanding access to food. The DGAprovides the nutritional foundation for this proposal. In developing this proposed definition, CMS worked closely with experts throughout HHS involved in the development of the DGA. The 2025-2030 DGA rests on a documented evidence-review process: subject-matter experts were selected through a federal contracting process; standardized protocols—covering inclusion criteria, risk of bias, synthesis, and evidence grading—were set in advance by a methodology expert; the review relied on rapid systematic reviews, umbrella reviews, and literature syntheses; and the review was subject to external peer review coordinated by the NIH Office of Nutrition Research, with two independent reviewers assigned to each topic. Reviewer financial interests were disclosed as part of this process.

CMS recognizes that the information and guidelines contained in the DGA are based on the preponderance of the scientific and medical knowledge which is current at the time the DGA is prepared and is subject to ongoing refinement as new research emerges. CMS believes this iterative process makes the DGA the most appropriate and reliable scientific anchor currently available for this definition, notwithstanding the inherent limitations of any evolving scientific field. Because the “healthy food” standard is anchored to the DGA rather than to a fixed guideline or definition, the standard can evolve as the science changes and future DGA cycles are completed, rather than being bound to a static standard that cannot adapt over time.
CMS recognizes that the DGA provides broad nutrition guidance for the general population and is not written as regulatory standards for MA supplemental benefits. CMS therefore developed this proposed definition to translate the core nutritional principles reflected in the DGA into a clear, administrable standard for MA plans offering food-related supplemental benefits to Medicare beneficiaries. d. Alternatives Considered
In sum, under proposed § 516.300(a), we propose to allow ADVaNCE MA model participants to target certain supplemental benefits to LIS-eligible individuals. Previously cited evidence demonstrates that individuals with low-income collectively comprise a high-needs population. It is our intent that this flexibility would provide ADVaNCE MA model participants of all sizes with an opportunity to focus resources towards identifying and engaging high-needs and high-cost enrollees who could greatly benefit from prevention-oriented supplemental benefits, but who may otherwise not be deemed eligible for such supplemental benefits.
Under the same rationale, we alternatively considered allowing ADVaNCE MA model participants to LIS-target additional supplemental benefits beyond healthy food and produce, TNMN, and support for caregivers of enrollees. This could have included: (1) allowing a limited number of additional supplemental benefits to be LIS-targeted based on the criteria, discussed above, of strong likelihood for improved health outcomes, alignment with our strategic focus on prevention and chronic disease, and potential for cost-savings to Medicare; or (2) broadening LIS-targeting outside of the discussed criteria to maximize ADVaNCE MA model participants' benefit flexibility and innovation and maximize choice of supplemental benefits among LIS-eligible individuals. However, we noted that allowing ADVaNCE MA model participants to LIS-target any primarily or non-primarily health related supplemental benefit could also impact the ADVaNCE MA model's quality improvement and reduction of avoidable health care utilization. We solicit comment on these alternatives allowing supplemental benefits beyond healthy food and produce, TNMN, and caregiver supports to be targeted to LIS-eligible individuals.
Additionally, we considered allowing ADVaNCE MA model participants to LIS-target supplemental benefits based on the LIS eligibility levels operationalized under the VBID model. That is, rather than solely allowing targeting of supplemental benefits to all LIS-eligible individuals, we considered allowing LIS-targeting of supplemental benefits to distinct, further delineated categories of LIS-eligible individuals based on the LIS eligibility categories and corresponding cost-sharing benefits that, as described in the Advance Notice, are sometimes referred to using category codes as follows:
Category Code 1
—Non-institutionalized Full Benefit Dual Eligible (FBDE) beneficiaries with incomes between 100 percent and 150 percent of FPL and full-subsidy-non-FBDE beneficiaries.
Category Code 2
—Non-institutionalized FBDE beneficiaries with incomes up to 100 percent of the FPL.
Category Code 3
—FBDE beneficiaries who are institutionalized or would be institutionalized if they were not receiving home and community-based services.
[
275
]
Under this alternative approach, an ADVaNCE MA model participant would be allowed to offer certain supplemental benefits to any, or all, of the aforementioned LIS levels/category codes. For example, an ADVaNCE MA model participant could choose to target healthy food and produce supplemental benefits exclusively to LIS-eligible individuals in LIS Category Code One, or to LIS-eligible individuals in LIS Category Codes One and Two but not Three, and so on. However, we believe the proposed approach of targeting supplemental benefits towards all LIS-eligible individuals offers greater simplicity for MA organizations and their enrollees while still allowing for discretion to target towards high-needs and high-cost enrollees who could greatly benefit from prevention-oriented supplemental benefits. We seek comment on this alternative of delineating LIS-eligible individuals for the purpose of offering certain supplemental benefits in a non-uniform manner under the ADVaNCE MA model.

H. Dialysis Carveout for Beneficiaries With End-Stage Renal Disease
a. Background
As discussed in more detail in section VIII.A.4.d and section VIII.A.2.d, ESRD and its treatment under Medicare payment policy have evolved considerably over the past five years. This section presents data on the consolidation of the dialysis market and summarizes relevant research findings on how that consolidation has affected beneficiary access, quality and cost, for dialysis. We are considering proposing a change to the dialysis coverage structure for beneficiaries who reside in one of the Mandatory States and who are enrolled in a plan subject to an ADVaNCE MA model contract.
The dialysis market is highly concentrated with 70 percent of the market controlled by two large organizations, DaVita and Fresnius. Because of this market concentration, these dialysis organizations have great leverage when negotiating payment rates with MA organizations.
[
277
]
A 2026 MedPAC report found that, in 2022, MA plans paid an average of 22 percent more for dialysis than OM, a trend that has continued ever since.
[

b. Potential Modification to the ADVaNCE MA Model Test
CMS is considering proposing a future modification to the ADVaNCE MA model that would exclude coverage for outpatient maintenance dialysis facility services from MA basic benefits for ADVaNCE MA model beneficiaries and would instead provide coverage for those services through OM, with reimbursement under the ESRD PPS. Beneficiaries would remain enrolled in their MA plan for all other covered Medicare services, consistent with the existing statutory exclusions for hospice services and organ acquisition costs. Under such a potential policy change, CMS would adjust MA benchmarks and capitation payments to reflect the transfer of dialysis payment responsibility to OM and waive other applicable statutory requirements that MA organizations cover dialysis services. Dialysis facilities would submit claims only to OM for carved-out services and would not be required to submit a separate claim to MA organizations. This potential change would reduce MA dialysis costs without reducing services available to beneficiaries.
We request comment on the potential policy to exclude dialysis coverage from the MA basic benefit and provide coverage though OM as a means for reducing spending, while improving choice and competition.
I. Proposed Waivers of Medicare Program Requirements
1. Background
Section 1115A of the Act authorizes the Secretary to test innovative payment and delivery models that have the potential to reduce Medicare, Medicaid, or CHIP expenditures while preserving or enhancing the quality of care furnished to beneficiaries. Section 1115A(d)(1) further authorizes the Secretary to waive such requirements of Titles XI and XVIII and of sections 1902(a)(1), 1902(a)(13), and 1903(m)(2)(A)(iii), and 1934 (other than subsections (b)(1)(A) and (c)(5) of such section) of the Act as may be necessary solely for purposes of carrying out section 1115A with respect to testing models described in section 1115A(b).
This section of the proposed rule details waivers necessary for testing the ADVaNCE MA model under the CMS Innovation Center's section 1115A authority. The ADVaNCE MA model proposes a restructuring of how quality performance is scored and associated payments are determined, how certain supplemental benefits are offered and targeted, how MA contracts are organized within Mandatory States to implement the ADVaNCE MA model test, and shadow testing of a new CMMI Inferred Risk Adjustment Model. These modifications are designed to improve the quality of care furnished to MA beneficiaries and reduce program expenditures.
These proposals require departures from existing statutory and regulatory requirements governing the MA program that would otherwise prohibit or constrain the proposed ADVaNCE MA model design. Accordingly, we propose the waivers described in this section to the extent necessary to test the ADVaNCE MA model. All waivers described in this section will apply across the model test as described in section VIII.C.2.
We seek comment on all aspects of the proposed waivers described, and on whether additional waivers would be necessary to test the ADVaNCE MA model as proposed.

b. Waivers and Other Considerations Supporting Operational Compliance for new ADVaNCE MA Model Contracts
(1) Total Beneficiary Cost
A plan's Total Beneficiary Cost (TBC) is a metric calculated by summing the plan-specific part B premium, plan premium, and estimated beneficiary out-of-pocket costs. The change in TBC
(
printed page 76509)
from one year to the next captures the combined financial impact of premium changes and benefit design changes in the PBP on plan enrollees. An increase in TBC is indicative of an increase in beneficiary costs or a reduction in benefits. CMS uses the TBC metric to evaluate whether an MA organization's bid proposes significant increases in cost sharing or decreases in benefits offered under the plan, in which case CMS has authority to deny the bid under section 1854(a)(5)(C)(ii) of the Act. This approach not only keeps MA plan cost sharing and benefit designs stable, but also ensures enrollees have access to viable and sustainable MA plan offerings.
At § 516.150(e)(1), we propose that MA plans in the ADVaNCE MA model would be treated as new plans for purposes of TBC threshold requirements during bid submission in 2028 for contract year 2029. New plans are excluded from the TBC analysis for their first year of operation to allow the plan to establish a baseline bid. Additionally, plans participating in the ADVaNCE MA model would be subject to the regular TBC evaluation criteria during bid submission in 2029 for contract year 2030, consistent with the process applicable to new plans, which applies TBC evaluation criteria to plans in their second year of operation. TBC is an important tool for CMS to regulate plans and protect beneficiaries. However, due to the significant changes proposed by the ADVaNCE MA model to pilot fundamental reforms in quality and supplemental benefits, we find it appropriate to treat plans in the ADVaNCE MA model like new plans for purposes of the TBC evaluation for CY 2029. This will ease operational burden and benefit design complexity for plans and avoid the intricacies associated with accurately capturing and incorporating the full range of model effects into TBC calculations. We expect that competitive market dynamics would discourage ADVaNCE MA model participants from significantly increasing cost sharing or reducing benefit availability. Furthermore, the TBC evaluation to be applied in CY 2030 of the ADVaNCE MA model provides a strong incentive for ADVaNCE MA model participants to maintain stable cost sharing and benefit design in contract year 2029, serving as a natural guardrail. Notably, D-SNP bids in the ADVaNCE MA model, like other D-SNPs, will continue to be excluded from TBC requirements, as the PBP data used in the TBC calculation does not capture the Medicaid component of a complete D-SNP benefit package.
We considered applying TBC requirements for ADVaNCE MA model participants in contract year 2029 without treating plans in the model as new plans, but, while this has the operational convenience of continuity, it would not incorporate the numerous changes proposed by the ADVaNCE MA model, many of which would likely affect the calculation of TBC. Thus, such an approach would not accurately encapsulate an ADVaNCE MA model benefit configuration. Additionally, we considered incorporating a range of factors relevant to the model into the TBC calculation itself. However, it would be operationally complex to do so accurately and comprehensively.
We propose to treat plans in the ADVaNCE MA model as new plans for purposes of TBC threshold requirements for contract year 2029 only.
We seek comment on our proposal to treat plans in the ADVaNCE MA model as new plans for purposes of TBC threshold requirements in contract year 2029 considering the significant changes expected from implementation of the model. Furthermore, we seek comment on alternative options to address the TBC requirement in the ADVaNCE MA model.

(4) Categorical Adjustment Index (CAI)
Currently, one way the MA and Part D Star Ratings system accounts for differences in a contract's enrolled population, such as social risk factors, is by adjusting overall and summary MA and Part D Star Ratings using a Categorical Adjustment Index (CAI). We are instead proposing that the Diamond Ratings system would create group participants within the Mandatory States into either a General Enrollment cohort or a D-SNP cohort based on the contract type, which would serve as the adjustment method.
