6. Risk Adjustment
As described in section VIII.E. of this proposed rule, the ADVaNCE MA model proposes to shadow test a CMMI inferred risk adjustment methodology in CY 2028. Because the risk scores generated from this new CMMI Inferred Risk Adjustment Model will not be used for payment purposes, the shadow test does not require CMS to depart from any existing statutory or regulatory requirements, and no waivers are necessary at this time. If CMS determines, following testing and validation, to use risk scores generated from this new model for payment or other purposes in future years, additional waivers or regulatory amendments may be necessary and would be proposed through rulemaking at that time.

2. Extreme and Uncontrollable Circumstances
a. Background
Events outside the control of ADVaNCE MA model participants can disrupt the delivery of care, the collection of quality data, and the operation of billing and payment processing systems in ways that would make performance-based assessment inaccurate or unfair to affected contracts and, ultimately, to the beneficiaries they serve. The existing MA regulatory framework addresses these disruptions in three distinct contexts, each of which has implications for the ADVaNCE MA model.
First,
42 CFR 422.100(m)
addresses disruptions in the availability of benefits arising from disasters or emergencies declared by the President, the Secretary, or a State Governor. These provisions require each MA organization to continue making covered benefits available during declared emergencies by waiving requirements for gatekeeper referrals where applicable, ensuring out-of-network access at in-network cost-sharing levels, and making changes that benefit enrollees effective immediately without the standard 30-day notification requirement. We propose to apply the requirements of
42 CFR 422.100(m)
, governing access to covered benefits during disasters or emergencies, to participating contracts in the ADVaNCE MA model without modification. No feature of the ADVaNCE MA model as proposed would necessitate modifying these requirements.
Second,
42 CFR 422.504(o)
requires each MA organization to develop, maintain, and implement a business continuity plan containing policies and procedures to ensure the restoration of essential operational functions following disruptions to business operations. Each MA organization must plan to restore essential functions within 72 hours after any essential function fails or otherwise stops functioning as usual. Section 422.504(o)(2) identifies two specific categories of essential functions subject to this requirement: benefit authorization (if not waived) for services to be immediately furnished and operation of call center customer services.
Third,
42 CFR 422.166(i)
addresses disruptions to the collection of quality data through surveys needed for accurate performance measurement under the MA Star Ratings program. These provisions establish a process by which CMS may account for extreme and uncontrollable circumstances in its quality calculations and shield affected contracts from adverse rating consequences attributable to events beyond their control.
Because the ADVaNCE MA model operates within the MA program, each of these provisions is applicable to participating contracts. However, the unique structural features of the model, including the Mandatory State construct and the parent organization-level unit of quality assessment, we are proposing modifications to
42 CFR 422.166(i)
and one addition to
42 CFR 422.504(o)(2)
to ensure these provisions operate as intended in the ADVaNCE MA context. We propose those modifications and that addition at § 516.625, as described in detail below.

3. ADVaNCE MA Model Overlaps
The ADVaNCE MA model would be a MA-focused CMS Innovation Center model. Because MA operates as a capitated, private managed care framework, whereas existing CMS Innovation Center models rely on OM claims attribution and total cost of care accountability, we do not anticipate substantial overlap between the ADVaNCE MA model and existing CMS Innovation Center models designed around OM. Medicare beneficiaries are generally enrolled either in OM or in MA for purposes of coverage of Medicare Parts A and B services. We recognize, however, that future CMS Innovation Center models or CMS programs may create circumstances in which an ADVaNCE MA model participant, its downstream providers or suppliers, or its enrolled beneficiaries are also affected by another CMS payment, quality, reporting, or benefit policy. In such circumstances, overlap may create operational, payment, or evaluation questions that CMS would need to address to preserve ADVaNCE MA model integrity, avoid duplicative incentives, and ensure accurate evaluation.
We are not, in this rule, proposing any specific overlap policy with an existing model other than recognizing that overlap with currently operating OM focused models is expected to be limited. We seek comment on our proposed approach to account for overlaps with other CMS programs and models.

b. Diamond Ratings System
We propose at § 516.205 to establish the Diamond Ratings system as a comprehensive redesign of the Star Ratings system that would measure and reward MA plan performance at the parent organization level within Mandatory States, utilizing cohorts to ensure fair comparisons among organizations serving similar beneficiary populations.
The Diamond Ratings system scores would be viewable on Medicare Plan Finder beginning with the CY 2031 Diamond Ratings and continue throughout the model and would compare entire parent organizations against each other within a Mandatory State and by cohort (one relative score for a parent organization's D-SNP population; another relative score for their General Enrollment population) to allow for meaningful beneficiary comparisons and to promote competition based on quality between plans locally for each parent organization that operates within an ADVaNCE MA Mandatory State. These ratings would be labeled as ADVaNCE MA Overall Diamond Ratings and would be displayed only for plans that are ADVaNCE MA model participants. The ADVaNCE MA Overall Diamond Ratings would provide usable data to support more informed beneficiary plan selection and to stimulate competition.
The proposed data sharing on Medicare Plan Finder complies with beneficiary confidentiality requirements specified in the regulations at
42 CFR 401.118
, which prohibits public disclosure of beneficiary identifying information and limits the release of such information to only when necessary for program purposes, consistent with applicable Federal laws and CMS data sharing procedures.
c. Supplemental Benefit Flexibility Data Sharing
We propose at § 516.300 to allow ADVaNCE MA model participants to engage in a targeting flexibility for offering MA supplemental benefits that is not currently available in the MA program, as well as offer certain non-primarily health related supplemental benefits to LIS-eligible individuals in a manner that would otherwise only be permissible as SSBCI. In the ADVaNCE MA model, CMS proposes to allow ADVaNCE MA model participants to target healthy food and produce, transportation for non-medical needs, or support for caregiver supplemental benefits (or any and all of the aforementioned) to enrollees eligible for Part LIS.
To evaluate the effectiveness of these supplemental benefits, CMS would exercise our authority to collect comprehensive data annually on supplemental benefit utilization and costs through PBP-level reporting as well as beneficiary-level reporting. To minimize reporting burden on MA organizations, these reporting requirements would align as closely as feasible to the established Part C Reporting Requirements in
42 CFR 422.516
. CMS would review the quality of this data, including examining variation in utilization patterns among MA organizations and assessing the accuracy, reliability, and validity of the reported information before making determinations about the impact of these benefits on beneficiary outcomes and program costs. As needed, CMS would provide additional sub-regulatory guidance specifying data reporting formats, definitions, and submission requirements for supplemental benefit utilization to ensure consistency and minimize administrative burden.
The PBP-level data collected for the evaluation and monitoring of these supplemental benefits would be de-identified and aggregated, not including any personally identifiable information that could be used to identify individual beneficiaries. However, the additional beneficiary-level supplemental benefits utilization and costs reporting would include private and sensitive data necessary to allow CMS to effectively monitor supplemental benefit utilization patterns and assess the model's impact on health outcomes and program costs.
5. Evaluation
Pursuant to
42 CFR 403.1110(b)

We would use such data to conduct an evaluation of the proposed ADVaNCE MA model in accordance with section 1115A(b)(4) of the Act, which requires the Secretary to evaluate each model tested by the CMS Innovation Center.
The evaluation would consider changes in the quality of care and changes in program spending that occurred due to the model. Because one of the goals of the ADVaNCE MA model is to assess market-level competitive effects, we would also consider examining the changes to market competition that occurred due to the model. We would also consider examining changes in utilization patterns, variations in impact, and the likelihood of unintended consequences or other effects.
We would select an independent evaluation contractor to perform this evaluation and would use a multilevel approach to evaluation. We are considering analyses at the State, parent organization, contract, plan, and beneficiary levels. Based on the State groupings method proposed in the section on selection of geographic areas, we believe there are several ways in which we can draw comparison groups and employ scientifically-sound, rigorous methods for evaluating the effect of the ADVaNCE MA model intervention. The evaluation effort may require participants in the ADVaNCE MA model to provide additional data specifically for evaluation purposes. Such requirements for additional data to carry out ADVaNCE MA model evaluation would be in compliance with

We would consider all parent organizations, and their subsidiaries providing plans under eligible contracts within a Mandatory State, to be participating in the testing of the ADVaNCE MA model because they would be receiving payment from CMS under the model.

CMS proposes to remove the network adequacy submission and review requirements for initial applicants and service area expansion (SAE) applicants under the MA application process. Under the current framework, prospective MA organizations are required to submit provider network data as part of the MA application, which is reviewed by CMS prior to contract approval.
Under this proposal, provider network submissions would no longer be required at the application stage. Instead, MA organizations would be required to submit provider network data during the first year the contract is operational, at which point CMS would conduct its network adequacy review.
This change does not eliminate the overall burden associated with network adequacy submissions; rather, it redistributes that burden from the pre-contract application period to the first operational contract year. (

Under the current framework, MA organizations are required to separately document and demonstrate network adequacy for Clinical Psychology and Clinical Social Work as distinct specialty categories. Under the proposed change, these two categories would be merged into the existing OBH standard, resulting in a single submission and review process for outpatient behavioral health network adequacy.
This consolidation is expected to result in a measurable reduction in respondent burden, as MA organizations will no longer be required to separately contract with, compile, document, and submit network data for two additional distinct behavioral health specialty categories. 8. ICRs Regarding Cost Sharing Standards for Ground Ambulance and Emergency Services (§§ 422.100 and 422.113)
As discussed in section III.D of this proposed rule, this proposal requires MA plans (including employer group waiver plans [EGWPs]) in-network cost sharing for ground ambulance and emergency services to be subject to the following cost sharing standards, beginning in contract year 2028:

X. Regulatory Impact Analysis
A. Statement of Need
This proposed rule addresses several critical needs in the Medicare Advantage (Part C), Medicare Prescription Drug Benefit (Part D), PACE organizations, and Medicare cost plans that require regulatory action to ensure program integrity, beneficiary protection, and statutory compliance. This rule also includes proposals intended to implement new requirements, codify existing subregulatory guidance, and provide greater clarity and operational consistency for plans operating in the MA and Part D spaces for contract year 2028.
This proposed rule includes a wide range of provisions to strengthen the MA and Part D programs for contract year 2028. Key proposals address beneficiary protections—including standardized healthy food definitions for supplemental benefits, improved provider termination notifications, continuity of care guarantees, and better-aligned cost-sharing for ambulance and emergency services. The rule also targets program integrity through tighter controls on the Disaster/Emergency SEP and enrollment capacity limits, while modernizing operations via mandatory use of a FHIR-based Prior Authorization API, policies to facilitate manufacturer effectuation of maximum fair prices for selected drugs administered or furnished to Medicare Advantage enrollees, and a streamlined agent and broker compensation framework. Additional provisions would update MA application and network adequacy requirements, and improve Medicaid coordination for Special Needs Plans serving dually eligible individuals.
This rule proposes to establish the Aligning Data and Value to Nurture Competition and Efficiency in Medicare Advantage (ADVaNCE MA) model under section 1115A of the Act to test whether alternative quality programs, targeted supplemental benefits, and an alternative risk adjustment methodology can improve care quality for MA enrollees without increasing costs to the Medicare program. The absence of a rigorous, mandatory testing mechanism limits CMS' ability to generate the evidence needed to drive data-informed improvements to MA payment and care delivery in future rulemaking.
The absence of regulatory action would result in ongoing operational inefficiencies and missed opportunities for program improvement and innovation. Therefore, this rulemaking is necessary to ensure the Medicare program operates effectively, efficiently, and in compliance with Federal law
(
printed page 76533)
while serving the best interests of Medicare beneficiaries.

1. Cost Sharing Standards for Ground Ambulance and Emergency Services (§ 422.100 and 422.113)
As discussed in section III.D. of this proposed rule, this proposal requires MA plans (including employer group waiver plans (EGWPs)) in-network cost sharing for ground ambulance and emergency services to be subject to the following cost sharing standards, beginning in contract year 2028: (1) ground ambulance—the range of cost sharing limits at §  422.100(f)(6)(iii); and (2) emergency services—dollar limits that are actuarially equivalent to 15-20 percent of the most recent Medicare FFS data projections. CMS expects that this proposal to update the cost sharing standards for ground ambulance and emergency services will result in MA plans changing cost sharing amounts across service categories and MOOP limits.
From an aggregate perspective, CMS assumes that this proposal will not result in: (1) additional out of pocket costs for MA enrollees compared to beneficiaries in Original Medicare; or (2) significant losses for MA organizations. This is because there is a statutory requirement for MA organizations to submit bids that are at least actuarially equivalent to coverage in Original Medicare. This statutory requirement is operationalized through an actuarial equivalence test based on a projection of MA cost sharing under each plan. At the time that the actuarially equivalent cost sharing amounts are calculated, the expectation is that there will be no costs or savings for the policy year in question. As a result, the plan will cover—and MA enrollees would receive—the same level of total benefits
(
printed page 76534)
on average in each contract year prior to and after implementation.
If this proposal is finalized, CMS would not experience additional burden because adjustments to the plan benefit package could be made as part of normal business operations as needed. In addition, CMS expects this proposal would prompt some organizations to adjust their plan benefit designs, primarily to come into compliance with this proposal, if: (1) any of their contract year 2027 plan benefits are not compliant with the proposed ground ambulance
[
290

cost-sharing standards for contract year 2028 and (2) they submit a bid to continue that plan offering for contract year 2028. Further, enrollees who remain in those continuing plans are expected to experience changes in cost that will change over time based on their health status and service utilization (for example, ground ambulance services or other service categories).
These potential impacts to organizations and enrollees are discussed in greater detail in the following section. In brief, CMS expects this proposal will result in:
Non-significant changes to total plan costs; as such MA plans will likely shift cost sharing by service category and MOOP limits to maintain benefits that are actuarially equivalent to current benefit packages.
Enrollees utilizing emergency services less often while increasing utilization of other services (for example, urgent care); which is likely to result in:
++ Neutral financial impacts given that that change in utilization may create savings or additional costs, depending on whether the forgone emergency services were necessary or not.
++ Negligible impacts on hospitalization rates given that most MA plans waive emergency services cost sharing when the enrollee is admitted as an inpatient to the same hospital within a 3-day window from an emergency department visit (the expectation being that an enrollee needing emergency services at an urgent care clinic would be transferred to an emergency department and then admitted as an inpatient with zero emergency department cost sharing).

b. Impact Analysis: Proposed Ground Ambulance and Emergency Services Cost-Sharing Standards
The aggregate, short term impact of this proposal on MA organizations and enrollees should be minimal due to the statutory requirement that plans remain actuarially equivalent to Original Medicare. However, as noted previously and shown in Tables III.D-5—III.D-7, MA plan cost sharing amounts for—and thus potential enrollee utilization of—emergency and ground ambulance and other service categories may change as a direct result of this proposal. 2. Enrollee Notification Requirements for Provider Terminations, Continuity of Care, and SEP Notice Consolidation (§§ 422.111(e), 422.112(b), and 422.2267(e)(12))
CMS is proposing several changes to regulations governing provider network terminations in MA. These proposals include: (1) revising the timing and content of required enrollee notices for provider terminations; (2) establishing new minimum continuity of care standards requiring MA organizations to cover services from a terminated provider for at least 90 days at in-network cost-sharing rates; (3) requiring MA organizations to include special election period (SEP) eligibility information in the provider termination notice when CMS has determined that the affected enrollee qualifies for the SEP at § 422.62(b)(23); (4) updating the affected enrollee definition to a uniform 1-year lookback period; and (5) codifying longstanding criteria used to identify whether a provider termination constitutes a significant change in a plan provider network at § 422.112(d).
a. Savings From Simplified and Streamlined Notice Requirements
CMS anticipates that the proposed revisions to the provider termination notice requirements will generate administrative savings for MA organizations. Most notably, the proposal to eliminate the telephonic notice requirement at § 422.111(e)(1)(i) removes a distinct and operationally burdensome notification pathway that currently requires MA organizations to maintain separate telephonic outreach processes in addition to written notice. The elimination of this requirement is expected to reduce per-termination administrative costs for MA organizations.
Additionally, the proposed update to the affected enrollee definition at § 422.111(e)(3) and § 422.62(b)(23)(ii) to a uniform 1-year lookback period is expected to reduce net administrative costs by eliminating the need for MA organizations to run separate queries and maintain separate enrollee populations by provider type. Under the proposed rule, MA organizations would identify affected enrollees through a single query, maintain one list, and issue one consolidated notice—rather than managing two separate enrollee populations for what is, in effect, a single network disruption event.
CMS is unable to quantify these savings at this time because the per-notice cost of telephonic outreach and the administrative cost of maintaining dual enrollee populations vary across MA organizations and are not available to CMS.
CMS solicits comment on the estimated per-notice cost savings associated with eliminating the telephonic notice requirement, the estimated administrative savings associated with consolidating the affected enrollee query and list maintenance process, and the number of provider termination events per year for which MA organizations currently issue notices.
b. Financial Burden on MA Organizations From 90-Day Continuity of Care Requirement
The proposed continuity of care requirement at § 422.112(b)(9), which would require MA organizations to cover services from a terminated provider for a minimum of 90 days at in-network cost-sharing rates, may impose financial costs on MA organizations. However, CMS is unable to quantify the financial burden of this requirement at this time because the costs depend on variables that are not available to CMS.
CMS solicits comment on the estimated number of provider terminations per year that would trigger the continuity of care requirement, the estimated number of affected enrollees who would utilize continuity of care services during the 90-day period, the types of services most commonly utilized during continuity of care periods, and the estimated differential between in-network and out-of-network rates for those services.
c. Net Effect of Codifying Significance Determination Criteria (§ 422.112(d))
The proposed codification of significance determination criteria at new § 422.112(d) formalizes a process that MA organizations are already expected to follow under sub-regulatory guidance in Chapter 4 of the Medicare Managed Care Manual. The proposed 60-day notification requirement is consistent with the existing § 422.202(d)(4) provider notification timeframe. Because this proposal codifies existing sub-regulatory practice rather than imposing an entirely new obligation, CMS does not anticipate a significant net increase in administrative burden attributable to this provision.
CMS solicits comment on the current frequency with which MA organizations submit significant provider termination notifications to CMS under the existing sub-regulatory guidance, whether the proposed codified criteria align with the standards MA organizations currently apply internally, and whether codification is expected to increase or decrease reporting volume relative to current practice.

4. Strengthening Maximum Fair Price Effectuation Policies for Medicare Advantage (§ 422.100 and § 422.504)
CMS is proposing to require that any out-of-network cost sharing for selected drugs payable under Part B subject to an MFP is calculated based on a price that does not exceed the MFP (as defined in proposed § 422.2). CMS is also proposing four changes to facilitate manufacturer effectuation of the MFP for selected drugs payable under Part B for which an MFP is in effect that are furnished or administered to MA enrollees. These proposals include: (1) at proposed § 422.504(p) requiring any contract between an MA organization and a provider, or between a first tier, downstream, or related entity and a provider on the MA organization's behalf, for participation in one or more of the MA organization's networks include a provision that if the provider furnishes or administers selected drugs payable under Part B during the period when such drugs are subject to an MFP, the provider must be enrolled in the Medicare Transaction Facilitator Data Module (MTF DM) and maintain and certify up-to-date, complete and accurate enrollment information with the MTF DM, in accordance with applicable terms and conditions of participation with the MTF DM, in a form and manner determined by CMS; (2) at proposed § 422.504(q)(1)(i)) requiring MA organizations to submit MA encounter data records involving the furnishing or administration of selected drugs payable under Part B for which an MFP is in effect on the claim-from date within 30 days of the claim-from date; (3) at proposed § 422.504(q)(1)(ii) requiring MA organizations to collect and submit NDC-11s on MA encounter data records for selected drugs payable under Part B for which an MFP is in effect on the claim-from date; and (4) at proposed § 422.504(q)(2) requiring MA organizations to certify, in a form and manner specified by CMS, that the data submitted under § 429.504(q)(1) is complete, accurate, and truthful.
a. Medicare Advantage Out-Of-Network Cost Sharing for Selected Drugs Payable Under Part B
Under this proposal, coinsurance for selected drugs subject to an MFP furnished or administered by an out-of-network provider would be calculated based on a price no greater than the MFP. We expect this policy to have no impact on overall MA expenditures.
MA plan sponsors are required to establish cost sharing for basic benefits specified by CMS that do not exceed levels annually determined by CMS to be discriminatory, as set forth at § 422.100(f)(6). MA plan sponsors that establish out-of-network cost sharing for Part B drugs are required to include this cost sharing in their prospective bid calculation. As a result, any plan-level cost changes arising from this proposal, including adjustments to beneficiary cost-sharing obligations, must be fully reflected in prospective bid calculations. Per § 422.100(j)(2), an MA plan's total cost sharing for all basic benefits must not exceed cost sharing for those benefits in original Medicare on a per member per month actuarially equivalent basis. Therefore, to the extent that this policy reduces cost-sharing on the selected drugs with an MFP below total financial liability, MA plan bids will likely respond by raising cost-sharing for other benefits (such as other Part B drugs) in order to maintain compliance with the requirements from paragraph (j)(2). These potential cost sharing adjustments must consider the projected utilization, so any changes in utilization resulting from changes to cost-sharing will be accounted for. Actuarial equivalence standards and cost-sharing adjustments neutralize any net effect on bids.
Under the proposed regulation, coinsurance for selected drugs payable under Part B with an MFP below the total financial liability furnished or administered by an out-of-network provider must be calculated based on a price that is equal to or less than the MFP, thereby potentially reducing beneficiary out-of-pocket costs for those selected drugs (not in aggregate from an actuarial perspective). However, given that drugs payable under Part B will have MFPs in effect for the first time in 2028, we are uncertain at this time the extent to which this proposed regulation would impact beneficiary cost sharing. Given that selected drugs furnished or administered by out-of-network providers and payable under Part B represent a minority of total spending by MA plans, we do not expect broader impacts resulting from the lower cost sharing.
b. Medicare Transaction Facilitator Requirements for Network Providers
The proposal of the “Medicare Transaction Facilitator Requirements for Providers” provision applies to MA organizations. The proposal would require any contract between an MA organization and a provider, or between a first tier, downstream, or related entity and a provider on the MA organization's behalf, for participation in one or more of the MA organization's networks include a provision that if the provider furnishes or administers selected drugs payable under Part B during the period when such drugs are subject to an MFP, the provider must be enrolled in the MTF DM. CMS notes that this provision in the proposed rule would have a negligible direct economic impact on MA organizations (associated with adding language to their contracts with providers) and will not have a direct significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities. CMS recognizes that providers (including those that are “small entities” under the meaning of the RFA) are indirectly involved in the downstream impacts of this provision as they fulfill the requirements of their contracts with MA organizations and enroll in the MTF DM. This one-time enrollment activity among providers is expected to have a nominal economic cost per entity associated with completing a brief web-based enrollment form, which CMS has described in the Medicare Transaction Facilitator Information Collection Request (CMS-10912, OMB 0938-NEW).

As discussed in section II.I.1 of this proposed rule, we believe that enrollment in the MTF DM by providers that furnish or administer selected drugs payable under Part B for which an MFP is in effect would facilitate continued beneficiary and provider access under the MA program to selected drugs that are payable under Part B. As discussed in this proposed rule, the MTF is designed to provide efficient, timely, and unified data exchange and payment flow where none currently exists between Primary Manufacturers and providers. c. Submission of Encounter Data Records for Selected Drugs Payable Under Part B
CMS is proposing to require MA organizations to submit MA encounter data records involving the furnishing or administration of selected drugs payable under Part B for which an MFP is in effect on the claim-from date within 30 days of the claim-from date. This proposal would not affect the existing deadline requirements or processes for submission of MA encounter data records for Part B drugs or any other service or item provided to an MA enrollee for the purpose of risk adjustment. However, MA encounter data for selected drugs payable under Part B and submitted to CMS under the proposal will be used for risk adjustment purposes unless the MA organization submits risk adjustment data required under § 422.310 by the final risk adjustment submission deadline under § 422.310(g).
This proposed requirement is necessary to ensure MA beneficiaries' access to selected drugs payable under Part B. Absent a requirement for MA organizations to submit encounter data for selected drugs payable under Part B for which an MFP is in effect within 30 days, providers could wait up to approximately 26 months to receive an MFP refund from the manufacturer. As such, providers could be inadvertently disincentivized from furnishing or administering selected drugs payable under Part B for which an MFP is in effect, thereby potentially impacting MA enrollee access to selected drugs payable under Part B. This proposed requirement will help facilitate manufacturer effectuation of the MFP for selected drugs payable under Part B and furnished or administered to MFP-eligible individuals enrolled in an MA plan under Part C and help ensure that providers furnishing or administering selected drugs payable under Part B receive MFP refund payments from manufacturers promptly, thereby enabling them to continue furnishing or administering to MA beneficiaries selected drugs payable under Part B. Following solicitation of public comment on the 30-day timeline in the Draft Guidance on Manufacturer Effectuation of the Maximum Fair Price in 2028 under the Medicare Drug Price Negotiation Program, we believe that a 30-day timeline appropriately balances increased burden on MA organizations with the need for prompt manufacturer MFP refund payments to providers.

5. Specialty Tier Eligibility With Respect to Selected Drugs and Technical Correction (§ 423.104)
In this rule, consistent with existing policy, we propose to revise our specialty-tier regulations to expressly state that, for selected drugs with an MFP in effect for the applicable contract year, CMS will use the MFP rather than the PDE claims history to determine specialty-tier placement eligibility. If a selected drug's maximum fair price for a 30-day equivalent supply is below the annually determined specialty threshold, which is set at $1,080 for 2027, it will be ineligible for the specialty tier. As this policy is already in effect, we do not expect an impact on Medicare Part D expenditures. The requirements for actuarial equivalence in Part D bid submissions prevent a change in tiering from changing the overall value of the Part D plan sponsor's benefit. While cost sharing may be lower for the drugs impacted by this policy, any specific utilization effects will be counterbalanced by increased cost sharing on other drugs to maintain equivalence.
When the maximum fair price for a selected drug is below the specialty tier threshold, such drugs would be ineligible for the specialty tier and would be required to be placed on non-specialty tiers. Part D plan sponsors are also required to submit actuarially sound bids that satisfy the actuarial equivalence standards set forth under
42 CFR 423.265
. As a result, any plan-level cost changes arising from this proposal—including adjustments to beneficiary cost-sharing obligations—must be fully reflected in prospective bid calculations. To the extent that this policy reduces cost-sharing on the selected drugs with a maximum fair price below the specialty tier threshold, the bids must respond by raising cost-sharing on other drugs. This adjustment must consider the projected utilization on all drugs, so any changes in utilization resulting from changes to cost-sharing will be accounted for. Actuarial equivalence standards and cost-sharing adjustments neutralize any net effect on bids and payments from CMS to Part D plan sponsors.
Finally, this policy may produce changes in utilization patterns for affected drugs. Under the proposed regulations, selected drugs with a maximum fair price below the specialty tier threshold are not eligible for the specialty tier. Selected drugs that may have had negotiated prices above the specialty tier threshold in previous years prior to their maximum fair price taking effect will instead be placed on a preferred tier, reducing the beneficiary cost-sharing. However, given that drugs with prices in the range to be impacted by this policy represent a minority of selected drugs for initial price applicability years 2026 and 2027, we do not expect broader impacts on population health from lower cost-sharing. We expect that Part D plan sponsors will continue to adjust their formularies to promote cost-effective drugs for their members.

There are two ways that Star Ratings changes will impact the Medicare Trust Fund:
A Star Rating of 4.0 or higher will result in a QBP for the MA contract, which, in turn, leads to a higher benchmark for the MA plans offered by the MA organization under that contract. In this proposed rule, we are proposing to amend the definition of FIDE SNP at § 422.2 to remove the requirement that the D-SNP provide access to Medicare and Medicaid under a single entity that holds both an MA contract with CMS and a Medicaid MCO and replace it with the same requirement currently applicable to HIDE SNPs under § 422.2: the requirement that the plan provides coverage of Medicaid benefits under a capitated contract that is between the State Medicaid agency and the MA organization, the MA organization's parent organization or another entity that is owned and controlled by its parent organization, or a local nonprofit public benefit corporation of which the MA organization, MA organization's parent organization, or another entity that is owned and controlled by its parent organization is a founding member where the local nonprofit public benefit corporation is responsible for the delivery of physical, behavioral, and dental health services.
Over the 10-year period from 2028 to 2037, we estimate that this proposal would result in total net transfers from the Medicare Trust Fund to MA organizations of approximately $609 million. The projected transfers are driven by the possibility that a subset of HIDE SNPs newly qualifying for FIDE SNP designation could become eligible for frailty-adjusted MA payments. The proposal does not change MA payment methodology, beneficiary eligibility, or enrollment requirements. Instead, it broadens the organizational structures that may qualify for FIDE SNP designation by allowing the Medicaid managed care contract to be held by the MA organization, its parent organization, or an affiliated entity under the same parent organization
The analysis assumes that several existing HIDE SNPs could become eligible for FIDE SNP status under the revised definition. Because plan-level qualification for the frailty adjustment is not publicly available, we assume that 30 percent of the potentially affected enrollment qualifies for frailty-adjusted payments. Approximately 60 percent of current FIDE SNP enrollment is in plans that qualify for the frailty adjustment. To account for uncertainty regarding whether the affected HIDE SNP populations would meet CMS's frailty criteria, we conservatively apply one-half of the observed FIDE qualification rate.
Estimated payment impacts were developed using the average frailty adjustment currently observed for existing FIDE SNPs and projected forward using MA payment trends from the 2025 Medicare Trustees Report. The proposal does not affect MA enrollment, benchmarks, or bid submission requirements, and therefore estimated transfers reflect only the potential increase in risk-adjusted payments associated with expanded eligibility for FIDE SNP designation.
While greater organizational alignment between Medicare and Medicaid may improve care coordination, we did not estimate any offsetting Medicare savings. The proposal does not require changes in enrollment alignment or care delivery, and we are not aware of sufficient evidence demonstrating measurable reductions in Medicare expenditures associated solely with the expanded FIDE SNP eligibility criteria.
Under these assumptions, estimated gross transfers from the Medicare Trust Fund to MA organizations increase from approximately $41 million in 2026 to $95 million in 2037, for a total gross cost of approximately $727 million over the 2028-2037 projection period. b. Update to Default Enrollment for States Transitioning From Medicaid FFS to Medicaid Managed Care
We are proposing allow default enrollment into a D-SNP for individuals who are eligible for Medicare and who are in the process of transitioning from Medicaid FFS into a Medicaid managed care plan affiliated with the D-SNP, as part of a State-initiated transition to Medicaid managed care.
This analysis estimates the impact of the proposed revision to § 422.66(c), which would allow default enrollment into an affiliated D-SNP for individuals transitioning from Medicaid FFS into Medicaid managed care at the time they become Medicare eligible. The analysis focuses on States where meaningful Medicaid FFS-to-managed care transition pathways remain for full-benefit dually eligibles.
States were grouped into three tiers based on the likelihood that newly Medicare-eligible duals would be in Medicaid FFS and subsequently transition into an aligned Medicaid managed care and D-SNP arrangement. Tier 1 States (Alabama, Georgia, Missouri, Mississippi) represent the highest-impact States due to greater reliance on FFS pathways for aged, blind, disabled, and LTSS populations. Tier 2 States (IN, NC, OK) have established managed care programs but retain some transition pathways. Tier 3 States (Arizona, New Jersey, Pennsylvania, Tennessee, Virgina) have mature managed care and MLTSS programs and are expected to experience only limited impacts.
Enrollment estimates were developed using beneficiary-level Medicare-Medicaid enrollment data, focusing on new full-benefit dual eligibles currently enrolled in Original Medicare. For 2028, the model projects approximately 3,300 additional MA enrollees attributable to the proposal, growing to approximately 14,300 active enrollees by 2037. Enrollment impacts were estimated using State-specific assumptions regarding: (1) the percentage of newly Medicare-eligible duals in Medicaid FFS at Medicare eligibility, (2) the percentage transitioning into Medicaid managed care, and (3) the percentage entering an affiliated/aligned D-SNP pathway. Tier 1 States were assumed to have the highest pathway rates (30 percent FFS at eligibility, 60 percent MCO transition, 60 percent aligned pathway), with lower assumptions applied to Tier 2 and Tier 3 States. A 25 percent annual cohort decay factor was applied to reflect mortality and other enrollment attrition among a high-need dual-eligible population.
Per-capita Original Medicare transfers were based on a projected-enrollment-weighted average of KFF's 2021 estimates for full-benefit dual eligibles under age 65 enrolled in Original Medicare, resulting in a baseline transfer of $23,511 from the Medicare Trust Funds to MA organizations. These transfers were then trended forward using the 2025 Medicare Trustees Report USPCC growth factors.
To estimate the Medicare Advantage cost differential, the analysis used observed experience from a cohort of beneficiaries who became newly Medicare eligible and full-benefit dual eligible in 2022. County-level Medicare Advantage and Original Medicare expenditures were compared for this cohort through 2025, and the resulting duration pattern was used to develop MA-to-Original Medicare transfer factors for newly enrolled beneficiaries. This approach recognizes that expenditures for newly Medicare-eligible duals differ materially from expenditures observed after several years of enrollment and avoids applying payment relationships derived from mature Medicare populations.
Under these assumptions, estimated gross transfers from the Medicare Trust Funds to MA organizations increase gradually over the projection period as additional cohorts are default enrolled into MA. Total gross transfers from the Medicare Trust Funds to MA organizations over the 2028-2037 period are estimated at approximately $133 million. Because beneficiary premiums finance approximately 25 percent of Part B transfers, only the remaining share is borne by the Medicare Trust Funds and general revenues. After applying the projected net-of-Part-B-premium factors (84.5 percent in 2028 declining to 83.5 percent by 2037), the estimated net transfers from the Medicare Trust Funds and general revenues to MA organizations is approximately $112 million.

c. Expanding the Definition of HIDE SNP
We are proposing to broaden the HIDE SNP definition at § 422.2 to allow for more flexible and innovative arrangements between D-SNPs and Medicaid MCOs.
We developed savings estimates for expanding the HIDE SNP definition to allow certain CO D-SNPs to qualify as HIDE SNPs through arrangements with Medicaid managed care organizations that are not under the same parent organization. We assume that this change would allow some CO D-SNPs to become more integrated with the Medicaid delivery system and could generate efficiencies in the provision of Medicare-covered benefits.
The analysis is limited to CO D-SNP enrollment in States where HIDE or FIDE SNPs already operate, providing evidence that the State's Medicaid delivery system can support integrated D-SNP arrangements. We apply State-specific assumptions regarding the share of CO D-SNP enrollment for which greater integration is feasible and assume that potentially affected enrollment transitions gradually over the 2028 through 2037 projection period. Lower transition rates are assumed where the same D-SNP contract already operates an integrated D-SNP because the current organizational requirements are less likely to be the primary barrier to additional integration.
Savings are estimated using observed differences in Medicare Advantage bids and rebates between CO D-SNPs and more integrated D-SNPs. Consistent with previous estimates of increased D-SNP integration, lower bid-to-benchmark ratios among more integrated D-SNPs are assumed to reflect, in part, greater efficiency in providing Medicare-covered benefits. The per capita savings and affected enrollment are projected forward using Medicare enrollment and expenditure trends.
We similarly estimate Part D savings using observed differences in combined Part D bid and reinsurance amounts between CO and more integrated D-SNPs. As with Part C, the estimate assumes that a portion of the observed difference would be realized as CO D-SNPs transition to more integrated arrangements. This approach is generally consistent with previous estimates of D-SNP integration, which projected Part D impacts using differences in bid and reinsurance amounts and the enrollment expected to become more integrated.
Under these assumptions, affected enrollment increases from approximately 27,000 in 2028 to 320,000 in 2037. Estimated net Part C savings are approximately $123 million over the 2028-2037 projection period, and estimated Part D savings are approximately $173 million. Overall, we examined the potential impacts of the three proposed provisions related to Improvements for Special Needs Plans on the Medicaid program. Changes in the level of Medicare-Medicaid integration could affect Medicaid expenditures, particularly through changes in the coordination and utilization of long-term services and supports and behavioral health services. For example, greater integration could reduce or delay institutional long-term care while increasing the use of home- and community-based services. Changes in enrollment in Medicaid managed care arrangements could also affect Medicaid service utilization and expenditures. However, available evidence does not provide a sufficient basis for estimating the net Medicaid impact of these provisions. Because many Medicaid services are provided through capitated managed care arrangements, changes in service utilization may not immediately affect Medicaid program expenditures but could affect future capitation rates. The timing and magnitude of these effects would depend on State-specific utilization experience, rate-setting methodologies, and other factors. Accordingly, we do not estimate Medicaid costs or savings associated with these proposals and welcome public comments that could inform such an estimate.
11. Aligning Data and Value To Nurture Competition and Efficiency in Medicare Advantage (ADVaNCE MA) Model
The proposed ADVaNCE MA model tests certain changes to MA program structure in the model geographies for the individual and D-SNP markets. The model would adjust quality bonus payments to plans in model geographies and allow plans to offer certain supplemental benefits targeted based on beneficiaries' Part D Low Income Subsidy (LIS) status. The model would also consider alternatives to the current risk adjustment methodology and ESRD payments; as these adjustments are either informational or not proposed in this rule, we do not opine on the potential savings/costs associated with those adjustments. Below we discuss the potential impacts associated with the modifications proposed in this rule.
a. Changes to Market Geographies
To construct a control group for evaluation, the ADVaNCE MA model would be isolated to a subset of States. Currently, MA parent organizations may have contracts that can span over State lines. For the purposes of conducting the model test, these contracts would need to be split so that they do not contain both ADVaNCE MA and non-ADVaNCE MA geographies. This change alone would result in parent organizations submitting more contracts and bids and, therefore, may result in additional administrative costs for parent organizations, although we expect these additional costs to be small. The contract splitting process would affect contracts that currently span mandatory and non-mandatory state boundaries. I-SNPs (including IE-SNPs and HI-SNPs) are excluded from model participation and, therefore, would be unaffected by the contract restructuring requirements.
Additionally, CMS is proposing Star Ratings in non-model areas be adjusted for the impact of excluding model area contracts from Star Ratings. We would need to consider how the exclusion of model area contracts from the Star Ratings program may affect national cut points, clustering algorithms, and CAI calculations used to determine Star Ratings for non-model area contracts. If finalized, CMS will monitor these potential spillover effects and make further adjustments as necessary to minimize unintended impacts on non-model area plans. Therefore, we expect no savings/costs impact for non-model plans.
Further, our payments to EGWPs are made based on calculations from bids submitted in the individual non-D-SNP market. CMS is proposing to exclude EGWPs from the ADVaNCE MA model. If finalized, we will make considerations on how to adjust EGWPs' payment calculations, including any future rulemaking, to keep EGWP disruption minimal. Our payments to EGWPs are based on the average bid-to-benchmark ratio for individual MA plans in their service area. The restructuring of model area contracts and the introduction of Diamond Ratings-based benchmark adjustments could affect both the bid-to-benchmark ratio and the implicit rebate calculation for EGWPs—potentially disrupting EGWP payment rates in mandatory geographic areas and, indirectly, in non-Mandatory States as well. If finalized, we will monitor these potential effects and make adjustments as necessary to minimize unintended impacts on EGWP payment rates, including through future rulemaking.
b. Changes to Quality Bonus Payments
The ADVaNCE MA model would make the following changes to how MA quality scores affect MA payments:
Testing an alternative to the Star Ratings program with a new Diamond Rating system (determined at the parent organization level for each state) with two distinct Diamond Ratings per parent organization—one for the D-SNP cohort and one for the General Enrollment cohort.
The applicable benchmark adjustment would be based on a linear interpolation of a particular parent organization's rating versus the range of the market. Specifically, the highest-rated plan in a given market would receive the maximum benchmark adjustment (proposed at up to five percent, though the final percentage is illustrative and subject to change based on forthcoming analytics, public comment, and budget review), and the lowest-rated plan would receive no additional benchmark adjustment (that is, zero percent), with all other plans receiving an adjustment between these two, based on the proposed formula. Also, the “double bonus counties” framework would not apply and there would be no additional adjustment for these counties.
The rebate percentage would be based on a linear interpolation of a particular parent organization's rating versus the range of the market (that is, the highest Diamond Rating plan would receive a rebate percentage of 70 percent and the lowest Diamond Rating plan would receive a rebate percentage of 50 percent with all other plans receiving a rebate percentage between these two, based on the proposed formula).
If finalized, CMS would retain the flexibility to make budget adjustments in future rulemaking, so that the other payment revisions do not result in costs to the MA program. Such adjustments would need to be regularly updated and could have different market implications depending on their structure (for example, changing the benchmark adjustment for the highest rated plan vs changes to benchmarks for all plans). Also, the adjustments to achieve this goal will likely be based on model experience, but will impact prospective payments. These adjustments may not fully offset past savings or losses.
The ADVaNCE MA model aims for budget savings at the overall model level, relative to the existing MA Quality Bonus Payment system. This may be challenging, as the determination of counterfactual costs to the model will be increasingly hard to determine over time. For example, if a parent organization leaves one of the Mandatory States due to revenue reductions, that would have an impact on payments beyond the proposed model changes to benchmark and rebate levels. It is possible that the model impact will be either higher or lower costs.
(
printed page 76546)
We note that the removal of the “double bonus counties” framework on its own would generate savings absent the other tests currently proposed in the model. We estimate this change could reduce a particular Mandatory State's total benchmarks anywhere from zero to 3.0 percent, with an average reduction of 0.6 percent across all States. The total payment reductions from any benchmark reduction would depend on reactions from market participants, for example, the amount of savings from rebate-based payments versus bid-based payments would depend on the change in plan bids and the resulting bid to benchmark ratio.
In addition to the cost/savings implications of the model, there are also implications for beneficiaries in the model geographies. Plans may leave certain ADVaNCE MA markets based on their forecasted revenue reductions, forcing currently enrolled beneficiaries to choose new MA plans or revert to Original Medicare. We have reviewed data on forecasted revenue changes to inform scenario analysis of potential market changes. In one hypothetical scenario, where MA organizations facing material revenue reductions pull out of ADVaNCE MA States representing less than 10 percent of their enrollment, approximately 400,000 enrollees would have to find a new plan. This is just one of many hypothetical scenarios. For example, it's also possible that new plans could enter markets due to new competitive considerations or more beneficiaries switching to MA from Original Medicare due to the new benefit offerings.
c. Changes to Supplemental Benefit Offerings
ADVaNCE MA model participants would also be allowed to offer certain supplemental benefits (including food and produce, transportation for non-medical needs, and caregiver support) to beneficiaries based on their LIS eligibility. There is some evidence in literature to support such benefits producing medical cost savings. However, such an impact would need to be weighed against the reduction of other supplemental benefits and their relative value. Increased use of targeted benefits may put upward pressure on risk scores. MA organizations offering these model supplemental benefits may have additional interactions with their enrollees, leading to more opportunities for new diagnoses. MA organizations' revenue is still tied to risk scores within the model, so new diagnoses could lead to higher payments to plans. This pattern was observed in the discontinued CMS Innovation Center Value-Based Insurance Design (VBID) model, although the additional benefits in that model targeted specific conditions, unlike in the ADVaNCE MA model.
Offering these supplemental benefits is optional for MA organizations. ADVaNCE MA model participants retain full discretion to use rebate dollars for other purposes (premium reductions, cost-sharing reductions, or other supplemental benefits). The ADVaNCE MA model creates a new pathway that gives plans the option to target food, transportation, and caregiver support specifically to LIS-eligible enrollees—something not available under current law.
d. Conclusion
The ADVaNCE MA model includes multiple tests of the MA program, and it is difficult to anticipate exactly how these tests will impact all interested parties. As it relates to assessing the regulatory impact, CMS could propose future policy adjustments to avoid unfavorable impacts to trust fund expenditures and to achieve model savings. For example, if the overall payments inside the model exceeded estimates of what they would have been absent the model, CMS could propose to modify ADVaNCE payments to reduce model payments in future years. The payment and incentive structures may have other impacts to enrollees or administrative costs. The impact of the supplemental benefit offerings is unclear.

While this alternative is the most protective of beneficiaries requiring ground ambulance services and ground ambulance providers, like alternative 1, this alternative does not improve the existing cost-sharing incentives for MA plans to establish lower MOOP amounts because the proposed ground ambulance cost-sharing standards would apply equally to all MOOP types. Given that the proposed changes to emergency services cost sharing limits (or alternative 3 in the following section X.D.1.d.(3). of this proposed rule) may reduce the existing cost sharing incentives for lower MOOP adoption, CMS believes another alternative that improves upon the existing cost-sharing incentives for lower MOOP types would be appropriate to consider.
Given the reasons discussed, CMS is not proposing this alternative.
(3) Alternative 3 (Proposed)
In this alternative/proposal, CMS proposes to set ground ambulance services cost sharing limits based on the range of cost sharing limits codified at § 422.100(f)(6)(iii), beginning in contract year 2028, and the most recent weighted average Medicare FFS data projections. As shown in Table X.9, this alternative results in ground ambulance cost
(
printed page 76553)
sharing limits ranging from $180 to $300 based on MOOP type. Given that the current ground ambulance cost sharing standard (50 percent coinsurance) applies equally to all MA plans, CMS expects this alternative—by itself—will improve upon the existing cost sharing incentives for lower MOOP adoption.
As shown in Tables III.D-7 and X.D-2, this alternative would result in approximately 65 percent of MA plans decreasing their ground ambulance cost sharing amounts by about $75 on average (or between $38 to $126, based on MOOP type). However, this expected impact to MA plan ground ambulance cost sharing is a rough estimate for the same reasons discussed in relation to alternative 1's impact assessment—and because it does not account for how this alternative (which assigns unique cost sharing limits based on MOOP type) may result in more MA plans choosing lower MOOP types (and the increased cost sharing flexibility for ground ambulance services). As a result, CMS emphasizes that all estimates of expected decreases to average MA plan ground ambulance cost sharing amounts are only rough parameters of impact.
Under this alternative, for example, MA plans may decrease their ground ambulance cost sharing amount by roughly $75 on average based on Table III.D-7. Given the flexibility afforded by the cost sharing standards proposed for emergency services, CMS believes a plan in this situation could make the necessary cost sharing offset ($75) by primarily increasing their emergency services cost sharing amount. For example, an existing MA plan with a mandatory MOOP type (that chooses not to switch MOOP types) and a $115 emergency services dollar limit (the maximum allowed under the current regulations) may choose to increase their emergency services cost sharing amount up to CMS's proposed limit for the mandatory MOOP type ($180). That would be a $65 increase and leave only $10 unaccounted for. Alternatively, if the MA plan chose to lower their MOOP type they would gain access to additional emergency services cost sharing flexibility (and not necessarily need to adjust other benefit category cost sharing amounts in response to maintain actuarial equivalence to original Medicare). As a result, CMS believes this alternative would: (1) better allocate cost sharing revenue between ground ambulance and emergency services, (2) reduce the risk for ground ambulance providers to gain uncollectable bad debt due, and (3) require minimal changes to other aspects of the plan's benefit design to come into compliance with the proposed and existing actuarial equivalence standard.
As discussed in section III.D. of this proposed rule, CMS is considerate that the $155 imbalance in ground ambulance cost sharing between original Medicare ($120 based on contract year 2027 Medicare FFS data projections) and MA ($275, based on contract year 2026 MA weighted average plan data) may result in significantly more uncollectable bad debt for ground ambulance providers when they provide ambulance services to MA enrollees over beneficiaries in original Medicare. Regarding this risk of uncollectable bad debt, this alternative is expected to reduce the difference in average ground ambulance cost sharing responsibility between MA plans and original Medicare from $155 (comparing the values in Table III.D-4) by about $75 (as shown in Table III.D-7 with the limitations noted throughout this section) to $80. In other words, CMS expects this proposal will reduce average MA plan ground ambulance cost sharing from $275 to about $200, based on the minimum $75 average change necessary for current plan designs to become compliant with the proposed standards (though this assumes current MOOP type allocation). While this alternative does not fully address the imbalance of cost sharing between original Medicare and MA for ground ambulance services, it may make a meaningful improvement (and thus address uncollectible bad debt concerns of ground ambulance providers).
In summary, CMS concludes that this alternative (in combination with the proposal for emergency services) best addresses the following goals because it:
Negates the potential financial incentive most MA organizations have under the current cost sharing standards to raise cost sharing for benefit categories that are not emergency services, such as ground ambulance services, to make up for the out-of-date cost sharing limit for emergency services.
Addresses concerns raised by interested parties, including ground ambulance providers, from uncollectable bad debt.
Maintains or improve upon the existing cost sharing incentives for MA organizations to adopt lower MOOP amounts.
Uses the most recent Medicare FFS data projections to set copayment and dollar limits for ground ambulance and emergency services that align with industry trends for that benefit.
E. Regulatory Review Cost Estimation
If regulations impose administrative costs on reviewers, such as the time needed to read and interpret the proposed rule, then we should estimate the cost associated with regulatory review. We have received approximately 20,000 comments specific to the provisions of our recent proposed rule, and we estimate that a similar number will review this rule upon publication in the
Federal Register
.
Using the BLS wage information for medical and health services managers (code 11-9111), we estimate that the cost of reviewing this proposed rule is $135.54 per hour, including fringe benefits, overhead, and other indirect costs (
http://www.bls.gov/​oes/​current/​oes_​nat.htm
). Assuming an average reading speed, we estimate that it will take approximately 10 hours for each person to review this proposed rule. For each entity that reviews the rule, the estimated cost is therefore $1,355.40 (10 hours × $135.54). Therefore, we estimated that the maximum total cost of reviewing the proposed rule is $27.1 million ($1,355.40 × 20,000 reviewers). However, we expected that many reviewers, for example pharmaceutical companies and PBMs, will not review the entire rule but review just the sections that are relevant to them. We expect that on average (with fluctuations) 10 percent of the proposed rule will be reviewed by an individual reviewer; we, therefore, estimate the total cost of reviewing to be $2.7 million. We welcome any comments on the approach in estimating the number of entities which will review this proposed rule.
We noted that this analysis assumes one reader per contract. Some alternatives included assuming one reader per parent organization. Using parent organizations instead of contracts would reduce the number of reviewers. However, we believe it is likely that review will be performed by contract. The rationale for this is that a parent organization might have local reviewers assessing potential region-specific effects from the rule.

G. Impact on Small Businesses—Regulatory Flexibility Act (RFA)
The RFA, as amended, requires agencies to analyze options for regulatory relief of small businesses if a rule has a significant impact on a substantial number of small entities. For purposes of the RFA, small entities include small businesses, nonprofit organizations, and small governmental jurisdictions.
We believe this proposed rule will have a direct economic impact on beneficiaries and health insurance plans. Based on the size standards set by the Small Business Administration (SBA) effective March 17, 2023, (for details, see the Small Business Administration's website at
https://www.sba.gov/​document/​support-table-size-standards
), Direct Health and Medical Insurance Carriers, classified using the NAICS code 524114, have a $47 million threshold for “small size.” Many Medicare Advantage organizations (about 30 to 40 percent) are not-for-profit,
[
298
]
which allows them to qualify as “small entities” so long as they are independently owned and operated and nondominant in their field. We believe all of the not-for-profit organizations qualify as small under the aforementioned criteria. Of the 1,071 businesses using this NAICS code, we believe 799 (or 74.6 percent) are small businesses.
Using CMS's own payment records, we have been able to make estimates as to the minimum size of the smallest Medicare Advantage and Part D insurance contracts. The smallest Medicare contracts are primarily those held by PACE programs, which must adhere to the majority of Part D requirements. For the last year for which we have complete financial records (2024), we believe the smallest PACE programs had gross receipts between $200,000 and $300,000. The vast majority of other Part D contracts and MA organizations must meet minimum size and financial thresholds that make them substantially larger. Excluding the smallest non-PACE contracts paid in 2024, which primarily represent those which did not operate for the full calendar year or new entities excluded from CMS enrollment thresholds, the smallest MA organizations averaged over $650,000 in total receipts.
The RFA does not define the terms “significant economic impact” or “substantial number.” The SBA advises that this absence of statutory specificity allows what is “significant” or “substantial” to vary, depending on the problem that is to be addressed in the rulemaking, the rule's requirements, and the preliminary assessment of the rule's impact. Nevertheless, HHS typically considers a “significant economic impact” to be 3 to 5 percent or more of the affected entity's costs or revenues, and a “substantial number” to mean 5 percent or more of affected small entities within a given industry.

1. Operational Aspects of the Medicare Program
To explain our position, we will first note certain operational aspects of the Medicare program. Each year, MA organizations submit a bid for each plan for furnishing Parts A and B benefits and the entire bid amount is paid to the plan by the government through the Medicare Trust Funds, if the plan's bid is below an administratively set benchmark. If the plan's bid exceeds that benchmark, the beneficiary pays the difference in the form of a basic premium (note that, historically, only 2 percent of plans bid above the benchmark, and they contain roughly 1 percent of all plan enrollees). Part D sponsors also submit a bid for each plan, and the payments made to stand-alone Part D plans (PDPs) are covered by the Supplementary Medical Insurance Medicare Trust Fund. PACE organizations are paid a capitation amount that is funded by both the Medicare Trust Funds (the Hospital Insurance and Supplementary Medical Insurance trust funds) as well as the State Medicaid programs they contract with.
MA plans can also offer enhanced benefits—that is, benefits not covered under Original Medicare. These enhanced benefits are paid for through enrollee premiums, rebates or a combination. Under the statutory payment formula, if the plan bid submitted by an MA organization for furnishing Part A and B benefits is lower than the administratively set benchmark, the government pays a portion of the difference to the plan in the form of a rebate. The rebate must be used to provide supplemental benefits (that is, benefits not covered under Original Medicare) and/or to lower beneficiary cost sharing, Part B or Part D premiums. Some examples of these supplemental benefits include vision, dental, and hearing, fitness and worldwide coverage of emergency and urgently needed services.
Part D sponsors submit bids and plans are paid through a combination of Medicare funds and beneficiary premiums. In addition, for enrolled low-income beneficiaries, Part D plans receive special government payments to cover most of premium and cost sharing amounts those beneficiaries would otherwise pay.
Thus, the cost of providing services by these insurers is funded by the government and, in some cases, by enrollee premiums. As a result, MA plans, Part D plans, Prescription Drug Plans, and PACE organizations are not
(
printed page 76555)
expected to incur burden or losses since the private companies' costs are being supported by the government and enrolled beneficiaries. This lack of expected burden applies to both large and small health plans.
In addition to the direct costs discussed earlier, there are certain indirect consequences of these provisions which also create impact. We have already explained that 98 percent of MA plans (including MA-PD plans) bid below the benchmark. Thus, their estimated costs for the coming year are fully paid by the Federal Government, given that as previously noted, under the statutory payment formula, if a bid submitted by a MA plan for furnishing Part A and B benefits is lower than the administratively set benchmark, the government pays a portion of the difference to the plan in the form of a beneficiary rebate, which must be used to provide supplemental benefits or lower beneficiary cost sharing or both, Part B or Part D premiums. If the plan's bid exceeds the administratively set benchmark, the beneficiary pays the difference in the form of a basic premium. However, as also noted previously, the number of MA plans bidding above the benchmark to whom this burden applies does not meet the RFA criteria of a significant number of firms.
In addition, section 1102(b) of the Act requires us to prepare a regulatory impact analysis if a rule may have a significant impact on the operations of a substantial number of small rural hospitals. For purposes of section 1102(b) of the Act, we define a small rural hospital as a hospital that is located outside of a metropolitan statistical area and has fewer than 100 beds. This analysis must conform to the provisions of section 603 of the RFA. Therefore, the Secretary has certified that this proposed rule would not have a significant impact on the operations of a substantial number of small rural hospitals.
If the provisions of the rule were to cause bids to increase and if the benchmark remains unchanged or increases by less than the bid does, the result could be a reduced rebate. Plans have different ways to address this in the short-term, such as reducing administrative costs, modifying benefit structures, or adjusting profit margins. These decisions may be driven by market forces. Part of the challenge in pinpointing the indirect effects is that there are many other factors combining with the effects of the rule, making it effectively impossible to determine whether a particular policy had a long-term effect on bids, administrative costs, margins, or supplemental benefits.
2. Anticipated Costs and Savings
As indicated in Table X.C-1, the proposals described in this rule are expected to result in cost savings amounting to approximately $240.5 million in 2028, with comparable cost savings expected in subsequent years. MA organizations and Part D sponsors will be the entities most economically impacted by this rule. Some provisions are expected to increase costs for insurers, but most MA organizations and Part D sponsors, including small entities, will likely have greater savings than costs.
The Updating Agent and Broker Compensation and Oversight provision is expected to save MA organizations and Part D sponsors $82.0 million annually. The Removing the Requirement for the TPMO Disclaimer provision is expected to save MA organizations and Part D sponsors $33,963 annually. The Expanding Electronic Delivery of Required Enrollee Communications provision is expected to save MA organizations and Part D sponsors $187.2 million annually. Averaged across all 761 entities, MA organizations and Part D contracts would be expected to save $353,666 each. While we anticipate that larger contracts may receive greater total cost savings due to their higher engagement with brokers and the reduced volume of paper deliveries resulting from this rule, smaller organizations could be expected to reap savings that are higher in proportion to their total revenues. D-SNPs, a type of plan offered by MA organizations, are also expected to have cost savings amounting to at least $1,161 per entity (as each D-SNP is required to have a minimum of one approved Model of Care).
The costs incurred by MA and Part D contracts fall below the HHS significance threshold. In the case of Medicare contracted insurers, we consider the 5 percent threshold to be more appropriate, as these insurers include the cost of following regulatory requirements in their bids. Part D-only contracts are expected to face new costs of $469 per entity, primarily from the information collection components of the Updating Agent and Broker Oversight provision—likely less than what many of these businesses will save due to that same provision.
In summation, this proposed rule will not have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities. The vast majority of MA organizations and Part D sponsors are expected to see cost savings as a result of this rule.
H. Unfunded Mandates Reform Act (UMRA)
Section 202 of UMRA also requires that agencies assess anticipated costs and benefits before issuing any rule whose mandates require spending in any 1 year of $100 million in 1995 dollars, updated annually for inflation. In 2026, that threshold is approximately $193 million. This proposed rule is not anticipated to have an unfunded effect on State, local, or Tribal governments, in the aggregate, or on the private sector of $193 million or more.

Definition.
For purposes of supplemental benefits under this section, healthy foods are defined as whole, nutrient-dense foods. Healthy foods include, but are not limited to the following:
