Section 422.2271 is added to read as follows:
§ 422.2271
MA requirements, MA reporting requirements, and MA oversight of agent/broker/TPMO requirements.
MA organizations are responsible for the actions of their first tier, downstream, related entities, and TPMOs, that represent the MA organization and must ensure the following requirements in paragraphs (a) through (c) of the section are met. Representation includes selling products (including Medicare Advantage plans, Medicare Advantage-Prescription Drug plans, Medicare Prescription Drug plans, and section 1876 Cost plans) as well as outreach to existing or potential enrollees and answering or potentially answering questions from existing or potential enrollees.
(a)
General MA oversight requirements.
MA organizations must do all of the following:
(1) Establish and implement an oversight plan that monitors agent and broker activities, identifies non-compliance with CMS requirements, and reports non-compliance to CMS.
(2) Oversee first tier, downstream, and related entities, including agents and brokers, to ensure agents and brokers abide by all applicable State and Federal laws, regulations, and requirements.
(3)
(i) Must comply with State requests for information about the performance of a licensed agent or broker as part of a state investigation into the individual's conduct.
(ii) CMS will share compliance and oversight information with States about licensed agents' and brokers' performance via a memorandum of understanding or other appropriate means.
(4) Must demonstrate to CMS's satisfaction that marketing resources are allocated to marketing to the disabled Medicare population as well as beneficiaries age 65 and over.
(b)
MA reporting requirements.
MA organizations must provide CMS, and the State, if specified, in the form and manner prescribed by CMS, the following:
(1) Terminated agents and brokers, reported as required:
(i) Report to the State all terminations of agents and brokers who are licensed and appointed, as required, in that State and the reasons for termination, as required by State law.
(ii) Report to CMS, in the form and manner prescribed by CMS, within 15 calendar days of the termination, all terminations of an agent or broker due to violations of Federal law, CMS regulations, or relevant State laws, as well as any other for cause termination of an agent or broker, and the reasons for termination.
(2) Report all enrollments made by unlicensed agents and brokers.
(3) On an annual basis, by the last Friday in July, report to CMS:
(i) Whether the MA organization intends to use employed, captive, and/or independent agents or brokers in the upcoming plan year;
(ii) The specific base compensation amounts, as defined at § 422.2260, the plan will pay independent agents and brokers for each plan.
(iii) Supplemental compensation, as defined at § 422.2260, the plan will pay independent agents and brokers for each plan, including—
(A) The specific type, such as bonuses, gifts, prizes or awards,
(B) Monetary amounts or retail value of non-monetary compensation; and
(C) Detailed explanation of supplemental compensation programs including payment schedules.
(iv) Documentation, including contracts regarding compensation associated with their relationships with first tier, downstream, related entities, and TPMOs as requested by CMS.
(c)
MA oversight of agent/broker/TPMO requirements.
MA organizations must ensure agents, brokers and TPMOs who represent MA organizations meet the requirements in paragraphs (c)(1) through (7) of this section.
(1) Agents and brokers are licensed and appointed under State law, if required.
(2) Agents and brokers are trained and tested annually meeting the following requirements:
(
printed page 76566)
(i) Training and testing must cover relevant Medicare rules and regulations and relevant State and Federal requirements, as well as any additional topics, as specified annually by CMS.
(ii) Must achieve at least 85 percent or higher on all testing.
(iii) If trained and tested by a third-party or another MA organization, agents and brokers must meet the requirements in (c)(2)(i) and (ii) of this section.
(3) Beneficiaries are not charged fees by agents, brokers, or TPMOs when operating under a health insurance license under State law.
(4) Meet the following requirements:
(i) Verify, prior to entering into a contract with an agent, broker, or TPMO, that the individual or entity is not currently terminated from participation in the Federally Facilitated Exchange (FFE), as outlined at
45 CFR 155.220(g)
by CMS.
(ii) Monitor the termination status with the FFE monthly for agents and brokers with whom they have existing contracts.
(iii) Terminate within 15 calendar days, any existing contract with an agent or broker upon determining that the agent or broker has been terminated from the FFE by CMS.
(5) All marketing and sales calls, including the audio portion of calls conducted via web-based technology, must be recorded and retained in their entirety for a minimum period of 6 years. For the first 3 years of the retention period, records must be maintained in audio format. For years 4, 5, and 6, records may be maintained in either audio format or as complete and accurate transcript recordings.
(6) The TPMO, when conducting lead generating activities, either directly or indirectly for an MA organization, must, when applicable:
(i) Disclose to the beneficiary that their information will be provided to a licensed agent for future contact. This disclosure must be provided as follows:
(A) Verbally, when communicating with a beneficiary through telephone.
(B) In writing, when communicating with a beneficiary through mail or other paper.
(C) Electronically, when communicating with a beneficiary through email, online chat, or other electronic messaging platform.
(ii) Disclose to the beneficiary that they are being transferred to a licensed agent who can enroll them into a new plan.
(7) Personal beneficiary data collected by a TPMO for marketing or enrolling them into an MA plan may only be shared with another TPMO when prior express written consent is given by the beneficiary. Prior express written consent from the beneficiary to share the data and be contacted for marketing or enrollment purposes must be obtained through a clear and conspicuous disclosure that lists each entity receiving the data and allows the beneficiary to consent or reject to the sharing of their data with each individual TPMO.

§ 422.2274
Agent, broker, and other third-party requirements.
If an MA organization uses independent agents and brokers to sell its Medicare plans, the requirements in § 422.2271 and paragraphs (a) and (b) of this section are applicable.
(a)
Compensation requirements.
MA organizations must comply with the requirements in paragraphs (a)(1) through (8) of this section in paying and recovering compensation. These compensation requirements only apply to independent agents and brokers.
(1)
Compensation amount.
MA organizations, in paying compensation, must pay the same base compensation amount to all agents and brokers for the same product line under a contract. CMS defines product lines as one of the following:
(i) HMO.
(ii) PPO.
(iii) PFFS.
(iv) RPPO
(v) MSA.
(vi) Cost.
(2)
Compensation payment schedule.
MA organizations who are paying compensation may determine their compensation payment schedule.
(3)
Initial enrollment year compensation.
For each enrollment in an initial enrollment year MA organizations may determine the amount of compensation to be paid, provided it complies with requirements outlined in this section.
(i) MA organizations may pay either a full or pro-rated initial enrollment year compensation for—
(A) A beneficiary's first year of enrollment in any plan; or
(B) A beneficiary's move from an employer group plan to a non-employer group plan (either within the same parent organization or between parent organizations).
(ii) MA organizations may pay pro-rated initial enrollment year compensation for—
(A) A beneficiary's plan change(s) during their initial enrollment year.
(B) A beneficiary's selection of an “unlike plan type” change. In that case, the new plan would only pay the months that the beneficiary is enrolled, and the previous plan would recoup the months that the beneficiary was not in the plan.
(4)
Renewal compensation.
For each enrollment in a renewal year, MA organizations may determine, the amount of compensation to be paid, provided it complies with requirements outlined in this section.
(i) MA plans may pay compensation for a renewal year—
(A) In any year following the initial enrollment year the beneficiary remains in the same plan; or
(B) When a beneficiary enrolls in a new “like plan type”.
(ii) [Reserved]
(5)
Changes to compensation.
MA organizations may make changes to compensation amounts reported in accordance with § 422.2271(b)(3), following a 30-day advance notice to CMS, made in the form and manner prescribed by CMS.
(i) Changes to base compensation amounts will be reviewed against CMS' original base compensation outlier review in accordance with paragraph (b) in this section.
(6)
Payment of compensation.
MA organizations may only pay compensation for the number of months a member is enrolled.
(7)
Other compensation scenarios.
When a beneficiary—
(i) Enrolls in an MA-PD, MA organizations may pay only the MA compensation (and not compensation for Part D enrollment under
42 CFR 423.2274
);
(ii) Enrolls in both a section 1876 Cost Plan and a stand-alone PDP, the 1876 Cost Plan sponsor may pay compensation for the cost plan enrollment and the Part D sponsor may pay compensation for the Part D enrollment;
(iii) Enrolls in an MA-only plan and a PDP plan, the MA plan sponsor may pay for the MA plan enrollment and the Part D plan may pay for the PDP plan enrollment; or
(iv) Changes from two plans (for example, an MA plan and a stand-alone PDP) (dual enrollments) to one plan (MA-PD), the MA organization may only pay compensation at the renewal rate for the MA-PD product.

Additional compensation, payment, and compensation recovery requirements (Charge-backs).
(i) MA organizations electing to pay compensation must retroactively pay or
(

recoup funds for retroactive beneficiary changes for the current and immediately preceding calendar years. MA organizations may choose to recoup or pay compensation for years prior to the immediately preceding calendar year, but they must do both (recoup amounts owed and pay amounts due) during the same year.

(A) A beneficiary makes any plan change (regardless of the parent organization) within the first 3 months of enrollment (known as rapid disenrollment), except as provided in paragraph (a)(8)(iii) of this section; and
(B) Any other time period a beneficiary is not enrolled in a plan, but the plan paid compensation based on that time period.

(b)
Compensation Outlier Review.
CMS reviews MA base compensation submissions annually, prior to the start of marketing, October 1 of each year, as required in § 422.2271(b)(3)(ii) and (iii), to ensure the base compensation submitted is within Fair Market Value. CMS has the authority to deny base compensation outliers as defined in § 422.2260.
(1) CMS will calculate two separate reviews based on geography. One review will be calculated for Puerto Rico and the Virgin Islands combined. The second review for all other geographic areas.
(2) CMS will provide MA organizations, whose compensation submission is determined to be an outlier, as follows:
(i) Prior to October 1 of each year, CMS will notify MA organizations that have outlier compensation rates, that their rates are considered outliers, and provide MA organizations with the CMS calculated FMV amount. After receipt, MA organizations—
(ii) Must submit revised compensation rates; and
(iii) Are prohibited from paying base compensation until submitted rates fall at or below FMV.
(c)
Payments other than compensation (administrative payments).
Payments made for services other than enrollment of beneficiaries (for example, training, customer service, agent recruitment, operational overhead, or assistance with completion of health risk assessments) must not exceed the value of those services in the marketplace. Administrative payments can be based on enrollment provided the payments are at or below the value of those services in the marketplace..

§ 423.2271
Part D requirements, Part D reporting requirements, and Part D oversight of agent/broker/TPMO requirements.
Part D sponsors are responsible for the actions of their first tier, downstream, related entities, and TPMOs, that represent the Part D sponsor and must ensure the following requirements in paragraphs (a) through (c) of the section are met. Representation includes selling products (including Medicare Advantage plans, Medicare Advantage-Prescription Drug plans, Medicare Prescription Drug plans, and section 1876 Cost plans) as well as outreach to existing or potential beneficiaries and answering or potentially answering questions from existing or potential beneficiaries.
(a)
General Part D oversight requirements.
Part D sponsors must do all of the following:
(1) Establish and implement an oversight plan that monitors agent and broker activities, identifies non-compliance with CMS requirements, and reports non-compliance to CMS.
(2) Oversee first tier, downstream, and related entities, including agents and brokers, to ensure agents and brokers abide by all applicable State and Federal laws, regulations, and requirements.
(3)(i) Must comply with State requests for information about the performance of a licensed agent or broker as part of a state investigation into the individual's conduct.
(ii) CMS will share compliance and oversight information with States about licensed agents' and brokers' performance via a memorandum of understanding or other appropriate means.
(4) Must demonstrate to CMS's satisfaction that marketing resources are allocated to marketing to the disabled Medicare population as well as beneficiaries age 65 and over.
(b)
Part D reporting requirements.
Part D sponsors must provide CMS, and the State, if specified, in the form and manner prescribed by CMS, the following:
(1) Terminated agents and brokers, reported as required:
(i) Report to the State all terminations of agents and brokers who are licensed and appointed, as required, in that State and the reasons for termination, as required by State law.
(ii) Report to CMS, in the form and manner prescribed by CMS, within 15 calendar days of termination, all terminations of an agent or broker due to violations of Federal law, CMS regulations, or relevant State laws, as well as any other for cause termination of an agent or broker, and the reasons for termination.
(2) Report all enrollments made by unlicensed agents and brokers.
(3) On an annual basis, by the last Friday in July, report to CMS:
(i) Whether the MA organization intends to use employed, captive, and/or independent agents or brokers in the upcoming plan year;
(ii) The specific base compensation amounts, as defined at § 423.2260, the plan will pay independent agents and brokers for each plan.
(iii) Supplemental compensation, as defined at § 423.2260, the plan will pay independent agents and brokers for each plan, including all of the following:
(A) The specific type, such as bonuses, gifts, prizes or awards.
(B) Monetary amounts or retail value of non-monetary compensation.
(C) Detailed explanation of supplemental compensation programs including payment schedules.
(iv) Documentation, including contracts regarding compensation associated with their relationships with first tier, downstream, related entities, and TPMOs as requested by CMS.
(c)
Part D oversight of agent/broker/TPMO requirements.
Part D sponsors must ensure agents, brokers and TPMOs who represent Part D sponsors meet the requirements in paragraphs (c)(1) through (7) of this section.
(1) Agents and brokers are licensed and appointed under State law, as required.
(2) Agents and brokers are trained and tested annually meeting the following requirements:
(i) Training and testing must cover relevant Medicare rules and regulations and relevant State and Federal requirements, as well as any additional topics, as specified annually by CMS.
(ii) Must achieve at least 85 percent or higher on all testing.
(iii) If trained and tested by a third-party or another Part D sponsor, agents and brokers must meet the requirements in paragraphs (c)(2)(i) and (ii) of this section.
(3) Beneficiaries are not charged fees by agents, brokers, or TPMOs when operating under a health insurance license under State law.
(4) Meet the following requirements:
(i) Verify, prior to entering into a contract with an agent, broker, or TPMO that the individual or entity is not currently terminated from participation in the Federally Facilitated Exchange (FFE), as outlined at
45 CFR 155.220(g)
by CMS.
(ii) Monitor the termination status with the FFE monthly for agents and brokers with whom they have existing contracts.
(iii) Terminate with 15 calendar days, any existing contract with an agent or broker upon determining that the agent or broker has been terminated from the FFE by CMS.
(5) All marketing and sales calls, including the audio portion of calls conducted via web-based technology, must be recorded and retained in their entirety for a minimum period of 6 years. For the first 3 years of the retention period, records must be maintained in audio format. For years 4, 5, and 6, records may be maintained in either audio format or as complete and accurate transcript recordings.
(6) The TPMO, when conducting lead generating activities, either directly or indirectly for a Part D sponsor, must, when applicable:
(i) Disclose to the beneficiary that their information will be provided to a licensed agent for future contact. This disclosure must be provided as follows:
(A) Verbally, when communicating with a beneficiary through telephone.
(B) In writing, when communicating with a beneficiary through mail or other paper.
(C) Electronically, when communicating with a beneficiary through email, online chat, or other electronic messaging platform.
(ii) Disclose to the beneficiary that they are being transferred to a licensed agent who can enroll them into a new plan.
(7) Personal beneficiary data collected by a TPMO for marketing or enrolling them into an Part D plan may only be shared with another TPMO when prior express written consent is given by the beneficiary. Prior express written consent from the beneficiary to share the data and be contacted for marketing or enrollment purposes must be obtained through a clear and conspicuous disclosure that lists each entity receiving the data and allows the beneficiary to consent or reject to the sharing of their data with each individual TPMO.

§ 516.1
Basis and scope.
(a)
Basis.
This part implements the test of the Aligning Data and Value to Nurture Competition and Efficiency in Medicare Advantage (ADVaNCE MA) model under section 1115A of the Act. Except as specifically noted in this part, the regulations under this part must not be construed to affect requirements (including those in part 422 of this chapter and Title XVIII of the Act) that apply to MA organizations and providers under this chapter.
(b)
Scope.
This part sets forth the following:
(1) Inclusion criteria and participation in the ADVaNCE MA model.
(2) The alternative Medicare Advantage quality program being tested in the model.
(3) Targeted supplemental benefit flexibilities being tested in the model.
(c)
Applicability.
Except as otherwise specified in this part, ADVaNCE MA model participants are subject to the standard provisions for Innovation Center models set forth in
42 CFR 512 subpart A
.
§ 516.2
ADVaNCE MA: Model duration.
(a) The ADVaNCE MA model pre-implementation period encompasses the period beginning on June 8, 2027, the CY 2028 bid deadline, and ending December 31, 2028, during which pre-performance contracting and operational activities required for appropriate implementation of the model would occur.
(b) The ADVaNCE MA model performance period consists of 10 consecutive performance years, each aligned with the calendar year, beginning January 1, 2029, and ending December 31, 2038, unless the ADVaNCE MA model is terminated earlier either in accordance with
42 CFR 512.165
or to effectuate an expansion of the model in accordance with section 1115A(c) of the Act.
(c) The ADVaNCE MA model post-implementation period consists of the 3 consecutive payment years that immediately follow the model performance period under paragraph (b) of this section (for example, if the model performance period ends December 31, 2038, the post-implementation period begins January 1, 2039, and end December 31, 2041). The purpose of the post-implementation period is for CMS to provide final payments associated with the model's Diamond Ratings system in accordance with subpart C of this part.

Opt-out process.

States, including the District of Columbia, in the United States are stratified into seven mutually exclusive groups according to the characteristics that CMS determines are necessary to ensure that the model is tested on a nationally representative sample of State MA Markets and to meet model evaluation requirements under section 1115A(b)(4) of the Act.

Non-ADVaNCE MA contracts.
Refers to MA contracts that include ineligible plans, as defined at § 516.100(b)(2), within Mandatory States and/or eligible plans, as defined at § 516.100(b)(1), operating outside of Mandatory States.

Criteria for Determining Contract Split Eligibility.
An existing MA contract is subject to a contract split if it—

(ii) Operates exclusively within a Mandatory State that offers both eligible and ineligible plans as described at § 516.100(b); or
(iii) Subject to § 516.100(c), operates exclusively in a Mandatory State that only offers eligible plans, as described at § 516.100(b)(1), and includes both eligible D-SNPs, described at § 516.100(b)(1)(v), and any eligible plans that are not D-SNPs.

Quality measurement.

ADVaNCE MA Diamond Ratings quality measures.
For a given measurement period, CMS will use the quality measure set used in the MA and Part D Star Ratings system of the same measurement period to assess performance for ADVaNCE MA model participants. Unless otherwise specified, CMS, will automatically add, remove, or make substantive or non-substantive updates to the measure set in alignment with changes made in the MA and Part D Star Ratings system. General.
CMS may, independently from the MA and Part D Star Ratings system, add, update, and remove measures used to calculate the ADVaNCE MA Individual Measure Diamonds and ADVaNCE MA Overall Diamond Ratings as set forth in paragraph (b)(2) through (b)(4) of this section.
(2)
Adding measures.
(i) CMS may add a measure to the ADVaNCE MA Diamond Ratings system if the Secretary determines that a quality measure achieves at least one of the following:
(A) Is meaningful to participating plans.
(B) Addresses a priority area.
(C) Supports or advances the overall goal of the ADVaNCE MA model.
(D) Improves the comprehensiveness of the ADVaNCE MA Diamond Ratings list of quality measures.
(ii) CMS may continue to review measures that are nationally endorsed and in alignment with the private sector, such as measures developed by National Committee for Quality Assurance (NCQA) and the Pharmacy Quality Alliance (PQA), or endorsed by the National Quality Forum (NQF) for adoption and use in the ADVaNCE MA Diamond Rating system.
(iii) CMS may develop its own measures when appropriate to measure and reflect performance specific to the Medicare program.
(iv) In advance of the measurement period, CMS may propose and finalize new measures through rulemaking. 3

Substantively updated Diamond Ratings measures will be on the CMS website for a minimum of one year prior to being used in the calculation of ADVaNCE MA Overall Diamond Rating. CMS may continue collection of performance data for the legacy measure and include it in Diamond Ratings until the updated measure has been on display for one year.
(4)
Removing measures.
(i) CMS will remove a measure from the ADVaNCE MA Diamond Ratings measure set for any of the following reasons:

(2) An ADVaNCE MA model participant will be assigned to the D-SNP cohort if the ADVaNCE MA model participant consists of only D-SNPs per § 516.100(b)(1)(v).
(b)
Measure scores.
The data reported on measures by each ADVaNCE MA model participant under § 516.205 will be pooled with such measure data reported by all other ADVaNCE MA model participants with the same parent organization in the same cohort in the same Mandatory State and would receive an overall score if the requirements under § 516.215(d)(1) are met.
(1) To pool data, contract-level data will be combined and measure scores will be calculated using enrollment-weighted averages based on enrollment data from July of the measurement period, except for survey-based measures.
(2) The survey-based measures will use the enrollment at the time the sample is pulled for the rating year for all ADVaNCE MA model participants within the same parent organization and same cohort in the same Mandatory State.
(3) All ADVaNCE MA model participants under a single parent organization, within a Mandatory State, and within the same cohort will receive one set of measure scores for each Diamond Ratings system quality measure.
(4) ADVaNCE MA model participants under the same parent organization in a Mandatory State may have up to two sets of measure scores, one for the ADVaNCE MA model participants in the D-SNP cohort and one for the ADVaNCE MA model participants in the General Enrollment cohort.

§ 516.625
Extreme and uncontrollable circumstances.
(a)
General.
When an extreme and uncontrollable circumstance negatively impacts a participating parent organization's ability to conduct surveys needed for accurate performance measurement, CMS calculates ADVaNCE MA Diamond Ratings as specified in paragraph (c)(2) of this section for that affected parent organization in that Mandatory State during the performance period. The start date of the incident period determines which performance year is affected, regardless of whether the incident period extends into a subsequent calendar year.
(b)
Modified application of § 422.166(i).
The quality measurement extreme and uncontrollable circumstances regulations at § 422.166(i)(1) through (8) apply to the ADVaNCE MA model, with the following modifications applied throughout those paragraphs:
(1) “Contract” is replaced by “participating parent organization”;
(2) “Star Ratings” is replaced by “ADVaNCE MA Diamond Ratings”; “Star Rating” is replaced by “ADVaNCE MA Diamond Rating”; and “Stars” is replaced by “ADVaNCE MA Measure Diamonds”; and when the term “measure stars” appears in the compound phrases “CAHPS measure stars,” “HOS and HEDIS-HOS measure stars,” and “HEDIS measure stars” in paragraph (i)(2)(iii), (i)(3)(iii), and (i)(4)(iii), it is replaced by “ADVaNCE MA Individual Measure Diamonds”;
(3) For purposes of paragraph (i)(5) of this section, “the contract's summary or overall rating” is replaced by “the participating parent organization's ADVaNCE MA Overall Score”;
(4) “Enrollees” is replaced by “enrollees of the ADVaNCE MA model,” meaning enrollees of participating contracts only;
(c)
Disaster policy.
If a participating parent organization operates contracts in more than one State, CMS evaluates a disaster or emergency declared in one State only for the enrollees and contracts within that State.

Department of Justice
Drug Enforcement Administration
[Docket No. DEA-1568A]
(
printed page 76268)
AGENCY:
Drug Enforcement Administration, Department of Justice.
ACTION:
Notice with request for comments.
SUMMARY:
The Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) proposes to adjust the 2026 aggregate production quotas for several controlled substances in schedules I and II of the Controlled Substances Act and the assessment of annual needs for the list I chemical phenylpropanolamine.
DATES:
Interested persons may file written comments on this notice in accordance with
21 CFR 1303.13(c)
and
1315.13(d)
. Electronic comments must be submitted, and written comments must be postmarked, on or before December 28, 2026. Commenters should be aware that the electronic Federal Docket Management System will not accept comments after 11:59 p.m. Eastern Time on the last day of the comment period.
Based on comments received in response to this notice, the Administrator may hold a public hearing on one or more issues raised. In the event the Administrator decides in his sole discretion to hold such a hearing, the Administrator will publish a notice of any such hearing in the
Federal Register
. After consideration of any comments or objections, or after a hearing, if one is held, the Administrator will publish in the
Federal Register
a final order establishing the 2026 adjusted aggregate production quotas for schedule I and II controlled substances, and an adjusted assessment of annual needs for the list I chemicals ephedrine, pseudoephedrine, and phenylpropanolamine, as relevant.
ADDRESSES:
To ensure proper handling of comments, please reference “Docket No. DEA-1568A” on all correspondence, including any attachments. DEA encourages that all comments be submitted electronically through the Federal eRulemaking Portal, which provides the ability to type short comments directly into the comment field on the web page or attach a file for lengthier comments. Please go to
www.regulations.gov
and follow the online instructions at that site for submitting comments. Upon completion of your submission, you will receive a Comment Tracking Number for your comment. Please be aware that submitted comments are not instantaneously available for public view on
www.Regulations.gov
.
If you have received a Comment Tracking Number, your comment has been successfully submitted and there is no need to resubmit the same comment. Paper comments that duplicate electronic submissions are not necessary and are discouraged. Should you wish to mail a paper comment
in lieu of
an electronic comment, it should be sent via regular or express mail to: Drug Enforcement Administration, Attention: DEA Federal Register Representative/DPW, 8701 Morrissette Drive, Springfield, Virginia 22152.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Heather E. Achbach, Regulatory Drafting and Policy Support Section, Diversion Control Division, Drug Enforcement Administration; Mailing Address: 8701 Morrissette Drive, Springfield, Virginia 22152, Telephone: 571-776-3882.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Posting of Public Comments
Please note that all comments received in response to this docket are considered part of the public record. They will, unless reasonable cause is given, be made available by the Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) for public inspection online at
www.regulations.gov
.
Such information includes personal identifying information (such as your name, address, etc.) voluntarily submitted by the commenter.
The Freedom of Information Act applies to all comments received. If you want to submit personal identifying information (such as your name, address, etc.) as part of your comment, but do not want it to be made publicly available, you must include the phrase “PERSONAL IDENTIFYING INFORMATION” in the first paragraph of your comment. You must also place all the personal identifying information you do not want made publicly available in the first paragraph of your comment and identify what information you want redacted.
If you want to submit confidential business information as part of your comment, but do not want it to be made publicly available, you must include the phrase “CONFIDENTIAL BUSINESS INFORMATION” in the first paragraph of your comment. You must also prominently identify confidential business information to be redacted within the comment.
Comments containing personal identifying information or confidential business information identified and located as directed above will generally be made available in redacted form. If a comment contains so much confidential business information or personal identifying information that it cannot be effectively redacted, all or part of that comment may not be made publicly available. Comments posted to
www.regulations.gov
may include any personal identifying information (such as name, address, and phone number) included in the text of your electronic submission that is not identified as directed above as confidential.
An electronic copy of this document is available at
www.regulations.gov
for easy reference.
Legal Authority and Background
Section 306 of the Controlled Substances Act (CSA) (
21 U.S.C. 826
) requires the Attorney General to establish aggregate production quotas (APQ) for each basic class of controlled substance listed in schedules I and II and for the list I chemicals ephedrine, pseudoephedrine, and phenylpropanolamine. The Attorney General has delegated this function to the Administrator of DEA pursuant to
28 CFR 0.100
.
DEA established the 2026 APQ for substances in schedules I and II and the assessment of annual needs (AAN) for the list I chemicals ephedrine, pseudoephedrine, and phenylpropanolamine on January 5, 2026.
[
1
]
That order stipulated that, in accordance with
21 CFR 1303.13
and
1315.13
, all APQ and AAN are subject to adjustment.
Analysis for Proposed Adjusted 2026 Aggregate Production Quotas and Assessment of Annual Needs
DEA proposes to adjust the established 2026 APQ for certain schedule I and II controlled substances and the AAN for certain list I chemicals to be manufactured in the United States in 2026 to provide for the estimated medical, scientific, research, and industrial needs of the United States, for lawful export requirements, and for the establishment and maintenance of reserve stocks. These quotas do not include imports of controlled substances for use in industrial processes.
(
printed page 76269)
Factors for Determining the Proposed Adjustments
In determining the proposed adjustments, the Administrator has taken into account the factors in
21 CFR 1303.13
(adjustment of APQ for controlled substances) and
21 CFR 1315.13
(adjustment of the AAN for ephedrine, pseudoephedrine, and phenylpropanolamine). The Administrator is authorized to increase or reduce the APQ and the AAN at any time.
[
2
]
DEA determined whether to propose an adjustment of the APQ for 2026 by considering the factors found at
21 CFR 1303.13(b)
:
(1) Changes in the demand for that class, changes in the national rate of net disposal of the class, changes in the rate of net disposal of the class by registrants holding individual manufacturing quotas for that class, and changes in the extent of any diversion in the class;
(2) Whether any increased demand for that class, the national and/or individual rates of net disposal of that class are temporary, short term, or long term;
(3) Whether any increased demand for that class can be met through existing inventories, increased individual manufacturing quotas, or increased importation, without increasing the aggregate production quota, taking into account production delays and the probability that other individual manufacturing quotas may be suspended pursuant to [21 CFR] 1303.24(b);
(4) Whether any decreased demand for that class will result in excessive inventory accumulation by all persons registered to handle that class (including manufacturers, distributors, practitioners, importers, and exporters), notwithstanding the possibility that individual manufacturing quotas may be suspended pursuant to [21 CFR] 1303.24(b) or abandoned pursuant to [21 CFR] 1303.27;
(5) Other factors affecting medical, scientific, research, and industrial needs in the United States and lawful export requirements, as the Administrator finds relevant, including changes in the currently accepted medical use in treatment with the class or the substances which are manufactured from it, the economic and physical availability of raw materials for use in manufacturing and for inventory purposes, yield and stability problems, potential disruptions to production (including possible labor strikes), and recent unforeseen emergencies such as floods and fires.
DEA also considered updated information obtained from 2025 year-end inventories, 2025 disposition data submitted by quota applicants, changes in estimates of the medical needs of the United States, export requirements, and other information made available to DEA after the initial APQ and AAN had been established. Additional factors the Administrator considered in calculating the APQ, but not the AAN, include product development requirements of both bulk and finished dosage form manufacturers.
After considering the changes in the extent of diversion of all controlled substances, as required by
21 CFR 1303.13(b)(1)
, DEA has determined that any changes from the initial calculations for all substances other than fentanyl are slight and not significantly different from the estimates of diversion that DEA applied to the initial APQ valuations.
DEA determined whether to propose an adjustment of the AAN for 2026 by considering the factors found at
21 CFR 1315.13(b)
and summarized below:
(1) Changes in the demand for that chemical, changes in the national rate of net disposal of the chemical, and changes in the rate of net disposal of the chemical by registrants holding individual manufacturing or import quotas for that chemical;
(2) Whether any increased demand for that chemical, the national and/or changes in individual rates of net disposal of that chemical are temporary, short term, or long term;
(3) Whether any increased demand for that chemical can be met through existing inventories, increased individual manufacturing quotas, or increased importation, without increasing the assessment of annual needs, taking into account production delays and the probability that other individual manufacturing quotas may be suspended pursuant to [21 CFR] 1315.24(b);
(4) Whether any decreased demand for that chemical will result in excessive inventory accumulation by all persons registered to handle that chemical (including manufacturers, distributors, importers, and exporters), notwithstanding the possibility that individual manufacturing quotas may be suspended pursuant to [21 CFR] 1315.24(b) or abandoned pursuant to [21 CFR] 1315.27;
(5) Other factors affecting medical, scientific, research, industrial, and importation needs in the United States, lawful export requirements, and reserve stocks, as the Administrator finds relevant, including changes in the currently accepted medical use in treatment with the chemical or the substances that are manufactured from it, the economic and physical availability of raw materials for use in manufacturing and for inventory purposes, yield and stability problems, potential disruptions to production (including possible labor strikes), and recent unforeseen emergencies such as floods and fires.
In evaluating whether there is a need for adjustment of the 2026 AAN for list I chemicals, DEA used the calculation methodology previously described in the 2010 and 2011 AAN.
[
3
]
DEA considered the total net disposals of the list I chemicals for the current and preceding two years, actual and estimated inventories, projected demand, industrial use, and export requirements from data provided by DEA registered manufacturers and importers on the relevant quota application forms.
[
4
]
Additional Considerations Applicable to Covered Controlled Substances
When setting APQ, the Administrator must estimate the amount of diversion of any substance that is considered a “covered controlled substance.”
[
5
]
The covered controlled substances are fentanyl, oxycodone, hydrocodone, oxymorphone, and hydromorphone.
[
6
]
DEA is required to “make appropriate quota reductions, as determined by the [Administrator], from the quota the [Administrator] would have otherwise established had such diversion not been considered.”
[
7
]
When estimating diversion, the Administrator “shall consider information” that he, in consultation with the Secretary of Health and Human Services (HHS), “determines reliable on rates of overdose deaths and abuse and overall public health impact related to the covered controlled substance in the United States;” and “may take into consideration” whatever other sources of information he determines reliable.
[
8
]
DEA solicited information from the Food and Drug Administration (FDA), Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), and the states in March and April 2026 on trends in the legitimate domestic use of select schedule I and II controlled substances and on trends in overdose death and overprescribing data that could be considered in estimating diversion of the covered controlled substances. DEA received information from the FDA in July 2026, the CDC in May 2026, and received Prescription Data Monitoring Program (PDMP) data from the states from April through June 2026. DEA considered this information in revising the APQs and developing the estimates of diversion for the five covered controlled substances for this proposed adjustment.
DEA also aggregated data for each covered controlled substance from Drug Theft and Loss Reports to determine the estimates of diversion. DEA gathered data involving employee theft, break-ins, armed robberies, and material lost in transit. DEA calculated the metric weight in grams of each active
(
printed page 76270)
pharmaceutical ingredient (API) of the controlled substances being diverted as identified in these reports. In calculating the estimates of diversion, DEA utilized the same methodology as published in the Proposed Aggregate Production Quotas for Schedule I and II Controlled Substances and Assessment of Annual Needs for the List I Chemicals Ephedrine, Pseudoephedrine, and Phenylpropanolamine for 2026.
[
9
]
Below, DEA provides an updated chart showing estimations of diversion for each of the covered controlled substances.

Proposed Adjustments for the 2026 Aggregate Production Quotas
DEA is proposing an increase to the APQ for schedule I substance betamethadol to support the manufacture of analytical standards for use in analytical testing in laboratories. Additionally, DEA is proposing an increase to the APQ for schedule I substances 3,4-methylenedioxy-N-methylcathinone, psilocybin, and psilocyn based on increased manufacturer interest in dosage form development for clinical trials in response to
Executive Order 14401
, which established a policy of accelerating innovative research models and appropriate drug approvals of new psychedelic-based treatments for serious mental illnesses that persist after standard therapy.
[
10
]
DEA is proposing an increase to the APQ for schedule II substances d,l-amphetamine and d-amphetamine (for sale). DEA reviewed the data provided by FDA on the domestic medical use of d,l-amphetamine and d-amphetamine. FDA predicted the domestic medical need for d,l-amphetamine and d-amphetamine will increase by 23.6 percent and 23.7 percent respectively when compared to their 2025 observed domestic medical need. DEA also reviewed the global sales data from Multi Internal Data Analysis System (MIDAS). Extrapolation of the global sales of d,l-amphetamine and d-amphetamine predicts an increase of 4.36 percent and 4.07 percent respectively from 2025. While sufficient quota was granted to meet legitimate global sales, it may be insufficient to allow for adequate reserve stocks to start the next calendar year.
DEA also received additional quota requests for product development activities by bulk and dosage form manufacturers of d,l-amphetamine and d-amphetamine (for sale) to synthesize engineering and validation batches to support the filing of new drug applications for FDA review. Year-to-date amounts approved for product development by bulk and dosage manufacturers have increased 173 percent for d,l-amphetamine and 32 percent for d-amphetamine (for sale) when compared to 2025, respectively. After considering all the data from FDA, DEA, and manufacturers regarding product development needs, DEA has determined that it is necessary to propose an increase to the 2026 d,l-amphetamine and d-amphetamine (for sale) APQs for the maintenance of reserve stocks and increased product development needs.
DEA is proposing an increase to the APQ for schedule II substance hydromorphone due to an increase in domestic medical need and exports. DEA reviewed the most recent domestic usage data from IQVIA, as well as data provided by the FDA on the domestic medical use of hydromorphone. FDA predicted the domestic medical need for hydromorphone in 2026 will increase by 20.9 percent compared to the 2025 observed medical need. DEA also reviewed export information provided by bulk manufacturers, export data from DEA's internal database, and global sales data from MIDAS. Export data shows that exports will increase 142% when compared to 2025 because one bulk manufacturer is planning to significantly increase their export of API in 2026. In determining the proposed adjusted APQ, DEA made the appropriate quota reductions pursuant to the updated estimate of the amount of diversion of hydromorphone that occurs in the United States, provided above.
DEA is proposing an increase to the APQ for schedule II substance lisdexamfetamine due to rising global demand for drug products containing this substance. DEA reviewed export data from DEA's internal database and global sales data from MIDAS. Extrapolation of the data predicts global consumption will increase by 19.2 percent when compared to 2025. This increase is due to the expanded approval of the brand name product, Vyvanse, in additional countries since 2025. Additionally, U.S. bulk manufacturers and dosage form manufacturers which support generic versions of Vyvanse have already begun exporting lisdexamfetamine API and finished dosage-form products according to the data extracted from DEA's internal databases. Extrapolation utilizing previous years' reported data suggests the export requirements for lisdexamfetamine API and finished dosages will likely continue to increase in 2026 and beyond. An increase in domestic manufacturing of the API and finished dosages is necessary to supply lisdexamfetamine products to both the domestic and foreign markets.
As a result of the increase to the APQ of lisdexamfetamine, DEA must make a corresponding increase to the APQ of d-amphetamine (for conversion) because this substance is used by some manufacturers as part of the synthesis pathway to manufacture lisdexamfetamine products. Without this corresponding increase, manufacturers of lisdexamfetamine API would not be able to utilize the entire amount of the increased lisdexamfetamine APQ.
DEA is proposing an increase to the APQ for schedule II substance methylphenidate (for sale) due to decreased global reserve stocks and the growth of global medical demands. DEA reviewed the methylphenidate export data from DEA's internal database, as well as global sales data from MIDAS. Data shows that 2025 methylphenidate exports from the United States increased 17.3% from 2024. Additionally, extrapolation of the sales data from MIDAS predicts global consumption will increase by 8.01 percent for methylphenidate drug products in 2026 when compared to 2025.
DEA also reviewed global production and consumption data of methylphenidate published in the 2025 Psychotropic Technical Report by the International Narcotics Control Board (INCB).
[
11
]
The INCB stated that methylphenidate is the most manufactured and traded substance among the scheduled II stimulants, with 111 countries and territories reporting imports in 2024. The INCB reported the United States as the leading manufacturer and noted increasing exports of methylphenidate from the country to others. Although the total manufacturing of methylphenidate was reported to be at the highest level since INCB began receiving data, the global stocks of methylphenidate decreased by 11 tons, from 91.6 tons in 2023 to 80.6 tons in 2024. After considering all the
(
printed page 76271)
data from FDA, DEA, and INCB, DEA has determined that it is necessary to propose an increase to the 2026 methylphenidate APQ to allow for the adjustment of reserve stocks to support the increase in global medical demand.
DEA is proposing an increase to the remifentanil APQ to support increasing domestic medical use and exports. Remifentanil is a schedule II synthetic opioid analgesic that is primarily administered intravenously to manage pain during and after surgical procedures. DEA reviewed the data provided by FDA, the most recent domestic usage data from IQVIA and export data from DEA's internal database. FDA projected a 27.0 percent increase in domestic medical usage of remifentanil in 2026 compared with 2025 and exports of this API showed an upward trend from 2023 to 2025.
DEA is proposing to decrease the APQ of fentanyl based on adjustments to the national diversion estimates for calendar year 2026. Revisions of the APQs for hydrocodone, oxycodone, hydrophone and oxymorphone, the four other covered controlled substances defined in
21 U.S.C. 826(i)(1)(A)
, are unnecessary because the updated diversion estimates are less than, or within one gram of, the previously published national diversion estimates for 2026.

[
12

DEA consolidated 13 of 15 existing drug codes and 18 additional substances meeting the definition of cannabimimetic agents under drug code 7000, except for JWH-018 and AM2201, which retained their existing drug codes and APQs to facilitate quota and international reporting requirements. The 18 additional substances that meet the structural and pharmacological definition of cannabimimetic agents are: AM-1220; AM-2233; EAM-2201; JWH-098; JWH-184; JWH-193; JWH-210; MAM-2201; JWH-007; JWH-022; JWH-147; JWH-302; JWH-307; JWH-412; WIN 55,212-2; CP-55,940; CP-47,497 C6 homolog; and CP-47,497 C9 homolog. That final rule did not change the current and continuing schedule I status for substances meeting the definition of cannabimimetic agents. DEA is proposing to establish an APQ value for cannabimimetic agents pursuant to
21 U.S.C. 826
and
21 CFR part 1303
.

Medical Marijuana
On April 28, 2026, the Acting Attorney General issued
Schedules of Controlled Substances: Rescheduling of Food and Drug Administration Approved Products Containing Marijuana From Schedule I to Schedule III; Corresponding Change to Permit Requirements
as a final rule which became effective the same day.
[
16
]
This final rule places in schedule III and assigns separate drug codes for marijuana in an FDA-approved product or subject to a state medical marijuana license, marijuana extract in an FDA-approved product or subject to a state medical marijuana license, and naturally-derived delta-9-tetrahydrocannabinols in an FDA-approved product or subject to a state medical marijuana license (drug codes 7362, 7353, 7386). FDA approves products under the authority granted by the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act. Additional information about FDA-approved products can be found on FDA's website.
[
17
]
The final rule outlines several control measures required to satisfy the United States obligations under the Single Convention on Narcotic Drugs, 1961, as well as the CSA. Two related control measures of the Single Convention require: (1) manufacturers and distributors of drugs listed in Schedule I of the Convention, including marijuana, to be licensed (Articles 29 & 30); and (2) licensed manufacturers of drugs listed in Schedule I of the Convention obtain quotas specifying the amounts of such drugs they may manufacture to prevent excessive production and accumulation beyond that necessary to satisfy legitimate needs. (Articles 21 & 29). DEA is currently in the process of registering the manufacturers and distributors who will be handling the substances that have been moved to schedule III under the CSA as outlined in the final rule. Concurrently, DEA is assessing data sources and methodologies to determine the most reliable and relevant datasets for the estimation of the United States' legitimate need and production requirements for these 3 substances. A separate notice will be published in the
Federal Register
once the proposed APQs for the schedule III substances (drug codes 7362, 7353, 7386) are determined.
As specified in the final rule, “any form of marijuana other than in an FDA-approved drug product or marijuana subject to a state medical marijuana license remains a schedule I controlled substance.”

Office of the Secretary
AGENCY:
Office of the Secretary (OST), Department of Transportation (DOT).
ACTION:
Notice of public meetings.
SUMMARY:
The Office of the Secretary of Transportation (OST) announces the next public meeting of the Beautifying Transportation Infrastructure Council (Council) on December 9, 2026. This notice announces the date, time, and location of the virtual meeting, which will be open to the public. The purpose of the Council is to advise the Secretary of Transportation on enhancing the aesthetic value of our Nation's transportation systems.
DATES:
The meeting will be held on December 9, 2026, beginning at 10:00 a.m. (EST) and ending at 2:30 p.m. (EST). The exact start and end times are subject to change; please monitor
https://www.transportation.gov/​beautifytransportation/​meetings
for the latest information.
ADDRESSES:
The Council will meet virtually. The public may join the meeting virtually, with information available on
https://www.transportation.gov/​beautifytransportation/​meetings
.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
The Council's Designated Federal Officer, Julianne Schwarzer, Office of the Assistant Secretary for Transportation Policy, Office of the Secretary,
BeautifyTransportation@dot.gov
or 617-999-9667.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Background
The U.S. Secretary of Transportation (Secretary) established the Council as a Federal Advisory Committee in accordance with the Federal Advisory Committee Act (Pub. L. 92-463,
5 U.S.C. Ch. 10
) to advise the Secretary of Transportation on enhancing the aesthetic value of our Nation's transportation systems. The Council provides recommendations on policies, designs, and funding priorities that beautify transportation infrastructure, including highways, bridges, and transit hubs, while maintaining safety and efficiency.
Agenda
At the meeting, the proposed agenda will cover the Call to Order, Official Statement of the Designated Federal Officer, Meeting Logistics, Opening Remarks, Committee Business, and Review of Next Steps. The agenda is subject to change.
Public Participation
The meeting will be open to the public through a virtual meeting. Registration for the meeting can be found here:
https://www.transportation.gov/​beautifytransportation/​meetings
.
Members of the public may submit comments to the Committee in advance, as well as any requests for an electronic meeting accommodation consistent with the relevant sections of the Rehabilitation Act, as amended,
29 U.S.C. 794
, by contacting the individual listed in the
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT
section of this notice no later than December 3, 2026.
All advance submissions will be reviewed by the Designated Federal Officer. If approved, advance submissions shall be circulated to the Council members for review prior to the meeting. All advance submissions will become part of the official record of the meeting.
Authority:
The Council is a discretionary advisory committee under the authority of the U.S. Department of Transportation and was established in accordance with the provisions of the Federal Advisory Committee Act, as amended,
5 U.S.C. Ch. 10
.
Loren A. Smith,
Deputy Assistant Secretary for Transportation Policy.

Health Resources and Services Administration
AGENCY:
Health Resources and Services Administration (HRSA), Department of Health and Human Services (HHS).
ACTION:
Notice.
SUMMARY:
HRSA is publishing this notice of petitions received under the National Vaccine Injury Compensation Program (the Program), as required by the Public Health Service (PHS) Act, as amended. While the Secretary of HHS is named as the respondent in all proceedings brought by the filing of petitions for compensation under the Program, the United States Court of Federal Claims is charged by statute with responsibility for considering and acting upon the petitions.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
For information about requirements for filing petitions, and the Program in general, contact Lisa L. Reyes, Clerk of Court, United States Court of Federal Claims, 717 Madison Place NW, Washington, DC 20005, (202) 357-6400. For information on HRSA's role in the Program, contact the Director, Division of Injury Compensation Programs, 5600 Fishers Lane, Room 14W-17, Rockville, Maryland 20857; 1-800-338-2382, or visit our website at:
https://www.hrsa.gov/​vaccine-compensation
.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
The Program provides a system of no-fault compensation for certain individuals who have been injured by specified childhood vaccines. Subtitle 2 of Title XXI of the PHS Act,
42 U.S.C. 300aa-10
et seq.,
provides that those seeking compensation are to file a petition with the United States Court of Federal Claims and to serve a copy of the petition to the Secretary of HHS, who is named as the respondent in each proceeding. The Secretary has delegated this responsibility under the Program to HRSA. The Court is directed by statute to appoint special masters who take evidence, conduct hearings as appropriate, and make initial decisions as to eligibility for, and amount of, compensation.
A petition may be filed with respect to injuries, disabilities, illnesses, conditions, and deaths resulting from vaccines described in the Vaccine Injury Table (the Table) set forth at
42 CFR 100.3
. This Table lists for each covered childhood vaccine the conditions that may lead to compensation and, for each condition, the time period for occurrence of the first symptom or manifestation of onset or of significant aggravation after vaccine administration. Compensation may also be awarded for conditions not listed in the Table and for conditions that are manifested outside the time periods specified in the Table, but only if the petitioner shows that the condition was caused by one of the listed vaccines.
Section 2112(b)(2) of the PHS Act,
42 U.S.C. 300aa-12(b)(2)
, requires that “[w]ithin 30 days after the Secretary receives service of any petition filed under section 2111 the Secretary shall publish notice of such petition in the
Federal Register
.” Set forth below is a list of petitions received by HRSA on October 1, 2026, through October 31, 2026. This list provides the name of the petitioner, city, and state of vaccination (if unknown then the city and state of the person or attorney filing the claim), and case number. In cases where the Court has redacted the name of a petitioner and/or the case number, the list reflects such redaction.
Section 2112(b)(2) also provides that the special master “shall afford all interested persons an opportunity to submit relevant, written information” relating to the following:
1. The existence of evidence “that there is not a preponderance of the evidence that the illness, disability, injury, condition, or death described in the petition is due to factors unrelated to the administration of the vaccine described in the petition,” and
2. Any allegation in a petition that the petitioner either:
a. “[S]ustained, or had significantly aggravated, any illness, disability, injury, or condition not set forth in the Vaccine Injury Table but which was caused by” one of the vaccines referred to in the Table, or
b. “[S]ustained, or had significantly aggravated, any illness, disability, injury, or condition set forth in the Vaccine Injury Table the first symptom or manifestation of the onset or significant aggravation of which did not occur within the time period set forth in the Table but which was caused by a vaccine” referred to in the Table.
In accordance with Section 2112(b)(2), all interested persons may
(
printed page 76257)
submit written information relevant to the issues described above in the case of the petitions listed below. Any person choosing to do so should file an original and three copies of the information with the Clerk of the United States Court of Federal Claims at the address listed above (under the heading
For Further Information Contact
), with a copy to HRSA addressed to Director, Division of Injury Compensation Programs, Health Systems Bureau, 5600 Fishers Lane, 14W-17, Rockville, Maryland 20857. The Court's caption (
Petitioner's Name
v.
Secretary of HHS
) and the docket number assigned to the petition should be used as the caption for the written submission.
Chapter 35 of Title 44, United States Code
, related to paperwork reduction, does not apply to information required for purposes of carrying out the Program.
Thomas J. Engels,
Administrator.

Notice of contract actions.
SUMMARY:
Notice is hereby given of contractual actions that have been proposed to the Bureau of Reclamation (Reclamation) and are new, discontinued, or completed since the last publication of this notice. This notice informs the public about proposed contractual actions for capital recovery and management of project resources and facilities consistent with section 9(f) of the Reclamation Project Act of 1939.
ADDRESSES:
The identity of the approving officer and other information pertaining to a specific contract proposal may be obtained by calling or writing the appropriate regional office at the address and telephone number given for each region in the
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION
section of this notice.

Individuals in the United States who are deaf, deafblind, hard of hearing, or have a speech disability may dial 711 (TTY TDD, or TeleBraille) to access telecommunications relay services. Individuals outside the United States should use the relay services offered within their country to make international calls to the point-of-contact in the United States.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Consistent with section 9(f) of the Reclamation Project Act of 1939 and the regulations at
43 CFR 426.22
, Reclamation publishes notice of proposed or amendatory contract actions for any contract for the delivery of project water for authorized uses.
The public participation procedures do not apply to proposed contracts for the sale of surplus or interim irrigation water for a term of 1 year or less. Either of the contracting parties may invite the public to observe contract proceedings. All public participation procedures will be coordinated with those involved in complying with the National Environmental Policy Act.
Pursuant to the “Final Revised Public Participation Procedures” for water resource-related contract negotiations, published in
47 FR 7763
, February 22, 1982, a tabulation is provided of all proposed contractual actions in each of the five Reclamation regions. When contract negotiations are completed, and prior to execution, each proposed contract form must be approved by the Secretary of the Interior, or pursuant to delegated or redelegated authority, the Commissioner of Reclamation or one of the regional directors. In some instances, congressional review and approval of a report, water rate, or other terms and conditions of the contract may be involved.
Public participation in and receipt of comments on contract proposals will be facilitated by adherence to the following procedures:
1. Only persons authorized to act on behalf of the contracting entities may negotiate the terms and conditions of a specific contract proposal.
2. Advance notice of meetings or hearings will be furnished to those parties that have made a timely written request for such notice to the appropriate regional or project office of Reclamation.
3. Written correspondence regarding proposed contracts may be made available to the general public pursuant to the terms and procedures of the Freedom of Information Act, as amended.
4. Written comments on a proposed contract or contract action must be submitted to the appropriate regional officials at the locations and within the time limits set forth in the advance public notices.
5. All written comments received, and testimony presented at any public hearings will be reviewed and summarized by the appropriate regional office for use by the contract approving authority.
6. Copies of specific proposed contracts may be obtained from the appropriate regional director or his or her designated public contact as they become available for review and comment.
7. In the event modifications are made in the form of a proposed contract, the appropriate regional director shall determine whether republication of the notice and/or extension of the comment period is necessary.
Factors considered in making such a determination shall include, but are not limited to, (i) the significance of the modification, and (ii) the degree of public interest which has been expressed over the course of the negotiations. At a minimum, the regional director will furnish revised contracts to all parties who requested the contract in response to the initial public notice.

Securities and Exchange Commission
[Release No. 34-106951; File No. SR-NYSEARCA-2026-112]
November 20, 2026.
Pursuant to Section 19(b)(1)
[
1
]
of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 (“Act”),
[
2
]
and Rule 19b-4 thereunder,
[
3
]
notice is hereby given that on November 16, 2026, NYSE Arca, Inc. (“NYSE Arca” or the “Exchange”) filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission (the “Commission”) the proposed rule change as described in Items I and II below, which Items have been prepared by the self-regulatory organization. The Commission is publishing this notice to solicit comments on the proposed rule change from interested persons.
I. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement of the Terms of Substance of the Proposed Rule Change
The Exchange proposes to modify the NYSE Arca Options Fee Schedule (“Fee Schedule”) to amend the Exchange's General Options and Options Trading Permit (“OTP”) Fees. The Exchange proposes implementing the fee change effective November 16, 2026. The proposed rule change is available on the Exchange's website at
www.nyse.com
and at the principal office of the Exchange.
II. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement of the Purpose of, and Statutory Basis for, the Proposed Rule Change
In its filing with the Commission, the self-regulatory organization included statements concerning the purpose of, and basis for, the proposed rule change and discussed any comments it received
(
printed page 76293)
on the proposed rule change. The text of those statements may be examined at the places specified in Item IV below. The Exchange has prepared summaries, set forth in sections A, B, and C below, of the most significant parts of such statements.
A. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement of the Purpose of, and the Statutory Basis for, the Proposed Rule Change
1. Purpose
The Exchange proposes to modify the Fee Schedule to amend OTP
[
4
]
Trading Participant Rights fees to introduce a distinct Floor Market Maker Fee that is assessed in addition to, and not in place of NYSE Arca Options OTP fees.
[
5
]
The Exchange proposes to introduce the new fee effective November 16, 2026.
[
6
]
Currently, a Market Maker does not pay a separate monthly fee to engage in Floor market making, because its Floor activity is covered by its existing OTPs. Apart from these OTP fees, a Market Maker's Floor-related costs are limited to negligible monthly communication, connectivity, equipment, and booth or podia fees charged to all Trading Floor participants.
The Exchange proposes to introduce a monthly fee of $5,000 per OTP for Floor Market Makers, in addition to their existing NYSE Arca Market Maker OTP fees. However, if a Floor Market Maker purchases no more than two OTPs per month and transacts at least 75% of its volume, excluding QCC and Strategy Executions, as Manual trades on the Trading Floor, the Floor Market Maker would be exempt from the NYSE Arca Market Maker OTP fees and would pay only the Floor Market Maker permit fee.
[
7
]
The Exchange's proposal is the result of its ongoing reassessment and rebalancing of its fee structure overall and, in this instance, its Market Maker permit fees. In addition, the proposal is consistent with monthly amount of the Floor Market Maker permit fees charged by the MIAX Sapphire Options Exchange ($5,350)
[
8
]
and BOX Options Market ($5,500/podium).
[
9
]
The Exchange believes the proposed fee is a reasonable part of its ongoing rebalancing of its Market Maker permit fees. Currently, Market Makers pay no permit fee specific to their Floor market making operation, even though they may benefit from access to the Trading Floor. The Exchange does not believe the proposed fee would discourage Floor Market Makers from directing order flow to the Exchange. To the extent they continue to do so, that activity would continue to promote market depth, tighter spreads, and price discovery for all market participants. The fee would apply equally to all similarly situated Market Makers, and the Exchange operates in a highly competitive market in which participants can direct order flow to any of the 20 options exchanges.
2. Statutory Basis
The Exchange believes that the proposed rule change is consistent with Section 6(b) of the Act,
[
10
]
in general, and furthers the objectives of Sections 6(b)(4) and (5) of the Act.
[
11
]
In particular, because it provides for the equitable allocation of reasonable dues, fees, and other charges among its members, issuers and other persons using its facilities and does not unfairly discriminate between customers, issuers, brokers or dealers. The charges are aligned with industry peer fee practices and will equally impact all similarly situated market participants.
The Exchange is subject to significant competitive forces in the market for options securities transaction services that constrain its pricing determinations in that market. The Commission has repeatedly expressed its preference for competition over regulatory intervention in determining prices, products, and services in the securities markets. In Regulation NMS, the Commission highlighted the importance of market forces in determining prices and SRO revenues and, also, recognized that current regulation of the market system “has been remarkably successful in promoting market competition in its broader forms that are most important to investors and listed companies.”
[
12
]
There are currently 20 registered options exchanges competing for order flow. Based on publicly available information and, excluding index-based options, no single exchange has more than 16% of the market share of executed volume of multiply-listed equity and ETF options trades.
[
13
]
Therefore, currently no exchange possesses significant pricing power in the execution of multiply-listed equity and ETF options order flow. More specifically, in September 2026, the Exchange had 9.23% market share of executed volume of multiply-listed equity and ETF options trades.
[
14
]
In such a low-concentrated and highly competitive market, no single options exchange possesses significant pricing power in the execution of options order flow. Within this environment, market participants can freely and often do shift their order flow among the Exchange and competing venues in response to changes in their respective pricing schedules.
The Exchange believes that the ever-shifting market share among the exchanges from month to month demonstrates that market participants can shift order flow or discontinue or reduce use of certain categories of products in response to fee changes. Accordingly, competitive forces constrain options exchange transaction fees. Specifically, as it relates to the instant proposal, Market Makers, like other market participants, retain the ability to adjust their trading behavior or reallocate order flow and liquidity-provision activity across competing exchanges in response to fee changes. In such a low concentrated and highly competitive market, no single options exchange possesses significant pricing power in the execution of option order flow Moreover, the proposed Floor Market Maker permit fee is lower than comparable monthly fees of industry peers (
e.g.,
MIAX Sapphire and BOX).
The Exchange believes that the proposed fee and waiver are equitably
(
printed page 76294)
allocated and not unfairly discriminatory because, even with their introduction, the Exchange believes that the fee will not discourage Floor Market Maker participation. The Exchange notes that the proposed fee remains competitive with and lower than the fee charged by other equity options exchanges to their floor market makers (
e.g.
MIAX Sapphire and BOX).
In addition, the Exchange believes that the proposed waiver would attract trades in open outcry on the Trading Floor to the benefit of all Exchange participants continuing to make the Exchange a more competitive venue. The additional liquidity would help contribute to a robust trading environment on the Exchange's Trading Floor. Moreover, the proposed fee and waiver would apply equally to all Floor Market Makers and reflects the uniquely advantaged position of Trading Floor-based Market Makers. Moreover, the proposed fee is not targeted at a specific type or category of any particular trading strategy. The Exchange notes that any participant can become a Floor-based Market Maker on the Exchange and avail themselves equally to all the benefits and obligations that such role entails.
B. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement on Burden on Competition
In accordance with Section 6(b)(8) of the Act, the Exchange does not believe that the proposed rule change would impose any burden on competition that is not necessary or appropriate in furtherance of the purposes of the Act.
Intramarket Competition.
The Exchange believes that the proposed fee and related waiver will not discourage Floor Market Maker participation. As noted above, the proposed fee remains competitive with and lower than the fee charged by other equity options exchanges to their floor market makers (
e.g.,
MIAX Sapphire and BOX). The Exchange notes that any participant can become a Floor-based Market Maker on the Exchange and avail themselves equally to all the benefits and obligations that such role entails. The Exchange believes that the proposed Market Maker Floor permit fee would not disincentivize Market Maker activity on the Trading Floor and that continued order flow would continue to increase opportunities for execution of other trading interest. does not put any market participants at a relative disadvantage compared to other market participants. Moreover, the proposed changes would apply to all Market Makers on the Trading Floor, and, accordingly, would not impose a disparate burden on competition among market participants on the Exchange.
Intermarket Competition.
The Exchange believes the proposed fee and waiver do not impose an undue burden on inter-market competition because the changes are to remain competitive with other options exchanges that offer a trading floor. The Exchange believes the proposed changes will help the Exchange remain competitive in order to be able to provide market participants with another choice of where to execute floor transactions. The Exchange notes that it operates in a highly competitive market in which market participants can readily favor one of the other 19 competing options exchanges if they deem the Exchange's fee levels to be excessive. In such an environment, the Exchange must continually adjust its fees to remain competitive with other exchanges and to attract order flow to the Exchange. Based on publicly available information, and excluding index-based options, no single exchange has more than 16% of the market share of executed volume of multiply-listed equity and ETF options trades.
[
15
]
Therefore, currently no exchange possesses significant pricing power in the execution of multiply-listed equity and ETF options order flow. More specifically, in September 2026, the Exchange had 9.23% market share of executed volume of multiply-listed equity and ETF options trades.
[
16
]
The Exchange believes that the proposed rule change reflects this competitive environment and considers that the ever-shifting market share among the exchanges from month to month demonstrates that market participants can shift order flow or discontinue or reduce use of certain categories of products in response to fee changes. For Floor-based Market Makers, they, like other market participants, retain the ability to adjust their trading behavior or reallocate order flow and liquidity-provision activity across competing exchanges in response to fee changes. In such a low concentrated and highly competitive market, no single options exchange possesses significant pricing power in the execution of option order flow. Moreover, the proposed Floor Market Maker permit fee is comparatively low, vis-a-vis industry peer standards (
e.g.,
MIAX Sapphire and BOX).
In such an environment, the Exchange must continually review, and consider adjusting, its fees and credits to remain competitive with other exchanges. For the reasons described above, the Exchange believes that the proposed rule change reflects this competitive environment.
C. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement on Comments on the Proposed Rule Change Received From Members, Participants, or Others
No written comments were solicited or received with respect to the proposed rule change.
III. Date of Effectiveness of the Proposed Rule Change and Timing for Commission Action
The foregoing rule change is effective upon filing pursuant to Section 19(b)(3)(A)
[
17
]
of the Act and subparagraph (f)(2) of Rule 19b-4
[
18
]
thereunder, because it establishes a due, fee, or other charge imposed by the Exchange.
At any time within 60 days of the filing of such proposed rule change, the Commission summarily may temporarily suspend such rule change if it appears to the Commission that such action is necessary or appropriate in the public interest, for the protection of investors, or otherwise in furtherance of the purposes of the Act. If the Commission takes such action, the Commission shall institute proceedings under Section 19(b)(2)(B)
[
19
]
of the Act to determine whether the proposed rule change should be approved or disapproved.
IV. Solicitation of Comments
Interested persons are invited to submit written data, views and arguments concerning the foregoing, including whether the proposed rule change is consistent with the Act. Comments may be submitted by any of the following methods:
Electronic Comments
Use the Commission's internet comment form (
https://www.sec.gov/​rules/​sro.shtml
); or
Send an email to
rule-comments@sec.gov
.
Please include file number SR-NYSEARCA-2026-112 on the subject line.
Paper Comments
Send paper comments in triplicate to Secretary, Securities and Exchange Commission, 100 F Street NE, Washington, DC 20549-1090.
(
printed page 76295)
All submissions should refer to file number SR-NYSEARCA-2026-112. This file number should be included on the subject line if email is used. To help the Commission process and review your comments more efficiently, please use only one method. The Commission will post all comments on the Commission's internet website (
https://www.sec.gov/​rules/​sro.shtml
). Copies of the filing will be available for inspection and copying at the principal office of the Exchange. Do not include personal identifiable information in submissions; you should submit only information that you wish to make available publicly.
