AGENCY:
Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), Department of Health and Human Services (HHS).
ACTION:
Notice of meeting.
SUMMARY:
In accordance with the Federal Advisory Committee Act, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) announces the following meeting of the National Committee on Vital and Health Statistics (NCVHS). The meeting is open to the public.
DATES:
The meeting will be held on December 16, 2026, from 11 a.m. to 4 p.m., EST.
ADDRESSES:
The public meeting will be held virtually. The public is welcome to obtain a link to attend this meeting by following the instructions posted on the Committee website:
https://www.cdc.gov/​faca/​committees/​ncvhs.html
.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Naomi Michaelis, MPA, Executive Secretary, National Committee on Vital Health and Statistics, Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, 3311 Toledo Road, Hyattsville, Maryland 20782. Telephone: (301) 458-4202; Email:
ncvhsmail@cdc.gov
.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Background:
The National Committee on Vital and Health Statistics assists and advises the Secretary of HHS on health data, data standards, statistics, privacy, national health information policy, and the Department's strategy to best address those issues. The original authorities of NCVHS are described at 42 U.S. Code § 242k. Additional authorities were added by the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act of 1996 (HIPAA,
Pub. L. 104-191
, 110 Stat. 1936, Aug. 21, 1996), under which NCVHS advises the Secretary on administrative simplification standards, including those for privacy, security, adoption and implementation of transaction standards, unique identifiers, code sets, and operating rules adopted under the
(
printed page 76251)
Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act (ACA,
Pub. L. 111-148
, 124 Stat, 119, Mar. 23, 2010). Included in HIPAA is the statutory reporting requirement that the Committee submit to Congress and make public, a report regarding the implementation of part C of title XI of the Social Security Act.
Purpose:
The National Committee on Vital and Health Statistics shall assist and advise the Secretary on health data, statistics, privacy, national health information policy, and the Department's strategy to best address those issues. The Committee also shall assist and advise the Department in the implementation of the Administrative Simplification provisions of HIPAA and shall inform decision making about data policy by HHS, states, local governments and the private sector.
Matters to be Considered:
The agenda will include drafting of the annual Report to Congress and a review of potential future topics. The Committee will reserve time on the agenda for public comment. Agenda items are subject to change as priorities dictate. Summaries of meetings and a roster of Committee members are available on the NCVHS website:
https://www.cdc.gov/​faca/​committees/​ncvhs.html
,
where further information including an agenda and instructions to access the broadcast of the meeting will be posted.
Should you require reasonable accommodation due to a disability, please contact Naomi Michaelis at
ncvhsmail@cdc.gov
(see
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT
) at least 7 days in advance of the meeting.

Federal Register
notices pertaining to announcements of meetings and other committee management activities, for both the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and the Agency for Toxic Substances and Disease Registry.

Director, Office of Strategic Business Initiatives, Office of the Chief Operating Officer, Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

Securities and Exchange Commission
[Release No. 34-106948; File No. SR-NYSENAT-2026-30]
November 20, 2026.
Pursuant to Section 19(b)(1)
[
1
]
of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 (“Act”)
[
2
]
and Rule 19b-4 thereunder,
[
3
]
notice is hereby given that on November 17, 2026, NYSE National, Inc. (“NYSE National” or the “Exchange”) filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission (the “Commission”) the proposed rule change as described in Items I, II, and III below, which Items
(
printed page 76281)
have been prepared by the self-regulatory organization. The Commission is publishing this notice to solicit comments on the proposed rule change from interested persons.
I. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement of the Terms of Substance of the Proposed Rule Change
The Exchange proposes to adopt a new rule within Section 6, Harmonized Conduct Rules, to conform to the rules of the Financial Industry Regulatory Authority, Inc. (“FINRA”) for purposes of an agreement between the Exchange and FINRA pursuant to Rule 17d-4 under the Act. The proposed rule change is available on the Exchange's website at
www.nyse.com
and at the principal office of the Exchange.
II. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement of the Purpose of, and Statutory Basis for, the Proposed Rule Change
In its filing with the Commission, the self-regulatory organization included statements concerning the purpose of, and basis for, the proposed rule change and discussed any comments it received on the proposed rule change. The text of those statements may be examined at the places specified in Item IV below. The Exchange has prepared summaries, set forth in sections A, B, and C below, of the most significant parts of such statements.
A. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement of the Purpose of, and the Statutory Basis for, the Proposed Rule Change
1. Purpose
The Exchange proposes to adopt a new rule within Section 6, Harmonized Conduct Rules, to conform to FINRA Rule 3220 for purposes of an agreement between the Exchange and FINRA pursuant to Rule 17d-2 under the Act. The Exchange notes that this filing is based on a filing recently submitted by FINRA, and approved by the Commission, to amend FINRA Rule 3220 (Influencing or Rewarding Employees of Others), and is intended to harmonize the Exchange's rules with those of FINRA so as to promote uniform standards across the securities industry.
[
4
]
The Exchange proposes to adopt the proposed rule to require compliance with FINRA Rule 3220. The proposed rule is intended to provide a limitation on gifts and thereby govern influencing or rewarding the employees of others. More specifically, the Exchange proposes to adopt NYSE National Rule 11.3220 (Influencing or Rewarding Employees of Others) with certain changes by FINRA to FINRA Rule 3220 to adopt a gift limit of $300. Additionally, NYSE National would adopt provisions covering: supervision and recordkeeping; gifts incidental to business entertainment; valuation of gifts; aggregation of gifts; personal gifts; bereavement gifts;
de minimis
gifts and promotional or commemorative items; donations due to federally declared major disasters; or gifts to an ETP Holder or ETP Holder's associated persons or individual retail customers. To further harmonize its rules with FINRA, the Exchange proposes to adopt these provisions in proposed Supplementary Material .01 through .09 to NYSE National Rule 11.3220 that is substantially similar to Supplementary Material .01 through .09 to FINRA Rule 3220 adopted in the FINRA Rule Change.
Pursuant to Rule 17d-2 under the Act,
[
5
]
the Exchange and FINRA have entered into an agreement to allocate regulatory responsibility for common rules (the “17d-2 Agreement”). The 17d-2 Agreement covers common members
[
6
]
of the Exchange and FINRA and allocates to FINRA regulatory responsibility, with respect to common members, for the following: (i) examination of common members of the Exchange and FINRA for compliance with certain federal securities laws, rules and regulations and rules of the Exchange that the Exchange has certified as identical or substantially similar to FINRA rules; (ii) investigation of common members of the Exchange and FINRA for violations of certain federal securities laws, rules or regulations, or Exchange rules that the Exchange has certified as identical or substantially similar to a FINRA rule; and (iii) enforcement of compliance by common members with certain federal securities laws, rules and regulations, and the rules of the Exchange that the Exchange has certified as identical or substantially similar to FINRA rules.
[
7
]
Proposed NYSE National Rule 11.3220 is based on FINRA Rule 3220. NYSE National Rule 11.3220(a) would state that no ETP Holder or person associated with an ETP Holder, shall, directly or indirectly, give or permit to be given anything of value, including gratuities, in excess of $300 per individual per year to any person, principal, proprietor, employee, agent to representative of another person where such payment or gratuity is in relation to the business of the employer of the recipient of the payment or gratuity. Proposed NYSE National Rule 11.3220(b) would provide for certain exceptions from the requirements enumerated in Rule 11.3220(a). Finally, proposed NYSE National Rule 11.3220(c) would require an ETP Holder to maintain a record of payments or gratuities of any amount for a specified period of time.
The Exchange believes that adopting NYSE National Rule 11.3220 will help to avoid confusion among ETP Holders that are also members of FINRA. The proposal to adopt NYSE National Rule 11.3220 is also designed to enable the Exchange to incorporate the entirety of NYSE National Rule 11.3220 in the 17d-2 Agreement, further reducing duplicative regulation of ETP Holders that are also members of FINRA. For the avoidance of doubt, NYSE National Rule 11.3220 would equally apply to Exchange-only ETP Holders as the Exchange believes it appropriately protects against improprieties, such as conflicts of interest, that might arise when an ETP Holder or person associated with an ETP Holder gives items of value to an employee of another person, such as an institutional customer, vendor or counterparty with the hope of strengthening the relationship with the customer.
Additionally, the Exchange proposes to adopt Supplementary Material .01 through .09 to NYSE National Rule 11.3220 to codify the provisions within FINRA Supplementary Materials 3220.01 through 3220.09. More specifically, proposed Supplementary Material .01 through .09 to NYSE National Rule 11.3220, like FINRA Supplementary Materials 3220.01 through 3220.09, would codify the FINRA Supplementary Materials to Rule 3220 related to gifts incidental to business entertainment, valuation of gifts, aggregation of gifts, personal gifts, bereavement gifts,
de minimis
gifts and promotional or commemorative items, donations due to federally declared major disasters, supervision and
(
printed page 76282)
recordkeeping, and gifts to an ETP Holder or ETP Holder's associated persons or individual retail customers.
Proposed Supplementary Material .01 (Gifts Incidental to Business Entertainment) would state that a gift given during the course of a business entertainment event is subject to Rule 11.3220 unless it is consistent with the requirements of proposed Supplementary Material .04 (Personal Gifts) or .06 (
De Minimis
Gifts and Promotional or Commemorative Items) which is substantially similar to FINRA Rule 3220 Supplementary Material .04 and .06. For the purpose of the $300 limit, the cost of the business entertainment event itself would not be included in the value of the gift.
Proposed Supplementary Material .02 (Valuation of Gifts) would require ETP Holders to value gifts (other than tickets for sporting or other events) at cost, exclusive of tax and delivery charges, and would require ETP Holders to value tickets for sporting or other events at the higher of cost or face value. If gifts are given to multiple recipients, ETP Holders must record the names of each recipient and calculate and record the value of the gift on a pro-rata, per-recipient basis, for purposes of ensuring compliance with the $300 limit in Rule 11.3220(a). FINRA Rule 3220 at Supplementary Material .02 requires Members to value gifts (other than tickets for sporting or other events) at cost rather than at the higher of cost or market value reduces complexity and subjectivity because market value can be difficult and burdensome to determine, while distinguishing tickets for sporting or other events accounts for the fact that such tickets are commonly purchased on secondary markets at costs that differ from face value.
Proposed Supplementary Material .03 (Aggregation of Gifts) would require ETP Holders to aggregate all gifts given by the ETP Holder and each person associated with an ETP Holder to a particular recipient over the course of the year for purposes of ensuring compliance with the $300 limit in Rule 11.3220(a), and would require each ETP Holder to state in its procedures whether it is aggregating all gifts given by the ETP Holder and each person associated with an ETP Holder on a calendar year, fiscal year, or on a rolling basis beginning with the first gift to any particular recipient. The aggregation requirement would not apply to personal gifts under proposed Supplementary Material .04 or to gifts of
de minimis
value or promotional or commemorative items under proposed Supplementary Material .06 as they are already not subject to the gift limit. This proposed provision, which is substantially similar to FINRA Rule 3220, would help ensure that persons who give multiple gifts in a year to the same recipient do not circumvent the gift limit.
Proposed Supplementary Material .04 (Personal Gifts) would state that gifts that are given for infrequent life events (
e.g.,
a wedding gift or a congratulatory gift for the birth of a child) are not subject to the restrictions in Rule 11.3220(a) or the recordkeeping requirements in Rule 11.3220(c), provided the gifts are customary and reasonable, personal in nature, and not in relation to the business of the employer of the recipient. In determining whether a gift is “personal in nature and not in relation to the business of the employer of the recipient,” ETP Holders should consider a number of factors, including the nature of any pre-existing personal or family relationship between the person giving the gift and the recipient and whether the associated person paid for the gift. When the ETP Holder bears the cost of the gift, either directly or by reimbursing an associated person, the Exchange will presume that such gift is not personal in nature and instead is in relation to the business of the employer of the recipient. This provision is substantially similar to FINRA Rule 3220 at Supplementary Material .04.
Proposed Supplementary Material .05 (Bereavement Gifts) separates bereavement gifts from personal gifts. Proposed Supplementary Material .05 would state that bereavement gifts that are customary and reasonable are not considered to be in relation to the business of the employer of the recipient and, therefore, are not subject to the restrictions in Rule 11.3220(a) or the recordkeeping requirements in Rule 11.3220(c). This provision is substantially similar to FINRA Rule 3220 at Supplementary Material .05.
Proposed Supplementary Material .06 (
De Minimis
Gifts and Promotional or Commemorative Items), at paragraph (a), would state that gifts of a
de minimis
value (
e.g.,
pens, notepads, or modest desk ornaments) or promotional items of nominal value that display the ETP Holder's logo (
e.g.,
umbrellas, tote bags, or shirts) are not subject to the restrictions in Rule 11.3220(a) or the recordkeeping requirements in Rule 11.3220(c), provided that the value of the gift or promotional item is substantially below the $300 limit. Proposed Supplementary Material .06(b) would state that customary and reasonable solely decorative items commemorating a business transaction are not subject to the restrictions in Rule 11.3220(a) or the recordkeeping requirements in Rule 11.3220(c). These provisions are substantially similar to FINRA Rule 3220 at Supplementary Material .06.
Proposed Supplementary Material .07 (Donations Due to Federally Declared Major Disasters) would state that donations by an ETP Holder or person associated with an ETP Holder to any person, principal, proprietor, employee, agent or representative of another person to provide assistance to the individual for losses sustained in a natural event that the President has declared to be a major disaster, such as a wildfire, hurricane, tornado, earthquake, or flood, are not considered “in relation to the business of the employer of the recipient” for purposes of Rule 11.3220(a) and are not subject to the restrictions in Rule 11.3220(a) or the recordkeeping requirements of Rule 11.3220(c). This provision is substantially similar to FINRA Rule 3220 at Supplementary Material .07 which recognizes that the nature of such disasters is unpredictable and catastrophic.
Proposed Supplementary Material .08 (Supervision and Recordkeeping) would state that Rules 11.3.2 and 11.5.1 require ETP Holders to have a supervisory system reasonably designed to achieve compliance with applicable securities laws and regulations and Exchange rules, including Rule 11.3220. To meet these standards, ETP Holders would be required to have systems and procedures reasonably designed to ensure that payments and gratuities in relation to the business of the employer of the recipient given by the ETP Holder or persons associated with an ETP Holder to employees of another person are (a) reported to the ETP Holder; (b) reviewed for compliance with Rule 11.3220; and (c) maintained in the ETP Holder's records. Such procedures must be reasonably designed to ensure that an associated person who is giving a payment or gratuity is not responsible for determining whether such payment or gratuity is in relation to the business of the recipient's employer. ETP Holders are not required to maintain records of gifts that are consistent with the requirements of proposed Supplementary Material .04 through .07 of Rule 11.3220. Requiring a person other than the associated person giving the gift to assess the nature of the gift is intended to encourage objectivity in making such determinations, consistent with existing FINRA Rule 3220.
Proposed Supplementary Material .09 (Gifts to an ETP Holder's Associated Persons or Individual Retail Customers) would state that Rule 11.3220 does not
(
printed page 76283)
apply to gifts from an ETP Holder to its own associated persons, or to gifts from an ETP Holder or person associated with an ETP Holder to individual retail customers. The Exchange believes that proposed Supplementary Material .09 would clarify, and improve awareness and understanding of, the scope of Rule 11.3220, consistent with FINRA Rule 3220 at Supplementary Material .09.
The Exchange notes that, although the FINRA Rule Change provides authority for FINRA to grant exemptive relief to FINRA Rule 3220, the Exchange's proposed rule change would not harmonize or align with FINRA through the inclusion of a corresponding provision.
[
8
]
The Exchange notes that, historically, it has not always aligned with FINRA with respect to providing exemptive relief to ETP Holders and in fact, has provided exemptive relief in very limited circumstances to ETP Holders, as illustrated in NYSE National Rule 10.9610.
The Exchange believes the proposed rule change would promote efficiency without reducing protection for investors and the public interest. The proposed rule change to adopt NYSE National Rule 11.3220 to conform to the rules of FINRA would improve transparency, awareness, and understanding of NYSE National Rule 11.3220's requirements. The Exchange believes these proposed changes would also help facilitate compliance with NYSE National Rule 11.3220 and would provide regulatory certainty to ETP Holders.
2. Statutory Basis
The proposed rule change is consistent with Section 6(b) of the Act,
[
9
]
in general, and furthers the objectives of Section 6(b)(5),
[
10
]
in particular, because it is designed to prevent fraudulent and manipulative acts and practices, to promote just and equitable principles of trade, to foster cooperation and coordination with persons engaged in facilitating transactions in securities, to remove impediments to, and perfect the mechanism of, a free and open market and a national market system and, in general, to protect investors and the public interest.
The Exchange believes that the proposed rule change will further these requirements by providing greater harmonization between Exchange and FINRA rules of similar purpose, resulting in greater uniformity and less burdensome and more efficient regulatory compliance. As such, the proposed rule change would foster cooperation and coordination with persons engaged in facilitating transactions in securities and would remove impediments to and perfect the mechanism of a free and open market and a national market system in accordance with Section 6(b)(5) of the Act.
[
11
]
As noted above, the proposed rule change to adopt proposed NYSE National Rule 11.3220 is designed to conform the Exchange's Rule to the comparable FINRA rule. The Exchange also notes the changes proposed herein would align proposed NYSE National Rule 11.3220 with a recent filing submitted by FINRA and approved by the Commission.
[
12
]
As described above, the Exchange believes the proposed change to adopt proposed Exchange Rule 11.3220 to conform to FINRA Rule 3220 is consistent with the Act because it is intended to harmonize the Exchange Rule with the comparable FINRA rule and will promote uniform standards across the securities industry. The Exchange also believes the proposed change to adopt Supplementary Material .01 through .09 to Exchange Rule 11.3220 is consistent with the Act because it is a conforming change to adopt the provisions within FINRA Supplementary Materials 3220.01 through 3220.09. The Exchange further believes that these changes will help to reduce and avoid potential confusion among ETP Holders and persons associated with ETP Holders of the Exchange that are also members of FINRA by harmonizing proposed Exchange Rule 11.3220 with FINRA Rule 3220. The proposed rule change is designed to enable the Exchange to incorporate proposed Exchange Rule 11.3220 into the 17d-2 Agreement, further reducing duplicative regulation of ETP Holders and persons associated with ETP Holders that are also members of FINRA. For the avoidance of doubt, proposed Exchange Rule 11.3220 would equally apply to Exchange-only ETP Holders as the Exchange believes it appropriately protects against improprieties that might arise when substantial gifts or monetary payments are given to certain persons.
The Exchange believes the proposed rule change would promote efficiency without reducing protection for investors and the public interest. The proposed changes to proposed Exchange Rule 11.3220 to conform to the rules of FINRA improve transparency, awareness, and understanding of the proposed Exchange Rule's requirements. The Exchange believes these proposed changes would also help facilitate compliance with proposed NYSE National Rule 11.3220.
B. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement on Burden on Competition
The Exchange does not believe that the proposed rule change will impose any burden on competition that is not necessary or appropriate in furtherance of the purposes of the Act. The proposed rule change is not designed to address any competitive issues but rather to provide greater harmonization among Exchange and FINRA rules of similar purpose, resulting in less burdensome and more efficient regulatory compliance for common members and facilitating FINRA's performance of its regulatory functions under the 17d-2 Agreement. As such, the Exchange does not believe that the proposed rule change will impose any burden on competition not necessary or appropriate in furtherance of the purposes of the Act.
C. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement on Comments on the Proposed Rule Change Received From Members, Participants, or Others
No written comments were solicited or received with respect to the proposed rule change.
III. Date of Effectiveness of the Proposed Rule Change and Timing for Commission Action
The Exchange has filed the proposed rule change pursuant to Section 19(b)(3)(A)(iii) of the Act
[
13
]
and Rule 19b-4(f)(6) thereunder.
[
14
]
Because the proposed rule change does not: (i) significantly affect the protection of investors or the public interest; (ii) impose any significant burden on competition; and (iii) become operative prior to 30 days from the date on which it was filed, or such shorter time as the Commission may designate, if consistent with the protection of investors and the public interest, the proposed rule change has become effective pursuant to Section 19(b)(3)(A)
(
printed page 76284)
of the Act and Rule 19b-4(f)(6)(iii) thereunder.
A proposed rule change filed under Rule 19b-4(f)(6)
[
15
]
normally does not become operative prior to 30 days after the date of the filing. However, pursuant to Rule 19b-4(f)(6)(iii),
[
16
]
the Commission may designate a shorter time if such action is consistent with the protection of investors and the public interest.
At any time within 60 days of the filing of such proposed rule change, the Commission summarily may temporarily suspend such rule change if it appears to the Commission that such action is necessary or appropriate in the public interest, for the protection of investors, or otherwise in furtherance of the purposes of the Act. If the Commission takes such action, the Commission shall institute proceedings under Section 19(b)(2)(B)
[
17
]
of the Act to determine whether the proposed rule change should be approved or disapproved.
IV. Solicitation of Comments
Interested persons are invited to submit written data, views and arguments concerning the foregoing, including whether the proposed rule change is consistent with the Act. Comments may be submitted by any of the following methods:
Electronic Comments
Use the Commission's internet comment form (
https://www.sec.gov/​rules/​sro.shtml
); or
Send an email to
rule-comments@sec.gov
.
Please include file number SR-NYSENAT-2026-30 on the subject line.
Paper Comments
Send paper comments in triplicate to Secretary, Securities and Exchange Commission, 100 F Street NE, Washington, DC 20549-1090.
All submissions should refer to file number SR-NYSENAT-2026-30. This file number should be included on the subject line if email is used. To help the Commission process and review your comments more efficiently, please use only one method. The Commission will post all comments on the Commission's internet website (
https://www.sec.gov/​rules/​sro.shtml
). Copies of the filing will be available for inspection and copying at the principal office of the Exchange. Do not include personal identifiable information in submissions; you should submit only information that you wish to make available publicly. We may redact in part or withhold entirely from publication submitted material that is obscene or subject to copyright protection. All submissions should refer to file number SR-NYSENAT-2026-30 and should be submitted on or before December 16, 2026.
For the Commission, by the Division of Trading and Markets, pursuant to delegated authority.
[
18
]
Stephanie J. Fouse,
Assistant Secretary.

Securities and Exchange Commission
[Release No. 34-106949; File No. 4-698]
November 20, 2026.
I. Introduction
By letter dated August 11, 2026, Consolidated Audit Trail, LLC (“CAT LLC”), on behalf of the Participants
[
1
]
in the National Market System Plan Governing the Consolidated Audit Trail (“CAT NMS Plan” or “Plan”),
[
2
]
requested that the Securities and Exchange Commission (“Commission” or “SEC”) provide exemptive relief to the Participants, pursuant to its authority under Section 36 of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 (“Exchange Act”)
[
3
]
and Rule 608(e) of Regulation NMS under the Exchange Act, in connection with the recovery of certain costs incurred during the period associated with the final of four target deadlines established for certain implementation milestones (the “FAM 4 period”) as set forth in Sections 11.6(a)(i)(D), 11.6(a)(iii), and11.3(b)(i)(D)(I) of the CAT NMS Plan.
[
4
]
Section 36(a)(1) of the Exchange Act grants the Commission the authority, with certain limitations, to “conditionally or unconditionally exempt any person, security, or transaction . . . from any provision or provisions of [the Exchange Act] or of any rule or regulation thereunder, to the extent that such exemption is necessary or appropriate in the public interest, and is consistent with the protection of investors.”
[
5
]
Under Rule 608(e) of Regulation NMS, the Commission may “exempt from [Rule 608], either unconditionally or on specified terms and conditions, any self-regulatory organization, member thereof, or specified security, if the Commission determines that such exemption is consistent with the public interest, the protection of investors, the maintenance of fair and orderly markets and the removal of impediments to, and perfection of the mechanism of, a national market system.”
[
6
]
For the reasons set forth below, this Order grants exemptive relief from Sections 11.6(a)(i)(D), 11.6(a)(iii), and 11.3(b)(i)(D)(I) of the CAT NMS Plan, as set forth below, to allow the recovery of
(
printed page 76285)
certain costs incurred during the FAM 4 period.
II. Background
The Commission adopted Rule 613 of Regulation NMS
[
7
]
on July 18, 2012, with the goal of creating a modernized consolidated audit trail system—the CAT—that would provide regulators with timely access to a comprehensive set of trading data that more efficiently and effectively facilitates cross-market surveillance, investigations, enforcement activities, and cross-market reconstructions and analyses, as appropriate. On November 15, 2016, the Commission approved the CAT NMS Plan as the national market system plan required by Rule 613.
[
8
]
Rule 613
[
9
]
and the CAT NMS Plan
[
10
]
both contemplate that the costs of building and operating the CAT would be allocated among Industry Members
[
11
]
and the Participants.
[
12
]
During the development and implementation stages of the CAT, however, the Participants fully funded the costs associated with building and operating the CAT through non-interest-bearing loans.
[
13
]
The CAT NMS Plan provides for the recovery of Industry Members' allocated share of CAT costs through fees assessed on Industry Members.
[
14
]
Any such fees must be filed with the Commission and are subject to Commission review for consistency with the Exchange Act and the Plan.
[
15
]
On May 15, 2020, after significant delays in the development and implementation of the CAT,
[
16
]
the Commission amended the CAT NMS Plan to establish target deadlines for four Financial Accountability Milestone (or “FAM”) provisions and to reduce the amount that the Participants could recover from Industry Members if they missed those deadlines.
[
17
]
Specifically, Section 11.6 of the CAT NMS Plan requires the Participants to satisfy four implementation milestones by specified deadlines in order to recover from Industry Members the full amount of the Industry Members' allocated share of the CAT costs incurred during each FAM period. Section 11.6 also sets forth a schedule detailing the extent to which those fees are reduced when a target deadline is missed.
The final FAM, “Full Implementation of CAT NMS Plan Requirements” or “FAM 4,” is defined as:
the point at which the Participants have satisfied all of their obligations to build and implement the CAT, such that all CAT system functionality required by Rule 613 and the CAT NMS Plan has been developed, successfully tested, and fully implemented at the initial Error Rates specified by Section 6.5(d)(i) or less, including functionality that efficiently permits the Participants and the Commission to access all CAT Data required to be stored in the Central Repository pursuant to Section 6.5(a), including Customer Account Information, Customer-ID, Customer Identifying Information, and Allocation Reports, and to analyze the full lifecycle of an order across the national market system, from order origination through order execution or order cancellation, including any related allocation information provided in an Allocation Report. This Financial Accountability Milestone shall be considered complete as of the date identified in a Quarterly Progress Report meeting the requirements of Section 6.6(c).
[
18
]
Section 11.6(a)(i)(D) of the CAT NMS Plan set forth the target date for completion of FAM 4 as December 30, 2022, stating that:
[t]he Participants will be entitled to collect the full amount of: . . . (D) Any Post-Amendment Industry Member Fees established or implemented to recover the Post-Amendment Expenses incurred from the date immediately following the achievement of Full Availability and Regulatory Utilization of Transactional Database Functionality to the date of Full Implementation of CAT NMS Plan Requirements (“Period 4”), so long as such date is no later than December 30, 2022.
Thus, absent an exemption, to be entitled to recover from Industry Members the full amount of the CAT costs incurred during the FAM 4 period and allocated to Industry Members pursuant to the Plan, the Participants were required to achieve the full implementation of all CAT functionality required by Rule 613 and the CAT NMS Plan, including both the transactional database and the functionality necessary to collect, process, and make available the required customer and account information, which at that time was implemented through the Customer and Account Information System (“CAIS”), a separate and distinct system in the CAT.
[
19
]
If this target deadline of
(
printed page 76286)
December 30, 2022 was missed, Section 11.6(a)(iii) states that the amount of Post-Amendment Industry Member Fees that the Participants may collect for Period 4 would be reduced according to the following schedule:
(A) By 25% if the Participants missed the deadline by less than 90 days;
(B) By 50% if the Participants missed the deadline by 90 days or more, but less than 180 days;
(C) By 75% if the Participants missed the deadline by 180 days or more, but less than 270 days; and
(D) By 100% if the Participants missed the deadline by 270 days or more.
When implementing these deadlines in the FAM Release, the Commission acknowledged that both Industry Member and Participant commenters urged the Commission to adopt a more flexible approach that could account for the possibility of reasonable or unforeseeable delays to CAT implementation.
[
20
]
These commenters recommended that the Commission include provisions or formal mechanisms in the CAT NMS Plan that would allow the Commission, “after the holistic assessment of all factors impacting the Participants' ability to meet a particular milestone date, flexibility to extend milestone dates without holding Participants directly accountable (financially or otherwise)” or to “suspend[ ] the proposed financial penalties based on the cause, foreseeability and attempts to mitigate the impact of the delay.”
[
21
]
In response, the Commission stated that its approach “would not allow further delays to occur without consequence,” but emphasized that it “has the authority to grant exemptive relief from any requirement associated with a particular Financial Accountability Milestone” and explained that “this ability, in particular, should alleviate . . . concerns regarding the potential impact of unforeseeable or reasonable delays.”
[
22
]
III. Request for Exemptive Relief
In the FAM 4 Exemption Request, CAT LLC, on behalf of the Participants, stated that the first three FAMs, including Full Availability and Regulatory Utilization of Transactional Database Functionality, were completed by the deadlines set forth in the Plan.
[
23
]
CAT LLC stated that the fourth milestone, FAM 4, required the completion of a novel and separate system for the submission of customer and account data (the CAIS) by December 30, 2022. According to CAT LLC, certain technical aspects associated with the construction and completion of the separate system were not completed until July 15, 2024.
[
24
]
CAT LLC also stated that during the FAM 4 time period (January 1, 2022 through July 15, 2024), it incurred costs of $99,307,505 related to the completion of the CAIS. And, during the same time, CAT LLC continued to operate the transactional database, incurring $364,219,549 in technology costs and $26,624,090 in other CAT LLC operating costs. The overall costs incurred during this time period totaled $490,151,144. Thus, pursuant to the schedule set forth in Section 11.6(a)(iii), the amount of Post-Amendment Industry Member Fees that the Participants could recover for FAM 4 would be reduced by 100%. In other words, Section 11.6(a)(iii) prevents recovery of any and all costs, including costs associated with operation of the previously completed transactional database, incurred by the Participants during this time period. CAT LLC requests that the Commission grant exemptive relief from the fee reduction that would be imposed by Sections 11.6(a)(i)(D) and 11.6(a)(iii).
CAT LLC stated that exemptive relief “would prevent an excessive and grossly disproportionate penalty from being imposed in connection with FAM 4.”
[
25
]
CAT LLC states that “the CAT NMS Plan requirements related to the transactional database were implemented prior to FAM 4,” such that only “certain technical aspects” of FAM 4 related to the CAIS “were not completed until July 15, 2024.”
[
26
]
Accordingly, CAT LLC stated that “the vast majority of Period 4 costs related to the operation of the transactional database, which was fully implemented and utilized by the Commission in both enforcement and rulemaking during this entire period.”
[
27
]
CAT LLC stated that, in spite of the limited impact of the delay in CAIS implementation, the FAM 4 provisions would prevent the recovery of any CAT costs incurred by CAT LLC during Period 4 (January 1, 2022 through July 15, 2024), including those related to the ongoing, successful operation of the transactional database that was completed on time.
[
28
]
CAT LLC further stated that such a result would not be a reasonable or equitable application of the financial accountability provisions adopted by the Commission.
[
29
]
CAT LLC stated that, for Period 4, it continued to operate the transactional database, incurring $364,219,549 in related technology costs and $26,624,090 in other operating costs (“non-CAIS FAM 4 costs”), and incurred CAIS-related costs of $99,307,505 (“CAIS FAM 4 costs”).
[
30
]
CAT LLC stated that total Period 4 costs were $490,151,144,
[
31
]
and this excludes remediation costs incurred by FINRA CAT relating to the delayed implementation of CAIS.
[
32
]
CAT LLC seeks exemptive relief as to the total $390,843,639 of non-CAIS FAM 4 costs.
[
33
]
CAT LLC stated that with such exemptive relief, based on the existing Funding Model,
[
34
]
CAT LLC would anticipate seeking recovery of $260,562,426 in costs related to FAM 4 from Industry Members (
i.e.,
two-thirds
(
printed page 76287)
of $390,843,639).
[
35
]
CAT LLC asked the Commission to consider materiality and proportionality because “treating FAM 4 as wholly unmet” would effectively impose “a $326 million strict liability penalty based solely on the late completion of certain technical CAIS elements,” and stated that the “delayed technical aspects of CAIS did not affect the overall utility of the transactional database.”
[
36
]
In addition, CAT LLC requested an exemption from Section 11.3(b)(i)(D)(I) of the CAT NMS Plan, which would allow for a shortened Historical Recovery Period.
[
37
]
Section 11.3 is part of the CAT NMS Plan that contains the provisions commonly referred to as the CAT funding model. Those provisions establish how the costs of developing, operating, and maintaining the CAT are allocated and recovered from Participants and Industry Members. Section 11.3 establishes the framework for calculating and assessing fees to fund the CAT. Section 11.3(b)(i)(D)(I) requires the Participants, when establishing fees to recover CAT costs previously paid by the Participants (“Historical CAT Costs”), to determine a reasonable period over which those costs will be recovered through such fees (“Historical Recovery Period”), and provides that this period may not be less than 24 months or more than five years.
[
38
]
However, another provision in the funding model, Section 11.3(f) of the CAT NMS Plan, prohibits billing or otherwise requesting the payment of CAT fees to fund the costs to build, operate, and administer the CAT from Industry Members after March 31, 2028, which is less than 24 months from the date of this request.
[
39
]
Accordingly, CAT LLC requested an exemption from Section 11.3(b)(i)(D)(I) of the CAT NMS Plan to allow for a Historical Recovery Period of one year.
[
40
]
CAT LLC currently estimates that the fee rate necessary to recover $260,562,426 would be approximately $0.000022 per executed equivalent share for a one-year recovery period,
[
41
]
which CAT LLC states is comparable to the fee rates previously charged to fund CAT costs and to recover CAT costs previously paid by the Participants.
[
42
]
As such, CAT LLC represented that using a Historical Recovery Period shorter than two years would continue to result in a reasonable fee rate.
IV. Discussion and Exemptive Relief
In the FAM 4 Exemption Request, the Participants seek exemptive relief from Sections 11.6(a)(i)(D), 11.6(a)(iii), and 11.3(b)(i)(D)(I) of the CAT NMS Plan that would permit them to seek to recover from Industry Members, over a one-year recovery period, Industry Members' share of the non-CAIS FAM 4 costs. These costs were incurred primarily in operating the CAT transactional database, a core regulatory system that captures trading in U.S. exchange-listed equities, listed options, and OTC equity securities and supports regulatory oversight of the national market system. After carefully considering the FAM 4 Exemption Request and the comment letters received,
[
43
]
the Commission has determined that granting such exemptive relief pursuant to Section 36(a)(1) of the Exchange Act is appropriate in the public interest and is consistent with the protection of investors. The Commission has further determined, pursuant to Rule 608(e), that this exemption is consistent with the public interest, the protection of investors, the maintenance of fair and orderly markets and the removal of impediments to, and the perfection of, the mechanisms of a national market system. The reasons for these determinations, and the Commission's responses to comments received, are discussed below.
A. The Commission's Authority to Grant Relief
Three commenters opposed the request for relief and urged the Commission to deny any exemptive relief for the recovery of FAM 4 costs.
[
44
]
Among other objections, these commenters questioned the Commission's authority to grant the requested relief. They asserted that the Participants' ability to recover FAM 4 costs from Industry Members was extinguished when the 270-day period following the FAM 4 deadline expired in 2023,
[
45
]
and one commenter asserted that Industry Members thereby acquired a right to be free of any obligation to contribute to FAM 4 costs.
[
46
]
According to these commenters, the requested relief would revive the extinguished recovery right, imposing new liability on Industry Members for past conduct contrary to the presumption against retroactivity, and they maintained that Section 36 provides no clear congressional authorization for such action.
[
47
]
Two commenters further asserted that Industry Members had set budgets and business plans in reliance on the FAMs operating according to their terms.
[
48
]
Contrary to the opposing commenters' assertions, the requested relief does not implicate the retroactivity doctrine. The FAMs placed conditions on the Participants' ability to recover Period 4 costs through CAT fees, subject from the outset to the Commission's exercise of exemptive authority. They did not confer on Industry Members a right to be free of those costs. When the Commission adopted the FAMs, it simultaneously made clear that it retained authority “to grant exemptive relief from any requirement associated with a particular Financial Milestone” in appropriate circumstances.
[
49
]
Indeed,
(
printed page 76288)
the Commission began to issue exemptive relief from various FAM requirements just months after the issuance of the FAM Release in May 2020
[
50
]
and continued to do so throughout the period during which the FAMs were applicable, including exemptive relief issued years after the target deadlines for FAMs 1-3 had passed
[
51
]
but before historical fees for FAMs 1-3 were established by the Participants for their members.
[
52
]
Industry Members thus could not have reasonably relied on the FAMs as granting them an unconditional entitlement not to bear any Period 4 costs in the event the FAM 4 deadline was not met.
Nor would the requested relief impose a “liability” on Industry Members for “past conduct.” Under the CAT NMS Plan, historical CAT assessments are calculated and charged based on Industry Members' executed equivalent share volume during the Historical Recovery Period, that is, based on
current
rather than past market activity.
[
53
]
Any fee to recover Period 4 costs would similarly be calculated using that method. And the requested relief would not itself impose any financial obligations on Industry Members. Any fee to recover Period 4 costs would be subject to the separate rule filing process under Section 19(b) of the Exchange Act,
[
54
]
including notice and comment, the Commission's authority to temporarily suspend the fee and institute proceedings, and the requirements of the Exchange Act and the CAT NMS Plan, including that fees be reasonable and equitably allocated. Thus, rather than imposing new liability for completed conduct, the requested relief represents a determination regarding the potential allocation of historical CAT costs going forward.
The Commission also disagrees that it could exercise its exemptive authority only before FAM 4 operated to reduce recoverable fees. Neither Section 36 nor the Commission's statements in the FAM Release limit the timing of such relief. And as discussed above, the Commission has previously granted exemptive relief from particular FAM 1-3 requirements after the target deadlines for those FAMs had passed but before historical fees for FAMs 1-3 were established.
[
55
]
The approach taken by the Commission in this Order, therefore, was explicitly contemplated by the FAM Release and is consistent with its previous practice. In any event, Industry Members have had advance notice that the issuance of exemptive relief could alter the application of the FAM provisions. CAT LLC first requested exemptive relief from FAM 4 in November 2022, publicly and before the FAM 4 deadline,
[
56
]
and the present request revises that and subsequent requests.
B. Relief From the Period 4 Fee Reduction
In the FAM 4 Exemptive Request Letter, CAT LLC stated that the “technical delay in certain aspects of CAIS” was “unforeseeable and reasonable.”
[
57
]
CAT LLC further stated that the “unforeseeable nature of an excessively large reduction in recoverable costs resulting from the delay in certain limited aspects of one part of the CAT system is exactly the type of circumstance that warrants the use of the Commission's exemptive authority.”
[
58
]
One commenter, a Participant, agreed and stated “CAT LLC was not building the CAT with a static set of requirements but rather with a framework that continued to evolve, impacting the ability to plan for and deliver on the timeline the Commission specified in the FAMs.”
[
59
]
This commenter supported recovery of all Period 4 costs—not just the non-CAIS FAM 4 costs—suggesting that the initial cost and data volume projections were too low, and the CAT, including aspects of CAIS, was largely available to regulators by the FAM 4 deadline.
[
60
]
Other commenters opposed the exemptive relief on the grounds that the delays were neither unforeseeable nor reasonable, and likewise disagreed that the magnitude of the financial consequences of the delay was
(
printed page 76289)
unforeseeable or would justify relief.
[
61
]
These commenters stated that the Participants provided the Commission with their own projected timelines to complete the FAMs and that the Participants had substantial time to complete FAM 4 by their chosen deadline.
[
62
]
Two commenters disputed that the timely completion of the transactional database and its continued operation and use during Period 4 justified relief from the FAM 4 requirements.
[
63
]
One of these commenters noted that FAMs 1-3 already required completion of the transactional database, and that the Participants are recovering the development costs for completing FAMs 1-3.
[
64
]
Both commenters also disputed that the Participants' inability to recover FAM 4 costs should be viewed as a “penalty” to “be analyzed under the civil enforcement framework that considers `materiality or proportionality.' ”
[
65
]
These commenters further stated that the Participants' request for exemptive relief is not necessary or appropriate in the public interest and would not be consistent with the protection of investors.
[
66
]
They asserted that the relief would not provide any benefit to investors or the markets, but instead transfer significant historical CAT costs to investors.
[
67
]
These commenters stated that, if relief is granted, it would weaken the incentive effects of future Commission-imposed regulatory deadlines.
[
68
]
Further, these commenters asserted that they or their members invested substantial amounts of their own money and resources to develop and maintain the reporting systems necessary to meet the implementation deadlines established by the Participants—particularly for building the necessary customer-database reporting infrastructure for CAIS—and that they continued to incur additional costs as implementation extended beyond the established deadlines.
[
69
]
They stated that those costs were not accounted for in the request for relief.
[
70
]
These commenters asserted that the financial consequences for failing to meet the FAMs were the entire point of the Commission implementing the FAMs, and that the public and the Participants understood that they would not be able to “recover any of the costs incurred in any FAM period during which they did not successfully complete all aspects of the milestone within 270 days after the relevant deadline.”
[
71
]
The Commission has determined that the requested relief is warranted under the standards set forth in Section 36 of the Exchange Act and Rule 608(e). In reaching this determination, the Commission does not find that the Participants satisfied all FAM 4 requirements on time, which they acknowledge they did not. Rather, the Commission has considered, among other things, the extent of CAT implementation during Period 4, the nature of the CAIS deficiencies, and the relationship between those deficiencies and the magnitude of the costs at issue, which is the type of case-specific assessment the Commission indicated its exemptive authority would permit when it adopted the FAMs.
By the FAM 4 deadline, the Participants had substantially completed implementation of the FAM 4 requirements, including the fully operational CAT transactional database, a significant undertaking that created a regulatory system capable of collecting and processing transaction data across the national market system and providing the Participants and the Commission with access to that data for regulatory purposes. Specifically, FAMs 1, 2, and 3 had been completed on time.
[
72
]
Effective as of September 2021, FINRA had retired its predecessor audit trail system, OATS, after determining that the CAT met the requisite accuracy and reliability standards.
[
73
]
CAT query tool functionality was available to the Participants and the Commission, and the average overall CAT error rate was below 5%.
[
74
]
Critical infrastructure for the transactional database—including functionality that enabled data ingestion, processing, validation, security, cloud storage, data retention, and regulatory access and use—was developed, successfully tested, and fully implemented. The Commission and the Participants relied on CAT transactional data throughout Period 4 for surveillance, investigations, enforcement activities, and cross-market reconstructions and analyses, as appropriate.
The Participants had also made meaningful progress towards the implementation of the remaining FAM 4 requirements related to the CAIS. As commenters have noted:
As of September 30, 2022, 99% of Industry Members and CAT Reporting Agents had completed CAIS production readiness certification and 96% of Data Submitters had completed the first interim reporting obligation of the CAIS implementation schedule. As of November 14, 2022, 92% of Data Submitters had completed the second interim reporting obligation of the CAIS implementation schedule, which required the submission of all active accounts to CAIS.
[
75
]
Industry Members were further reporting customer and account information to CAIS on a daily basis, such data was accepted and validated by CAIS, and the CAIS data was accessed and used by regulators during this period to perform surveillance, investigations, enforcement activities, and cross-market reconstructions and analyses, as appropriate.
[
76
]
However, certain CAIS functionality was not fully implemented by the FAM 4 deadline. Various technical issues, including data load defects, deficiencies in the error corrections process, and other processing defects affected the reliability of CAIS data and the availability of information to regulators, and these issues were not fully resolved until July 15, 2024.
[
77
]
Nevertheless, all other functionality required for “Full Implementation of CAT NMS Plan Requirements” was implemented on time consistent with the requirements of the Plan and applicable exemptive
(
printed page 76290)
relief.
[
78
]
And the progress made by the Participants in fully implementing the CAT transactional database and partially implementing the CAIS substantially achieved the Commission's expressed goal in adopting Rule 613 of improving the accuracy, completeness, accessibility, and timeliness of the data available to regulators—even without full use of the CAIS.
[
79
]
Absent the requested relief, the Participants would be unable to recover from Industry Members, through CAT fees, any portion of the $490,151,144 in CAT costs they incurred during Period 4. The vast majority of those costs relate to the transactional database that the Participants implemented on time and that was fully operational throughout the period, which the Participants represent totals $364,219,549 in technology costs unrelated to CAIS and $26,624,090 in other CAT LLC operating costs (separate and apart from any CAIS-related costs), while approximately 20% of the costs ($99,307,505) relate to the CAIS system that was partially but not fully implemented by the FAM 4 deadline.
[
80
]
CAT LLC requested exemptive relief only for the non-CAIS FAM 4 costs, which CAT LLC characterized as being separate and apart from any CAIS-related costs. Providing this relief would permit them to seek to recover up to $260,562,426 (two-thirds of those costs) from Industry Members with respect to these costs.
[
81
]
The Exchange Act permits the Participants, as self-regulatory organizations, to recover the costs of their regulatory activities from their members. Consistent with the statutory presumption of cost-recovery, the CAT NMS Plan generally provides that the Participants and Industry Members are to share the costs of the CAT. The interim funding model currently in effect splits historical and prospective CAT costs evenly among the buyer, seller, and market regulator in transactions reportable to the CAT.
[
82
]
The Commission has previously found that this approach, which allocates CAT costs among the primary parties that participate in and benefit from the trading activity that generates those costs and the market oversight the CAT enables, is reasonable and consistent with the public interest and the protection of investors.
[
83
]
The FAMs represent an exception to that general cost-sharing premise, placing conditions on the Participants' ability to recover Industry Members' share of costs in order to reduce the likelihood of implementation delays that “prevent regulators and market participants from reaping the regulatory benefits of the CAT.”
[
84
]
In adopting the FAMs, the Commission responded to the recommendation of both Participants and Industry Members to build into the Plan a flexible, holistic assessment of whether to hold the Participants financially accountable for missed implementation milestones by emphasizing that it retained the authority to grant exemptive relief from “any requirement associated with a [FAM]” where “appropriate.”
[
85
]
The Commission believes it is appropriate to exercise that reserved authority based on the specific circumstances of Period 4.
A 100% reduction of all CAT costs incurred during Period 4 would extend not only to the costs of the one component that the Participants did not fully implement on time, but also to the full costs of operating the transactional database, a separate system that was completed on time. A reduction of that scope, totaling $326,767,429 (two-thirds of the FAM 4 total costs), would not be commensurate with the significance of the CAIS deficiencies relative to the CAT as a whole or with their effect on the CAT's regulatory utility during Period 4. Those deficiencies did not prevent regulators from obtaining the substantial regulatory benefits of the transactional database or from meaningfully benefiting from the data reported to CAIS, and regulators relied on both systems in carrying out their responsibilities to maintain the integrity of the securities markets and enforce the securities laws. Moreover, the magnitude of Period 4 costs, and associated reduction in CAT fees, was driven in significant part by unanticipated growth in trading activity, as well as data processing and storage costs, that the Commission has recognized were largely outside the Participants' control.
[
86
]
The Commission disagrees with the commenters who argued that the requested relief must be rejected to preserve the incentive effects of future Commission regulatory deadlines or to account for the costs incurred by Industry Members to meet CAIS-implementation deadlines. Granting the requested relief would not allow the delay in completing FAM 4 to occur “without consequence.”
[
87
]
Even with the relief, the Participants are still precluded from imposing CAT fees to recover the $66.2 million share of CAIS-related costs that would otherwise have been allocable to Industry Members. That is a significant financial consequence, directed at the component that the Participants failed to complete on time.
The Commission acknowledges that Industry Members made expenditures to build internal systems to comply with CAIS reporting, but those expenditures do not alter its determination that the requested relief is appropriate. Commenters have presented no specific evidence or analysis regarding the alleged adverse financial impact on Industry Members caused by the delays in CAIS implementation. Moreover, regulators were able to make meaningful use of a substantial portion of the CAIS data reported by Industry Members during Period 4. As discussed above, CAIS accepted, validated, and stored the data reported by Industry Members and that data was made available to regulators and used for surveillance and oversight. Although the above-described CAIS defects prevented certain CAIS data from being properly uploaded to the CAT's primary data stores for some period of time, such data was not lost. Rather, as described by the Participants in a previous exemptive relief request, all CAIS data reported to the CAT was preserved, and the Plan Processor later “reload[ed] historical CAIS data (both accepted and rejected) from October 2022 to present to all relevant data stores so that it [was] fully available to both regulators and Industry Members.”
[
88
]
Contrary to the assertions of certain commenters, the Commission's reservation of exemptive authority was not limited to delays that the
(
printed page 76291)
Participants are able to establish were unforeseeable or outside the Participants' control. The FAM Release identified the potential impact of unforeseeable or reasonable delays as one circumstance in which exemptive relief could be appropriate; but the Commission's exemptive relief authority under Section 36 and Rule 608(e) is not limited to that circumstance. Under the particular circumstances here, including the Participants' substantial implementation of the CAT by the FAM 4 deadline, the nature of the remaining technical CAIS deficiencies, the substantial regulatory utility derived from the CAT despite those deficiencies, and the magnitude of the cost reductions that would otherwise be required (due largely to market developments outside of the Participants' control), the Commission concludes that relief limited to the non-CAIS FAM 4 costs is appropriate in the public interest and consistent with the protection of investors, as discussed above.
At the same time, the Commission does not believe it would be appropriate to go beyond the requested relief and permit the Participants to seek to recover Industry Members' two-thirds share of all Period 4 costs, as one commenter, who is a Participant, requested.
[
89
]
As the Participants have acknowledged, CAIS was not fully implemented by the FAM 4 deadline, and as a result, regulators and market participants lacked the full benefit of certain CAIS functionality during that period.
[
90
]
The reduction in recoverable fees under the Participants' requested relief is commensurate with their failure to timely complete CAIS: it applies FAM 4's reduction to the costs of the component the Participants did not complete within the period the FAMs provided. Extending relief to all Period 4 costs would leave the Participants' failure to timely implement CAIS without meaningful financial consequence, contrary to the purpose of the FAMs.
Another commenter supported granting the requested relief on the condition that an independent accountant verify that the $390,843,639 in non-CAIS FAM 4 costs was correctly classified.
[
91
]
The Commission notes that CAT LLC already publicly provides its independently audited annual financial statements on the CAT NMS Plan website.
[
92
]
CAT LLC also publicly provides its annual “Financial and Operating Budget” on the Plan website.
[
93
]
Moreover, to recover from Industry Members their share of the non-CAIS FAM 4 costs, the Participants will need to separately file proposed rule filings pursuant to Section 19(b) of the Exchange Act establishing the amounts of the fees to be charged.
[
94
]
Such fee filings would be published for public comment and subject to Commission review.
[
95
]
Additionally, as discussed above, the Participants would be required to include certain cost information, including detailed information regarding the amount and type of costs proposed for recovery, and provide sufficient information to demonstrate that any proposed fees are consistent with the Exchange Act and the rules thereunder.
[
96
]
In light of CAT LLC's existing financial reporting and audit processes and the requirements of the Section 19(b) fee filing process, and absent any basis to conclude that the reported non-CAIS FAM 4 costs were materially misclassified, the Commission declines to condition this exemptive relief on the engagement of an independent auditor.
Finally, opposing commenters argued that the Commission did not consider the economic effects of imposing approximately $260.6 million (two-thirds) of the Period 4 costs on broker-dealers, and that it cannot grant the requested relief without analyzing those effects.
[
97
]
In its order approving the Funding Model, the Commission explained that the economic effects of CAT costs should be assessed on a per-share basis, by comparing CAT fee rates to other costs of execution and regulatory fees, because that approach most accurately reflects how the costs will be experienced by those that ultimately bear them.
[
98
]
In the approval order, a historical CAT fee rate of $0.000013 per executed equivalent share was used in that comparison.
[
99
]
The Commission concluded that CAT fee rates in general, including the historical CAT fee rate of $0.000013, are smaller than other regulatory fees. Here, the estimated fee rate of $0.000022 per executed equivalent share
[
100
]
for a one-year recovery period of the exempted FAM 4 costs is larger than the historical CAT fee rate of $0.000013 used in the order approving the Funding Model. The sum of the historical CAT fee rate in the approval order and the estimated fee rate for exempted FAM 4 costs would be $0.000035 per executed equivalent share.
[
101
]
However, even that combined higher fee rate of $0.000035 is still smaller than other regulatory fees and of the same order of magnitude as the historical CAT fee rate evaluated in the approval order.
[
102
]
Therefore, permitting the Participants to seek recovery of the exempted FAM 4 costs does not materially change the Commission's assessment of the economic impact of CAT fees set forth in the order approving the Funding Model.
C. Relief Relating to the Recovery Period
CAT LLC has also requested that the Participants be granted relief that would allow them to recover the non-CAIS FAM 4 costs under a Historical Recovery Period shortened to one-year.
[
103
]
CAT LLC estimated that, “based on the recovery of $260,562,426 and based on recent executed equivalent share volumes, the estimated fee rate would be approximately $0.000022 for a one-year recovery period.”
[
104
]
CAT LLC stated that this rate would be comparable to the fee rates previously
(
printed page 76292)
charged to fund CAT costs (ranging from $0.000035 to $0.000001).
[
105
]
Four commenters opposed a shortened Historical Recovery Period.
[
106
]
While one commenter stated that they are opposed to any recovery over any period of time, they stated that the “proposed one-year recovery period, however, would compound the harm to Industry Members and investors . . .”
[
107
]
Three commenters stated that the Commission has not analyzed the economic effects of imposing those Period 4 costs over the course of a single year, considering that the Funding Model imposes a Historical Recovery Period of two to five years.
[
108
]
One commenter stated that the proposed rate is not “comparable” to recent rates, as the “proposed rate equals one, is below one, and exceeds four. It is 22 times the most recent prospective fee and 11 times the most recent historical assessment.”
[
109
]
The commenter also stated that the “request does not state the combined rate if this assessment runs alongside prospective fees.”
[
110
]
The Commission concludes that it is appropriate in the public interest to grant the Participants' request for a limited exemption from CAT NMS Plan Section 11.3(b)(i)(D)(I) to shorten the period over which the Participant may seek full recovery of the exempted FAM 4 costs to one year. The Commission recognizes that it could, alternatively, extend Section 11.3(f)'s March 31, 2028, deadline for CAT billing to Industry Members to permit recovery of FAM 4 costs over a 24-month period, but declines to do so. The Commission adopted that deadline because it is “engaged in a comprehensive review of the CAT” that is “intended to include” the CAT's “design and functionality, the scope of information it collections, and an examination of CAT costs,” and it would therefore have been “premature to adopt a new, permanent funding model.”
[
111
]
The Commission today is separately proposing to rescind Rule 613 and implement a new reporting rule that would require self-regulatory organizations and broker-dealers to record and electronically report to a central repository substantially the same information required to be recorded and reported pursuant to Rule 613, the CAT NMS Plan, and related compliance rules, incorporating applicable exemptive relief issued by the Commission. This proposal would eliminate the diffuse ownership structure over the CAT and subject it to the Commission's direct control, such that the Commission anticipates that the Participants would dissolve CAT LLC and rescind the CAT NMS Plan. Extending the duration of CAT billing to Industry Members by CAT LLC beyond the current March 31, 2028 deadline would potentially introduce unnecessary complexity and uncertainty as it considers these potential changes to the CAT. Moreover, as discussed above, the estimated fee rate of $0.000022 for a one-year recovery period of the exempted FAM 4 costs is comparable to other approved rates for previous CAT costs.
[
112
]
As such, the Commission has determined that further exemptive relief to permit a one-year recovery period for the exempted FAM 4 costs is appropriate under the circumstances.
V. Conclusion
Based on the foregoing, the Commission believes that, pursuant to Section 36(a)(1) of the Exchange Act, this exemption is appropriate in the public interest and consistent with the protection of investors, and that pursuant to Rule 608(e), this exemption is consistent with the public interest, the protection of investors, the maintenance of fair and orderly markets and the removal of impediments to, and the perfection of a national market system to exempt the Participants from Sections 11.6(a)(i)(D), 11.6(a)(iii) and 11.3(b)(i)(D)(I) of the CAT NMS Plan in connection with the recovery of certain costs incurred during FAM 4.
Accordingly,
it is hereby ordered,
pursuant to Section 36(a)(1) of the Exchange Act,
[
113
]
and Rule 608(e) of the Exchange Act
[
114
]
that exemptive relief is granted from:
1. Sections 11.6(a)(i)(D) and 11.6(a)(iii) of the CAT NMS Plan, to the extent that such provisions would prevent the recovery of Post-Amendment Industry Member Fees for non-CAIS FAM 4 costs in the amount of $390,843,639 (two-thirds of which, or $260,562,426, the Participants may seek to recover from Industry Members); and
2. Section 11.3(b)(i)(D)(I) of the CAT NMS Plan, as a one year recovery period is less than the 24-month minimum period otherwise required by the CAT NMS Plan.

U.S. International Development Finance Corporation
AGENCY:
U.S. International Development Finance Corporation.
ACTION:
Announcement of public hearing.
SUMMARY:
The Board of Directors of U.S. International Development Finance Corporation (DFC), in accordance with the Better Utilization of Investments Leading to Development (BUILD) Act of 2018, as amended by the DFC Modernization and Rehabilitation Act of 2025, will hold a public hearing to provide an opportunity for stakeholders to present their views. Those wishing to attend, present at, or submit a written statement to the Board prior to the public hearing must provide advance notice to the agency as detailed below.
DATES:
12:30 p.m. EST, Friday, December 11, 2026.
ADDRESSES:
The public hearing will take place virtually. Access information will be provided following attendee registration.
Registration:
To attend, present at, or submit a written statement to the Board prior to the public hearing, individuals must notify DFC Corporate Secretary Heather Carroll at
corporate.secretary@dfc.gov
by 5:00 p.m. EST, Friday, December 4, 2026.
Notices of intent to attend or present at the public hearing must include the individual's name, title, organization, address, email address, phone number, and a concise summary of the subject matter to be presented. Oral presentations may not exceed five minutes and may be reduced proportionately, if necessary, to afford all participants an opportunity to be heard.
Written statements submitted to the Board prior to the public hearing must include the individual's name, title, organization, address, email address, and phone number. Statements must be typewritten, double-spaced, and less than ten pages in length.
Heather Carroll,
Corporate Secretary, U.S. International Development Finance Corporation.
